text: Put a finger on A and move one square at a time, saying each move.
When you stop, read the number below your finger, then the number beside it.

families.title: Counting sides and corners of flat shapes
explanations: one-of-each (procedural): Each kind of shape was counted only once. Every shape in the group has its own sides and corners.
circle-corner (conceptual): A circle was given a corner. A circle has one curved line all round and no corners.
counted-shapes (conceptual): The shapes were counted, not their corners.
missed-one (procedural): One corner was missed. Put a finger on one and go round, counting each once.

teach.idea: A side is a straight edge of a flat shape; a corner is where two sides meet. A shape with straight sides has as many corners as sides; a circle has none.
teach.method: Put a finger on one corner and go round the shape, counting each side (or corner) once. For several shapes, add the counts for every shape.

alternatives.title: Skip count for many shapes
text: Three triangles have 3 sides each: count 3, 6, 9.
Add the counts for each kind of shape.

families.title: Things that roll and things that slide
explanations: round-only (conceptual): Only the things that are round all over were counted. A tin or a pipe also rolls on its curved side.
counted-sliders (procedural): The things that slide were counted. Things with a curved surface roll.
flat-only (conceptual): Things with a curved side were left out. A tin standing on its flat end slides too.
counted-rollers (procedural): The things that roll were counted. Things with a flat face slide.
roll-for-both (conceptual): Everything that rolls was counted. A ball cannot slide: it has no flat face. Only things with a flat face AND a curved side do both.
or-for-and (conceptual): Things that roll OR slide were counted. 'Both' means a thing must do the two.

teach.idea: A curved surface lets a thing roll; a flat face lets it slide. A thing with both, like a tin, can do both.
teach.method: For each thing, ask: does it have a curved surface? Does it have a flat face? Then count the ones that fit the question.

alternatives.title: Try it on a slope
text: Put a ball, a box and a tin on a tilted book.
The ball rolls, the box slides, and the tin rolls on its side or slides on its end.

families.title: Faces, edges and corners of solids
explanations: only-visible (conceptual): Only the corners you can see in a drawing were counted. A box also has corners at the back and underneath.
one-of-each (procedural): Each kind of solid was counted once. Every solid has its own faces, edges and corners.
pyramid-as-box (conceptual): The pyramid was counted like a box. A square pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 corners.

teach.idea: A face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a corner is where edges meet. A cube and a cuboid have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners; a square pyramid has 5, 8 and 5.
teach.method: Hold the solid (or picture it) and count the top, the bottom and all round, marking each one as you go. For several solids, add the counts for each one.

alternatives.title: Count in layers
text: For a box: 4 corners on top and 4 on the bottom make 8.
Edges: 4 round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 standing up make 12.

families.title: Letters that fold onto themselves
explanations: other-kind (procedural): The other kind of letter was counted. The question asks for letters that are NOT symmetrical.
repeats-once (procedural): A letter that appears twice was counted only once. Count every letter you see.
standing-fold-only (conceptual): Only a standing fold (left onto right) was tried. Letters like B, C, D and E fold top onto bottom.

teach.idea: A shape is symmetrical when a fold line splits it into two halves that match exactly when folded. The fold can stand up (left onto right) or lie down (top onto bottom).
teach.method: For each letter, imagine a standing fold through the middle; if the halves do not match, try a lying fold. If either works, the letter is symmetrical.

alternatives.title: Use a mirror
text: Stand a small mirror on the middle line of the letter.
If the letter looks whole with its reflection, that line is a fold line.

families.title: Comparing how many cups containers hold
explanations: added (conceptual): The two amounts were added. 'How many more' asks for the difference.
gave-bigger (conceptual): The cups for the bucket were given. Take away the cups for the jug.
gave-smaller (procedural): The smaller amount was given instead of the difference.
wrong-bar (procedural): A different bar was read. Find "Bucket" under the chart first.
biggest (conceptual): The container that holds the most was read. Read the bar for the container asked about.

teach.idea: When every container is filled with the same cup, the one that takes more cups holds more water.
teach.method: Read the number of cups for each container. To find how many more, take the smaller number from the bigger one.

alternatives.title: Line up the cups
text: Picture the cups for each container standing in a row.
Match the rows cup by cup; the cups with no partner are how many more.

families.title: Reading millilitres on a measuring jug
explanations: mark-below (procedural): The number on the mark just below the level was read. The level is halfway between two marks, so add half of 200 mL.
steps-as-hundreds (conceptual): Each step of the scale was taken as 100 mL. Read the numbers on the scale: each step is 200 mL.
counted-steps (procedural): The steps of the scale were counted instead of reading the amount.
gave-level (conceptual): The water already in the jug was given. The question asks how much MORE is needed to reach the top.
stopped-at-hundred (procedural): Counting up stopped at the next hundred. Keep counting on from there all the way to 2000 mL and add the jumps.
top-as-litre (conceptual): The top was taken as 1000 mL. This jug holds 2000 mL: read the number at the top of the scale.

teach.idea: A measuring jug has a scale like a number line standing up; the water level points to how many millilitres are inside. 1 litre is 1000 mL.
teach.method: Read the numbers on the marks and find what one step is worth. Read the level; for 'how much more', count up from the level to the top.

alternatives.title: Count up to the top
text: Start at the water level and jump to the next hundred, then on to the top.
Add the jumps: that is how much more water is needed.

families.title: Reading the time on a clock
explanations: hands-swapped (conceptual): The long and short hands were mixed up. The short hand shows the hour; the long hand shows the minutes.
number-as-minutes (conceptual): The number the long hand points to was read as the minutes. Each number on the clock is 5 minutes for the long hand: it points to 11, so it is 55 minutes.
next-hour (procedural): The hour was read from the number the short hand is moving towards. After 12 o'clock it stays 12 until the short hand reaches the next number.

teach.idea: The short hand shows the hour; the long hand shows the minutes. When the long hand is at 12 it is o'clock; when it is at 6 it is half past.
teach.method: Read the hour from the short hand (the last number it has passed). Then count the long hand in fives from 12: 5, 10, 15 …

alternatives.title: Count the long hand in fives
text: Each number the long hand passes is 5 more minutes: 1 is 5, 2 is 10, 3 is 15, 6 is 30.
Skip count in fives from 12 to where the long hand points.

families.title: Finding the change
explanations: stopped-at-ten (procedural): Counting up stopped at the next ten (₹100). Keep counting on to ₹100 and add both jumps.
added (conceptual): The price and the money paid were added. Change is what is left after paying: take the price away.
no-exchange (procedural): The smaller digit was taken from the bigger in each column. 50 − 49 needs a ten changed into ones; or count up from ₹49 to ₹50.

teach.idea: Change is the money you get back: what you paid take away the price.
teach.method: Count up from the price to the money paid: first to the next ten, then in tens. Add the jumps. Or take the price away from the money paid.

alternatives.title: Count up like a shopkeeper
text: Start at the price and give coins until you reach the money paid: up to the next ten, then tens.
The coins you gave are the change.

families.title: How much more money is needed
explanations: coins-as-ones (conceptual): Each coin was counted as ₹1. Look at the number on each coin: a ₹10 coin is ten rupees.
gave-total (conceptual): The money Anu has was given. The question asks how much MORE she needs to reach the price.
added (conceptual): The price and the money were added. Take what she has away from the price.

teach.idea: First find how much money there is by adding the coins' values. If it is less than the price, the difference is how much more is needed.
teach.method: Add the coins, biggest first. Then count up from that amount to the price.

alternatives.title: Count on to the price
text: Start at the money you have.
Count on to the price; the number of rupees you count is how much more you need.

families.title: Measuring length with a ruler
explanations: read-end (conceptual): The number at the far end was read. The pencil does not start at 0: count the centimetres from 8 to 15.
counted-marks (procedural): The marks were counted, including the first one. Count the spaces between the marks: each space is 1 cm.
started-at-one (procedural): Counting started from 1 at the end of the ruler. Measuring starts at 0.

teach.idea: Length on a ruler is the number of 1 cm spaces the object covers, so it starts counting from where the object starts.
teach.method: Line one end up with 0 if you can. If it starts at another mark, take the start number from the end number (or count the spaces).

alternatives.title: Count the spaces
text: Put your finger at the start mark and hop to the next mark: that is 1 cm.
Count the hops until you reach the end.

families.title: Weighing on a balance in kilograms and grams
explanations: kg-as-100 (recall): 1 kg was taken as 100 g. 1 kg is 1000 g.
left-out-kg (procedural): The kilogram weight was left out because it is in kg. Change it to grams and add it too.
counted-weights (conceptual): The weights were counted, not added. Each weight has its own number of grams.

teach.idea: When a balance is level, both sides weigh the same, so the bag weighs as much as all the weights together. 1 kg = 1000 g.
teach.method: Change any kilograms to grams (1 kg = 1000 g). Add the grams of all the weights, biggest first.

alternatives.title: Build up to 1000
text: 500 g and 500 g make 1 kg; 200 g + 200 g + 100 g make 500 g.
Group the weights into easy amounts (hundreds), then add.

families.title: Equal groups: how many in all
explanations: one-group (conceptual): Only one group was counted. Count every group.
missed-group (procedural): One group was missed while skip counting. Touch each plate as you say the next number.
extra-group (procedural): One group too many was counted: the count went on after the last plate. Say one number for each plate and stop at the last one.
added-numbers (conceptual): 10 and 10 were added. There are 10 groups of 10: add 10 again and again, 10 times.

teach.idea: Equal groups can be added again and again: 4 groups of 3 is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3, which we also write 4 × 3.
teach.method: Skip count by the number in one group, once for each group: 3, 6, 9, 12. The last number is how many in all.

alternatives.title: Jumps on a number line
text: Make one jump for each group, each jump as long as one group.
Where you land after the last jump is the total.

families.title: Hundreds, tens and ones from blocks
explanations: missing-zero (conceptual): A place with nothing in it needs a 0.
counted-blocks (conceptual): The blocks were counted one each. A big square is 100 and a stick is 10.
tens-ones-swapped (procedural): The tens and the ones were written in each other's places. Tens come before ones.

teach.idea: Ten ones make a ten and ten tens make a hundred. A three-digit number tells how many hundreds, tens and ones, in that order.
teach.method: Count the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones. Write the three digits in order, putting 0 in any place that has nothing.

alternatives.title: A place-value table
text: Draw three boxes labelled H, T and O.
Write how many hundreds, tens and ones in the boxes; read the digits across.

families.title: Building a number from extra tens or ones
explanations: wrote-side-by-side (conceptual): The numbers were written next to each other. 15 tens is 1 hundred and 5 tens, so it must be exchanged.
dropped-extra (conceptual): Only the last digit of 15 was kept. The extra ten tens make a hundred: add it to the next place.

teach.idea: Ten tens make a hundred and ten ones make a ten, so a number can be built with more than 9 tens or ones; exchange them to write it.
teach.method: Change ten ones into a ten (or ten tens into a hundred). Then write the hundreds, tens and ones digits in order.

alternatives.title: Add the parts
text: Turn each part into a number: 2 hundreds is 200, 13 tens is 130, 4 ones is 4.

families.title: The four directions: North, South, East and West
explanations: left-right (conceptual): Left and right were mixed up. Facing North, East is on your right and West on your left.
opposite (conceptual): The opposite direction was given. A quarter turn moves to the next direction, not across.
no-turn (procedural): The direction faced was given. Behind is the opposite way.
from-other-end (conceptual): The direction from the post office to the well was given. Start at the well and look towards the post office.

teach.idea: The four main directions are North, East, South and West. Facing North, East is on your right, West on your left and South behind you. On maps North is at the top.
teach.method: Picture yourself facing the direction given. A quarter turn right goes North → East → South → West; a quarter turn left goes the other way; a half turn faces the opposite way.

alternatives.title: Use the sun
text: The sun rises in the East. Stand with your right arm pointing at the morning sun.
You are facing North, your left arm points West and South is behind you.

families.title: Distances on a map: using a scale and choosing the shortest route
explanations: squares-not-scale (conceptual): The squares were counted but the scale was not used. Each square stands for 2 km.
one-direction (procedural): Only the first part of the walk was counted. Add both parts of the walk.
second-part-only (procedural): Only the second part of the walk was counted. Add both parts of the walk.
direct-is-shortest (conceptual): The direct road was taken to be the shortest. A road with no village on the way is not always shorter: add the lengths and compare.
other-route (procedural): The longer of the two routes through a village was chosen. Work out both totals and take the smaller one.
shortest-road (conceptual): The shortest single road was given. A route is made of all the roads along it, added together.

teach.idea: A map scale tells how much real distance one unit on the map stands for. A route's length is the sum of its parts; the shortest route is the one with the smallest total.
teach.method: Count the squares along the path and multiply by the scale. For routes, add the roads along each one, then compare the totals.

alternatives.title: Use a string
text: Lay a string along the path on the map, then hold it against the scale.
Each scale length along the string stands for the same real distance.

families.title: Shapes with straight sides, curved sides or both
explanations: half-as-straight (conceptual): The half circles were counted as straight. A half circle has one straight side but also a curved one.
full-circles-only (conceptual): Only the full circles were counted. A half circle has a curved side too.
counted-straight (procedural): The shapes with only straight sides were counted instead.
any-curve (conceptual): Every shape with a curve was counted. A circle has no straight side; only the half circles have both.

teach.idea: A side can be straight, like the side of a triangle, or curved, like the edge of a circle. A half circle has one straight side and one curved side.
teach.method: Run a finger along the edge of each shape. If it never bends, the side is straight; if it bends, it is curved. Sort the shapes, then count.

alternatives.title: The ruler test
text: Lay a ruler along each side.
A straight side lies along the ruler all the way; a curved side moves away from it.

families.title: Sides, corners and diagonals of flat shapes, and sorting by them
explanations: one-of-each (procedural): Each kind of shape was counted only once. Every shape has its own sides and corners.
rectangle-two (conceptual): A rectangle was given only 2 sides (a long one and a short one). It has 4 sides: two long and two short.
sides-for-diagonals (conceptual): The sides were counted instead of the diagonals. A diagonal is a straight line inside the shape joining two corners that are not next to each other.
one-corner-only (procedural): Only the diagonals from one corner were counted. Draw the diagonals from every corner (each one is shared by two corners).
circle-sides (conceptual): A circle was counted as if it had sides or diagonals. A circle has no sides, no corners and no diagonals.
rectangle-square (conceptual): The rectangle was left out. A rectangle has 4 sides, 4 corners and 2 diagonals, just like a square.

teach.idea: A shape with straight sides has as many corners as sides. A diagonal joins two corners that are not next to each other: a triangle has none, a square or rectangle 2, a pentagon 5, a hexagon 9.
teach.method: For each shape, count its sides (or corners, or diagonals), then add for every shape. To sort, check each shape against the rule and count the ones that fit.

alternatives.title: Draw them from each corner
text: Put a finger on one corner and draw lines to every corner that is not next to it.
Do this for each corner, but do not draw a line twice.

families.title: Faces, curved surfaces, edges and corners of cylinders, cones and spheres
explanations: curved-as-face (conceptual): The curved surface was counted as a flat face. A cylinder has 2 flat faces and 1 curved surface; a sphere has no flat face.
cone-no-corner (conceptual): The point of the cone was not counted. A cone has one corner (vertex) at its tip.
one-of-each (procedural): Each kind of solid was counted only once. Every solid has its own faces, edges and corners.
sphere-edge (conceptual): The sphere was given an edge or a face. A sphere has one curved surface and no edges or corners.
sphere-both (conceptual): The sphere was counted as having both. A sphere has only a curved surface.

teach.idea: A cylinder has 2 flat faces, 1 curved surface, 2 curved edges and no corners; a cone has 1 flat face, 1 curved surface, 1 edge and 1 corner (its tip); a sphere has only a curved surface.
teach.method: Picture each solid: count its flat faces, its curved surfaces, the edges where surfaces meet and the corners. Then add for every solid.

alternatives.title: Roll and stand
text: A solid with a curved surface can roll; one with a flat face can stand still.
A cylinder and a cone can do both; a sphere only rolls; a cube only stands.

families.title: Everyday things with straight or curved edges
explanations: other-kind (procedural): The things with only straight lines were counted instead.
missed-one (procedural): One thing was missed. Go through the list and tick each one that fits.

teach.idea: Some things have outlines made only of straight lines, like a book or a door; others have curved outlines, like a bangle or a plate.
teach.method: Picture each thing and trace its outline in the air. If your finger never has to bend, the lines are straight; if it bends, the outline is curved.

alternatives.title: Could you draw it with a ruler?
text: Ask: can I draw this thing's outline using only a ruler?
If yes, it has only straight lines; if you need to draw freehand, it has a curve.

families.title: Ordering containers by how much they hold
explanations: taller-holds-more (conceptual): The containers were ordered by height. A tall, thin container can hold less than a short, wide one; the cups tell how much each holds.
reversed (procedural): The order was turned round. Start with the one that holds the least.
label-order (procedural): The numbers were written in counting order. Order them by the cups each one holds.

teach.idea: How much a container holds is measured by how many cups of water fill it, not by how tall it looks.
teach.method: Read the cups for each container. Find the biggest number (or the smallest) and write that container first, then the next, and so on.

alternatives.title: Pour and compare
text: Fill one container and pour it into another.
If it overflows, the first holds more. Do this two at a time to put them in order.

families.title: Volume of an object from the rise in water level
explanations: final-reading (conceptual): The new reading was given. The water was already there; only the rise is the object's volume.
added-readings (procedural): The two readings were added. Take the first reading away from the second.
subtracted (conceptual): The volume was taken away from the reading. The stone pushes the water up, so the level goes up by its volume.
not-shared (procedural): The volume of all 2 marbles was given. Share the rise equally among the 2 marbles.

teach.idea: An object that sinks pushes away as much water as its own volume, so the water level rises by exactly the object's volume (1 ml takes up 1 cm³).
teach.method: Read the level before and after. The rise (after − before) is the volume. For several equal objects, share the rise equally.

alternatives.title: The overflow can
text: Fill a can to the brim and drop the stone in.
Catch the water that spills out and measure it: that is the stone's volume.

families.title: The total cost of two things
explanations: subtracted (conceptual): The prices were subtracted. Buying both things means paying for both, so add.
counted-start (procedural): When counting on, 15 itself was counted as the first step. Start at 15 and say the next number for each rupee.

teach.idea: To find what two things cost together, add their prices.
teach.method: Start at the bigger price and count on the smaller one, or add the two numbers.

alternatives.title: Put out the coins
text: Put out coins for the first price and coins for the second.
Count all the money together.

families.title: Is the money enough for two things?
explanations: one-price (conceptual): The money was compared with one price only. Both things must be paid for: add the two prices first.
exact-not-enough (conceptual): Having exactly the price was taken as not enough. If the money equals the total, it is just enough, with nothing left.

teach.idea: To know whether money is enough for two things, add the prices and compare the total with the money.
teach.method: Add the two prices. If the money is more, it is more than enough; if it is the same, exactly enough; if it is less, not enough.

alternatives.title: Pay one at a time
text: Take the price of the first thing away from the money.
Then see whether what is left covers the second price.

families.title: Writing equal groups as repeated addition and as multiplication
explanations: one-row-short (procedural): One row was missed. Write one addend for each row.
one-row-extra (procedural): One addend too many was written. Touch each row once as you write its number.
added-numbers (conceptual): The number of rows and the number in a row were added. 7 rows of 10 means adding 10 again and again, 7 times.
plus-for-times (conceptual): The addition was written as 7 + 10. Adding 10 again and again 7 times is 7 × 10.
miscounted (procedural): The number of addends was counted wrongly. Count how many times the same number is added.

teach.idea: Equal groups can be written as a repeated addition (3 + 3 + 3 + 3) or as a multiplication: 4 × 3 means 4 groups of 3.
teach.method: Write the number in one group once for every group, with + between. The number of groups goes first in the multiplication, then the number in each group.

alternatives.title: Equal jumps
text: On a number line, make one jump for each group, each as long as the group.
Each jump is one addend; the number of jumps is the first number in the multiplication.

families.title: Reading a metre tape (whole, half and quarter metres) and a ruler in millimetres
explanations: counted-marks (procedural): The marks were counted instead of the spaces between them. There is one more mark than spaces.
read-end (conceptual): The number at the end was read, but the rope does not start at 0. Take the start mark away from the end mark.
steps-as-metres (conceptual): Each quarter metre was counted as a whole metre. It takes 4 quarter metres to make 1 m.
cm-not-mm (conceptual): The length was given in centimetres. 1 cm is 10 mm, so the length in mm is 10 times the centimetres plus the extra millimetres.
mm-ignored (procedural): Only the whole centimetres were read. Count the small millimetre marks after the last centimetre too.

teach.idea: A length is the distance from one end to the other: on a tape, the end mark minus the start mark. 1 m = 100 cm, and 1 cm = 10 mm.
teach.method: Read the mark at each end and subtract. For quarter metres, each small step is ¼ m; for millimetres, count the whole centimetres (each 10 mm) and add the small marks.

alternatives.title: Count the steps
text: Put a finger on the start and count each space up to the end.
Multiply by what one space is worth: 1 m, ¼ m or 1 mm.

families.title: Choosing a unit and a tool, and estimating lengths and distances
explanations: unit-too-big (conceptual): A unit that is too small was chosen. Think how many of that unit it would take: the best unit gives a number that is not too big and not too small.
tool-size (conceptual): A tape was chosen for a long road. Distances of many kilometres are measured with the odometer of the bus or car that travels them.
wrong-unit (conceptual): The number is right but the unit is not: "about 20 m" does not fit at all. Picture 1 m and compare.
ten-times (procedural): "about 200 cm" is ten times too much. Compare with something you know, like your own height (about 1 m) or a hand span (about 15 cm).

teach.idea: Small lengths are measured in millimetres or centimetres, longer ones in metres, and distances between places in kilometres. 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km.
teach.method: Compare with lengths you know: a fingernail is about 1 cm wide, a big step about ½ m, a door about 2 m, a 15-minute walk about 1 km. Pick the unit (or tool, or estimate) that fits.

alternatives.title: Body benchmarks
text: Measure your hand span, your step and your height once.
Use them to picture other lengths: a bed is a little more than your height, a classroom about 10 big steps.

families.title: Choosing mg, g or kg, judging recorded weights, and estimating weights
explanations: unit-slip (conceptual): Grams were chosen for something heavy. Things that are hard to lift are weighed in kilograms (1 kg = 1000 g).
number-only (conceptual): Only the number was looked at, not the unit. Check whether the number and unit together fit what the thing is like.
wrong-unit (conceptual): The number is right but the unit is not: "about 30 kg" is far too heavy: compare with a 1 kg packet of salt.
ten-times (procedural): "about 300 g" is ten times too heavy. Compare with things you have lifted.

teach.idea: Very light things are weighed in milligrams, light things in grams and heavy things in kilograms: 1000 mg = 1 g and 1000 g = 1 kg.
teach.method: Compare with weights you know: a ₹1 coin is about 4 g, an egg about 50 g, a packet of salt 1 kg, a school bag about 3 kg.

alternatives.title: Lift and compare
text: Hold a 1 kg packet in one hand and the thing in the other.
Is it much lighter, about the same, or heavier? Then choose g or kg.

families.title: Grams written as kilograms and grams
explanations: hundred-grams (conceptual): 1 kg was taken as 100 g. 1 kg is 1000 g, so the kilograms are the thousands.
dropped-zero (procedural): A zero in the grams was dropped. The grams left over are a three-digit amount: write all of it.

teach.idea: 1 kg = 1000 g, so every full thousand grams is one kilogram and the rest stay as grams.
teach.method: The digit in the thousands place gives the kilograms; the last three digits give the grams: 2075 g is 2 kg 75 g.

alternatives.title: Fill 1 kg packets
text: Picture pouring the grams into 1 kg packets, 1000 g in each.
Count the full packets; what does not fill a packet is the grams.

families.title: Seats in rows and columns
explanations: seat-row-swapped (procedural): The seat was written first. Write the row first, then the seat.
from-the-back (conceptual): The rows were counted from the back. Row 1 is at the front.
from-the-right (conceptual): The seats were counted from the right. Seat 1 is on the left.
behind-as-front (conceptual): Behind was taken as nearer the front. Behind means a bigger row number, further from the front.
swapped-moves (procedural): The moves were swapped: the rows were moved by the seat number and the seats by the row number.

teach.idea: A seat in a hall is found by two numbers: the row (counted from the front) and the seat in that row (counted from the left).
teach.method: Find the row first, counting from row 1 at the front; then go along the row from the left to the seat. Write (row, seat).

alternatives.title: Like a cinema ticket
text: A cinema ticket says the row and the seat, like 'Row C, Seat 7'.
Walk to the row first, then along it to the seat.

families.title: Clock times to the minute, and half and quarter hours in minutes
explanations: read-the-number (conceptual): The number the minute hand has just passed was read as the minutes. Each number on the clock stands for 5 minutes; count the small marks too.
nearest-five (procedural): The time was read only to the nearest 5 minutes. Count the small marks after the last number.
minutes-past (procedural): The minutes past the hour were given. The question asks how many minutes are left until the next hour.
quarter-25 (conceptual): A quarter of an hour was taken as 25 minutes (as a quarter of 100). An hour has 60 minutes, so a quarter is 15 minutes.
decimal-hours (conceptual): 5 and three quarters hours was read like 5.75 with 100 minutes in an hour. An hour has 60 minutes.

teach.idea: The minute hand goes once round the clock in 60 minutes; each number stands for 5 minutes and each small mark for 1 minute. Half an hour is 30 minutes and a quarter of an hour is 15 minutes.
teach.method: Count in fives to the last number the minute hand has passed, then count on the small marks. For hours, use 60 minutes for each hour, 30 for a half and 15 for a quarter.

alternatives.title: A clock is a pie
text: Cut the clock face into 4 equal parts: each part is a quarter of an hour, 15 minutes.
Two parts are half an hour, 30 minutes; three parts are 45 minutes.

families.title: 12-hour and 24-hour clock times
explanations: twelve-rule (conceptual): 12 was not added for a p.m. time (or 12 noon was changed). After noon, add 12 to the hour; 12 noon stays 12:00 and 12 midnight is 00:00.
am-pm (conceptual): a.m. and p.m. were mixed up. Times from 00:00 to 11:59 are a.m.; from 12:00 to 23:59 they are p.m.
took-ten (procedural): 10 was taken away instead of 12. To change a 24-hour time after noon, take 12 from the hours.

teach.idea: The 24-hour clock counts the hours from midnight (00:00) to 23:59. Times after noon have 12 added: 3:40 p.m. is 15:40. 12 noon is 12:00 and 12 midnight is 00:00.
teach.method: 12-hour to 24-hour: for p.m. times after 12 noon add 12 to the hour; for a.m. times keep the hour (12 a.m. becomes 00). 24-hour to 12-hour: if the hour is 13 or more take away 12 and write p.m.

alternatives.title: A day line
text: Draw a line from 0 (midnight) to 24 (the next midnight) with noon at 12.
Morning times are left of 12; afternoon and evening times are right of 12, so their 24-hour number is 12 more.

families.title: Casting out nines: the nines check number
explanations: not-reduced (procedural): The digit sum was not reduced to one digit. Keep adding the digits until one digit is left.
nine-kept (procedural): A 9 was kept. Casting out nines means 9 counts as 0.
not-cast-again (procedural): The product of the check numbers was not cast out again. Reduce it to one digit, with 9 as 0.
multiplied (conceptual): The check numbers were multiplied. Do to the check numbers what the sum does: add them.
added (conceptual): The check numbers were added. Do to the check numbers what the sum does: multiply them.

teach.idea: Adding the digits of a number again and again (with 9 counting as 0) leaves its remainder when divided by 9. A correct sum or product has the check number you get by adding or multiplying the check numbers.
teach.method: Find each number's check number. Add (or multiply) them and cast out nines again. Then find the check number of the answer: if they differ, the answer is wrong.

alternatives.title: The nine pattern
text: The digits of 9, 18, 27, 36, 45 … always add up to 9 (or a multiple of 9).
So a multiple of 9 has check number 0, and any number's check number is how far it is past a multiple of 9.

families.title: Pascal's triangle: building rows, row sums and diagonals
explanations: copied-above (procedural): The number just above was copied. Each number is the sum of the two numbers above it.
plus-one (conceptual): 1 was added to the number above, as in a counting pattern. Add the two numbers above instead.
one-row-short (procedural): The row was built one too few times. Count the rows below the last one shown.
one-row-off (procedural): The sum of the row before was given. The row that begins 1, n has sum 2 multiplied by itself n times.
double-the-second (conceptual): The second number was doubled (12 × 2). Add every number in the row: the sums go 1, 2, 4, 8, … doubling each row.
same-difference (conceptual): The last difference was added again. On this diagonal the differences grow: they are the numbers on the diagonal before.

teach.idea: Pascal's triangle starts with 1; each row starts and ends with 1 and each other number is the sum of the two above it. Its rows add up to 1, 2, 4, 8, … and its diagonals are 1s, the counting numbers, the triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10 …
teach.method: To build a new row, write 1, then add each pair of neighbours in the row above, then write 1. Use the patterns to check.

alternatives.title: Count the paths
text: Each number tells how many ways there are to walk down from the top 1 to it, moving down-left or down-right.
Two paths arrive from the two numbers above, so their counts add.

families.title: Adding and taking away tens or hundreds in your head
explanations: changed-ones (conceptual): 300 was treated as 3 ones. 300 is 3 hundreds, so the hundreds digit changes, not the ones.
wrong-place (procedural): The tens digit was changed instead of the hundreds digit.
no-carry (procedural): The tens went past 9 but the extra hundred was not carried on.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): There were not enough tens, so 4 was taken from 9 instead. Break one hundred into ten tens first.

teach.idea: Adding tens changes the tens digit; adding hundreds changes the hundreds digit. The ones stay the same.
teach.method: Say how many tens (or hundreds) you are adding, then count on (or back) that many tens (or hundreds) from the number.

alternatives.title: Jump along a number line
text: Start at the first number.
Make one jump of ten (or a hundred) for each ten (or hundred) you add, and say each new number.

families.title: Multiplying in your head by splitting into tens and ones
explanations: ones-not-multiplied (conceptual): Only the tens were multiplied (90 × 5); the 9 ones must be multiplied by 5 too.
tens-as-ones (conceptual): The tens digit 9 was multiplied as if it were 9 ones; it stands for 90.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (9 × 5) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Splitting a number into tens and ones lets you multiply each part separately and add: 23 × 4 = 20 × 4 + 3 × 4.
teach.method: Split the two-digit number into tens and ones. Multiply the tens, multiply the ones, then add the two answers.

alternatives.title: Double and double again
text: For × 2 double the number; for × 4 double it twice; for × 8 double it three times.
For × 5, multiply by 10 and halve.

families.title: Finding a number on a number line
explanations: count-by-ones (conceptual): Each gap was counted as 1, but the marks go up by 100 each time.
count-by-tens (conceptual): Each gap was counted as 10, but the marks go up by 100. Look at two labelled marks next to each other to find the step.

teach.idea: On a number line the marks are equally spaced, so every gap is worth the same amount.
teach.method: Find the step from two labelled marks next to each other, then count on in that step to the ?.

alternatives.title: Skip count aloud
text: Say the first number, then keep adding the step: for steps of 5, say 35, 40, 45 …
Touch one mark for each number you say until you reach the ?.

families.title: Counting on and back in jumps on a number line
explanations: count-start (procedural): The starting number was counted as the first jump. A jump starts at the number and ends at the next one.
extra-jump (procedural): One jump too many was made. Count the jumps as you make them.
wrong-way (procedural): The jumps went the wrong way: back means to smaller numbers.
jumps-of-one (conceptual): Each jump was taken as 1, but each jump is 10.

teach.idea: Each jump moves the same amount along the line: forward to bigger numbers, back to smaller numbers.
teach.method: Put your finger on the start. Make one jump at a time, saying the new number each time, and count the jumps.

alternatives.title: Find the total jump first
text: k jumps of s are k × s altogether.
Add (or take away) that total in one go, then check by jumping.

families.title: How many whole numbers lie between two numbers
explanations: difference (conceptual): 9815 − 9805 = 10 counts the jumps from 9805 to 9815, not the numbers in between. There is one fewer number between them than jumps.
both-ends (procedural): 9805 and 9815 were counted too; "between" leaves out both ends.

teach.idea: The numbers between two numbers leave out both end numbers.
teach.method: Find the difference (the number of jumps), then take away 1: that is how many numbers sit strictly between.

alternatives.title: Try a small case
text: Between 5 and 8 are 6 and 7: two numbers, although 8 − 5 = 3.
So the count between is always one less than the difference.

families.title: Sharing equally and making equal groups
explanations: gave-total (procedural): The answer given was the total number of objects; the total has to be split up.
took-away-once (conceptual): 5 was taken away once. Sharing keeps giving out until none are left: count how many each gets (or how many groups you make).
gave-divisor (conceptual): The answer given was the size of each group (5); the question asks how many groups.

teach.idea: Sharing equally means every share has the same number and nothing is left over.
teach.method: Deal the objects out one at a time to each share (or make groups of the given size) and count one share (or the groups).

alternatives.title: Use a times fact
text: Ask: what number times the number of shares gives the total?
For 15 shared among 3, 3 × 5 = 15, so each gets 5.

families.title: Subtracting two-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In the ones, 8 − 7 was worked out instead of 7 − 8. When the top digit is smaller, break a ten into 10 ones first.
tens-not-reduced (procedural): A ten was broken into ones, but the tens digit was not made one less.
fact-slip-sub (recall): A take-away fact (17 − 8) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: If there are not enough ones to take away, break one ten into 10 ones. The number stays the same; only how it is grouped changes.
teach.method: Start with the ones. If the top digit is smaller, take 1 ten and make it 10 ones, then subtract the ones and then the tens.

alternatives.title: Count up from the smaller number
text: Jump from the smaller number to the next ten, then on to the bigger number.
Add the jumps: that is the difference.

families.title: Subtracting three-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In a column where the top digit was smaller, the top was taken from the bottom. Break one from the next column into ten first.
next-not-reduced (procedural): A ten (or hundred) was broken up, but the column it came from was not made one less.

teach.idea: Breaking one hundred into ten tens, or one ten into ten ones, keeps the number the same, so you can always take away column by column.
teach.method: Work from the ones to the hundreds. When the top digit is smaller, break one from the next column on the left and make that column one less.

alternatives.title: Check by adding back
text: Add your answer to the number you took away.
If you get the first number back, your answer is right.

families.title: Naming the shaded part: a half, a quarter or three quarters
explanations: shaded-to-unshaded (conceptual): The shaded part was compared with the unshaded part. A fraction compares the shaded part with the whole shape.
count-only (conceptual): Only the shaded squares were counted (36); the fraction is shaded squares out of all 48 squares.
unshaded (procedural): The fraction of the shape that is NOT shaded was given.

teach.idea: A half is 1 of 2 equal parts; a quarter is 1 of 4 equal parts; three quarters is 3 of 4 equal parts.
teach.method: Count all the squares and the shaded squares. If the shaded squares are half of all, it is 1/2; a quarter of all, 1/4; three quarters, 3/4.

alternatives.title: Fold into equal parts
text: Fold the shape in half, then in half again: you get 4 equal parts.
Count how many of the 4 parts are shaded.

families.title: A half, a quarter or three quarters of a number of things
explanations: doubled (conceptual): The number was doubled. Half means splitting into 2 equal parts and taking one part.
take-two (conceptual): 2 was taken away. Half means 2 equal parts, not taking away 2.
quarter-as-half (conceptual): The things were split into 2 parts. A quarter is one of 4 equal parts.
take-four (conceptual): 4 was taken away. A quarter means one of 4 equal parts.
one-quarter (procedural): Only one quarter was found. Three quarters is 3 of the 4 equal parts.
take-three (conceptual): 3 was taken away. Three quarters means 3 out of 4 equal parts.

teach.idea: To find a half, share into 2 equal parts; a quarter, into 4 equal parts. Three quarters is 3 of those 4 parts.
teach.method: Deal the things out into 2 (or 4) equal piles. Count one pile for a half or a quarter; count three piles for three quarters.

alternatives.title: A quarter is half of a half
text: Halve the number, then halve it again: that is a quarter.
Three quarters is the whole minus one quarter.

families.title: Choosing whether to add, take away, multiply or share
explanations: took-away (conceptual): 6 was taken away from 48, but the story shares equally, so we divide.
added (conceptual): 6 and 7 were added, but the story has 6 equal groups of 7, so we multiply (or add 7 again and again).
multiplied (conceptual): 48 and 6 were multiplied, but sharing makes each share smaller than the total.

teach.idea: First picture what happens in the story: things put together (add), taken away (subtract), equal groups (multiply) or shared equally (divide).
teach.method: Ask: does the amount get bigger or smaller? Are the groups equal? Then choose the operation and work it out.

alternatives.title: Act it out with counters
text: Use beads or stones for the things in the story.
Do exactly what the story says with them, then count what you have.

families.title: Reading a pictograph with a key
explanations: wrong-row (procedural): The row for Cycle was read instead. Put a finger on the right label and follow its row.
no-key (conceptual): The pictures were counted, but each picture stands for 10 children, not 1.

teach.idea: In a pictograph every picture stands for the same number of things: the number in the key.
teach.method: Count the pictures in the row, then count in the key's number once for each picture (or multiply).

alternatives.title: Turn it into a table
text: Write each label with its number of pictures.
Multiply each by the key and write the real number beside it.

families.title: Comparing two rows of a pictograph
explanations: added (conceptual): "How many more" asks for the difference, so take the smaller number from the bigger one; the two rows were added.
bigger-only (procedural): Only the bigger row was read. Compare it with the smaller row by taking away.
no-key (conceptual): The difference in pictures was found, but each picture stands for 10.

teach.idea: "How many more" compares two amounts: it is the bigger amount minus the smaller one.
teach.method: Read both rows using the key, then take the smaller number from the bigger one.

alternatives.title: Count the extra pictures
text: Line up the two rows. Count the pictures the longer row has that the shorter one does not.
Then count in the key's number once for each extra picture.

families.title: Making both sides of a number sentence equal
explanations: equals-gives-answer (conceptual): The answer to 20 − 17 was written in the box. The = sign means both sides have the same value.
add-all (conceptual): All the numbers were added together. Find what the box must be so that the right side has the same value as the left side.
took-away (procedural): 8 was taken away again; the box must be 8 MORE than 3, so that taking 8 from it leaves 3.

teach.idea: The = sign means "has the same value as", like a balance that is level: both sides must be worth the same.
teach.method: Work out the side you can finish. Then find the number in the box that makes the other side worth the same.

alternatives.title: Compare without adding up
text: In 9 + 7 = □ + 8, the 8 on the right is one less than the 9 on the left, so the box must be one more than 7: it is 8.
If one number goes up by some amount, the other must go down by the same amount for the sides to stay equal.

families.title: Finding the missing number in a number sentence
explanations: added-both (conceptual): The two numbers you can see were added. Taking the box away from 39 leaves 19, so the box is 39 − 19.
took-away-again (conceptual): 19 was taken away again. The box is the number we started with before 19 was taken away, so add 19 back.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (10 × 10) is not yet reliable.
took-away (conceptual): 10 was taken away from 100. The box is how many times 10 goes into 100: use the 10 times table.

teach.idea: Adding and taking away undo each other, and so do multiplying and dividing, so you can work backwards to the missing number.
teach.method: Read the sentence and ask what was done to the box. Do the opposite to the other number, then check by putting your answer in the box.

alternatives.title: Count on to find the gap
text: For □ + 7 = 15, start at 7 and count on to 15: 8, 9, … 15 is 8 counts.
The number of counts is the missing number.

families.title: Continuing a growing pattern
explanations: next-only (procedural): Only the next step (step 4) was found. Keep adding 6 until step 8.
one-too-many (procedural): 6 was added 8 times, but step 1 already has 10; from step 1 to step 8 there are 7 jumps.
times-step (conceptual): The step number was multiplied by 6, but the pattern started at 10, not at 6.

teach.idea: In a growing pattern the same amount is added each time; find that amount and keep adding it.
teach.method: Find how much the pattern grows from one step to the next. Keep adding that amount, step by step, until you reach the step you want.

alternatives.title: Extend the table
text: Write the step numbers 1, 2, 3, … in one row and the counts under them.
Fill each new box by adding the same amount as before.

families.title: Matchstick shapes in a row
explanations: no-sharing (conceptual): Each hexagon was given 6 sticks, but neighbours share a stick, so each new hexagon needs only 5 more.
forgot-first (procedural): Every hexagon was given 5 sticks, but the first one needs all 6.

teach.idea: The first shape needs all its sticks; every shape after it shares one stick with its neighbour, so it needs one stick fewer.
teach.method: Start with the sticks for one shape, then add (sides − 1) for each extra shape.

alternatives.title: Count all sides, then remove the shared ones
text: If the shapes were apart, n shapes need n × sides sticks.
Joining them in a row shares one stick between each pair of neighbours: take away one fewer than the number of shapes.

families.title: Counting line segments and lines through points
explanations: neighbours-only (conceptual): Only the short segments between neighbouring points were counted. Longer segments, such as from the first point to the third, count too.
counted-twice (procedural): Each segment was counted twice (AB and BA are the same).
counted-points (conceptual): The points were counted; a segment needs two points.

teach.idea: Every pair of points gives exactly one line segment (or one straight line), and AB is the same as BA.
teach.method: Start with the first point and join it to every point after it; then the second point to every point after it; and so on. Add up the counts.

alternatives.title: Make a list
text: Write the pairs in order: AB, AC, AD, then BC, BD, then CD.
Never write a pair you already have the other way round.

families.title: How many tiles cover a floor
explanations: counted-squares (conceptual): The squares were counted, but each tile covers 4 squares.
one-row (procedural): Only the tiles for the top two rows were counted. The same number fits in every pair of rows.
two-squares (conceptual): Each tile was taken to cover 2 squares, but it covers 4.

teach.idea: Tiles that fit with no gaps and no overlaps cover the floor exactly, so the floor splits into equal tile-sized pieces.
teach.method: Find how many tiles fit across one row of tiles and how many rows of tiles there are, then multiply (or add the rows).

alternatives.title: Share the squares among the tiles
text: Count all the squares on the floor.
Each tile covers the same number of squares (count them on one tile), so share the squares into groups of that size.

families.title: How long something lasts, from the clock
explanations: hand-number (recall): The minute hand points to 10, which means 50 minutes (count in 5s), not 10 minutes.
hour-as-100 (conceptual): The times were taken away like ordinary numbers (1230 − 1145), but an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
minutes-only (procedural): Only the minute numbers were compared and the hour that went past was forgotten. Count on to the next o'clock first.

teach.idea: Time is counted in hours of 60 minutes, so count on from the start to the next o'clock, then on to the end.
teach.method: Read the start time from the clock. Count on in 5s to the next o'clock, then count on to the end time, and add the two parts.

alternatives.title: Use a time line
text: Draw a line from the start time to the end time with a mark at the o'clock in between.
Write the minutes for each jump and add them.

families.title: Changing metres and centimetres
explanations: wrote-together (conceptual): 9 and 3 were written side by side (93); 9 m is 900 cm, so 3 cm goes in the ones place: 903.
added-numbers (conceptual): The numbers 9 and 95 were added, but metres and centimetres are different sizes: change the metres to centimetres first.
took-metres (conceptual): 9 was taken away, but 9 m is 900 cm.
ten-cm (recall): A metre was taken as 10 cm; 1 metre is 100 centimetres.

teach.idea: 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so each metre is a hundred in centimetres.
teach.method: Change the metres to centimetres by multiplying by 100, then add the extra centimetres (or take the metres away to find what is left).

alternatives.title: Metres are hundreds
text: In centimetres the metres go in the hundreds place.
3 m 7 cm is 3 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones: 307 cm.

families.title: Changing rupees and paise into paise
explanations: ten-paise (recall): ₹1 was taken as 10 paise; ₹1 is 100 paise.
added-numbers (conceptual): 20 and 60 were added, but a rupee and a paisa are different sizes: change the rupees to paise first.
paise-only (procedural): Only the paise after the dot (60) were given; the ₹20 before the dot are 2000 paise more.
wrote-together (conceptual): 20 and 5 were written side by side; ₹20 is 2000 paise, so the answer is 2000 + 5.

teach.idea: ₹1 is 100 paise, so each rupee is a hundred paise; in ₹3.45 the 3 is rupees and the 45 is paise.
teach.method: Multiply the rupees by 100 to get paise, then add the paise.

alternatives.title: Read the digits as paise
text: Write the amount with two digits after the dot: ₹3.05, ₹12.40.
Read all the digits without the dot: ₹3.05 is 305 paise, ₹12.40 is 1240 paise.

families.title: Adding and taking away rupees and paise
explanations: paise-over-100 (conceptual): The paise came to 180, which is more than 100: 100 paise make ₹1, so 180 paise is ₹1 and 80 paise.
no-carry (procedural): The rupee made from 100 paise was not carried to the rupees.
smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In the paise, 85 − 75 was worked out instead. Change ₹1 into 100 paise first.
rupee-not-reduced (procedural): ₹1 was changed into 100 paise, but the rupees were not made one less.

teach.idea: Rupees and paise work like hundreds: 100 paise make ₹1, so paise over 100 become a rupee, and a rupee can be broken into 100 paise.
teach.method: Write the amounts one under the other with the dots in line. Add (or take away) the paise first, carrying or breaking ₹1 when needed, then the rupees.

alternatives.title: Work in paise
text: Change both amounts to paise: ₹12.50 is 1250 paise.
Add or take away the whole numbers, then put the dot back two places from the right.

families.title: Small number stories: adding or taking away within 9
explanations: count-on-start (procedural): When counting on from 8, the 8 itself was counted as the first step. The first step on lands on 9.
took-away (conceptual): The smaller number was taken from the bigger one, but in the story more come, so we add.
added (conceptual): The two numbers were added, but in the story some go away, so we take away.
count-back-start (procedural): When counting back from 9, the 9 itself was counted as the first step. The first step back lands on 8.

teach.idea: In a number story, things are either put together (add) or some go away (take away).
teach.method: Ask: do more come, or do some go? Then count on or count back that many from the first number.

alternatives.title: Show it with fingers or stones
text: Hold up fingers (or put down stones) for the first number.
Put up more for the ones that come, or fold down the ones that go, then count what is left.

families.title: Subtracting two-digit numbers without regrouping
explanations: added (conceptual): The two numbers were added; the − sign means take away.
ones-only (procedural): Only the ones were taken away. The 8 tens of 87 must be taken from the tens too.
tens-only (procedural): Only the tens were taken away. The 7 ones of 87 must be taken from the ones too.

teach.idea: Take away ones from ones and tens from tens. When each top digit is big enough, no ten needs to be broken.
teach.method: Write the numbers one under the other. Subtract the ones, then the tens.

alternatives.title: Jump back in tens, then ones
text: Start at the first number. Jump back one ten at a time for the tens of the second number.
Then jump back the ones.

families.title: Are the parts equal? Checking halves and quarters
explanations: counted-pieces (conceptual): There are 4 pieces, but that alone does not make them quarters: they must all be the same size. Count the m in each piece.

teach.idea: Halves are 2 EQUAL parts and quarters are 4 EQUAL parts of the same whole. Cutting into 2 or 4 pieces is not enough: the pieces must be the same size.
teach.method: Count (or measure) each piece. If every piece is the same size, each is a half (of 2) or a quarter (of 4); if not, they are not halves or quarters.

alternatives.title: Fold and match
text: Fold the strip so that one piece lies on top of the other.
If the pieces match exactly, they are equal; if one sticks out, they are not halves.

families.title: Comparing four-digit numbers by where they lie on a number line
explanations: ones-digit (conceptual): The numbers were compared by their ones digits. Compare the thousands first, then the hundreds, then the tens: the first place where the digits differ decides.
left-is-bigger (conceptual): The biggest number was put at the left. On a number line the numbers get bigger to the right.

teach.idea: On a number line, a number further to the right is bigger. Four-digit numbers are compared place by place from the thousands.
teach.method: Look at the thousands digits; if they are the same, the hundreds; then the tens; then the ones. The first place that differs tells which number is bigger and so further right.

alternatives.title: Line up the digits in a place-value table
text: Write each number in a Th H T O table, one under another.
Go down the columns from the left; the first column that differs decides.

families.title: Comparing lengths written in metres and centimetres
explanations: tens (conceptual): 9 m 8 cm was taken as 980 cm. 8 cm is only 8 ones of centimetres: 9 m 8 cm = 908 cm.
joined (conceptual): 9 m 8 cm was read as 98 cm, the two numbers side by side. 9 m is 900 cm, so 9 m 8 cm is 908 cm.

teach.idea: 1 m = 100 cm, so a m b cm is a hundreds of centimetres and b more: 3 m 5 cm = 305 cm.
teach.method: Change the length in metres and centimetres into centimetres, then compare the two numbers of centimetres.

alternatives.title: Compare metres, then centimetres
text: Write the centimetre length in metres and centimetres too: 350 cm = 3 m 50 cm.
Compare the metres; if they are the same, compare the centimetres.

families.title: Placing digit cards to make the largest or smallest sum or difference
explanations: big-number-first (procedural): The biggest two-digit number was made first and the other two cards were used for the second number. For the largest sum, both tens places need the two biggest digits.

small-number-first (procedural): The smallest two-digit number was made first and the other two cards were used for the second number. For the smallest sum, both tens places need the two smallest digits.

second-not-smallest (procedural): The second number was made with the larger of the two cards left in the tens place. To take away as little as possible, it must be the smallest number those cards make: 67.

teach.idea: A digit in the tens place is worth ten times as much as in the ones place, so the digits that matter most go in the tens places.
teach.method: For the largest sum, put the two biggest digits in the tens places; for the smallest sum, the two smallest. For the largest difference, make the biggest number you can and take away the smallest number the other two cards make.

alternatives.title: Try and improve
text: Make any two numbers and work out the answer.
Swap two cards and see whether the answer gets better; keep the swap if it does.

families.title: Time intervals in hours and minutes
explanations: hours-only (procedural): Only the hours were counted; the minutes from the start to the end were left out.
hours-not-added (procedural): Only the minutes were added; the 3 hours of the duration were left out.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): In the minutes, 55 − 30 was worked out instead of 30 − 55. Count on from 8:55 p.m. to the next o'clock first.
hour-as-100 (conceptual): An hour was broken into 100 minutes, as if time were counted in hundreds. An hour has 60 minutes.
no-carry (conceptual): The minutes came to 90, but 60 minutes make 1 hour: change 60 of them into an hour.
carry-kept-minutes (procedural): One hour was added for the 60 minutes, but those 60 minutes were not taken away from the minutes.

teach.idea: Time is counted in hours of 60 minutes, so we count on to the next o'clock, then whole hours, then the minutes left.
teach.method: To find a duration: count on from the start to the next o'clock, then the whole hours, then on to the end, and add. To find an end time: add the hours, then the minutes, changing 60 minutes into an hour.

alternatives.title: Draw a time line
text: Mark the start, the o'clocks in between and the end on a line.
Write the minutes or hours of each jump and add them.

families.title: Pictographs and tables: completing, totals and the largest group
explanations: one-each (conceptual): One ● was drawn for each child, but each ● stands for 10 children: share the number into groups of 10.
no-key (conceptual): The pictures in the longest row were counted, but each ● stands for 10 children.
missed-row (procedural): One row was left out of the total. Add every row.
smallest (procedural): The shortest row was read. The largest group has the longest row of pictures.

teach.idea: Every picture stands for the key's number of children, so the number of pictures is the number of children shared into groups of the key, and the children are the pictures times the key.
teach.method: To draw a row, divide the number by the key. To read the pictograph, count the pictures and multiply by the key; for the total, add all the pictures first.

alternatives.title: Write the table beside the pictograph
text: Make a column for the pictures and a column for the children.
Fill each row: pictures × key = children, or children ÷ key = pictures.

families.title: Related facts: addition and subtraction, multiplication and division
explanations: kept-order (conceptual): The numbers were kept in the order of the multiplication. A division fact starts with the product and divides it by one factor.
added-given (conceptual): The two numbers of the subtraction were added. To check c − b = a, add the answer a back to b: you should get c.
divisor-as-dividend (conceptual): The divisor was written as the dividend. The dividend is the number being divided, and it equals divisor × quotient.

teach.idea: Adding and taking away undo each other, and so do multiplying and dividing: a + b = c gives c − a = b and c − b = a; a × b = c gives c ÷ a = b and c ÷ b = a.
teach.method: Start the subtraction (or division) with the biggest number of the family, the total (or product). To check a subtraction, add the answer to the number taken away; to check a division, multiply the divisor by the quotient.

alternatives.title: A fact triangle
text: Write the whole (the total or the product) at the top of a triangle and the two parts at the bottom.
Every fact of the family uses these three numbers: the top is always the result of + or ×, and the start of − or ÷.

families.title: Millimetres, centimetres, metres and kilometres
explanations: cm-as-100 (recall): A centimetre was taken as 100 mm; 1 cm = 10 mm.
added (conceptual): The numbers were added as they are; change the centimetres into millimetres first.
took-a (conceptual): 9 was taken away, but 9 km is 9,000 m.
gave-cm (procedural): The whole centimetres were given; the question asks for the millimetres left over.
km-as-100 (recall): A kilometre was taken as 100 m, so the metres were divided by 100; 1 km = 1000 m.
km-as-10 (recall): The metres were divided by 10; 1 km = 1000 m.
multiplied (conceptual): The millimetres were multiplied by 10; going to a bigger unit gives a smaller number, so divide.

teach.idea: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m and 1000 m = 1 km. Going to a smaller unit gives a bigger number; going to a bigger unit makes groups.
teach.method: To change to the smaller unit, multiply by 10 (cm to mm) or 1000 (km to m) and add the rest. To change to the bigger unit, make groups of 10 or 1000; what is left stays in the smaller unit.

alternatives.title: Look at a ruler
text: Between two centimetre numbers on a ruler there are 10 small marks: millimetres.
So 4 cm 3 mm is 4 groups of 10 small marks and 3 more: 43 mm.

families.title: Patterns in calendars and on the clock
explanations: used-first-date (conceptual): The first date (15) was used in place of the middle date. The pattern works with the middle date, 23: each date is as much above it as its partner is below it.
one-row (procedural): Only the middle row was added. All three rows must be added (or the middle date taken 9 times).
divided-by-3 (conceptual): The sum was divided by 3, but there are 9 dates, each balancing around the middle one: divide by 9.
no-wrap (conceptual): The hours were counted on past 12, but on a clock the hand goes round: after 12 comes 1 again.
wrapped-once (procedural): 12 was taken away only once; take 12 away for every full turn of the hand.

teach.idea: In a calendar the date below is 7 more and the date to the right is 1 more, so in a 3 × 3 block every date is balanced by a partner around the middle date. On a clock the hour hand comes back to the same place every 12 hours.
teach.method: Find the middle date and multiply it by how many dates you add. For the clock, take away 12 hours for every full turn, then count on what is left.

alternatives.title: Pair up the dates
text: In a block, the top-left and bottom-right dates add up to twice the middle date, and so do the other opposite pairs.
So nine dates are four pairs and the middle: 9 times the middle date.

families.title: Reading a pictograph with half pictures
explanations: no-key (conceptual): The pictures were counted, but each ● stands for 20 children.
half-as-whole (conceptual): The half ● was counted as a whole ●. A half picture stands for half the key: 10.
half-left-out (procedural): The half ● was left out. It stands for 10 children.

teach.idea: A whole picture stands for the key; a half picture stands for half the key.
teach.method: Count the whole pictures and multiply by the key, then add half the key for a half picture.

alternatives.title: Count in halves
text: Count every half of a picture: a whole picture is two halves.
Multiply the number of halves by half the key.

families.title: Writing a length in a larger unit as a decimal
explanations: m-as-10 (recall): The metres were multiplied by 10; 1 m = 100 cm.
m-as-1000 (recall): The metres were multiplied by 1000; 1 m = 100 cm.
cm-as-100 (recall): The millimetres were divided by 100; 1 cm = 10 mm, so divide by 10.
km-as-100 (recall): The metres were divided by 100; 1 km = 1000 m, so divide by 1000.
km-as-10 (recall): The metres were divided by 10; 1 km = 1000 m.

teach.idea: 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 cm is one hundredth of a metre; 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 mm is a tenth of a centimetre; 1 km = 1000 m, so 1 m is a thousandth of a kilometre.
teach.method: To write a length in the bigger unit, divide by 100, 10 or 1000: move the digits that many places to the right of the decimal point. To go back, multiply.

alternatives.title: Split into whole units and the rest
text: 245 cm is 2 m and 45 cm.
45 cm is 45 hundredths of a metre, so 245 cm = 2.45 m.

families.title: Parallel, perpendicular or neither
explanations: slant-not-parallel (conceptual): Lines were taken to be parallel only when they go straight across or straight up. Slanting segments are parallel when they go the same number of squares across for the same number up.
must-touch (conceptual): Perpendicular segments do not have to touch: if they were made longer, they would meet at a right angle.
looks-parallel (procedural): The segments slope nearly the same way, but count the squares: AB goes 4 across for 3 up, CD goes 5 across.

teach.idea: Parallel lines go in the same direction and never meet; perpendicular lines meet (or would meet, if made longer) at a right angle.
teach.method: Count how many squares each segment goes across and up. The same for both: parallel. Across and up swapped, with one going the other way: perpendicular. Otherwise: neither.

alternatives.title: Slide and turn a set square
text: Lay a ruler along AB and slide it without turning: if it lies along CD, they are parallel.
Put the corner of a set square on the lines: if both edges lie along them, they are perpendicular.

families.title: One-step word problems with four-digit numbers
explanations: took-away (conceptual): The smaller number was taken from the bigger one, but the story puts the two amounts together, so we add.
no-carry (procedural): A ten, hundred or thousand made in one column was not carried to the next.
added (conceptual): The numbers were added, but in the story some are taken away (or one part is asked for), so we subtract.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): In a column where the top digit was smaller, the top was taken from the bottom. Regroup from the next column first.

teach.idea: Decide first what happens in the story: two amounts put together (add), or one taken from another, or one part of a total asked for (subtract).
teach.method: Write the numbers one under the other, thousands under thousands, and work from the ones, regrouping as needed. Check with an estimate in thousands.

alternatives.title: Draw a bar model
text: Draw one long bar for the total and split it into the two parts.
Label what you know; the box with the question mark tells you whether to add the parts or take one from the total.

families.title: Changing paise into rupees
explanations: divided-by-10 (recall): The paise were divided by 10, as if ₹1 were 10 paise; ₹1 = 100 paise.
divided-by-1000 (recall): The paise were divided by 1000; ₹1 = 100 paise, so divide by 100.

teach.idea: 100 paise make ₹1, so every hundred paise is a rupee and the paise under 100 are written after the point.
teach.method: Divide the paise by 100: the hundreds become rupees and the last two digits are the paise. 1245 paise = ₹12.45.

alternatives.title: Put the point two places from the right
text: Write the number of paise.
Put the decimal point before the last two digits: 805 paise = ₹8.05.

families.title: Comparing two expressions with <, > or =
explanations: first-only (procedural): Only the first numbers (10 and 11) were compared. The second numbers change too, so look at both changes.
minus-as-plus (conceptual): Taking away more was treated as giving more. In a − b, a bigger number taken away leaves less.
add-changes (conceptual): The changes were balanced as in adding (one up, one down, so equal). For multiplying that does not work: work out or picture both rectangles.

teach.idea: You can often compare two expressions by seeing how the numbers change: in a sum, a bigger part makes a bigger sum; in a difference, taking away more leaves less.
teach.method: Match up the numbers on the two sides and see how much each goes up or down. Add up the effects; if they cancel, the sides are equal. For products, work them out if the changes pull different ways.

alternatives.title: Think of a balance
text: Put each side on a pan of a balance.
If one side gets 2 more on one number and 3 less on the other, it is 1 lighter: the other side is greater.

families.title: Total cost and cost of one item, with paise
explanations: paise-not-multiplied (procedural): Only the rupees were multiplied by 9; the 65 paise must be multiplied too.
paise-over-100 (conceptual): The paise came to 585, more than 100: 100 paise make ₹1, so carry the rupees.
multiplied (conceptual): The total was multiplied by 8; the cost of one item is the total shared into 8 equal parts.

teach.idea: Money in rupees and paise can be worked in paise: ₹12.75 is 1275 paise, a whole number you can multiply or divide.
teach.method: Change the price to paise, multiply (or divide) by the number of items, then change back to rupees by putting the point two places from the right.

alternatives.title: Split rupees and paise
text: Multiply the rupees and the paise separately: 3 × ₹12.75 is 3 × ₹12 and 3 × 75 paise.
Change every 100 paise into ₹1 and add.

families.title: Which three points are collinear?
explanations: by-eye (procedural): Point A looks almost in line, but count the squares: each step along the line is 3 across and 2 up, and A is one square off.

teach.idea: Points are collinear when they lie on one straight line: the steps from one to the next all go the same way.
teach.method: Pick three points. Count the squares across and up from the first to the second and from the second to the third. If the steps are in the same ratio (same direction), the three are collinear.

alternatives.title: Lay a ruler
text: Lay a ruler through two of the points.
If the edge also passes exactly through a third point, the three are collinear; one square off is not enough.

families.title: Journeys across midnight: railway and bus timetables
explanations: same-day (conceptual): The two times were taken away as if they were on the same day. The train passes midnight: count on to 24:00 first, then on to the arrival.
day-as-12 (recall): A day was taken as 12 hours. On a 24-hour timetable a whole day is 24 hours.
past-24 (conceptual): The hours were added past 24. After 23:59 the clock starts again at 00:00, so take 24 away for each midnight.
minus-12 (recall): 12 was taken away, as on a 12-hour clock; on a 24-hour clock take away 24.

teach.idea: A 24-hour clock goes from 00:00 to 23:59 and then starts again; a journey past midnight is the time up to 24:00 plus the time after it.
teach.method: For a journey time, count on from the departure to 24:00, then from 00:00 to the arrival (adding 24 hours for each extra day). For an arrival time, add the journey and take away 24 hours for each midnight passed.

alternatives.title: A time line with midnight marked
text: Draw a line from the departure to the arrival and mark 24:00 on it.
Work out the two jumps and add them.

families.title: Preparing and checking a bill
explanations: rates-added (conceptual): The rates were added without multiplying by the quantities. Each amount is quantity × rate.
missed-row (procedural): One row was left out of the total; add every amount.
rate-only (conceptual): The rate was copied as the amount, but 4 kg were bought: the amount is quantity × rate.
added-quantity (conceptual): The quantity was added to the rate; the amount is the rate taken as many times as the quantity.

teach.idea: Each line of a bill is quantity × rate; the total is the sum of the amounts.
teach.method: Multiply the quantity by the rate for each row (work in paise if it helps), write the amounts, then add them for the total. To check a bill, redo each multiplication and the addition.

alternatives.title: Check with an estimate
text: Round each rate to the nearest rupee and multiply.
The total of the estimates should be close to the bill's total.

families.title: The perimeter of a shape from its side lengths
explanations: missed-side (procedural): One side was left out. Tick each side as you add it, and go all the way round.
side-twice (procedural): One side was added twice. Start at one corner and stop when you are back at it.
lost-ten (recall): A ten was lost while adding the lengths. Add the sides one at a time and check each step.
multiplied-sides (conceptual): Two sides were multiplied, as for the space inside. The perimeter is the distance around the edge: add all the sides.

teach.idea: The perimeter is the length of the boundary: the distance all the way around a shape.
teach.method: Start at one corner. Add the length of each side in turn, ticking it, until you are back where you started.

alternatives.title: Straighten the boundary
text: Imagine a string laid along every side of the shape, then pulled straight.
Its length is the perimeter: one jump on the number line for each side.

families.title: A missing side from the perimeter
explanations: added-perimeter (conceptual): The perimeter was added to the other sides. The perimeter is already the whole way round, so take the known sides away from it.
known-sum (procedural): The known sides were added, but the total was not taken away from the perimeter.
one-side-taken (procedural): Only one known side was taken away from the perimeter. Take away every side you know.

teach.idea: The perimeter is all the sides added together, so the missing side is what is left when the known sides are taken away.
teach.method: Add the sides you know. Take that total away from the perimeter. Check: all the sides together should make the perimeter.

alternatives.title: Count on to the perimeter
text: Jump along a number line by each known side.
The last jump, up to the perimeter, is the missing side.

families.title: Hours and minutes into minutes
explanations: hour-as-100 (conceptual): An hour was taken as 100 minutes, as if time were counted in hundreds. An hour has 60 minutes.
not-converted (conceptual): The hours and minutes were added as they are. Hours must first be changed to minutes: 1 hour = 60 minutes.
minutes-left-out (procedural): The hours were changed to minutes, but the extra 55 minutes were not added.

teach.idea: 1 hour is 60 minutes: the minute hand goes once all the way round the clock.
teach.method: Change the hours to minutes (60 for each hour), then add the extra minutes.

alternatives.title: Once round the clock
text: Each time the minute hand goes all the way round, 60 minutes pass and the hour hand moves to the next number.
Count 60, 120, 180 … for the hours, then count on the extra minutes.

families.title: Minutes into hours and minutes
explanations: minutes-as-hours (conceptual): The number of minutes was written as hours. Change minutes to hours by making groups of 60.
hour-as-100 (conceptual): The minutes were split into hundreds, as if an hour were 100 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes.
hour-left-in (procedural): Not every hour was taken out: 115 minutes is still more than an hour, so it makes one more hour.

teach.idea: Every 60 minutes make 1 hour. The minutes left over, fewer than 60, stay as minutes.
teach.method: Take away 60 minutes as many times as you can. Count the 60s: that is the hours. What is left is the minutes.

alternatives.title: Use the 60 times table
text: Say 60, 120, 180, 240 … and stop before you pass the number of minutes.
The count of 60s is the hours; the difference to the total is the minutes.

families.title: Minutes and seconds into seconds
explanations: minute-as-100 (conceptual): A minute was taken as 100 seconds. A minute has 60 seconds.
not-converted (conceptual): The minutes and seconds were added as they are. Change the minutes to seconds first: 1 minute = 60 seconds.
seconds-left-out (procedural): The minutes were changed to seconds, but the extra 55 seconds were not added.

teach.idea: 1 minute is 60 seconds: the seconds hand goes once round the clock in a minute.
teach.method: Change the minutes to seconds (60 for each minute), then add the extra seconds.

alternatives.title: Just like hours and minutes
text: Minutes and seconds work the same way as hours and minutes: 60 of the small unit make one of the big unit.
So 2 minutes 10 seconds = 60 + 60 + 10 seconds.

families.title: Comparing two fractions with the same bottom or top number
explanations: more-parts-wrong-way (procedural): Both fractions count parts of the same size (a whole cut into 12 equal parts), so the one with more parts is greater. The smaller one was mixed up.
bigger-bottom-bigger (conceptual): The fraction with the smaller bottom number was chosen as smaller. A bigger bottom number means the whole is cut into more parts, so each part is smaller.
