teach.idea: Same bottom number: the parts are the same size, so more parts is more. Same top number: the same number of parts, but a bigger bottom number cuts the whole into more, smaller parts.
teach.method: Look at which number is the same. If the bottoms match, compare the tops. If the tops match, the smaller bottom number gives the greater fraction.

alternatives.title: Shade both in the same whole
text: Draw two strips of the same length. Cut one into the first fraction's parts and the other into the second's, and shade.
The longer shaded part is the greater fraction.

alternatives.title: More sharers, smaller shares
text: Share one roti among 2 children, then another among 4.
With more children each piece is smaller: 1/4 is less than 1/2.

families.title: Ordering three fractions with the same bottom or top number
explanations: largest-first (procedural): The fractions were put from the largest to the smallest. The question asks for the smallest first.
as-given (procedural): The fractions were written in the order they were given. Compare them first, then write the smallest one first.
bigger-bottom-bigger (conceptual): The fractions were put in order of their bottom numbers. With the same top number, a bigger bottom number means smaller parts, so the order goes the other way.

teach.idea: With the same bottom number the parts are the same size, so order by the top numbers. With the same top number, a bigger bottom number means smaller parts.
teach.method: Find the smallest fraction and write it first, then the next, then the largest. Check each one is smaller than the next.

alternatives.title: Line up fraction strips
text: Shade each fraction on a strip of the same length, one under another.
Read the shaded lengths from the shortest to the longest.

families.title: Naming the shaded fraction of a shape
explanations: shaded-to-unshaded (conceptual): The shaded squares were put over the unshaded ones. The bottom number is ALL the equal parts of the whole.
count-only (conceptual): Only the shaded squares were counted. A fraction also says how many equal parts make the whole.
unshaded (procedural): The unshaded squares were counted. The question asks about the shaded part.

teach.idea: A fraction names equal parts of a whole: the bottom number is how many equal parts make the whole, the top number is how many we mean.
teach.method: Count all the equal parts for the bottom number. Count the shaded parts for the top number.

alternatives.title: The same fraction as a round cake
text: Cut a round cake into the same number of equal pieces and colour the same number.
The fraction is the same: it does not depend on the shape of the whole.

families.title: Building a fraction from unit fractions
explanations: add-bottoms (conceptual): The bottom numbers were added too. Every piece is still a 1/12 piece: the bottom number names the size of the piece and stays 12.
count-only (conceptual): Only the number of pieces was written. Say what size the pieces are too: that is the bottom number.
bottom-number (conceptual): The bottom number 12 was given. It says how many pieces make the WHOLE; the top number says how many pieces we have.
pieces-left (procedural): The pieces that are left over were counted. Count the pieces that make the fraction.

teach.idea: A unit fraction 1/n is one of n equal parts. Putting k of those parts together gives k/n: the top number counts the parts.
teach.method: Count how many pieces there are (the top number). The size of each piece (the bottom number) does not change.

alternatives.title: Count pieces like objects
text: Say the pieces like counting things: one eighth, two eighths, three eighths.
Three eighths is written 3/8: 3 pieces, each an eighth.

families.title: A fraction of a collection of objects
explanations: what-is-left (procedural): The part that is left was found (60 minus the fraction). The question asks for the fraction itself.
one-part-only (procedural): 60 was shared into 10 equal groups, but only one group was counted. 9/10 means 9 of those groups.
divide-by-top (conceptual): 40 was divided by the top number 8. Share into 10 equal groups first (the bottom number), then take 8 of them.

teach.idea: To find a fraction of a collection, share it into as many equal groups as the bottom number, and take as many groups as the top number.
teach.method: Divide by the bottom number to find one group. Multiply by the top number.

alternatives.title: Deal them out like cards
text: Make as many piles as the bottom number. Give one object to each pile in turn until none are left.
Count the objects in as many piles as the top number.

families.title: A fraction of an hour, a metre, a kilogram, a day or ₹100
explanations: hour-as-100 (conceptual): An hour was taken as 100 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes.
one-part-only (procedural): Only 1/12 was found. 11/12 is 11 of those parts.
divide-by-top (conceptual): The whole was divided by the top number 8. Divide by the bottom number 12 to find one part, then take 8 parts.
kg-as-100 (recall): A kilogram was taken as 100 grams. 1 kg = 1000 g.

teach.idea: First change the whole into small units (an hour is 60 minutes, a metre is 100 cm, a kilogram is 1000 g, a day is 24 hours). Then find the fraction of that number.
teach.method: Write the whole in the small unit, divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.

alternatives.title: Fractions of an hour on a clock
text: Half past is the minute hand halfway round: 30 minutes. A quarter past is a quarter of the way round: 15 minutes.
Three quarters of an hour is three of those quarter turns: 45 minutes.

families.title: Adding and subtracting three-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: no-carry (conceptual): A ten (or a hundred) made in one column was not carried to the next column.
first-carry-forgotten (procedural): The hundred was carried, but the ten carried from the ones was forgotten in the tens column. Add every carried 1 to the next column.
smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In each column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, regroup first: exchange 1 ten from the next column for 10 ones.

borrow-not-taken (procedural): A ten (or a hundred) was exchanged for 10 ones (or 10 tens), but the column it came from was not made one less. When you regroup, the next column gives one away, so it goes down by 1.

teach.idea: Ten ones make a ten and ten tens make a hundred, so a column that gets too big passes a ten (or a hundred) on, and a column that is too small can break one from the next column.
teach.method: Write the numbers one under the other, ones under ones. Work from the ones to the hundreds, regrouping as you go: carry a ten when adding, exchange a ten for 10 ones when subtracting. Check with an estimate.

alternatives.title: Jump by hundreds, tens and ones
text: Start at the first number. Jump by the hundreds of the second number, then its tens, then its ones (forwards to add, backwards to subtract).
Each jump is easy to do in your head.

families.title: Writing a number from its place-value parts
explanations: blocks-as-ones (conceptual): Every block was counted as 1. A flat is 100 and a long is 10.
tens-ones-swapped (procedural): The tens and the ones were written in each other's places.
parts-side-by-side (conceptual): The parts were written next to each other. Add them: each digit goes in its own place.
zero-left-out (conceptual): A place with nothing in it was left out. Write 0 to keep the other digits in their places.

teach.idea: Each place is worth ten of the place on its right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. A digit shows how many of that place there are.
teach.method: Write the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones digits in a place-value table. Write 0 for an empty place.

alternatives.title: Build it with blocks
text: Show the number with flats (100), longs (10) and cubes (1); a big cube is 1000.
Count each kind and write the counts in order: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.

families.title: How much more makes 1000
explanations: made-999 (procedural): The number was made up to 999, one short of 1000.
ones-dropped (procedural): The ones were left out: only the tens and hundreds were made up.
each-digit-to-ten (conceptual): Each digit was made up to 10. Only the ones make 10; the tens and the hundreds each make 9, because the ten and the hundred carried over fill the rest.

teach.idea: Counting up in friendly jumps (to the next ten, then the next hundred, then 1000) finds the difference without regrouping.
teach.method: Jump from the number to the next ten, then to the next hundred, then to 1000. Add the jumps.

alternatives.title: Make 999, then one more
text: Each digit of the number and the missing number add up to 9: that makes 999.
One more makes 1000, so add 1 to what you found.

families.title: How many whole numbers lie between two numbers
explanations: difference-only (procedural): The difference 17 counts the steps from one number to the other, which includes the last number. The numbers between are one fewer.
both-ends (procedural): Both end numbers were counted. 'Between' leaves them out.

teach.idea: Subtracting counts the steps from one number to the other; the last step lands on the end number, so the numbers in between are one fewer than the steps.
teach.method: Subtract the smaller number from the larger, then take away 1.

alternatives.title: Try a small case
text: Between 3 and 7 are 4, 5 and 6: three numbers, and 7 − 3 = 4.
So the count between is always the difference minus one.

families.title: Estimating a sum or difference by rounding to tens
explanations: always-down (conceptual): Both numbers were rounded down. Round to the NEAREST ten: 5 or more in the ones goes up.
one-rounded (procedural): Only the first number was rounded. Round both numbers before working it out.
exact (procedural): The exact answer was worked out. An estimate uses the rounded numbers, so it is quick to find in your head.

teach.idea: A number rounded to the nearest ten is the ten it is closest to on the number line. Rounded numbers are easy to add or subtract in your head, and the estimate shows whether an exact answer is sensible.
teach.method: Look at the ones digit: 0 to 4 round down, 5 to 9 round up. Round both numbers, then work out the answer with the tens.

alternatives.title: Which ten is closer?
text: Put the number on a number line between two tens.
Count the steps to each ten: it rounds to the closer one (halfway goes up).

families.title: Reading a bar chart
explanations: next-bar (procedural): The bar next to the one asked about was read. Find the label first, then go straight up its bar.
counted-lines (conceptual): The lines on the scale were counted as 1 each. Each line on this scale stands for 5.
added (conceptual): The tallest and shortest bars were added. 'How many more' means the difference.
one-bar (procedural): Only the larger bar was read. Compare it with the other bar by subtracting.
missed-bar (procedural): One bar was left out of the total. Add every bar, ticking each one.
tallest-only (procedural): Only the tallest bar was read. Subtract the shortest bar from it.

teach.idea: In a bar chart the height of each bar shows a number. The scale on the side tells how much each line stands for.
teach.method: Find the label under the bar, go to the top of the bar and read across to the scale. For 'how many more', subtract; for 'in all', add.

alternatives.title: Turn the chart into a table
text: Write each label with the number its bar shows.
Then answer from the table: compare, add or subtract the numbers.

families.title: Reading tally marks in a table
explanations: bundle-as-one (conceptual): Each bundle ||||/ was counted as 1 instead of 5.
bundle-as-four (conceptual): Only the four upright marks of each bundle were counted. The line across is the fifth mark.
wrong-row (procedural): The marks in another row were counted. Find the right row first.
missed-row (procedural): One row was left out of the total. Add every row.
added (conceptual): The two rows were added. 'How many more' asks for the difference.
one-row (procedural): Only one row was counted. Subtract the smaller count from the larger.

teach.idea: Tally marks record one mark for each thing counted; every fifth mark crosses the four before it, so the marks come in easy bundles of 5.
teach.method: Count the bundles in fives (5, 10, 15 …), then count on the single marks.

alternatives.title: Bundles as half ten frames
text: Each bundle of 5 fills half a ten frame; two bundles fill a whole frame.
Count the full frames as tens, then add the rest.

families.title: A missing number in a two-way table
explanations: added-to-total (conceptual): The total and the other number were added. The total is already both parts together, so take the other part away from it.
gave-total (procedural): The total of the row was given. The missing number is only one part of that total.
subtracted (conceptual): The two numbers were subtracted. A total puts the parts together: add them.
one-part (procedural): Only one of the numbers was given. The total includes both.
double-total (procedural): Both the row totals and the column totals were added, so every child was counted twice.
one-total (procedural): Only one group's total was given. Add the totals of both groups.

teach.idea: In a two-way table every row and every column adds up to its total, so any one missing number can be found from the others.
teach.method: Look along the row (or down the column) with the gap. If the gap is a total, add the parts; if it is a part, take the other part from the total.

alternatives.title: See the parts as bars
text: Draw the total as one long bar, split into the two parts.
The missing part is the piece of the bar that is not yet labelled.

families.title: Unit fractions such as 1/2 and 1/4 on a number line
explanations: bigger-bottom-bigger (conceptual): A bigger bottom number was taken to mean a bigger fraction. 1/10 cuts the whole into more parts than 1/8, so each part is smaller and its dot is nearer to 0.

teach.idea: On a number line from 0 to 1, 1/2 is halfway and 1/4 is halfway to the half: cutting the line into more equal parts makes each part shorter, so 1/4 is nearer to 0 than 1/2.
teach.method: Picture the line from 0 to 1 cut into as many equal parts as the bottom number; the first mark is the unit fraction. More parts means the first mark is closer to 0.

alternatives.title: Fold a strip
text: Fold a paper strip in half and mark the fold: that is 1/2.
Fold it in half again: the first fold from the start is 1/4, closer to the start.

families.title: Estimating and checking weights and capacities
explanations: added (conceptual): The guess and the weighing were added. How far off the guess was is the difference: take the smaller from the larger.
kept-guess (procedural): The guess was given again. Check it: find how many mugs of that size the bucket really holds.
subtracted (conceptual): The glass was taken away from the jug once. Filling glasses takes the glass away again and again: count how many times.
kg-as-100 (recall): A kilogram was taken as 100 g; 1 kg = 1000 g.
added-numbers (conceptual): The numbers were added without changing kilograms into grams first.
litre-as-100 (recall): A litre was taken as 100 mL; 1 L = 1000 mL.
litres-only (conceptual): The number of litres was given; change the litres into millilitres and see how many mugs fit.

teach.idea: An estimate is a sensible guess; checking it by weighing or pouring tells how close it was. Estimates get better when we compare with things we know (a 1 kg packet of salt, a 1 L bottle).
teach.method: Make a guess using a known weight or container, then measure. The difference between the guess and the measurement shows how good the guess was.

alternatives.title: Compare with things you know
text: A packet of salt weighs 1 kg; a water bottle often holds 1 L.
Ask: is it about as heavy as 2 packets? 5 packets? That gives a sensible guess.

families.title: Hours in days, days in weeks and months, months in years
explanations: not-converted (conceptual): The numbers were added as they are; change the years into months first.
day-as-12 (recall): A day was taken as 12 hours. A whole day and night is 24 hours.
extra-days-left-out (procedural): The weeks were changed into days, but the extra 6 days were not added.
thirty-each (recall): Every month was taken to have 30 days. Months have 28, 30 or 31 days: use the knuckle rhyme or a calendar.
thirty-one-each (recall): Every month was taken to have 31 days. Some months have 30 days, and February has 28 (29 in a leap year).
year-as-10 (recall): A year was taken as 10 months, as if time were counted in tens. A year has 12 months.

teach.idea: 1 day = 24 hours, 1 week = 7 days, 1 year = 12 months; months have 28, 30 or 31 days.
teach.method: Multiply the bigger unit by how many small units it holds, then add the extra small units. For days in a month, use a calendar or the knuckle rhyme.

alternatives.title: The knuckle way
text: Make two fists. Say the months along the knuckles and the gaps between them.
Months on a knuckle have 31 days; months in a gap have 30, except February (28, or 29 in a leap year).

families.title: Number names and expanded form of four-digit numbers
explanations: zero-place (conceptual): The 0 in 6,073 was read in the wrong place. A 0 keeps its place empty: here there are no hundreds.
thousand-as-zero (procedural): A 0 was written for the word "thousand", giving five digits. The thousands digit is just the number before "thousand", and the number has four digits.
face-values (conceptual): The digits were added as they are. In the expanded form each digit is written with its place value: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.

teach.idea: A four-digit number has thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. The name and the expanded form say each digit with its place; a 0 means that place is empty.
teach.method: Write the number in a Th H T O table. Read it as (thousands digit) thousand, (hundreds digit) hundred, then the tens and ones; skip a place with 0. The expanded form adds the value of each non-zero digit.

alternatives.title: Think of notes
text: ₹4,507 is 4 bundles of ₹1000 (ten ₹100 notes each), 5 more notes of ₹100, no ₹10 notes and 7 coins of ₹1.
So it is 4000 + 500 + 7, four thousand five hundred seven.

families.title: Continuing number patterns up to 10,000
explanations: wrong-way (conceptual): The numbers go up each time; the step was taken the other way.
step-ten (procedural): The pattern was continued in tens, but each step is 1,000: look at the gap between two numbers next to each other.
no-carry (procedural): The digit went past 9 but the next place was not made one more.

teach.idea: In a number pattern that adds (or takes away) the same step each time, find the step and keep going; when a place goes past 9, the next place goes up by one.
teach.method: Subtract two numbers next to each other to find the step. Add (or take away) the step from the last number, regrouping if a place passes 9 or 0.

alternatives.title: Watch the place that changes
text: Steps of 100 change the hundreds digit; steps of 1000 change the thousands digit.
When the hundreds go from 9 to 10, write 0 hundreds and add one thousand.

families.title: Checking an answer by estimating
explanations: estimate-must-match (conceptual): The answer was rejected because it is not exactly 850. An estimate is only close: 851 is near 850, so it is sensible.
trusted-working (procedural): The working was trusted without checking. The estimate is about 850, which is far from 617, so something went wrong.

teach.idea: An estimate made with rounded numbers is close to the exact answer, so an answer far from the estimate must be wrong.
teach.method: Round each number to the nearest ten and work out the estimate in your head. If the answer is close (within about 15 here), it is sensible; if it is much smaller or bigger, check the working again.

alternatives.title: Use the hundreds first
text: Add (or subtract) the hundreds only: 468 + 57 is more than 400 + 50 = 450.
An answer below that cannot be right.

families.title: Column addition and subtraction from three to five digits, with and without regrouping
explanations: misaligned (procedural): 11 was written under the wrong places (its tens under the hundreds). Line up the ones under the ones.
smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In each column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, regroup: exchange 1 from the next column for 10.
not-reduced (procedural): A column was regrouped, but the column it came from was not made one less.
no-carry (conceptual): A ten (or hundred, or thousand) made in one column was not carried to the next column.

teach.idea: Write the numbers with ones under ones, tens under tens and so on; each column is added or subtracted on its own, passing a 1 to the next column (or taking one from it) when needed.
teach.method: Start with the ones and work left. Adding: if a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry 1. Subtracting: if the top digit is smaller, regroup 1 from the next column as 10.

alternatives.title: Check with the inverse
text: After subtracting, add your answer to the number you took away: you should get the first number.
After adding, take one number away from your answer: you should get the other.

families.title: Only one, both or neither: reading a two-way table
explanations: only-cell (conceptual): Only the children who play cricket and not kho-kho were counted; those who play both also play cricket.
added-neither (conceptual): The children who play neither game were counted too.
both-twice (procedural): The children who play both were counted once for each game, so twice.
missed-neither (procedural): The children who play neither game were left out; they are in the class too.
counted-both (conceptual): The children who play both games were counted too. 'Exactly one' leaves out those who play both and those who play neither.
one-cell (procedural): Only one of the 'only one game' cells was taken; there are two such groups.

teach.idea: Each child is in exactly one cell: both games, cricket only, kho-kho only, or neither. 'Exactly one' is the two 'only' cells; 'cricket' includes those who play both; 'at least one' is everyone except 'neither'.
teach.method: Decide which cells fit the question, then add only those cells.

alternatives.title: Two overlapping circles
text: Draw a circle for cricket and one for kho-kho that overlap. Both games go in the overlap; only one game in the rest of a circle; neither outside both circles.
Read the question and shade the parts it asks for.

families.title: How many squares to shade to show a fraction
explanations: top-number (conceptual): 8 squares were shaded, the top number. The top number counts parts of size 1/9 of the WHOLE grid, and each such part here is 4 squares.
unshaded (procedural): The squares left unshaded were counted.
one-part (procedural): Only 1/9 of the grid was found (4 squares); 8/9 is 8 of those parts.

teach.idea: The same fraction can be shown on wholes of different sizes: 3/4 of 8 squares is 6 squares, 3/4 of 12 squares is 9 squares, but each time it is 3 of 4 equal parts of the whole.
teach.method: Share the squares into as many equal groups as the bottom number, then shade as many groups as the top number.

alternatives.title: Same fraction, different wholes
text: Shade 1/2 of a 2 × 2 grid and 1/2 of a 2 × 4 grid.
Different numbers of squares are shaded (2 and 4), but each is half of its own grid.

families.title: Mental shortcuts: making 100 and 10,000, and taking away or adding 9 or 99
explanations: each-to-ten (conceptual): Each digit was made up to 10. Only the ones make 10; the other places each make 9, because the ten carried over fills the rest.
made-nines (procedural): The number was made up to 9,999, one short of 10,000.
no-adjust (procedural): 100 was added, but the extra 1 was not taken away: 99 is one less than 100.
adjust-wrong-way (procedural): 100 was added and then 1 more was added; since 100 is one too many, take 1 away.

teach.idea: Round numbers are easy: 9 is 10 − 1 and 99 is 100 − 1. To make 100 or 10,000, every digit pairs to 9 except the ones, which pair to 10.
teach.method: To take away 9, take away 10 and add 1 back; to add 99, add 100 and take 1 away. To make 10,000, find what makes each digit 9 and the ones digit 10.

alternatives.title: Too much, then fix it
text: Taking away 99 is taking away 100, which is 1 too many.
So give that 1 back: 562 − 99 = 462 + 1 = 463.

families.title: Race times, and choosing seconds, minutes or hours
explanations: seconds-only (conceptual): Only the numbers of seconds were compared and the minutes were left out. Change each time into seconds first: 1 min 5 s is 65 s.
more-is-faster (conceptual): The smallest time was taken as the slowest. In a race, the fastest runner takes the LEAST time.

teach.idea: 1 minute = 60 seconds. In a race the fastest runner takes the least time. Short things (a clap, a 100 m run) are timed in seconds, longer ones in minutes, very long ones in hours.
teach.method: Change every time into seconds (minutes × 60 + seconds), then compare. For choosing a unit, think how long the activity usually takes.

alternatives.title: Count it out
text: Say 'one thousand one, one thousand two …': each is about a second.
If you would be counting for a long time, minutes (or hours) are the better unit.

families.title: Adding durations and changing seconds into minutes and seconds
explanations: small-unit-left-out (procedural): Only the minutes were added.
no-carry (conceptual): The seconds came to 75, but 60 of them make one minute.
carry-kept (procedural): One minute was carried, but its 60 seconds were not taken away.
minute-as-100 (conceptual): The seconds were split into hundreds, as if a minute were 100 seconds. A minute has 60 seconds.
one-minute-only (procedural): Only one minute was taken out; keep taking out 60 seconds while you can.

teach.idea: 60 minutes make 1 hour and 60 seconds make 1 minute, so when the small units add up to 60 or more, 60 of them become one big unit.
teach.method: Add the small units, then the big units. If the small units are 60 or more, take 60 away and add 1 to the big units. To change seconds into minutes and seconds, take out 60 seconds as many times as you can.

alternatives.title: Like carrying, but at 60
text: It works like carrying in addition, but you carry when you reach 60, not 10.
45 min + 30 min = 75 min = 1 h 15 min.

families.title: True or false? Checking statements about a bar chart
explanations: believed-order (procedural): The statement was accepted without looking at the two bars. Compare their heights: the taller bar is the larger number.
missed-bar (procedural): One bar was left out when checking the total, so the wrong total looked right. Add every bar.
added (conceptual): The two bars were added, so the sum looked like the answer. 'How many more' is the difference.

teach.idea: A statement about a chart is true only if the numbers read from the bars make it so: check it, do not guess from how it sounds.
teach.method: Read the bars the statement talks about. Work out what it claims (compare, add or subtract) and see whether you get the same.

alternatives.title: Write the numbers down first
text: Make a small table of each label and its number.
Then test the statement on the table.

families.title: Perimeter of a square or regular polygon from one side, and the side from the perimeter
explanations: one-side (procedural): Only the marked side was given. The perimeter goes all the way round: every side counts.
four-sides (conceptual): The side was multiplied by 4, as for a square, but a regular octagon has 8 sides.
halved (conceptual): The perimeter was halved, as when finding length + breadth of a rectangle. Here all the sides are equal, so share the perimeter among all of them.
multiplied (conceptual): The perimeter was multiplied by 8; the side is the perimeter shared equally among the 8 sides.
divided-by-4 (conceptual): The perimeter was divided by 4, as for a square, but a regular octagon has 8 equal sides.
area (conceptual): The side was multiplied by itself, which gives the area (the space inside). The perimeter is the distance round: 4 sides.

teach.idea: A regular polygon has all its sides equal, so its perimeter is the number of sides times one side: 4 × side for a square, 3 × side for an equilateral triangle, n × side in general.
teach.method: Count the sides. Multiply the side by that number for the perimeter; divide the perimeter by it for the side.

alternatives.title: Add the equal sides
text: Write the side once for every side of the shape and add: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 30 for a pentagon of side 6.
Adding the same number again and again is multiplying.

families.title: Measuring lengths with fractional units
explanations: counted-strips (conceptual): The number of strips was given as metres. Each strip is only 1/10 m, so 29 strips are 29 of those parts.
multiplied (conceptual): 29 was multiplied by 10. The strips are smaller than a metre, so 29 strips are fewer metres than 29: 29 × 1/10.
divided (conceptual): The metres were divided by 10. A short strip fits into a metre 10 times, so you need MORE strips than metres.
one-metre (procedural): Only the strips for one metre were counted; there are 6 metres.

teach.idea: A unit can be a fraction of a metre: if a strip is 1/b of a metre, b strips make 1 metre, and k strips make k/b of a metre.
teach.method: For a length, write the number of strips over b (and change to a mixed number if you like). For how many strips, multiply the metres by b.

alternatives.title: Jump along a number line
text: Mark 0, 1, 2 … metres and cut each metre into b equal jumps.
Count the jumps: k jumps land on k/b.

families.title: Comparing two fractions with different tops and bottoms
explanations: bigger-bottom-bigger (conceptual): The fraction with the smaller bottom number was chosen. The bottom number alone does not decide: change both to the same bottom number first.
bigger-top-bigger (conceptual): The fraction with the bigger top number was chosen. The parts are different sizes, so compare with a common bottom number.

teach.idea: Fractions with different bottom numbers count parts of different sizes; writing them with a common bottom number makes the parts the same size, so the tops can be compared.
teach.method: Find a common multiple of the bottom numbers (the smallest is easiest). Change both fractions to it, then the one with the bigger top is greater.

alternatives.title: Compare with 1/2
text: If one fraction is more than half and the other less than half, the first is greater.
3/5 is more than 1/2 (3 is more than half of 5); 3/8 is less than 1/2.

alternatives.title: Cross-multiply
text: For a/b and c/d, compare a × d with c × b.
The bigger product goes with the greater fraction.

families.title: Ordering three unlike fractions
explanations: by-bottom (conceptual): The fractions were ordered by their bottom numbers. With different tops and bottoms, change them to a common bottom number first.
by-top (conceptual): The fractions were ordered by their top numbers, but the parts are different sizes. Use a common bottom number.

teach.idea: To order fractions with different bottom numbers, write them all with one common bottom number; then their tops are in the same order as the fractions.
teach.method: Find a common multiple of all three bottom numbers. Change each fraction to it, order the tops, and write the original fractions in that order.

alternatives.title: Sort by 0, 1/2 and 1
text: First put each fraction into 'less than 1/2' or 'more than 1/2'.
Then compare only the fractions in the same group.

families.title: Estimating the total cost of several items
explanations: exact (procedural): The exact total was worked out. An estimate uses the rounded prices, so it can be found quickly in your head.
always-down (conceptual): Every price was rounded down. Round to the NEAREST ten: 5 or more in the ones goes up.

teach.idea: Rounding each price to the nearest ten gives friendly numbers that are easy to add in your head; the estimate tells you roughly how much money you need.
teach.method: Look at the ones digit of each price: 0 to 4 round down, 5 to 9 round up. Add the rounded prices.

alternatives.title: Which ten is nearer?
text: Put the price on a number line between two tens.
It rounds to the ten it is closer to; exactly halfway goes up.

families.title: Recording a list in a two-way table
explanations: whole-row (procedural): All the girls were counted, whatever they chose. The cell needs both: girls AND dosa.
whole-column (procedural): Everyone who chose dosa was counted, boys and girls. The cell is only for the girls.
one-cell (procedural): Only the boys who chose idli were counted; girls who chose idli count too.

teach.idea: A two-way table sorts each child two ways at once (boy or girl, and idli or dosa), so every child goes in exactly one cell.
teach.method: Draw the table. Go down the list one child at a time, put a tally mark in the cell for both answers, and tick the child off. Count the tallies in each cell; add along a row or down a column for totals.

alternatives.title: Sort into four piles
text: Write each child's name on a card.
Sort the cards into four piles: boy-idli, boy-dosa, girl-idli, girl-dosa, and count each pile.

families.title: Using a pattern rule to find a later number
explanations: n-jumps (conceptual): 12 jumps of 8 were added to the start, but the 1st number is the start itself: the 12th number is only 11 jumps along.
forgot-start (procedural): Only the jumps (12 × 8) were counted; the pattern starts at 30, not at 0.
next-only (procedural): Only the next number after those shown was found; keep using the rule until you reach the place asked for.

teach.idea: A rule like "add 5 each time" tells you how to get from one number to the next. The 1st number is the start, so the n-th number is n − 1 jumps after it.
teach.method: Count the jumps from the 1st number to the one asked for (one less than its place), multiply by the amount added each time, and add that to the start.

alternatives.title: Keep writing the pattern
text: Write the numbers in a row and keep adding the same amount.
Number each one with its place (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and stop at the place asked for.

families.title: Moving on a 1–100 number grid
explanations: down-adds-one (conceptual): Moving down was counted as adding 1 and moving right as adding 10; on the grid one row down adds 10 and one square right adds 1.
down-is-up (procedural): The move went up instead of down: going up takes away 10 for each row.
one-row (procedural): Only one row was moved; each of the 3 rows down adds another 10.

teach.idea: Each row of the grid holds 10 numbers, so the number just below is always 10 more, and the number just to the right is 1 more.
teach.method: Add 10 for every row you move down, then add 1 for every square you move right.

alternatives.title: Watch the tens digit
text: Moving down one row changes only the tens digit: 34 → 44 → 54.
Moving right changes only the ones digit: 54 → 55 → 56 (until the end of a row).

families.title: Picking out an acute, right, obtuse or straight angle
explanations: acute-obtuse-swap (recall): The names were mixed up: an obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle; an acute angle is smaller.
right-as-acute (conceptual): An angle of exactly 90° is a right angle; an acute angle is less than 90°.
straight-as-right (conceptual): A straight angle (180°) was taken for a right angle; a right angle is a square corner, half of a straight angle.
straight-as-obtuse (conceptual): A straight angle (180°) is not obtuse; an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°.
biggest-bent (conceptual): The biggest bent angle was chosen; a straight angle is exactly 180°, its arms make one straight line.
upright-as-straight (recall): A right angle (an arm standing straight up) was taken for a straight angle; a straight angle is a flat line, 180°.

teach.idea: A right angle (90°) is a square corner. Smaller than a right angle is acute, between a right angle and a straight line is obtuse, and a straight line is a straight angle (180°).
teach.method: Compare each angle with 90°: less is acute, equal is right; more than 90° but less than 180° is obtuse; exactly 180° is straight.

alternatives.title: Check with a folded-paper corner
text: Fold a paper twice to make a square corner: that is a right angle.
Hold the corner in the angle: if the angle fits inside the corner it is acute; if the corner fits inside the angle (and the arms are not one straight line) it is obtuse.

families.title: Angles as turns on a clock face
explanations: anticlockwise (procedural): The turn was counted the other way round (anticlockwise); clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move.
minutes-not-degrees (conceptual): The minutes were counted (5 for each number) instead of degrees; each number on the clock is 30° of turn.
count-start (procedural): The starting number was counted as a step too; count only the moves from one number to the next.

teach.idea: An angle is an amount of turn. A full turn is 360°, a half turn 180°, and a quarter turn is a right angle, 90°. On a clock, each number is one twelfth of a full turn: 30°.
teach.method: Count how many numbers the hand moves past clockwise, then multiply by 30°.

alternatives.title: Use quarter turns
text: 12 to 3 is a quarter turn (90°), 12 to 6 a half turn (180°), 12 to 9 three quarters (270°).
Each quarter turn is 3 numbers; find the nearest quarter and add or take away 30° for each number more or less.

families.title: Radius and diameter of a circle
explanations: same-length (conceptual): The diameter and the radius were taken as the same length; the radius goes only from the centre to the edge, half of the diameter.
halved (conceptual): The radius was halved; the radius is the shorter one (centre to edge), so the diameter is twice as long.
doubled (conceptual): The diameter was doubled; the diameter is the longer one, so the radius is half of it.

teach.idea: The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is made of two radii.
teach.method: To find the diameter, double the radius. To find the radius, halve the diameter.

alternatives.title: Fold a paper circle
text: Cut out a circle and fold it in half: the fold is a diameter, and it passes through the centre.
Fold again: the two folds cross at the centre, and each half of the first fold is a radius.

families.title: Letters with a vertical or horizontal line of symmetry
explanations: axis-swap (conceptual): The letters were folded the other way (up and down); a horizontal line goes across, so the top half must match the bottom half.
turn-not-fold (conceptual): N, S or Z look the same when turned upside down, but folding them does not make the halves match: turning is not a line of symmetry.
any-line (procedural): Letters with any line of symmetry were counted; the question asks only for a horizontal one.

teach.idea: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves of a shape match exactly, like a mirror image.
teach.method: Imagine folding each letter along the line (or stand a mirror on it): if the half you see in the mirror finishes the letter exactly, the letter has that line of symmetry.

alternatives.title: Use a mirror
text: Write the letter big and stand a small mirror on the line down its middle (or across its middle).
If the letter you see, half on paper and half in the mirror, looks just like the real letter, that line is a line of symmetry.

families.title: Reflecting a point in a mirror line on a grid
explanations: wrong-coordinate (conceptual): The wrong coordinate was changed: a mirror line y = 9 goes across, so the point moves up or down and only y changes.
onto-line (procedural): The point was moved only as far as the mirror line; the image is as far beyond the line as P is in front of it.

teach.idea: A mirror image is as far behind the mirror line as the object is in front of it, straight across, at right angles to the line.
teach.method: Count how far P is from the mirror line, then count the same distance on the other side. Only the coordinate that crosses the line changes.

alternatives.title: Fold the grid paper
text: Draw the point on squared paper and fold the paper along the mirror line.
Press hard on the point: the mark it makes on the other side is the image.

families.title: Translating a point on a grid
explanations: swap-moves (conceptual): The across move was added to y and the up-down move to x; the first coordinate tells how far across, the second how far up.
wrong-way-across (procedural): The point was moved to the right instead of the left: moving right makes x bigger, moving left makes it smaller.
wrong-way-updown (procedural): The point was moved up instead of down: moving up makes y bigger, moving down makes it smaller.

teach.idea: A translation slides a shape without turning or flipping it: every point moves the same distance across and the same distance up or down.
teach.method: Add the move to the right to x (take away a move to the left), and add the move up to y (take away a move down).

alternatives.title: Walk it on the grid
text: Put a finger on P. Count the squares across first, one at a time, then the squares up or down.
Read the coordinates where your finger stops: across first, then up.

families.title: Writing a 12-hour time in 24-hour form
explanations: am-add (conceptual): 12 was added to a morning time; a.m. times keep the same hour in 24-hour time.
pm-no-add (conceptual): 12 was not added for a p.m. time; after noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting: 1 p.m. is 13, 2 p.m. is 14 …
add-ten (procedural): 10 was added instead of 12 to the hours.
midnight-12 (conceptual): 12 a.m. is just after midnight, the start of the day: in 24-hour time its hour is 00.
noon-plus-12 (conceptual): 12 was added to 12 noon; 12 noon is already 12:00 in 24-hour time (there is no 24:00 in the day's times).

teach.idea: The 24-hour clock counts the hours of the whole day from 00 at midnight to 23. Morning (a.m.) hours stay the same; afternoon and evening (p.m.) hours go on past 12: 1 p.m. is 13, 2 p.m. is 14, and so on.
teach.method: For a.m., keep the hour (but 12 a.m. becomes 00). For p.m., add 12 to the hour (but 12 noon stays 12). The minutes do not change.

alternatives.title: A line for the whole day
text: Draw a line from 0 (midnight) to 24 (the next midnight), with 12 (noon) in the middle.
Morning times are on the first half; for an afternoon time, count on past 12: 3 p.m. is 3 more than 12, which is 15.

families.title: Reading a 24-hour time on a 12-hour clock
explanations: midnight-zero (conceptual): 00 hours is midnight; a 12-hour clock shows it as 12 (12 a.m.), not 0.
noon-minus-12 (conceptual): 12 was taken away from 12; 12:00 in 24-hour time is 12 noon, so the clock shows 12.
minus-ten (procedural): 10 was taken away instead of 12; for times after 12 noon, take away 12 from the hours.
no-change (conceptual): The 24-hour number was kept; a 12-hour clock only goes up to 12, so 23 hours is 11 p.m.

teach.idea: After 12 noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting (13, 14, … 23), but a 12-hour clock starts again at 1. 00 hours is midnight, shown as 12.
teach.method: If the hours are more than 12, take away 12 (it is p.m.). 12 stays 12 (noon). 00 becomes 12 (midnight, a.m.). Keep the minutes.

alternatives.title: Two rings of numbers
text: Picture a clock face with an inner ring 1 to 12 and an outer ring 13 to 24 (13 beside 1, 14 beside 2 …).
The 24-hour number on the outer ring sits next to the 12-hour number on the inner ring.

families.title: Time between two 24-hour times
explanations: subtract-as-number (conceptual): The times were subtracted like ordinary numbers, so 1 hour was exchanged for 100 minutes. An hour has only 60 minutes: when you regroup, change 1 hour into 60 minutes.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): The smaller number of minutes was taken from the larger one; when the end minutes are fewer, change 1 hour into 60 minutes first.
hours-only (procedural): Only the hours were counted and the minutes were left out.

teach.idea: Time is counted in sixties: 60 minutes make 1 hour. So when you take away times and need to regroup, 1 hour is exchanged for 60 minutes, not 100.
teach.method: Count on from the start to the next full hour, then the full hours, then the minutes to the end time, and add them up.

alternatives.title: Count on in jumps
text: Jump from the start time to the next o'clock (for example 09:45 → 10:00 is 15 minutes).
Jump whole hours to the last o'clock before the end, then jump the leftover minutes. Add the jumps.

families.title: Area of a rectangle by counting unit squares
explanations: perimeter (conceptual): The edges round the outside were counted; that is the perimeter. Area counts the squares that cover the inside.
border-only (procedural): Only the squares along the border were counted; the squares in the middle are part of the area too.
add-sides (conceptual): The rows and the columns were added (10 + 12); there are 10 rows of 12 squares, so multiply.

teach.idea: Area is how much flat space a shape covers. We measure it by counting how many unit squares cover it with no gaps and no overlaps.
teach.method: Count the squares in one row, then count the rows. Equal rows can be counted by multiplying: rows × squares in each row.

alternatives.title: See the rows as an array
text: The squares sit in equal rows, like chairs in a hall.
Skip-count one row at a time: 6, 12, 18, … until every row is counted.

families.title: Choosing area or perimeter in a problem
explanations: perimeter-for-area (conceptual): The perimeter was found, but covering the inside needs the area (how many squares fit inside).
two-sides (procedural): Only one length and one width were added (14 + 16). Going round passes all four sides.
area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The area was found, but going round the edge needs the perimeter (the length all the way round).

teach.idea: Area is the space inside a shape (how many unit squares cover it). Perimeter is the distance all the way round its edge.
teach.method: Ask: am I covering the inside (area: multiply length × width) or going round the edge (perimeter: add all four sides)?

alternatives.title: Act it out
text: Covering a floor: you lay tiles all over it, so you count squares (area).
Fencing a garden: you walk round the edge, so you add lengths (perimeter).

families.title: Adding and subtracting measures in two units
explanations: no-regroup (conceptual): 1900 mL was left as it is; 1000 mL make 1 L, so change 1000 of them into 1 L.
carry-lost (procedural): 1000 mL were taken away, but the 1 L they make was not added to the L.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): 450 − 950 cannot be done, so 450 was taken from 950; instead, change 1 L into 1000 mL first.
borrow-not-taken (procedural): 1 L was changed into 1000 mL, but the L were not made 1 less.
borrow-100 (conceptual): 1 L was changed into 100 mL; 1 L = 1000 mL.

teach.idea: Measures in two units work like tens and ones, but the change-over is 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 g = 1 kg and 1000 mL = 1 L.
teach.method: Add or subtract the small units first. If the small units reach the change-over number, change them into 1 large unit; if there are too few to subtract, change 1 large unit into small units. Then do the large units.

alternatives.title: Change everything into the small unit
text: Write both measures in the small unit only (for example 2 m 45 cm = 245 cm).
Add or subtract these numbers, then change the answer back (310 cm = 3 m 10 cm).

families.title: Multiplying a measure in two units
explanations: no-regroup (conceptual): 5400 mL was left as it is; every 1000 mL make 1 L.
big-only (procedural): Only the L were multiplied; the mL must be multiplied by 6 too.
carry-lost (procedural): The extra mL were changed into L but those L were not added on.

teach.idea: Multiplying a measure is repeated adding: multiply the small units and the large units, then change extra small units into large ones.
teach.method: Multiply the small units; take out every full 100 cm (or 1000 g, 1000 mL) as a large unit. Multiply the large units and add the ones you took out.

alternatives.title: Work in the small unit
text: Change the measure into the small unit only (1 kg 250 g = 1250 g).
Multiply, then change back: 3 × 1250 g = 3750 g = 3 kg 750 g.

families.title: Changing a measure into the smaller unit
explanations: wrong-factor (recall): 1 g was taken as 100 mg; 1 g = 1000 mg.
added (conceptual): The two numbers were simply added; first change the large units into small units.
write-side-by-side (conceptual): The two numbers were written side by side; 75 m needs 3 places, so empty places are filled with zeros.

teach.idea: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 L = 1000 mL and 1 km = 1000 m. A measure in two units is the large part changed into small units, plus the small part.
teach.method: Multiply the large units by 100 or 1000, then add the small units. Check the small part fills its places: 3 kg 25 g = 3000 g + 25 g = 3025 g.

alternatives.title: Use a place-value chart
text: Write the large units in the thousands place (for g, mL, m) or hundreds place (for cm).
Write the small units ending in the ones place, and fill any empty places with 0.

families.title: How many parts make a kilogram or a litre
explanations: hundred (recall): 1 L was taken as 100 mL; 1 L = 1000 mL.
one-only (procedural): The parts in only 1 L were found; there are 9 of them.
times-n (conceptual): 9 and the number of parts in 1 L were added instead of multiplied.

teach.idea: 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 L = 1000 mL. Two 500 g packets make 1 kg, four 250 g packets make 1 kg, and so on.
teach.method: Find how many parts make 1 kg (or 1 L): 1000 ÷ the part. Then multiply by the number of kilograms (or litres).

alternatives.title: Skip-count to 1000
text: Count up in parts: 250, 500, 750, 1000 — that is 4 parts in 1 kg.
Each extra kilogram needs the same number of parts again.

families.title: Writing ones, tenths and hundredths as a decimal
explanations: places-swapped (conceptual): The tenths and hundredths were put in each other's places: the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths.
cubes-as-tenths (conceptual): The small cubes were counted as tenths too; a small cube is ten times smaller than a rod.
whole-number (conceptual): All the pieces were counted as whole ones; only the flats are wholes.
zero-tenths-dropped (conceptual): The zero tenths were left out, so the hundredths moved into the tenths place; write 0 in the tenths place to keep it.

teach.idea: Splitting 1 whole into 10 equal parts gives tenths; splitting each tenth into 10 gives hundredths. After the decimal point, the first place is tenths and the second is hundredths.
teach.method: Write the wholes, then the point, then the number of tenths, then the number of hundredths. Use 0 for an empty place.

alternatives.title: Shade a hundred grid
text: A grid of 100 squares is 1 whole: one row (10 squares) is a tenth, one square is a hundredth.
Shade the rows for the tenths and single squares for the hundredths; 3 rows and 4 squares is 34 hundredths, 0.34.

families.title: Comparing a tenths decimal with a hundredths decimal
explanations: longer-is-larger (conceptual): 3.39 was taken as greater because 39 is more than 9; compare the tenths first: 9 tenths are more than 3 tenths.
shorter-is-larger (conceptual): 3.6 was taken as greater because hundredths are small pieces; but 3.89 has more tenths (8 against 6).

teach.idea: Decimals are compared place by place from the left, like whole numbers: first the wholes, then the tenths, then the hundredths. More digits does not mean bigger.
teach.method: Write both with the same number of places (0.7 = 0.70) and compare them as hundredths: 70 hundredths is more than 65 hundredths.

alternatives.title: Think of rupees
text: ₹0.70 is 70 paise and ₹0.65 is 65 paise.
70 paise is more, so 0.7 is greater than 0.65.

families.title: Picking out the even numbers
explanations: first-digit (conceptual): The first digit was looked at; whether a number is even depends only on its ones digit (the last digit).
zero-not-even (conceptual): Numbers ending in 0 were left out; 0 is even (0 things can be shared into pairs with none left over), so 10, 20, 30 … are even.
odd-for-even (recall): The odd numbers were picked; even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

teach.idea: An even number of things can be put into pairs with none left over; an odd number always leaves one. Tens and hundreds always pair up, so only the ones digit decides.
teach.method: Look at the last digit: 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 means even; 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 means odd.

alternatives.title: Make pairs
text: Draw dots for the ones digit and join them in pairs.
If every dot has a partner the number is even; if one dot is left alone it is odd.

families.title: Writing a number in lakhs and thousands in figures
explanations: no-zeros (conceptual): The numbers heard were written one after another, without zeros for the empty places; each period has a fixed number of places (lakhs, then 2 for thousands, then 3 for hundreds, tens and ones).
lakh-as-ten-thousand (recall): A lakh was written like ten thousand, so the 9 went into the ten-thousands place; 1 lakh = 100 thousand = 1,00,000 (six digits).

teach.idea: In the Indian system the places are grouped as ones–tens–hundreds, then thousands–ten thousands, then lakhs–ten lakhs. Every place gets a digit, so empty places get 0.
teach.method: Draw a place-value chart (L, TTh, Th, H, T, O). Write each part in its own places, fill empty places with 0, then put commas: 4,07,052.

alternatives.title: Fill the periods
text: Write three boxes for hundreds-tens-ones, two boxes for thousands, and one or two for lakhs.
Fill each period from its right, and put 0 in any empty box.

families.title: Putting large numbers in ascending order
explanations: first-digit-only (conceptual): The numbers were compared by their first digits only; a number with fewer digits is always smaller, so count the digits first.
descending (procedural): The list was written from greatest to smallest; ascending means smallest first.

teach.idea: A number with more digits is bigger. When two numbers have the same number of digits, the first place where their digits differ decides.
teach.method: First sort by how many digits each number has. Then, for numbers with the same number of digits, compare ten thousands, then thousands, then hundreds … until the digits differ.

alternatives.title: Line them up in a place-value chart
text: Write each number in a place-value chart so the ones are in one column.
Read down the chart from the left: the first column where the digits differ shows which number is bigger.

families.title: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000
explanations: zeros-short (procedural): Too few zeros were taken off: ÷ 1000 takes 3 zeros off the end.
zeros-extra (procedural): Too many zeros were taken off: ÷ 1000 takes off only 3 zeros.
added (conceptual): 1000 was added instead of multiplied.
subtracted (conceptual): 1000 was subtracted instead of divided.

teach.idea: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much, so each digit moves one place to the left and a 0 fills the ones place. Dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right.
teach.method: × 10, × 100, × 1000: write 1, 2 or 3 zeros on the end. ÷ 10, ÷ 100, ÷ 1000 (of a number ending in enough zeros): take 1, 2 or 3 zeros off the end.

alternatives.title: Swap each block for a bigger one
text: × 10 changes every one into a ten, every ten into a hundred, every hundred into a thousand.
So 34 (3 tens, 4 ones) × 10 is 3 hundreds and 4 tens: 340.

families.title: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 or 100
explanations: zeros-forgotten (procedural): 99 × 9 was found but the zeros of 900 were not put back on the end.
zeros-extra (procedural): One zero too many was put on the end; 900 has two zeros.
tens-only (procedural): Only the tens digit of 99 was multiplied; the ones digit must be multiplied too.

teach.idea: Multiplying by 40 is multiplying by 4 and then by 10, because 40 = 4 × 10.
teach.method: Multiply by the non-zero digit first, then put the zeros of the multiplier on the end of the answer.

alternatives.title: Split the two-digit number
text: Break the two-digit number into tens and ones: 23 × 40 = 20 × 40 + 3 × 40.

families.title: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
explanations: always-down (conceptual): The digits after the thousands were just changed to zeros; when the next digit is 5 or more, round up.
always-up (conceptual): The number was rounded up, but the next digit is less than 5, so it is nearer to 9,000.
wrong-place (procedural): The number was rounded to the wrong place (to the nearest hundred instead of the nearest thousand).

teach.idea: Rounding finds the nearest 'round' number: on a number line, which ten (hundred, thousand) is the number closer to? A number exactly halfway is rounded up.
teach.method: Look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 0–4, round down (keep the place, zeros after). If it is 5–9, round up (add 1 to the place, zeros after).

alternatives.title: The rounding hill
text: Picture the numbers from one ten to the next as a hill, with the halfway number at the top.
A number before the top rolls back down to the lower ten; at the top or after it, it rolls on to the higher ten.

families.title: Estimating a sum or difference by rounding
explanations: exact (procedural): The exact answer was worked out; an estimate rounds the numbers first so it can be done in your head.
round-down (conceptual): Both numbers were rounded down (digits just cut off); round up when the next digit is 5 or more.
round-answer (procedural): The exact answer was rounded at the end; the question asks you to round each number first.

teach.idea: An estimate is a quick, close answer. Rounding each number to a ten or hundred first makes the sum or difference easy to do in your head, and it tells you if an exact answer is sensible.
teach.method: Round each number to the place asked for, then add or subtract the rounded numbers.

alternatives.title: Use the estimate as a check
text: Work the exact answer, then compare it with the estimate.
If they are far apart, look again for a mistake in the exact working.

families.title: Shopping: total cost and change
explanations: no-multiply (procedural): The price of one of each item was used; the prices must be multiplied by how many were bought.
total-not-change (procedural): The total cost was given; the question asks for the change, so take the total away from the note.
one-item (procedural): Only the first item was paid for; add the cost of both kinds of item before finding the change.

teach.idea: A multi-step problem is a chain of small questions: what does each kind of item cost, what is the whole bill, and what is left from the note.
teach.method: Multiply to find the cost of each kind of item, add the costs to get the bill, then subtract the bill from the money paid.

alternatives.title: Count up like a shopkeeper
text: After finding the bill, count up from the bill to the note: ₹265 → ₹270 → ₹300 → ₹500.
Add the jumps: 5 + 30 + 200 = ₹235 change.

families.title: Water lost from a dripping tap
explanations: hours-as-minutes (conceptual): The hours were used as if they were minutes; 12 hours are 720 minutes.
hundred-minutes (recall): An hour was taken as 100 minutes; 1 hour = 60 minutes.
one-hour (procedural): Only the water for 1 hour was found; multiply by 12 for all the hours.

teach.idea: When something happens at the same rate every minute, the total is the amount each minute times the number of minutes. Hours must be changed into minutes first.
teach.method: Change the hours into minutes (× 60), then multiply by the millilitres lost each minute.

alternatives.title: One hour first
text: Find the water lost in one hour: 60 × the millilitres each minute.
Then add that amount once for every hour (or multiply by the number of hours).

families.title: Spotting right angles in pictures and objects
explanations: corner-reversed (conceptual): The paper-corner test was read the wrong way round: if the angle fits inside the square corner it is smaller; if the square corner fits inside the angle it is bigger.
nearly-square (conceptual): The angle at a corner of a samosa is not far from a square corner, but a folded-paper right angle would not fit it exactly.
looks-big (conceptual): The square corner was judged by eye as a little too wide; a right angle fits the folded-paper corner exactly, with no gap on either side.
straight-as-right (conceptual): A flat, straight angle (an open book lying flat) was taken for a right angle; a right angle is only half of a straight angle.

teach.idea: A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a page: a quarter of a full turn. Folding a paper twice makes a right-angle tester.
teach.method: Hold the folded corner in the angle with one edge along one arm. If the other arm lies along the other edge, it is a right angle; if the angle fits inside the corner it is smaller; if the corner fits inside the angle it is bigger.

alternatives.title: A quarter turn on a clock
text: The hands of a clock at 3 o'clock make a right angle: the minute hand at 12, the hour hand a quarter of the way round.
Fewer than 3 hours apart is smaller than a right angle; more (up to 6) is bigger.

families.title: Classifying angles, including reflex angles
explanations: acute-obtuse-swap (recall): The names were mixed up: an angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse; acute is smaller than 90°.
upright-as-straight (recall): An arm standing straight up was taken for a straight angle; a straight angle is a flat line (180°), and a square corner is a right angle.
big-is-reflex (conceptual): Every angle bigger than a right angle was called reflex; a reflex angle is bigger than a straight angle (more than 180°).
biggest-bent (conceptual): A straight angle is not obtuse: its two arms make one straight line, exactly 180°.
inner-angle (conceptual): The smaller angle between the arms (360° − 355° = 5°) was named; the angle meant goes the long way round, so it is more than 180°: a reflex angle.

teach.idea: Angles are named by comparing them with a right angle (90°) and a straight angle (180°): acute < 90° < obtuse < 180° < reflex < 360°.
teach.method: Look at how far the arc turns. Less than a square corner: acute; a square corner: right; less than a straight line: obtuse; a straight line: straight; more than a straight line: reflex.

alternatives.title: Every pair of arms makes two angles
text: Two arms from one point make two angles that add up to 360°: one the short way round and one the long way round.
If the short one is 120°, the long one is 240° — a reflex angle. The shading shows which one is meant.

families.title: The vertex and arms of an angle, and comparing angles by turning
explanations: first-letter (conceptual): The first letter was taken as the vertex, so the arms were drawn from the wrong point; both arms start at the middle letter.
join-ends (conceptual): The segment joining the two outer points was taken as an arm; the arms are the two rays that start at the vertex.
longer-arms (conceptual): ∠Y was taken as bigger because its arms are longer; the size of an angle is the amount of turn between the arms, not how long the arms are drawn.

teach.idea: An angle is made by two rays (its arms) starting from one point (its vertex). Its size is the amount of turn from one arm to the other.
teach.method: In ∠ABC the middle letter B is the vertex and the arms are BA and BC. To compare two angles, put one on the other with vertices and one arm together: the one whose second arm turns further is bigger.

alternatives.title: Trace and lay on top
text: Trace one angle on thin paper and lay it on the other, vertex on vertex and one arm along one arm.
If the traced second arm lies inside the other angle, the traced angle is smaller — however long the arms are.

families.title: Naming the parts of a circle
explanations: centre-radius (recall): The centre is a point; the radius is the distance (or segment) from the centre to the circle.
radius-diameter (conceptual): A radius and a diameter were mixed up: a segment across the whole circle through the centre is a diameter (two radii).
chord-as-diameter (conceptual): Every segment across the circle was called a diameter; a diameter must pass through the centre, and this one does not.
arc-chord (conceptual): The curved piece was called a chord; a chord is the straight segment joining the two points, the curved piece is an arc.
sector-segment (conceptual): Sector and segment were mixed up: a region cut off by a chord is a segment; a sector is cut off by two radii.

teach.idea: Every point of a circle is the same distance from the centre. A radius joins the centre to the circle; a chord joins two points of the circle, and the chord through the centre is a diameter. An arc is a piece of the circle itself.
teach.method: Ask: is it a point, a straight segment, a curved piece or a region? For a segment, where do its ends lie and does it pass through the centre? For a region, is it cut off by two radii (sector) or by a chord (segment)?

alternatives.title: Think of food
text: A slice of a round cake, cut from the middle, is a sector.
Cutting a straight line across a chapati, not through the middle, cuts off a segment; the cut itself is a chord.

families.title: Counting the lines of symmetry of a design or a shape
explanations: diagonals-missed (procedural): Only the up-and-down and across lines were counted; a square also folds along both diagonals.
looks-balanced (conceptual): The design was counted as symmetric because it looks balanced; a fold line works only when every shaded square lands on a shaded square.
one-line (conceptual): Only the up-and-down line was found; a regular shape has a line of symmetry through every corner.
diagonals-counted (conceptual): The diagonals were counted as fold lines; folding along a diagonal of this shape does not make the two halves match.
two-ways (procedural): A second fold line (across) was counted; for this shape only the up-and-down fold makes the halves match.
half-turn (conceptual): A parallelogram looks the same after a half turn, but that is not a fold: no fold line makes its halves match.
corners-only (procedural): Only the lines through opposite corners were counted; lines through the middles of opposite sides are lines of symmetry too.
any-shape (conceptual): A fold was taken to work for this triangle, but with three different sides (or two different shorter sides) no fold makes the halves match.

teach.idea: A line of symmetry is a fold line where one half lands exactly on the other. A shape can have none, one, or several.
teach.method: Try each possible fold: up and down, across, and along the diagonals (and, for regular shapes, through every corner and every side's middle). Count only the folds where every part matches.

alternatives.title: Use a mirror
text: Stand a small mirror on the line you are testing.
If the half you see plus its reflection looks exactly like the whole design, the line is a line of symmetry.

families.title: Lines of symmetry in digits and numbers
explanations: axis-swap (conceptual): The numbers were folded the other way (down the middle); a horizontal line goes across, so the top half must land on the bottom half.
digit-by-digit (conceptual): Each digit was checked on its own, but folding a whole number down its middle also swaps the order of the digits: 80 folds onto 08, which is different.

teach.idea: On a digital clock each digit is made of straight bars. Some digits, like 8 and 0, match when folded either way; 3 matches only when folded across.
teach.method: For a fold across, check each digit's top and bottom halves. For a fold down the middle of a whole number, the left end must match the right end: read the mirrored digits in reverse order and see if you get the same number.

alternatives.title: Hold a mirror
text: Stand a mirror along the middle of the number (across or up and down).
If the half on paper and its reflection together show the same number, that line is a line of symmetry.

families.title: Which word looks the same in a mirror
explanations: palindrome-only (conceptual): NUN reads the same backwards, but its letters themselves flip in a mirror (N look different), so it does not look the same.
letters-only (conceptual): Each letter of WITH looks the same in a mirror, but a mirror beside the word also reverses the order of the letters: it shows HTIW.
side-rule (conceptual): The rule for a mirror standing beside the word was used; water below flips each letter top to bottom and keeps the order, and T, U look different upside down.
one-letter (procedural): Not every letter of HIDES was checked: S looks different when flipped top to bottom.

teach.idea: A mirror standing beside a word flips it left to right: the letters come in the reverse order and each letter is flipped. Water below flips it top to bottom: the order stays, but each letter is turned upside down.
teach.method: For a mirror beside the word: every letter must have an up-and-down line of symmetry AND the word must read the same backwards. For water below: every letter must have an across line of symmetry.

alternatives.title: Try it with a mirror
text: Write the word in big capitals and hold a mirror beside it, then below it.
Read what the mirror shows, letter by letter, and compare it with the card.

families.title: Even or odd by putting things in pairs
explanations: tens-digit (conceptual): The tens digit (5) was looked at; tens always pair up, so only the ones (or the counter left over) decide.

teach.idea: An even number of things can be put into pairs with none left over. An odd number always leaves exactly one without a partner.
teach.method: Join the things two by two (a full ten frame is 5 pairs: each counter in the top row with the one below it). If every one has a partner, the number is even; if one is left over, it is odd.

alternatives.title: Check with the last digit
text: Count them and look at the ones digit.
0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 means even; 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 means odd — the same answer as pairing.

families.title: Patterns in reverse-and-add sums and in the addition chart
explanations: no-carry (procedural): The ones (8 + 9 = 17) were added but the ten was not carried.
doubled (procedural): 98 was doubled; the second number is 98 with its digits reversed, 89.
count-start (procedural): The starting number was counted as a step; count only the reverse-and-add steps.
stop-early (procedural): The count stopped too early: keep going until the sum itself reads the same both ways.
half-of-eleven (conceptual): Even and odd sums take turns, but 11 sums cannot split equally: starting with 20 (even), there is one more even sum than odd.
row-zero-missed (procedural): Row 0 (or column 0) was left out; 0 + a number is a cell of the chart too.
diagonal-length (conceptual): The cells with the same sum lie on a slanting line; past 10 that line gets shorter again, because rows and columns stop at 10.

teach.idea: Addition makes patterns: the sums in an addition chart grow by 1 to the right and down, the same sum lies along a slanting line, and a two-digit number plus its reverse is always 11 × (sum of its digits).
teach.method: Work out a few cases, look for what repeats, then use the rule: even and odd sums alternate along a row, and ab + ba = 11 × (a + b).

alternatives.title: Colour the chart
text: Draw a small addition chart and colour the even sums.
The colours make a chessboard pattern, and equal sums run in slanting lines from top-right to bottom-left.

families.title: Sums of consecutive numbers
explanations: k-times-start (procedural): 6 × 40 was found, but each number after the first is 1, 2, 3 … more than 40.
first-last (procedural): Only the first and last numbers were added; all the numbers in between belong to the sum too.
middle-given (procedural): The sum ÷ 5 gives the middle number; the smallest is 2 less.
largest-given (procedural): The largest of the numbers was given; the question asks for the smallest.

teach.idea: In a run of consecutive numbers, the middle number is the average: 3 consecutive numbers add up to 3 × the middle one. The first and last together make the same total as the second and second-last.
teach.method: To add them: number of terms × (first + last) ÷ 2. To find them from the sum (an odd number of them): sum ÷ how many = the middle; count back to the smallest.

alternatives.title: Make a staircase
text: Draw the numbers as towers of blocks: each tower is one block taller than the last.
Move blocks from the tall end to the short end: all towers become as tall as the middle one.

families.title: Number names, commas and expanded forms of large numbers
explanations: zero-dropped (conceptual): A zero was skipped, so the digits after it moved into the wrong places; a 0 holds its place even though it is not said aloud.
extra-place (procedural): The digits were read one place too high (an extra place was counted); count the places from the ones.

international-commas (conceptual): The commas were placed every three digits, as in the International system; in the Indian system the first comma is after three digits from the right, then after every two.
from-left (procedural): The commas were counted from the left; periods are always counted from the right, starting with the ones.
indian-commas (conceptual): The commas were placed as in the Indian system (3, then 2s); the International system groups every three digits from the right.

teach.idea: Digits are grouped into periods from the right. Indian system: ones (3 digits), thousands (2), lakhs (2), crores. International system: ones, thousands, millions, each 3 digits.
teach.method: Starting from the right, mark off three digits, then twos (Indian) or threes (International). Read each period with its name; a zero keeps its place even when it is not said.

alternatives.title: Use a place-value chart
text: Write the number in a chart with the periods labelled (Cr, L, Th, ones).
Read the number in each period followed by the period's name, left to right.

families.title: Rounding large numbers in real situations
explanations: too-fine (procedural): The number was rounded to a smaller place than asked (ten lakhs instead of crores).
wrong-place (procedural): The number was rounded to the wrong place (the nearest ten crore instead of the nearest crore).
always-down (conceptual): The digits after the crores place were just changed to zeros; when the next digit is 5 or more, round up.

teach.idea: Large numbers in news and plans are usually rounded: 4,37,862 people is 'about 4,40,000' to the nearest ten thousand. Rounding finds the nearer of the two round numbers on either side.
teach.method: Find the place you round to, look at the digit just to its right: 0–4 keep the place and write zeros after it; 5–9 add 1 to the place and write zeros after it.

alternatives.title: Which two round numbers?
text: Write the round number just below and just above (for example 4,30,000 and 4,40,000).
The halfway number is 4,35,000; the number is past halfway, so it rounds up.

families.title: Estimating a product by rounding
explanations: exact (procedural): The exact product was worked out; an estimate rounds the numbers first so it can be done in your head.
round-down (conceptual): Both numbers were rounded down (the digits just cut off); round up when the next digit is 5 or more.
one-only (procedural): Only 969 was rounded; round both numbers before multiplying.
zeros (procedural): 10 × 3 was found, but the zeros of 1000 and 30 were not all put back.

teach.idea: Rounding both numbers turns a hard product into an easy one (48 × 32 ≈ 50 × 30). The estimate shows roughly how big the exact answer must be.
teach.method: Round each number as asked, multiply the non-zero digits, then put back all the zeros of both rounded numbers.

alternatives.title: Think of a rectangle
text: A product is the area of a rectangle. Rounding the sides a little changes the area only a little.
50 by 30 is easy to picture: 15 hundreds.

families.title: Judging answers with an estimate
explanations: not-equal (conceptual): The answer was thought wrong because it is not exactly the estimate; an estimate only has to be close.
trust-working (procedural): The worked answer was trusted without comparing it with the estimate; it is many times too small, so there must be a mistake (often a digit put in the wrong column).

big-means-exact (conceptual): A large or important-sounding number was taken to need an exact answer; an estimate is enough when only the rough size matters (news, planning), but money handed over and doses must be exact.
zeros-short (procedural): A zero was lost when multiplying the rounded numbers; put back all the zeros of both.
zeros-extra (procedural): One zero too many was put on; count the zeros of both rounded numbers.

teach.idea: An estimate is a quick, nearly-right answer. It tells you how big an exact answer should be, so a worked answer far from it must have a mistake. Some situations (giving change, a medicine dose) need exact answers; others (a crowd, a distance for planning) need only an estimate.
teach.method: Round each number (to the nearest ten or hundred), work out the estimate in your head, and compare. Close: reasonable. Many times bigger or smaller: check the working.

alternatives.title: Look for a column slip
text: If an answer is about ten times too big or too small, a digit was probably written in the wrong column.
Line the numbers up by their ones digits and work it again.

families.title: Rounding a decimal to a whole number, tenths or hundredths
explanations: cut-off (conceptual): The digits after the place were simply dropped; when the next digit is 5 or more, the place goes up by 1.
wrong-place (procedural): The number was rounded to the tenths instead of the hundredths: the first place after the point is tenths, the second hundredths.

teach.idea: Rounding a decimal works like rounding whole numbers: find which of the two numbers on either side, at the place asked for, it is nearer to.
teach.method: Find the place you round to. Look at the digit just to its right: 0–4 keep the place and drop the digits after it; 5–9 add 1 to the place and drop the digits after it.

alternatives.title: Think of rupees and paise
text: ₹23.47 to the nearest rupee: is it nearer ₹23 or ₹24? 47 paise is less than 50, so ₹23.
To the nearest tenth (10 paise): ₹23.47 is between ₹23.40 and ₹23.50, nearer ₹23.50.

families.title: Dividing a measure in two units
explanations: left-over-dropped (conceptual): 39 L ÷ 8 leaves 7 L over; those 7 L must be changed into mL (7000 mL) and shared too.
change-100 (recall): The L left over were changed into 100 mL each; 1 L = 1000 mL.

teach.idea: Dividing a measure shares the large units first; whatever large units are left over are changed into small units and shared with the small units.
teach.method: Divide the large units. Change the ones left over into small units (× 100 or × 1000), add the small units, and divide those. Check: multiply the answer back.

alternatives.title: Work in the small unit
text: Change the whole measure into the small unit (7 m 20 cm = 720 cm).
Divide (720 ÷ 4 = 180 cm) and change back (1 m 80 cm).
