families.title: Changing a measure into the larger unit and what is left
explanations: wrong-factor (recall): 1 g was taken as 100 mg; 1 g = 1000 mg.
left-dropped (procedural): The mg left over were dropped; 18 mg remain after taking out the whole g.

teach.idea: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 g = 1000 mg, 1 L = 1000 mL, 1 km = 1000 m. To change into the larger unit, see how many whole large units fit, and what is left.
teach.method: Divide by 100, 10 or 1000: the whole number of times is the large unit; the remainder is the small unit (3450 g = 3 kg 450 g).

alternatives.title: Split the digits
text: For × 1000 units, the last three digits are the small unit: 3|450 g = 3 kg 450 g; 3|045 g = 3 kg 45 g.
For cm to m, the last two digits; for mm to cm, the last digit.

families.title: Writing a measure as a decimal of the larger unit
explanations: wrong-factor (recall): 1 g was taken as 100 mg; 1 g = 1000 mg.
zero-lost (conceptual): The 18 mg were written straight after the point, but they are thousandths of a g, so they need 3 decimal places: put zeros in the empty places.

teach.idea: A small unit is a fraction of the large unit: 1 g is one thousandth of a kg, so 3450 g = 3450 thousandths of a kg = 3.450 kg = 3.45 kg.
teach.method: Divide by 1000 (or 100, or 10): move the decimal point 3 (or 2, or 1) places to the left, filling empty places with zeros (3045 g = 3.045 kg).

alternatives.title: A place-value chart
text: Write the amount in a chart with kg in the ones column and g in the tenths, hundredths and thousandths columns.
3045 g: 3 in the ones, then 0, 4, 5: 3.045 kg.

families.title: Comparing weights in different units with <, = or >
explanations: side-by-side (conceptual): 6 g 600 mg was read as 6600 mg by writing the numbers side by side; it is 6 × 1000 + 600 = 6600 mg.
bigger-number (conceptual): The numbers were compared without the units (6560 looks bigger than 6 and 600); change both weights into the same unit first.

teach.idea: Weights can be compared only in the same unit: 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 g = 1000 mg.
teach.method: Change the weight in two units into the small unit (2 kg 50 g = 2050 g), then compare the numbers.

alternatives.title: Compare the large units first
text: Change the single amount into large and small units (2500 g = 2 kg 500 g).
Compare kilograms first; only if they are equal, compare the grams.

families.title: Feet, inches and centimetres, and estimating with a known length
explanations: ten-inches (recall): A foot was taken as 10 inches; 1 foot = 12 inches.
inches-as-cm (conceptual): The inches were counted as centimetres; an inch is about 2.5 cm.
foot-12cm (recall): A foot was taken as 12 cm (the number of inches in it); 1 foot is about 30 cm.
added (conceptual): The known length and the number of times were added; 12 of them end to end is 12 × 25 m.

teach.idea: Feet and inches are older units still used for heights: 12 inches make 1 foot, 1 inch is about 2.5 cm and 1 foot about 30 cm. A known length (a door, a step, a bus) can be used as a ruler to estimate bigger lengths.
teach.method: Change feet to cm (× 30) and inches to cm (× 2.5) and add. To estimate with a known length, count how many of it fit and multiply.

alternatives.title: Use your body
text: Your foot is close to a foot long for an adult; a thumb-width is close to an inch.
Your step is about half a metre: 10 steps make about 5 m.

families.title: Converting units with a conversion factor
explanations: factor-upside-down (conceptual): The amount was divided by 88 instead of multiplied; each dollar is worth many rupees, so the number of rupees is bigger.
metres-only (procedural): Only the kilometres and metres were changed; the hours and seconds must be changed too (1 hour = 3600 s).

teach.idea: A conversion factor says how many of one unit make one of the other: 1 inch = 2.54 cm, 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s. Converting is multiplying by the factor, because the amount is proportional.
teach.method: Write the factor as 'new units per old unit' and multiply. Check the direction: going to a smaller unit gives a bigger number.

alternatives.title: Change one unit at a time
text: For speeds, change km into m (× 1000), then per hour into per second (÷ 3600).

families.title: Dividing a multiple of 10, 100 or 1000 by a one-digit number
explanations: zero-lost (procedural): 81 ÷ 9 = 9 was right, but a zero was lost: 81000 is 81 thousands, so the answer is 9 thousands.
extra-zero (procedural): One zero too many was written; 81000 has 3 zeros after 81, and the answer keeps exactly those.
fact-slip (prerequisite): The division fact 81 ÷ 9 is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: 2400 is 24 hundreds, so 2400 ÷ 6 is 24 hundreds ÷ 6 = 4 hundreds = 400.
teach.method: Cover the zeros, divide using the table fact, then put the zeros back on the answer.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Multiply the answer by the divisor: 400 × 6 = 2400.
If you get the number you started with, the division is right.

families.title: A table of quantities and costs with missing values
explanations: missing-left-out (procedural): The cost of the packets of crayons (missing in the table) was left out; work it out first: 2 × ₹25.
price-for-cost (procedural): The price of one packet of crayons was added instead of the cost of all 2.
subtract (conceptual): The price was taken away from the cost; the cost is number × price, so divide.
other-column (procedural): The wrong column was read: the question asks for the number bought.

teach.idea: In each row, cost = how many × price of one. Knowing any two of the three gives the third: multiply for the cost, divide the cost to find the number or the price.
teach.method: Fill each missing value first (multiply or divide in its row), then answer the question, adding the costs for a total.

alternatives.title: One row at a time
text: Cover all rows except one and ask: which of number, price and cost is missing?
Cost missing: multiply. Price or number missing: divide the cost by the other.

families.title: Problems that combine time, distance and money
explanations: hours-times-rate (conceptual): The hours were multiplied by the fare per km; first find the distance (speed × time), then multiply by the fare per km.
speed-times-rate (procedural): Only one hour was paid for (60 km); the taxi travels for 5 hours.
one-way (procedural): Only the trip to the island was counted; the boat must come back too.
km-for-hours (conceptual): The kilometres were paid for as if they were hours; the hire is by the hour, so find the time (distance ÷ speed) first.

teach.idea: Speed links distance and time: distance = speed × time, and time = distance ÷ speed. A charge per km or per hour then turns the distance or the time into money.
teach.method: Decide what the money depends on (km or hours). Find that quantity first from the speed, then multiply by the charge.

alternatives.title: Make a table
text: Write a row for each hour: the km travelled that hour and the money for those km.
Add the rows up, or multiply when every row is the same.

families.title: Multi-step problems with large numbers
explanations: both-added (conceptual): The people who moved away were added; they leave the town, so take them away.
both-taken (conceptual): The babies born were taken away; they join the town, so add them.
one-item (procedural): Only one computer was paid for; 9 computers cost 9 × ₹66,500.
cost-not-left (procedural): The total cost was given; the question asks how much money is left.
one-week (procedural): Only one week was counted; the truck runs for 13 weeks.
added (conceptual): The numbers were added; equal trips every week are counted by multiplying.

teach.idea: Large numbers in real life (people, rupees, kilometres) follow the same rules as small ones: decide what joins (add), what leaves (subtract) and what repeats (multiply).
teach.method: Write the steps in order in words first, then calculate each one, keeping the places lined up. Use Indian commas to read the answer.

alternatives.title: Estimate first
text: Round the numbers and get a rough answer before calculating.
If the exact answer is far from the estimate, check the working.

families.title: An attribute-matching puzzle
explanations: not-read-as-yes (procedural): The clue "Priya does not play the violin." was read as if it said Priya does; a "not" clue only rules Priya out.

teach.idea: In a matching puzzle every person goes with exactly one thing and every thing with exactly one person. Each clue rules out (or fixes) some pairs; when only one choice is left in a row or column, it must be the answer.
teach.method: Draw a 4 × 4 grid (people down, things across). Mark ✗ for each 'does not' clue and ✓ for each 'does' clue (with ✗ for the rest of that row and column). Keep filling until every row has one ✓.

alternatives.title: Try the possibilities
text: Start with the person who has the most ✗: try each thing still possible for them.
If a choice breaks a clue later, go back and try the next one.

families.title: Estimating the area of an irregular shape and comparing two areas
explanations: every-part (conceptual): Every square the leaf touches was counted as 1; squares less than half covered are left out, and half-covered squares count as ½.
full-only (procedural): Only the fully covered squares were counted; squares more than half covered count as 1 and half-covered ones as ½.
half-as-one (procedural): Half-covered squares were counted as whole ones; each counts ½.
total (procedural): The two areas were added; the question asks how many MORE squares the bigger shape covers (the difference).
bigger-only (procedural): Only the bigger shape's squares were counted; take away the smaller shape's squares to find how many more.

teach.idea: Area is the number of unit squares a shape covers. For a curved shape the squares on the edge are only partly covered, so we estimate: more than half counts as a whole square, exactly half as ½, less than half as nothing.
teach.method: Count the full squares, then the more-than-half squares, then the half squares (each ½). Add them. To compare two shapes, count each and subtract.

alternatives.title: Pair up the bits
text: A square that is a bit more than half covered and one a bit less than half covered together make about one whole square.
That is why more than half counts as 1 and less than half as 0: the extras roughly balance out.

families.title: Place value, expanded form and place-value form of decimals with thousandths
explanations: next-place (conceptual): The digit's place was counted one place off; after the point the places are tenths, hundredths, thousandths, so the 9 is in the tenths place.
zero-dropped (conceptual): The 0 in the tenths place was skipped, so the digits after it moved one place to the left; a 0 keeps its place.
tens-ones (recall): The tens and ones digits were swapped; the digit just before the point is the ones.

teach.idea: Each place is ten times the place to its right: tens, ones, then after the point tenths (1/10), hundredths (1/100), thousandths (1/1000). A digit's place value is the digit times its place.
teach.method: Write the number in a place-value chart (T, O . t, h, th). Read each digit with its place; for the expanded form, add the place values of the non-zero digits.

alternatives.title: Think of kilograms and grams
text: 1 g is one thousandth of a kilogram, so 2.305 kg is 2 kg, 3 tenths, 0 hundredths and 5 thousandths.

families.title: Ordering decimals
explanations: longer-is-larger (conceptual): The digits after the point were compared as whole numbers, so more digits looked bigger; compare tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths (0.5 = 0.500 is more than 0.45).
descending (procedural): The decimals were written from greatest to smallest; ascending means smallest first.

teach.idea: Decimals are compared place by place from the left: wholes, then tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. Writing them all with the same number of places (0.5 = 0.500) makes this easy.
teach.method: Fill each number with zeros to three decimal places, then compare them like whole numbers of thousandths: 0.500, 0.450, 0.505, 0.550.

alternatives.title: Place them on a number line
text: Draw a line from the whole number to the next one, marked in tenths.
Put each decimal in its tenth, then decide the order inside the tenth by the hundredths and thousandths.

families.title: Decimals as fractions and fractions as decimals
explanations: place-wrong (conceptual): The last digit of 0.24 is in the hundredths place, so the bottom number is 100.
not-simplified (procedural): 65/100 is equal to 0.65, but it is not in simplest form: divide the top and bottom by their highest common factor.
upside-down (conceptual): The fraction was turned upside down; the decimal's digits go on top and the place value on the bottom.
digits-as-decimal (conceptual): 13/20 was written as 13.20 by putting a point between the top and bottom numbers; a fraction is a division: 13 ÷ 20.

teach.idea: A decimal is a fraction with a bottom number of 10, 100 or 1000: 0.07 = 7/100, 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4. A fraction is a division, so 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
teach.method: Decimal to fraction: write the digits over 10, 100 or 1000 (by the last place) and simplify. Fraction to decimal: make the bottom 10, 100 or 1000 by multiplying, or divide the top by the bottom.

alternatives.title: Use rupees and paise
text: ₹0.25 is 25 paise, a quarter of a rupee: 0.25 = 1/4.
Half a rupee is 50 paise: 1/2 = 0.50 = 0.5.

families.title: Writing a 24-hour time with a.m. or p.m.
explanations: am-pm-swap (conceptual): Times after 12 noon are p.m.; a.m. is for times between midnight and noon.
zero-hour (conceptual): A 12-hour clock has no 0; the hour after midnight and the hour after noon are both shown as 12.
kept-24 (conceptual): The 24-hour number was kept; a 12-hour clock only goes up to 12, so 23 hours is 11 o'clock in the afternoon or evening.
minus-ten (procedural): 10 was taken away instead of 12.

teach.idea: a.m. means before noon (from midnight to 12 noon); p.m. means after noon (from 12 noon to midnight). 12 a.m. is midnight and 12 p.m. is noon.
teach.method: If the 24-hour hour is 0 to 11 it is a.m. (00 becomes 12). If it is 12 to 23 it is p.m.: take away 12 from 13 to 23 (12 stays 12).

alternatives.title: Think of your day
text: Waking up and the school assembly are in the morning: a.m.
Lunch after 12, playtime in the evening and dinner are p.m.

families.title: The HCF by repeated division, step by step
explanations: last-not-counted (procedural): The last division, the one that leaves remainder 0, was not counted; it is still a division (and it shows the HCF divides exactly).
hcf-given (procedural): The HCF was given; the question asks how many divisions were needed to reach it.
first-remainder (procedural): The remainder of the first division (240 ÷ 23) was given; the second division is 23 ÷ 10.
quotient (procedural): The quotient of 23 ÷ 10 was given instead of its remainder.

teach.idea: Any number that divides both a and b also divides the remainder of a ÷ b. So the HCF does not change when (a, b) is replaced by (b, remainder), and the numbers shrink until the remainder is 0: the last divisor is the HCF.
teach.method: Divide the larger by the smaller; then divide the divisor by the remainder; repeat until the remainder is 0. The last non-zero remainder is the HCF.

alternatives.title: Why Fibonacci numbers take longest
text: For two neighbouring Virahanka–Fibonacci numbers, every division has quotient 1 and the remainders are the earlier Fibonacci numbers: 89, 55, 34, 21, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2, 1.
So neighbouring Fibonacci numbers need more divisions than any smaller pair, and their HCF is always 1.

families.title: Adding two-digit numbers without regrouping, and totals up to 200
explanations: tens-ones-mixed (conceptual): The tens digit of one number was added to the ones digit of the other; line up tens under tens and ones under ones.
hundred-lost (conceptual): The tens added up to 10 or more, but the new hundred was not written; 10 tens make 1 hundred.
no-regroup (prerequisite): The ten made by the ones (3 + 7 = 10) was not carried to the tens.

teach.idea: Adding tens to tens and ones to ones works because each digit counts a different place. When the ones stay under 10, nothing needs to be regrouped.
teach.method: Split both numbers into tens and ones, add the tens, add the ones, and put them together. On a number line, jump the tens first, then the ones.

alternatives.title: Use base-ten blocks
text: Show each number with tens rods and ones cubes.
Push the rods together and the cubes together, then count: rods first (by tens), then cubes.

families.title: Adding three-digit numbers without regrouping
explanations: one-column (procedural): The ones column was copied from the first number without adding; add every column.
misaligned (conceptual): 11 was written under the hundreds and tens of 846; line up the ones digits first: 11 has no hundreds.

teach.idea: In column addition each column counts one place: ones, tens, hundreds. When no column adds up to 10 or more, each column's sum is simply written below it.
teach.method: Line up the ones digits. Add the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds, writing each sum under its column.

alternatives.title: Split into places
text: Write each number as hundreds + tens + ones: 342 = 300 + 40 + 2.
Add the hundreds, the tens and the ones separately and put them together.

families.title: Adding and subtracting four- and five-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: no-carry (prerequisite): The tens made in a column were not carried to the next column; 10 ones make a ten, 10 tens a hundred, and so on.
smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In some columns the smaller digit was taken from the larger one; when the top digit is smaller, regroup 1 from the next column first.
regroup-not-reduced (procedural): A column was regrouped, but the digit it was taken from was not made 1 less.

teach.idea: Large numbers are added and subtracted column by column, exactly as with small ones. Ten in any place makes one of the next place (and one of a place can be broken into ten of the place to its right).
teach.method: Write the numbers with the ones lined up. Start at the ones: carry (when adding) or regroup (when subtracting) as needed, then move one column left at a time.

alternatives.title: Check with the inverse
text: After adding, subtract one number from the answer: you should get the other.
After subtracting, add the answer to the smaller number: you should get the larger.

families.title: Solving an inequation over whole numbers, natural numbers or integers
explanations: boundary-included (procedural): With < the boundary x = −2 is not included: it makes both sides equal, not smaller.
zero-left-out (recall): 0 was left out; the whole numbers start at 0 (the natural numbers start at 1).
boundary-left-out (procedural): ≤ includes the boundary: x = −3 makes both sides equal, so it is in the solution set.
zero-put-in (recall): 0 was put in; the natural numbers start at 1.
sign-kept (conceptual): Both sides were divided by −1, a negative number, without reversing the sign.

teach.idea: An inequation has many solutions. When x must be a whole number, natural number or integer, the solution set is the list of those numbers on the right side of the boundary.
teach.method: Solve it like an equation to find the boundary (reverse the sign if you divide by a negative number). Then list the allowed numbers on the correct side; include the boundary only for ≤ or ≥. Show them as dots on a number line.

alternatives.title: Try each number
text: Put x = 0, 1, 2, … (or −5 to 5) into the inequation one by one.
Keep each number that makes it true; stop when they stop working.

families.title: Solving a system of two linear inequalities
explanations: sign-kept (conceptual): In the second inequality both sides were divided by −4 without reversing the sign, giving x ≥ 16 instead of x ≤ 16.
union (conceptual): The two solution sets were joined (or) instead of overlapped (and); a system needs x to satisfy both inequalities at once.
ends (procedural): The ends were included or left out wrongly: > and < leave the end out (round bracket); ≥ and ≤ include it (square bracket).

teach.idea: A system of inequalities in one variable asks for the numbers that satisfy every inequality at the same time: the overlap (intersection) of their solution sets.
teach.method: Solve each inequality on its own (reverse the sign when dividing by a negative number). Draw both on one number line and take the part covered by both; use [ ] for ≤ or ≥ and ( ) for < or >.

alternatives.title: Test a point in each part
text: The two boundaries cut the number line into three parts.
Try one number from each part in both inequalities: the part where both are true is the answer.

families.title: Modelling a word problem with a linear inequality
explanations: average-as-mark (conceptual): The required average (85) was used as the mark needed; the three marks together must be at least 3 × 85 = 255.
no-cap (procedural): The upper limit was left out; a test is out of 100, so x ≤ 100 as well.
fixed-ignored (procedural): The bus cost (₹1000) was left out of the total; it is paid whatever the number of students.
wrong-way (conceptual): 'At most' means the cost is less than or equal to the limit, so x ≤ the boundary, not x ≥.
no-32 (procedural): The + 32 in F = 9C/5 + 32 was left out.
upside-down (conceptual): The fraction was used upside down (5/9 instead of 9/5).

teach.idea: Words like 'at least', 'at most', 'no more than' and 'between' describe inequalities. Turning them into symbols and solving gives the whole range of answers that work.
teach.method: Name the unknown, write the condition with ≥, ≤, < or >, solve it like an equation (reversing the sign if you divide by a negative), then check that the answer makes sense in the story (marks up to 100, numbers of people not negative).

alternatives.title: A table of key words
text: at least → ≥; at most, no more than → ≤; more than → >; less than → <.
'between A and B, both included' → A ≤ x ≤ B.

families.title: Neighbourhoods of a point in interval notation
explanations: sign-of-centre (conceptual): |x − 10| is the distance from x to 10, not to −10.
brackets (procedural): ≤ includes the ends: square brackets.
one-side (conceptual): Only one side of 10 was taken; the distance 9 can be on either side, so the set runs from 1 to 19.
inside (conceptual): |x − a| > 9 means x is MORE than 9 away from 10: outside the interval, on both sides.

teach.idea: |x − a| is the distance from x to a on the number line. The δ-neighbourhood of a is every x less than δ away from a: the open interval (a − δ, a + δ).
teach.method: Mark a on the number line and go δ to the left and δ to the right. Less than δ: the open interval between; at most δ: include the ends; more than δ: the two outside pieces.

alternatives.title: Unfold the absolute value
text: |x − a| < δ means −δ < x − a < δ.
Add a to all three parts: a − δ < x < a + δ.

families.title: Word problems that lead to a linear equation
explanations: years-once (procedural): The 8 years were added only once; both people get 8 years older, so add 2 × 8.
future-ignored (procedural): The ages now were made to add up to 76; that is their sum in 8 years.
middle (procedural): 390 ÷ 3 gives the middle multiple; the smallest is 10 less.
consecutive-numbers (conceptual): The numbers were taken as x, x + 1, x + 2; consecutive multiples of 10 go up by 10.
half-perimeter (conceptual): Length + width was set equal to the perimeter; the perimeter goes round all four sides: 2 × (length + width).
length-given (procedural): The length was given; the question asks for the width.
fraction-of-result (conceptual): 4/5 of the result was taken away; the fraction is of the unknown number, so the equation is x + 4x/5 = 108.
savings-added (conceptual): The two weekly savings were added; the gap closes by the DIFFERENCE of what they save each week.
gap-only (procedural): The difference in money now was given; divide it by how much the gap closes each week.

teach.idea: A word problem becomes an equation when the unknown gets a letter and each sentence is written in symbols. Solving the equation and checking the answer in the story finishes the problem.
teach.method: Let x be what is asked. Write the other quantities with x (mother's age kx, next multiple x + k, length x + k). Write the fact the story gives as an equation, solve it, and check in the words of the story.

alternatives.title: Draw a bar model
text: Draw a bar for the unknown and bars for the other quantities in terms of it.
The total length of the bars is the given total: share out what is left after the known parts.

families.title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing surds
explanations: add-under-root (conceptual): The numbers under the roots were added; √a + √b is not √(a + b). Simplify each surd first, then add like surds (like terms).
multiply-coefficients (procedural): The numbers in front were multiplied; like surds are added like like terms: 3√2 + 2√2 = 5√2.
subtract-under-root (conceptual): The numbers under the roots were subtracted; √a − √b is not √(a − b). Simplify each surd first, then subtract like surds.
add-coefficients (procedural): The numbers in front were added instead of subtracted.
add-for-multiply (conceptual): The numbers under the roots were added; √a × √b = √(ab).
square-not-rooted (procedural): The quotient under the root was not square-rooted; √a ÷ √b = √(a ÷ b).
subtract-for-divide (conceptual): The numbers under the roots were subtracted; √a ÷ √b = √(a/b).

teach.idea: Surds behave like letters: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2 (like surds), but √2 + √3 cannot be combined. For multiplying and dividing, √a × √b = √(ab) and √a ÷ √b = √(a/b).
teach.method: To add or subtract, first simplify each surd (take out square factors) and then combine like surds. To multiply or divide, combine under one root and simplify.

alternatives.title: Check with decimals
text: √2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732. Work out both the question and your answer with these decimals.
If the decimals agree, the surd answer is right.

families.title: Recognising surds and comparing their sizes
explanations: any-root (conceptual): √64 has a root sign, but it is a whole number (8); a surd is a root that cannot be written exactly as a fraction.
fraction-root (conceptual): √(25/36) is a fraction under a root, but both its top and bottom are perfect squares, so it is a rational number.
coefficient-only (conceptual): Only the numbers in front were compared; the number under the root matters too. Square both: (p√m)² = p²m.
root-only (conceptual): Only the numbers under the roots were compared; the numbers in front matter too. Square both and compare p²m with q²n.

teach.idea: A surd is a root of a rational number that is itself irrational, like √2 or √12. √9 = 3 and ∛8 = 2 are not surds. To compare p√m with q√n, compare their squares p²m and q²n.
teach.method: For 'is it a surd?', check whether the number under the root is a perfect square (or cube). For 'which is greater?', put the outside number inside: 3√2 = √18 and 2√5 = √20, so 2√5 is greater.

alternatives.title: Move everything under the root
text: Then the surd with the bigger number under the root is bigger.

families.title: Rationalising the denominator
explanations: top-only (procedural): Only the top was multiplied by √15; multiply the top and the bottom by √15, so the bottom becomes 15.
root-dropped (conceptual): The root sign was simply removed from the bottom; that changes the value. Multiply top and bottom by the root instead.
plus-c-squared (conceptual): (√15 + 3)(√15 − 3) = 15 − 9; the product of a sum and a difference is a difference of squares, not 15 + 9.
c-not-squared (procedural): 3 was not squared in the denominator: it should be 15 − 3² = 6.
sign-of-denominator (procedural): The denominator was worked out as 9 − 15 instead of 15 − 9, which changes the sign of the answer.

teach.idea: Multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same number does not change its value. Choosing √b (or the conjugate √b ∓ c) makes the bottom a whole number, because √b × √b = b and (√b + c)(√b − c) = b − c².
teach.method: For a/√b, multiply by √b/√b. For a/(√b ± c), multiply by (√b ∓ c)/(√b ∓ c). Then simplify, cancelling any common factor.

alternatives.title: Check with decimals
text: Work out the original fraction with a calculator-style estimate (√2 ≈ 1.414).
Your answer must give the same decimal.

families.title: Finding a missing digit in a sum or difference
explanations: carry-forgotten (procedural): The ten carried from the column on the right was forgotten. When a column adds up to 10 or more, 1 goes to the next column.
add-not-undo (conceptual): To find a missing part of an addition, take the other number away from the total; the digits were added instead.
borrow-forgotten (procedural): The column on the right was regrouped (1 from this column was exchanged for 10 there), but this column was not made one less.
subtract-not-undo (conceptual): To find the first number of a subtraction, add the answer and the number taken away; the digits were subtracted instead.

smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In that column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, regroup first: exchange 1 from the next column on the left for 10 in this column.

teach.idea: A sum or difference is a true sentence, so each column must work out, including any regrouping with the column on its right (a ten carried in, or 1 exchanged for 10 ones).
teach.method: Start from the ones column and move left. In each column, note whether the column regroups: a ten carried (addition) or 1 exchanged for 10 in the column on the right (subtraction), then find the digit that makes the hidden column right. Check by doing the whole calculation.

alternatives.title: Try the digits and check
text: Put a digit in the box and work out the whole sum.
If it is not right, see whether the answer came out too big or too small and try a better digit. Only one digit works.

alternatives.title: Undo the operation
text: A missing part of an addition is total − other part.
A missing first number of a subtraction is answer + number taken away. Work out that calculation and read off the digit.

families.title: Winning move in a take-away game
explanations: groups-of-k (conceptual): The safe numbers to leave go up in steps of 6, not 5: whatever the other player takes (1 to 5), you can take enough to make 6.
take-most (conceptual): Taking as many as possible (3) does not always win. Look for the counts you want to leave for the other player.
wrong-goal (conceptual): This game was played as if taking the last counter wins. Here you want to leave the other player exactly 1 counter at the end.

teach.idea: Work backwards from the end. Some numbers of counters are "safe" to leave for the other player: from them, whatever they take, you can get back to the next safe number.
teach.method: If each turn takes 1 to k, the safe numbers go up in steps of k + 1 (0, k + 1, 2(k + 1) … when the last counter wins; 1 more than these when it loses). Take enough to leave a safe number.

alternatives.title: Play small games first
text: Play with 1, 2, 3 … counters and write W (the player to move wins) or L (loses) under each number.
A number is W if you can move to an L. The L numbers form a pattern; leave your partner an L number.

families.title: Counting every combination (one from each group)
explanations: add-choices (conceptual): The numbers of choices were added. Each choice from the first group goes with every choice from the next, so multiply.
add-last-group (procedural): The pairs were found (6 × 6), but then the sweets were added. Every pair goes with each of the 4 sweets, so multiply again.
forgot-group (procedural): One group was left out. A meal has one item from each of the three groups.

teach.idea: Every choice from one group can be matched with every choice from the next, so the number of combinations is the product of the numbers of choices.
teach.method: Fix the first choice and count how many ways the rest can go; that number is the same for every first choice, so multiply. With a third group, multiply again.

alternatives.title: Make an organised list
text: Take the first shirt and list it with every skirt, then the second shirt with every skirt, and so on.
Each row of the list has the same length, so the total is rows × length of a row.

alternatives.title: Draw a tree
text: Draw one branch for each first choice; from the end of each, draw one branch for each second choice.
Count the ends of the last branches.

families.title: How many numbers can be made from given digits
explanations: repeat-rule (procedural): A digit may be used again, so every place has all the choices; repeats were left out.
add-choices (conceptual): The choices for each place were added. Each first digit goes with every choice for the next place, so multiply.
zero-first (conceptual): Numbers starting with 0 were counted. A number does not start with 0 (07 is just 7), so 0 cannot be the first digit.

teach.idea: Fill the places one at a time from the left. The number of ways is the product of the choices for each place.
teach.method: Count the choices for the first place (0 is not allowed there), then for the next place (one fewer if digits cannot repeat), and so on; multiply.

alternatives.title: List by the first digit
text: Write all the numbers that start with the first digit, then those that start with the next digit, and so on.
Each starting digit gives the same number of numbers, so multiply.

families.title: Reading a pie chart
explanations: equal-parts (conceptual): The 5 parts were treated as equal. Look at the size of each part: they are not all the same.
the-rest (procedural): The number for all the other parts was found instead of this part.
denominator-only (procedural): Only the bottom of the fraction was used (240 ÷ 3). Then multiply by the top: that many of those pieces.

teach.idea: A pie chart shows the whole group as a full circle; each part's size is a fraction of the whole group.
teach.method: Find the fraction for the part (the whole circle is 1, so a missing part is 1 minus the others). Then find that fraction of the total: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top.

alternatives.title: Cut into equal pieces
text: Imagine the circle cut into equal pieces (for example 8 eighths). Share the total equally among the pieces.
Count how many pieces the part covers, and add up their shares.

families.title: Sector angles in a pie chart
explanations: count-as-degrees (conceptual): The number of students was used as the angle. The whole class is the full circle of 360°, so first find what fraction of the class this is.
percent-not-degrees (procedural): The angle was treated as a percentage (out of 100). Compare it with 360°, the whole circle.
half-circle (recall): A full turn is 360°, not 180°.
degrees-as-count (conceptual): The angle was given as the number of students. The angle is a fraction of 360°; the same fraction of the class chose cricket.

teach.idea: The whole group is the whole circle, 360°. Each part gets the same fraction of 360° as it is of the group.
teach.method: Angle = (part ÷ total) × 360°. Going back: part = (angle ÷ 360°) × total.

alternatives.title: Degrees for one person
text: Share 360° among everyone: each person gets 360 ÷ total degrees.
Multiply by the number in the part (or divide the angle by the degrees for one person).

families.title: Reading a bar chart with a scale
explanations: count-lines (conceptual): The lines were counted as 1 each. On this chart each line on the scale stands for 100.
assume-tens (procedural): Each line was taken as 10. Read the numbers on the scale: they tell how much each line stands for.
add-for-more (conceptual): "How many more" asks for the difference between the bars, not their total.
difference-for-total (procedural): "Together" asks for the total of the two bars; the difference was found instead.

teach.idea: On a scaled bar chart each line on the side stands for more than 1 (for example 5 or 50). The height of a bar is read off the scale, not by counting squares as ones.
teach.method: Find how much one line stands for (the difference between two numbers on the scale). Read each bar against the scale, then add or subtract as the question asks.

alternatives.title: Skip-count up the scale
text: Put a finger at the bottom of the bar and count up the lines in steps of the scale: 5, 10, 15 …
Stop at the top of the bar: that number is its value.

families.title: Writing a number rule with a letter
explanations: times-for-add (conceptual): 12m means 12 × m. Adding 12 is written m + 12.
reversed (conceptual): 12 − m takes m away from 12. Taking 12 away from m is written m − 12.
add-for-take (procedural): The rule takes away, so use −, not +.
add-for-times (conceptual): m + 12 adds 12. Multiplying by 12 is written 12 × m, or 12m.
brackets (procedural): 12(m + 9) adds 9 first and then multiplies. The machine multiplies first, then adds 9.
all-added (conceptual): Multiplying by 12 was written as adding 12.
joined-numbers (procedural): 9 was put with the 12 in front of m. 21m means 21 × m; the 9 is added on its own.

teach.idea: A letter stands for any number. A rule written with the letter works for every number at once.
teach.method: Do to the letter exactly what you would do to a number: 'add 5' gives n + 5; 'multiply by 4' gives 4n (4 × n). Test your rule with a small number.

alternatives.title: Try numbers first
text: Make a small table: put in 1, 2, 3 and write what comes out.
Look at what you did to each number every time, and write the same thing with the letter.

families.title: Writing the rule of a growing pattern with a letter
explanations: step-added (conceptual): n + 6 adds 6 once. The pattern adds 6 for every shape, so the rule has 6n (6 × n).
counted-from-zero (procedural): The shapes were numbered from 0. Check your rule with n = 1: it must give the first shape.
start-forgotten (procedural): 6n gives 6 for shape 1, but shape 1 has 11. Add the extra 5.
first-times-n (conceptual): 11n would add 11 each time, but the pattern grows by 6 each time.

teach.idea: If a pattern grows by the same amount each time, that amount is the number multiplied by n; a fixed extra makes the first shape right.
teach.method: Find how much the pattern grows each time (say 3): the rule starts 3n. Compare 3 × 1 with shape 1 to find what to add. Check with shape 4.

alternatives.title: See the groups in the shape
text: Look for the part that is added each time (for example a ⊓ of 3 matchsticks) and the part that is there from the start (one extra stick).
Shape n has n of the repeating parts plus the starting part.

families.title: Continuing square, triangular and other number patterns
explanations: same-gap (conceptual): The last gap (4) was added again and again. In this pattern the gap changes each time.
double-for-square (recall): A square number is n × n (25 × 25), not n × 2.
square-instead (conceptual): This picture has 20 rows and 21 columns, so 20 × 21; 20 × 20 would be a square.
times-three (recall): A cube number is n × n × n (10 × 10 × 10), not n × 3.
times-two (conceptual): Each number is double the one before; 2 × n adds 2 each time instead of doubling.
off-by-one (procedural): The 30th odd number is 2 × 30 − 1; 2 × 30 + 1 is the next one.

teach.idea: Square numbers come from square dot pictures (n rows of n), triangular numbers from triangles (1 + 2 + … + n), rectangular numbers from n rows of n + 1.
teach.method: Find the rule that makes each term from its position (for squares, n × n), test it on the terms you know, then use it for the term asked.

alternatives.title: Look at the gaps
text: Write the gaps between the terms: for square numbers they are 3, 5, 7, 9 … (the odd numbers); for triangular numbers 2, 3, 4, 5 ….
Keep adding the next gap until you reach the term you need.

families.title: Links between square, odd and triangular numbers
explanations: last-term (procedural): Only the last odd number was given; the question asks for the total of all of them.
count-terms (procedural): There are 25 odd numbers from 1 to 49, so the total is the 25th square number.
differ-by-one (conceptual): The two squares come next to each other in the list, but they are not next to each other as numbers: they differ by more than 1.
missed-one (procedural): Going from 30 × 30 to 31 × 31 adds a row of 30, a column of 30 and one corner dot.
doubled-one (procedural): The 20th triangular number was doubled; the question adds the 19th and the 20th.
wrong-square (procedural): The two triangles fit together into a square of side 20.
counted-one-end (procedural): One of the two squares was counted. "Between" leaves out both 625 and 676.
counted-both-ends (procedural): Both squares were counted; numbers between them do not include the ends.

teach.idea: Dot pictures show the links: odd numbers wrap round a square to make the next square; two neighbouring triangles fit together into a square.
teach.method: Draw (or imagine) the dot picture. Going from n × n to (n + 1) × (n + 1) adds n + n + 1 dots, an odd number; so adding the odd numbers from 1 gives the square numbers.

alternatives.title: Check small cases
text: Work the first few by hand: 1 = 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 ….
Spot the pattern (here, square numbers), then use it for the case asked.

families.title: Reading an angle from a protractor
explanations: wrong-scale (procedural): The number was read from the wrong scale. Start from the 0 that one arm lies on and read the same scale up to the other arm.
one-reading (conceptual): The reading at one arm was given as the angle. Neither arm is on 0, so the angle is the difference between the two readings.
mixed-scales (procedural): One reading came from the inner scale and the other from the outer scale. Use the same scale for both arms.

teach.idea: A protractor has two scales running in opposite directions. Both arms must be read on the same scale; the angle is how far apart the readings are.
teach.method: Put the centre on the corner. Find the scale that reads 0 on one arm (or use either scale for both arms). Read the other arm on that same scale; if neither arm is on 0, subtract the smaller reading from the larger.

alternatives.title: Estimate first
text: Look at the angle: is it smaller than a right angle (less than 90°) or bigger?
If your reading says acute but the angle looks obtuse (or the other way round), you read the wrong scale.

families.title: Missing angle in a complementary or supplementary pair
explanations: wrong-total (recall): Supplementary angles make a straight angle, 180°. 90° is for complementary angles.
full-turn (recall): 360° is a full turn. Supplementary angles add up to 180°.

teach.idea: Complementary angles together make a right angle (90°); supplementary angles together make a straight angle (180°).
teach.method: Take the given angle away from 90° (complementary) or 180° (supplementary). Check: the two angles should add up to the total.

alternatives.title: Count on to the total
text: Start at the angle you know and count on to 90 (or 180), in tens and then ones.

families.title: Angles where two straight lines cross
explanations: opposite-as-linear (conceptual): Vertically opposite angles are equal; they do not add up to 180°. Angles next to each other on a straight line add to 180°.
full-turn (recall): Two angles on a straight line add up to 180°, not 360°.
neighbour-equal (conceptual): Angles next to each other are not equal (unless both are 90°); together they make a straight line, 180°.
straight-only (procedural): Only one neighbouring angle was found. All four angles together make a full turn, 360°.
all-equal (conceptual): The four angles are not all equal: only opposite angles are equal.

teach.idea: Where two straight lines cross, angles next to each other make a straight line (180°), so opposite angles are equal; all four make a full turn (360°).
teach.method: Opposite angle: the same. Angle next to it: 180° minus it. All the others together: 360° minus it.

alternatives.title: Go round the crossing
text: Start at the angle you know. The next angle round makes a straight line with it, so it is 180° minus it.
The next one makes a straight line with that one, so it is back to the first angle: opposite angles match.

families.title: Turns between compass directions as fractions of a full turn
explanations: other-way (conceptual): The turn was counted the other way round. Clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move: North → East → South → West.
quarters (procedural): Each step between neighbouring directions was counted as a quarter turn. With the in-between directions (North-East …) there are 8 steps in a full turn, so each is one eighth.
steps-not-fraction (procedural): The number of steps was given. A full turn has 8 steps, so write it as a fraction of 8.

teach.idea: A full turn brings you back to where you started. The four main directions split it into quarters; with the in-between directions (North-East and so on) it is split into eighths.
teach.method: Count the steps from the starting direction to the final one, going the way of the turn (clockwise is the way clock hands move). Each step is 1/8 of a turn; two steps make a quarter.

alternatives.title: Use a clock face
text: Imagine North at 12, East at 3, South at 6, West at 9.
North to East clockwise is like the minute hand going from 12 to 3: a quarter turn.

families.title: Degrees turned by the minute hand
explanations: six-per-number (procedural): Each number was counted as 6°. 6° is one minute mark; from one number to the next is 5 minutes, which is 30°.
minutes-not-degrees (conceptual): The minutes that passed were given, not the angle. A full turn of 60 minutes is 360°.
other-way (procedural): The angle the other way round the clock was found. The hand turned clockwise, so count the numbers it passes going clockwise.

teach.idea: The minute hand makes a full turn (360°) in an hour, passing 12 numbers, so it turns 30° from one number to the next.
teach.method: Count how many numbers the hand moves past (clockwise), then multiply by 30°. A quarter turn (3 numbers) is 90°; a half turn (6 numbers) is 180°.

alternatives.title: Fractions of a turn
text: Moving 3 numbers is a quarter turn (90°), 6 numbers a half turn (180°), 9 numbers three-quarters (270°).
For other moves, start from the nearest quarter and add or take away 30° for each number.

families.title: Counting the pieces at a stage of a repeating pattern
explanations: same-increase (conceptual): The pattern was taken to grow by the same number each stage (16). Every piece is replaced, so the number is multiplied by 5 each stage.
stage-off-by-one (procedural): Stage 0 is the start, so stage 3 has had 3 replacements; one stage too few was counted.
times-stage (conceptual): 4 × 5 × 3 multiplies by 5 only once. Multiply by 5 once for every stage: 3 times.

teach.idea: In a fractal pattern the same rule is used again and again on every piece, so the number of pieces is multiplied by the same number at every stage.
teach.method: Start with the pieces at stage 0 and multiply by the number of new pieces each piece becomes, once for every stage. A table of stages helps you keep count.

alternatives.title: A table of stages
text: Write the stages 0, 1, 2, … in a row.
Under each stage write the number of pieces: each is the one before times the number of new pieces per piece.

families.title: Faces, edges and vertices of prisms and pyramids
explanations: forgot-ends (conceptual): Only the 10 side faces were counted. A prism also has two ends (the top and the bottom decagon).
one-end (procedural): Only one end was counted; a prism has two.
euler-sign (procedural): Vertices = 2 + edges − faces; the 2 was taken away instead of added.
euler-forgot-2 (recall): The 2 in Euler's rule was left out.
forgot-side-edges (procedural): The edges round the top and bottom (10 + 10) were counted, but not the 10 edges joining them.
one-end-edges (procedural): The edges of only one end were counted.
one-end-vertices (procedural): Only the corners of one end were counted. The other end has 10 more.
forgot-base (conceptual): Only the 10 triangles were counted; the base (decagon) is a face too.
base-only (procedural): Only the 10 edges of the base were counted. There are also 10 edges going up to the top point.
extra-edge (procedural): An edge was counted twice: count the base edges, then the edges to the top point.
forgot-apex (procedural): The top point (apex) is a vertex too.

teach.idea: A prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles; a pyramid has one base joined to a top point by triangles. Counting part by part makes the counts easy.
teach.method: Prism on an n-sided base: faces n + 2, edges 3n, vertices 2n. Pyramid: faces n + 1, edges 2n, vertices n + 1. Check with Euler's rule: faces + vertices − edges = 2.

alternatives.title: Count part by part
text: Count the base, then the top (or the top point), then what joins them.
For edges: round the bottom, round the top, then the ones going up.

alternatives.title: Unfold it into a net
text: Imagine cutting the solid open and laying it flat: each face becomes one shape of the net.
Count the shapes in the net to get the faces.

families.title: Painted faces in a block of small cubes
explanations: kept-corners (procedural): The corner cubes were counted along each edge; corner cubes have paint on three faces, so leave them out (2 from each edge).
whole-faces (procedural): Every cube on a face was counted. Cubes on the edges of a face have paint on two or three faces; only the middle part of each face counts.
one-layer (procedural): Only one layer was taken off each length. The paint is on both sides, so take 2 from each length.
outside-cubes (conceptual): The question asks for the cubes with no paint: the hidden ones inside, not the ones on the outside.

teach.idea: Where a small cube sits decides its paint: corners get three faces, the rest of each edge two, the middle of each face one, and the hidden inside none.
teach.method: Take 2 off each length (the two outer layers). Edges: 4 × (sum of the shortened lengths). Faces: 2 × (sum of the products of pairs). Inside: the product of all three.

alternatives.title: Look layer by layer
text: Look at the top layer: count its corner, edge and middle cubes.
Then a middle layer: its outside ring has paint, its centre does not. Add up the layers.

families.title: Classifying quadrilaterals from their sides and angles
explanations: square-not-rectangle (conceptual): The squares were left out. A square has four right angles and opposite sides equal, so every square is also a rectangle.
opposite-sides-only (conceptual): Shapes with opposite sides equal were counted even without right angles. A rectangle needs all four angles to be 90°.
square-not-rhombus (conceptual): The squares were left out. A rhombus has four equal sides, so every square is also a rhombus.
rhombus-needs-right-angles (conceptual): Only the squares were counted. A rhombus needs four equal sides; its angles do not have to be 90°.
only-slanted (conceptual): Only the slanted shapes with unequal sides were counted. Squares, rectangles and rhombuses also have opposite sides equal and parallel, so they are parallelograms too.
right-angles-excluded (conceptual): Shapes with right angles were left out; rectangles and squares are parallelograms as well.
trapezium-included (conceptual): A trapezium was counted. Its opposite sides are not equal and only one pair is parallel, so it is not a parallelogram.

teach.idea: Shape names describe properties, so one shape can have several names: a square is a rectangle (four right angles), a rhombus (four equal sides) and a parallelogram (opposite sides equal and parallel).
teach.method: For each shape, check the property the name needs. Rectangle: all angles 90°. Rhombus: all sides equal. Parallelogram: opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal. Count every shape that has it.

alternatives.title: A family tree of shapes
text: Parallelograms are a big family. Rectangles and rhombuses are inside it, and squares are inside both rectangles and rhombuses.
When you count a family, count everyone inside it too.

families.title: Unknown angles in a parallelogram or rhombus
explanations: opposite-as-adjacent (conceptual): Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal; it is angles next to each other that add to 180°.
all-equal (conceptual): Only opposite angles are equal. Angles next to each other add up to 180°.
full-turn (recall): Neighbouring angles add to 180°; 360° is all four angles together.
no-split (conceptual): The diagonal of a rhombus cuts angle A into two equal halves; the whole angle was given.
wrong-angle-halved (procedural): Angle B was halved instead of angle A. The diagonal AC starts at A, so it splits angle A.

teach.idea: In a parallelogram (and so in a rhombus) opposite angles are equal, and angles next to each other add up to 180°. In a rhombus each diagonal also cuts its angles in half.
teach.method: Opposite angle: the same. Neighbouring angle: 180° minus it. Rhombus diagonal: half the angle it starts from.

alternatives.title: Think of parallel lines
text: Two sides of a parallelogram are parallel; a third side crosses them.
The two angles between the parallel sides on the same side of that crossing line add to 180°.

families.title: Order and angle of rotational symmetry
explanations: missed-full-turn (procedural): The last position, back at the start after a full turn, was not counted. Count every time it looks the same, including the full turn.
doubled (procedural): Each matching position was counted twice (once for each direction of turning). Turn one way only.
half-turn-shared (conceptual): 180° was shared out instead of a full turn, 360°.
gave-order (procedural): The order (how many times) was given instead of the angle. Share 360° by the order.
upside-down (procedural): The fraction was written the wrong way up. The turn is 1 out of 8 equal parts of a full turn: 1/8.
angle-not-fraction (procedural): The angle in degrees was given. As a fraction of a full turn, divide by 360.
counted-start (procedural): The starting position was counted as the first time. The first time it looks the same is after the smallest turn.
first-angle (procedural): Only the smallest angle was given; the 7th time is 7 of those turns.
counted-corners (conceptual): The corners were counted. Turn the shape: it only fits onto itself after a half turn and a full turn.
mirror-only (conceptual): It has no mirror line, but it still looks the same after a half turn. Rotational symmetry is about turning, not folding.

teach.idea: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a turn of less than a full turn. The order is how many times it fits onto itself in one full turn.
teach.method: Count the identical parts that go round the centre (sides of a regular shape, blades, petals): that is usually the order. The smallest turn is 360° ÷ order, which is 1/order of a full turn.

alternatives.title: Trace and turn
text: Trace the shape on thin paper, put a pin through the centre and turn the tracing slowly.
Count each time the tracing sits exactly on the shape before you get back to the start.

families.title: Classifying triangles by their angles
explanations: one-acute-enough (conceptual): A triangle was called acute-angled because it has an acute angle. Every triangle has at least two acute angles; an acute-angled triangle has all three less than 90°.
right-as-acute (recall): A 90° angle is a right angle, not an acute one. Acute means less than 90°.
big-as-right (recall): Triangles with an angle bigger than 90° were counted. A right angle is exactly 90°; bigger is obtuse.
right-as-obtuse (recall): A 90° angle was counted as obtuse. Obtuse means more than 90°.
biggest-first (procedural): Only the first angle of each triangle was checked. Look at all three angles: the largest one decides the type.

teach.idea: Every triangle has at least two acute angles, so the type is decided by its largest angle: less than 90° acute-angled, exactly 90° right-angled, more than 90° obtuse-angled.
teach.method: For each triangle find the largest angle and compare it with 90°. Then count the ones asked for.

alternatives.title: The square-corner test
text: Hold the corner of a sheet of paper (a right angle) against each angle.
If one angle fits exactly it is right-angled; if one is wider it is obtuse-angled; if all are narrower it is acute-angled.

families.title: Classifying triangles by their sides
explanations: not-equilateral (conceptual): Every triangle that is not equilateral was counted. A triangle with two equal sides is not scalene.
names-swapped (recall): Isosceles and scalene were mixed up. Isosceles: two sides equal. Scalene: all different.
two-equal-enough (conceptual): Triangles with only two equal sides were counted. Equilateral needs all three sides equal.
equilateral-included (procedural): The equilateral triangles were counted too; the question asks for exactly two equal sides.

teach.idea: Triangles are named by how many sides are equal: all three equal is equilateral, exactly two equal is isosceles (with two equal sides), none equal is scalene.
teach.method: For each triangle compare the three lengths in pairs (first and second, second and third, first and third). Count the equal pairs, name the triangle, then count the ones asked for.

alternatives.title: Sort the lengths first
text: Write the three lengths from smallest to largest.
Equal lengths are now next to each other, so they are easy to spot.

families.title: Rectangles with the same area or the same perimeter
explanations: same-perimeter (conceptual): Rectangles with the same area do not always have the same perimeter. Find the other side first, then go round the new rectangle.
half-perimeter (procedural): Only two sides were added. A rectangle has four sides: two of each length.
gave-area (procedural): The area was given; the question asks for the distance round the edge.
same-area (conceptual): Rectangles with the same perimeter do not always have the same area. Find the other side first, then multiply.
forgot-halve (procedural): The other side was found as perimeter − 17. The perimeter has two of each side: the other side is half the perimeter minus 17.
gave-perimeter (procedural): The perimeter was given; the question asks for the area (the squares inside).

teach.idea: Area counts the squares inside; perimeter is the distance round the edge. Rearranging the same squares can change the perimeter, and the same length of fence can enclose different areas.
teach.method: Same area: find the other side by dividing the area by the side you know, then add all four sides. Same perimeter: half the perimeter is one long side plus one short side, so take away the side you know, then multiply.

alternatives.title: Rearrange the squares
text: Imagine cutting the rectangle into its unit squares and laying them out in rows of the new length.
Count the rows to get the other side, then walk round the edge to get the perimeter.

families.title: River-crossing puzzles: the fewest crossings
explanations: forward-only (conceptual): Only the trips across were counted. The boat has to come back each time, and the return trips count as crossings too.
rower-forgotten (conceptual): Each trip across was taken to move 6 people for good. Someone rows the boat back, so each round trip moves only 6 − 1 = 5 more people across (the last trip moves 6).

children-not-back (procedural): Only the soldier's trip and one trip back were counted for each soldier. The boat is with the children, so for every soldier: both children cross, one brings the boat back, the soldier crosses, and the other child brings it back: 4 crossings.
last-return (procedural): The last trip back was left out. The children must end on the starting bank with their boat, so the final return counts too.

teach.idea: Act the puzzle out one trip at a time and look for the pattern that repeats. A round trip (across and back) is what moves people, and the boat's rower has to come back each time.
teach.method: Work out what one full round achieves (how many more people end up across), count how many rounds are needed before the last trip, then add the last trip.

alternatives.title: Act it out with counters
text: Use counters for the people and a coin for the boat on two sides of a line.
Move them trip by trip and write each trip in a table; count the rows at the end.

alternatives.title: Solve smaller puzzles first
text: Try the same puzzle with 1, 2 and 3 people (or soldiers) and count the crossings.
See how much the count grows each time one more person is added, and use that to reach the number asked.

families.title: The compass direction faced after a turn
explanations: other-way (conceptual): The turn was made the other way. Clockwise is the way clock hands move: North → North-East → East → …
eighth-as-quarter (procedural): Each eighth was taken as a quarter turn. A quarter turn is 2 of the 8 steps, so one eighth is just one step, to the next direction.
quarter-as-eighth (procedural): Each quarter turn was taken as one step between neighbouring directions. With the in-between directions there are 8 steps in a full turn, so a quarter turn is 2 steps.

teach.idea: The eight compass directions split a full turn into eight equal steps; a quarter turn is two steps and a half turn is four. Clockwise goes North → East → South → West.
teach.method: Change the turn into eighths (a quarter = 2, a half = 4, three quarters = 6), then count that many steps round the compass, the way of the turn.

alternatives.title: Stand up and turn
text: Face the starting direction and point your arm straight ahead.
Turn your body step by step (each step to the next direction on the compass) and say the directions aloud as you pass them.

alternatives.title: Use a clock face
text: Put North at 12, East at 3, South at 6 and West at 9; the in-between directions sit half-way.
A quarter turn clockwise moves the minute hand from 12 to 3: from North to East.

families.title: Naming a quadrilateral from its properties (kites and trapeziums included)
explanations: sides-only (conceptual): Only the sides were looked at. Four equal sides make a rhombus, but these angles are all 90° as well, so the most special name is square.
angles-only (conceptual): Only the angles were looked at. Four right angles make a rectangle, but all four sides are equal too, so the most special name is square.
general-name (conceptual): A rectangle is a parallelogram, but its four right angles make 'rectangle' the more special name.
right-angles-square (conceptual): Four right angles were taken to mean a square. A square also needs all four sides equal; here the sides are not all equal.
equal-sides-square (conceptual): Four equal sides were taken to mean a square. A square also needs four right angles; these angles are not 90°.
general-kite (conceptual): Pairs of equal sides next to each other do fit a kite, but all four sides are equal and opposite sides are parallel: the more special name is rhombus.
opposite-sides-rectangle (conceptual): Opposite sides equal were taken to mean a rectangle. A rectangle also needs four right angles; these angles are not 90°.
pairs-rhombus (conceptual): A rhombus has all four sides equal. Here there are two different lengths, each used for two sides next to each other: a kite.

pairs-parallelogram (conceptual): Two pairs of equal sides were taken to mean a parallelogram. In a parallelogram the equal sides are OPPOSITE each other and parallel; here the equal sides are next to each other and no sides are parallel: a kite.

one-pair-parallelogram (conceptual): One pair of parallel sides was taken to be enough for a parallelogram. A parallelogram needs BOTH pairs of opposite sides parallel; with exactly one pair it is a trapezium.
any-kite (conceptual): A kite has two pairs of equal sides next to each other; here all four sides are different.

teach.idea: Each name is a list of properties. A square has every property; a kite has two pairs of equal sides NEXT to each other; a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides. The best name is the most special one whose properties all hold.
teach.method: Check, in order: both pairs of opposite sides parallel? (parallelogram family: then all sides equal → rhombus, right angles → rectangle, both → square). Exactly one pair parallel? → trapezium. No parallel sides but two pairs of equal neighbouring sides? → kite.

alternatives.title: A family tree of quadrilaterals
text: Parallelograms hold rectangles and rhombuses; squares sit inside both. Kites and trapeziums are separate branches.
A shape is named by the lowest branch whose properties it has.

alternatives.title: Sketch it from the table
text: Sketch the shape roughly, marking equal sides with the same tick and parallel sides with arrows.
Look at the sketch: which ticks and arrows does it have? Match them to a name.

families.title: Unknown sides of a parallelogram or rhombus
explanations: whole-perimeter (procedural): 20 was taken from the whole perimeter. The perimeter has two sides of each length, so first halve it: AB + BC = 34.
all-equal (conceptual): The perimeter was shared equally among four sides, as for a rhombus. In a parallelogram only OPPOSITE sides are equal.
half (conceptual): The perimeter was halved. A rhombus has four equal sides, so divide by 4.
x-not-side (procedural): x = 9 was given, but the question asks for a length: put x = 9 back into the expression.
sign-slip (procedural): When the numbers were moved across the equals sign, their signs were not changed (2x = 9 − 9). Moving +9 to the other side makes it −9, and moving −9 makes it +9: 2x = 9 + 9.
side-not-perimeter (procedural): The side (36 cm) was given. The perimeter is all four equal sides: 4 × 36.

teach.idea: In a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, so the perimeter is twice (one side + the next side). In a rhombus all four sides are equal.
teach.method: Parallelogram: halve the perimeter and take away the side you know. Rhombus: divide the perimeter by 4. When sides are given as expressions, set the two equal sides equal, solve for x, then substitute.

alternatives.title: Walk round the shape
text: Walking round a parallelogram you go along AB, BC, then the same lengths again.
So half the walk is AB + BC: the side you know plus the side you want.

alternatives.title: Equal sides balance
text: Write the two equal sides on the two pans of a balance: px + q = rx − s.
Take px from both sides and add s to both; then divide to find x.

families.title: Counting the rectangles, squares or triangles hidden in a figure
explanations: small-only (conceptual): Only the smallest squares were counted. Bigger squares are made of 2 × 2, 3 × 3, … small squares.
rows-only (procedural): Only rectangles one row high were counted. Count rectangles of every height as well as every width.
small-and-whole (procedural): Only the small squares and the biggest ones were counted; the middle sizes were missed.

thin-only (conceptual): Only the smallest triangles, at the top above the first line across, were counted. Two or more of them together make a triangle too, and every line across is the base of more triangles.
thin-and-whole (procedural): Only the thin triangles and the whole triangle were counted; triangles made of two, three, … thin ones were missed.
one-layer (procedural): Only the triangles standing on the base were counted (45). Each line across makes another set of triangles with the top corner.

teach.idea: Counting hidden figures goes wrong when we just look and count. Instead, describe each figure by the lines that make it, and count the choices of lines systematically.
teach.method: Rectangles in a grid: choose 2 of the upright lines and 2 of the lines across, and multiply the numbers of ways. Squares: count each size separately and add. Triangles from one corner: choose 2 of the lines from the corner, times the number of lines across.

alternatives.title: Count size by size
text: Make a table: figures made of 1 piece, of 2 pieces, of 3 pieces, ….
Count each row of the table carefully, then add the rows.

alternatives.title: Start with a smaller figure
text: Count the figures in a 1 × 2 grid, then a 1 × 3 grid, then a 1 × 4 grid.
Notice the pattern 3, 6, 10, … (the triangular numbers) and use it to count bigger figures.

families.title: Cube nets: opposite faces, and which shapes fold into a cube
explanations: round-corner (procedural): D does not touch B in the net, but after folding it is next to it. Fold the net in your mind one square at a time to see where each square ends up.
next-door (conceptual): A shares an edge with B in the net, so after folding it is next to B, not opposite. A face is never opposite a square it touches in the net.
six-is-enough (conceptual): Six squares were taken to be enough. When this shape is folded, two squares land on the same face of the cube and one face is left open.
looks-odd (conceptual): The shape looks unusual, but folding it square by square gives six different faces, so it is a cube net. Many different shapes fold into a cube (there are 11 nets).

teach.idea: A net is a solid unfolded flat. For a cube the six squares must fold into six different faces; a square's neighbours in the net become its neighbours on the cube, and the face opposite it is one that never touches it.
teach.method: Pick a square as the bottom and fold up the squares round it one at a time, saying which face each becomes (front, back, left, right, top). Opposite pairs are bottom–top, front–back, left–right; in a straight row of squares, the squares one apart are opposite.

alternatives.title: Squares one apart in a row
text: In a straight line of three squares, the first and the third fold onto opposite faces.
Use this rule along every straight row and column of the net; the face left over pairs with the last one.

alternatives.title: Make it from paper
text: Copy the net on squared paper, cut it out and fold it.
Write the letters on both sides so you can check which faces end up opposite each other.

families.title: Matching solids with their nets and views
explanations: count-slip (conceptual): These views were not checked carefully against the heptagonal pyramid: count the sides of the shape seen from above, and look whether the front view is a rectangle or a triangle.

similar-solid (conceptual): The views of an octagonal prism were mixed up with these. Check both views: the view from above shows the base, the front view shows whether the sides go up straight (a rectangle) or meet at a point (a triangle).

other-view (conceptual): This view belongs to another solid. From the front, a prism or cylinder shows straight upright sides (a rectangle); a pyramid or cone shows sides meeting at a point (a triangle).

teach.idea: A net is the solid's faces unfolded flat; a view is what you see from one side. Both come from the solid's parts: a prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles, a pyramid a base joined by triangles to a point; a cylinder has two circles and a curved side, a cone one circle and a curved side.
teach.method: For a net, count the pieces and look at their shapes: the ends or base name the solid. For a view, picture yourself looking from that side: from above you see the base's outline; from the front, straight upright sides look like a rectangle and sides meeting at a point look like a triangle.

alternatives.title: Unroll the curved surface
text: Cut a cylinder's curved side straight down and it unrolls into a rectangle; a cone's curved side unrolls into a fan shape (a sector).
So a cylinder's net is 2 circles and a rectangle, and a cone's is 1 circle and a sector.

alternatives.title: Look at real objects
text: A tin of oil is a cylinder, a birthday cap a cone, a Toblerone box a triangular prism.
Hold one at eye level and then look down on it from above; say what shape you see each time.

families.title: Top, front and side views of a building of cubes
explanations: all-cubes (conceptual): Every cube was counted. From the side, cubes in the same row hide each other: in each row you see only as high as the tallest stack.
whole-mat (procedural): An empty square of the mat was counted too. Where nothing is stacked you see no cube.
front-row-only (procedural): Only the front row was looked at. A taller stack further back shows above the front row.
front-for-side (procedural): The front view was counted instead of the side view. From the right-hand side, each ROW of the plan (from the front to the back) becomes one column of the view.

teach.idea: A view shows only what faces you: from above, the top of each stack; from the front, the tallest stack in each column (cubes behind are hidden); from the side, the tallest stack in each row.
teach.method: Top view: count the squares that have cubes. Front view: for each column find the biggest number and add these. Side view: for each row find the biggest number and add these.

alternatives.title: Build it with blocks
text: Build the stacks with cubes or matchboxes on squares drawn on paper.
Crouch down to eye level in front of them and count the squares you see, then do the same from the side.

alternatives.title: Draw each view on squared paper
text: For the front view, draw one column for each column of the plan, as tall as its tallest stack.
Count the squares in your drawing.

families.title: Which rule makes the sequence?
explanations: first-gap (procedural): Only the first step (512 to 1024) was checked. A rule must work for every step; here the steps are 512, 1024, 2048, 4096.
untested-rule (conceptual): A rule was chosen without testing it on the numbers. Try it on each number: does it really give 1024, 2048, 4096, …?
odd-even (conceptual): The numbers go up in 2s, as the even numbers do, but 59, 61, … are odd numbers (they end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9).
step-miscount (procedural): The step from one number to the next was miscounted by one: 12 to 23 is 11. Count on from 12 to check.
step-miscount-down (procedural): The step was counted one too small: 12 + 10 = 22, not 23.

teach.idea: A rule must explain EVERY number of the sequence, not just the first step. Look at the steps between numbers: equal steps mean 'add the same each time'; steps that grow by 1 give triangular numbers, by 2 square numbers; numbers that double are powers of 2.
teach.method: Write the steps (differences) between neighbouring numbers. If they are equal, the rule adds that number. If not, test the special sequences (squares, triangular, cubes, doubling) on all the numbers.

alternatives.title: A table of steps
text: Write the numbers in a row and the steps between them underneath.
If the steps themselves follow a pattern, write the steps of the steps: for square numbers they are all 2.

alternatives.title: Draw the numbers as dots
text: Square numbers make squares of dots, triangular numbers make triangles, and doubling makes two copies of the last picture.
Draw the first few as dots and see which picture fits.

families.title: Distance covered in one hour or one minute
explanations: multiply-not-divide (conceptual): The distance was multiplied by the time. In 1 minute the distance is less than the whole journey, so share it out: divide by 6.
whole-distance (conceptual): The whole distance was given. The question asks for the part covered in just 1 minute.
subtract-time (procedural): 6 was taken away from the distance. Sharing a distance equally over 6 minutes means dividing by 6.
division-slip (prerequisite): A slip in dividing 540 by 6. Check by multiplying back: the answer × 6 must give 540.

teach.idea: Speed tells how far something goes in ONE hour (or one minute). If the speed is steady, every hour covers the same part of the journey.
teach.method: Share the whole distance equally among the hours: distance ÷ time. Check by multiplying back.

alternatives.title: Build an hour-by-hour table
text: Make a table: after 1 hour, after 2 hours, and so on.
Guess the distance for 1 hour, keep adding it, and adjust the guess until the last row gives the whole distance.

families.title: Comparing two speeds from distance and time
explanations: farther-is-faster (conceptual): The child who went farther was taken as faster. Going farther may just mean cycling for longer: compare the distance in ONE minute.
bigger-distance (procedural): The longer distance was given instead of a speed. Speed is the distance in 1 minute: distance ÷ minutes.
less-time-is-faster (conceptual): The child with the shorter time was taken as faster, but they cycled different distances. Work out each child's metres in one minute.

teach.idea: To compare speeds fairly, compare the distance each covers in the SAME time: one minute (or one hour).
teach.method: For each one, divide distance by time to get the distance in 1 minute. The bigger result is the faster one.

alternatives.title: Stretch both to the same time
text: Find a time both can be scaled to, e.g. 12 minutes for 3 and 4 minutes.
Multiply each distance up to that time; the one that goes farther in the same time is faster.

families.title: Adding and subtracting decimals with different places
explanations: right-align (conceptual): The digits were lined up from the right, as for whole numbers, so tenths were added to hundredths. Line up the decimal points: write 19.8 as 19.80.
no-carry (procedural): A column added up to 10 or more, but the 1 was not carried to the next place on the left.
bring-down (procedural): The empty hundredths place in 19.8 was skipped and the 6 was brought down. Write 19.8 as 19.80: the empty place is a 0, and you take 6 away from it by exchanging.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): In each column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, exchange 1 from the next place first.

teach.idea: Each place has a value: ones, tenths, hundredths. Only digits of the same place can be added or taken away, so the decimal points must line up.
teach.method: Write the numbers one under the other with the decimal points in a line. Fill empty places with 0, then add or subtract from the right as with whole numbers, and keep the point in the answer.

alternatives.title: Think of rupees and paise
text: Read 4.5 as ₹4.50 and 2.37 as ₹2.37: 50 paise and 37 paise are both paise, so they go together.
Add the paise, then the rupees, exchanging 100 paise for ₹1 when needed.

families.title: Adding and subtracting money in rupees and paise
explanations: paise-over-100 (conceptual): The paise were added to 150 and all written after the point. 150 paise is ₹1 and 50 paise, so carry ₹1 to the rupees.
rupee-not-carried (procedural): 100 paise were taken away from the paise but the ₹1 they make was not added to the rupees.
smaller-paise-from-larger (procedural): 55 paise is less than 95 paise, so 55 was taken from 95 instead. Change ₹1 into 100 paise first: 155 − 95.
rupee-not-reduced (procedural): ₹1 was changed into paise, but the rupees were not made one less (₹80 becomes ₹79).

teach.idea: 100 paise make ₹1. Paise go with paise and rupees with rupees, and 100 paise can be swapped for ₹1 (or ₹1 for 100 paise).
teach.method: Line up the decimal points. Work on the paise first, exchanging ₹1 and 100 paise when needed, then the rupees.

alternatives.title: Change everything into paise
text: ₹45.50 is 4550 paise and ₹28.75 is 2875 paise.
Add or subtract the paise as whole numbers, then put the point back two places from the right: 7425 paise = ₹74.25.
