families.title: Listing all the factors of a number
explanations: forget-1-and-n (conceptual): 1 and 100 were left out. Every number has 1 and itself as factors: 1 × 100 = 100.
half-the-pairs (procedural): Only the first number of each factor pair was written. Each factor comes with a partner: write both numbers of every pair.
multiples-for-factors (conceptual): Multiples of 100 were listed. Factors divide 100 exactly, so they are never bigger than 100.

teach.idea: A factor of a number divides it exactly. Factors come in pairs: if a × b = n, both a and b are factors of n.
teach.method: Try 1, 2, 3, … in order. Each time one divides exactly, write it and its partner. Stop when the numbers meet in the middle.

alternatives.title: Make rectangles of dots
text: Arrange the number as dots in a rectangle: rows × columns.
Every rectangle you can make gives a factor pair; a number with only one rectangle (1 row) is prime.

families.title: Common factors of two numbers
explanations: hcf-only (conceptual): Only the highest common factor was given. The question asks for every number that divides both.
forget-1 (conceptual): 1 was left out; 1 divides every number, so it is always a common factor.
factors-of-one (procedural): All the factors of 56 were listed. Check each one: does it also divide 60?

teach.idea: A common factor divides both numbers exactly. 1 is always one; the largest is the HCF.
teach.method: List the factors of the smaller number, then keep only the ones that also divide the larger number.

alternatives.title: Find the HCF first
text: Find the largest number that divides both (the HCF).
Every common factor is a factor of the HCF: list the factors of the HCF.

families.title: Common multiples from jumps on a number line
explanations: first-only (procedural): Only the first meeting point was given. After 24 they meet again every 24: keep going up to 60.
one-animal (conceptual): These are all the frog's landing places. A common multiple must be a landing place for the rabbit too.
product (conceptual): Only multiples of 6 × 10 were used. 6 and 10 share a factor, so they meet sooner, at 30.

teach.idea: A number where both animals land is in both times tables: a common multiple. After the first one, they meet again at regular steps of that same size.
teach.method: Write the multiples of the bigger jump and check each one: does the smaller jump also land there? Collect those up to the end of the line.

alternatives.title: Two lists side by side
text: Write the frog's landing places in one row and the rabbit's in the row below.
Circle the numbers that appear in both rows.

families.title: The lowest common multiple of two numbers
explanations: hcf-for-lcm (conceptual): The highest common factor was found. The LCM is the smallest number that BOTH divide into: it is never smaller than the larger number.
larger-number (procedural): 24 was given, but 24 is not in the 23 times table. Keep going along the 24 times table.
common-not-lowest (procedural): A common multiple was found, but not the lowest one. Check the smaller multiples first.
product (conceptual): 22 × 24 is a common multiple, but 22 and 24 share the factor 2, so a smaller one comes first.

teach.idea: A common multiple is in both times tables. The lowest one is the first time they meet.
teach.method: Go up the times table of the larger number and stop at the first one the smaller number divides exactly.

alternatives.title: Use prime factors
text: Write each number as a product of primes, e.g. 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3.
Take each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either: 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36.

alternatives.title: Divide both together
text: Divide both numbers by a common factor and write the quotients below; repeat until no common factor is left.
Multiply the divisors on the left by the numbers left at the bottom.

families.title: The highest common factor of three numbers
explanations: two-only (procedural): This is the HCF of 54 and 66 only. Check that it divides 70 too.
smallest-number (conceptual): The smallest number, 60, was given, but 60 does not divide all of them.
a-common-factor (conceptual): A common factor was found, but not the highest one. Look for a bigger number that divides all three.

teach.idea: The HCF is the biggest number that divides every one of the numbers exactly.
teach.method: Find the HCF of the first two numbers, then find the HCF of that result and the third number.

alternatives.title: List and compare factors
text: List the factors of the smallest number, biggest first.
The first one that divides the other two numbers exactly is the HCF.

alternatives.title: Common prime factors
text: Write each number as a product of primes.
Multiply the primes that appear in all three (as many times as they appear in every one).

families.title: Writing a mixed number as an improper fraction
explanations: add-whole-to-top (conceptual): 9 was added to the numerator. Each whole is 10/10, so 9 wholes are 90 pieces of size 1/10.
forget-numerator (procedural): Only the wholes were changed into pieces; the 9/10 was not added on.
fact-slip (prerequisite): The multiplication 9 × 10 is not yet reliable.
times-numerator (procedural): The whole number was multiplied by the numerator and the denominator was added. Multiply the whole number by the DENOMINATOR, then add the numerator.

teach.idea: A whole cut into d equal pieces is d/d. So w wholes are w × d pieces, and the fraction part adds a few more pieces of the same size.
teach.method: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and write the total over the same denominator.

alternatives.title: Cut every whole into pieces
text: Draw each whole as a bar cut into the same number of pieces as the denominator.
Count all the pieces, including the extra ones: that count goes on top.

families.title: Writing an improper fraction as a mixed number
explanations: swap (procedural): The quotient and the remainder swapped places. 99 ÷ 10 = 9 remainder 9: 9 wholes, and the 9 pieces left over go on top.
too-few-wholes (procedural): One whole was missed: 19/10 is more than 1, so another whole can be taken out.
remainder-as-denominator (conceptual): The pieces keep their size: the denominator stays 10.
division-slip (prerequisite): A slip in dividing 99 by 10. Check: 10 × whole number + numerator must give 99.

teach.idea: A whole is made of d pieces of size 1/d. Dividing the numerator by the denominator tells how many wholes there are; the remainder is the pieces left.
teach.method: Divide the numerator by the denominator. The quotient is the whole number, the remainder is the new numerator, and the denominator stays the same.

alternatives.title: Count out the wholes
text: Take away d/d (one whole) again and again, counting the wholes.
When less than a whole is left, that is the fraction part.

families.title: Order of operations with brackets
explanations: left-to-right (conceptual): The adding was done first. Division comes before addition: work out 12 ÷ 6 first.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (11 × 3) is not yet reliable.
ignore-brackets (conceptual): The brackets were ignored. Work out what is inside the brackets first.
add-before-subtract (conceptual): 11 + 8 was worked out first. Adding and taking away have equal rank: go from left to right, 39 − 11 first.

teach.idea: Everyone agrees on one order so an expression has only one value: brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −; equal ranks go from left to right.
teach.method: Look for brackets and work them out. Next do every × and ÷, left to right. Last do + and −, left to right.

alternatives.title: Draw it as a tree
text: Put the last operation at the top of a tree, with its two parts as branches: 6 + 4 × 3 has + at the top, with 6 on one branch and 4 × 3 on the other.
Work from the bottom of the tree upwards: 4 × 3 = 12, then 6 + 12 = 18.

alternatives.title: Split into terms
text: Cut the expression at every + and − that is not inside brackets: each piece is a term.
Work out each term on its own, then add and take away the terms from left to right.

families.title: Writing a fraction or decimal as a percentage
explanations: numerator-as-percent (conceptual): The numerator was taken as the percentage. Per cent means out of 100: change 49/50 into hundredths first.
add-not-scale (procedural): The same number was added to the top and bottom to make the bottom 100. To keep the fraction the same size, MULTIPLY both by 2.
unit-fraction (procedural): 1/100 is 1%, but there are 99 of them: 99 × 1 = 99.
one-place (conceptual): The point moved only one place. Per cent means hundredths: 0.99 is 99 hundredths, so it is 99%.
zero-ignored (conceptual): The 0 straight after the point was ignored. 0.09 is 9 hundredths, not 9 tenths.

teach.idea: Per cent means 'out of 100'. A percentage is a number of hundredths: 37% = 37/100 = 0.37.
teach.method: Turn the fraction into hundredths by multiplying top and bottom by the same number; for a decimal, read how many hundredths it is. That number of hundredths is the percentage.

alternatives.title: Shade a hundred square
text: A 10 × 10 square has 100 small squares; each one is 1%.
Shade the part the fraction or decimal stands for and count the small squares.

families.title: Writing a percentage as a decimal
explanations: tenths (conceptual): 150% was written as 150 tenths. Per cent means hundredths: 150% = 150/100.
thousandths (procedural): The point moved three places. Dividing by 100 moves the point two places to the left.
drop-sign (conceptual): The % sign was just dropped. 150% is 150 out of 100, which is 1.5.

teach.idea: Per cent means hundredths, so x% is x/100. Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right of where it was.
teach.method: Write the percentage over 100, then write it as a decimal: the last two digits of the number become the tenths and hundredths.

alternatives.title: Think of paise in a rupee
text: ₹1 has 100 paise, so 1% of a rupee is 1 paisa.
7% of a rupee is 7 paise = ₹0.07; 45% is 45 paise = ₹0.45.

families.title: Listing the prime numbers in a range
explanations: odd-is-prime (conceptual): Some odd numbers that are not prime were included (87, 91, 93). Being odd is not enough: test whether 3, 5, 7 or another number divides it.
one-is-prime (conceptual): 1 was counted as prime. A prime has exactly two factors; 1 has only one factor.
two-not-prime (conceptual): 2 was left out because it is even. 2 has exactly two factors (1 and 2), so it is prime: the only even prime.

teach.idea: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.
teach.method: For each number, try dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7 (enough up to 100, unless the number is that prime). If none divides it exactly, it is prime.

alternatives.title: Use a sieve
text: Write the numbers in a grid. Cross out 1.
Keep 2 and cross out every other multiple of 2; keep 3 and cross out its multiples; do the same for 5 and 7. The numbers left are prime.

alternatives.title: Only one rectangle
text: Try to arrange the number as dots in a rectangle with more than one row.
If the only rectangle is a single row, the number is prime.

families.title: Finding a counterexample to a claim
explanations: confirming-example (conceptual): 9 agrees with the claim, so it does not show the claim is wrong. To show a claim is not always true, find ONE number where it fails.

teach.idea: A claim that says 'every' must work for ALL numbers. One number where it fails, a counterexample, is enough to show it is not always true; numbers where it works never prove it.
teach.method: Test each number: does it fit the first part of the claim? If yes, does the rest of the claim hold? The number that fits the first part but not the rest is the counterexample.

alternatives.title: Two ticks
text: Make two columns: 'is it one the claim talks about?' and 'does the claim hold?'.
The counterexample has a tick in the first column and a cross in the second.

families.title: Fractions greater than 1 on a number line
explanations: counted-start (procedural): The starting point 0 was counted as a jump. Count the jumps (the arcs), not the marks they start and end on.
jumps-as-wholes (conceptual): Each jump was counted as 1 whole. Each jump is only 1/7: 7 jumps make 1 whole.
not-simplest (procedural): 3 6/8 is the right amount but not in its simplest form: 6/8 = 3/4.

teach.idea: On a number line every whole is cut into equal parts. A fraction greater than 1 lies beyond 1: its whole-number part says how many wholes are passed, and the fraction part how far into the next whole.
teach.method: Count the jumps: that many parts is (jumps)/(parts in a whole). Take out the whole ones (each is one full set of parts) and write the rest as the fraction part; simplify it.

alternatives.title: Count whole by whole
text: Every whole on the line holds the same number of jumps (the denominator).
Count how many wholes the jumps fill, then count the jumps past the last whole number.

alternatives.title: Use fraction strips
text: Lay strips of 1/d end to end along a ruler marked in whole units.
Where the last strip ends is the number: wholes, and a part of the next whole.

families.title: Which pair of numbers is co-prime?
explanations: odd-means-coprime (conceptual): Two odd numbers were taken to have no common factor. Odd numbers have no factor 2, but they can share another one: 45 and 75 are both divisible by 15.
prime-means-coprime (conceptual): A pair with a prime number in it was taken to be co-prime. A prime has no factors except 1 and itself, but it can still divide the other number: 51 = 17 × 3.

teach.idea: Co-prime numbers have no common factor except 1, so their HCF is 1. Neither number needs to be prime: 8 and 15 are co-prime, but 9 and 15 are not.
teach.method: For each pair, test the small primes 2, 3, 5, 7, … : if one of them divides both numbers, the pair is not co-prime. If none does, it is.

alternatives.title: Compare factor lists
text: List the factors of both numbers.
If 1 is the only number in both lists, they are co-prime.

alternatives.title: Look at prime factors
text: Write each number as a product of primes: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2, 15 = 3 × 5.
No prime appears in both, so they are co-prime.

families.title: Writing an expression for a situation
explanations: brackets (conceptual): The mangoes taken out were taken away only once. They are taken from EVERY box, so take them from each box first (inside brackets), then multiply by the number of boxes.
order-of-story (procedural): The numbers were mixed up: it is the mangoes in each box, minus those taken out, that is multiplied by the number of boxes.

teach.idea: An expression is the story written in numbers and signs. Brackets show what must be worked out first; without brackets, × and ÷ are done before + and −.
teach.method: Say the story in steps: what is there at the start, what is added or taken away, what is repeated. Write each step, and put brackets round anything that must happen before a multiplication.

alternatives.title: Check with the story's answer
text: Work the story out step by step without any expression.
Evaluate each option (brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −); the one that gives the story's answer is right.

alternatives.title: Draw the story as a tree
text: The last step of the story goes at the top of the tree; what it uses hangs below as branches.
Read the tree back as an expression, with brackets round each branch that is an operation.

families.title: The terms of an expression
explanations: counted-numbers (conceptual): The numbers were counted. A term is a part joined to the rest by + or −; a product like 4 × 3 is one term.
split-brackets (procedural): The + inside a bracket was taken to start a new term. A bracket is worked out as one piece, so (5 + 2) × 3 is a single term.
sign-dropped (conceptual): The minus sign in front was left off. The term includes its sign: after a minus sign the term is negative.
first-number (procedural): Only the first number of the term was taken. The term is everything up to the next + or − outside brackets: 5 × 9.

teach.idea: The terms of an expression are the parts joined by + and − (outside brackets). Each term carries the sign in front of it: 20 − 3 × 4 + 6 is 20 + (−12) + 6, with terms 20, −3 × 4 and 6.
teach.method: Read along the expression and cut it at every + and − that is not inside brackets. Each piece, with the sign before it, is a term; work out each term on its own.

alternatives.title: Underline each term
text: Underline each piece between the + and − signs; a whole bracket and whatever multiplies it stays in one piece.
Count the underlined pieces, and write the sign in front of each.

alternatives.title: Think of money in and out
text: Each term is one amount of money: + means money coming in, − money going out.
4 × 3 after a minus sign is one payment of ₹12 going out: the term −12.

families.title: Measurement problems with two units (m and cm, kg and g, km and m, L and mL)
explanations: units-not-matched (conceptual): 550 mL was taken from 9.7 L as if they were the same unit. Change mL into L first: 550 mL = 0.55 L.
wrong-factor (recall): The mL were changed into L by dividing by 100. 1 L = 1000 mL, so divide by 1000.

teach.idea: Only amounts in the same unit can be added or taken away. 1 m = 100 cm, and 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 km = 1000 m, 1 L = 1000 mL, so the smaller unit becomes a decimal of the larger one.
teach.method: Change the amount in the smaller unit into the larger unit (divide by 100 or 1000), line up the decimal points, then add or subtract.

alternatives.title: Work in the smaller unit
text: Change both amounts into the smaller unit: 2.5 kg = 2500 g.
Add or subtract the whole numbers, then change back: 2500 g + 750 g = 3250 g = 3.25 kg.

alternatives.title: Use a place-value table
text: Write the amounts in a table with columns ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths of the larger unit.
750 g is 0.750 kg: the 7 goes in the tenths column.

families.title: The lowest common multiple of three numbers
explanations: product (conceptual): 15 × 16 × 20 is a common multiple, but the numbers share factors, so a smaller one comes first.
two-only (procedural): This is the LCM of 16 and 20 only. Check that 15 divides it too.
hcf-for-lcm (conceptual): A common factor was found. The LCM is the smallest number that all three divide into: it is never smaller than the largest number.
common-not-lowest (procedural): A common multiple was found, but not the lowest. Check the smaller multiples first.

teach.idea: The LCM of three numbers is the smallest number in all three times tables.
teach.method: Find the LCM of two of the numbers, then the LCM of that and the third. Or go up the times table of the largest number until the other two both divide it.

alternatives.title: Divide all three together
text: Divide by a prime that divides at least two of the numbers; write the quotients (and copy any number it does not divide).
Repeat until no two numbers share a factor; multiply all the divisors and the numbers left at the bottom.

alternatives.title: Highest powers of primes
text: Write each number as a product of primes.
Take each prime as many times as it appears in the number that has most of it, and multiply.

families.title: Sharing, grouping and timing problems: HCF or LCM?
explanations: lcm-for-hcf (conceptual): The LCM was found. Sharing or cutting into the greatest equal parts needs the greatest number that divides both: the HCF.
a-common-factor (procedural): A number that divides both was found, but not the greatest one.
hcf-for-lcm (conceptual): The HCF was found. Waiting until two repeating things happen together needs the smallest number both divide into: the LCM.
product (procedural): 25 × 30 is a common multiple, but 25 and 30 share the factor 5, so they meet sooner.

teach.idea: Sharing or cutting into the biggest equal parts with nothing left over uses the HCF (it divides both). Waiting for two repeating events to happen together, or buying equal amounts in packets, uses the LCM (both divide it).
teach.method: Ask: is the answer smaller than the numbers (a part of them)? Then it is the HCF. Is it bigger (a time or amount both reach)? Then it is the LCM. Then work it out.

alternatives.title: Try it out
text: For a timing problem, list the times each event happens: 6, 12, 18, … and 8, 16, 24, ….
The first time in both lists is the answer. For sharing, try the number of plates from the biggest down.

alternatives.title: Is the answer bigger or smaller?
text: Groups and pieces must fit INTO the amounts: the answer is at most the smaller number (HCF).
Meeting times come AFTER both: the answer is at least the bigger number (LCM).

families.title: Using HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers
explanations: product-is-lcm (conceptual): The product 30 × 105 was given as the LCM. The product equals HCF × LCM, so divide it by the HCF, 15.
hcf-times (procedural): The HCF was multiplied by the product instead of dividing it into the product.
forgot-hcf (procedural): The LCM was divided by 70, leaving out the HCF. HCF × LCM = 70 × (other number), so the other number is 14 × 490 ÷ 70.
lcm-over-hcf (procedural): The LCM was divided by the HCF. Use HCF × LCM ÷ (the number you know).
lcm-over-number (procedural): The LCM was divided by one number. The HCF is the product of the two numbers ÷ the LCM.
product-is-hcf (conceptual): The product of the numbers was not divided by the LCM. HCF × LCM = product, so the HCF = product ÷ LCM.

teach.idea: For two numbers, HCF × LCM = the product of the numbers: the common prime factors are counted once in the HCF and the rest in the LCM, so together they use every prime factor of both numbers exactly once.
teach.method: Write HCF × LCM = first number × second number, put in the three values you know, and divide to find the fourth.

alternatives.title: Check with a small example
text: Use the same pattern with the numbers in the question.

alternatives.title: Split into prime factors
text: Write both numbers as products of primes; the HCF takes the shared primes, the LCM takes the rest of them as well.
Multiplying HCF and LCM uses every prime of both numbers, the same as multiplying the numbers.

families.title: Writing a percentage or a decimal as a fraction in its simplest form
explanations: not-simplified (procedural): 98/100 is right but not in its simplest form: divide the top and bottom by 2.
percent-as-tenths (conceptual): 198% was written over 10. Per cent means out of 100: 198% = 198/100.
hundredths-always (conceptual): Every decimal was put over 100. 0.98 has 2 decimal places, so it is 98 over 100.

teach.idea: A percentage is a number of hundredths, and a decimal is a number of tenths, hundredths or thousandths. Either can be written as a fraction and then simplified.
teach.method: Percentage: write it over 100 (multiply top and bottom by 10 to clear a decimal point, as 12.5/100 = 125/1000). Decimal: write the digits over 10, 100 or 1000 (one zero for each decimal place). Then divide the top and bottom by their HCF.

alternatives.title: Find the HCF in one go
text: Find the HCF of the top and bottom (for 375 and 1000 it is 125).
Divide both by it once: 375/1000 = 3/8.

families.title: Writing a fraction as a decimal or a percentage
explanations: digits-joined (conceptual): The numerator and denominator were just written next to each other. 99/50 means 99 ÷ 50, and then × 100 for a percentage.
divided-wrong-way (procedural): 50 was divided by 99. The fraction 99/50 is 99 ÷ 50: the top divided by the bottom.

teach.idea: A fraction n/d means n ÷ d. Dividing gives the decimal; a percentage is that decimal × 100 (the number of hundredths).
teach.method: Divide the numerator by the denominator (long division, adding zeros after the point), or scale the fraction to a denominator of 10, 100 or 1000. For a percentage, multiply the decimal by 100.

families.title: Testing for primes by dividing up to the square root
explanations: up-to-half (conceptual): Primes up to half of 997 were tried. If 997 had a factor bigger than its square root, it would have a partner factor smaller than the square root, already tested. So stop at √997 ≈ 31.
root-not-prime (procedural): 31 is the whole number below √997, but only primes need to be tried: 31 is not prime.
half-a-check (procedural): A factor was guessed without checking. Every prime up to √997 ≈ 31 leaves a remainder, so 997 is prime.
stopped-early (procedural): Only 2, 3 and 5 were tried, and 989 was called prime. Keep going with 7, 11, 13, … up to √989 ≈ 31: 23 divides 989.
largest-factor (conceptual): 43 is a factor, but the question asks for the smallest prime factor: 989 = 23 × 43.

teach.idea: Factors come in pairs: if n = a × b, one of a and b is at most √n. So if no prime up to √n divides n, n has no factor other than 1 and itself: it is prime.
teach.method: Find the whole number just below √n (the largest k with k² ≤ n). Divide n by each prime up to k. The first one that divides exactly is the smallest prime factor; if none does, n is prime.

alternatives.title: Use a list of squares
text: Try each prime whose square is not more than n; stop at the first prime whose square is bigger than n.

alternatives.title: Factor pairs meet at the square root
text: For 91: 1 × 91, 7 × 13. The pairs close in on √91 ≈ 9.5 from both sides.
Once you pass the square root, every factor you would find is the partner of one already found.

families.title: The steps of Euclid's division algorithm
explanations: last-not-counted (procedural): The last division, the one with remainder 0, was not counted. It is the step that shows the algorithm is finished.
first-remainder (procedural): The remainder of the first division was given. In the second division, 857 is divided by 142.
quotient-for-remainder (procedural): The quotient of the second division was given. 857 = 142 × 6 + 5: the remainder is what is left over.

teach.idea: If a = bq + r, every common factor of a and b is also a factor of r, so HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, r). Repeating with smaller and smaller numbers must end with remainder 0; the last divisor is the HCF. (Aryabhata's 'mutual division' uses the same chain of divisions.)
teach.method: Write a = b × q + r. Replace (a, b) by (b, r) and repeat. Stop when the remainder is 0: the divisor at that step is the HCF.

alternatives.title: Cut squares from a rectangle
text: Cutting the biggest squares from a rectangle is one division: the number of squares is the quotient, the leftover strip the remainder.
Keep cutting squares from the strip; the side of the last squares, which fit exactly, is the HCF.

alternatives.title: Keep a table
text: Make columns: dividend, divisor, quotient, remainder.
Each new row starts with the last row's divisor and remainder; count the rows at the end.

families.title: HCF and LCM from prime factorisations
explanations: highest-for-hcf (conceptual): The higher power of each prime was taken. The HCF uses each COMMON prime with the LOWER power (the most that divides both numbers).
primes-once (procedural): Each common prime was taken only once. The HCF takes each common prime to the lower of its two powers.
lowest-for-lcm (conceptual): The lower powers of the common primes were taken: that is the HCF. The LCM takes every prime that appears, with the HIGHER power.
product (conceptual): The two numbers were multiplied. They share primes, so the LCM is 24 × 2205 ÷ HCF.

teach.idea: By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic every number has exactly one prime factorisation. A common factor can only use primes both numbers have, as often as both allow; a common multiple must contain every prime of each number.
teach.method: HCF: multiply the common primes, each to the LOWER of its two powers. LCM: multiply every prime that appears, each to the HIGHER power. Check: HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers.

alternatives.title: Sort the primes in a Venn diagram
text: Put the shared prime factors in the middle and the rest on each side.
The middle multiplied is the HCF; everything multiplied is the LCM.

alternatives.title: A table of powers
text: Make a row for each number and a column for each prime, writing its power (0 if missing).
Take the smaller entry in each column for the HCF and the bigger for the LCM.

families.title: Proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers
explanations: reversed-rule (conceptual): The rule was turned round. In a proper fraction the top number is SMALLER than the bottom one, as in 11/12: it is less than 1.
one-is-proper (conceptual): 12/12 is exactly 1, so it was taken as proper. A proper fraction is less than 1; when the top equals the bottom (or is bigger) the fraction is improper.

more-than-one-mixed (conceptual): 35/12 is more than 1, so it was called a mixed number. It is written as one fraction with the top bigger than the bottom: an improper fraction. A mixed number has a whole number written in front.
more-than-one-improper (conceptual): 4 11/12 is more than 1, so it was called improper. It is written as a whole number and a proper fraction side by side: a mixed number.

teach.idea: A proper fraction is less than 1 (top smaller than bottom). An improper fraction has the top equal to or bigger than the bottom, so it is 1 or more. A mixed number writes a value over 1 as a whole number and a proper fraction.
teach.method: Is there a whole number in front? Then it is a mixed number. If not, compare the top and the bottom: top smaller → proper; top equal or bigger → improper.

alternatives.title: Count the pieces
text: 7/4 of a pizza cut in quarters is 7 quarters: more than one whole pizza.
1 3/4 is the same amount written as 1 whole pizza and 3 quarters.

alternatives.title: Place it on a number line
text: Fractions between 0 and 1 are proper.
From 1 onwards they are improper, or can be written as mixed numbers.

families.title: The value of an expression given as a tree diagram
explanations: read-flat (conceptual): The numbers and signs were read in a line from left to right (12 − 7 × 5 + 8), ignoring the branches. A box must be worked out before the box above it uses its value: that is what brackets do.

bodmas-without-brackets (conceptual): The expression was written without brackets (12 − 7 × 5 + 8) and worked out by the usual order. The tree says which part comes first: write it with brackets, (12 − 7) × (5 + 8).

teach.idea: A tree diagram shows the order of work: the operation at the top is done last, and each branch that is a box must be worked out first. Written as an expression, every such branch goes in brackets.
teach.method: Start at the bottom: work out each box whose branches are both numbers. Put its value in place of the box, and move up until the top box is done.

alternatives.title: Write it with brackets
text: Write the top box as (left branch) op (right branch).
Replace each branch that is a box by its own expression in brackets; then work out the brackets first.

alternatives.title: Children before parents
text: Think of each box as a parent and its branches as children.
A parent can only be worked out when all its children have values.

families.title: Solving a one-step equation
explanations: same-operation (conceptual): 20 was divided by 10; x ÷ 10 = 20 is undone by multiplying by 10.
subtract-coefficient (conceptual): 10 was taken away from 190; 10x means 10 × x, so divide by 10.
add-for-multiply (procedural): 10 was added to 20; undoing ÷ 10 needs × 10.

teach.idea: An equation is a balance: both sides have the same value. Doing the opposite operation to both sides keeps it balanced and leaves x alone.
teach.method: Look at what is done to x (+, −, ×, ÷). Do the opposite to both sides. Then put your answer back into the equation to check it.

alternatives.title: Guess, check and improve
text: Ask: which number makes the equation true? Try one, work out the left side, and compare.
If the left side is too big, try a smaller number; too small, try a bigger one.

alternatives.title: Keep the balance level
text: Picture the two sides on a balance.
Whatever you take off or add on one side, do the same on the other, until x is alone.

families.title: Collecting like terms
explanations: unlike-combined (conceptual): x terms and y terms were added together into one term. Only like terms (the same letter) can be added: x terms with x terms, y terms with y terms.
squared-letters (conceptual): Adding x terms was written as a power (like x + x = x²). Adding like terms only adds the numbers in front: 2x + 3x = 5x.
sign-dropped (prerequisite): A minus sign in front of a term was lost. The sign belongs to the term that follows it.

teach.idea: Like terms have the same letter part: 3x and −5x are like terms, 3x and 2y are not. Like terms can be added because they count the same thing.
teach.method: Group the x terms and the y terms, keeping each sign with the term after it. Add the numbers in front of each group and write one term for each letter.

alternatives.title: Count things of the same kind
text: Read x as 'apples' and y as 'bananas': 3 apples + 2 bananas + 4 apples is 7 apples + 2 bananas.
You cannot add apples to bananas to get 'applebananas', just as 3x + 2y is not 5xy.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Put x = 2 and y = 1 into the question and into your answer.
If the two values are different, a term has been combined wrongly.

families.title: Subtracting one expression from another
explanations: minus-first-term-only (procedural): The minus sign was used on 5x but not on −4. A minus in front of a bracket changes the sign of every term inside it.
added-instead (procedural): The two expressions were added. The question takes the second bracket away.
wrong-order (procedural): The first expression was taken away from the second. The order matters: (first) − (second).

teach.idea: Taking away a bracket takes away every term inside it, so each sign in the bracket changes: −(3x − 4) = −3x + 4.
teach.method: Remove the brackets, changing every sign in the second one. Then collect the x terms and the number terms.

alternatives.title: Add the opposite
text: Subtracting is adding the opposite: (5x + 2) − (2x − 3) = (5x + 2) + (−2x + 3).
Now add like terms as usual.

alternatives.title: Line up like terms
text: Write the first expression above the second, x terms under x terms and numbers under numbers.
Subtract each column, taking care with negative numbers.

families.title: Coefficients and the constant term
explanations: sign-dropped (conceptual): The sign was left out. The coefficient includes the sign in front of the term: in 5 − 3y the coefficient of y is −3.
invisible-one (conceptual): A term with no number in front was given coefficient 0. A term like xy means 1 × xy, so its coefficient is 1 (or −1 with a minus sign).
power-for-coefficient (conceptual): The power 2 in x² was taken as the coefficient. The coefficient is the number multiplying x², written in front of it.

teach.idea: An expression is a sum of terms. Each term is a number (the coefficient, with its sign) times letters; a term with no letter is the constant term.
teach.method: Split the expression at each + or −, keeping the sign with the term after it. The coefficient is the signed number in front of the letters; no number means 1.

alternatives.title: Make a table of terms
text: Write each term in its own column: for 4x² − xy + 3y − 9 the terms are 4x², −xy, 3y, −9.
Under each, write its number part: 4, −1, 3 and −9.

families.title: The top of a number pyramid
explanations: bottom-row-sum (conceptual): Only the bottom row was added up. Each block is used again in the rows above, so the middle blocks count more than once.
three-rows (procedural): The middle blocks were counted twice, as in a pyramid with three rows. With four rows, each middle block of the bottom row reaches the top 3 times.
x-counted-once (procedural): The x terms were not all collected: x appears in more than one block on the way up, and each one must be added.

teach.idea: In a four-row pyramid the corner blocks of the bottom row reach the top once and the two middle blocks reach it 3 times each, so the top is 1, 3, 3, 1 times the bottom blocks.
teach.method: Write the second row as sums, then the third row, then the top, collecting like terms at each step.

alternatives.title: Count the paths to the top
text: Each bottom block adds into the top once for every path upward.
A corner block has 1 path; a middle block has 3 paths. So top = first + 3 × second + 3 × third + fourth.

alternatives.title: Try a number for x
text: Put x = 0 and build the pyramid: that gives the number part of the answer.
Then put x = 1: the top grows by the coefficient of x.

families.title: An expression for a growing pattern
explanations: step-as-expression (conceptual): The rule 'add 9 each time' was written as n + 9. Figure n has 9 added n times, which is 9n, plus a fixed part.
first-term-as-coefficient (conceptual): The first figure's count, 18, was used as the number multiplying n. The number that multiplies n is how many are added each time (9).
first-term-as-constant (procedural): The first figure's count was added on as the fixed part. Check Figure 1: 9 × 1 + 18 is not 18.
constant-forgotten (procedural): Only the growing part 9n was written. Check with Figure 1: 9 × 1 = 9, but the figure has 18.

teach.idea: If a pattern grows by the same amount d each time, Figure n is d × n plus a fixed part. The fixed part is what makes Figure 1 come out right.
teach.method: Find how many are added each time: that number multiplies n. Then compare d × 1 with Figure 1 to find what to add or take away. Check with Figure 2.

alternatives.title: Go back to Figure 0
text: Step back once from Figure 1: Figure 0 would have (Figure 1) − d.
That is the fixed part; then add d for each figure: d n + (Figure 0).

alternatives.title: See the groups in the picture
text: In a row of squares made of matchsticks, each new square needs 3 more sticks and the first square needs one extra.
So n squares need 3n + 1 sticks: 3 for each square, plus the first stick.

families.title: Why a 'think of a number' trick works
explanations: bracket-not-multiplied (procedural): Only 9n was multiplied by 5, not the 9 added to it. Multiplying 'the result' multiplies the whole of 9n + 9.
number-not-multiplied (procedural): The 9 was multiplied by 5 but 9n was not. Every term in the bracket is multiplied by 5.

teach.idea: Using a letter for the number lets you follow the trick for every number at once. When the added numbers cancel, the answer depends only on n, which is why the trick always works.
teach.method: Write each step as an expression, using brackets when a whole result is multiplied. Expand the brackets and collect like terms.

alternatives.title: Try a few numbers first
text: Play the trick with n = 1, 2 and 3 and write the results.
Look for the pattern (each result is a fixed multiple of n), then show it with algebra.

alternatives.title: Bags and counters
text: Picture n as a closed bag of counters and the numbers as loose counters.
Follow the steps with bags and counters: the loose counters all leave at the end, so only the bags are left.

families.title: Terms from a recursive rule
explanations: started-late (procedural): The list started at t₂. The first term is t₁ = 9 itself; the rule makes the terms after it.
add-before-multiply (procedural): 9 was added before multiplying by 2. The rule multiplies the term first, then adds.
sign-dropped (prerequisite): The minus sign in the rule was lost: tₙ₊₁ = … − 1 takes 1 away.
multiplier-ignored (procedural): Only the addition was used. Each new term is 2 times the last one, then plus 9.

teach.idea: A recursive rule tells you how to get each term from the one before it; the first term starts the chain.
teach.method: Write t₁. Put it into the rule to get t₂, put t₂ in to get t₃, and so on. Do the operations in the order the rule gives.

alternatives.title: A table of n and tₙ
text: Make two columns: n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and tₙ.
Fill each row from the row above using the rule, showing the working.

alternatives.title: A number machine
text: Think of the rule as a machine: a term goes in, the next term comes out.
Feed each output back in as the next input.

families.title: From a recursive rule to a formula for tₙ
explanations: one-jump-too-many (procedural): t₁ = 20 was used as the fixed part. To reach tₙ from t₁ there are n − 1 jumps of −1, not n.
step-added-to-n (conceptual): The rule was copied with n in place of tₙ. Each step adds −1, so n steps add −1 × n.
swapped (procedural): The first term and the step were swapped. The number multiplying n is the step (what is added each time).

teach.idea: Adding d each time means tₙ is the first term plus (n − 1) steps of d: tₙ = t₁ + (n − 1)d.
teach.method: Write t₁ + (n − 1)d with the numbers, open the bracket and collect the numbers. Check that n = 1 gives t₁ and n = 2 gives t₂.

alternatives.title: Find term number 0
text: Step back once from t₁: t₀ = t₁ − d.
Then tₙ = dn + t₀, since n steps of d take you from t₀ to tₙ.

families.title: A Virahanka-Fibonacci style sequence
explanations: off-by-one (procedural): The terms were miscounted by one. Number each term as you write it: term 1 is the first number given.
arithmetic (conceptual): The sequence was treated as adding −2 each time. Here each term is the sum of the two before it, so the jumps grow.

teach.idea: Each new term is made from the two terms before it, so you must keep the last two terms in view as you go.
teach.method: Write the terms in a numbered row: add the last two to get the next, until you reach the term you need.

alternatives.title: Virahanka's rhythms
text: Virahanka counted rhythms made of short (1 beat) and long (2 beat) syllables: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 … rhythms for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 beats.
A rhythm of n beats ends in a short syllable (after n − 1 beats) or a long one (after n − 2 beats), so the counts add.

alternatives.title: Number every term
text: Write 1, 2, 3 … above the terms as you go, so you stop at the right term.
Check each sum before moving on.

families.title: An inverse proportion
explanations: direct-for-inverse (conceptual): y was scaled the same way as x, as in a direct proportion. Here more of x means less of y: the product x × y stays 312.
not-divided (procedural): The product 12 × 29 = 348 is right, but it must then be shared by 6.
additive (conceptual): The change in x was taken off y. In an inverse proportion the product stays the same, not the sum.

teach.idea: In an inverse proportion, when one quantity is multiplied by some number the other is divided by it, so their product never changes (workers × days = the total work).
teach.method: Multiply the two given values to get the fixed product, then divide it by the new value.

alternatives.title: Go through one worker
text: If a workers take d days, 1 worker takes a × d days (one person does all the work).
Then b workers share it: (a × d) ÷ b days.

alternatives.title: Invert the ratio
text: If x becomes twice as big, y becomes half as big.
So y(new) = y(old) × x(old) ÷ x(new).

families.title: Time taken working together
explanations: add-times (conceptual): The two times were added. Working together is faster than either one alone, so the answer must be less than both times.
average (conceptual): The average of the two times was taken. Two people together finish sooner than either one alone.
rate-not-flipped (procedural): The work per day, 1/19 + 1/20, was given as the answer. That is the part of the job done in one day; the days needed is 1 divided by it.

teach.idea: Think of the work done in one day: a person who takes p days does 1/p of the job each day. Working together, the parts done per day add up.
teach.method: Add 1/p and 1/q to get the part of the job done in one day together; the number of days is 1 divided by that fraction.

alternatives.title: Count units of work
text: Pretend the job is p × q units of work (for example, bricks).
One person lays q units a day, the other p units a day; together p + q a day, so the job takes pq ÷ (p + q) days.

families.title: An equation with fractions of x
explanations: denominators-combined (conceptual): x/8 − x/9 was written as x/1, subtracting the bottom numbers. Fractions with different denominators are first written with a common denominator.
lcd-one-side (procedural): The left side was multiplied by 72 but the right side (2) was not. Multiply every term on both sides by the same number.
one-fraction-only (procedural): Only x/8 was used, as if x/8 = 2. Both fractions of x are part of the left side.

teach.idea: Multiplying every term on both sides by the same number keeps an equation true; choosing the least common multiple of the denominators clears all the fractions.
teach.method: Find the LCM of the denominators, multiply every term by it, collect the x terms, then divide.

alternatives.title: Combine the fractions first
text: Write both fractions over a common denominator: x/3 + x/4 = 4x/12 + 3x/12 = 7x/12.
Then 7x/12 = c gives x = 12c ÷ 7.

alternatives.title: Think in equal parts
text: If the whole is cut into (LCM) equal parts, x/a is LCM ÷ a of them and x/b is LCM ÷ b of them.
Find how many parts the right side is, and how big one part is.

families.title: An equation with x on both sides
explanations: x-sign-kept (procedural): 5x was moved to the left side without changing its sign. Taking 5x from both sides leaves 4x on the left.
number-sign-kept (procedural): 15 was moved to the right side without changing its sign. To remove + 15 from the left, take away 15 on both sides.
wrong-way-round (procedural): The numbers were subtracted the wrong way round, giving the right size with the wrong sign. Check by putting the answer back into both sides.

teach.idea: An equation stays balanced when the same thing is added to or taken from both sides, including a number of x's.
teach.method: Take the smaller x term from both sides so x is on one side only, move the numbers to the other side, then divide by the coefficient of x. Check by substituting.

alternatives.title: Remove x's from both pans
text: Picture x-bags and counters on a balance.
Take the same number of bags off both pans, then the same number of counters, until one bag is balanced by counters.

families.title: Reading the coordinates of a point
explanations: sign-dropped (conceptual): A coordinate left of the y-axis or below the x-axis is negative; the minus sign was left out.
swapped (conceptual): The coordinates were written the wrong way round. The x-coordinate (across) comes first, then the y-coordinate (up or down).

teach.idea: A point's coordinates say how to reach it from the origin: first across (x), then up or down (y). Left and down are negative.
teach.method: Start at the origin. Count squares across to the point's line: that is x (negative if left). Then count up or down: that is y. Write (x, y).

alternatives.title: Along the corridor, then up the stairs
text: You walk along the corridor (x) before you climb the stairs (y).
So the across number always comes first.

alternatives.title: Drop lines to the axes
text: From the point, imagine a line straight down (or up) to the x-axis: where it meets is x.
And a line straight across to the y-axis: where it meets is y.

families.title: Which quadrant a point is in
explanations: clockwise (recall): The quadrants were numbered clockwise. They go anticlockwise from the top right: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), IV (+, −).

teach.idea: The two axes cut the plane into four quadrants, numbered anticlockwise from the top right. The signs of x and y tell which one a point is in.
teach.method: Look at the sign of x (right +, left −) and of y (up +, down −). (+, +) is I, (−, +) is II, (−, −) is III, (+, −) is IV.

alternatives.title: Sketch it
text: Draw two crossing lines and mark I, II, III, IV anticlockwise starting top right.
Move right or left for x, up or down for y, and see where you land.

families.title: Moving on a grid
explanations: axes-swapped (conceptual): The left–right move was added to y and the up–down move to x. Moving right or left changes x; moving up or down changes y.
direction-ignored (prerequisite): A move left or down was added. Moving left or down makes the coordinate smaller.

teach.idea: Moving right or left changes only the x-coordinate; moving up or down changes only the y-coordinate. Right and up add; left and down take away.
teach.method: Add the across move to x (subtract for left). Add the up move to y (subtract for down). Write the new (x, y).

alternatives.title: Plot the start and walk
text: Mark the starting point on a grid.
Count the squares across, then up or down, and read off the point where you stop.

families.title: The third angle of a triangle
explanations: used-360 (recall): The angles were taken from 360°. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°; 360° is the sum around a point or in a quadrilateral.
added (procedural): The two angles were added, but the third angle is what is left over from 180° after them.
one-angle-only (procedural): Only one of the two angles was taken from 180°. Both known angles must be taken away.

teach.idea: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°: tear off the corners and they fit together on a straight line.
teach.method: Add the two angles you know, then take the sum from 180°.

alternatives.title: Tear off the corners
text: Cut out a paper triangle, tear off its three corners and place them side by side.
They make a straight line, which is 180°.

alternatives.title: Count on to 180
text: Start from the sum of the two angles and count up to 180 in easy jumps (to the next ten, then tens).
The total of the jumps is the third angle.

families.title: The exterior angle of a triangle
explanations: third-interior (conceptual): The third interior angle was found instead. The exterior angle sits outside, next to that angle, on the straight line.
one-angle (procedural): Only one of the opposite angles was used. The exterior angle equals the sum of both interior opposite angles.
exterior-as-interior (conceptual): The exterior angle was used as if it were inside the triangle (180° − 101° − 78°). The exterior angle equals the two opposite interior angles together.
added (procedural): The two angles were added. The exterior angle is the sum, so the missing part is the difference.
adjacent-interior (conceptual): The interior angle next to the exterior angle was found (180° − exterior). The question asks for the other opposite angle.

teach.idea: An exterior angle and the interior angle next to it make a straight line (180°), and the three interior angles also make 180°, so the exterior angle equals the two far interior angles together.
teach.method: To find the exterior angle, add the two interior opposite angles. To find one of those, subtract the other from the exterior angle.

alternatives.title: Go through the third angle
text: Find the third interior angle with the angle sum (180° minus the other two).
The exterior angle is 180° minus that third angle, because they lie on a straight line.

families.title: Angles of an isosceles triangle
explanations: not-halved (procedural): 180° − 160° = 20° is shared by the two equal angles, so each one is half of it.
all-equal (conceptual): All three angles were taken to be equal. In an isosceles triangle only the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
one-base-angle (procedural): Only one 85° angle was taken from 180°. There are two equal angles of 85°.
halved (procedural): The remaining angle was halved, but here only one angle (the third) is missing.

teach.idea: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the two equal sides are equal; with the angle sum of 180°, one angle tells you the other two.
teach.method: Vertex angle known: take it from 180° and halve. Base angle known: double it and take that from 180°.

alternatives.title: Fold it in half
text: Fold an isosceles triangle along the line from the top to the middle of the base: the two halves match.
So the two base angles are the same size.

families.title: How long can the third side be?
explanations: equal-allowed (conceptual): A third side of 40 cm was allowed. If it equals 20 + 20, the two sides lie flat along it and there is no triangle: it must be shorter.
longest-given (conceptual): The third side was thought not to be longer than 20 cm. It can be longer, as long as it is less than 19 + 20.
any-length (conceptual): It was thought any length will do. The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side, so the third side must be more than 20 − 19.

teach.idea: In a triangle, any two sides together are longer than the third. So the third side is less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference.
teach.method: Longest: one less than the sum of the two sides. Shortest: one more than their difference (for whole numbers).

alternatives.title: Try it with sticks
text: Hold two sticks at a hinge. Open them wide: the gap grows but never reaches their total length.
Close them up: the gap shrinks but never reaches their difference.

families.title: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles
explanations: alphabetical-match (conceptual): P, Q, R were matched with A, B, C in alphabetical order. The order of the letters in the congruence statement shows the matching: the first letters match, the second letters match, and the third letters match.

teach.idea: When ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, the letters are written in matching order: A goes with X, B with Y, C with Z. Matching parts are equal.
teach.method: Write the two names one above the other. Find the asked letters in the second name, read the letters above them in the first name, and use that side or angle.

alternatives.title: Stack the names
text: Write A B C on one line and the second triangle's name under it.
Each column is a matching pair of vertices; a side is two columns.

alternatives.title: Trace and place
text: Imagine tracing triangle ABC and placing the tracing exactly on the other triangle.
Each vertex lands on its matching vertex, so matching sides lie on top of each other.

families.title: Angles made by a transversal with parallel lines
explanations: supplementary-for-equal (conceptual): The vertically opposite angle was taken from 180°. With parallel lines, vertically opposite angles are equal.
equal-for-supplementary (conceptual): The linear pair angle was taken to be equal. Angles in a linear pair add up to 180°.

teach.idea: A transversal crosses parallel lines at the same slant, so the angles at the two crossings repeat: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add to 180°.
teach.method: Decide whether the two angles are the same 'shape' (equal: corresponding, alternate, vertically opposite) or together make a straight line (add to 180°: co-interior, linear pair).

alternatives.title: F, Z and C shapes
text: Corresponding angles sit in an F shape, alternate angles in a Z shape: they are equal.
Co-interior angles sit inside a C (or U) shape: they add up to 180°.

alternatives.title: Slide one crossing onto the other
text: Slide the upper crossing along the transversal until it lies on the lower one.
Because the lines are parallel the angles match exactly: that is why corresponding angles are equal.

families.title: Finding x from angles at parallel lines
explanations: gave-angle (procedural): The size of an angle was given instead of x. Once x is found, the angle is 5x + 30 worked out, but the question asks for x.
supplementary-for-equal (conceptual): The two angles were added to make 180°. Alternate angles at parallel lines are equal.
equal-for-supplementary (conceptual): The two angles were set equal. Co-interior angles at parallel lines add up to 180°.

teach.idea: The angle facts become equations: alternate angles give 'angle = angle', co-interior angles give 'angle + angle = 180'.
teach.method: Write the equation from the angle fact, collect the x terms and the numbers, and divide. Then check both angles with your x.

alternatives.title: Check the angles
text: Put your x into both expressions to get the two angles.
Alternate angles must come out equal; co-interior angles must add to 180°.

families.title: A missing side of a right triangle
explanations: added-sides (conceptual): The two sides were added. The theorem adds the squares of the sides, then takes the square root.
no-square-root (procedural): 9409 − 4225 = 5184 is the square of the side; its square root is the length.
subtracted-sides (conceptual): The sides were subtracted. Subtract the squares, then take the square root.

teach.idea: In a right-angled triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides (Baudhayana's rule for the diagonal of a rectangle).
teach.method: Hypotenuse: add the squares of the two shorter sides and take the square root. Shorter side: subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse, then take the square root.

alternatives.title: Squares on the sides
text: Draw a square on each side of the triangle. The two smaller squares together have the same area as the big one.
So the area of the big square is a² + b², and its side is the square root.

alternatives.title: Spot a triple
text: Many whole-number right triangles are multiples of 3-4-5, 5-12-13 or 8-15-17.
Divide the sides by a common factor, recognise the triple, then scale back.

families.title: The missing angle at a point of a tiling
explanations: exterior-for-interior (prerequisite): The angle of each polygon was taken as 360° ÷ (number of sides), which is its exterior angle. A tile's corner is the interior angle, 180° − 360° ÷ n.
straight-line (recall): The corners were made to add up to 180°. Angles all the way round a point add up to 360°.
not-shared (procedural): The whole gap was given as one corner. Two equal tiles share the gap, so each corner is half of it.

teach.idea: Tiles fit around a point with no gaps or overlaps only when their corner angles add up to exactly 360°.
teach.method: Find each regular polygon's interior angle (180° − 360° ÷ number of sides), add the angles already at the point, and take the total from 360°; share the gap if more than one tile fills it.

alternatives.title: Know the polygon angles
text: Triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°, octagon 135°, decagon 144°, dodecagon 150°.
Squares (4 × 90°), triangles (6 × 60°) and hexagons (3 × 120°) tile on their own; pentagons do not, since 360 ÷ 108 is not whole.

alternatives.title: Split into triangles
text: A polygon with n sides splits into n − 2 triangles from one corner, so its angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°.
In a regular polygon all n corners are equal: divide by n.

families.title: Naming corresponding, alternate, co-interior and vertically opposite angles
explanations: gave-vertically-opposite (conceptual): The vertically opposite angle was given. Corresponding angles sit in the same corner at each line: same side of t, and both above (or both below) their line.
gave-alternate-interior (conceptual): The alternate interior angle was given. Vertically opposite angles are at the same crossing point, facing each other across it.
gave-co-interior (conceptual): The co-interior angle was given. Alternate interior angles are between the two lines, on OPPOSITE sides of t (they make a Z shape).
gave-corresponding (conceptual): The corresponding angle was given. Vertically opposite angles are at the same crossing point, facing each other across it.
mixed-names (conceptual): Corresponding angles are at different lines; these two are at the same crossing point and face each other: they are vertically opposite angles.

teach.idea: Where a transversal crosses two lines it makes the same four angles at each line. Corresponding angles are in matching places; alternate interior angles are between the lines on opposite sides of t; co-interior angles are between the lines on the same side; vertically opposite angles face each other at one crossing.
teach.method: Find the given angle: which line, above or below it, which side of t. Corresponding: same place at the other line. Alternate interior: other line, other side of t, still between the lines. Co-interior: other line, same side of t, between the lines. Vertically opposite: same line, both other side and other position.

alternatives.title: Look for F, Z and C shapes
text: Corresponding angles sit in an F shape, alternate angles in a Z shape, co-interior angles in a C (or U) shape.
Trace the letter through the two angles to check.

alternatives.title: Slide one crossing onto the other
text: Imagine sliding the crossing at l down t until it sits on the crossing at m.
Each angle lands on its corresponding angle; then turn half way round the point to find the vertically opposite one.

families.title: Counting rhythms, climbs and tilings: Virahanka numbers
explanations: one-term-back (procedural): The count for 17 was given. Each number in the sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, … is the sum of the two before it; count on to length 18.
count-up (conceptual): The counts were taken to grow by 1 each time. They grow by adding the two previous counts: endings with a short part plus endings with a long part.
all-of-them (procedural): All the arrangements were counted. Only those that start with the given part are asked: after it, the rest can be any arrangement of the remaining length.
wrong-rest (procedural): The rest was taken to have length 16. After a short (1) part, 17 remains.

teach.idea: Every arrangement of length n ends with a short part (after an arrangement of length n − 1) or a long part (after one of length n − 2). So the counts follow Virahanka's rule: each is the sum of the two before (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …).
teach.method: Start with length 1: 1 way, length 2: 2 ways. Add the last two counts to get the next, up to the length asked. For arrangements that must start with a given part, count the arrangements of what is left.

alternatives.title: List the small cases
text: Length 3: S S S, S L, L S (3 ways). Length 4: S S S S, S S L, S L S, L S S, L L (5 ways).
Notice 3 + 5 = 8 for length 5, and continue.

alternatives.title: Count by the number of long parts
text: With k long parts there are n − 2k short ones: n − k parts in all.
Choose which k of the n − k places are long, and add up over every possible k.

families.title: Which figure is congruent to the given one?
explanations: same-shape (conceptual): This figure has the same shape but is twice as big. Congruent figures are the same shape AND the same size: one fits exactly on the other.
same-perimeter (conceptual): This triangle has the same perimeter, but its sides are different. Congruent triangles have all three sides equal in pairs.
same-area (conceptual): This rectangle has the same area, but different sides, so it will not fit exactly on the first one.
radius-diameter (conceptual): The radius was taken for the diameter (or the other way round). A circle of radius r has diameter 2r; congruent circles have the same radius.
half-size (conceptual): Half the diameter was used as the radius twice. The diameter here must be 2 × the radius.

teach.idea: Two figures are congruent when one can be placed exactly on the other (perhaps after turning or flipping it): the same shape and the same size, so all matching sides and angles are equal.
teach.method: Compare the measurements, not their order: list each figure's sides from smallest to largest (or its radius) and check they match exactly. The same shape at a different size, or the same area or perimeter, is not enough.

alternatives.title: Trace and place
text: Trace one figure on thin paper and lay it on the other; you may turn it or flip it over.
If every edge lies exactly on an edge, they are congruent.

alternatives.title: Sort the measurements
text: Write each figure's sides in order of size: 4, 6, 7 and 7, 4, 6 both become 4, 6, 7.
Equal lists mean congruent (for triangles this is the SSS rule).

families.title: Expanding with (a + b)², (a − b)² and (a + b)(a − b)
explanations: middle-not-doubled (conceptual): The middle term was written as ab. The identity has 2ab: the two products 5x × 9 and 9 × 5x are both there.
middle-sign (procedural): The middle term of (a − b)² is −2ab: it carries the minus sign.
minus-squared (conceptual): (−9)² was written as −81. The square of a negative number is positive: the last term of (a − b)² is +b².
q-doubled (procedural): 9 was doubled instead of squared: b² = 9 × 9.
p-not-squared (procedural): 5x was not squared fully: (5x)² = 5x × 5x = 25x².
doubled-not-squared (procedural): 5 was doubled instead of squared: 5² = 25.
sign-of-b2 (conceptual): The last term of (a + b)(a − b) is −b²: the middle terms cancel and the product of +b and −b is negative.
q-not-squared (procedural): 9 was not squared: b² = 9 × 9 = 81.

teach.idea: (a + b)² is the area of a square of side a + b: it splits into a square a², a square b² and two rectangles ab. So (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², and (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² because the two ab terms cancel.
teach.method: Decide what a and b are (a = px, b = q). Work out a², then 2ab (with its sign), then b², and write them in order.

alternatives.title: Draw the square
text: Draw a square of side a + b and cut it into a² , b² and two rectangles a × b.
The two rectangles are why the middle term is 2ab, not ab.

alternatives.title: Multiply it out to check
text: Write (px + q)² as (px + q)(px + q) and multiply each term by each term.
Collect the two middle products: they always come out equal.

families.title: Quick calculation with identities
explanations: no-middle (conceptual): Only a² + b² was worked out. (100 + 4)² also has the middle term 2ab = 2 × 100 × 4 = 800.
middle-not-doubled (procedural): The middle term was taken as ab. It is 2ab = 800.
as-difference (conceptual): (100 − 4)² was taken as 100² − 4². The square of a difference is a² − 2ab + b².
minus-b2 (procedural): The last term was subtracted. In (a − b)² the b² is added: (−b)² is positive.
plus-b2 (conceptual): b² was added. (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b²: subtract 16.
b-not-squared (procedural): 4 was taken away instead of 4² = 16.

teach.idea: A number near a round number is easy to square with an identity: 103 = 100 + 3, so 103² = 100² + 2 × 100 × 3 + 3². Products like 103 × 97 are (100 + 3)(100 − 3) = 100² − 3².
teach.method: Write the number as a ± b with a a multiple of 10. Work out a², 2ab and b² (all easy) and combine them with the right signs.

alternatives.title: See it as an area
text: 103² is a 100 by 100 square, two 100 by 3 strips and a 3 by 3 corner.
Add the parts: 10000 + 600 + 9.

alternatives.title: Check the last digit
text: The last digit of 103² must be the last digit of 3² = 9.
If your answer ends in another digit, look for a slip.

families.title: Expanding (x ± a)³, (x + a)(x + b)(x + c) and (x + ay + b)²
explanations: no-three (conceptual): The 3 in the identity was left out: the coefficient is 3 × 6².
square-pattern (procedural): The pattern of (a + b)² (2ab) was used. In a cube the middle coefficients are 3a²b and 3ab².
cube-sign (conceptual): (−6)³ is negative: −216.
cube-as-square (procedural): 6 was squared instead of cubed.
product-for-sum (procedural): The x² coefficient is the SUM 3 + 4 + 6; the product is the number at the end.
two-products (procedural): Only some of the pair products were added. The x coefficient is ab + bc + ca: all three pairs.
sum-for-pairs (procedural): The sum a + b + c belongs to x²; the x coefficient is the sum of the products of pairs.
sum-for-product (procedural): The number at the end is the product abc, not the sum.
no-doubling (conceptual): The cross term was not doubled. (a + b + c)² has 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
cross-forgotten (procedural): A cross term was missed out (counted as 0); every pair of the three terms gives a doubled product.

teach.idea: (a + b)³ = (a + b)(a + b)²: multiplying out gives a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³. (x + a)(x + b)(x + c) collects the sum of the numbers, the sum of their pair products and their product. (a + b + c)² has each square and every pair product twice.
teach.method: Name the parts (a, b, c), then fill the identity term by term, keeping track of signs: (x − a)³ has alternating signs.

alternatives.title: Multiply two at a time
text: First expand two brackets, then multiply that by the third.
Collect like terms carefully: write the powers of x in columns.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Put x = 1 (and y = 1) into both sides.
Both sides must give the same number; if not, a coefficient is wrong.

families.title: Is the triangle right-angled? The converse of Pythagoras
explanations: last-side-as-longest (procedural): The last side listed (52) was used as the longest. The test uses the LONGEST side: is the square of 65 equal to the sum of the squares of the other two?
nearly-equal (conceptual): The two sides of the test came out close, so it was taken as right-angled. The converse needs them EXACTLY equal; if they differ at all, the angle is not 90°.

teach.idea: The converse of Baudhayana–Pythagoras: if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the angle opposite the longest side is a right angle. If not, there is no right angle.
teach.method: Find the longest side. Square it, and add the squares of the other two. Equal: right-angled. Not equal, even by a little: not right-angled.

alternatives.title: The knotted rope
text: Builders once made a right angle with a rope of 12 equal parts, pegged into a triangle 3, 4, 5.
Because 3² + 4² = 5², the corner between the 3 and the 4 is a right angle.

alternatives.title: Look for a known triple
text: Divide the sides by a common factor: 30, 40, 50 → 3, 4, 5.
If you get a known triple (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), it is right-angled.

families.title: Generating Pythagorean triples by a rule
explanations: m-is-2m (procedural): 2m = 40, so m = 20; 40 itself was used as m.
m-squared-only (procedural): Only m² = 400 was worked out; the rule says m² − 1.
not-squared (procedural): m and n were not squared (or 2mn was taken as 2m + n).
other-member (procedural): Another member of the triple was given; the question asks for m² + n².

teach.idea: (m² + 1)² − (m² − 1)² = 4m² = (2m)², so 2m, m² − 1 and m² + 1 always form a Pythagorean triple. In the same way (m² + n²)² = (m² − n²)² + (2mn)².
teach.method: From the even member 2m, halve it to get m, then work out m² − 1 and m² + 1. With m and n given, substitute into the three expressions.

alternatives.title: Check the triple
text: Square the two smaller numbers and add them; square the largest.
If they are equal, the triple is right.

alternatives.title: From odd squares
text: Every odd square is a sum of consecutive odd numbers: 9 = 1 + 3 + 5.
When an odd square is itself the next odd number in such a sum, as 9 after 16 = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7, it gives 9 + 16 = 25: the triple 3, 4, 5.

families.title: Direct proportion, inverse proportion or neither?
explanations: not-equal-steps (conceptual): x and y do not change by equal steps, so it was taken as neither. Inverse proportion is about PRODUCTS: here x × y is the same in every row.
equal-steps-needed (conceptual): The steps between the numbers were compared. Direct proportion is about RATIOS: y ÷ x is the same in every row.
both-grow (conceptual): Both quantities grow, so they were taken as directly proportional. In direct proportion y ÷ x stays the same; here the same number is added instead, so the ratio changes.
one-falls (conceptual): One quantity rises while the other falls, so it was taken as inverse proportion. In inverse proportion x × y stays the same; here the products change.

teach.idea: Two quantities are in inverse proportion when their product stays the same (double one, the other halves). They are in direct proportion when their ratio stays the same. One going up while the other goes down is not enough for inverse proportion.
teach.method: Multiply x × y in every row: all equal means inverse proportion. Divide y ÷ x in every row: all equal means direct proportion. Otherwise neither.

alternatives.title: Double and see
text: Find two rows where x doubles (or triples).
If y halves (or becomes a third), it is inverse; if y doubles too, it is direct.

alternatives.title: Picture the graph
text: Direct proportion is a straight line through 0; inverse proportion is a curve that never meets the axes.
A straight line that does not pass through 0 is neither.

families.title: Inverse proportion: workers and time, speed and time
explanations: used-direct (conceptual): It was treated as direct proportion (more cows, more days). Here more cows means fewer days: the product stays the same.
take-away-difference (conceptual): The difference 9 was added to the days. Inverse proportion multiplies and divides: 24 × 30 = 15 × ?.

teach.idea: When one quantity goes up and the job stays the same, the other goes down in the same ratio: workers × days (or speed × time) is constant.
teach.method: Multiply the first pair to get the whole job (worker-days, or distance). Divide by the new number of workers (or the new speed).

alternatives.title: Go through one
text: If 6 workers take 10 days, 1 worker takes 6 × 10 = 60 days.
Then 4 workers take 60 ÷ 4 = 15 days.

alternatives.title: Ask: more or less?
text: More workers should finish SOONER; a faster car should take LESS time.
If your answer goes the other way, the proportion was used the wrong way round.

families.title: Compound variation: workers, hours and days
explanations: hours-ignored (procedural): Only the change in workers was used. The hours a day changed too (6 to 8): fewer hours a day means more days.
all-direct (conceptual): Both changes were treated as direct proportion. More workers, or more hours a day, mean FEWER days: divide, do not multiply.
saris-ignored (procedural): Only the change in weavers was used. The number of saris changed too (40 to 20): more saris take more days.
weavers-direct (conceptual): More weavers were taken to need more days. More weavers finish SOONER: days go down in the same ratio as weavers go up.

teach.idea: With two changes, look at each separately: more workers or more hours a day mean fewer days (inverse); more work to do means more days (direct). The total work (worker-hours, or worker-days per item) stays the same.
teach.method: Write the total work for the first situation (workers × hours a day × days). The second situation needs the same total, so divide it by workers × hours a day. For items, scale by the new number of items first.

alternatives.title: Change one thing at a time
text: First change only the workers (inverse): days × old workers ÷ new workers.
Then change only the hours (or items) and adjust again.

alternatives.title: Use a table with arrows
text: Make columns for workers, hours, days. Put arrows: up means up or down?
Multiply the old days by each ratio in the direction the arrows say.

families.title: Patterns in calendar and number-grid squares
explanations: next-is-plus-one (conceptual): Each number was taken to be 1 more than the last: n, n + 1, n + 2, n + 3. The number below n is n + 10, because a row has 10 numbers.
four-n (procedural): Only 4n was used; the numbers are n, n + 1, n + 10 and n + 11, so add 22 too.
divide-by-four (procedural): The sum was divided by 4, giving the average of the four numbers, not the smallest. Solve 4n + 22 = 378.
forgot-constant (procedural): The 22 was added instead of taken away.
centre-times-nine (procedural): 9 × (the smallest number) was used. 9 times the MIDDLE number (89) gives the sum.
row-plus-one (conceptual): The numbers below were taken to go up by 1. Each row down adds 10.
gave-centre (procedural): Sum ÷ 9 = 89 is the MIDDLE number. The smallest is 11 less.
one-row-back (procedural): Only one row back was taken from the middle number; the smallest is one row up AND one column left.

teach.idea: In a grid with w numbers in each row, the number to the right of n is n + 1 and the number below it is n + w. So every square of numbers can be written in terms of n, and its sum is an expression in n.
teach.method: Write the numbers of the square in terms of n (as in the picture) and add them: a 2 × 2 square gives 4n + 2w + 2, a 3 × 3 square gives 9n + 9(w + 1). Substitute n, or solve the equation for n.

alternatives.title: Use the middle
text: In a 3 × 3 square the numbers balance round the middle one: the sum is 9 × the middle number.
In a 2 × 2 square, the sum is 4 × the average of the smallest and largest.

alternatives.title: Try one on a real calendar
text: Pick a square on a calendar, add its numbers, and compare with the expression.
If they agree, the expression works for every square.

families.title: Using a coordinate grid for a floor plan
explanations: wrong-corner (procedural): B and C were added and A taken away, which finds a point across from A. D is next to A and C: it has A's x-coordinate and C's y-coordinate.
swapped (conceptual): The coordinates were written in the wrong order. A point is (x, y): across first, then up.
added-not-halved (procedural): The x-coordinates of A and B were added but not halved. Half-way is the average: (first + second) ÷ 2.
half-the-width (procedural): Half the width (2) was given as the x-coordinate. Start from A's x-coordinate and add half the width.
half-sizes (procedural): Half the length and half the width were given as the coordinates. Start at corner A (2, 1) and move half way across and half way up.
corner-c (procedural): The far corner was given. The centre is half way between A and C.

teach.idea: A grid turns a plan into numbers: each place is (across, up) from the origin. Walls of a rectangular room run along grid lines, so corners share x- or y-coordinates.
teach.method: Fourth corner: it lines up with one corner across and with another up and down, so copy those coordinates. Half-way: average the two x-coordinates and the two y-coordinates.

alternatives.title: Walk it on the grid
text: From A, walk along the wall to B: count the steps across.
From A, walk up to D: the same number of steps as from B up to C.

alternatives.title: Sketch the room
text: Mark the three corners you know on squared paper.
Complete the rectangle; read the last corner's coordinates.

families.title: From an explicit rule to its terms and its recursive rule
explanations: start-at-zero (procedural): The terms were started at n = 0. The first term is t₁: put n = 1, 2, 3.
added-b-only (procedural): a and n were added instead of multiplied: 9n means 9 × n.
b-as-t1 (procedural): The constant 9 was taken as the first term. t₁ = 9 × 1 + 9 = 18.
b-as-d (conceptual): The constant was taken as the step. The step d is the number multiplying n (9): each term is 9 more than the one before.
t1-times-r (procedural): t₁ was taken as 9 × 5. For n = 1 the power is 5⁰ = 1, so t₁ = 9.
swapped (procedural): The ratio and the first term were swapped.

teach.idea: An explicit rule gives any term straight from its position n; a recursive rule gives the first term and how each term comes from the one before. For tₙ = an + b each term is a more than the last; for tₙ = b × aⁿ⁻¹ each term is a times the last.
teach.method: Put n = 1, 2, 3 into the explicit rule to get the terms. The first term is t₁; the step d = t₂ − t₁ (or the ratio r = t₂ ÷ t₁).

alternatives.title: Make a table
text: Write n = 1, 2, 3, 4 in one row and tₙ under each.
Look at how each term gets from the one before: that is the recursive rule.

alternatives.title: Check that both rules agree
text: Use your recursive rule to make the first five terms.
Use the explicit rule for the same five; they must match exactly.
