families.title: Finding an unknown coefficient from a condition on the zeros
explanations: sign (procedural): The coefficient of x must be 0, so k − 9 = 0 means k = 9; the sign was changed.
forgot-a (procedural): The coefficient of x² (5) was left out: sum = −k/5.
divided-by-a (procedural): The product of the zeros is c/a = k/5, so k = 5 × −3; it was divided instead.
one-zero-only (procedural): Only the zero 6 was used for k. Substitute x = 6 into p(x) = 0 and solve for k.

teach.idea: For ax² + bx + c the zeros α, β satisfy α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. A condition on the zeros therefore becomes an equation for the unknown coefficient.
teach.method: Write the condition with the relations: sum = −b/a, product = c/a, or substitute a known zero into p(x) = 0. Solve the equation for k.

alternatives.title: Substitute a zero
text: If r is a zero, then p(r) = 0.
Put x = r into the polynomial and solve the resulting equation for k.

alternatives.title: Use the factor form
text: p(x) = a(x − α)(x − β) = a x² − a(α + β)x + aαβ.
Compare coefficients with the given polynomial.

families.title: Is it a perfect square? Last digits of squares
explanations: last-digit-enough (conceptual): 3610 ends in a digit that squares can end in, but that only rules numbers OUT; it does not prove 3610 is a square. Check it: it lies between two neighbouring squares.
ends-badly (recall): 3608 ends in 8. No perfect square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8.
doubled (procedural): The last digit was doubled instead of squared: 9 × 9 = 81, which ends in 1.
same-digit (conceptual): The square was taken to end in the same digit as 99. Only the last digit of 9 × 9 matters: 81.

teach.idea: The last digit of a square depends only on the last digit of the number: 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. So a number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a perfect square; a number ending in another digit may or may not be one.
teach.method: Rule out the numbers ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8. For the others, find the two squares the number lies between (e.g. 30² = 900 and 31² = 961); a perfect square must be one of them exactly.

alternatives.title: Make a last-digit table
text: The last digits 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, 9 are the only ones a square can have.

alternatives.title: Squeeze between squares
text: Every number lies between two neighbouring squares.
If it is not equal to one of them, it is not a perfect square.

families.title: The square root of a non-square, to one decimal place
explanations: truncated (procedural): The digits were cut off after the first decimal place without rounding. Work out the second decimal place too, then round.
nearest-whole (procedural): Only the nearest whole number was given. The square root lies between two whole numbers; find the tenths too.
halved (conceptual): 200 was halved. The square root is the number that, multiplied by ITSELF, gives 200.

teach.idea: A non-square has a square root between two whole numbers that never ends as a decimal. The long-division method finds its digits one at a time; one more digit than needed lets you round.
teach.method: Pair the digits from the decimal point and use the long-division method to two decimal places, then round to one. Check: the square of your answer should be close to the number.

alternatives.title: Squeeze between squares
text: Find the whole numbers: 7² = 49 < 55 < 64 = 8², so √55 is between 7 and 8.

alternatives.title: Think of a square's side
text: √n is the side of a square of area n.
A bigger area needs a longer side, but the side grows more slowly than the area.

families.title: The missing angle of a polygon
explanations: n-triangles (conceptual): The angle sum was taken as 8 × 180°. An octagon splits into 6 triangles from one corner, so its angles add to 1080°.
assumed-regular (conceptual): The angle sum was shared equally, as if the octagon were regular; its angles are not all equal, so take the given angles away from 1080°.
sum-not-subtracted (procedural): The angle sum 1080° was found, but the given angles were not taken away from it.

teach.idea: From one corner, the diagonals cut a polygon with n sides into n − 2 triangles, and each triangle's angles add to 180°. So the angles of the polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°.
teach.method: Find the angle sum (n − 2) × 180°, add the angles you know, and take that total from the angle sum.

alternatives.title: Walk around the edge
text: Walk around the polygon: at each corner you turn through 180° minus the angle there.
One full walk turns you once round, 360°. Add the turns you know; the last turn is what is left of 360°, and the last angle is 180° minus that turn.

families.title: Angle sums and regular polygons
explanations: n-triangles (conceptual): 36 triangles were counted; from one corner a polygon with 36 sides splits into 34 triangles.
always-360 (conceptual): The angle sum was taken as 360° for every polygon; that is only true for quadrilaterals.
forgot-add-two (procedural): 6120 ÷ 180 = 34 gives the number of triangles; the polygon has 2 more sides than that.
add-one (procedural): One was added instead of two: sides = triangles + 2.
exterior-for-interior (conceptual): 360° ÷ 36 is each exterior angle (the turn at a corner); the interior angle is 180° minus it.
sum-not-shared (procedural): The angle sum was found but not shared among the 36 equal angles.
half-turn (conceptual): 180° was divided; walking once round a polygon turns through 360°.
exterior-as-interior (conceptual): 10° was treated as the inside angle; it is the exterior angle, the turn at each corner.

teach.idea: A polygon with n sides splits into n − 2 triangles from one corner, so its angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. In a regular polygon all the angles are equal, and the turns at the corners (exterior angles) add to 360°.
teach.method: For the sum, work out (n − 2) × 180°. For one angle of a regular polygon, divide the sum by n (or take 360° ÷ n from 180°). For the number of sides, divide 360° by the exterior angle.

alternatives.title: Build a table
text: Triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°: each new side adds one more triangle, 180° more.
Continue the pattern to the number of sides you need.

families.title: Euler's formula F + V − E = 2
explanations: forgot-two (procedural): The 2 in F + V − E = 2 was forgotten: V = E − F + 2.
two-wrong-way (procedural): The 2 was added instead of taken away: from F + V − E = 2, E = F + V − 2.
added-all (procedural): The faces were added to the edges; V = 2 + E − F.

teach.idea: For every polyhedron without holes, faces + vertices − edges = 2. Knowing any two of the counts gives the third.
teach.method: Write F + V − E = 2, put in the two numbers you know, and solve for the third.

alternatives.title: Check it on a cube first
text: A cube has 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.
Use the same pattern with the numbers in the question: the answer must make F + V − E come to 2.

families.title: Faces, edges and vertices of prisms and pyramids, from a name or a net
explanations: ends-forgotten (conceptual): Only the side faces were counted; a prism also has two end faces.
side-edges-forgotten (conceptual): Only the edges round the two ends were counted; there are also 10 edges joining the ends.
net-sides-counted (conceptual): Every corner of every piece of the net was counted; when the net folds up, several corners meet at each vertex.
one-end-only (conceptual): Only the corners of one end were counted; the other end has just as many.
base-forgotten (conceptual): Only the triangular faces were counted; the base is a face too.
base-edges-only (conceptual): Only the edges round the base were counted; 10 more edges go up to the top point.
apex-forgotten (conceptual): The top point (apex) was forgotten; it is a vertex too.

teach.idea: A prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles; a pyramid has one base and triangles meeting at a top point. The shape of the end or base tells you all the counts.
teach.method: For a prism on an n-sided end: n + 2 faces, 3n edges (n round each end and n joining them), 2n vertices. For a pyramid on an n-sided base: n + 1 faces, 2n edges, n + 1 vertices.

alternatives.title: Fold the net in your mind
text: Each piece of the net becomes one face.
When the net folds, sides of two pieces meet to make one edge, so the solid has half as many edges as the pieces have sides.

families.title: The fourth angle of a quadrilateral
explanations: angle-left-out (procedural): Only two of the three given angles were taken from 360°; all three (170°, 85° and 40°) must be taken away.
total-given (procedural): The three angles were added, but the total was not taken from 360°.

teach.idea: A diagonal cuts a quadrilateral into two triangles, so its four angles add to 2 × 180° = 360°.
teach.method: Add the three angles you know and take the total from 360°.

alternatives.title: Tear off the corners
text: Cut out a four-sided shape and tear off its four corners.
Put the corners together point to point: they make a full turn, 360°.

families.title: Angles of a parallelogram or rhombus
explanations: all-equal (conceptual): All the angles were taken to be equal; only opposite angles are equal. Neighbouring angles add to 180° because AB is parallel to DC.
neighbours-360 (conceptual): Neighbouring angles were taken to add to 360°; it is all four angles that add to 360°, and two neighbours add to 180°.
rhombus-square (conceptual): A rhombus was treated as a square; its sides are equal but its angles need not be right angles.
opposite-supplementary (conceptual): Opposite angles were taken to add to 180°; in a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add to 180°.

teach.idea: In a parallelogram (a rhombus is one), opposite sides are parallel, so neighbouring angles add to 180° and opposite angles are equal.
teach.method: Decide whether the angle you want is opposite ∠A (then it equals ∠A) or next to ∠A (then it is 180° − ∠A).

alternatives.title: See the parallel lines
text: AD and BC are parallel, and AB crosses them.
∠A and ∠B are co-interior angles between parallel lines, so they add to 180°. Going round, ∠C comes back to the same size as ∠A.

families.title: Diagonals of rectangles and parallelograms
explanations: whole-diagonal (procedural): The whole diagonal was given; the diagonals of a rectangle are equal and cut each other in half, so OB is half of BD.
side-for-half-diagonal (conceptual): The side AB was used; OB is half of the diagonal BD, not a side.
diagonals-equal (conceptual): The diagonals of a parallelogram were taken to be equal; they cut each other in half but need not be equal (that is only true in a rectangle).
not-doubled (procedural): OA is only half of AC; O is the midpoint of AC.
added-halves (procedural): OA and OB were added; they lie on different diagonals. AC = OA + OC = 2 × OA.

teach.idea: The diagonals of every parallelogram cut each other in half. In a rectangle they are also equal in length.
teach.method: Mark O as the midpoint of each diagonal. For a rectangle, BD = AC, so OB = AC ÷ 2. For a parallelogram, AC = 2 × OA.

alternatives.title: Fold and measure
text: Draw a rectangle and both diagonals, then fold the paper so A lands on C: the crease passes through O, the middle of AC.
Measure OA, OB, OC and OD: in a rectangle all four are equal.

families.title: Map scale: 1 cm stands for k km
explanations: divided (conceptual): The map distance was divided by 50; every 1 cm on the map is 50 km, so multiply.
multiplied (conceptual): The real distance was multiplied by 50; the map is smaller, so divide by 50.
added (conceptual): 50 was added; each of the 15 centimetres stands for 50 km.
subtracted (conceptual): 50 was taken away; find how many lots of 50 km make the distance.

teach.idea: A map scale says how much real distance each centimetre on the map stands for; distances on the map and on the ground are in the same proportion.
teach.method: Map to real: multiply the map length by the scale. Real to map: divide the real distance by the scale.

alternatives.title: A ratio table
text: Write 1 cm → k km in the first column.
Scale both sides by the same number to reach the length you know, then read the other side.

families.title: Ratio scales 1 : n with unit conversion
explanations: not-converted (procedural): The length was found in centimetres but not changed to kilometres (100 000 cm = 1 km).
thousand-for-hundred (recall): It was divided by 1000; 100 cm make 1 m.
thousand-for-km (recall): It was divided by 1000; 1 km = 1000 m = 100 000 cm.
metres-only (procedural): The centimetres were changed to metres but not on to kilometres.

teach.idea: A scale 1 : n means every length in the real world is n times the length on the drawing, in the same unit.
teach.method: Multiply the drawing length by n to get centimetres, then change units: ÷ 100 for metres, ÷ 100 000 for kilometres.

alternatives.title: What does 1 cm stand for?
text: Change the scale first: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm stands for 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km.
Then multiply by the number of centimetres on the drawing.

families.title: Volume of a cuboid or cube from its edges
explanations: added-edges (conceptual): The edges were added; volume multiplies length, width and height.
one-layer (conceptual): Only the base (length × width) was found; there are as many layers as the height.
surface-for-volume (conceptual): The area of the outside faces was found; volume measures the space inside.

teach.idea: Volume counts how many 1 cm cubes fill a solid. One layer on the base holds length × width cubes, and there are as many layers as the height.
teach.method: Volume = length × width × height. For a cube with edge a, volume = a × a × a = a³.

alternatives.title: Count in layers
text: Imagine filling the box with 1 cm cubes: the bottom layer is a rectangle of cubes, length × width.
Stack the same layer once for every centimetre of height.

families.title: Capacity of a tank in litres
explanations: cm3-not-litres (procedural): The volume in cm³ was given; 1000 cm³ make 1 litre, so divide by 1000.
hundred-for-thousand (recall): It was divided by 100; 1 litre is 1000 cm³.
m3-not-litres (procedural): The volume in m³ was given; each m³ holds 1000 litres.

teach.idea: Capacity is volume measured in litres. A 10 cm cube holds exactly 1 litre (1000 cm³), and a 1 m cube holds 1000 litres.
teach.method: Find the volume (length × width × height), then change units: cm³ ÷ 1000 = litres; m³ × 1000 = litres.

alternatives.title: Count litre cubes
text: A 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm cube holds 1 litre.
Count how many such cubes fit along each edge, and multiply the three counts.

families.title: Packing cubes into a box
explanations: volume-divided (conceptual): The box's volume was divided by a cube's volume; that counts cut pieces of cubes too. Count how many whole cubes fit along each edge instead.
rounded-up (procedural): A part of a cube was counted as a whole one; only whole cubes fit, so round each count down.

teach.idea: Only whole cubes fit, so a gap smaller than a cube is wasted. Count whole cubes along each edge first.
teach.method: Divide each edge of the box by the cube's edge and drop any remainder; multiply the three whole numbers.

alternatives.title: Build one layer
text: Fill the floor of the box: (cubes along) × (cubes across).
Then see how many such layers fit in the height, rounding down.

families.title: Area of a triangle from base and height
explanations: no-half (conceptual): Base × height gives the rectangle around the triangle; the triangle is half of it.
added (conceptual): Base and height were added; area multiplies them and then halves.

teach.idea: A triangle is exactly half of a rectangle (or parallelogram) with the same base and height.
teach.method: Area = ½ × base × height. Multiply the base by the height and halve the result.

alternatives.title: Half a rectangle
text: Draw the rectangle with the same base and height around the triangle.
The diagonal cuts it into two equal triangles, so each is half the rectangle's area.

families.title: A missing base or height of a triangle
explanations: not-doubled (conceptual): The area was divided by 20 without doubling it first; area = ½ × base × height, so the other length is 2 × area ÷ 20.
subtracted (conceptual): The known length was taken from the area; area and length are linked by multiplying, so undo it by dividing.

teach.idea: Area = ½ × base × height, so twice the area is base × height: the area of the matching rectangle.
teach.method: Double the area, then divide by the length you know.

alternatives.title: Write an equation
text: Write ½ × base × height = area with a letter for the missing length.
Multiply both sides by 2, then divide by the known length.

families.title: Circumference of a circle
explanations: radius-as-diameter (procedural): π × radius was found; the circumference is π × diameter = 2πr.
area-for-circumference (conceptual): πr² is the area (the space inside); the circumference is the distance around, 2πr.
doubled-diameter (procedural): The diameter was doubled again; C = π × diameter, or 2 × π × radius.

teach.idea: In every circle, the distance around (the circumference) divided by the diameter is the same number, π (about 22/7 or 3.14).
teach.method: C = π × diameter = 2 × π × radius. Double the radius first if you are given the radius.

alternatives.title: Measure with a string
text: Wrap a string around a bangle or a lid and lay it flat against a ruler.
It is a little more than 3 diameters long: that number is π.

families.title: Area of a circle
explanations: circumference-for-area (conceptual): 2πr is the circumference (the distance around); the area is πr².
diameter-squared (procedural): The diameter was squared; the formula uses the radius, half the diameter.
not-squared (procedural): π × r was found; the radius must be squared (r × r).

teach.idea: Cut a circle into many thin slices and lay them head to tail: they make a shape close to a rectangle, half the circumference (πr) long and r high. So the area is πr × r = πr².
teach.method: Find the radius (half the diameter), square it, and multiply by π.

alternatives.title: Compare with squares
text: Draw the square on the radius: its area is r².
The circle covers a little more than 3 of these squares — exactly π of them.

families.title: Distance travelled by a wheel
explanations: cm-not-m (procedural): The distance was left in centimetres; 100 cm = 1 m.
radius-for-diameter (procedural): The diameter was used as if it were the radius (2 × π × diameter); one turn rolls π × diameter.
one-turn (conceptual): Only one turn was counted; each turn rolls one circumference.
m-not-cm (procedural): Metres were divided by centimetres; change the distance to centimetres first.
diameter-for-circumference (conceptual): The distance was divided by the diameter; each turn rolls the circumference, π × diameter.

teach.idea: In one full turn, a wheel rolls a distance equal to its circumference, π × diameter.
teach.method: Distance = circumference × number of turns; turns = distance ÷ circumference. Keep the units the same (change m to cm or cm to m).

alternatives.title: Mark and roll
text: Put a chalk mark on a wheel and roll it until the mark touches the ground again.
The gap between the two marks on the ground is the circumference.

families.title: Arc length, area and perimeter of a sector
explanations: area-for-arc (conceptual): The area formula (πr²) was used; the arc is part of the circumference, 2πr.
whole-circle (conceptual): The whole circle's area was given; the sector is only 300/360 of it.
over-180 (procedural): The angle was divided by 180; a full circle is 360°.
arc-for-area (conceptual): The arc-length formula (2πr) was used; area uses πr².
radii-forgotten (procedural): Only the arc was found; the perimeter of a sector also has the two straight radii.
one-radius (procedural): Only one radius was added; a sector has two straight edges.

teach.idea: A sector with angle θ is θ/360 of the whole circle, so its arc is θ/360 of the circumference and its area is θ/360 of the circle's area.
teach.method: Arc = θ/360 × 2πr; area = θ/360 × πr²; perimeter = arc + 2r.

alternatives.title: Think of a clock face
text: 90° is a quarter of a full turn, so a 90° sector is a quarter of the circle; 60° is a sixth.
Find the whole circle's circumference or area, then take that fraction of it.

families.title: Area of a circular path (a ring)
explanations: width-squared (conceptual): π × width² (or π(R − r)²) was found; the path is the big circle minus the small one, π(R² − r²): square each radius first.
outer-only (procedural): The area of the big circle was found but the garden was not taken away.

teach.idea: A ring is a big circle with a small circle taken out of the middle.
teach.method: Outer radius R = inner radius + width. Area of the path = πR² − πr² = π(R² − r²).

alternatives.title: Two circles
text: Work out the area of the whole circle including the path.
Work out the area of the garden alone, then subtract.

families.title: Area and perimeter of a parallelogram
explanations: slant-for-height (conceptual): The slanting side was used; the height is the straight-up distance between the parallel sides.
halved (conceptual): The answer was halved as for a triangle; for a parallelogram area = base × height, so height = area ÷ base.
subtracted (conceptual): The base was taken from the area; divide the area by the base.
two-sides (procedural): Only two sides were added; a parallelogram has four sides, two of each length.
height-for-side (conceptual): The height was used for the slanting sides; the perimeter goes along the sides.
area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The area was found; the perimeter is the distance around.

teach.idea: Cut a triangle off one end of a parallelogram and slide it to the other end: it becomes a rectangle with the same base and height.
teach.method: Area = base × height (the height is at right angles to the base, not the slanting side). Perimeter = 2 × (base + slanting side).

alternatives.title: Cut and slide
text: Draw the parallelogram on squared paper and draw its height from one top corner.
Cut off the triangle and move it to the other side: count the squares of the rectangle you made.

families.title: Area of a rhombus from its diagonals
explanations: not-doubled (conceptual): The area was divided by 30 without doubling it first; area = ½ × d₁ × d₂.
subtracted (conceptual): The diagonal was taken from the area; undo the multiplying by dividing.
no-half (conceptual): The diagonals were multiplied but not halved; the rhombus fills half of the rectangle drawn round it.
added (conceptual): The diagonals were added; the area is half their product.

teach.idea: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and cut it into four equal right triangles; together they fill half of the rectangle d₁ by d₂.
teach.method: Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂. To find a missing diagonal, double the area and divide by the diagonal you know.

alternatives.title: Four triangles
text: Each of the four triangles has sides d₁/2 and d₂/2 at the right angle.
Each has area ½ × d₁/2 × d₂/2; four of them make ½ × d₁ × d₂.

families.title: Total surface area of a cuboid or cube
explanations: three-faces (procedural): Only three faces were added; each face has an equal face opposite it, so double the total.
volume (conceptual): The volume was found; surface area is the total area of the six faces.
walls-only (procedural): Only the four side faces were added; the top and bottom count too.

teach.idea: A cuboid has six rectangular faces in three matching pairs: top and bottom, front and back, two ends.
teach.method: Total surface area = 2(lw + wh + hl). For a cube with edge a, it is 6a².

alternatives.title: Unfold into a net
text: Unfold the box flat: it makes six rectangles.
Find each rectangle's area and add all six.

families.title: Area of the four walls of a room (lateral surface area)
explanations: two-walls (procedural): Only two walls were counted; a room has four walls, two of each size.
with-floor (procedural): The floor was added; the question asks for the four walls only.
total-surface (conceptual): Floor and ceiling were included; the walls are only the four sides.

teach.idea: Unrolled, the four walls of a room make one long rectangle: as long as the distance round the floor and as tall as the room.
teach.method: Lateral surface area = 2(l + w) × h.

alternatives.title: Wall by wall
text: Two walls are length × height; two walls are width × height.
Add all four.

families.title: Volume of a cylinder
explanations: curved-area (conceptual): 2πrh is the curved surface area; the volume is base area × height, πr²h.
not-squared (procedural): The radius was not squared: the base is a circle of area πr².
diameter-squared (procedural): The diameter was squared; use the radius, half the diameter.

teach.idea: A cylinder is a stack of equal circles, like a pile of coins: the volume is the area of one circle times the height.
teach.method: Volume = πr²h. Halve the diameter first if you are given it.

alternatives.title: Like a prism
text: For a cuboid, volume = base area × height.
A cylinder works the same way; only the base is a circle (πr²).

families.title: Curved and total surface area of a cylinder
explanations: forgot-two (procedural): πrh was found; the curved surface unrolls to a rectangle as long as the circumference, 2πr.
volume (conceptual): The volume (πr²h) was found; the curved surface is an area, 2πrh.
no-ends (procedural): Only the curved surface was found; a closed cylinder also has a top and a bottom circle.
one-end (procedural): Only one circle was added; a closed cylinder has two, top and bottom.

teach.idea: Cut the curved surface of a cylinder straight down and unroll it: it is a rectangle, as long as the circumference (2πr) and as tall as the cylinder.
teach.method: Curved surface area = 2πrh. Total surface area = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r).

alternatives.title: Peel the label
text: Peel the paper label off a can and lay it flat: it is a rectangle.
Its length went once round the can, so it equals the circumference.

families.title: Area of a trapezium
explanations: no-half (conceptual): The sum of the parallel sides × height was not halved; two copies of the trapezium make that parallelogram.
long-side-only (conceptual): Only the longer parallel side was used, as for a rectangle; the trapezium is narrower at the top, so use the average of the two sides.

teach.idea: Two copies of a trapezium, one turned upside down, fit together into a parallelogram with base (a + b) and the same height. The trapezium is half of it.
teach.method: Area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height.

alternatives.title: Split into pieces
text: Draw a diagonal: the trapezium becomes two triangles with the same height, bases a and b.
Add their areas: ½ × a × h + ½ × b × h.

families.title: Area and perimeter of an L-shape
explanations: whole-rectangle (procedural): The whole rectangle was found but the cut-out corner was not taken away.
perimeter-for-area (conceptual): The sides were added (the perimeter); area counts the squares inside.
added-cut (procedural): The cut-out was added instead of taken away.
cut-shortens (conceptual): Cutting the corner was thought to shorten the perimeter; the two new edges (11 cm and 2 cm) replace exactly the edges that were removed.
area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The area was found; the perimeter is the distance around the edge.
missed-side (procedural): One of the six sides was missed; go all the way round.

teach.idea: An L-shape is a big rectangle with a small rectangle taken away. Its area is less than the big rectangle's, but its perimeter is the same: the two new edges replace the two that were cut off.
teach.method: Area = big rectangle − cut-out. Perimeter: add all six sides (here it equals 2 × (width + height) of the big rectangle).

alternatives.title: Split into two rectangles
text: Draw one line to split the L into two rectangles.
Find each rectangle's area and add them.

families.title: Area of a rectangular path
explanations: width-once (procedural): The path width was taken off only once; the path is on both sides, so the inner rectangle is 26 m by 16 m.
corners-missed (conceptual): The four strips along the sides were found, but the four corner squares were missed.
outer-only (procedural): The outer rectangle was found but the garden was not taken away.
corners-twice (conceptual): The four strips along the sides were added, so the corner squares were counted twice.
inner-only (procedural): The inner rectangle (the part without the path) was given.

teach.idea: A path around (or inside) a rectangle is the space between two rectangles: the bigger one minus the smaller one.
teach.method: Outside path: (L + 2x)(W + 2x) − LW. Inside path: LW − (L − 2x)(W − 2x). The width is added (or taken off) on both sides.

alternatives.title: Strips and corners
text: Split an outside path into two long strips (L by x), two short strips (W by x) and four corner squares (x by x).
Add them all: do not forget the corners.

families.title: Multiplying decimals
explanations: points-lined-up (procedural): The decimal point was placed as in addition (lined up); in a product, the decimal places of both numbers are added.
point-ignored (procedural): The digits were multiplied but the decimal point was left out.
one-place-off (procedural): The point was moved one place too far; the answer has 2 decimal places.

teach.idea: Tenths times tenths make hundredths (0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01), so the answer has as many decimal places as the two numbers together.
teach.method: Multiply the numbers as if there were no decimal points, count the decimal places in both, and give the answer that many decimal places. Estimate to check (e.g. 1.9 × 3.1 is about 2 × 3 = 6).

alternatives.title: Use fractions
text: Write each decimal as a fraction: 0.7 × 1.3 = 7/10 × 13/10.

families.title: Dividing decimals
explanations: divisor-only-shifted (procedural): The divisor was made a whole number (× 100) but the dividend was not multiplied by the same amount.
point-wrong-way (procedural): The decimal point was moved the wrong way; check with an estimate.
one-place-off (procedural): The decimal point in the answer is one place out; line up the point in the quotient with the dividend's point.

teach.idea: Multiplying both numbers in a division by the same amount does not change the answer (12 ÷ 4 = 120 ÷ 40), so you can make the divisor a whole number first.
teach.method: Move the decimal point in the divisor to make it whole, move the dividend's point the same number of places, then divide as usual, keeping the point in line.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Estimate first: 7.2 ÷ 0.8 is like 72 ÷ 8.
Check: the answer × the divisor must give the dividend.

families.title: Multiplying and dividing decimals by 10, 100 and 1000
explanations: wrong-way (conceptual): The point was moved the wrong way; multiplying makes the number bigger, so the point moves right.
places-off (procedural): The point was moved the wrong number of places; 100 has 2 zeros, so move it 2 places.

teach.idea: Multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth ten times as much, so every digit moves one place to the left; dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right.
teach.method: Count the zeros in 10, 100 or 1000 and move the decimal point that many places: right for ×, left for ÷. Fill empty places with zeros.

alternatives.title: A place-value table
text: Write the number in a place-value table (hundreds, tens, ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
Slide every digit across one column for each zero; the point stays where it is.

families.title: Multiplying fractions and mixed numbers
explanations: cross-multiplied (procedural): The fractions were cross-multiplied (top × other bottom); to multiply fractions, multiply top by top and bottom by bottom.
added (conceptual): The fractions were added; 'of' and '×' mean multiply.
whole-kept-apart (procedural): Only the fraction part was multiplied and 2 was kept as it was; change the mixed number to an improper fraction first (2 11/12 = 35/12).

teach.idea: a/b × c/d means c/d of a/b: cutting each of the b pieces into d smaller ones makes pieces of size 1/(b × d), and you take a × c of them.
teach.method: Change mixed numbers to improper fractions, multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms, and simplify.

alternatives.title: Area model
text: Draw a square. Shade a/b of it across and c/d of it down.
The part shaded both ways is the product: a × c small rectangles out of b × d.

families.title: Dividing fractions using reciprocals
explanations: no-flip (procedural): The fractions were multiplied without turning the second one upside down; dividing by c/d is multiplying by d/c.
flipped-first (procedural): The first fraction was turned upside down instead of the second; only the divisor is replaced by its reciprocal.
multiplied-by-whole (conceptual): The fraction was multiplied by 9; sharing into 9 equal parts makes each part smaller.

teach.idea: Dividing asks 'how many lots of the divisor fit?'. Dividing by c/d is the same as multiplying by d/c, its reciprocal, because c/d × d/c = 1.
teach.method: Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, turn the second fraction upside down, then multiply and simplify.

alternatives.title: Same-size pieces
text: Write both fractions with the same denominator: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6/8 ÷ 1/8.
Now count: how many 1-eighths fit in 6-eighths? 6.

families.title: Adding and subtracting integers
explanations: negatives-make-positive (conceptual): Two negatives were taken to make a positive; that rule is for multiplying. Adding two debts makes a bigger debt.
minus-negative-as-minus (conceptual): Taking away (−11) was done as taking away 11; subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
sign-lost (procedural): The size is right but the sign is wrong; check which way you moved on the number line.
sizes-added (conceptual): The sizes were added; with one positive and one negative number, they cancel, so find the difference of the sizes.
difference-of-sizes (procedural): 33 was taken off towards zero; subtracting a positive number moves left on the number line, further below zero.

teach.idea: On a number line, adding a positive number moves right and adding a negative number moves left. Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite.
teach.method: Change any subtraction into adding the opposite. Same signs: add the sizes and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract the sizes and take the sign of the larger size.

alternatives.title: Positive and negative tokens
text: Use + tokens and − tokens; a + and a − together make zero and can be removed.
To take away tokens you do not have, first add zero pairs (+ and −), then remove what you need.

families.title: Integer differences in temperature and height
explanations: ignored-negative (conceptual): −1 was treated as 1; going from −1 up to 0 is 1 steps, then on to 20.
sizes-added (conceptual): The sizes were added; both values are below zero, so the gap is the difference of the sizes.

teach.idea: The change from one value to another is end − start. On a number line it is the distance between the two points, counting through zero.
teach.method: Subtract the start from the end; subtracting a negative start means adding its size.

alternatives.title: Go through zero
text: Count up from the start to 0, then from 0 to the end.
Add the two parts (when both values are below zero, just count the gap).

families.title: Dividing a whole number by a fraction
explanations: multiplied (conceptual): 12 was multiplied by 9/10. Dividing by a fraction less than 1 gives MORE than 12: multiply by the reciprocal 10/9.
numerator-only (procedural): 12 was divided by the numerator 9 only. Dividing by 9/10 means multiplying by 10 and dividing by 9.
wrong-reciprocal (procedural): The reciprocal of 12 was taken instead of the reciprocal of 9/10. Keep 12 and turn the divisor over.

teach.idea: w ÷ (c/d) asks how many c/d's fit into w. Each whole holds d/c of them, so w wholes hold w × d/c: dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal.
teach.method: Turn the divisor upside down (its reciprocal) and multiply the whole number by it; simplify.

alternatives.title: Count the pieces
text: 6 ÷ 3/4: each whole has 4 quarters, so 6 wholes have 24 quarters.
Group them in threes: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 pieces of 3/4.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Multiply your answer by the fraction.
You should get back the whole number you started with.

families.title: Word problems with multiplying or dividing fractions
explanations: wrong-operation (conceptual): The amount was divided. Taking a fraction OF an amount (… of …) is a multiplication.
flipped-dividend (procedural): The fractions were divided the wrong way round. Divide the whole amount by the size of one part.
added (conceptual): The fractions were added. 'A fraction of' a quantity means multiplying.

teach.idea: 'How many parts of size … fit into …' is a division; 'a fraction of an amount' is a multiplication. Deciding which comes first, then the calculation.
teach.method: Ask what the question wants: a number of equal parts (divide the amount by the size of a part) or a part of an amount (multiply the fraction by the amount). Then multiply by the reciprocal to divide, or multiply tops and bottoms.

alternatives.title: Try easy numbers first
text: Replace the fractions with whole numbers: '6 litres into 2-litre bottles' is 6 ÷ 2.
The same operation works when the numbers are fractions.

alternatives.title: Draw a bar
text: Draw the whole amount as a bar and mark the fraction (or the part size) on it.
Count how many parts fit, or shade the fraction of the bar asked for.

families.title: Expressions and stories with several integer operations
explanations: sign-rule (conceptual): The sign of (−48) ÷ 6 was wrong. Dividing numbers with the same sign gives a positive answer; different signs give a negative one.
left-to-right (procedural): The subtraction was done before the division. Multiplication and division come first.
wrong-added (conceptual): The wrong answers were added. Each wrong answer is −1: 5 × (−1) = −5.
right-only (procedural): Only the right answers were counted; the wrong answers take marks away.
rose (conceptual): The temperature was made to rise. A fall is a negative change: add −4 for each hour.
one-hour (procedural): Only one hour's fall was taken. It fell 4 °C every hour for 3 hours: 3 × (−4).

teach.idea: Brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −, also for integers. A product or quotient of two numbers with the same sign is positive; with different signs it is negative. Repeated falls or losses are multiplication by a negative number.
teach.method: Work out each product or quotient with the sign rule, then add or subtract the results from left to right.

alternatives.title: Picture it on a number line
text: A fall of 3 °C each hour for 4 hours is 4 jumps of −3 on the number line.
Start at the first temperature and make the jumps.

alternatives.title: A sign table
text: Decide the sign first, then multiply the sizes.

families.title: Several integer changes in a row: temperatures, lifts and divers
explanations: fall-added (conceptual): The dive down of 21 was added. Going down is a negative change: take 21 away.
start-sign (conceptual): The start was read as 3 instead of −3. Below zero the numbers are negative.
sign-dropped (procedural): After a negative running total (−23), the minus sign was dropped, so 23 + 10 was worked out. Keep the sign: −23 + 10.

teach.idea: Rises and trips up are positive changes, falls and trips down are negative changes. Apply them one after another, in order.
teach.method: Start at the first value. Add each rise, subtract each fall, one at a time; when you cross zero, count down to 0 and carry on into the negatives.

alternatives.title: Use a vertical number line
text: Draw a thermometer (or a lift shaft) with 0 in the middle.
Move up and down it step by step and read where you end.

alternatives.title: Find the net change
text: Add all the rises, add all the falls, and subtract: +x + z − y.
Then add the net change to the starting value.

families.title: Estimating decimal products and quotients
explanations: cut-off (procedural): The decimals were just cut off. Rounding to the nearest whole number looks at the tenths: 5 or more rounds up.
exact-not-estimate (conceptual): The exact answer was worked out and rounded. An estimate rounds the numbers FIRST, so it can be done in your head; here it is the rounded numbers' result.

teach.idea: An estimate tells roughly how big an answer should be, so a misplaced decimal point shows up at once. Rounding the numbers first makes the calculation easy to do in your head.
teach.method: Round each number to the nearest whole number (look at the tenths: 5 or more, round up). Multiply or divide the rounded numbers. Compare with the exact answer: they should be close.

alternatives.title: Use it to check the point
text: 4.8 × 6.1 ≈ 5 × 6 = 30, so the exact answer 29.28 is sensible; 292.8 or 2.928 is not.
Always estimate before placing the decimal point.

alternatives.title: Round on a number line
text: Mark the decimal between the two whole numbers it lies between.
It rounds to the nearer one.

families.title: Areas of fields and polygons split into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums
explanations: no-half (procedural): The trapezium's area was not halved: area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × distance between them.
one-triangle (procedural): Only one of the two triangles was found; the field is both triangles together.
triangle-not-halved (procedural): The triangle was counted as a full rectangle. Its area is ½ × width × height.
rectangle-only (procedural): Only the rectangle was found. The triangle on top is part of the wall too.
area-only (procedural): The area was found but not the cost. Multiply the area by the cost per m².
no-double (procedural): The area was divided by the sum of the parallel sides without doubling it first. Area = ½ × (a + b) × h, so h = 2 × area ÷ (a + b).
one-side (procedural): The area was divided by one parallel side only.

teach.idea: Any polygon can be cut into triangles, rectangles and trapeziums whose areas you know; the pieces' areas add up to the whole. A trapezium's area is ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × the distance between them.
teach.method: Split the shape along a diagonal or a line you know, find each piece's area, and add. For a cost, multiply the area by the rate; to find a missing distance, put the area into the formula and solve.

alternatives.title: A surveyor's field book
text: Measure along one diagonal and the offsets (the perpendicular distances) to the other corners.
Each offset makes a triangle with the diagonal: add ½ × diagonal × offset for each.

alternatives.title: Draw it on squared paper
text: Draw the field to scale on squared paper.
Count whole squares and pair up half squares to check your answer.

families.title: Circumference ÷ diameter, and values of π through history
explanations: upside-down (procedural): The diameter was divided by the circumference. π is circumference ÷ diameter, a little more than 3.
radius (conceptual): The circumference was divided by the radius (300 mm). Dividing by the radius gives 2π, about 6.28; π uses the diameter.
too-few-places (procedural): Only two decimal places were given; four are asked.
diameter-as-radius (conceptual): The diameter was used as the radius in C = 2πr, which doubles the circumference. With the diameter, C = π × d.
radius-times-pi (procedural): Half the diameter (192.5 mm) was multiplied by π. C = π × d, or 2 × π × r with r = 192.5 mm.

teach.idea: For every circle, big or small, the circumference is a little more than 3 times the diameter: C ÷ d is always the same number, π ≈ 3.1416. Mathematicians in India and elsewhere found better and better fractions for it (Aryabhata: 62832/20000).
teach.method: Divide the circumference by the diameter (both in the same unit) and round to the places asked. For a fraction, divide the top by the bottom.

alternatives.title: Measure with a string
text: Wrap a string round a bangle, a plate and a wheel; measure the string and each diameter.
Divide each time: the answers all come out close to 3.14.

alternatives.title: Three diameters and a bit
text: Lay three diameters of string round the circle: a small gap is left.
So C is a bit more than 3d, about 3.14 d.

families.title: Convex, non-convex, or not a quadrilateral?
explanations: obtuse-is-dent (conceptual): An obtuse angle (more than 90°) was taken as a dent. A figure is non-convex only when an angle is more than 180°.
all-convex (conceptual): Every four-sided figure was taken to be convex. One corner here points inwards (the figure has a dent), so it is non-convex.
four-points-enough (conceptual): Four points were taken to make a quadrilateral. A, B and C lie on one straight line, so the figure is a triangle, not a 4-gon.

teach.idea: A quadrilateral (4-gon) is a closed figure of four line segments meeting only at their ends, with no three corners in a line. It is convex when every inside angle is less than 180° (no dents); if one angle is more than 180°, it is non-convex.
teach.method: Check for a straight angle (180°) or three corners in a line: then it is not a quadrilateral. Otherwise look for an angle bigger than 180° (a corner pointing inwards): non-convex. If none, convex.

alternatives.title: Look at the diagonals
text: In a convex quadrilateral both diagonals lie inside it.
In a non-convex one, one diagonal lies outside.

alternatives.title: The rubber-band test
text: Imagine stretching a rubber band round the four corners.
If the band touches every side, it is convex; if it skips a corner that is pushed in, it is non-convex.

families.title: Areas of wipers, tile designs and lighthouse beams
explanations: whole-sector (conceptual): The whole sector out to 56 cm was found. The blade does not reach the part within 42 cm of the pivot: take that smaller sector away.
difference-squared (procedural): The radii were subtracted before squaring (56 − 42)². Find each sector's area, then subtract: the area depends on b² − a².
one-quarter (procedural): Only one quarter circle was taken away. There is one at each of the four corners: together they make a whole circle.
side-as-radius (procedural): The side of the tile (84 cm) was used as the radius.
one-segment (procedural): Only one half of the leaf was found. The leaf is two equal segments, one from each quarter circle.
quarter-circle (conceptual): The area of a whole quarter circle was given. The leaf is the part where the two quarter circles overlap: quarter circle − triangle, twice.
full-circle (conceptual): The area of the whole circle was found. The light covers only 135/360 of it.
arc-not-area (procedural): The arc length was found instead of the area. The area of a sector is (θ/360) × πr².

teach.idea: A sector of angle θ is θ/360 of a circle, so its area is (θ/360) × πr². Shapes from wipers and designs are built from sectors, squares and triangles by adding and taking away.
teach.method: Split the shape: a wiper's path is a big sector minus a small one; corner quarter circles together make a whole circle; a leaf is two segments, each a quarter circle minus a right triangle. Work out each part, then combine.

alternatives.title: Think in fractions of a circle
text: 90° is a quarter of a full turn, 120° a third, 60° a sixth.
So the sector is that fraction of πr².

alternatives.title: Add and take away
text: Write the shaded area as (big shape) − (pieces cut out) or (piece) + (piece).
Work out each piece separately and combine them at the end.

families.title: Surface area and volume of a hollow cylinder (a pipe)
explanations: outside-only (procedural): Only the outside curved surface was found. A pipe has an inside surface too: 2πrh.
radius-difference (conceptual): The difference of the radii was used. The two curved surfaces ADD: 2πh(R + r).
no-ends (procedural): The two ring-shaped ends were left out of the total surface.
full-circle-ends (conceptual): The ends were taken as full circles. Each end is a ring: πR² − πr².
difference-squared (conceptual): (R − r)² was used. The metal's cross-section is πR² − πr², not π(R − r)².
outer-only (procedural): The whole cylinder's volume was found. Take away the hollow inside: πr²h.

teach.idea: A hollow cylinder is a big cylinder with a smaller one taken out. Its curved surface has an outside part 2πRh and an inside part 2πrh; each end is a ring of area πR² − πr²; its volume is π(R² − r²)h.
teach.method: Work out the outer and inner curved surfaces and add them. For the total surface, add two rings. For the volume, find the ring's area and multiply by the length.

alternatives.title: Unroll the pipe
text: Cut the pipe along its length: the outside unrolls into a rectangle 2πR by h, the inside into one 2πr by h.
The ends are rings, like flat bangles.

alternatives.title: Big minus small
text: Volume: (volume of the solid cylinder of radius R) − (volume of the hole of radius r).
Ring: πR² − πr² = π(R + r)(R − r).

families.title: Finding the radius or diameter from the circumference
explanations: gave-diameter (procedural): C ÷ π gives the diameter. The radius is half of it.
times-pi (conceptual): The circumference was multiplied by π. To undo C = 2πr, divide by 2π.
gave-radius (procedural): The radius was found. The diameter is twice the radius: C ÷ π.
halved-c (conceptual): The circumference was halved. Dividing by π (about 3.14) gives the diameter.
whole-distance (procedural): The whole distance was used. In one turn the wheel rolls its circumference: 440 m ÷ 100 turns.

teach.idea: C = πd = 2πr. Working backwards: d = C ÷ π and r = C ÷ 2π. A wheel rolls its circumference in one turn.
teach.method: Divide the circumference by 22/7 (multiply by 7/22) to get the diameter; halve it for the radius. For a wheel, first divide the distance by the number of turns (in the same unit).

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Put your radius back into C = 2 × 22/7 × r.
You should get the circumference you started with.

alternatives.title: Rough size first
text: The circumference is a little more than 3 diameters.
So the diameter is a little less than C ÷ 3, and the radius about C ÷ 6.

families.title: Word problems with dividing decimals
explanations: point-slip (procedural): The decimal point was moved in only one of the numbers. Multiply the dividend and the divisor by the SAME power of 10 so the divisor becomes a whole number.
point-slip-other (procedural): The answer's decimal point is one place out. Estimate first: the answer must be about 21 ÷ 1.
multiplied (conceptual): The numbers were multiplied. Sharing or cutting into equal parts is a division.

teach.idea: Dividing by a decimal asks how many of it fit (or how much each gets). Multiplying both numbers by the same power of 10 does not change the answer, and makes the divisor a whole number.
teach.method: Move the decimal point in both numbers the same number of places until the divisor is whole. Then divide as usual, placing the point in the answer above the point in the dividend. Estimate to check.

alternatives.title: Think in paise or centimetres
text: 7.5 m ÷ 0.25 m is the same as 750 cm ÷ 25 cm = 30.

alternatives.title: Estimate first
text: Round both numbers: 7.5 ÷ 0.25 is about 8 ÷ 0.25 = 32.
Your exact answer should be close to the estimate.

families.title: Ordering positive and negative integers
explanations: ignore-sign (conceptual): The numbers were ordered by their size without the minus sign. On the number line, −4 is to the left of −3, so −4 is smaller.
negatives-reversed (conceptual): Among the negative numbers, the one with the bigger digit was taken as bigger. −4 is further below zero than −3, so −4 is the smaller number.
decreasing (procedural): The numbers were written largest first; increasing order starts with the smallest.

teach.idea: On a number line, numbers get bigger as you move to the right. Every negative number is left of 0, and the further a negative number is from 0, the smaller it is.
teach.method: Mark the numbers on a number line, then read them from left to right.

alternatives.title: Think of a thermometer
text: −8 °C is colder than −3 °C: it is further below zero.
So start with the coldest (most negative) temperature and go up to the warmest.

families.title: Multiplying by a number near 100 using the distributive property
explanations: wrong-sign-correction (conceptual): 102 is 100 plus 2, so 99 × 2 must be added to 99 × 100.
correction-not-multiplied (procedural): Only 2 was added; every one of the 99 lots gains 2, so it is 99 × 2.
part-left-out (procedural): Only 99 × 100 was found; the 99 × 2 part was left out.

teach.idea: Multiplication spreads over addition and subtraction: k × (100 − 2) = k × 100 − k × 2.
teach.method: Write the number near 100 as 100 plus or minus a little, multiply k by each part, then add or take away.

alternatives.title: Split a rectangle
text: Think of k × 98 as the area of a rectangle k by 98.
It is a k by 100 rectangle with a k by 2 strip cut off: k × 100 − k × 2.

families.title: Removing brackets after a minus sign
explanations: sign-not-changed (conceptual): When brackets after a minus sign are removed, every sign inside changes: 99 − (49 + 10) = 99 − 49 − 10.
last-term-dropped (procedural): The 10 inside the brackets was forgotten after the brackets were removed.

teach.idea: Taking away a bracket takes away everything inside it: taking away (b − c) takes away b but gives c back.
teach.method: Remove the brackets and change the sign of every term inside, then group numbers that are easy to combine.

alternatives.title: Money in and out
text: Spending ₹47 and then getting ₹8 back is the same as spending ₹(47 − 8).

families.title: Writing a number as a product of primes
explanations: composite-left (procedural): The splitting stopped too early: 25 is not prime, so it can still be split into 5 × 5.
one-included (conceptual): 1 was written as a factor. 1 is not a prime number, so it is not part of the list.
repeat-missed (conceptual): Each prime was written only once. A prime must be written as many times as it divides the number.

teach.idea: Every whole number greater than 1 is either prime or can be split into primes in exactly one way (apart from order).
teach.method: Divide by the smallest prime that goes exactly (2, then 3, then 5 …) again and again until 1 is left. The divisors are the prime factors.

alternatives.title: A factor tree
text: Split the number into any two factors, for example 72 = 8 × 9.
Keep splitting every factor that is not prime: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 9 = 3 × 3.
The primes at the ends of the branches are the answer: 2, 2, 2, 3, 3.

families.title: The smallest multiplier that makes a perfect square
explanations: itself (conceptual): 500 × 500 is a perfect square, but it is not the smallest; only the primes without a partner are needed.
largest-prime (procedural): The largest prime factor of 495 was used; the primes without a partner decide the multiplier, not the largest prime.
one-unpaired (procedural): Only one of the primes without a partner was used; every prime without a partner needs one more copy.

teach.idea: In a perfect square every prime factor comes in pairs, because the number is something times itself.
teach.method: Write the number as a product of primes and pair equal primes. Multiply together the primes that have no partner: that is the smallest multiplier.

alternatives.title: Even powers
text: Write the number in index form, for example 180 = 2² × 3² × 5.
A perfect square has only even powers, so multiply by each prime with an odd power once: here by 5.

families.title: A ratio in its simplest form
explanations: not-simplest (procedural): Both numbers were divided by 2, but they still have a common factor; divide by their highest common factor, 10.
order-reversed (conceptual): The ratio was written the other way round; the first quantity named comes first.
units-not-matched (conceptual): The two lengths were compared in different units. Change metres to centimetres first (1 m = 100 cm).

teach.idea: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind. Dividing both by the same number gives an equal ratio, like an equivalent fraction.
teach.method: Make the units the same, then divide both numbers by their highest common factor.

alternatives.title: Equal groups
text: 18 : 24 means 18 of one thing for every 24 of another.
Make groups of 6: 3 groups and 4 groups. So for every 3 of the first there are 4 of the second: 3 : 4.

families.title: The missing term of an equivalent ratio
explanations: additive (conceptual): The same amount was added to both terms. Equivalent ratios multiply both terms by the same number (here 10).
scale-factor-given (procedural): 10 is how many times bigger the terms became; the missing term is 12 × 10.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (9 × 2) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying (or dividing) both terms by the same number, just like equivalent fractions.
teach.method: Find what the known term was multiplied by, then multiply the other term by the same number.

alternatives.title: A ratio table
text: Write the ratio in two rows: 2 | 3.
Keep doubling, tripling … both rows together: 4 | 6, 6 | 9, 8 | 12, until you reach the known number.

families.title: Finding a unit rate
explanations: multiplied (conceptual): The total was multiplied by 11. To find the amount for one, share the total equally: divide by 11.
subtracted (conceptual): 11 was taken away from the total; sharing equally means dividing.
division-slip (recall): A division step slipped. Check by multiplying back: the answer × 11 should give 1089.

teach.idea: A unit rate is the amount for one unit: one kilogram, one hour, one kilometre or one day.
teach.method: Divide the total by the number of units. Check by multiplying back.

alternatives.title: Share it out
text: Imagine the total being shared equally among the units, one by one.
Each unit gets the same amount: that amount is the rate.

families.title: The better buy by unit price
explanations: bigger-pack (conceptual): The bigger pack was taken to be the better value. A bigger pack is not always cheaper per item: compare the price of one soap.
price-difference (procedural): The difference between the two prices per soap was given; the question asks for the price of one soap in the better pack.
lower-total (conceptual): The pack with the lower total price was chosen. The packs hold different numbers of soaps, so compare the price of one soap.

teach.idea: To compare packs of different sizes, compare the same amount from each: the price of one item is the fairest comparison.
teach.method: Divide each pack's price by the number of items, then choose the lower price per item.

alternatives.title: Buy the same number
text: Find a number of soaps both packs can make, for example 12 from packs of 4 and 6.
Work out what 12 soaps cost using each pack, and see which is cheaper.

families.title: Time taken working together
explanations: add-days (conceptual): The days were added. Working together is faster than either alone, so the answer must be less than both.
average-days (conceptual): The average of the two times was found. Two people working together finish sooner than the faster one alone.
rate-not-inverted (procedural): The work done in one day (1/23 + 1/24) was given; the number of days is 1 divided by that.

teach.idea: Rates add: if Arun does 1/6 of the job each day and Bala 1/12, together they do 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 each day.
teach.method: Add the work done per day, then divide 1 whole job by that rate.

alternatives.title: Count pieces of a bigger job
text: Pretend the job has 12 pieces (a number both times divide).
In one day Arun does 12 ÷ 6 = 2 pieces and Bala 12 ÷ 12 = 1: together 3 pieces a day, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 days.

families.title: Laws of exponents with one base
explanations: reversed-subtraction (procedural): The powers were subtracted the wrong way round: it is the top power minus the bottom power.
added-exponents (procedural): The powers were added; that is the rule for multiplying, not dividing.
multiplied-exponents (conceptual): The powers were multiplied. aᵐ × aⁿ puts 12 factors and 8 factors together, so the powers add.
added-for-power (conceptual): The powers were added. (aᵐ)ⁿ is aᵐ written 6 times, so the powers multiply.
power-of-power (procedural): The first power was raised to the second; the powers simply multiply.
divided-exponents (conceptual): The powers were divided. Dividing cancels factors, so the powers subtract.

teach.idea: A power counts how many times the base is multiplied. Multiplying joins the factors (add the powers), dividing cancels them (subtract), and a power of a power repeats them (multiply).
teach.method: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. A negative power means a fraction: a⁻² = 1/a².

families.title: The units digit of a large power
explanations: multiplied (conceptual): The units digit 9 was multiplied by 19; a power multiplies 9 by itself 19 times.
last-digit-of-power (procedural): The last digit of the power (0) was used; use the remainder when 60 is divided by the length of the cycle.
remainder-zero (procedural): 60 divides exactly by the length of the cycle, so the answer is the LAST digit of the cycle, not 1.

teach.idea: Only the units digit affects the units digit of a product, and the units digits of powers repeat in a short cycle.
teach.method: Write the units digits of the first few powers until they repeat. Divide the power by the cycle length; the remainder tells the place in the cycle (remainder 0 means the last place).

alternatives.title: A table of units digits
text: Powers of 7: 7, 9, 3, 1, then 7 again: a cycle of 4.
7³⁰: 30 = 4 × 7 + 2, so it is the 2nd in the cycle: 9.

families.title: Zero and negative powers
explanations: negative-as-minus (conceptual): 10⁻⁴ was read as a negative number. A negative power means a fraction: 10⁻⁴ = 1/10⁴.
multiplied (conceptual): 10 was multiplied by −3. A power is repeated multiplication; a negative power is 1 over the positive power.
reciprocal-missed (procedural): The value of the positive power was given; a negative power turns it into 1 over that number.
sign-ignored (procedural): The powers were added as 5 + 2; the second power is −2, so it is 5 − 2.

teach.idea: Each step down in the power divides by the base once: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4.
teach.method: Combine the powers first (add them, keeping the signs), then a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.

alternatives.title: Keep dividing
text: Write the powers of the base in a row and divide by the base each time you go left.
The pattern shows a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, never a negative number.

families.title: Crores and lakhs in millions
explanations: crore-is-million (conceptual): 1 crore was taken as 1 million. 1 million is 10 lakh, so 1 crore (100 lakh) is 10 million.
crore-hundred-million (recall): 1 crore was taken as 100 million; 1 crore is 10 million (and 100 crore is 1 billion).
lakh-is-million (conceptual): 1 lakh was taken as 1 million. 1 lakh is 1,00,000 = one hundred thousand; 10 lakh make a million.

teach.idea: Both systems use the same digits; only the grouping differs. 10 lakh = 1 million, and 1 crore = 10 million.
teach.method: Rewrite the number with international commas (groups of three: 34,000,000) and read the millions.

alternatives.title: Count the zeros
text: 1 lakh has 5 zeros, 1 million has 6, 1 crore has 7.
So 1 crore = 10 million, and 10 lakh = 1 million.

families.title: Multiplying integers
explanations: sign-rule (conceptual): A positive times a negative was made positive. The product of a positive and a negative number is negative.
added (conceptual): The two numbers were added instead of multiplied.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (12 × 2) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Multiplying by a negative number reverses the direction: so a negative times a positive is negative, and a negative times a negative is positive.
teach.method: Multiply the sizes, then decide the sign: same signs give +, different signs give −.

alternatives.title: Follow a pattern
text: Keep going: −3 × (−1) = 3, −3 × (−2) = 6. A negative times a negative is positive.

families.title: Selling price or cost price from a profit or loss per cent
explanations: amount-only (procedural): Only the loss (40% of ₹1,000) was found; the selling price is the cost price minus it.
wrong-direction (conceptual): The loss was added. A profit means selling for more than the cost; a loss means selling for less.
applied-forward (procedural): The loss was applied to the selling price as if it were the cost price. Here the selling price is known and the cost price is the unknown.
percent-of-sp (conceptual): 40% of the selling price was added to it. Profit and loss per cent are of the COST price, so the selling price is 60% of the cost price: divide by 60 and multiply by 100.
percent-as-rupees (conceptual): 40% was used as ₹40; 40% of ₹1,000 means 40 out of every 100 rupees.

teach.idea: Profit or loss per cent compares the profit or loss with the cost price: 20% profit means the selling price is 120% of the cost price.
teach.method: To find the selling price, find p% of the cost price and add it (profit) or take it away (loss). To find the cost price, divide the selling price by (100 ± p) and multiply by 100.

alternatives.title: Think of 100 parts
text: Split the cost price into 100 equal parts.
With a 15% profit the selling price is 115 of those parts; with a 15% loss it is 85 parts.

families.title: Simple interest, amount, rate or time
explanations: no-hundred (conceptual): The interest was divided by 13 × 3 but not multiplied by 100. 13% means 13 out of 100, so P = SI × 100 ÷ (R × T).
one-year (procedural): Only one year's interest was added; the money is lent for 3 years.
amount-given (procedural): The amount (principal + interest) was given; the question asks for the interest only.
interest-only (procedural): Only the interest was found; the amount is the principal plus the interest.
time-forgotten (procedural): The time was left out: the interest is for 3 years, so divide by R × T = 13 × 3.
one-year-interest (conceptual): One year's interest in rupees was given; the rate compares it with the principal, out of 100.
rate-and-time (conceptual): The interest was divided by the rate; divide it by one year's interest (P × R ÷ 100) to count the years.
year-interest-given (procedural): One year's interest was given; the time is how many years of that interest make the total.
multiplied-back (conceptual): The interest formula was used forwards on the interest itself. Here the interest is known and the principal is the unknown: P = SI × 100 ÷ (R × T).

teach.idea: Simple interest is the same every year: R% of the principal, so T years give T times as much. SI = P × R × T ÷ 100.
teach.method: Write SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, put in the three numbers you know, and work out the fourth.

alternatives.title: Year by year
text: Find one year's interest first: R% of P.
Add it once for every year. To find the time, count how many years of interest make the total.

families.title: Discount and GST
explanations: discount-only (procedural): Only the discount was found; the selling price is the marked price minus the discount.
wrong-direction (conceptual): The discount was added; a discount makes the price lower.
tax-only (procedural): Only the GST was found; the price including GST is the price plus the tax.
percent-as-rupees (conceptual): 50% was used as ₹50; 50% of ₹3,000 means 50 rupees for every 100 rupees.

teach.idea: A discount is a per cent of the marked price taken off; GST is a per cent of the price added on.
teach.method: Find the per cent of the price, then subtract it (discount) or add it (GST).

alternatives.title: One multiplication
text: A 20% discount leaves 80% of the price: multiply by 80 and divide by 100.
18% GST makes 118% of the price: multiply by 118 and divide by 100.

families.title: Sharing an amount in a given ratio
explanations: one-part (procedural): The value of one part (₹460 ÷ 23) was given; Ravi gets 9 parts.
shared-equally (conceptual): The money was shared equally. In a ratio the shares are different: count the parts first.
other-share (procedural): Someone else's share was given; check whose part of the ratio is asked for.
ratio-as-fraction (conceptual): The ratio 7 : 6 was read as the fraction 7/6 of the whole. The whole is 13 parts, so Anu gets 7/13 of it.

teach.idea: A ratio a : b splits the whole into a + b equal parts; the first person gets a of them and the second b.
teach.method: Add the terms to find the number of parts, divide the total by it to find one part, then multiply by the person's number of parts.

alternatives.title: A bar model
text: Draw one bar for each person: a boxes, b boxes (and c boxes).
All the boxes are equal; the total divided by the number of boxes is the value of one box.

families.title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing rational numbers
explanations: add-tops-and-bottoms (conceptual): The tops and the bottoms were added (or subtracted) separately. Write both fractions with the same denominator first.
sign-error (conceptual): The sign is wrong: compare the sizes of the two fractions to see whether the answer is above or below zero.
minus-negative (conceptual): Subtracting −1/6 was done as subtracting 1/6. Taking away a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
cross-multiplied (procedural): The fractions were cross-multiplied. To multiply fractions, multiply top by top and bottom by bottom.
not-flipped (procedural): The fractions were multiplied without turning the second one upside down. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.
flipped-first (procedural): The first fraction was turned upside down; it is the second one (the divisor) that is flipped.

teach.idea: Rational numbers follow the same rules as fractions, together with the sign rules for integers.
teach.method: For + and −, write both with a common denominator and combine the tops. For ×, multiply tops and bottoms. For ÷, multiply by the reciprocal of the second. Then fix the sign and simplify.

alternatives.title: Move on the number line
text: Adding a negative fraction moves left; subtracting a negative fraction moves right.
Mark the first fraction and move by the second to see the sign of the answer before working it out.

families.title: Compound interest and depreciation
explanations: simple-interest (conceptual): Simple interest was found. With compound interest, each year's interest is added on and earns interest too.
amount-given (procedural): The amount was given; compound interest is the amount minus the principal.
simple-depreciation (conceptual): 20% of the ORIGINAL value was taken off every year. Each year the loss is 20% of that year's starting value, which keeps getting smaller.
loss-given (procedural): The total loss in value was given; the question asks what the machine is worth.
growth (conceptual): The value was increased; depreciation means the value goes down each year.
full-rate-each-half (procedural): For half-yearly compounding the rate for each half-year is 10%, not 20%, and there are 4 half-years.
compounded-yearly (procedural): The interest was compounded once a year; half-yearly means 4 periods at 10% each.

teach.idea: With compound interest, each period's interest joins the principal, so the next period's interest is bigger. Depreciation works the same way, downwards.
teach.method: Amount = P × (1 + R/100)ⁿ (depreciation: 1 − R/100). Half-yearly: use R/2 for each half-year and 2n half-years. Interest = amount − principal.

alternatives.title: A year-by-year table
text: Year 1: interest on the principal, add it on.
Year 2: interest on the new amount, add it on. Repeat for each year, then subtract the starting principal.

families.title: Cubes and cube roots
explanations: times-three (conceptual): 25³ was worked out as 25 × 3; a cube multiplies 25 by itself three times.
squared (procedural): 25 was multiplied by itself only twice (that is 25²).
near-cube (recall): A cube next to the right one was used; check: −30 × (−30) × (−30) = −27000.
divided-by-three (conceptual): The number was divided by 3; a cube root is the number that, multiplied by itself three times, gives it.
square-root (procedural): The square root was found; a cube root needs three equal factors, not two.
sign-dropped (conceptual): A negative number has a negative cube root, because a negative × negative × negative is negative.

teach.idea: A cube is a number times itself three times; a cube root undoes it. Three negative factors make a negative, so negative numbers have negative cube roots.
teach.method: For a cube root, use the units digit to guess the last digit of the root and the size to guess the tens, then check by cubing. Or use prime factors in groups of three.

alternatives.title: Group prime factors in threes
text: Write the number as a product of primes, e.g. 1728 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3.
Take one prime from each group of three equal primes: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.

families.title: The smallest multiplier that makes a perfect cube
explanations: one-each (procedural): Each incomplete group got one more prime; a group of one needs two more to make three.
leftover-given (procedural): The primes left over after taking out the complete groups of three were given; the multiplier is what is MISSING to complete those groups.
square-of-number (conceptual): Multiplying by 2000 × 2000 does make a cube (2000³), but it is not the smallest; only the missing primes are needed.
square-thinking (conceptual): The primes were paired as for a perfect square. A perfect cube needs every prime in groups of three.

teach.idea: In a perfect cube every prime factor comes in groups of three, because the number is something times itself three times.
teach.method: Write the number as a product of primes and group equal primes in threes. Multiply by whatever primes are needed to complete every group.

alternatives.title: Powers that divide by 3
text: Write the number in index form, e.g. 72 = 2³ × 3².
A perfect cube has every power a multiple of 3: 3² needs one more 3, so multiply by 3.

families.title: When doubling overtakes adding
explanations: last-day-behind (procedural): The last day on which Plan A was still ahead (or equal) was given; the question asks for the first day Plan B is ahead.
start-as-day-one (procedural): The start was counted as day 1; here the start is day 0.
power-as-multiplication (conceptual): After n days of doubling the amount is ₹7 × 2ⁿ, not ₹7 × 2 × n: each day multiplies by 2 again.
doubling-as-adding (conceptual): Doubling was treated as adding ₹10 each day. Doubling adds the whole current amount, which itself keeps growing.

teach.idea: Adding grows by the same amount each step (linear); doubling grows by more and more each step (exponential), so doubling always overtakes in the end.
teach.method: Make a table of the two plans day by day: add for one, double for the other, and look for the first day the doubling plan is bigger.

alternatives.title: Folding paper
text: Fold a sheet in half again and again: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 … layers.
Adding one sheet each time gives only 2, 3, 4, 5 …: doubling soon leaves adding far behind.

families.title: A numeral in another base, in base ten
explanations: read-as-ten (conceptual): The digits were read as a base-ten number. In base 9 the places are worth 1, 9, 81, …, not 1, 10, 100.
digit-sum (conceptual): The digits were simply added; each digit must be multiplied by the value of its place first.
places-reversed (procedural): The place values were taken from the left; the rightmost digit is the ones place, then 9s, then 81s.

teach.idea: In base b, each place is worth b times the place to its right: 1, b, b², b³, … just as base ten has 1, 10, 100.
teach.method: Multiply each digit by the value of its place and add the results.

alternatives.title: Multiply and add from the left
text: Start with the first digit. Multiply by the base and add the next digit; repeat to the end.

families.title: A base-ten number in another base
explanations: remainders-top-down (procedural): The remainders were written in the order they were found. The first remainder is the ones digit, so read them from the last one up.
one-division (procedural): Only one division was done: 199 = 22 × 9 + 1, but 22 is 9 or more, so it must be divided by 9 again.
unchanged (conceptual): The base-ten digits were kept. In base 9 only the digits 0 to 8 are used and the places are worth 1, 9, 81, ….

teach.idea: Writing a number in base b means making groups of 1, b, b², … : the remainders after dividing by b are the digits, ones first.
teach.method: Divide by b again and again, writing each remainder. Stop at 0, then read the remainders from the last to the first.

alternatives.title: Take away the biggest places
text: List the place values: for base 3, 1, 3, 9, 27, 81.
Take away as many of the biggest place value as fit; the count is that digit. Repeat with the next place.

families.title: Divisibility and co-primeness from prime factorisations
explanations: bigger-divisible (conceptual): The larger number was taken to be divisible by the smaller one. One number is divisible by another only when every prime factor of the second appears in the first at least as many times.
not-dividing-is-coprime (conceptual): Because neither number divides the other, they were called co-prime. Co-prime means the two numbers share no prime factor at all; these two share one.
direction-reversed (conceptual): The direction was reversed. 'A is divisible by B' means B goes into A exactly, so every prime factor of B must appear in A at least as often.
coprime-means-prime (conceptual): Co-prime was taken to mean that both numbers must be prime. Co-prime means the two numbers have no prime factor in common, even when neither of them is prime.

teach.idea: B divides A exactly when every prime of B appears in A at least as many times. Two numbers are co-prime when they share no prime factor, so their only common factor is 1.
teach.method: Compare the powers prime by prime: if each power in B is at most the power in A, A is divisible by B. If no prime appears in both, they are co-prime.

alternatives.title: Prime boxes
text: Put the primes of each number into boxes: 2, 2, 2, 3 for 24 and 2, 3 for 6.
If all of B's primes can be matched with primes of A, then B goes into A. If no prime can be matched at all, the numbers are co-prime.

families.title: Integers on the number line and in real situations
explanations: wrong-direction (conceptual): P was moved the wrong way. Moving left on the number line gives smaller numbers, moving right gives larger ones.
start-counted (procedural): The marks were counted instead of the jumps between them.
sign-missing (conceptual): "a withdrawal of ₹4 from a bank account" is on the negative side, so it is written with a minus sign.
sign-swapped (conceptual): Above zero, above sea level, a gain or a deposit is written as a positive number; negative numbers are for the opposite.
unchanged (conceptual): The number was copied. The opposite of a number is the same distance from 0 on the other side, so its sign changes.
situation-not-opposite (procedural): The situation itself was written as an integer. Its opposite goes the other way, so the sign changes.
sizes-added (conceptual): The sizes were added, but −3 and −1 are both below 0; count from one to the other.
