sizes-subtracted (conceptual): The sizes were subtracted, but −1 and 9 are on opposite sides of 0: it is 1 units to 0 and 9 more.

teach.idea: On a number line, positive integers are to the right of 0 and negative integers to the left. Every integer has an opposite, the same distance from 0 on the other side.
teach.method: Decide the direction first (above or below, gain or loss, left or right), then count the units from 0 or from the starting point.

alternatives.title: A lift in a building
text: Think of the ground floor as 0, floors above as 1, 2, 3 and basements as −1, −2, −3.
Going up adds, going down subtracts; the opposite of 3 floors up is 3 floors down.

families.title: Crores and lakhs in figures; millions and billions in lakhs and crores
explanations: no-place-holder (procedural): The numbers were written next to each other without zeros for the empty places. Lakhs take two places and thousands two places, so missing digits must be filled with 0.
crore-six-zeros (recall): 1 crore was written with six zeros (10,00,000), which is 10 lakh. 1 crore is 1,00,00,000: seven zeros, so 99 crore = 99,00,00,000.
lakh-as-ten-lakh (recall): 1 lakh was written as 10,00,000; 1 lakh is 1,00,000 (five zeros).
million-is-lakh (conceptual): 1 million was taken as 1 lakh. 1 million is 10,00,000, which is 10 lakh.
million-is-crore (conceptual): 1 million was taken as 1 crore (100 lakh). 1 million is 10 lakh, and 1 crore is 10 million.
billion-is-crore (conceptual): 1 billion was taken as 1 crore. 1 billion = 1000 million, and 1 crore = 10 million, so 1 billion = 100 crore.
billion-thousand-crore (procedural): 1 billion is 1000 million, but a crore is 10 million, not 1 million: 1 billion = 100 crore.

teach.idea: In the Indian system the places after thousands are lakhs and crores: 1 lakh = 1,00,000 and 1 crore = 1,00,00,000. 10 lakh = 1 million and 100 crore = 1 billion.
teach.method: Write each period in its own places (crores, then two places for lakhs, two for thousands, three for the rest), filling empty places with 0. To convert, use 1 million = 10 lakh and 1 billion = 100 crore.

alternatives.title: Count the zeros
text: 1 lakh has 5 zeros, 1 million 6, 1 crore 7 and 1 billion 9.
So a million is 10 lakh (one more zero) and a billion is 100 crore (two more zeros).

families.title: The greatest of four numbers in lakhs and crores
explanations: first-digit (conceptual): The numbers were compared by their first digits. A number with more digits is greater, so count the digits (or the crores and lakhs) first.
last-groups (procedural): The last digits (thousands and ones) were compared. When two numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the left: crores first, then lakhs.

teach.idea: A number with more digits is greater. With the same number of digits, compare place by place from the left: crores, then lakhs, then thousands.
teach.method: Count the digits of each number. Among those with the most digits, compare the crores, then the lakhs, and so on.

alternatives.title: A place-value table
text: Write each number in a table with columns for crores, lakhs, thousands and the last three digits.
Read down the first column that differs; the largest digit there is the greatest number.

families.title: Comparing two expressions without working them out
explanations: inner-sign (conceptual): When the bracket after the minus sign was removed, the sign inside was kept. Taking away a bracket changes every sign inside: a − (b − c) = a − b + c and a − (b + c) = a − b − c.
plus-bracket (conceptual): The signs inside a bracket after a plus sign were changed. Only a minus sign in front of a bracket changes the signs inside: a + (b − c) = a + b − c.
distribute-one (conceptual): Only the first number in the bracket was multiplied. The multiplier spreads over every term inside: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.

teach.idea: Two expressions can be compared by rewriting one to look like the other: removing a bracket after a minus sign changes the signs inside, and a multiplier spreads over every term of a bracket.
teach.method: Rewrite the side with brackets without them, then see what is left over: if the two sides now differ only by an extra + c or − c, you know which is bigger without working anything out.

alternatives.title: Think of money
text: a − (b − c): you spend b but get c back, so you have a − b + c.
a − (b + c): you spend b and then c more, so you have a − b − c, which is less.

families.title: Naming the property: closure, commutative, associative, distributive, identity and inverse
explanations: confuse-0 (conceptual): Changing the order was called associative. Associative is about regrouping with brackets; swapping the order is the commutative property.
confuse-1 (conceptual): Regrouping with brackets was called commutative. The order of the numbers is the same on both sides; only the brackets moved, so it is associative.
confuse-2 (conceptual): Moving the brackets was taken as the associative property. Here a multiplication is spread over an addition, which is the distributive property.

confuse-5 (conceptual): 'The answer is again a number of the same kind' was read as an identity property. An identity leaves a number unchanged; here the result is new but stays in the same set, which is closure.

teach.idea: Closure: the result stays in the set. Commutative: the order can change. Associative: the grouping can change. Distributive: multiplication spreads over addition. Identity: 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication. Inverse: what brings a number back to the identity.
teach.method: Compare the two sides: same numbers in a different order (commutative), same order with brackets moved (associative), a product spread over a sum (distributive), a 0 or 1 that changes nothing (identity), or a result of 0 or 1 (inverse).

alternatives.title: Spot the change
text: Cover the brackets and look at the order of the numbers: if it changed, it is commutative.
If the order is the same and only the brackets moved, it is associative. If one number now appears twice, it is distributive.

families.title: Inverses of rational numbers and the distributive property
explanations: reciprocal-instead (conceptual): The reciprocal was given. The additive inverse is the number that ADDS to give 0: just change the sign.
reciprocal-signed (conceptual): The fraction was turned upside down; the additive inverse keeps the numerator and denominator and only changes the sign.
sign-changed (conceptual): The sign was changed as well. The reciprocal keeps the sign, because the product must be +1 (a negative times a negative is positive).
additive-instead (conceptual): The additive inverse was given. The multiplicative inverse is the number that MULTIPLIES to give 1: turn the fraction upside down.
factor-dropped (procedural): After taking out the common factor, only the bracket was worked out: 3/8 + 5/8 = 1 must still be multiplied by 9/8.
sign-error (conceptual): The sign was lost: the common factor is negative, so the answer is negative too.

teach.idea: The additive inverse of x is −x, because x + (−x) = 0. The multiplicative inverse of a/b is b/a, because a/b × b/a = 1. The distributive property x × y + x × z = x × (y + z) can make a calculation easy.
teach.method: Additive inverse: change the sign. Multiplicative inverse: turn the fraction upside down and keep the sign. For x × y + x × z, add y and z first and multiply once.

alternatives.title: Check by combining
text: Add your additive inverse to the number: you must get 0.
Multiply your multiplicative inverse by the number: you must get 1.

families.title: Numbers that are sums of two cubes in two ways
explanations: no-cube-root (procedural): 443889 − 38³ = 389017 was found, but the box holds the number whose CUBE is 389017: take the cube root.
root-by-three (conceptual): The cube root was found by dividing by 3. The cube root is the number that, multiplied by itself three times, gives the result.
times-three (conceptual): The cubes were worked out as 3 times the number. A cube is the number multiplied by itself three times.
cube-of-sum (conceptual): The two numbers were added first and then cubed; (a + b)³ is not a³ + b³.

teach.idea: Some numbers are the sum of two cubes in two different ways, like 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³ (Ramanujan's taxicab number).
teach.method: Subtract the known cube from the number, then find the cube root of what is left (by prime factorisation, or by trying numbers whose cube ends in the right digit).

alternatives.title: Use the last digit
text: The last digit of a cube decides the last digit of its cube root: cubes ending in 8 come from numbers ending in 2, ending in 7 from 3, and so on.
Then estimate the size: 10³ = 1000, 20³ = 8000, 30³ = 27,000.

families.title: Comparing two ratios, or deciding whether they are equivalent
explanations: first-terms (procedural): Only the first terms were compared. A ratio depends on both terms: bring the second terms to the same number first.
additive (conceptual): The ratios were compared by the difference between their terms. Ratios compare by multiplication: compare a/b with c/d, for example by cross-multiplying.

teach.idea: Ratios compare by multiplication. a : b and c : d are equivalent when a/b = c/d; the one with the larger fraction is the greater ratio.
teach.method: Cross-multiply: compare a × d with b × c. Equal products mean equivalent ratios; otherwise the larger product shows the greater ratio. Or write both with the same second term.

alternatives.title: Make the second terms equal
text: To compare 3 : 4 and 5 : 8, write 3 : 4 as 6 : 8.
Now 6 : 8 and 5 : 8 have the same second term, so 3 : 4 is greater.

families.title: Total cost from a fixed rate per kilometre or metre
explanations: added (conceptual): The rate and the distance were added. Every one of the 22 units costs ₹30, so multiply.
rate-only (procedural): The rate for one unit was given; the question asks for the cost of all of them.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (12 × 3) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: At a fixed rate, every kilometre (or metre) costs the same, so the total is the rate times the number of units.
teach.method: Multiply the rate by the distance. Check by estimating: about ₹10 a km for about 10 km is about ₹100.

alternatives.title: A rate table
text: 1 km costs ₹12, 2 km cost ₹24, 3 km cost ₹36 …
Keep adding ₹12 for each kilometre, or jump: 10 km cost ₹120.

families.title: Profit or loss in rupees, and a missing price
explanations: reversed (conceptual): It was called a loss. Selling for more than the cost price gives a profit, so the answer is positive.
prices-added (procedural): The two prices were added. Profit or loss is the difference: selling price − cost price.
wrong-direction (conceptual): The profit was taken away. With a profit the selling price is MORE than the cost price.
applied-to-sp (conceptual): The profit was added to the selling price. The selling price already includes the profit, so take it away to get the cost price.

teach.idea: Profit = selling price − cost price when the selling price is more; loss = cost price − selling price when it is less.
teach.method: To find a price: SP = CP + profit (or CP − loss), and CP = SP − profit (or SP + loss).

alternatives.title: On a number line
text: Mark the cost price. A profit moves to the right to reach the selling price; a loss moves to the left.
The size of the move is the profit or loss.

families.title: Dividing integers
explanations: sign-rule (conceptual): Two negatives were divided to give a negative. A negative divided by a negative is positive.
multiplied (conceptual): The numbers were multiplied instead of divided.

teach.idea: Division undoes multiplication, so the sign rules are the same: same signs give a positive quotient, different signs a negative one.
teach.method: Divide the sizes, then decide the sign. Check by multiplying the answer by the divisor.

alternatives.title: Use multiplication
text: −48 ÷ 6 asks: what times 6 gives −48? The answer is −8.
−48 ÷ (−6) asks: what times −6 gives −48? The answer is 8.

families.title: A rational number in standard form
explanations: not-reduced (procedural): The sign was put in the right place, but 44 and 48 still have the common factor 4; divide both by it.
sign-lost (conceptual): The two minus signs were not cancelled correctly: a negative divided by a negative is positive.
part-reduced (procedural): Only the common factor 2 was divided out; 4 is the highest common factor.

teach.idea: A rational number is in standard form when its denominator is positive and the numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1.
teach.method: If the denominator is negative, multiply top and bottom by −1. Then divide both by their highest common factor.

alternatives.title: Like equivalent fractions
text: 36/−48: first write −36/48, then divide by 12 to get −3/4.

families.title: Comparing two rational numbers
explanations: negatives-by-size (conceptual): The numbers were compared by size without their signs. For negative numbers, the one further from 0 is the smaller.
numerators-only (procedural): Only the numerators were compared. With different denominators, write both with a common denominator first.

teach.idea: On the number line, the number to the right is greater. Every positive number is greater than every negative number; between two negatives, the one closer to 0 is greater.
teach.method: Write both with the same positive denominator and compare the numerators (−8/12 < −3/12 because −8 < −3).

alternatives.title: Cross-multiply
text: With positive denominators, a/b > c/d exactly when a × d > c × b.

families.title: Rational numbers on the number line, and one halfway between two
explanations: negative-direction (conceptual): From a negative number, moving right still adds and moving left still subtracts: 0 − 6/9.
other-end (procedural): The marks were counted from the other end. P is 8 parts from 2.
marks-as-parts (procedural): The 8 marks were taken as the number of parts; 8 marks cut the gap into 9 parts.
not-halved (procedural): The two numbers were added but not halved. Halfway is their sum divided by 2.
mediant (conceptual): The numerators and the denominators were added: (a + c)/(b + d) lies between the two numbers but not halfway. Halfway is (x + y) ÷ 2.

teach.idea: Between two integers the number line can be cut into q equal parts; each part is 1/q. A rational number halfway between x and y is their average.
teach.method: Start at the named end and move s parts of 1/q (right adds, left subtracts). For halfway, add the two numbers and divide by 2.

alternatives.title: Like a ruler
text: A ruler cuts each centimetre into 10 parts; here each unit is cut into q parts.
Count the small parts from the end you are told, just as you count millimetres.

families.title: Compound interest half-yearly or quarterly, and compared with simple interest
explanations: annual-rate-each-period (procedural): The yearly rate 14% was used for each half-year. Each period earns 14% ÷ 2 = 7%.
simple-interest (conceptual): Simple interest was found. With compounding, each period's interest is added on and earns interest in the next period.
amount-given (procedural): The amount was given; compound interest is the amount minus the principal.
compounded-yearly (procedural): The interest was compounded once a year. Half-yearly means 2 periods at 7% each.
ci-only (procedural): Only the compound interest was found; the question asks how much MORE it is than the simple interest.
amount-minus-si (procedural): The simple interest was taken away from the amount; take it away from the compound interest (amount − principal).

teach.idea: Compounding more often means more periods at a smaller rate: half-yearly uses R/2 per half-year, quarterly R/4 per quarter. Compound interest is more than simple interest because interest earns interest.
teach.method: Amount = P × (1 + r/100)ⁿ with r the rate per period and n the number of periods; CI = amount − P. For the difference, also find SI = P × R × T ÷ 100 and subtract.

alternatives.title: Period by period
text: Write the balance at the start of each period, add that period's interest, and carry it on.
For simple interest, add the same interest (on the original principal) each year.

families.title: Factorising a difference of squares or a perfect square
explanations: squares-in-brackets (conceptual): The squares were written in the brackets. The brackets hold the square roots: 144x² = (12x)² and 49 = 7².
factor-not-taken (procedural): The common factor 9 must be taken out first; then x² − 144 is a difference of squares.
constant-not-rooted (procedural): After taking out 9, the bracket is x² − 144 = x² − 12²: the number in the brackets is 12, the square root of 144.

teach.idea: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)² and a² − 2ab + b² = (a − b)². An expression that matches one of these can be factorised at once.
teach.method: Take out any common factor first. Then find a and b as the square roots of the first and last terms; for a perfect square, check that the middle term is 2ab.

alternatives.title: Cut and move a square
text: Cut a b × b square from the corner of an a × a square.
The L-shape that is left can be cut and moved into an (a + b) × (a − b) rectangle.

families.title: Factorising with the cube identities
explanations: square-middle (conceptual): The middle term of a square, 2ab, was used. In the cube identities the second bracket has ab: a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca.
squares-multiplied (procedural): The two squares 25 and 81 were multiplied; the middle term is a × b = 5 × 9.
three-abc (procedural): The coefficient 3abc = 192 was copied into the bracket; each cross term in the second bracket is just the product of two of the terms.

teach.idea: a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), and a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca).
teach.method: Write each cube term as (something)³ to find a, b (and c), then fill the second bracket from the identity.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Multiply the two brackets out: the x² and x terms must cancel, leaving only the cubes.
If a middle term is left over, the number in the box is wrong.

families.title: Factorising by a common factor or by grouping
explanations: only-letters (procedural): Only xy was taken out. The numbers 81 and 63 also have the common factor 9; the highest common factor includes it.
second-group-sign (procedural): When −2 is taken out of the last two terms, the signs inside the bracket change: −10x + 18 = −2(5x − 9).

teach.idea: Factorising undoes expanding: a common factor of every term can be taken outside a bracket, and after grouping, a common bracket can be taken out too.
teach.method: Find the highest common factor of the numbers and the letters. For four terms, take a common factor out of each pair so that the same bracket appears twice, then take that bracket out.

alternatives.title: Expand to check
text: Multiply your answer out again.
If you get back the expression you started with, the factorisation is right.

families.title: Factorising ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term
explanations: swapped (procedural): The two numbers were put in the wrong brackets. Multiplying out (5x + 7)(6x + 9) gives the middle term 87x, not 89x.
signs-reversed (procedural): The signs were reversed: check the sign of the middle term after multiplying out. The constant only fixes whether the two signs are the same or different.

teach.idea: If ax² + bx + c = (px + q)(rx + s), then b splits into two parts whose product is a × c: ps and qr.
teach.method: Find two numbers that multiply to a × c and add to b. Write bx as their sum, group the four terms in pairs, take out the common factor of each pair, then the common bracket.

alternatives.title: Algebra tiles
text: Lay out a x² tiles, b x-tiles and c unit tiles into one rectangle.
The length and breadth of the rectangle are the two factors.

families.title: The zeros of a quadratic polynomial by factorising
explanations: zero-signs (procedural): The zeros were read with the wrong signs: 6x + 5 = 0 gives x = −5/6.
coefficient-ignored (procedural): x was not divided by its coefficient: 6x + 5 = 0 gives 6x = −5, so x = −5/6.

teach.idea: A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero, so the zeros of (px + q)(rx + s) are −q/p and −s/r.
teach.method: Factorise by splitting the middle term, set each bracket equal to 0 and solve. Check: the zeros add to −b/a and multiply to c/a.

alternatives.title: Substitute to check
text: Put each zero back into p(x).
If the result is 0 both times, the zeros are right.

families.title: Checking zeros against the coefficients
explanations: sum-sign (conceptual): The sum of the zeros was compared with b/a. The sum of the zeros is −b/a.
product-sign (conceptual): The product of the zeros was compared with −c/a. The product of the zeros is c/a, with no minus sign.

teach.idea: For p(x) = ax² + bx + c with zeros α and β, α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. A pair that fails either check cannot be the zeros.
teach.method: Add the claimed zeros and compare with −b/a; multiply them and compare with c/a. Both must agree.

alternatives.title: Why it works
text: a(x − α)(x − β) = ax² − a(α + β)x + aαβ.
Matching with ax² + bx + c gives −a(α + β) = b and aαβ = c.

families.title: Writing a number in scientific notation
explanations: positive-power (conceptual): The power was written as positive. A number less than 1 has a negative power of 10: 9.81 is divided by 10 again and again, not multiplied.
counted-zeros-after-point (procedural): Only the zeros after the decimal point were counted. The point must move past the first non-zero digit too, so it moves one place more.
not-between-1-and-10 (conceptual): The digits were kept as a whole number (981). In scientific notation the first number must be at least 1 and less than 10, so the point goes after the first digit.
counted-digits (procedural): The number of digits was used as the power. The point moves one place fewer than the number of digits: count the jumps from the first digit to the end.
counted-zeros (procedural): Only the zeros at the end were counted. The point also moves past the other digits after the first one.

teach.idea: Each place the decimal point moves left divides by 10, so to keep the value the same we multiply by 10 that many times: 45,200 = 4.52 × 10⁴. Moving the point right multiplies by 10, so it is balanced by a negative power: 0.0045 = 4.5 × 10⁻³.
teach.method: Put the point just after the first non-zero digit to get a. Count how many places the point moved: to the left gives a positive n, to the right gives a negative n.

alternatives.title: Use the place value of the first digit
text: Find the place of the first non-zero digit. In 4,52,000 the 4 is in the lakhs place, and 1,00,000 = 10⁵, so n = 5.
In 0.00045 the 4 is in the ten-thousandths place, and 1/10000 = 10⁻⁴, so n = −4.

families.title: Writing a number in scientific notation as an ordinary number
explanations: one-place-extra (procedural): The point moved one place too many: one zero too many was written after the decimal point.
one-place-short (procedural): The point moved one place too few. Count each jump of the point; every jump is one ÷ 10.
wrong-direction (conceptual): The point moved the wrong way. A negative power of 10 makes the number smaller: 10⁻¹ means divide by 10 1 time.
zeros-added (conceptual): 8 zeros were written after the digits 987. The power tells how many places the point moves, and the point already has digits after it to move past.

teach.idea: × 10ⁿ moves the decimal point n places to the right; × 10⁻ⁿ moves it n places to the left. Empty places are filled with zeros.
teach.method: Look at the sign of the power. Move the point that many places (right for positive, left for negative), writing zeros in any empty places.

alternatives.title: Multiply by 10 one step at a time
text: Write 10ⁿ as 10 × 10 × … and multiply by 10 once for each factor: 3.07 → 30.7 → 307 → 3070.
For a negative power, divide by 10 once for each step instead: 3.07 → 0.307 → 0.0307.

families.title: Square root of a larger perfect square or decimal
explanations: halved (conceptual): The number was halved. The square root is the number that multiplied by itself gives the number.
wrong-last-digit (procedural): Two numbers have squares ending in 1: 91 and 99. Check which one by squaring, or by comparing with the square of the middle number 95.
each-prime-once (procedural): Each different prime was taken once. The square root takes one prime from each PAIR of equal primes, so a prime that appears four times gives two.
point-dropped (procedural): The decimal point was left out. 98.01 has two decimal places, so its square root has one.
point-two-places (procedural): The point was put two places in. A number with two decimal places has a square root with one decimal place (0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01).

teach.idea: In a perfect square every prime factor appears an even number of times, so the primes split into equal pairs; the square root takes one prime from each pair.
teach.method: Write the number as a product of primes, group equal primes in pairs and multiply one prime from each pair. For a decimal, find the root without the point, then give the answer half as many decimal places.

alternatives.title: Tens and the last digit
text: Find two square tens around the number: 70² = 4900 and 80² = 6400, so √5476 is in the seventies.
The last digit 6 comes from 4² or 6², so try 74 and 76: 74² = 5476.

families.title: Between which two whole numbers a square root lies
explanations: halved (conceptual): 999 was halved. The square root is the number that multiplied by itself gives 999.
next-squares (procedural): The wrong pair of squares was used. Check by squaring: the smaller number squared must be below 999 and the larger one squared above it.
divided-by-ten (conceptual): 999 was divided by 10. Square to check: 99 × 99 is far more than 999.

teach.idea: If a² < N < (a + 1)², then a < √N < a + 1, because bigger numbers have bigger square roots.
teach.method: List the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 … until you pass the number. The two square roots on either side of it are the answer.

alternatives.title: A table of squares
text: Write a table: 10² = 100, 20² = 400, 30² = 900. Find the tens first.
Then square the numbers in that ten one by one until you pass the number.

families.title: How many numbers lie between two consecutive squares
explanations: difference-of-squares (procedural): The two squares were subtracted (199). That counts the steps from one square to the next; the numbers strictly between are one fewer.
ends-included (procedural): The two squares themselves were counted. The question asks only for the numbers between them.
just-n (conceptual): The answer was taken as 99. Try a small case: between 2² = 4 and 3² = 9 there are 5, 6, 7, 8 — four numbers, which is 2 × 2.

teach.idea: (n + 1)² − n² = 2n + 1, so the jump from one square to the next is 2n + 1, and the numbers strictly between them are 2n.
teach.method: Use the pattern: between n² and (n + 1)² there are 2n whole numbers. Check with a small case such as 3² and 4² (10 to 15: six numbers).

alternatives.title: Grow a square
text: A square of n × n dots grows to (n + 1) × (n + 1) by adding a row and a column: n + n + 1 dots.
So the next square is 2n + 1 more; the numbers in between are 2n.

families.title: Probability from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain)
explanations: odds (conceptual): The other marbles were compared with the blue ones. Divide by the total number of marbles.
count-only (procedural): The number of red marbles was given. A probability is a fraction of all the marbles, between 0 and 1.
colours-equal (conceptual): Colours were counted instead of marbles.
event-itself (procedural): The probability of blue was found. 'Not blue' means every other marble.
small-chance (conceptual): An impossible event was given a small chance. There are no yellow marbles at all, so it cannot happen: its probability is 0.
swap-certain (conceptual): Impossible and certain were swapped. Certain is 1; impossible is 0.
swap-impossible (conceptual): Certain and impossible were swapped. Every marble in the bag fits, so it is certain: probability 1.
counted-marbles (conceptual): The number of marbles was given. A probability is never more than 1; a certain event has probability 1.

teach.idea: Probability measures chance on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). When every marble is equally likely to be picked, P(event) = favourable marbles ÷ all the marbles. P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
teach.method: Count all the marbles. Count the ones that fit the event. Write favourable over total. Nothing fits: 0. Everything fits: 1.

alternatives.title: Words on the scale
text: Draw a line from 0 to 1. Mark 0 'impossible', 1/2 'even chance' and 1 'certain'.
Place the event: no matching marbles at 0, all of them at 1, some of them in between — more matching marbles means nearer 1.

families.title: Experimental probability from a frequency table
explanations: theoretical (conceptual): The theoretical probability (1/4) was given. The question asks what happened in this experiment: use the counts in the table.
odds (conceptual): The count was compared with the other results (19 to 61). Divide by the total number of trials, 80.
count-only (procedural): The count was given. The probability is the count as a fraction of all the trials.

teach.idea: Experimental probability is the fraction of the trials in which the event really happened: (number of times it happened) ÷ (number of trials).
teach.method: Read the count for the event from the table, add all the counts to get the number of trials, and divide.

alternatives.title: Experiment and theory
text: Theory says a fair coin gives a head half of the time, but in 20 tosses you might get 12 heads: an experimental probability of 12/20.
The experiment uses what actually happened. With many more trials, the two usually get closer.

families.title: Counting the outcomes of choices made in stages
explanations: added (conceptual): The numbers of choices were added. Each choice at the first stage can go with every choice at the next, so multiply.
two-stages (procedural): Only the first two stages were counted. Each of the 36 pairs can go with each of the 5 choices at the last stage.
added-then-multiplied (procedural): Two stages were added and then multiplied by the third. Multiply all the stages.

teach.idea: If the first stage can happen in a ways and, for each of them, the next stage in b ways, there are a × b outcomes altogether (the multiplication principle).
teach.method: Count the choices at each stage and multiply them. A tree diagram or table shows why: every branch splits into the same number of branches.

alternatives.title: Draw a tree diagram
text: Draw one branch for each first choice. From the end of each branch, draw one branch for each second choice.
Count the ends of the last branches: that is every possible outcome.

families.title: Probability from the sample space of two dice or spinners
explanations: totals-equally-likely (conceptual): The 11 possible totals were taken as equally likely. They are not: list all 36 pairs and count the ones that fit.
added-sides (procedural): The sample space was taken as 6 + 6 = 12 outcomes. Each of the 6 first numbers goes with each of the 6 second numbers: 6 × 6 = 36.
order-ignored (conceptual): Pairs such as (1, 3) and (3, 1) were counted once. They are different outcomes: the first and second number are different.
more-than (procedural): '12 or more' was read as 'more than 12'. Totals of exactly 12 count too.
equal-included (procedural): Pairs with equal numbers were counted. 'Bigger' leaves out pairs where both numbers are the same.

teach.idea: For two stages, the sample space is every pair (first, second). With equally likely numbers, all m × n pairs are equally likely, so P(event) = pairs that fit ÷ all pairs.
teach.method: Draw a table: first numbers down the side, second numbers along the top, the total in each cell. Count the cells that fit the event and divide by the number of cells.

alternatives.title: Tree diagram
text: Draw a branch for each first number, then from each, a branch for each second number.
Each path is one outcome; tick the paths that fit the event and count them.

families.title: Tracing a step-by-step algorithm with a loop
explanations: stopped-early (procedural): The loop stopped one time too early. When K = 39, K is still 40 or less, so Step 2 adds it before stopping.
one-more-loop (procedural): K = 44 was added too. Check the rule in Step 4 before going back: 44 is more than 40, so stop.
gave-k (procedural): The final value of K was given. The question asks for S.

teach.idea: An algorithm is a list of exact steps. Tracing it means doing every step in order and writing down each value as it changes, checking the stopping rule each time.
teach.method: Make a table with columns K and S. Do Step 2 and Step 3, write the new values, then test Step 4 before going round again.

alternatives.title: See the sequence
text: The values of K that get added form a sequence: the start, then the start plus the step, and so on, up to the last one that is not more than the limit.
List them and add them; then compare with your trace.

families.title: Where the repeated-subtraction game ends
explanations: one-move (procedural): Only one move was made. Keep going until both cards show the same number.
smaller-card (procedural): The smaller starting number was given. The game changes the cards until they are equal.
past-the-end (procedural): One move too many was made (x − x = 0). The game stops as soon as the two cards are equal.
always-one (conceptual): It was guessed that the game always ends at 1. It ends at the largest number that divides both starting numbers.

teach.idea: Subtracting the smaller number does not change which numbers divide both cards, so the game ends at the largest number that divides both starting numbers: their HCF.
teach.method: Write the pair after each move in a table. Keep replacing the larger number by the difference until the two numbers are equal.

alternatives.title: Jump with division
text: Subtracting the smaller number many times in a row is division: the number left is the remainder.
Divide the larger by the smaller, keep the smaller and the remainder, and repeat until the remainder is 0. The last divisor is the end number.

families.title: One step of Kaprekar's routine
explanations: no-leading-zero (procedural): The smallest number was written without a 0 in front. In this routine the 0 may go first, which makes the smallest number smaller.
used-original (procedural): The number 9597 itself was subtracted. Rearrange its digits to make the smallest number first.
added (procedural): The two numbers were added. The routine subtracts the smaller from the larger.

teach.idea: Kaprekar noticed that repeating this routine on four-digit numbers always seems to reach 6174 — a conjecture you can test with your own numbers. Each step must be done exactly.
teach.method: Sort the four digits from largest to smallest for the big number and from smallest to largest for the small one (keep any 0 at the front), then subtract.

alternatives.title: Test the conjecture
text: Use your answer as the new number and do the routine again (write it with four digits, adding a 0 in front if needed).
Within at most seven steps you should reach 6174, which gives 7641 − 1467 = 6174 again.

families.title: Terms of a Collatz sequence
explanations: off-by-one (procedural): The start was not counted as the 1st number, so one step too many was made. 60 is the 1st number.
one-short (procedural): One step too few was made. Number each term as you write it.
forgot-plus-one (recall): For an odd number, only 3 times was used. The rule is 3 times plus 1.

teach.idea: Each number comes from the one before by a fixed rule. The Collatz conjecture says every starting number eventually reaches 1 — it has been checked for huge numbers, but nobody has proved it.
teach.method: Write the numbers in a row and number them 1st, 2nd, 3rd …. For each one, check even or odd before using the rule.

alternatives.title: Keep a table
text: Make two columns: term number and value. Write 1st and the start number.
On each new row, write whether the last value was even or odd and the result of the rule.

families.title: Using the odd-number pattern for squares
explanations: last-squared (conceptual): The last odd number (97) was squared. The pattern squares how MANY odd numbers are added from 1: 1 to 97 is 49 odd numbers.
miscounted-terms (procedural): The odd numbers were miscounted. From 1 to 97 there are (97 + 1) ÷ 2 = 49 of them.
start-ignored (procedural): The sum was taken from 1. It starts at 39, so take away 1 + 3 + … + 37 = 19².
removed-too-many (procedural): Too many odd numbers were taken away. Below 39 there are 19 odd numbers, so subtract 19².

teach.idea: Each odd number is an L-shaped layer that turns a square into the next square: 1, then 1 + 3 = 2 × 2, then + 5 = 3 × 3. So the first n odd numbers add to n².
teach.method: Count how many odd numbers there are from 1 to the last one ((last + 1) ÷ 2) and square it. If the sum starts later, subtract the square for the odd numbers that are missing.

alternatives.title: Pair from the ends
text: Pair the first and last numbers, the second and second-last, and so on: each pair has the same total.
Multiply that total by the number of pairs (half the number of terms).

families.title: The smallest missing digit that makes a number divisible
explanations: not-smallest (procedural): A digit that works was chosen, but not the smallest. Try 0, 1, 2 … in order.
used-rule-for-9 (recall): The digit sum was made a multiple of 9. For 3, a multiple of 3 is enough.
used-rule-for-3 (recall): The digit sum was made a multiple of 3. For 9 the digit sum must be a multiple of 9.
wrong-side (procedural): The missing digit was put in the wrong group of alternate digits. Count its place from the right.
digit-sum-for-11 (recall): All the digits were added. The test for 11 uses the DIFFERENCE between the sum of alternate digits (1st, 3rd, … from the right) and the sum of the others.
only-test-for-2 (procedural): Only the test for 2 was used. A number divisible by 6 must also have a digit sum that is a multiple of 3.
only-test-for-3 (procedural): Only the test for 3 was used. A number divisible by 6 must pass the tests for BOTH 2 and 3: its last digit must also be even.

teach.idea: A number is divisible by 3 (or 9) exactly when its digit sum is; by 11 when the sums of alternate digits differ by a multiple of 11 (0, 11, 22 …); by 6 when it passes the tests for both 2 and 3. These come from place value: 10 = 9 + 1, 100 = 99 + 1, 10 = 11 − 1.
teach.method: Use the test with the digits you know, work out what the missing digit must be to pass, and choose the smallest digit from 0 to 9 that does.

alternatives.title: Try the digits in order
text: Put 0 in the box and apply the test, then 1, then 2, and so on.
The first digit that passes is the smallest one.

families.title: Finding a hidden number in a magic square
explanations: not-subtracted (procedural): The two numbers in the line were added, but their total was not taken away from the magic total.
one-subtracted (procedural): Only one of the two numbers in the line was taken away from the magic total. Take away both.
gave-total (procedural): The magic total was given. The hidden number is what the line still needs to reach that total.

teach.idea: If one line is complete, its total is the magic total. Any line with only one gap tells you the gap: the magic total minus the two numbers in that line.
teach.method: Find a row, column or diagonal with no hidden number and add it. Then find the line through ? whose other two numbers are visible, and subtract them from the total.

alternatives.title: Use the centre
text: In a 3 × 3 magic square the total is 3 times the centre number.
Two numbers opposite each other through the centre add up to twice the centre.

families.title: Finding letters that stand for digits in an addition
explanations: copied-ones (procedural): The ones digit of the answer (0) was copied. P plus 1 must end in 0.
tens-of-answer (procedural): The tens digit of the answer was copied. Q is what must be added to the tens digit of the first number to make it.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): 1 was taken from 0 the other way round. P + 1 ends in 0, so P + 1 = 10: P = 10 − 1.
carry-forgotten (procedural): The carry from the ones column was forgotten. P + 1 = 10, so 1 ten is carried into the tens column.

teach.idea: A letter puzzle is an ordinary addition with some digits hidden. Working column by column from the ones, as in column addition, each column fixes one digit and tells whether a ten is carried.
teach.method: Start with the ones column: find the digit that makes the ones come out right (remember it may make 10 or more). Then do the tens column, adding any carried ten.

alternatives.title: Check by putting the digits in
text: Once you have a value for each letter, write the addition with the digits in place.
Add it normally. If the total matches, the digits are right.

families.title: Deciding whether sums and products are even or odd
explanations: odd-plus-odd (conceptual): Adding or subtracting odd numbers was taken to give an odd number. Two odd numbers each have one left over; the two left-overs make a pair, so odd + odd is even.
first-number-only (procedural): Only the first number of each calculation was looked at. Every number affects whether the answer is even or odd.
odd-times-anything (conceptual): A product with an odd number in it was taken as odd. If any number being multiplied is even, the product is even (it is made of pairs).

teach.idea: An even number is made of pairs; an odd number is pairs with one left over. In a sum, the left-overs pair up, so the sum is odd only when there is an odd number of odd numbers. A product is odd only when every number multiplied is odd.
teach.method: For each calculation, look only at whether each number is even or odd (its last digit). Count the odd numbers in a sum or difference; check whether every number in a product is odd.

alternatives.title: Picture the pairs
text: Draw each odd number as pairs of dots with one extra dot.
Put two odd numbers together: the two extra dots make a new pair, so nothing is left over and the total is even.

families.title: Scaling in proportion, not by adding
explanations: added-difference (conceptual): The same amount was added (15). Keeping the amount per person means multiplying both numbers by the same factor, 27 ÷ 12.
ratio-flipped (procedural): The factor was found the wrong way round. Compare the new number of people with the old one: 27 ÷ 12.
factor-only (procedural): Only the factor 27 ÷ 12 was found. Multiply the cups of rice by it.

teach.idea: Keeping the shape (or the amount per person) means keeping the ratio the same, so both numbers are multiplied by the same factor. Adding the same amount to both changes the ratio.
teach.method: Find the scale factor: new ÷ old for the pair you know. Multiply the other number by the same factor (or find the amount for 1 first, then multiply).

alternatives.title: Why adding goes wrong
text: A photo 2 cm wide and 4 cm tall, made 10 cm wide by adding 8 cm to both sides, would be 10 by 12: it now looks squashed.
Multiplying both by 5 gives 10 by 20: the height is still twice the width, so the shape is kept.

alternatives.title: Unitary method
text: Find the amount for one unit first: cups for 1 person = cups ÷ people.
Multiply by the new number of people.

families.title: Finding the key of a shift cipher
explanations: counted-back (procedural): The places were counted backwards (from the code letter to the plain letter). The code moves letters FORWARD.
counted-start (procedural): The starting letter was counted as one of the places. Count only the jumps: from A to C is 2 places.

teach.idea: In a shift (Caesar) code every letter moves the same number of places, going round from Z back to A. So comparing one plain letter with its code letter gives the key; the other letters check it.
teach.method: Number the letters A = 1 to Z = 26. Subtract the plain letter's number from the code letter's number; if the answer is negative, add 26. Check with a second letter.

alternatives.title: A letter wheel
text: Write the alphabet round a circle, so that A comes after Z.
Put a finger on the plain letter and count the jumps forward to the code letter.

families.title: The number a 'think of a number' trick always gives
explanations: added-not-divided (conceptual): Only the 20 × n part was divided by 5. Dividing by 5 divides the whole amount, including the 60 that was added: 60 ÷ 5 = 12.
divisor-given (procedural): The number divided by was given. Follow each step with n for the secret number to see what is left.
last-step-missed (procedural): The last step (add 6) was left out.

teach.idea: Call the secret number n and write each step as an expression. The steps are chosen so that the n's cancel out, leaving only a number: that is why the trick works for EVERY starting number, not just the ones you tried.
teach.method: Write n for the number. Multiply, add and divide the whole expression step by step, then take away the n's. What is left is the answer.

alternatives.title: Examples suggest, algebra shows
text: Try the trick with 1, then with 10: both give the same end number. That suggests the trick works, but trying examples cannot check every number.
Writing n for the number and simplifying shows it works for all numbers at once — that is a proof.

families.title: Counting from raw data with a frequency table
explanations: missed-one (procedural): One value was missed. Cross off each value as you tally it, and check that the tallies add up to the number of values.
counted-twice (procedural): One value was counted twice. Cross off each value once it has a tally mark.
included-boundary (conceptual): The values equal to 7 were counted too. 'More than 7' does not include 7 itself.
next-value-only (procedural): Only the value just above 7 was counted. Every value bigger than 7 counts.

teach.idea: A frequency table shows how many times each value occurs, so the raw data can be read at a glance. The frequencies add up to the number of values collected.
teach.method: List the possible values in order. Go through the data once, making a tally mark (bundles of five: four lines and one across) beside each value and crossing it off. Count the tallies.

alternatives.title: Sort the data first
text: Write the values in order from smallest to largest.
Equal values now sit together, so each group is easy to count.

families.title: Counting a class interval in grouped data
explanations: upper-included (conceptual): Marks of exactly 40 were counted in 30–40. The upper limit belongs to the next class.
missed-one (procedural): One mark was missed. Tally each mark and cross it off.
lower-excluded (conceptual): Marks of exactly 40 were left out. The lower limit belongs to this class.

teach.idea: Grouping puts the data in class intervals of equal width. Each value must go in exactly one class, so a value on a boundary goes in the class that starts with it.
teach.method: For each mark, find the class whose lower limit is at most the mark and whose upper limit is more than it. Tally the class, then count.

alternatives.title: Look at the tens digit
text: With classes of width 10 starting at 0, a mark's class is fixed by its tens digit: 27 and 20 go in 20–30, 30 goes in 30–40.
Count the marks with the right tens digit.

families.title: Reading a percentage from a bar chart
explanations: value-as-percent (conceptual): The bar's value (150) was given as the percentage. A percentage compares the bar with the total of all bars, 500.
compared-with-largest (procedural): The bar was compared with the tallest bar. Compare it with the total of ALL the bars.
compared-with-rest (conceptual): The bar was compared with the other bars only. The whole is all the bars together.

teach.idea: A bar chart shows amounts; a percentage compares one amount with the whole. The whole is the total of all the bars.
teach.method: Read every bar against the scale, add them to get the total, then work out (bar ÷ total) × 100.

alternatives.title: Scale the total to 100
text: If the total is 400, divide every bar by 4 to see how many there would be out of 100.
The bar's share out of 100 is its percentage.

families.title: Finding the median
explanations: not-ordered (procedural): The middle number of the list as given was taken. Put the numbers in order first.
mean-for-median (conceptual): The mean was worked out. The median is the middle value once the numbers are in order.
one-middle (procedural): With 10 numbers there are two middle numbers (49 and 58); the median is halfway between them.

teach.idea: The median is the middle value when the data are in order: half the values are below it and half above, so a few very large or very small values do not pull it.
teach.method: Write the values in order. With an odd number of values, the median is the middle one; with an even number, it is halfway between the two middle ones.

alternatives.title: Cross off from both ends
text: Write the values in order, then cross off the smallest and the largest, again and again.
The one value left (or halfway between the last two) is the median.

families.title: Finding the mode
explanations: frequency-given (conceptual): The number of times the mode appears (3) was given. The mode is the VALUE that appears most often.
largest-value (conceptual): The largest value was given. The mode is the value that occurs most often, not the biggest one.
median-for-mode (conceptual): The middle value was found. The mode is the most common value.

teach.idea: The mode is the value that occurs most often. It is useful for things like shoe sizes, where a shop wants to know the most common size.
teach.method: Make a frequency table (or sort the values) and choose the value with the highest frequency.

alternatives.title: Sort and look for the longest run
text: Write the values in order. Equal values sit together in runs.
The value with the longest run is the mode.

families.title: The mean of data in a frequency table
explanations: divided-by-rows (procedural): The total was divided by the number of rows (5). Divide by the number of families, 28.
mean-of-frequencies (conceptual): The frequencies were averaged. The mean is of the values, each counted as often as it occurs.
values-only (conceptual): The values were averaged without their frequencies. Each value must be counted as many times as it occurs.

teach.idea: A frequency table is a short way of writing a long list: a value with frequency 4 stands for that value written 4 times. The mean shares the total of ALL the values equally.
teach.method: Multiply each value by its frequency and add these to get the total. Add the frequencies to get how many values there are. Divide the total by that number.

alternatives.title: Write the list out
text: Write each value as many times as its frequency, e.g. 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, ….
Add them all and divide by how many there are; multiplying by the frequency is a shortcut for this.

families.title: Reading a histogram of grouped data
explanations: next-bar (procedural): A bar next to the one asked about was read. Find the group's label under the bar first.
missed-bar (procedural): One bar was left out of the total. Add every bar, ticking each one.
counted-bars (conceptual): The bars were counted. Each bar's height is how many are in that group: add the heights.
class-below-included (conceptual): The bar just below the value was included. Its values are all less than the boundary.
boundary-class-left-out (conceptual): The bar starting exactly at the value was left out. It includes its lower value, so it counts.
boundary-class-included (conceptual): The bar starting at the value was included. Its values are that value or more, so it does not count.
one-class-short (procedural): The bar just below the value was left out. Every bar that ends at or below the value counts.

teach.idea: A histogram is a bar chart for grouped data: the bars touch because the groups follow on without gaps, and each bar's height is how many values are in that group.
teach.method: Read the group labels under the bars. For 'or more', add the bars that start at the value and above; for 'less than', add the bars that end at the value and below.

alternatives.title: Mark the boundary
text: Imagine the groups along a number line. Draw a line at the value in the question.
The bars wholly on the correct side of the line are the ones to add.

families.title: Which number is divisible: tests for 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10
explanations: trap-0 (conceptual): The first digit was checked. Only the ones digit decides divisibility by 2: it must be 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
trap-1 (conceptual): A 5 somewhere in the number was taken to mean divisible by 5. Only the ones digit decides: it must be 0 or 5.
trap-2 (conceptual): A number ending in 5 was taken as divisible by 10. A multiple of 10 must end in 0.
trap-3 (conceptual): A number ending in 0 was chosen. It is divisible by 5, but it is also divisible by 10.
trap-4 (conceptual): Only the ones digit was checked (it is even). For 4, the number formed by the last two digits must be divisible by 4.
trap-5 (conceptual): Only the last two digits were checked. For 8, the number formed by the last three digits must be divisible by 8.

teach.idea: Because 10 is divisible by 2 and 5, only the ones digit decides divisibility by 2, 5 and 10. Because 100 is divisible by 4 and 1000 by 8, only the last two (for 4) or last three (for 8) digits matter.
teach.method: By 2: ones digit 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. By 5: ones digit 0 or 5. By 10: ones digit 0. By 4: the number made by the last two digits is divisible by 4. By 8: the last three digits are divisible by 8.

alternatives.title: Why the last digits
text: 3456 = 3400 + 56. 3400 is a number of hundreds, and 100 = 4 × 25, so 3400 is divisible by 4.
So 3456 is divisible by 4 exactly when 56 is.

families.title: Testing digit conjectures: Kaprekar's 6174, repeated digit sums, reverse-and-add palindromes
explanations: counted-start (procedural): The starting number was counted as a step. Count only the times the routine is carried out.
stopped-early (procedural): The count stopped one step early; keep going until the palindrome itself appears.
nine-as-zero (conceptual): The answer 9 was given as 0 (the remainder on dividing by 9). Repeated digit sums never give 0 for a positive number; a multiple of 9 ends at 9.
one-round (procedural): Only one round of adding was done: 30 still has two digits, so add its digits again.

teach.idea: A conjecture is a guess from patterns: every four-digit number (not all digits equal) reaches 6174 by Kaprekar's routine in at most 7 steps; repeated digit sums give the remainder on dividing by 9 (or 9); reversing and adding usually reaches a palindrome. Testing many numbers builds confidence, but only a proof makes it certain.
teach.method: Carry out the process carefully, writing every number, and count the steps. Check against the conjecture: the answer for Kaprekar is never more than 7; the digit-sum answer is the remainder on dividing by 9.

alternatives.title: Keep a table
text: Write the step number and the number you get in two columns.
Stop as soon as the target appears and read the last step number.

families.title: How a Collatz sequence behaves: steps to reach 1, and its highest number
explanations: counted-terms (procedural): The numbers in the sequence were counted, including the start. Count the steps (the arrows) between them.
stopped-at-two (procedural): The count stopped at 2; the sequence must reach 1.
start-taken (conceptual): The starting number was taken as the largest. Odd numbers make the sequence climb (3 × n + 1) before it falls.

teach.idea: Every starting number tried so far reaches 1 and then loops 4, 2, 1 — the Collatz conjecture — but no one has proved it. The sequences can climb high before they fall.
teach.method: Write each number with an arrow to the next. Count the arrows for the number of steps, and look along the row for the largest number.

alternatives.title: Share the work
text: Sequences join up: once you reach a number you have done before, the rest is the same.
So 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 takes 6 steps, and 20 takes one more.

families.title: The largest of four numbers in scientific notation
explanations: front-number-only (conceptual): The numbers in front were compared. The power of 10 decides the size first: one more power of 10 is ten times as big.
negative-power (conceptual): A larger negative power was taken as larger. 10⁻⁷ is much smaller than 10⁻³: the more negative the power, the smaller the number.

teach.idea: In scientific notation the power of 10 tells the size: a number with a higher power is bigger, whatever number stands in front (that number is always between 1 and 10).
teach.method: Compare the powers of 10 first (for negative powers, −3 is higher than −7). Only when the powers are equal compare the numbers in front.

alternatives.title: Write them out
text: Written out, the number of digits shows which is bigger.

families.title: Orders of magnitude of real quantities, and judging a claim
explanations: digits-counted (procedural): The number of digits (12) was used. A number with 12 digits is between 10¹¹ and 10¹², so n = 11.
one-factor-left-out (procedural): One of the multiplications was left out; every factor in the calculation changes the size.
difference-reversed (procedural): The difference was taken the other way round: claim's power minus the true power.
digits-for-power (procedural): The number of digits was used as the true power; the true power is one less than the number of digits.

teach.idea: The order of magnitude of a quantity is the power of 10 nearest below it: it tells the size at a glance (thousands, lakhs, crores, billions) and lets you spot a claim that is wildly wrong.
teach.method: Multiply the facts (round them if you like), write the result as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10, and read n. To judge a claim, compare its power of 10 with yours.

alternatives.title: Multiply the powers
text: Round each fact to a power of 10 times a small number: 365 ≈ 3.65 × 10², 24 ≈ 2.4 × 10.
Multiply the small numbers and add the powers; adjust if the front number reaches 10.

families.title: Multiplying and dividing numbers in scientific notation
explanations: powers-multiplied (conceptual): The powers were multiplied. When multiplying, add the powers: 10⁻³ × 10¹⁰ = 10⁷.
not-normalised (procedural): 0.99 is not between 1 and 10, so it must be rewritten: the power of 10 changes by one.
powers-added (conceptual): The powers were added. When dividing, subtract the powers: 10³ ÷ 10³ = 10⁰.

teach.idea: (a × 10ᵐ) × (b × 10ⁿ) = (a × b) × 10ᵐ⁺ⁿ and (a × 10ᵐ) ÷ (b × 10ⁿ) = (a ÷ b) × 10ᵐ⁻ⁿ. Then the front number may need adjusting to lie between 1 and 10.
teach.method: Work out the front numbers, add (or subtract) the powers, then if the front number is 10 or more divide it by 10 and add 1 to the power (if it is less than 1, multiply by 10 and subtract 1).

alternatives.title: An example
text: 20 is not below 10, so write 2 × 10¹⁰.

families.title: Letter puzzles with several letters, in additions and multiplications
explanations: letters-share-digit (conceptual): A solution was found in which two different letters stand for the same digit. Different letters must stand for different digits, so that solution does not count.
carry-forgotten (procedural): The carry from the column to the right was forgotten. Work column by column from the ones, and add any carried ten.

teach.idea: A letter puzzle is an ordinary sum or product with digits hidden. Each column gives a clue: what the ones must add (or multiply) to, and whether a ten is carried.
teach.method: Start with the clue that fixes a letter at once (a three-digit total of two two-digit numbers starts with 1; a letter repeated in the answer limits the choice), then work column by column, trying the few digits that are left and checking the carry.

alternatives.title: Try and check
text: List the possible digits for one letter.
For each, work out what the others must be; drop any choice that makes two letters equal or breaks a column.

families.title: Placing an event on the probability scale
explanations: impossible-as-unlikely (conceptual): An event that cannot happen at all was called unlikely. It has probability 0, so it is impossible.
two-outcomes-even (conceptual): It was thought that with two possible results (this or not this) the chance is always even. The chance depends on how many of the outcomes are in the event.
certain-as-likely (conceptual): An event that must happen was called likely. Every outcome is in it, so its probability is 1: certain.

teach.idea: The probability scale runs from 0 (impossible) through 1/2 (even chance) to 1 (certain). Fewer than half the outcomes: unlikely; more than half: likely.
teach.method: Count the outcomes in the event and all the outcomes. None: impossible; all: certain; exactly half: even chance; otherwise compare with half.

alternatives.title: What random means
text: A random pick means every marble has the same chance; we cannot say which one will come out.
We can still say how likely each colour is from how many there are.

families.title: Listing a sample space, and an event as a subset of it
explanations: order-ignored (conceptual): RY and YR were taken as the same. Red then yellow is a different outcome from yellow then red.
colour-not-suit (conceptual): The colours were listed. The question asks for the suit, and there are four suits.
parts-separately (conceptual): The results of the coin and the die were listed separately. Each outcome is a pair, such as H3.
odd-even (conceptual): The even numbers were listed. Odd numbers are those that leave 1 when divided by 2.
one-prime (conceptual): 1 was counted as prime. A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself, so 1 is not prime.
factor-for-multiple (conceptual): The factors were listed instead of the multiples. A multiple of 5 is 5 times a whole number: 5, 10, 15, ….
boundary-included (conceptual): The boundary number itself was included. 'Less than' does not include the number itself.
ends-left-out (conceptual): 1 and the number itself were left out. They are factors too.
roots-listed (conceptual): The numbers that are squared were listed, not the squares. The perfect squares are 1, 4, 9, 16, ….

teach.idea: The sample space is the list of every possible outcome of an experiment. An event is a part (subset) of the sample space: the outcomes that make it happen.
teach.method: Build the outcomes systematically (for two coins: first coin H with each of H, T, then first coin T with each). For an event, go through the sample space one outcome at a time and keep those that fit.

alternatives.title: A tree diagram
text: Draw a branch for each result of the first part, and from each a branch for each result of the second part.
Each path from start to end is one outcome: HT and TH are different paths.

families.title: Counting arrangements that meet a condition
explanations: condition-ignored (procedural): Every arrangement was counted; only those that meet the condition count.
pair-one-way (procedural): The two friends were kept in one order only; they can stand side by side in two ways (A B or B A).
one-end (procedural): Only one end was ruled out; the friend may stand at neither end.

teach.idea: Listing in an organised way (fix the first place, then the next …) makes sure no arrangement is missed or counted twice. A condition fixes or removes some places first.
teach.method: Deal with the condition first (put the fixed person at the end, glue the pair together, or choose the last digit), then count the ways to fill the remaining places one at a time and multiply.

alternatives.title: List them
text: For small numbers, write every arrangement in order: first all those starting with A, then with B, and so on.
Tick the ones that meet the condition and count the ticks.

families.title: Direct proportion, inverse proportion or neither?
explanations: products-only (procedural): Only x × y was checked; it changes from column to column, so 'neither' was chosen. Check y ÷ x as well: here it is the same in every column, so y is in direct proportion to x.
not-equal-steps (conceptual): Because y does not go down by equal steps, it was called neither. Inverse proportion means x × y stays the same, and here it does.
both-increase (conceptual): It was thought that y is in direct proportion because both increase. In direct proportion y ÷ x stays the same; here the same amount is added instead.
one-decreases (conceptual): It was thought that y is in inverse proportion because y goes down as x goes up. In inverse proportion x × y stays the same; check it for each column.

teach.idea: Direct proportion: y ÷ x is the same for every pair (doubling x doubles y). Inverse proportion: x × y is the same for every pair (doubling x halves y).
teach.method: Work out y ÷ x for each column; if they are all equal, it is direct. Otherwise work out x × y; if they are all equal, it is inverse. If neither stays the same, it is neither.

alternatives.title: Double and see
text: Find two columns where x doubles.
If y doubles too, try direct; if y halves, try inverse; then check the other columns.

families.title: Tracing a flowchart with decision boxes
explanations: wrong-branch (procedural): The other branch of a decision box was followed. Answer the question in the diamond for this input: Yes and No lead to different boxes.
loop-once-more (procedural): The loop ran one extra time. Check the decision before going round again.
loop-stopped-early (procedural): The loop stopped one time too early. Check the decision after each step.

teach.idea: A flowchart shows an algorithm as boxes joined by arrows: an oval to start and stop, a parallelogram for input and output, a rectangle for a step, and a diamond for a question with a Yes and a No arrow.
teach.method: Start at the oval and follow the arrows. At each diamond, answer the question for your number and take that arrow. Keep a note of each value as it changes.

alternatives.title: A trace table
text: Write a column for each value and the box you are in.
Every time a value changes, write the new value on a new row.

families.title: Encoding and decoding with shift and substitution codes
explanations: counted-start (procedural): Each letter was moved back only 24 places because the starting letter was counted.
moved-back (procedural): The letters were moved backward. To encode, move each letter forward.
moved-forward (procedural): The code letters were moved forward again. To decode, undo the code: move each letter back.
key-backwards (procedural): The key was read the wrong way: the code letters were looked up in the Plain row. To decode, find each letter in the Code row and read the Plain letter above it.

teach.idea: A code replaces each letter by another by a rule. A shift code moves every letter the same number of places; a substitution code uses a key table. Decoding undoes the rule.
teach.method: To encode with a shift of k, move each letter forward k places, going from Z back to A. To decode, move back k places. With a key table, look the letter up in the right row.

alternatives.title: Use letter numbers
text: Number the letters A = 1 to Z = 26 and add k to each number.
If the result is more than 26, take away 26.

families.title: Primary or secondary data?
explanations: copied-is-primary (conceptual): Copying figures out yourself was taken as collecting primary data. The figures were collected by someone else, so they are secondary data, whoever copies them.
asking-is-secondary (conceptual): Asking other people questions was taken as secondary data. A survey you carry out yourself is primary data, even though other people give the answers.

teach.idea: Primary data is collected first-hand by the person who will use it (counting, measuring, asking). Secondary data was collected by someone else and is reused (a census, a newspaper, a website, a report).
teach.method: Ask: did the person collect these numbers themselves, for this purpose? Yes: primary. No, they were taken from somewhere else: secondary.

alternatives.title: Two examples
text: Meena times her classmates running 100 m: primary.
Meena copies last year's sports-day times from the school magazine: secondary.

families.title: Mutually exclusive and exhaustive events
explanations: complement-not-exclusive (conceptual): Events that cover every outcome were thought to overlap. Here no outcome is in both and every outcome is in one: they are complementary.
overlap-missed (conceptual): The one outcome that is in both events was missed, so they were called mutually exclusive. Check every outcome against both events.

exclusive-as-complement (conceptual): Because A and B have no outcome in common, they were taken to cover every outcome. Mutually exclusive only means they cannot happen together; some outcomes are in neither.

teach.idea: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (no common outcome). Exhaustive events between them cover every outcome. Events that are both are complementary: B is 'not A', and P(A) + P(B) = 1.
teach.method: List the outcomes of each event. Any outcome in both? Then not mutually exclusive. Any outcome in neither? Then not exhaustive.

alternatives.title: Two circles
text: Draw two circles for A and B inside a box for all outcomes.
Overlapping circles: not mutually exclusive. Space left in the box outside both circles: not exhaustive.

families.title: Multiplying a binomial by a trinomial
explanations: b-times-first-only (procedural): 6 was multiplied by the first term of the second bracket only; every term of the first bracket multiplies every term of the second.
drop-minus (procedural): The minus sign of −1 was lost when multiplying; −1 × −5 must carry the sign.
power-not-added (conceptual): x × x² was written as x² (and x × x as x); when you multiply, the powers add: x × x² = x³.

teach.idea: Multiplication distributes over addition: each term of the first bracket multiplies every term of the second, and when powers of x are multiplied their indices add.
teach.method: Multiply the second bracket by ax, then by b. Write the two rows under each other, power below power, and add like terms.

alternatives.title: Use a multiplication grid
text: Draw a grid with ax and b down the side and cx², dx and e along the top.
Fill each cell with the product of its row and column, then add the cells on each diagonal (they hold the same power of x).

families.title: The quotient when a cubic is divided by x − r
explanations: sign-of-r (procedural): The number −4 was used in the division; dividing by x − 4 uses 4 (the value that makes x − 4 zero).
remainder-in-quotient (conceptual): The last number of the bottom row is the remainder, not part of the quotient; the quotient has one power less than p(x).
no-placeholder (procedural): A missing power of x was skipped; write 0 for it so each column keeps its own power.

teach.idea: Dividing by x − r leaves p(x) = (x − r) × quotient + remainder; synthetic division finds the quotient's coefficients one at a time.
teach.method: Write the coefficients of p(x) (0 for a missing power). Bring down the first; multiply by r and add to the next, again and again. The last number is the remainder; the others are the quotient.

alternatives.title: Long division
text: Divide the first term of p(x) by x to get the first term of the quotient; multiply x − r by it and subtract.
Repeat with what is left until only a number remains: that is the remainder.

families.title: The remainder theorem
explanations: sign-of-r (procedural): p(−2) was found; the remainder on dividing by x − 2 is p(2), the value that makes the divisor zero.
constant-term (conceptual): The constant term was taken as the remainder; that is only the value of p(0).
cube-of-negative (prerequisite): (−3)³ was taken as positive; a negative number cubed stays negative.

teach.idea: p(x) = (x − r) × quotient + remainder. Put x = r: the first part becomes 0, so the remainder is p(r).
teach.method: Find the value of x that makes the divisor zero, substitute it into p(x), and work out the powers carefully with their signs.

alternatives.title: Synthetic division
text: Write the coefficients, bring down the first, multiply by r and add to the next, and so on.
The last number you get is the remainder: the same number as p(r).

families.title: Finding k so that x − r is a factor
explanations: sign-of-r (procedural): x = −3 was substituted; x − 3 is a factor when p(3) = 0.
sign-moving (procedural): The known part was moved to the other side without changing its sign; p(r) = 0 gives k = −(the rest).

teach.idea: x − r is a factor of p(x) exactly when p(r) = 0 (the factor theorem).
teach.method: Substitute x = r into p(x), keeping k as a letter; set the result equal to 0 and solve for k.

alternatives.title: Make the remainder zero
text: Do synthetic division by r with k left as a letter.
The last number contains k: it must be 0, which gives k.

families.title: All the zeros of a cubic, by the factor theorem
explanations: bracket-signs (procedural): The numbers in the brackets were taken as the zeros; x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2, so each sign flips.
stop-at-one (procedural): Only the zero found by trial was given; after dividing, the quadratic quotient gives the other two.

teach.idea: If p(a) = 0 then x − a is a factor; a whole-number zero of a polynomial with leading coefficient 1 must divide the constant term.
teach.method: Try divisors of the constant term (±1 first) until p(a) = 0. Divide p(x) by x − a, factorise the quadratic quotient, and read off all three zeros.

alternatives.title: Quick tests for 1 and −1
text: If the coefficients add up to 0, then p(1) = 0 and x − 1 is a factor.
If the coefficients of the even powers add up to those of the odd powers, then p(−1) = 0 and x + 1 is a factor.

families.title: The straight-line rule behind a table
explanations: step-only (procedural): Only the step was used; the rule also needs the value of y when x = 0.
step-sign (procedural): The values go down, so the step is negative; the sign of the step was lost.
first-value-as-start (conceptual): The first y in the table was taken as the starting value, but the table starts at x = 2; the starting value is y when x = 0.

teach.idea: When y changes by the same amount each time x goes up by 1, the rule is y = (step) × x + (value of y at x = 0).
teach.method: Find the step from two neighbouring values. Work back to x = 0 to find the starting value. Check your rule with one more pair from the table.

alternatives.title: Plot the points
text: Plot the pairs on squared paper: they lie on one straight line.
The line rises (or falls) by the step for each 1 across, and crosses the y-axis at the starting value.

families.title: Completing a solution of ax + by = c
explanations: add-instead (procedural): 45 was added to 57; it must be taken away from both sides.
no-divide (procedural): 8y = 32 was taken as y = 32; divide by 8 as well.

teach.idea: A solution of an equation in two variables is a pair (x, y) that makes it true; choosing x fixes y.
teach.method: Substitute the given x, take that part away from the right side, then divide by the coefficient of y.

alternatives.title: Make a table of solutions
text: List x = 0, 1, 2, … and work out y each time.
Each row is one solution; there are infinitely many, all on one straight line.

families.title: GCD of two quadratics
explanations: factor-of-one (conceptual): A factor of only one of the polynomials was given; the GCD must divide both.
lcm-instead (conceptual): Every factor was multiplied together: that is the LCM; the GCD keeps only the factors they share.
factor-sign (procedural): A factor was written with the wrong sign; check by expanding the brackets back.

teach.idea: Like the HCF of numbers, the GCD of polynomials is the product of the factors they have in common.
teach.method: Factorise each polynomial completely, then multiply the factors that appear in every one (with the smaller power).

alternatives.title: Look for a shared zero
text: Each factor x + a belongs to a zero x = −a.
A value of x that makes both polynomials zero gives a common factor.

families.title: LCM of two quadratics
explanations: product (conceptual): The two polynomials were multiplied; the common factor x + 6 is then counted twice. The LCM takes each factor once, with its highest power.
gcd-instead (conceptual): The common factor was given; that is the GCD. The LCM must be divisible by both polynomials.
drop-common (procedural): The shared factor was left out; the LCM needs every factor of each polynomial.

teach.idea: The LCM is the smallest polynomial both divide into: every factor that appears, each with its highest power. GCD × LCM equals the product of the two polynomials.
teach.method: Factorise both. Write down every different factor once (the highest power that appears) and multiply.

alternatives.title: Product divided by the GCD
text: Multiply the two polynomials as factors.
Divide by their GCD (cross out the shared factor once): what is left is the LCM.

families.title: A rational expression in lowest terms
explanations: zero-for-number (procedural): The zeros were written instead of the numbers in the brackets: x + 5 has p = 5, not −5.
cancel-wrong (conceptual): The wrong bracket was cancelled; only a factor that is in both the top and the bottom can be cancelled.

teach.idea: A fraction is unchanged when the top and bottom are divided by the same non-zero factor; only factors (not terms) can be cancelled.
teach.method: Factorise the top and the bottom fully, then cancel the bracket that appears in both.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Put a value such as x = 1 into the original fraction and into your answer.
They must give the same value; cancelling x² terms (not factors) fails this test.

families.title: Excluded values of a rational expression
explanations: after-cancel (conceptual): The value was found after cancelling; x = −6 still makes the original denominator zero, so it is excluded too.
numerator (conceptual): The zeros of the numerator were given; the expression is undefined where the DENOMINATOR is zero.
sign (procedural): The numbers in the brackets were given; x + 3 = 0 when x = −3.

teach.idea: Division by zero has no meaning, so a rational expression is undefined wherever its denominator is zero, even if a factor later cancels.
teach.method: Factorise the denominator and set each factor equal to zero.

alternatives.title: Test the values
text: Put each value you found into the original denominator.
If it gives 0, the value is excluded; values that only make the top zero are fine.

families.title: Evaluating a composite function
explanations: order (conceptual): The functions were used in the wrong order; (f ∘ g)(x) means f(g(x)): g first, then the other.
product (conceptual): f(x) and g(x) were multiplied; composition puts the output of one function into the other.

teach.idea: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)): the output of g becomes the input of f. The order matters.
teach.method: Work from the inside out: find the inner function's value at the number, then put that value into the outer function.

alternatives.title: Two machines in a row
