text: Think of g and f as machines: a number goes into the first, and what comes out goes into the second.
For f ∘ g, the number goes into g first (the one nearest the bracket).

families.title: The composite of two linear functions
explanations: order (conceptual): g(f(x)) was found; (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)) puts g(x) into f.
constants-added (procedural): Only the x term was multiplied by 5; the whole of g(x), including −4, is multiplied.
product (conceptual): f(x) and g(x) were multiplied; composition substitutes one into the other.

teach.idea: f(g(x)) means: wherever f has x, put the whole of g(x) in its place.
teach.method: Write f with a bracket in place of x, put g(x) inside the bracket, multiply out and collect terms.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Pick x = 1: work out g(1), then f of that.
Your simplified answer at x = 1 must give the same number.

families.title: Solving a pair of linear equations
explanations: swapped (procedural): The values were written in the wrong order; the pair is (x, y): x first.

added-to-eliminate (procedural): After making the x coefficients equal, the two equations were added and the x terms were then crossed out as if they had cancelled; x terms with the same sign cancel only when the equations are subtracted.

teach.idea: The solution is the one pair (x, y) that makes both equations true: the point where the two lines cross.
teach.method: Elimination: multiply the equations so x has the same coefficient in both, subtract to remove x, solve for y, then substitute back to find x. Check in both equations.

alternatives.title: Substitution
text: Make x (or y) the subject of the simpler equation.
Put that expression into the other equation, solve it, then substitute back.

families.title: A pair of linear equations from a shopping problem
explanations: swapped (procedural): The prices were given in the wrong order; the question asks for (pen, notebook).

added-to-eliminate (procedural): After making the pen numbers equal, the two equations were added and the pen terms were then crossed out as if they had cancelled; equal pen terms cancel only when the equations are subtracted.

teach.idea: Each purchase gives one equation in the two unknown prices; together they fix both prices.
teach.method: Let x and y be the two prices, write one equation per purchase, solve by elimination or substitution, and check that both totals come out right.

alternatives.title: Compare the two baskets
text: Scale the baskets so both have the same number of pens.
The difference in cost is then caused only by the difference in notebooks.

families.title: How many solutions a pair of equations has
explanations: x-ratio-only (conceptual): Only a₁/a₂ was compared; the lines are parallel or the same only when b₁/b₂ is in the same ratio too.
equal-ratios-parallel (conceptual): Equal ratios a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ were taken to mean parallel lines; when c₁/c₂ is equal as well, the two equations describe the same line.
equal-ratios-same-line (conceptual): a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ was taken to mean the same line; the lines coincide only when c₁/c₂ is also in that ratio, otherwise they are parallel.

teach.idea: Two lines either cross once, are parallel (never meet) or are the same line. The ratios of the coefficients tell which.
teach.method: If a₁/a₂ ≠ b₁/b₂: exactly one solution. If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂: no solution. If all three ratios are equal: infinitely many.

alternatives.title: Compare the slopes
text: Write each equation as y = mx + c.
Different slopes: the lines cross once. Same slope, different c: parallel. Same slope and same c: the same line.

families.title: Solving three linear equations in three variables
explanations: order (procedural): The values were written in a different order; give them as (x, y, z).
one-sign (procedural): A sign was lost while eliminating, so one value has the wrong sign; check each value in all three equations.

teach.idea: Each equation removes one degree of freedom; three independent equations fix x, y and z. Eliminating one variable turns the problem into a pair of equations.
teach.method: Pick a variable, eliminate it from two different pairs of equations, solve the resulting pair, then substitute back to find the third value. Check in all three.

alternatives.title: Substitute from the simplest equation
text: Make one variable the subject of the equation with coefficient 1.
Put it into the other two equations and solve that pair.

families.title: The square root of a perfect-square polynomial
explanations: all-positive (procedural): Every term was given a plus sign; the signs must make the cross terms (like 2bc x) come out with their signs when you square back.
not-halved (procedural): The x³ term was divided by 4 only; it is 2 × (4x²) × (the next term), so divide by 8.
constant-sign (procedural): √(1) = 1, but the sign must match the x term: (4x² + 6x + 1)² has the wrong x term.

teach.idea: (ax² + bx + c)² = a²x⁴ + 2abx³ + (b² + 2ac)x² + 2bcx + c², so the terms of the root can be read off one at a time.
teach.method: Take the square root of the first term; divide the x³ term by twice that to get the x term; find the constant from the x term (divide by twice the x term). Square your answer to check.

alternatives.title: The long-division method
text: As for numbers: the first term of the root squared is taken away, the root so far is doubled as the next divisor.
Bring down two terms at a time; when nothing is left, the polynomial is a perfect square.

families.title: A symmetric expression in the zeros of a quadratic
explanations: forgot-2ab (procedural): α² + β² was taken as (α + β)²; subtract 2αβ first.
plus-2ab (procedural): 2αβ was added instead of subtracted in α² + β².
sum-sign (recall): The sum of the zeros was taken as b/a; it is −b/a.
flipped (procedural): 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ); the fraction was turned upside down.

teach.idea: For ax² + bx + c, the zeros satisfy α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a. Any expression that stays the same when α and β swap can be written using only these two.
teach.method: Write the expression in terms of α + β and αβ (for example α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ), then substitute.

alternatives.title: Check with easy zeros
text: Try a polynomial whose zeros you know, such as x² − 5x + 6 with zeros 2 and 3.
Work the expression out directly and with the formula: both must agree.

families.title: A quadratic polynomial from its zeros
explanations: sum-sign (recall): The x term was given the sign of the sum; x² − (sum)x + (product): the sum is subtracted.
product-plus (procedural): (6 + √15)(6 − √15) = 36 − 15: the product of a sum and a difference is a difference of squares.
swapped (recall): The sum and product were put in each other's places; the x coefficient comes from the sum and the constant is the product.

teach.idea: A quadratic with zeros α and β is (x − α)(x − β) = x² − (α + β)x + αβ.
teach.method: Find the sum and the product of the zeros (for m + √n and m − √n: sum 2m, product m² − n), then write x² − (sum)x + (product).

alternatives.title: Multiply the brackets
text: Write (x − α)(x − β) with the zeros in place.
Multiply out; with surd zeros, group as ((x − m) − √n)((x − m) + √n) = (x − m)² − n.

families.title: Which line to draw with y = ax² to solve a quadratic
explanations: no-sign-change (procedural): The other terms were copied to the line without changing their signs; moving a term to the other side of = changes its sign.
one-sign-changed (procedural): Only one of the two terms changed sign when it moved; both px and q move to the other side, so both change sign.

teach.idea: At a point where y = ax² meets the line y = mx + c, the y values are equal: ax² = mx + c. So the solutions of ax² − mx − c = 0 are the x-coordinates of the meeting points.
teach.method: Keep the ax² term on one side and move every other term to the other side (changing signs). The other side is the line to draw.

alternatives.title: Test with one x
text: Choose x = 1. On the curve, y = a.
Your line at x = 1 must satisfy: a − (line value) = the quadratic at x = 1.

families.title: Solving a quadratic equation from a table of values
explanations: sign-of-k (procedural): The x values where y = 1 were read; the right-hand side is −1.
read-zero (procedural): The x values where y = 0 were read; the equation asks where y = −2.

teach.idea: Solving f(x) = k means finding the x values where the graph of y = f(x) is at height k, where it meets the line y = k.
teach.method: Look along the y row of the table for the value k, and read the x above each one. A quadratic gives at most two.

alternatives.title: Plot and draw the line
text: Plot the points from the table and join them with a smooth curve.
Draw the horizontal line y = k: the x-coordinates where it cuts the curve are the solutions.

families.title: Sums of natural numbers, odd numbers, squares and cubes
explanations: one-short (procedural): n − 1 was used in place of n; the sum 1 + 2 + … + n has n terms.
last-as-count (procedural): The last term 59 was taken as the number of terms; there are 30 odd numbers up to 59.
all-numbers (conceptual): All the numbers up to 59 were added, not only the odd ones.
natural-formula (recall): The formula for 1 + 2 + … + n was used; the sum of squares is n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
cubes-formula (recall): The formula for the sum of cubes was used; the sum of squares is n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
not-squared (recall): n(n + 1)/2 was not squared; the sum of the first n cubes is (n(n + 1)/2)².
squares-formula (recall): The formula for the sum of squares was used; the sum of cubes is (n(n + 1)/2)².

teach.idea: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 (pair the first and last terms); the first n odd numbers add to n²; 1² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; 1³ + … + n³ = (n(n + 1)/2)².
teach.method: Count the number of terms n first (for odd numbers up to L, n = (L + 1)/2), then use the matching formula.

alternatives.title: Pair the ends (Gauss)
text: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add: every column is n + 1.
There are n columns, so twice the sum is n(n + 1).

families.title: Sums of powers that start partway
explanations: subtract-to-m (procedural): The sum up to 14 was taken away, which removes 14³ as well; take away the sum up to 13.
count-from-one (conceptual): The formula was used with n = 17 (the number of terms), as if the sum started at 1.

teach.idea: A sum from m to n is the sum from 1 to n minus the sum from 1 to m − 1.
teach.method: Use the formula with n, then with m − 1, and subtract.

alternatives.title: Cut off the start
text: Imagine the full sum 1 + 2 + … + n as a staircase.
Remove the first m − 1 steps: what is left is the part you want.

families.title: The distance between two points as a surd
explanations: added-sides (conceptual): The across and up distances were added; the straight distance is the hypotenuse: √(across² + up²).
no-root (procedural): The square root was not taken at the end.
sign-slip (prerequisite): A difference of coordinates lost a sign: from −2 to 3 is 5, not 1.
subtract-squares (procedural): The squares were subtracted; for the hypotenuse they are added.

teach.idea: The segment AB is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose other sides are the across and up distances, so AB² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² (Baudhayana–Pythagoras).
teach.method: Subtract the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates, square both, add, take the square root and simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: Draw the right triangle
text: Draw across from A and up (or down) to B: the corner is a right angle.
Count the two sides on the grid, then use the Baudhayana–Pythagoras theorem.

families.title: Midpoints, and the other end of a segment
explanations: half-difference (conceptual): Half the difference of the coordinates was found; that is how far to go, not where you land. The midpoint averages them: add and halve.
no-halve (procedural): The coordinates were added but not halved.
midpoint-of-given (conceptual): The midpoint of A and M was found; M is the middle, so B is as far beyond M as A is before it.
difference (procedural): M − A was found; that is the step from A to M, which must be added to M once more: B = 2M − A.

teach.idea: The midpoint is halfway across and halfway up: its coordinates are the averages of the endpoints' coordinates.
teach.method: Midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). For a missing end B with midpoint M: B = (2·Mx − Ax, 2·My − Ay).

alternatives.title: Count the steps
text: Count the steps across and up from A to the other point on the grid.
For a midpoint, take half of each; for a missing end, take the same steps again from M.

families.title: The fourth vertex of a parallelogram
explanations: wrong-diagonal (conceptual): A and C were not used as opposite corners; in ABCD the diagonals are AC and BD, and they share a midpoint.
wrong-pair (conceptual): A and B were treated as opposite corners; in ABCD, B is opposite D.

teach.idea: In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, and opposite sides are equal and parallel: going from A to B is the same step as going from D to C.
teach.method: D = A + C − B (add the coordinates of A and C, subtract those of B). Check that the midpoints of AC and BD agree.

alternatives.title: Copy the step
text: Count the step from B to C (across and up).
Make the same step from A: that is D.

families.title: Is the triangle right-angled or isosceles?
explanations: grid-lengths (conceptual): The sides were measured by counting across plus up along the grid; a slanting side is √(across² + up²).
only-angle-a (procedural): Only the angle at A was tested; the right angle can be at any vertex, so test the longest side against the other two.

teach.idea: Squared side lengths decide the shape: two equal sides make it isosceles, and if two squared sides add up to the third it has a right angle (converse of the Baudhayana–Pythagoras theorem).
teach.method: Find AB², BC² and CA² with the distance formula (no need for square roots). Compare them for equal pairs, and test whether the two smaller add up to the largest.

alternatives.title: Use the steps of the sides
text: Write each side as a step (across, up). Two sides are at right angles when across × across + up × up = 0 for their steps.
Equal sides have equal across² + up².

families.title: The area of a triangle from its vertices
explanations: no-half (procedural): The ½ in front of the formula was left out.
forward-only (procedural): Only the products x₁y₂, x₂y₃, x₃y₁ were added; the products x₂y₁, x₃y₂, x₁y₃ must be taken away.
negative-area (procedural): The result was left negative; an area is the absolute value: take away the minus sign.

teach.idea: Area = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|: the formula comes from boxing the triangle in a rectangle and taking away right triangles (or trapeziums).
teach.method: Substitute carefully with signs, add the three products, take the absolute value and halve.

alternatives.title: Box it in a rectangle
text: Draw the smallest rectangle on the grid that holds the triangle.
Take away the right triangles in the corners from the rectangle's area.

families.title: The unknown coordinate that makes three points collinear
explanations: slope-upside-down (conceptual): The slope was found as change in x ÷ change in y; it is change in y ÷ change in x.
mixed-points (procedural): The slope was used from one point but the steps counted from the other; measure both from the same point.

teach.idea: Three points are collinear exactly when the 'triangle' they make has area 0.
teach.method: Put the points into ½[x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)] = 0 with k in place, and solve the linear equation for k.

alternatives.title: Equal slopes
text: The slope from the first point to the second must equal the slope from the first point to the third.
Write (k − y₁)/(x₃ − x₁) = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) and solve.

families.title: Angles in a circle
explanations: equal (conceptual): The two angles at A and B were taken as equal; that is only true when C is halfway round.
halved (conceptual): The angle was halved, as for an angle at the circumference; equal chords make EQUAL angles at the centre.
doubled (conceptual): The angle at the centre was doubled; the angle at the circumference is half of it.
opposite-equal (conceptual): Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral were taken as equal; they add up to 180°.
complement (recall): 90° was used; opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°, not 90°.
bracket-slip (procedural): 180° − 90° − ∠CAB was worked out as 180° − (90° − ∠CAB): the given angle was added back instead of taken away. Both 90° and ∠CAB come off 180°.
not-halved (procedural): 180° − 150° was not shared between the two equal base angles.
half-centre (conceptual): The base angle was taken as half the angle at the centre; in triangle OAB the two base angles share 180° minus the angle at O.
supplement (conceptual): The two angles at the centre were taken to add up to 180°; equal chords make equal angles at the centre.
centre-angle-given (procedural): The angle at the centre was given; the question asks for the base angle of the isosceles triangle OCD, which shares 180° minus that angle with the other base angle.
whole-centre-angle (procedural): ∠AOB was found; OM bisects it, and the question asks for half of it, ∠AOM.
no-right-angle (conceptual): The right angle at M was not used; the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord, so ∠AOM = 90° − ∠OAM.

teach.idea: An arc makes twice the angle at the centre that it makes at any point on the rest of the circle. From this: angles in the same segment are equal, the angle in a semicircle is 90°, and opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add up to 180°.
teach.method: Name the fact that links the given angle to the one asked for, write the relation (×2, ÷2, 180° − , 90° − ), then work it out.

alternatives.title: Draw the radii
text: Join the centre to the points on the circle: every radius is the same length, so the triangles formed are isosceles.
Equal base angles and the angle sum of 180° in each triangle lead to the same results.

families.title: Chords and their distance from the centre
explanations: not-doubled (procedural): Only half the chord was found; the perpendicular from the centre cuts the chord into two equal halves, so double it.
added-squares (procedural): The squares were added; the radius is the hypotenuse, so subtract: distance² = r² − (half chord)².
subtract-lengths (conceptual): The lengths were subtracted without squaring; Pythagoras works with the squares of the sides.
full-chord (procedural): The whole chord was used in the right triangle; the triangle uses HALF the chord.

teach.idea: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it, so the radius, the distance from the centre and half the chord form a right triangle with the radius as hypotenuse.
teach.method: Half chord² + distance² = radius². Find the unknown side, and double the half chord if the whole chord is asked.

alternatives.title: Fold the circle
text: Fold a paper circle so that the two ends of a chord meet: the fold passes through the centre and is perpendicular to the chord.
The fold cuts the chord into two equal halves.

families.title: Which circle fact justifies a step
explanations: mixed-up-fact (conceptual): The fact about the perpendicular bisecting a chord was chosen; this step compares two equal chords.

teach.idea: Each step in a geometry argument needs a reason: a definition or a theorem already proved. Matching the situation (where the angle is, what the chord does) to the theorem is the first part of writing a proof.
teach.method: Look at what the step uses: an angle at the centre, two angles on the same arc, a diameter, a cyclic quadrilateral, a perpendicular to a chord, or equal chords. Pick the fact about exactly that.

alternatives.title: Sketch it first
text: Make a quick sketch and mark what is given and what is claimed.
The theorem you need is the one whose picture looks like your sketch.

families.title: Recognising and classifying polynomials
explanations: negative-power (conceptual): A term like a/x was accepted; a/x is a × x⁻¹, and a polynomial allows only whole-number powers 0, 1, 2, … of x.
root-of-x (conceptual): √x was accepted as a term; √x is x to the power ½, which is not a whole number. (A root in the coefficient, like √2 x, is allowed.)
two-terms-linear (conceptual): An expression with two terms was taken as linear; linear means the highest power of x is 1, and here it is 2.
terms-as-degree (conceptual): The number of terms was taken as the degree; the degree is the highest power of x.
first-term-power (procedural): The power of the first term written was taken; the terms are not written in order here, so look for the highest power anywhere.
degree-as-terms (conceptual): The degree was used to name it; monomial, binomial and trinomial count the terms, not the power.
like-terms-counted (procedural): Like terms were counted separately; terms with the same power of x are collected into one term first.

teach.idea: A polynomial in x is a sum of terms a·xⁿ with n a whole number (0, 1, 2, …). Its degree is the highest power of x; by degree it is constant, linear, quadratic or cubic, and by its number of terms a monomial, binomial or trinomial.
teach.method: Write each term as a power of x: 1/x is x⁻¹ and √x is x^½, so they are not allowed. Collect like terms, then read the highest power (the degree) and count the terms.

alternatives.title: Rewrite every term as a power
text: Rewrite 3/x as 3x⁻¹ and √x as x^½; √2 x is just the number √2 times x¹.
If every power is 0, 1, 2, 3, …, it is a polynomial; the largest power is its degree.

families.title: Degree and coefficients of a polynomial
explanations: terms-as-degree (conceptual): The number of terms was given; the degree is the highest power of x.
largest-coefficient (conceptual): The largest number in front of a term was given; the degree is a power, not a coefficient.
first-term-power (procedural): The power of the first term written was taken; the terms are not in order, so look for the highest power anywhere.
power-for-coefficient (conceptual): The power was given instead of the number multiplying it; the coefficient is the number in front.
sign-dropped (procedural): The minus sign in front of the term was left off; the sign belongs to the coefficient.
missing-is-one (conceptual): A missing term was given coefficient 1; when a power does not appear, its coefficient is 0.
highest-exponent (conceptual): The highest power of a single letter was taken; the degree of a term adds the powers of x and y, and the polynomial takes the largest of these.
exponents-multiplied (procedural): The powers were multiplied; the degree adds them.
count-variables (conceptual): The number of different letters was counted; the degree adds their powers.
all-exponents (procedural): All the powers in the polynomial were added together; add only within one term, then take the largest term.
first-term (procedural): The degree of the first term was given; another term has a higher degree.

teach.idea: The degree of a monomial is the sum of the powers of its variables (3x²y³ has degree 5); the degree of a polynomial is the highest degree of its terms. The coefficient of a power is the number multiplying it, with its sign.
teach.method: Collect like terms. For each term add the powers of its letters; the largest such sum is the degree. For a coefficient, find the term with that power and read the number (and sign) in front; 0 if it is missing.

alternatives.title: Make a table of terms
text: Write each term on its own line with its coefficient and the powers of each letter.
Add the powers on each line; the biggest total is the degree.

families.title: Adding and subtracting polynomials
explanations: sign-dropped (procedural): A minus sign inside the second bracket was lost while adding; keep each coefficient's own sign.
sign-first-term-only (procedural): Only the first term of the second bracket changed sign; the minus in front of the bracket changes the sign of every term inside.

teach.idea: Only like terms (the same power of x) can be added; subtracting a polynomial adds its negative, so every sign inside the bracket changes.
teach.method: Remove the brackets (changing every sign of the second polynomial for subtraction), then collect the x³ terms, the x² terms, the x terms and the numbers.

alternatives.title: Line up in columns
text: Write the two polynomials one under the other, x³ under x³, x² under x², and so on (leave a gap for a missing power).
Add (or subtract) each column.

families.title: The value of a polynomial and the zero of a linear polynomial
explanations: power-as-product (prerequisite): A power was worked out as a multiplication (for example 2² as 2 × 2); a power multiplies the number by itself.
negative-squared (prerequisite): (−2)² was taken as negative; a negative number squared is positive.
zero-sign (procedural): ax + b = 0 gives x = −b/a; the sign of 2 was not changed when it moved across.
zero-upside-down (procedural): The fraction was turned upside down: x = −b/a, not −a/b.

teach.idea: The value of p(x) at x = t is what you get by putting t in place of x; a zero of p(x) is a value of x that makes p(x) = 0.
teach.method: Substitute the number in brackets, work out the powers with their signs first, then multiply and add. For a zero of ax + b, solve ax + b = 0: x = −b/a.

alternatives.title: Nested multiplication
text: Start with the first coefficient; multiply by t and add the next coefficient, again and again.
The last number is p(t) — the same as the synthetic-division remainder.

families.title: Dividing a polynomial by a monomial
explanations: first-term-only (procedural): Only the first term was divided by 9; every term of the polynomial is divided by the monomial.
sign-lost (procedural): A minus sign was lost when dividing; a negative term divided by a positive monomial stays negative.

teach.idea: Dividing a sum by a monomial divides each term separately: (A + B + C) ÷ m = A/m + B/m + C/m, and xᵃ ÷ xᵇ = xᵃ⁻ᵇ.
teach.method: Split the division into one division per term; divide the coefficients and subtract the powers of x.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying back
text: Multiply your quotient by the monomial.
You must get the original polynomial term by term.

families.title: The division algorithm with a non-monic or quadratic divisor
explanations: not-divided-by-a (procedural): Synthetic division was done with x = −5/3, but the bottom row was not divided by 3; that row is 3 times the quotient.
root-sign (procedural): x = 5/3 was used in the synthetic division; the divisor 3x + 5 is zero at x = −5/3.
added-not-subtracted (procedural): Each line was added instead of subtracted during the long division; after multiplying the divisor by the quotient term, change its signs and add.

teach.idea: For any polynomials p(x) and d(x) ≠ 0 there are a quotient q(x) and a remainder r(x) with p(x) = d(x)q(x) + r(x) and deg r < deg d (the division algorithm).
teach.method: Long division: divide the leading term of what is left by the leading term of d(x), multiply d(x) by it, subtract, and repeat until the degree of what is left is less than that of d(x). For Ax + B, synthetic division at x = −B/A gives A times the quotient.

alternatives.title: Synthetic division for Ax + B
text: Do synthetic division with x = −B/A: the last number is the remainder.
Divide the other numbers of the bottom row by A to get the quotient's coefficients.

alternatives.title: Compare coefficients
text: Write p(x) = d(x)(ax² + bx + c) + r (or the quadratic-divisor form) with unknown letters.
Multiply out and match the coefficients of each power from the top down.

families.title: Splitting the middle term of ax² + bx + c
explanations: product-c-only (procedural): rs was taken as −20 (the constant term only); when the x² coefficient is not 1, rs = a × c.
zero-signs (procedural): The numbers in the brackets were taken as the zeros; mx + p = 0 gives x = −p/m, so the sign changes.
not-divided (procedural): The coefficient of x in each bracket was ignored; mx + p = 0 gives x = −p/m, not −p.

teach.idea: If ax² + bx + c = (mx + p)(nx + q), then a × c = (mn)(pq) = (mq)(np), and b = mq + np. So bx splits into two parts whose product is ac.
teach.method: Find two numbers with sum b and product a × c. Write bx as the sum of those two terms, group the four terms in pairs, take out the common factor of each pair, and then the common bracket.

alternatives.title: List the factor pairs of ac
text: Write all pairs of whole numbers whose product is a × c (with signs).
Pick the pair that adds up to b.

families.title: GCD of cubics, and of three polynomials
explanations: one-common-factor (procedural): Only one shared factor was taken; both polynomials also share a second factor, and the GCD takes every common factor.
lcm-instead (conceptual): Every factor was multiplied together: that is the LCM; the GCD keeps only the factors they share.
two-only (procedural): The common factors of the first and last polynomials only were taken; the GCD must divide all three.
factor-sign (procedural): A factor was written with the wrong sign; check by expanding the brackets back.

teach.idea: The GCD of several polynomials is the product of the factors common to ALL of them, each with the smallest power in which it appears.
teach.method: Factorise every polynomial completely (try small numbers as zeros for the cubics), list the factors, and multiply those that appear in every list.

alternatives.title: Two at a time
text: Find the GCD of the first two polynomials.
Then find the GCD of that result and the third polynomial.

families.title: Using GCD × LCM = the product of two polynomials
explanations: lcm-over-p (procedural): The LCM was divided by p(x) but not multiplied by the GCD; q(x) = GCD × LCM ÷ p(x).
lcm-over-gcd (procedural): The LCM was divided by the GCD; that gives the factors that are not shared, not q(x).
divided-twice (procedural): The product was divided by the GCD twice; LCM = product ÷ GCD, once.
product-as-lcm (conceptual): The product itself was given; it contains the common factor twice, while the LCM contains it once.

teach.idea: For two polynomials, GCD × LCM = p(x) × q(x) (up to a constant factor): the shared factors are counted once in each of GCD and LCM, and twice in the product.
teach.method: Rearrange the relation for what is unknown (q = GCD × LCM ÷ p, or LCM = product ÷ GCD) and divide by factorising or by long division.

alternatives.title: Count the factors
text: Write p, GCD and LCM as products of brackets.
q must contain the GCD's factors and the LCM's factors that p does not have.

families.title: Multiplying, dividing, adding and subtracting rational expressions
explanations: zero-for-number (procedural): The zeros were written instead of the numbers in the brackets: x + 6 has p = 6, not −6.
inverted-first (procedural): The first fraction was turned upside down instead of the second; dividing by a fraction multiplies by the second one inverted.
cross-swapped (procedural): Each numerator was multiplied by its own denominator's number; 3/(x + 4) becomes 3(x + 5) over the common denominator — it is multiplied by the OTHER bracket.
minus-not-distributed (procedural): The minus sign was applied to 6x only; −6(x + 4) = −6x − 24.

teach.idea: Rational expressions follow the rules of fractions: multiply tops and bottoms, divide by multiplying by the reciprocal, and add or subtract over a common denominator. Only common FACTORS cancel.
teach.method: Factorise every numerator and denominator first. For × and ÷ cancel the shared brackets; for + and − multiply each numerator by the other denominator's bracket, then collect terms.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Put x = 1 (or another value that does not make a denominator 0) into the question and into your answer.
Both must give the same number.

families.title: The value of k for equal roots
explanations: four-dropped (recall): The 4 in b² − 4ac was left out.
no-square-root (procedural): k² was found but its square root was not taken.
discriminant-sign (recall): The discriminant was written b² + 4ac; it is b² − 4ac.

teach.idea: A quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 has two equal real roots exactly when its discriminant b² − 4ac is 0 (two different real roots when it is positive, none when negative).
teach.method: Write b² − 4ac with k in its place, set it equal to 0 and solve for k (take the positive square root if a positive k is asked).

alternatives.title: Make a perfect square
text: Equal roots means the quadratic is a constant times (x − r)².
For x² + kx + 9 that is (x + 3)² = x² + 6x + 9, so k = 6.

families.title: The area of a quadrilateral from its vertices
explanations: no-half (procedural): The ½ in front of the formula was left out.
not-in-order (procedural): The vertices were not taken in order round the quadrilateral (A, C, B, D); go round the boundary A → B → C → D.
forward-only (procedural): Only the products x₁y₂, x₂y₃, x₃y₄, x₄y₁ were added; the products the other way round must be taken away.

teach.idea: Area = ½ |(x₁y₂ − x₂y₁) + (x₂y₃ − x₃y₂) + (x₃y₄ − x₄y₃) + (x₄y₁ − x₁y₄)| when the vertices are taken in order round the quadrilateral; it is the sum of the two triangles ABC and ACD.
teach.method: List the vertices in order (and the first again at the end), multiply across in both directions, take the difference, the absolute value and half.

alternatives.title: Split into two triangles
text: Draw the diagonal AC: ABCD is triangle ABC plus triangle ACD.
Find each area with the triangle formula and add.

families.title: Steady increase or decrease: a linear polynomial to predict
explanations: start-left-out (conceptual): Only the change r × t was worked out; the polynomial also needs the starting amount as its constant term.
one-step-short (procedural): The change was counted 2 times; after 3 hours it has happened 3 times.
wrong-direction (conceptual): The steady change was added; the amount goes DOWN each step, so the coefficient of t is negative.

teach.idea: A quantity that changes by the same amount every step is modelled by a linear polynomial p(t) = (start) + (change per step) × t; the change is negative for a steady decrease (linear decay).
teach.method: Read the starting amount (the value when t = 0) and the change per step with its sign, write p(t) = start + change × t, and substitute the number of steps.

alternatives.title: Make a table
text: Write t = 0, 1, 2, 3 and the amount each time: the amounts go up (or down) by the same step.
The pattern start + step × t gives every row; use it for the t asked.

families.title: Solutions of a linear equation in two variables
explanations: not-substituted (procedural): A pair was accepted without substituting it into the equation; put x and y in and check that both sides are equal.

one-solution-only (conceptual): A linear equation in two variables was thought to have only one solution, so a second, different pair was rejected; there are infinitely many pairs, all on one straight line.

teach.idea: A linear equation in two variables has infinitely many solutions: each value of x gives one y. All the solutions lie on one straight line.
teach.method: To test a pair, substitute x and y and check that the left side equals the right side. Finding one solution does not rule out others.

alternatives.title: Step along the line
text: From one solution (x, y) of ax + by = c, the pair (x + b, y − a) is also a solution: ab is added and taken away.
Repeating this gives as many solutions as you like.

families.title: Substitution, elimination and cross-multiplication: the key step
explanations: bracket-first-term (procedural): When 4y was replaced by 4(−5x − 10), 4 multiplied only one term of the bracket; it multiplies every term.
subject-sign (procedural): When y was made the subject, 5x was moved across without changing its sign; y = −5x − 10.
constant-sign (procedural): The constants were taken with the signs they have on the right of ax + by = c; in a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 the constant is c₁ as it stands on the left.
added (procedural): The two equations were added instead of subtracted; with the y coefficients made equal, subtracting removes y.
constants-not-multiplied (procedural): Only the left-hand sides were multiplied; the numbers on the right must be multiplied too.
multipliers-swapped (procedural): Equation (1) was multiplied by the y coefficient of (1) and (2) by its own: the multipliers were swapped, so y does not cancel.
y-pattern (procedural): The y denominator was written a₁c₂ − a₂c₁, continuing the x pattern; it is c₁a₂ − c₂a₁.
denominator-sign (procedural): The last denominator was written a₁b₂ + a₂b₁; it is a₁b₂ − a₂b₁.

teach.idea: Substitution replaces y by an expression in x; elimination scales the equations so that one variable has equal coefficients and subtracts; cross-multiplication uses x/(b₁c₂ − b₂c₁) = y/(c₁a₂ − c₂a₁) = 1/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁) for a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0.
teach.method: Follow the method step by step: write the expression or the multiplied equations in full, keep every sign (a bracket multiplies every term inside), and simplify to an equation in x alone (or the three ratios).

alternatives.title: The cross-multiplication arrows
text: Write the coefficients b₁, c₁, a₁, b₁ above b₂, c₂, a₂, b₂.
Each denominator is (down-right product) − (up-right product) of a neighbouring pair: b₁c₂ − b₂c₁, then c₁a₂ − c₂a₁, then a₁b₂ − a₂b₁.

families.title: The value of k for no solution or infinitely many
explanations: ratio-upside-down (procedural): The ratio was turned upside down: the second equation is 2 times the first, so its coefficient is 2 times as big, not 2 times smaller.
coefficients-equal (conceptual): The two coefficients were made equal; the ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂ (and c₁/c₂) must be equal to each other, not the coefficients.

teach.idea: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂ have no solution when a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ ≠ c₁/c₂ (parallel lines) and infinitely many when all three ratios are equal (the same line).
teach.method: Write the ratio condition for the case asked, put in the known coefficients, and solve the resulting equation for k. Check that the other ratio does (or does not) match.

alternatives.title: Spot the multiple
text: If the known coefficients of the second equation are m times those of the first, the unknown one must be m times too.
Then compare the constants: equal ratio → the same line; different → parallel lines.

families.title: Pairs of linear equations from ages, digits, speeds and rectangles
explanations: swapped (procedural): The two values were given in the wrong order; check the order the question asks for.
years-one-side (procedural): 5 years were taken from the father's age only; 5 years ago the son was younger too.
not-halved (procedural): The stream's speed was taken as the difference of the two speeds; the downstream speed is u + v and the upstream speed u − v, so their difference is 2v.
half-perimeter (conceptual): The perimeter was taken as length + width; it is 2 × (length + width).

teach.idea: Each condition in the problem becomes one equation in the two unknowns: ages now and years ago, a number 10a + b and its reverse 10b + a, speeds u + v downstream and u − v upstream, or perimeter 2(l + w).
teach.method: Name the two unknowns, write one equation for each sentence of the problem, solve the pair (by elimination or substitution), and check the answer against the words of the problem.

alternatives.title: Make a table first
text: Write a table with a column for 'now' and for 'then' (or downstream and upstream).
Fill it with expressions in x and y; each condition compares two cells.

families.title: Sum, difference, product and quotient of functions
explanations: multiplied (conceptual): f(t) and g(t) were multiplied; (f + g)(t) = f(t) + g(t).
minus-first-term (procedural): Only the x-term of g was subtracted; (f − g)(x) = f(x) − (px + c), so the constant is subtracted too.
added (conceptual): f(t) and g(t) were added; (fg)(t) = f(t) × g(t).
upside-down (procedural): The fraction was turned upside down: (f/g)(t) = f(t) ÷ g(t).
zero-of-f (conceptual): The zero of f was given; f/g is undefined where the DENOMINATOR g is zero.
sign (procedural): px + c = 0 gives x = −c/p; the sign of 5 was not changed.

teach.idea: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x), (f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x), (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x) and (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x). The domain of each is where both are defined; for f/g also leave out the x with g(x) = 0.
teach.method: Work out f(t) and g(t), then combine them. For the domain of f/g, solve g(x) = 0 and remove that number.

alternatives.title: Find the formula first
text: Combine the formulas: (f + g)(x) = (a + p)x + (b + c), (fg)(x) = (ax + b)(px + c), …
Then substitute the number; both ways agree.

families.title: Sums of series whose general term is a polynomial in k
explanations: product-of-sums (conceptual): Σ k²(k + a) was worked out as (Σ k²) × (Σ (k + a)); expand the general term to k³ + ak² first.
constant-once (procedural): Σ 9 was taken as 9; adding a constant n times gives 9n.
square-of-sum (conceptual): The terms were added first and the total squared; each term is squared before adding.
cross-term-dropped (procedural): (ak + b)² was expanded as a²k² + b²; the middle term 2abk is missing.
wrong-power (procedural): Σ 4k² was taken as 4 × Σ k; the second part of the general term is 4k².

teach.idea: A sum is linear: Σ(ak² + bk + c) = aΣk² + bΣk + cn. So a series whose k-th term is a polynomial in k can be summed with the formulas for Σk, Σk² and Σk³.
teach.method: Write the k-th term (look at how the first factors and the second factors grow), expand it into powers of k, and replace each Σkᵐ by its formula; a constant term adds up to n times itself.

alternatives.title: Check with n = 2
text: Add the first two terms by hand.
Your formula with n = 2 must give the same number.

families.title: Parts of a circle and its symmetry
explanations: mixed-up-part (conceptual): Reflection in a line through the centre keeps every distance from the centre the same, so the image is still on the circle.

teach.idea: A chord joins two points of a circle; a diameter is a chord through the centre; a radius joins the centre to the circle. An arc is part of the circle; a sector is the region between two radii and an arc; a segment is the region between a chord and an arc. Every line through the centre is a line of symmetry, so a circle has infinitely many.
teach.method: Ask: is it a point, a straight line, a curve or a region? Where are its ends (on the circle, at the centre)? What bounds the region (two radii, or a chord)? Then name it.

alternatives.title: Think of a pizza and a roti
text: A slice of pizza cut from the centre is a sector; its crust edge is an arc.
One straight cut across a roti that misses the centre cuts off a segment; the cut itself is a chord.

families.title: Chords and their distances from the centre: which is longer, which is nearer
explanations: equal-not-decided (conceptual): Equal chords were thought possibly at different distances; in one circle, equal chords are equidistant from the centre.
farther-longer (conceptual): The shorter chord was taken as nearer the centre; the longer chord is the nearer one.

teach.idea: In one circle, half a chord, its distance from the centre and the radius make a right triangle: (half chord)² + distance² = r². So equal chords are equidistant, equidistant chords are equal, and a longer chord is nearer the centre.
teach.method: Compare the distances (or the lengths) directly with the facts, or work out each half chord (or distance) with Pythagoras and compare.

alternatives.title: Slide a chord towards the centre
text: Imagine a chord moving towards the centre, staying parallel to itself.
Its ends move apart along the circle: it gets longer, and is longest (a diameter) when it passes through the centre.

families.title: Deciding whether four points lie on a circle
explanations: not-decidable (conceptual): It was thought the angles cannot decide it; the converse of the theorem says equal angles on the same side (or supplementary angles on opposite sides) put the four points on one circle.
adjacent-angles (conceptual): Two neighbouring angles adding up to 180° was taken as the test; the test is that OPPOSITE angles add up to 180°.
same-side-supplementary (conceptual): The angles were tested for adding up to 180°; with C and D on the SAME side of AB, the points are concyclic when the angles are equal.
opposite-side-equal (conceptual): The angles were tested for being equal; with C and D on OPPOSITE sides of AB, the points are concyclic when the angles add up to 180°.

teach.idea: Converses: if the opposite angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180°, it is cyclic; if a segment AB subtends equal angles at C and D on the same side of it, A, B, C, D are concyclic (on opposite sides, the angles must add up to 180°).
teach.method: For a quadrilateral add a pair of opposite angles; for two angles on the same segment compare them (same side: equal; opposite sides: supplementary).

alternatives.title: The circle of equal angles
text: All the points from which AB is seen at the same angle, on one side of AB, lie on one arc through A and B.
So if C and D see AB at the same angle from the same side, D is on the arc through A, B and C.

families.title: The number of zeros of a polynomial from its graph
explanations: turning-points (conceptual): The turning points (the tops and bottoms of the curve) were counted; the zeros are where the curve meets the x-axis.
degree-as-count (conceptual): The degree (3) was given; a polynomial of degree 3 has AT MOST 3 zeros, and the graph shows how many there really are.
touch-not-counted (conceptual): A point where the curve only touches the x-axis was not counted; touching the axis is also a zero.

teach.idea: A zero of p(x) is an x with p(x) = 0, that is, where the graph of y = p(x) meets the x-axis (crossing it or just touching it). A quadratic has at most 2 zeros and a cubic at most 3.
teach.method: Follow the curve from left to right and count each point where it meets the x-axis; count a point where it touches the axis without crossing as well.

alternatives.title: Look at the signs
text: Where the curve is above the axis p(x) > 0; below, p(x) < 0.
Each change from above to below (or back) passes through a zero; a touch is a zero without a change of sign.

families.title: How many solutions a system of three linear equations has
explanations: contradiction-as-many (conceptual): Ending with 0 = a non-zero number was read as 'infinitely many'; that equation can never be true, so there is no solution.
always-one (conceptual): Three equations in three unknowns were assumed always to have exactly one solution; check whether one equation follows from the others.
zero-equals-zero (conceptual): Ending with 0 = 0 was read as 'no solution'; 0 = 0 is always true, so the third equation adds nothing and there are infinitely many solutions.

teach.idea: Each equation is a plane. Three planes can meet in one point (one solution), have no point common to all three (no solution), or share a whole line (infinitely many). When one equation is a combination of the others, elimination ends with 0 = 0 (infinitely many) or 0 = a non-zero number (none).
teach.method: Eliminate one variable from two pairs of equations, then eliminate a second. If you reach one value for each variable there is one solution; 0 = k (k ≠ 0) means no solution; 0 = 0 means infinitely many.

alternatives.title: Look for a combination
text: Check whether the left side of one equation is the sum (or a multiple-sum) of the other two left sides.
If it is, compare the right sides in the same way: equal → infinitely many; different → none.

families.title: Slant height and surface area of a cone
explanations: add-legs (conceptual): The radius and the height were added. The slant height is the longest side of a right triangle, so l² = r² + h².
no-root (procedural): r² + h² was found, but its square root was not taken.
subtract-squares (procedural): h² − r² was used. The slant height is the hypotenuse, so the two squares are added.
height-for-slant (conceptual): The height was used instead of the slant height in πrl.
cylinder-formula (conceptual): 2πrl was used, as for a cylinder. A cone's curved surface is πrl.
added-base (procedural): The base circle was added. The curved surface area leaves the base out.
no-base (procedural): Only the curved surface was found. The total surface area also includes the circular base, πr².
two-bases (procedural): Two circles were added, as for a cylinder. A cone has only one base.

teach.idea: Cut a cone's curved surface along a slant line and flatten it: it becomes a sector of a circle of radius l whose arc is the base circumference 2πr, so its area is ½ × 2πr × l = πrl.
teach.method: Find the slant height first: l = √(r² + h²). Curved surface area = πrl; total surface area = πrl + πr² = πr(l + r).

alternatives.title: The hidden right triangle
text: Slice the cone straight down through its tip: the radius, the height and the slant height form a right triangle.
The slant height is the hypotenuse, so l² = r² + h².

families.title: Volume of a cone
explanations: no-third (conceptual): πr²h is the volume of a cylinder. A cone holds one third of that: V = ⅓πr²h.
not-squared (procedural): The radius was not squared. The base is a circle of area πr².
half (recall): ½ was used instead of ⅓, as for a triangle's area.
slant-for-height (conceptual): The slant height was used as the height. The height is measured straight up from the centre of the base: h = √(l² − r²).

teach.idea: A cone fits exactly three times into a cylinder with the same base and height, so its volume is one third of the cylinder's: ⅓πr²h.
teach.method: If the slant height is given, find the height first with h = √(l² − r²). Then V = ⅓ × π × r² × h.

alternatives.title: Pour and count
text: Fill a paper cone with sand and pour it into a cylinder with the same base and height.
It takes three cones to fill the cylinder.

families.title: Surface area and volume of a sphere or hemisphere
explanations: circle-area (conceptual): πr² is the area of a flat circle. A sphere's surface is four times that: 4πr².
cubed (procedural): The radius was cubed. A surface area is an area, so the radius is squared: 4πr².
diameter-as-radius (procedural): The diameter (98 cm) was used as the radius. The radius is half of it, 49 cm.
squared (procedural): The radius was squared. A volume uses r³.
no-third (recall): 4πr³ was used. The volume of a sphere is 4/3 πr³.
curved-only (procedural): Only the curved surface (2πr²) was found. A solid hemisphere also has a flat circular face, πr².
whole-sphere (conceptual): The whole sphere's volume (4/3 πr³) was found. A hemisphere is half of it: 2/3 πr³.

teach.idea: A sphere's surface is exactly four circles of the same radius (4πr²), and its volume is 4/3 πr³. A hemisphere is half a sphere: curved surface 2πr², volume 2/3 πr³.
teach.method: Halve a diameter to get the radius. For a solid hemisphere's total surface add the flat circle: 2πr² + πr² = 3πr².

alternatives.title: Peel an orange
text: Draw round an orange four times on paper, then peel it.
The peel just fills the four circles: the surface of a sphere is 4πr².

families.title: Hollow spheres and hemispherical bowls
explanations: outer-only (conceptual): The volume of a solid hemisphere of the outer radius was found; the space inside the bowl must be taken away.
thickness-cubed (procedural): The thickness was cubed. R³ − r³ is not (R − r)³.
whole-shell (conceptual): 4/3 was used, as for a whole sphere. A bowl is half a shell: 2/3 π(R³ − r³).
no-rim (procedural): The flat ring at the rim, π(R² − r²), was left out.
solid-hemisphere (conceptual): The bowl was treated as a solid hemisphere (3πR²). A bowl has an inside surface too, and only a ring at the top.
outside-only (procedural): The inside surface of the bowl, 2πr², was left out.

teach.idea: A hollow solid is the big solid with the small one taken out, so its volume is the difference of the two volumes.
teach.method: Outer radius R = inner radius + thickness. Metal in a hollow sphere = 4/3 π(R³ − r³); in a hemispherical bowl = 2/3 π(R³ − r³). The bowl's total surface = 2πR² + 2πr² + π(R² − r²).

alternatives.title: Two solids, one taken away
text: Work out the volume of the solid with the outer radius.
Work out the volume of the empty space with the inner radius, and subtract.

families.title: Area of a triangle by Heron's formula
explanations: perimeter-for-s (procedural): The whole perimeter was used for s. In Heron's formula s is the semi-perimeter, half the perimeter.
no-root (procedural): s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c) was found, but its square root was not taken.
half-two-sides (conceptual): ½ × one side × another side works only when the angle between them is a right angle; it is not this triangle's area.

teach.idea: Three sides fix a triangle, so they fix its area. Heron's formula gives it without the height: area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), where s is half the perimeter.
teach.method: Find s = (a + b + c)/2, then s − a, s − b and s − c. Multiply the four numbers and take the square root, simplifying the surd.

alternatives.title: Find the height instead
text: Drop a perpendicular from the top corner to the longest side; it splits the triangle into two right triangles.
Use Pythagoras on both to find where the foot lies and how tall the height is, then area = ½ × base × height.

families.title: Area of a quadrilateral split along a diagonal
explanations: one-triangle (procedural): Only one of the two triangles was found. The diagonal splits the field into two triangles; add both areas.
cyclic-formula (conceptual): Brahmagupta's formula was used on the four sides. It works only when the corners lie on a circle; split along the diagonal instead.

teach.idea: A diagonal cuts any quadrilateral into two triangles, and each triangle's three sides are known, so Heron's formula gives each area.
teach.method: Use Heron's formula on ΔABC (sides AB, BC, AC) and on ΔACD (sides CD, DA, AC), then add the two areas.

alternatives.title: Two triangular plots
text: Imagine a fence along the diagonal: it makes two triangular plots.
Measure each plot separately; the field is the two plots together.

families.title: Area of a cyclic quadrilateral by Brahmagupta's formula
explanations: no-root (procedural): (s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d) was found, but its square root was not taken.
perimeter-for-s (procedural): The whole perimeter was used for s. s is the semi-perimeter, half the perimeter.
heron-extra-s (conceptual): An extra factor s was put in, as in Heron's formula. Brahmagupta's formula has only the four factors s − a, s − b, s − c, s − d.

teach.idea: For a quadrilateral whose corners lie on a circle, the area depends only on its sides: √((s − a)(s − b)(s − c)(s − d)), with s half the perimeter (Brahmagupta, 7th century).
teach.method: Find s = (a + b + c + d)/2, then the four differences s − a, s − b, s − c, s − d. Multiply them and take the square root, simplifying the surd.

alternatives.title: Heron's formula hides inside
text: Let side d shrink to 0: the quadrilateral becomes a triangle with sides a, b, c.
Then s − d = s, and the formula becomes √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), which is Heron's formula.

families.title: Surface area of a square pyramid
explanations: no-half (procedural): Each face was taken as base × slant height. A triangle's area is ½ × base × height.
added-base (procedural): The square base was added. The lateral surface is only the four triangular faces.
height-for-slant (conceptual): The vertical height was used as the height of each face. Each triangular face slopes, so use the slant height l = √(h² + (half the base)²).
no-base (procedural): Only the four triangular faces were found. The total surface also includes the square base.

teach.idea: The lateral surface of a square pyramid is four equal triangles, each with the base side as its base and the slant height as its height.
teach.method: Lateral surface = 4 × ½ × side × slant height = 2 × side × slant height. Add side² for the total. If the vertical height is given, find the slant height first: l = √(h² + (side/2)²).

alternatives.title: Unfold the net
text: Unfold the pyramid: a square with a triangle on each edge.
Add the areas of the five pieces (or only the four triangles for the lateral surface).

families.title: Volume of a pyramid
explanations: no-third (conceptual): Base area × height is the volume of a prism. A pyramid holds one third of that.
half (recall): ½ was used instead of ⅓.
triangle-no-half (prerequisite): The base triangle's area was taken as x × y. A right triangle's area is ½ × x × y.

teach.idea: Three equal pyramids fill a prism with the same base and height, so a pyramid's volume is ⅓ × base area × height.
teach.method: Find the base area (side², length × breadth, or ½ × the two shorter sides for a right triangle), multiply by the height and divide by 3.

alternatives.title: A cube cut into pyramids
text: A cube can be cut into three equal pyramids, each with one face of the cube as its base and the cube's edge as its height.
So each pyramid is ⅓ of base × height.

families.title: Volume of a solid made of two or three basic solids
explanations: sphere-for-hemisphere (conceptual): 4/3 πr³ (a whole sphere) was used for the dome. A hemisphere is half: 2/3 πr³.
cone-no-third (recall): πr²h was used for the cone. A cone is ⅓πr²h.
one-part (procedural): Only the cylinder was found. Add the hemisphere on top.
one-hemisphere (procedural): Only one hemisphere was added. A capsule has one on each end, which together make a whole sphere.

teach.idea: Volume adds up: a solid made of two pieces holds what the two pieces hold together.
teach.method: Name each basic solid in the object, find each volume (cylinder πr²H, cone ⅓πr²h, hemisphere 2/3 πr³), and add them.

alternatives.title: Take the object apart
text: Sketch the object and draw lines where one solid meets the next.
Write each piece's formula under it, then add.

families.title: Surface area of a combined solid (only the outside faces)
explanations: hidden-faces (conceptual): The surface areas of the separate solids were added, including the circles where they are joined. Those faces are inside the solid and are not part of its outside.
height-for-slant (conceptual): The cone's height was used in πrl. The cone's surface needs the slant height.
no-base (procedural): The circular base the solid stands on was left out. It is part of the outside surface.
cylinder-only (procedural): Only the cylinder (with its two flat ends) was found. The ends are covered by the hemispheres, whose curved surfaces must be used instead.

teach.idea: When two solids are joined, the faces where they touch disappear inside; only the faces you could still touch from outside count.
teach.method: List the outside pieces (cone πrl, cylinder side 2πrH, hemisphere 2πr², a flat base πr²), find each and add. Do not include the circle where two pieces meet.

alternatives.title: The paint test
text: Imagine dipping the solid in paint: which faces get wet?
A face pressed against another piece stays dry, so leave it out.

families.title: Melting and recasting solids
explanations: radius-ratio (conceptual): The radii were divided. Volume grows with the cube of the radius, so divide the volumes.
squared (conceptual): The ratio of the radii was squared, as for surface areas. Volumes use cubes.
hemisphere-as-sphere (conceptual): The small hemispheres were treated as whole spheres. Each holds only half as much: 2/3 πr³, so twice as many are made.
no-third (conceptual): The cones were treated as cylinders. A cone holds ⅓πr²h, so three times as many are made.
not-squared (procedural): The radii were not squared. Volumes use πr².

teach.idea: Melting and recasting changes the shape but not the amount of metal, so the volume before equals the total volume after.
teach.method: Write volume before = volume after (× the number of pieces), cancel π, and solve for the unknown.

alternatives.title: Squash the clay
text: Roll a ball of clay into a long snake: it looks bigger, but there is the same amount of clay.
So the snake's volume equals the ball's volume.

families.title: Volume and surface area of a frustum of a cone
explanations: no-Rr (recall): The middle term Rr was left out. The volume is ⅓πh(R² + r² + Rr).
no-third (recall): The ⅓ was left out. A frustum is part of a cone, so its volume formula has ⅓.
average-cylinder (conceptual): The frustum was treated as a cylinder with the average radius. Its sides slope, so that does not give its volume.
height-for-slant (conceptual): The height was used instead of the slant height in π l (R + r).
difference (recall): π l (R − r) was used. The curved surface uses the sum of the radii: π l (R + r).
one-end (procedural): Only one circular end was added. A closed frustum has two ends, πR² and πr².
no-ends (procedural): Only the curved surface was found. The total surface also includes both circular ends.

teach.idea: A frustum is a big cone with a small cone cut off its top, so its volume and curved surface are the big cone's minus the small cone's.
teach.method: Volume = ⅓πh(R² + r² + Rr). Slant height l = √(h² + (R − r)²); curved surface = π l (R + r); total = π l (R + r) + πR² + πr².

alternatives.title: Big cone minus small cone
text: Extend the sloping side up to a point: you get a big cone, and the part cut off is a small cone of the same shape.
Similar triangles give the big cone's height; subtract the two cone volumes.

families.title: Area of a segment of a circle
explanations: sector-only (conceptual): The area of the sector was given. The segment is the sector with the triangle OAB taken away.
added-triangle (procedural): The triangle was added to the sector. The segment is the sector minus the triangle.
major-sector (conceptual): The major sector was found. The major segment is the whole circle minus the minor segment, so the triangle must be counted.
gave-minor (procedural): The minor segment was given. The question asks for the major (larger) segment: subtract the minor one from the whole circle.
right-triangle (prerequisite): The triangle OAB was taken as ½ × r × r, which is right only for a 90° angle. For 120° its area is (√3/4)r².

teach.idea: A chord cuts a circle into two segments. The minor segment is the sector OAB with the triangle OAB taken away; the major segment is the rest of the circle.
teach.method: Sector = θ/360 × πr². Triangle OAB = ½r² for 90°, or (√3/4)r² for 60° and 120°. Minor segment = sector − triangle; major = πr² − minor.

alternatives.title: Cut the slice
text: Cut a slice (sector) out of a paper circle, then cut straight along the chord.
The triangle falls away; the curved strip left is the segment.

families.title: Area swept and distance travelled by a clock hand
explanations: minutes-as-degrees (conceptual): 55 minutes was used as 55°. The minute hand turns 6° each minute (360° in 60 minutes).
arc-formula (conceptual): The arc-length formula was used. The area swept is a sector, a part of πr².
whole-circle (procedural): The whole circle was given. The hand only turns part of the way round.
area-formula (conceptual): The area formula was used. The distance the tip travels is an arc length, a part of 2πr.
six-per-hour (conceptual): The hour hand was turned 6° per hour, like the minute hand per minute. The hour hand turns 30° each hour (360° in 12 hours).

teach.idea: A clock hand sweeps out a sector. The minute hand turns 360° in 60 minutes (6° a minute); the hour hand turns 360° in 12 hours (30° an hour).
teach.method: Find the angle turned, then take that fraction of 360° of the whole circle: area θ/360 × πr², or distance θ/360 × 2πr.

alternatives.title: Think of the fraction of a turn
text: 15 minutes is a quarter of an hour, so the minute hand sweeps a quarter of the circle.
In general, the minute hand turns minutes/60 of a full turn and the hour hand hours/12.

families.title: Finding the angle or radius of a sector
explanations: pi-r (recall): πr was used for the whole circumference. The circumference is 2πr.
over-180 (recall): 180° was used for a full turn. A full turn is 360°.
arc-formula (conceptual): The arc-length formula was used. The area of a sector is θ/360 × πr².
not-squared (procedural): The radius was not squared: the whole circle's area is πr².
no-root (procedural): r² was found, but its square root was not taken.

teach.idea: A sector is θ/360 of its circle, so the arc is θ/360 of the circumference and the area is θ/360 of the circle's area. Knowing the part and the whole gives θ.
teach.method: Angle = (arc ÷ 2πr) × 360°, or (area ÷ πr²) × 360°. For the radius, r² = area × 360 ÷ (θπ), then take the square root.

alternatives.title: Fraction of the circle first
text: Work out the whole circle (2πr or πr²).
Divide the given part by it: that fraction of 360° is the angle.

families.title: Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction
explanations: over-ten (conceptual): The decimal was cut off after one digit (9.8). It goes on for ever, so it equals 8/9, not 8/10, after the whole part.
whole-part-lost (procedural): The whole-number part 2 was dropped.
over-hundred (conceptual): The decimal was cut off after two digits; it goes on for ever.
one-nine (procedural): Only one 9 was used. A block of two repeating digits needs 99 (100x − x).
all-repeating (conceptual): Both digits were treated as repeating (0.9898…). Only the 8 repeats.
no-subtract (procedural): 98 was put over 90 without taking away the part that does not repeat (98 − 9).

teach.idea: A recurring decimal is rational: multiplying by a power of 10 shifts the repeating part, and subtracting makes the endless tail cancel.
teach.method: Let x be the number. Multiply by 10 for one repeating digit, by 100 for two, and subtract so the repeating tails cancel; then divide and simplify.

alternatives.title: The nines rule
text: 0.ddd… = d/9 and 0.ababab… = ab/99.
If one digit comes before the repeat, as in 0.2777…, use (27 − 2)/90.

families.title: Will the decimal terminate or recur?
explanations: odd-recurs (conceptual): An odd denominator was taken to mean a recurring decimal. 25 is made only of 5s, so the decimal stops.
forever-irrational (conceptual): A decimal that goes on for ever was taken to never repeat. Every fraction of whole numbers either stops or repeats; only irrational numbers never repeat.
not-simplified (procedural): The factor 3 in 1200 was looked at before simplifying. 39/1200 = 13/400, and that denominator has only 2s and 5s.

teach.idea: A fraction in its simplest form terminates exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5, because only then can it be written over a power of 10.
teach.method: Simplify the fraction first. Factorise the denominator: only 2s and 5s means it terminates; any other prime means it recurs.

alternatives.title: Make the denominator a power of 10
text: With a factor like 3 or 7 in the denominator, no multiplying can make a power of 10.

families.title: How many decimal places before a fraction terminates
explanations: smaller-power (procedural): The smaller power was used. The number of places is the larger of the two powers.
add-powers (conceptual): The two powers were added. To make 10s, each 2 pairs with a 5, so the number of places is the larger power.
not-simplified (procedural): The fraction was not simplified first: 58/20000 = 29/10000.

teach.idea: p/(2^m 5^n) can be rewritten over 10^k, where k is the larger of m and n, so it has exactly k decimal places (after simplifying).
teach.method: Simplify the fraction, write the denominator as 2^m × 5^n, and take the larger power.

alternatives.title: Make a power of 10
text: 3/40 = 3/(2³ × 5): multiply top and bottom by 5² to get 75/1000.
1000 = 10³, so there are 3 decimal places: 0.075.

families.title: Picking out the irrational number
explanations: 22-7-is-pi (conceptual): 22/7 was taken to be π. It is only close to π; as a fraction of whole numbers it is rational.
product-of-roots (procedural): Each factor is irrational, but √2 × √8 = √16 = 4, which is rational.
square-of-root (procedural): (√7)² = 7, a whole number.
root-means-irrational (conceptual): A square-root sign was taken to mean irrational. √64 = 8, a whole number.
forever-decimal (conceptual): A decimal that goes on for ever was taken as irrational. A repeating decimal is rational.

teach.idea: A number is rational if it can be written as p/q with whole numbers p and q (q ≠ 0); its decimal stops or repeats. √n is irrational unless n is a perfect square.
teach.method: Simplify each number first: √49 = 7, √2 × √8 = √16 = 4, (√5)² = 5, a repeating decimal is a fraction. Whatever is still a non-square root is irrational.

alternatives.title: The decimal test
text: Rational numbers have decimals that stop or repeat a block for ever.
√2 = 1.41421356… never repeats; 22/7 = 3.142857142857… repeats, so it is rational even though it is close to π.

families.title: Unknown side of similar triangles
explanations: add-difference (conceptual): The same amount (2.8 cm) was added to every side. Similar triangles are scaled by multiplying: every side is × 1.4.
inverted-scale (procedural): The scale factor was turned upside down (7 ÷ 9.8). ΔPQR's sides are ΔABC's sides × PQ/AB.
wrong-match (procedural): The wrong side was matched. RP matches CA, from the order of the letters in ΔABC ~ ΔPQR.
not-scaled (procedural): The perimeter of ΔABC was given. ΔPQR's perimeter is scaled by the same factor as its sides.

teach.idea: Similar triangles have the same shape: matching angles are equal and every side is multiplied by the same scale factor.
teach.method: Match the sides from the order of the letters (AB ↔ PQ, BC ↔ QR, CA ↔ RP). Scale factor = PQ ÷ AB; multiply the matching side by it.

alternatives.title: Write a proportion
text: Write PQ/AB = QR/BC, put in the numbers you know and cross-multiply.
Check: the larger triangle should have the larger sides.

families.title: The basic proportionality theorem
explanations: inverted (procedural): The ratio was turned round: EC was matched with AD. AD/DB = AE/EC, so EC goes with DB.
whole-side (conceptual): AD was compared with the whole side AB instead of with DB. In AD/DB = AE/EC both ratios compare the two parts of a side.
add-difference (conceptual): The same difference was added on both sides. The theorem is about equal ratios, not equal differences.
parts-ratio (conceptual): AE/AC was taken as AD/DB. Compare the part with the whole side: AE/AC = AD/AB.
half (conceptual): DE was taken as half of BC, as if D were the midpoint. That is only true when AD = DB.
gave-ec (procedural): EC was found instead of AE.

teach.idea: A line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts off a smaller triangle of the same shape, so it divides the other two sides in the same ratio.
teach.method: Use AD/DB = AE/EC for the parts of the sides, or AD/AB = AE/AC = DE/BC when a whole side is involved. Cross-multiply to find the unknown.

alternatives.title: See the small triangle
text: Shade ΔADE: it is ΔABC shrunk by the factor AD/AB.
Every length in ΔADE is that fraction of the matching length in ΔABC.

families.title: Areas of similar triangles
explanations: linear (conceptual): The area was scaled by 7/6, like a side. Areas of similar triangles are in the ratio of the squares of the sides.
inverted (procedural): The ratio was turned upside down, which makes the larger triangle smaller.
area-ratio-for-sides (conceptual): The side was scaled by the area ratio 81/64. Sides scale by the square root of the area ratio, 9/8.
root-of-area (procedural): The square root of the larger area was given. Use the ratio of the areas, not one area alone.

teach.idea: If every side is multiplied by k, every height is multiplied by k too, so the area (½ × base × height) is multiplied by k².
teach.method: Area ratio = (side ratio)². To go from areas to sides, take the square root of the area ratio.

alternatives.title: Count small triangles
text: Double every side of a triangle and draw it: it is made of 4 copies of the original.
Triple every side: 9 copies. The area grows with the square of the scale factor.

families.title: Length of a tangent from an external point
explanations: added-squares (conceptual): The squares were added. OP is the hypotenuse, so OT² = OP² − PT².
subtract-lengths (procedural): The lengths were subtracted directly. Use the squares.
no-root (procedural): OP² − OT² was found, but its square root was not taken.
subtracted-squares (conceptual): The squares were subtracted. OP is the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle at T), so OP² = OT² + PT².
added-lengths (procedural): The lengths were added. Use the squares: OP = √(OT² + PT²).

teach.idea: A tangent meets the radius at the point of contact at a right angle, so the centre O, the point P and the point of contact T make a right triangle with OP as the hypotenuse.
teach.method: Use Pythagoras in ΔOTP: OP² = OT² + PT². Then PT = √(OP² − r²), and simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: Always draw the radius
text: Join the centre to the point of contact and mark the right angle.
Now it is a Pythagoras question with OP as the longest side.

families.title: Angles made by tangents
explanations: double (conceptual): ∠AOB was taken as twice ∠APB, as for an angle at the centre and an angle on the circle. P is outside the circle; use the quadrilateral OAPB with two right angles.
complement (conceptual): 90° − x was used.
equal (conceptual): ∠OAB was taken to equal ∠APB; it is half of it.
half (procedural): ∠APB was halved. ∠PAB is a base angle of the isosceles triangle PAB: (180° − x)/2.
supplement (procedural): 180° − x was given; that is the sum of the two base angles, so halve it.
gave-pab (procedural): ∠PAB was given. ∠OAB is what is left of the right angle OAP: 90° − ∠PAB.
right-angle (conceptual): ∠OAP = 90° was given; ∠OAB is only part of it.

teach.idea: Tangents from an outside point are equal, and each is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact; so OAPB has two right angles and ΔPAB is isosceles.
teach.method: ∠AOB = 180° − ∠APB. ∠PAB = ∠PBA = (180° − ∠APB)/2. ∠OAB = 90° − ∠PAB. The tangent–chord angle equals the angle in the alternate segment.

alternatives.title: OAPB is a kite
text: OA = OB (radii) and PA = PB (tangents), so OAPB is a kite with right angles at A and B.
Its angles add to 360°, so the angles at O and P add to 180°.

families.title: Tangent lengths in shapes drawn round a circle
explanations: opposite-equal (conceptual): DA was taken to equal BC, as in a parallelogram. For a quadrilateral round a circle it is the SUMS of opposite sides that are equal: AB + CD = BC + DA.
adjacent-sum (procedural): Adjacent sides were paired. The rule pairs opposite sides: AB with CD, and BC with DA.
half-side (conceptual): AF was taken as half of AB, as if F were the midpoint. The touching point divides AB into the tangent lengths from A and from B, which are usually different.
wrong-corner (procedural): s − CA was found; that is the tangent length from B. From A it is s − BC.
semi-perimeter (procedural): The semi-perimeter s was given; subtract the side opposite A.

teach.idea: The two tangents from any corner to the circle are equal, so every side is made of two tangent lengths, one from each end.
teach.method: Quadrilateral: AB + CD = BC + DA. Triangle: the tangent length from A is s − BC, where s is half the perimeter.

alternatives.title: Label the tangent lengths
text: Call the tangent lengths from the corners w, x, y, z; then AB = w + x, BC = x + y, CD = y + z, DA = z + w.
Add opposite sides: both sums are w + x + y + z.

families.title: Ceva's and Menelaus' theorems: the missing ratio
explanations: not-inverted (conceptual): The two ratios were multiplied and the result used as AF : FB. The product of all three ratios is 1, so AF/FB is the reciprocal of that product.
added-ratios (procedural): The parts of the ratios were added. The theorem multiplies the ratios.
not-simplified (procedural): The ratio was not given in its simplest form.

teach.idea: Going round the triangle, the three ratios (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB) multiply to 1, both when three lines from the corners meet at a point (Ceva) and when one straight line cuts the three sides, one of them extended (Menelaus).
teach.method: Put the two known ratios into the product, solve for AF/FB (it is the reciprocal of their product), and simplify.

alternatives.title: Balance the corners (mass points)
text: Hang weights at B and C so that D balances them: weight at B × BD = weight at C × DC.
Do the same at E for C and A; the weights at A and B then give AF : FB = weight at B : weight at A.

families.title: Using the midpoint theorem
explanations: equal (conceptual): BC was taken to equal DE.
double (procedural): BC was doubled. DE is half of BC.
halved (procedural): DE was halved. BC is twice DE.
full-perimeter (procedural): The perimeter of ΔABC was given. Each side of ΔDEF is half of a side of ΔABC.
quarter (procedural): The perimeter was divided by 4; it is halved.

teach.idea: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long (it cuts off a half-size copy of the triangle).
teach.method: DE = ½ BC, so BC = 2 DE. Joining all three midpoints gives a triangle with half the perimeter.

alternatives.title: Fold the triangle
text: Fold the top corner of a paper triangle down to the middle of the base: the crease joins the midpoints of the two sides.
The crease is parallel to the base and half its length.

families.title: Finding x and y so a quadrilateral is a parallelogram
explanations: sign-slip (procedural): In each equation the number beside the first expression was moved to the other side without changing its sign (added instead of subtracted).
swapped (procedural): x and y were swapped: the first pair of lengths gives x, the second pair gives y.

teach.idea: A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if its diagonals bisect each other, or if both pairs of opposite sides are equal (the converses of the parallelogram's properties).
teach.method: Write one equation for each pair that must be equal, solve each for its letter, and check the lengths are positive.

alternatives.title: Check by putting the numbers back
text: Put your x and y back into all four expressions.
Each pair must give the same length, and no length may be zero or negative.

families.title: Choosing the reason for a step in an angle proof
explanations: mix-0 (conceptual): The linear-pair reason was chosen, but the two angles are opposite each other at a crossing, and they are equal.
mix-1 (conceptual): Vertically opposite angles was chosen, but these two angles sit side by side on a straight line and add up to 180°.
mix-2 (conceptual): Corresponding angles was chosen, but these angles are on opposite sides of the crossing line, between the parallels (a Z shape): they are alternate angles.
mix-3 (conceptual): Alternate angles was chosen, but these angles are in matching positions at the two crossings (an F shape): they are corresponding angles.
mix-4 (conceptual): The linear-pair reason was chosen, but the two angles are at different points, between the parallel lines on the same side (a C shape): they are co-interior angles.
mix-5 (conceptual): The exterior-angle reason was chosen, but the step uses the three angles inside the triangle.
mix-6 (conceptual): The angle-sum reason was chosen, but the step finds an exterior angle directly as the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
