teach.idea: Each step of a proof must follow from something already accepted: a definition, an axiom or a theorem. The reason names it.
teach.method: Look at where the two angles are: at one crossing (vertically opposite or linear pair), at two crossings of parallel lines (Z = alternate, F = corresponding, C = co-interior), or in a triangle (angle sum, exterior angle).

alternatives.title: Z, F and C shapes
text: Trace the lines around the two angles with your finger.
A Z shape means alternate (equal), an F shape corresponding (equal), a C shape co-interior (adding to 180°).

families.title: Which congruence rule applies?
explanations: rule-0 (conceptual): It was thought that an angle is always needed. Three pairs of equal sides are enough on their own (SSS).
rule-1 (conceptual): ASA was chosen, but two sides and the angle between them are given: that is SAS.
rule-2 (conceptual): AAS was chosen, but the equal side lies between the two equal angles: that is ASA.
rule-3 (conceptual): ASA was chosen, but the equal side is not between the two equal angles: that is AAS.
rule-4 (conceptual): It was thought that two sides and an angle not between them are never enough. With a right angle, the hypotenuse and one side do fix the triangle (RHS).
rule-5 (conceptual): SAS was chosen, but the equal angle is not between the two equal sides. Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) can fit two different triangles, so they are not enough.

teach.idea: Some sets of three facts fix a triangle completely, so two triangles sharing them are congruent: SSS, SAS (the angle between the sides), ASA or AAS, and RHS for right triangles. Two sides with an angle that is not between them (SSA) do not.
teach.method: Mark the equal parts. Count sides and angles, then check where the angle is: between the two sides (SAS) or not; is the side between the two angles (ASA) or not (AAS); is there a right angle with the hypotenuse (RHS)?

alternatives.title: Try to build it
text: With straws and a protractor, try to build a triangle from the facts.
If only one triangle can be built, the facts fix it; with SSA you can often swing the last side to two different places.

families.title: The angle bisector theorem
explanations: midpoint (conceptual): D was taken as the midpoint of BC. The bisector of the angle splits BC in the ratio AB : AC, not equally.
swapped (procedural): The ratio was turned round: AC goes with DC, so AC = AB × DC/BD.
add-difference (conceptual): The same difference was added. The theorem is about equal ratios.

teach.idea: The bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite side in the ratio of the two sides that make the angle: BD/DC = AB/AC.
teach.method: Write BD : DC = AB : AC. To find BD, share BC in that ratio: BD = BC × AB/(AB + AC). To find a side, cross-multiply.

alternatives.title: Share in a ratio
text: If AB : AC = 3 : 5, then BC is cut into 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts.
BD is 3 of those parts and DC is 5 of them.

families.title: How many tangents from a point
explanations: inside-two (conceptual): It was thought that two tangents can be drawn from any point, as from a point outside the circle. P is inside, so every line through it cuts the circle twice and none just touches it.
inside-one (conceptual): It was thought that one line through a point inside the circle can just touch it. Every line through an inside point crosses the circle at two points.
on-two (conceptual): It was thought that two tangents pass through P, as for a point outside the circle. P is on the circle, so there is just one tangent there, at right angles to the radius.
diameter-as-radius (procedural): The distance 22 cm was compared with the diameter, 24 cm. It must be compared with the radius, half the diameter.
outside-one (conceptual): It was thought that only one tangent can be drawn from P, as at a point on the circle. From a point outside the circle there are two, one touching each side.

teach.idea: A tangent touches a circle at exactly one point. Compare the point's distance from the centre with the radius: inside, on, or outside.
teach.method: Distance less than the radius: 0 tangents. Equal to the radius: 1 tangent. Greater: 2 tangents.

alternatives.title: Turn a ruler
text: Put a pin at P and turn a ruler around it over a drawn circle.
Count how many times the ruler's edge just touches the circle without cutting it.

families.title: Natural, whole, integer, rational or irrational?
explanations: trap-0 (conceptual): 0 was taken as a natural number. The natural numbers start at 1; 0 is a whole number.
trap-1 (conceptual): A negative integer was taken as a whole number. Whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, …; they have no negatives.
trap-2 (conceptual): A negative fraction was taken as an integer. Integers are …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …; a fraction such as −5/2 lies between two of them.
trap-3 (conceptual): A fraction that simplifies to an integer was taken as not an integer. Work it out first. 40/8 = 5.
trap-4 (conceptual): A fraction or a repeating decimal was taken as irrational. 22/7 is only close to π, and decimals that repeat (0.333…) are rational.

teach.idea: Natural numbers 1, 2, 3, …; whole numbers add 0; integers add the negatives; rational numbers are all p/q (q ≠ 0), whose decimals end or repeat; irrational numbers (√2, π) have decimals that never end or repeat. Together they are the real numbers.
teach.method: Simplify each number first (√16 = 4, −12/4 = −3, 0.333… = 1/3), then place it in the smallest set it belongs to.

alternatives.title: Sets inside sets
text: Draw circles inside each other: natural inside whole inside integer inside rational.
Irrational numbers sit outside the rational circle, but inside the real numbers.

families.title: Absolute values and distances of rational numbers on the number line
explanations: sign-kept (conceptual): The minus sign was kept. An absolute value is a distance from 0, so it is never negative.
sign-dropped-inside (procedural): The minus sign inside was read as a plus. Work out the inside first, then take its distance from 0.
added (procedural): The two numbers were added; the distance between them is the difference (larger minus smaller).
sizes-subtracted (conceptual): The sizes were subtracted, but the two numbers are on opposite sides of 0: the distance is the sum of their distances from 0.
wrong-way (procedural): P was moved the wrong way. Left means subtracting 9/2.

teach.idea: Every rational number has a place on the number line. |x| is the distance of x from 0, and the distance between x and y is |x − y|.
teach.method: Work out the expression inside the bars, then drop the sign. For a distance, subtract the smaller number from the larger. To place p/q, cut each unit into q parts and count.

alternatives.title: Count small steps
text: Write both numbers with the same denominator, say 12ths.
Count the twelfths from one to the other: that count over 12 is the distance.

families.title: Cyclic patterns in recurring decimals (sevenths and thirteenths)
explanations: remainder-place (procedural): 59 ÷ 6 leaves remainder 5, but digit 6 of the block was taken (one place too far). The remainder itself is the place in the block: digit 5.
unit-fraction-digits (conceptual): The digits of 1/13 were used. 12/13 uses the same cycle but starts at a different digit: 12/13 = 0.923076….

teach.idea: Dividing by 7 can leave only the remainders 1 to 6, so the digits must repeat within 6 places. Every k/7 runs through the same remainders, so its digits are the cycle 142857 started at a different point.
teach.method: Find where the cycle of k/d starts (k/7 = k × 0.142857…, or from the first remainders), then use the remainder of n on division by 6 to find the place in the block.

alternatives.title: Multiply the cycle
text: 3/7 = 3 × 0.142857… = 0.428571…: the same digits, rotated.
The block for 3/7 starts with 4, the next digit after 1 in the cycle 1, 4, 2, 8, 5, 7.

families.title: A fraction as a terminating or recurring decimal
explanations: digits-joined (conceptual): The numerator and denominator were written after the point (0.2425). 24/25 means 24 ÷ 25: divide.
upside-down (procedural): 25 ÷ 24 was worked out. 24/25 means 24 divided by 25.
stopped (procedural): The division was stopped too early. Keep dividing until the remainder is 0.

teach.idea: n/d means n ÷ d. If d has no prime factors other than 2 and 5, the division ends (a terminating decimal); otherwise a remainder comes back and the digits repeat for ever (a recurring decimal).
teach.method: Do the long division, writing each remainder. Stop when the remainder is 0, or when a remainder you have seen before comes back: the digits from that point repeat.

alternatives.title: Make the denominator a power of 10
text: 7/16: 16 = 2⁴, so multiply top and bottom by 5⁴ = 625: 4375/10000 = 0.4375.
This works only when the denominator has just 2s and 5s.

families.title: Operations on real numbers: adding and multiplying surds
explanations: square-not-taken-out (procedural): √125 was taken as √5, so the coefficients 9 and 6 were just added. First write √125 = 5√5: it is 5 times √5.
sign-of-square (procedural): (√7)² was added instead of subtracted: (a + √m)(a − √m) = a² − m.
square-of-sum (conceptual): The square of a sum was taken as the sum of the squares; the middle term 2√(mk) is missing.
root-times-root (procedural): √2 × √2 was taken as √2; it is 2.

teach.idea: Real numbers can be added and multiplied like algebra: √a × √a = a and √a × √b = √(ab). The sum or product of two irrational numbers can be rational (as in (2 + √3)(2 − √3) = 1) or irrational, so the irrationals are not closed.
teach.method: Simplify each surd (√12 = 2√3), collect like surds, and expand brackets term by term, replacing (√m)² by m.

alternatives.title: Like terms
text: Treat √3 like a letter: 2√3 + 5√3 = 7√3, just as 2x + 5x = 7x.
√2 and √3 are unlike, so √2 + √3 cannot be combined.

families.title: Surface area and volume of a cube combined with a hemisphere or cylinder
explanations: covered-not-removed (procedural): The inside of the hollow was added, but the circle cut away from the top face was not taken off.
flat-face-counted (conceptual): The flat face of the hemisphere was counted as outside, but it is glued to the cube.
sphere-for-hemisphere (conceptual): 4/3 πr³ (a whole sphere) was used; a hemisphere is half of it, 2/3 πr³.
curved-only-no-change (procedural): The cylinder's top circle was left out; it is part of the outside surface.
cone-formula (recall): ⅓πr²h was used; that is a cone. A cylinder's volume is πr²h.
hollow-subtracted (conceptual): The circle was taken away, but the curved inside of the hollow, 2πr², is now part of the outside surface.
hollow-added (conceptual): The hollow was added. A scooped-out part is taken away from the cube.

teach.idea: For surface area, only the faces that stay outside count: where two solids meet, the hidden circle is lost from one solid and does not appear on the other. Volume simply adds (or, for a hollow, subtracts).
teach.method: Surface: start with 6a², take away each circle that is covered or cut away, then add the curved surfaces (and any flat top) that are now outside. Volume: a³ plus or minus the volume of the other solid.

alternatives.title: Think of painting it
text: Imagine painting the finished object: the glued faces never get paint.
A scooped hollow gets painted inside, so its curved surface counts.

families.title: Modelling real objects (tents, bowls, tanks, cones) as combinations of solids
explanations: floor-added (procedural): The floor πr² was added. The tent has no canvas floor, so only the walls and roof count.
diameter-as-radius (procedural): The diameter 28 m was used as the radius; the radius is half of it.
whole-ball (conceptual): A whole ball was used for the scoop; it is half a ball, 2/3 πr³.
surface-for-volume (conceptual): The curved surface area 2πr² was found. How much the bowl holds is its volume.
dome-left-out (procedural): Only the upright part was counted; the dome holds water too.
cone-no-third (recall): πr²h was used for the cone; a cone holds a third of that, ⅓πr²h.

teach.idea: Real objects are modelled by the basic solids they look like: upright walls round a circle are a cylinder, a roof rising to a point is a cone, a rounded bowl or dome is a hemisphere. Canvas or paint needs only the surfaces that are really there; capacity needs the volume inside.
teach.method: Sketch the object, name each part as a solid, decide whether the question needs surface (which surfaces?) or volume, then add the parts.

alternatives.title: Which surfaces?
text: A tent has no canvas floor and no canvas between its walls and roof: only the curved surfaces count.
A bowl holds what fits inside it: its volume, not the area of its surface.

families.title: Area and perimeter of composite shapes with semicircles, quadrants, triangles and trapeziums
explanations: full-circle (conceptual): A whole circle was added; the flower bed is a semicircle.
diameter-as-radius (procedural): The diameter 28 m was used as the radius; r = 14 m.
side-counted (procedural): The straight side under the semicircle was counted too; it is inside the shape, not on its edge.
half-not-quarter (conceptual): Half a circle was taken away; a quadrant is a quarter, πr²/4.
added (procedural): The quadrant was added. It is cut away, so subtract it.
no-half (recall): The triangle was taken as base × height; its area is half of that.
trapezium-no-half (recall): The trapezium was taken as (a + b) × h; its area is ½(a + b)h.

teach.idea: A composite shape is cut into pieces whose areas are known (rectangle, triangle, trapezium, semicircle πr²/2, quadrant πr²/4); the area is the sum of the pieces, or a whole minus the piece cut away. A perimeter goes round the outside only.
teach.method: Split the shape along straight lines, find each piece's area and add (or subtract a cut-out). For a perimeter, add only the outer edges: a semicircle's curved edge is πd/2 and it replaces the side it stands on.

alternatives.title: Sketch and label
text: Draw the shape and shade each piece in a different colour.
Write the formula and the numbers inside each piece before adding.

families.title: Using the converse of the midpoint theorem
explanations: half-of-ab (procedural): Half of AB was given; DE is half of BC.
whole-side (conceptual): AE was taken as the whole of AC. The parallel line through the midpoint D cuts AC exactly in half.
de-equals-bc (conceptual): DE was taken as equal to BC. DE joins the midpoints of AB and AC, so it is half of BC.
halved-instead (procedural): AE was halved. E is the midpoint of AC, so AC is twice AE.
ab-added (procedural): AB was added to AE; AC = 2 × AE because E is the midpoint of AC.

teach.idea: Converse of the midpoint theorem: the line through the midpoint of one side of a triangle, parallel to another side, meets the third side at its midpoint. So E is the midpoint of AC, and then DE = ½ BC by the midpoint theorem.
teach.method: Check the two conditions (D is a midpoint, the line is parallel to a side). Then halve the third side for AE or EC, and halve the parallel side for DE.

alternatives.title: Why it works
text: ΔADE and ΔABC have the same angles (corresponding angles on parallel lines), and AD is half of AB.
So every side of ΔADE is half of the matching side of ΔABC.

families.title: Surface area of pyramids with rectangular, triangular, hexagonal and other bases
explanations: base-left-out (procedural): Only the sloping faces were added; the total surface area includes the base.
one-slant-height (conceptual): The same slant height was used for all four faces. A rectangular base has two different slant heights, one for each pair of faces.
no-half (recall): Each face is a triangle, so its area is ½ × base × slant height; the ½ was left out.
square-base (conceptual): The base was taken as a square (a²). The base here is a regular polygon; its area involves √3.

teach.idea: The surface of a pyramid is its base plus one triangle for each side of the base. Each triangle has area ½ × base edge × slant height, so for a regular base the lateral area is ½ × perimeter × slant height.
teach.method: Lateral area = ½ × perimeter × slant height (for a rectangle, two pairs of faces with different slant heights). Total surface area = lateral area + area of the base (for an equilateral triangle (√3/4)a², a regular hexagon (3√3/2)a²).

alternatives.title: Unfold the net
text: Cut along the slanting edges and lay the faces flat: the base with a triangle on each side.
Add the area of the base and of every triangle.

families.title: Which similarity criterion applies: AA, SSS, SAS, or not similar?
explanations: crit-0 (conceptual): It was thought that two angles are not enough. If two angles are equal, the third angles are equal too, so the triangles are similar (AA).
crit-1 (conceptual): Because the triangles have different sizes, they were called not similar. Similar triangles can be different sizes: here every side is multiplied by the same number (SSS).
crit-2 (conceptual): SSS was chosen, but only two pairs of sides are given, with the angle between them equal: that is SAS.
crit-3 (conceptual): The triangles were called similar because the sides grow, but the three ratios are not all equal, so they are not similar.
crit-4 (conceptual): SAS was chosen, but the equal angle is not between the two proportional sides; that is not enough to show similarity.

teach.idea: Two triangles are similar when their angles are equal and their sides are in the same ratio. It is enough to show AA (two pairs of equal angles), SSS (all three side ratios equal) or SAS (two side ratios equal and the angles between those sides equal).
teach.method: Divide each side of ΔPQR by the matching side of ΔABC. Three equal ratios: SSS. Two equal ratios with the angle between them equal: SAS. Two equal angles: AA. Otherwise the facts do not show similarity.

alternatives.title: A ratio table
text: Write the matching sides in two rows: AB, BC, CA above PQ, QR, RP.
Divide the bottom by the top in each column and see whether the answers agree.

families.title: Unknown angles from AA similarity
explanations: wrong-vertex (procedural): ∠Q was copied for ∠C. ∠Q matches ∠B, not ∠C.
one-angle (procedural): Only ∠P was taken from 180°; take away both ∠P and ∠R.
third-angle (procedural): ∠R was given. ∠Q matches ∠B; find it from the angle sum of ΔPQR.

teach.idea: If two angles of one triangle equal two angles of another, the third angles are equal too (each triangle's angles add to 180°): the triangles are similar (AA), and matching vertices have equal angles.
teach.method: Match the vertices (A with P, B with Q, C with R). The angle you want equals its partner in the other triangle; find a missing one as 180° minus the other two.

alternatives.title: An angle table
text: Write the vertices in two rows: A B C above P Q R.
Fill in every angle you know; partners in the same column are equal, and each row adds to 180°.

families.title: Altitudes and perimeters of similar triangles
explanations: ratio-inverted (procedural): The ratio was used the wrong way round: the second triangle's lengths are 8/9 of the first's.
difference-added (conceptual): The difference between the sides was added. Similar figures scale by multiplying.
area-ratio-used (conceptual): The area ratio was used for the altitude. Areas are in the ratio of the squares of the sides, so the altitudes are in the ratio 9 : 8.

teach.idea: In similar triangles every length (side, altitude, median, perimeter) is multiplied by the same scale factor k; areas are multiplied by k².
teach.method: Find the scale factor from the sides (or as the square root of the area ratio) and multiply the given length by it.

alternatives.title: Enlarge on a grid
text: Draw a triangle on squared paper and double every side.
The altitude doubles too, but the area becomes 4 times as big.

families.title: Using the converses of the BPT and the angle bisector theorem
explanations: mixed-ratio (procedural): AD/AB was compared with AE/EC. Compare like with like: AD/DB with AE/EC (or AD/AB with AE/AC).
differences (conceptual): The differences of the lengths were compared. The converse needs equal RATIOS: compare the two fractions.
midpoint (conceptual): D being the midpoint of BC was taken to decide it. The bisector of ∠A divides BC in the ratio AB : AC, which is equal halves only when AB = AC.

teach.idea: Converse of the BPT: if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, it is parallel to the third side. Converse of the angle bisector theorem: if D on BC divides it so that BD/DC = AB/AC, then AD bisects ∠A.
teach.method: Work out the two ratios as fractions (or decimals) and compare. Equal: the conclusion of the converse holds. Not equal: it fails.

alternatives.title: Cross-multiply
text: AD/DB = AE/EC exactly when AD × EC = DB × AE.
Multiplying avoids decimals: 3 × 7.5 = 22.5 and 5 × 4.5 = 22.5, so the ratios are equal.

families.title: Tangent, secant or not meeting the circle?
explanations: near-is-touching (conceptual): A line close to the edge was taken to touch it. If the distance is less than the radius, the line cuts the circle at two points: it is a secant.
touch-is-cut (conceptual): A line at a distance equal to the radius was thought to cut the circle. It touches it at exactly one point: a tangent.
diameter-as-radius (procedural): The distance was compared with the diameter, 30 cm. Compare it with the radius, half the diameter.

teach.idea: A line and a circle can meet in two points (a secant), one point (a tangent) or not at all. It depends only on the distance from the centre to the line compared with the radius.
teach.method: Distance less than the radius: secant. Equal: tangent. Greater: the line does not meet the circle.

alternatives.title: Slide a ruler
text: Slide a ruler across a drawn circle, keeping it straight.
It crosses at two points, then just touches at one, then misses the circle.

families.title: Common tangents to two circles: how many, and how long
explanations: overlap-four (conceptual): Overlapping circles were given four common tangents. Crossing tangents would have to pass between the circles, where they overlap, so only the two direct tangents exist.
only-two (conceptual): Only the two outer (direct) tangents were counted. Circles that do not overlap also have tangents that cross between them.
inside-has-tangents (conceptual): A circle completely inside another has no common tangent: every line touching the inner circle cuts the outer one.
inside-touch (conceptual): Circles touching on the inside were taken to have none. They share the one tangent at the touching point.
touching-as-apart (conceptual): Circles that touch on the outside were treated as separate. The two crossing tangents become one tangent at the point where they touch: 3 in all.
no-root (procedural): The square root was not taken at the end.
wrong-kind (procedural): r1 − r2 was used; for a transverse (crossing) common tangent the leg is r1 + r2.

teach.idea: Two circles far apart have 4 common tangents; touching outside, 3; overlapping, 2; touching inside, 1; one inside the other, 0. A tangent length comes from a right triangle with the line of centres as hypotenuse.
teach.method: Compare d with r1 + r2 and r1 − r2 to count. For a length, L² = d² − (r1 − r2)² (direct) or d² − (r1 + r2)² (transverse).

alternatives.title: Draw it
text: Draw two coins and lay a ruler against both: try along the outside and crossing between them.
Move the coins closer and see the crossing tangents disappear.

families.title: Testing concurrency with Ceva's theorem and collinearity with Menelaus' theorem
explanations: ratio-flipped (procedural): One ratio was turned upside down (FB : AF instead of AF : FB). Go round the triangle in one direction: BD/DC, then CE/EA, then AF/FB.

teach.idea: Ceva: lines AD, BE and CF from the vertices meet at one point exactly when (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB) = 1. Menelaus: points D, E and F on the three side lines (one of them extended) lie on one straight line exactly when the same product is 1.
teach.method: Go round the triangle in order (B to C, C to A, A to B), write the three ratios as fractions and multiply. A product of exactly 1 means concurrent (Ceva) or collinear (Menelaus).

alternatives.title: Check with the medians
text: The medians cut every side in the ratio 1 : 1, so the product is 1 × 1 × 1 = 1.
So the three medians meet at one point: the centroid.

families.title: The least non-negative residue modulo n
explanations: negative-remainder (conceptual): The remainder of 7 was given a minus sign. A residue must be one of 0, 1, …, 5: add 6 to a negative remainder.
sign-ignored (conceptual): The minus sign of −7 was ignored. −7 is 7 steps below 0, so count back from a multiple of 6 below it.
quotient-given (procedural): The quotient (19) was given; the congruence asks for the remainder.
count-up (procedural): The gap up to the next multiple of 13 was given; the residue is the gap down from the multiple below.

teach.idea: a ≡ r (mod n) means n divides a − r. Every integer is congruent to exactly one of 0, 1, …, n − 1 — its least non-negative residue.
teach.method: Find the largest multiple of n that is not more than the number (for a negative number this multiple is more negative), then subtract it.

alternatives.title: Wrap around a clock
text: Think of a clock with n hours marked 0 to n − 1.
Moving a steps from 0 lands on the residue: every full turn of n steps brings you back to 0, and going backwards is turning the other way.

alternatives.title: Add or take away the modulus
text: Adding or subtracting n does not change the class: 17 ≡ 12 ≡ 7 ≡ 2 (mod 5).
Keep adding n to a negative number until it lands between 0 and n − 1.

families.title: Solving a linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod n)
explanations: coefficient-dropped (procedural): The 12 in front of x was left out; x must be the number that 12 times leaves 12.
multiplied (conceptual): 12 was multiplied by 12 instead of undoing the multiplication by 12.
subtracted (conceptual): 12 was taken away as if the congruence were x + 12 ≡ 12; 12x means 12 times x.

teach.idea: ax ≡ b (mod n) asks for x so that a × x leaves remainder b. Since b, b + n, b + 2n … are all ≡ b, one of them divides exactly by a.
teach.method: Write b, b + n, b + 2n, … until one is a multiple of a; divide it by a. Check: a times your answer leaves remainder b.

alternatives.title: Try every residue
text: Only 0, 1, …, n − 1 need checking.
Work out a × x for each and find the one whose remainder on division by n is b.

alternatives.title: Multiply by an inverse
text: Find c with a × c ≡ 1 (mod n) (for example 3 × 5 = 15 ≡ 1 mod 7).
Multiply both sides by c: x ≡ c × b (mod n).

families.title: Day of the week after d days (modulo 7)
explanations: count-today (procedural): Today was counted as the first of the days; the first day from today is tomorrow.
weeks-not-days (conceptual): The number of whole weeks (19) was counted on; whole weeks bring you back to the same day, so only the 6 extra days move the day on.
counted-back (procedural): The days were counted backwards; days from today go forwards.

teach.idea: The days repeat every 7, so d days from today land on the same day as d mod 7 days from today.
teach.method: Divide d by 7 and keep the remainder. Count that many days forward from today (tomorrow is 1).

alternatives.title: Jump whole weeks on a calendar
text: On a calendar, jumping 7 days moves straight down one row: same day of the week.
Take away as many 7s as you can; only the leftover days move you across the row.

families.title: Probability of a colour drawn from a bag
explanations: odds (conceptual): The green balls were compared with the other balls; a probability compares them with all 25 balls.
colours-equally-likely (conceptual): Each colour was taken as equally likely; the colours have different numbers of balls, and it is the balls that are equally likely.
count-not-probability (procedural): The number of green balls was given; a probability is that number out of the total.

teach.idea: When every outcome is equally likely, P(event) = (number of outcomes in the event) ÷ (total number of outcomes).
teach.method: Count all the balls, count the balls of the asked colour, and write the second over the first.

alternatives.title: Out of how many?
text: Imagine numbering every ball. Each number is as likely as any other.
The probability is how many of the numbers belong to the colour, out of how many numbers there are.

families.title: Probability with numbered cards
explanations: one-in-k (conceptual): "One card in every 7" was used, but 60 is not a multiple of 7; count the multiples of 7 up to 60.
complement-counted (procedural): The cards WITHOUT the property were counted; count the cards the question asks about.
one-is-prime (recall): 1 was counted as a prime number; a prime has exactly two factors, and 1 has only one.
one-not-square (recall): 1 was left out; 1 = 1 × 1 is a perfect square.

teach.idea: Each card is equally likely, so the probability is the number of cards with the property divided by the number of cards.
teach.method: List or count the numbers from 1 to N that have the property (multiples: divide N by k and drop the remainder), then divide by N.

alternatives.title: Write the list
text: Write the numbers that work: for multiples of 4 up to 30 that is 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 — seven cards.
Then P = 7/30.

families.title: Probability with two dice
explanations: order-ignored (conceptual): (1, 2) and (2, 1) were counted as one outcome; the two dice are different, so they are two of the 36 outcomes.
sums-equally-likely (conceptual): The 11 sums 2 to 12 were taken as equally likely; a sum like 7 can happen in more ways than 2 or 12.
twelve-outcomes (conceptual): 6 + 6 = 12 outcomes were used; each of the 6 numbers on one die goes with each of the 6 on the other, so there are 6 × 6 = 36.
double-counted (procedural): (6, 6) was counted twice, once for each die; it is one outcome.
one-die-only (conceptual): Only one die was considered; both dice must show a number above it.

teach.idea: Two dice give 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely ordered pairs (first die, second die); (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different outcomes.
teach.method: Draw the 6 × 6 grid of pairs, mark the pairs in the event, count them and divide by 36.

alternatives.title: Count row by row
text: Fix the first die at 1, 2, …, 6 in turn.
For each, count how many numbers on the second die work, and add the six counts.

families.title: Two counters drawn one after the other
explanations: as-if-replaced (conceptual): The second draw was worked out as if the first counter had been put back; without replacement there is one counter fewer, and one fewer of the colour already drawn.
one-colour-only (procedural): Only 'both red' was counted; 'both blue' is also the same colour.
one-order-only (procedural): Only red-then-blue was counted; blue-then-red also gives one of each.
added-branches (conceptual): The two probabilities along the path were added; 'this and then that' multiplies along the branches.
exactly-one (conceptual): 'Exactly one red' was found; 'at least one' also includes two reds.

teach.idea: In a tree diagram each branch carries a probability; along a path the probabilities multiply, and different paths that give the same event add.
teach.method: Draw the first draw (red or blue), then the second draw from each branch — with one counter fewer if the first is not put back. Multiply along each path you need and add those paths.

alternatives.title: A table of ordered pairs
text: Number the counters and make a table: first counter down the side, second across the top.
Without replacement cross out the diagonal (the same counter twice). Count the cells in the event over all the cells left.

families.title: Complementary and exhaustive events
explanations: reciprocal (conceptual): The fraction was turned upside down; 'not E' is what is left when E is taken from the sure event: 1 − P(E).
rest-over-event (conceptual): The outcomes against E were compared with the outcomes for E; a probability is always out of all the outcomes.
one-subtracted (procedural): Only the win was taken from 1; the draw must be taken away too, since win, draw and loss together make 1.

teach.idea: The outcomes of an experiment together form the sure event, with probability 1. So P(E) + P(not E) = 1, and the probabilities of outcomes that cannot happen together and cover everything add to 1.
teach.method: Add the probabilities you know (with a common denominator) and take the sum from 1.

alternatives.title: Think of tickets
text: Write the probabilities with one denominator, say 20: imagine 20 equally likely tickets.
The event takes some tickets; the rest of the tickets are 'not E'.

families.title: The addition rule P(A or B)
explanations: overlap-not-taken (conceptual): P(A) and P(B) were added without taking away P(A and B); the outcomes in both were counted twice.
overlap-twice (procedural): P(A and B) was taken away twice; that gives 'exactly one of A, B'. Take it away once.
and-for-or (conceptual): 'A or B' was read as 'A and B'; 'or' means at least one of them happens.

teach.idea: P(A) + P(B) counts the outcomes in both A and B twice, so P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B).
teach.method: Add P(A) and P(B) with a common denominator, then take away P(A and B) once.

alternatives.title: Fill a Venn diagram
text: Put P(A and B) in the overlap first.
Then 'A only' = P(A) − overlap and 'B only' = P(B) − overlap. P(A or B) is the three regions added.

families.title: Which number cannot be a probability
explanations: one-not-allowed (conceptual): 1 was thought impossible as a probability; an event that is sure to happen has probability 1.
zero-not-allowed (conceptual): 0 was thought impossible as a probability; an impossible event has probability 0.

teach.idea: A probability is (favourable outcomes) ÷ (all outcomes), and the favourable outcomes are some of all the outcomes. So it is never negative and never more than 1; 0 means impossible and 1 means sure.
teach.method: Check each number: is it at least 0 and at most 1? A fraction whose top is bigger than its bottom is more than 1.

alternatives.title: The probability line
text: Draw a line from 0 (impossible) to 1 (sure), with 1/2 (even chance) in the middle.
Every probability has a place on this line; a number off the line cannot be one.

families.title: Deciding the shape of three points from their distances
explanations: squares-added (conceptual): The squares of the distances were added, as for a right angle. For points on one line the distances themselves add up: the two shorter ones make the longest.
equal-sides-only (procedural): Only equal sides were looked for. Also test Pythagoras: do the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest?
right-angle-only (procedural): Only a right angle was tested. Also compare the three lengths: two equal sides make the triangle isosceles.

teach.idea: Distances decide the shape: if the two shorter distances add up to the longest, the points are on one line; if their squares add up to the square of the longest, there is a right angle (Pythagoras' converse); two equal distances make an isosceles triangle.
teach.method: Find PQ², QR² and PR² with (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)². Test the line first, then the right angle, then equal sides — and state which test decided it.

alternatives.title: Compare slopes
text: Points are on one line when the slope from P to Q equals the slope from Q to R.
Two sides are perpendicular when the product of their slopes is −1 (or one is horizontal and the other vertical).

families.title: The largest product from four digits
explanations: largest-number-first (conceptual): The biggest possible first number (98) was made, leaving the small digits for the second. Both numbers matter: the two largest digits should both be tens digits.

big-with-big (conceptual): The larger units digit was put with the larger tens digit. With the tens fixed, the product is larger when the two numbers are closer together, so the larger units digit goes with the smaller tens digit.

teach.idea: A tens digit counts ten times as much as a units digit, so the two largest digits belong in the tens places. Then, for a fixed total, two numbers have the largest product when they are as close together as possible.
teach.method: Put the two largest digits in the tens places. Give the larger units digit to the number with the smaller tens digit. Multiply, and check one swap to see it is smaller.

alternatives.title: Compare the two pairings
text: With tens digits a > b and units c > d, compare (10a + d)(10b + c) and (10a + c)(10b + d).
Their difference is 10(a − b)(c − d), which is positive: so the first pairing wins.

families.title: Can aⁿ end in 0? Reasoning with prime factors
explanations: even-is-enough (conceptual): Being even was taken as enough to end in 0. A number ending in 0 is a multiple of 10 = 2 × 5, so it needs the prime 5 as well, and powers of 148 never gain new primes.
big-powers (conceptual): It was assumed that a large enough power must end in 0. The primes in aⁿ are exactly the primes in a, so 2 and 5 can never appear.
five-is-enough (conceptual): Having the factor 5 was taken as enough to end in 0. Ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5, and 145 is odd, so every power of it is odd.

teach.idea: By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, aⁿ has exactly the same prime factors as a. A number ends in 0 only when 2 and 5 both divide it.
teach.method: Factorise a. If both 2 and 5 appear, aⁿ ends in 0; if one or both are missing, no power can ever gain them.

alternatives.title: Watch the last digits
text: The last digit of aⁿ depends only on the last digit of a: 6, 36, 216, 1296 all end in 6.
List the last digits of a, a², a³, a⁴ — they repeat — and see whether 0 ever appears.

families.title: Modelling with a pair of linear equations
explanations: swapped (procedural): The two values were written the wrong way round; the question asks for (x, y): the child's ticket first.

teach.idea: Two unknown prices and two facts about them: each fact is one linear equation, and the pair that makes both true is the answer.
teach.method: Name the unknowns, write one equation per fact, eliminate one unknown (multiply so its coefficients match, then subtract), solve, substitute back, and check both facts.

alternatives.title: Substitution
text: From the equation with a coefficient 1, write one unknown in terms of the other.
Put it into the other equation, solve, and check both facts with the prices.

families.title: Modelling with a quadratic and rejecting the impossible root
explanations: negative-root (conceptual): The negative root was kept. A width cannot be negative, so that solution of the equation does not fit the situation.
length-given (procedural): The length was given; the question asks for the width, which is the shorter side.

teach.idea: Call the width x; then the length is x + d and the area condition is x(x + d) = A, a quadratic. A quadratic has two roots, but only a positive width fits a real plot.
teach.method: Write x² + dx − A = 0, factorise (two numbers with product −A and sum d) or use the formula, then reject the root that cannot be a length.

alternatives.title: Estimate first
text: The width is a bit less than √A, because the length is bigger than the width.
Try whole numbers near there: x(x + d) = A picks out the width — then confirm with the equation.

families.title: Counting a class of a grouped frequency table from raw data
explanations: upper-included (conceptual): The values equal to 50 were counted in this class too; 50 belongs to the next class (50–55).
boundaries-shifted (conceptual): Values on 45 were put in the class before and values on 50 in this one; a class includes its lower limit and not its upper limit.

teach.idea: A grouped frequency table puts every value in exactly one class. With classes like 10–20, 20–30, a value on a boundary (20) goes in the class that starts there.
teach.method: Go through the data once, tallying each value in its class (a boundary value goes up into the class it starts). Check that the tallies add up to the number of values.

alternatives.title: Sort first
text: Write the values in order from smallest to largest.
The values in a class then sit together: count from the first value at or above the lower limit to the last value below the upper limit.

families.title: Mean of an ungrouped frequency distribution
explanations: frequencies-ignored (conceptual): The five values were averaged without their frequencies; a value that occurs 8 times counts 8 times.
divided-by-rows (procedural): Σfx was divided by 5 (the number of different values); divide by Σf = 34, the number of observations.

teach.idea: The mean shares the total equally. In a frequency table each value x occurs f times, so the total is Σfx and the number of observations is Σf.
teach.method: Make an fx column, add it (Σfx), add the frequencies (Σf), and divide: mean = Σfx ÷ Σf.

alternatives.title: Use deviations from a guess
text: Guess a mean A (the middle value). Work out d = x − A and add f × d.
Mean = A + Σfd ÷ Σf. The deviations from the true mean add up to zero, which is a check.

families.title: Absolute numbers versus proportions in bar charts
explanations: counts-for-shares (conceptual): The class with more walkers was chosen. A 100% stacked bar shows each class as a whole (100%), so it compares the share of walkers, not the number.

teach.idea: A clustered or ordinary stacked bar shows amounts; a 100% stacked bar makes every bar the same length (100%) and shows each part as a share of its whole.
teach.method: For each class, divide the walkers by the class total (or turn it into a percentage), then compare the shares, not the counts.

alternatives.title: Out of 100
text: Ask: if each class had exactly 100 children, how many would walk?
That number is the length of the walk part in a 100% stacked bar.

families.title: The percentage of a part in a 100% stacked bar
explanations: count-given (conceptual): The number of children was given; a 100% stacked bar shows the part as a percentage of the whole class.
fraction-not-percent (procedural): The fraction 3/60 was found but not turned into a percentage (multiply by 100).
part-to-rest (conceptual): The part was compared with the rest (57) instead of with the whole class (60).

teach.idea: In a 100% stacked bar the whole bar stands for the whole group, 100%; each part's length is its share of the group.
teach.method: Add the counts to get the whole, divide the part by the whole and multiply by 100.

alternatives.title: Each child is a slice
text: Share the 100% bar equally among all the children: each child gets 100 ÷ total percent.
A part with k children gets k of those slices.

families.title: The combined mean of two groups
explanations: average-of-averages (conceptual): The two means were averaged. The sections are of different sizes, so the bigger section must count more: work with the total marks.
divided-by-two (procedural): The total marks were divided by 2 (the number of sections); divide by the number of students, 75.
sizes-swapped (procedural): Each mean was multiplied by the size of the other section.

teach.idea: A mean hides a total: total = number × mean. The combined mean is the combined total shared among everyone, so a larger group pulls it towards its own mean.
teach.method: Find each group's total (size × mean), add the totals, and divide by the total number of people.

alternatives.title: A see-saw between the two means
text: Place the two means on a number line. The combined mean lies between them, nearer the bigger group.
It splits the gap in the ratio of the group sizes, the other way round: the bigger group's side is shorter.

families.title: How the mean changes when a value is added or removed
explanations: mean-with-value (conceptual): The old mean and 78 were averaged, as if there were only two numbers; the old mean stands for 20 numbers.
count-unchanged (procedural): The new total was divided by 20; after removing a number there are 19 numbers.

teach.idea: The mean times the count gives the total. Adding or removing a value changes both the total and the count.
teach.method: Old total = count × mean. Add or take away the value, change the count by one, and divide again.

alternatives.title: How far it pulls
text: A value bigger than the mean pulls the mean up when it joins; smaller pulls it down.
The new mean moves by (value − mean) ÷ (new count): a quick check on your answer.

families.title: Mean of grouped data
explanations: lower-limits (procedural): The lower limits of the classes were used as x; use the class marks (the middle of each class).
upper-limits (procedural): The upper limits of the classes were used as x; use the class marks (the middle of each class).
divided-by-classes (procedural): Σfx was divided by 5, the number of classes; divide by Σf = 50, the number of observations.
frequencies-ignored (conceptual): The class marks were averaged without their frequencies; each class mark counts as many times as its frequency.

teach.idea: In grouped data the exact values are lost, so each class is represented by its class mark (its midpoint); then the mean is Σfx ÷ Σf as for a frequency table.
teach.method: Find each class mark x, multiply by the frequency f, add the products (Σfx) and the frequencies (Σf), and divide.

alternatives.title: Step-deviation method
text: Choose an assumed mean a (a middle class mark) and the class width h. For each class, u = (x − a) ÷ h is a small whole number.
Mean = a + h × Σfu ÷ Σf — the numbers stay small.

alternatives.title: Assumed-mean method
text: Take d = x − a for an assumed mean a.
Mean = a + Σfd ÷ Σf.

families.title: Median of grouped data
explanations: upper-limit (procedural): The upper limit of the median class (110) was used for l; l is its lower limit, 90.
own-cf (procedural): The cumulative frequency up to and including the median class was used; cf is the cumulative frequency of the class before it (27).
class-mark (conceptual): The middle of the median class was given; the formula places the median inside the class according to how many observations are needed.
n-plus-one (procedural): (n + 1)/2 was used, as for ungrouped data; for grouped data use n/2 = 35.5.

teach.idea: The median is the value with half the observations below it. In grouped data we find the class where the cumulative frequency passes n/2, and assume the values are spread evenly across that class.
teach.method: Make a cumulative frequency column, find n/2 and the median class, then use median = l + ((n/2 − cf) ÷ f) × h with l its lower limit, cf the cumulative frequency before it, f its frequency and h the width.

alternatives.title: Read it from an ogive
text: Plot cumulative frequency against upper class limits and join the points.
Go across from n/2 to the curve and down: the reading is the median — the formula is the same thing done with a straight line inside the class.

families.title: Mode of grouped data
explanations: frequency-for-mode (conceptual): The highest frequency (19) was given; the mode is a value of the data, inside the modal class.
neighbours-swapped (procedural): f₂ (the class after) was used in the top of the formula; it is f₁ − f₀, with f₀ = 9 the class before.
upper-limit (procedural): The upper limit of the modal class was used for l; l is its lower limit, 70.
class-mark (conceptual): The middle of the modal class was given; the mode leans towards the bigger of the two neighbouring classes.

teach.idea: The modal class has the highest frequency. Inside it, the mode is pulled towards whichever neighbouring class is bigger.
teach.method: Pick the modal class; with l its lower limit, f₁ its frequency, f₀ and f₂ the frequencies before and after, and h the width: mode = l + ((f₁ − f₀) ÷ (2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)) × h.

alternatives.title: Crossing lines on a histogram
text: Draw the modal bar and its neighbours. Join the top-left corner of the modal bar to the top-left corner of the next bar, and the top-right corner to the top-right corner of the bar before.
The lines cross above the mode.

alternatives.title: Check with the empirical relation
text: For many distributions, mode ≈ 3 × median − 2 × mean.
Use it as a rough check, not as the answer.

families.title: Heights and distances with one right triangle
explanations: sine-for-tan (conceptual): The sine was used. Sine is opposite ÷ hypotenuse, but here the height (opposite) and the distance on the ground (adjacent) are involved: that is tan.
ratio-upside-down (conceptual): The ratio was turned upside down: tan θ = height ÷ distance, so height = distance × tan θ.
multiplied-by-tan (conceptual): The height was multiplied by tan θ; since tan θ = height ÷ distance, the distance is height ÷ tan θ.
line-of-sight (conceptual): The length of the line of sight (the hypotenuse) was found; the question asks for the distance along the ground.
cos-for-sin (conceptual): The cosine was used. The height is opposite the angle and the string is the hypotenuse: that is sin θ.
multiplied-by-sin (conceptual): The height was multiplied by sin θ; since sin θ = height ÷ length, the length is height ÷ sin θ.
ground-distance (conceptual): The distance along the ground was found; the string is the hypotenuse.

teach.idea: The height, the distance along the ground and the line of sight form a right triangle; the angle of elevation (or depression, which is equal to it by alternate angles) links two of its sides.
teach.method: Draw the triangle, mark the known side and the side you want, choose the ratio that uses exactly those two (tan for height and distance, sin or cos with the hypotenuse), and solve.

alternatives.title: Use the special triangles
text: A 30°–60°–90° triangle has sides in the ratio 1 : √3 : 2; a 45°–45°–90° triangle has sides 1 : 1 : √2.
Match the known side to its place in the ratio and scale.

families.title: Heights and distances with two observation points
explanations: far-only (conceptual): 80 m was taken as the whole distance from the first point to the tower; it is only the distance walked, and the rest (x) is unknown.
near-only (conceptual): 80 m was taken as the distance from the second point to the tower; the second point is x m from the tower, an unknown.
angle-difference (conceptual): The difference of the angles (30°) was used in one triangle; the two angles belong to two different right triangles that share the height.
height-given (procedural): The height of the tower was given; the question asks for the distance from the second point.
far-distance (procedural): The distance from the first point (x + 80) was given; the question asks for x, from the second point.

teach.idea: Each observation point gives a right triangle; the two triangles share the height h, and their bases differ by the distance walked.
teach.method: Let x be the distance from the nearer point. Write h = x tan β and h = (x + d) tan α, set them equal, solve for x, then find h.

alternatives.title: Subtract the bases
text: The bases are h cot α and h cot β, and they differ by d: h (cot α − cot β) = d.
So h = d ÷ (cot α − cot β).

families.title: Using sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 when sec θ + tan θ is known
explanations: sum-not-product (conceptual): cosec θ² − cot θ² = 1 was used as if (cosec θ + cot θ) + (cosec θ − cot θ) = 1; it factorises as a product: (cosec θ + cot θ)(cosec θ − cot θ) = 1.
not-halved (procedural): The two equations were subtracted but the result was not halved: that gives 2cot θ.
add-subtract-swapped (procedural): The equations were added; subtracting cancels cosec θ and leaves 2cot θ.
upside-down (recall): The ratio was turned upside down: cos θ = cot θ ÷ cosec θ.

teach.idea: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 factorises: (sec θ + tan θ)(sec θ − tan θ) = 1. So knowing the sum gives the difference as its reciprocal, and the sum and difference together give each ratio.
teach.method: sec θ − tan θ = 1 ÷ (sec θ + tan θ). Add the two equations and halve for sec θ; subtract and halve for tan θ. Then sin θ = tan θ ÷ sec θ. (The same works for cosec θ and cot θ.)

alternatives.title: Build the triangle
text: Once sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent and tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent are known, draw the right triangle with those sides.
Every other ratio can be read off it; check with Pythagoras.

families.title: Simplifying with the trigonometric identities
explanations: identity-slip (recall): 1 − cos²θ was taken as cos²θ; since sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 − cos²θ = sin²θ.
factor-dropped (procedural): The factor 6 in front was lost while simplifying; it multiplies the whole result.

teach.idea: Three facts do almost everything: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (and, dividing by cos²θ or sin²θ, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ), the reciprocals (sec = 1/cos, cosec = 1/sin, cot = 1/tan), and tan = sin/cos.
teach.method: Write everything in sin θ and cos θ, use sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 to replace 1 − sin²θ or 1 − cos²θ, cancel, and name the result.

alternatives.title: Check with an angle
text: Put θ = 30° (or 60°) into the question and into your answer using the known values.
If the two numbers differ, the simplification has a slip; if they agree for two angles, it is very likely right.

families.title: Evaluating expressions with standard angles
explanations: sin-cos-swapped (recall): The values of sin and cos were swapped (and tan taken as cot): for example sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 30° = √3/2.
angles-combined (conceptual): tan 60° − tan 45° was worked out as tan(60° − 45°); a trigonometric ratio does not add or subtract that way.
square-as-double (procedural): sin²θ was taken as 2 × sin θ; the small 2 means the value multiplied by itself.
squares-forgotten (procedural): The squares were left out; each value must be squared before adding or subtracting.

teach.idea: The ratios of 30°, 45° and 60° come from two triangles: half an equilateral triangle of side 2 (sides 1, √3, 2) and half a square of side 1 (sides 1, 1, √2).
teach.method: Write down each value (sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2, cos the reverse order, tan = sin ÷ cos), then do the arithmetic with surds exactly.

alternatives.title: The square-root pattern
text: cos θ is the same list backwards, and tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ.

alternatives.title: Draw the two triangles
text: Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2 in half: the half has sides 1, √3 and 2 and angles 30°, 60°, 90°.
Cut a unit square along its diagonal: sides 1, 1, √2 and angles 45°, 45°, 90°. Read any ratio off these.

families.title: Finding the other trigonometric ratios from one
explanations: subtracted-sides (prerequisite): The hypotenuse was taken as 9 + 4; by Pythagoras it is √(9² + 4²).
reciprocal (recall): The ratio was turned upside down: sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent.
opposite-adjacent-swapped (conceptual): The opposite and adjacent sides were swapped; the opposite side is the one facing θ.

teach.idea: A ratio fixes the shape of the right triangle: sin θ = 3/5 means opposite : hypotenuse = 3 : 5, whatever the size (similar triangles). Pythagoras gives the third side, and then every ratio can be read off.
teach.method: Draw a right triangle with the two given sides, find the third by Pythagoras, then write the asked ratio (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) and rationalise any surd in the denominator.

alternatives.title: Use the identities
text: From sin θ, cos θ = √(1 − sin²θ); from tan θ, sec θ = √(1 + tan²θ).
Then tan = sin ÷ cos and the reciprocals give the rest.

families.title: Complementary angles: sin(…) = cos(…)
explanations: angles-equated (conceptual): The two angles were set equal. sin x = cos y does not mean x = y: since cos y = sin(90° − y), it means x + y = 90°.
supplement (conceptual): The angles were made to add up to 180°; sin and cos of complementary angles (adding to 90°) are equal.

teach.idea: In a right triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, and the side opposite one is adjacent to the other. So sin x = cos(90° − x): the sine of an angle is the cosine of its complement.
teach.method: If sin(first angle) = cos(second angle) with both acute, the angles add to 90°. Write that equation in A and solve it.

alternatives.title: Rewrite as one function
text: Replace cos(y) by sin(90° − y).
Now sin(first) = sin(90° − y) with both acute, so first = 90° − y.

families.title: When the average of two means is not the mean of everyone
explanations: always-right (conceptual): The average of the two means was taken as the mean of everyone; that is only true when the groups are the same size. Here the bigger section must count more.
pull-reversed (conceptual): The pull was taken the wrong way; the combined mean is pulled towards the mean of the LARGER section.

teach.idea: The mean of everyone is total ÷ count. The average of two group means gives each GROUP equal weight, so it is right only when the groups are the same size; otherwise the larger group pulls the true mean towards its own mean.
teach.method: Find each total (size × mean), add, divide by the number of people, and compare with the average of the means.

alternatives.title: Try an extreme case
text: Imagine 99 students with mean 90 and 1 student who scored 40.
The average of the means is 65, but nearly everyone scored 90: the true mean is 89.5.

families.title: The assumed-mean and step-deviation methods for a grouped mean
explanations: a-minus-x (procedural): The deviations were worked out as a − x; they are x − a, so classes above the assumed mean have positive deviations.
frequencies-ignored (conceptual): The deviations were added without multiplying by the frequencies; each deviation counts as many times as its frequency.
not-divided-by-h (procedural): The deviations were not divided by the class width h = 20; u = (x − a)/h.

teach.idea: Mean = a + Σfd/Σf (assumed mean) = a + h × Σfu/Σf (step deviation): shifting every value by a and scaling by h makes the numbers small, and the mean shifts and scales back the same way.
teach.method: Choose a (a middle class mark) and h (the class width). Work out d = x − a (or u = d/h) for each class, multiply by f, add, then mean = a + Σfd/Σf (or a + h·Σfu/Σf).

alternatives.title: Compare with the direct method
text: The direct method gives Σfx/Σf; the assumed-mean method gives a + Σf(x − a)/Σf.
Both must give the same mean: a useful check.

families.title: The median of a frequency table
explanations: middle-value (conceptual): The middle value of the table was taken; the frequencies matter: the median is the middle of all the observations.
median-of-frequencies (conceptual): The median of the frequencies was found; the median is a value x, found with the cumulative frequencies.
position-n-over-2 (procedural): The 6th observation was taken; with 13 observations the middle one is the 7th.

teach.idea: The median has half the observations at or below it. In a frequency table the cumulative frequency (cf) says how many observations are at or below each value.
teach.method: Find N = Σf. If N is odd the median is the ((N + 1)/2)th observation; if even, the mean of the (N/2)th and (N/2 + 1)th. Find them by reading down the cf column to the first cf that reaches the position.

alternatives.title: Write the list out
text: Write each value as many times as its frequency, in order.
Cross off from both ends; what is left in the middle is the median.

families.title: The mode of a frequency table and the empirical relation
explanations: frequency-for-mode (conceptual): The highest frequency (12) was given; the mode is the VALUE that occurs most often.
middle-value (conceptual): The middle value of the table was given; the mode is the value with the largest frequency.
mean-median-swapped (recall): The mean and median were swapped: mode = 3 median − 2 mean.
two-one (recall): mode = 2 median − mean was used; the relation is mode = 3 median − 2 mean.
average (conceptual): The mean was taken as the average of the median and the mode; from mode = 3 median − 2 mean, mean = (3 median − mode)/2.
weights-swapped (recall): median = (2 mode + mean)/3 was used; it is (mode + 2 mean)/3.
sign (procedural): The relation was rearranged with a sign slip: mean = (3 median + mode)/2 was used.

teach.idea: The mode is the value that occurs most often (the largest frequency). For moderately skewed data, mean − mode ≈ 3(mean − median), that is mode ≈ 3 median − 2 mean (Karl Pearson's empirical relation).
teach.method: For a table, find the largest frequency and read its value. For the relation, write mode = 3 median − 2 mean, put in the two known numbers and solve for the third.

alternatives.title: Picture it on a line
text: Mark the mean and the mode on a number line.
The median lies between them, one third of the way from the mean to the mode.

families.title: Sure, impossible or neither
explanations: small-chance (conceptual): The event was thought to have some small chance; no outcome makes it happen, so it is impossible and P = 0.
unlikely-impossible (conceptual): An unlikely event was called impossible; some outcome makes it happen, so its probability is more than 0.
likely-sure (conceptual): A very likely event was called sure; some outcome does not make it happen, so its probability is less than 1.
not-sure (conceptual): The event was thought not certain; EVERY outcome makes it happen, so it is a sure event and P = 1.

teach.idea: An event that cannot happen is impossible, P = 0; an event that happens for every outcome is sure, P = 1; every other event has a probability strictly between 0 and 1.
teach.method: List (or count) the outcomes of the experiment and check each one against the event: none, all, or some.

alternatives.title: The probability line
text: Put impossible at 0 and sure at 1.
Unlikely events sit near 0 and likely ones near 1, but only 'no outcome' is at 0 and only 'every outcome' is at 1.

families.title: Which assignment of probabilities is valid
explanations: negative-accepted (conceptual): An assignment with a negative value was accepted because its values add up to 1; every probability must also be at least 0.
sum-not-checked (conceptual): Each value was checked to lie between 0 and 1, but the total was not; the probabilities of all the outcomes must add up to exactly 1.

teach.idea: An assignment of probabilities to the outcomes of a finite sample space is valid when every value is at least 0 and at most 1 and the values add up to exactly 1 (the axioms).
teach.method: For each assignment, write the values with a common denominator, check that none is negative or above 1, and add the numerators: they must give the denominator.

alternatives.title: Think of tickets
text: With denominator 12, imagine 12 tickets shared among the four outcomes.
A negative number of tickets is impossible, and all 12 must be shared out — no more, no fewer.

families.title: Simplifying with complementary angles
explanations: numbers-dropped (procedural): Each ratio of complementary functions is 1, but the numbers in front were dropped; they multiply those 1s.
minus-lost (procedural): The minus sign between the two parts was lost; each part simplifies to its number, and then they are subtracted.
tan-complement-negative (recall): tan(90° − θ) was taken as −tan θ; for complementary angles tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, so the product is 1.
angles-added (conceptual): The two angles were added inside one cosine, as cos²90° = 0; cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, and cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.

teach.idea: For complementary angles θ and 90° − θ: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, cot(90° − θ) = tan θ, sec(90° − θ) = cosec θ, cosec(90° − θ) = sec θ.
teach.method: Spot the pairs of angles that add up to 90°, rewrite one function of each pair as the co-function of the other angle, and simplify (a ratio of equal values is 1; tan θ × cot θ = 1; sin²θ + cos²θ = 1).

alternatives.title: One right triangle
text: In a right triangle the two acute angles are θ and 90° − θ.
The side opposite one is adjacent to the other, so each ratio of one angle is the co-ratio of the other.

families.title: Reading trigonometric tables (degrees, minutes, mean differences)
explanations: mean-difference-left-out (procedural): Only the entry for 51°42′ was read; the extra 5′ need the mean difference from the same row.
next-column (procedural): The entry for 48°54′ (the next column) was read; take the column just below the minutes and add the mean difference.
minutes-as-decimal (conceptual): 57°39′ was read as 57.39°; there are 60 minutes in a degree, not 100.
mean-difference-added (procedural): The mean difference was added; cosines DEcrease as the angle grows, so for a cosine it is subtracted.

teach.idea: A table gives each ratio to four decimal places for every 6′; for the minutes in between, the mean-difference columns give the small change to add (for sine and tangent, which increase) or to subtract (for cosine, which decreases).
teach.method: Find the row of the degrees and the column of the largest multiple of 6′ not above the minutes; read the value. Then read the mean difference for the extra minutes in the same row and add it (subtract for cosines) in the last decimal place.

alternatives.title: It must lie between two entries
text: Your answer must lie between the table entries for the 6′ just below and just above the angle.
For a cosine the later entry is smaller: so the mean difference is taken away.

families.title: Probability by counting selections
explanations: with-replacement (conceptual): Each choice was treated as independent with the same chance, as if each one were put back; the selection is made together, so count selections with combinations.
rest-not-chosen (procedural): Only the ways to choose the 3 faulty bulbs were counted; the other one must be chosen from the 8 good bulbs too, and the two counts multiply.
exactly-one (conceptual): 'Exactly one girl' was found; 'at least one' also includes two or more girls — easiest as 1 − P(no girl).
complement-of-one (procedural): 1 − P(exactly one girl) was found; the complement of 'at least one girl' is 'no girl'.

teach.idea: When r things are chosen together at random, every selection is equally likely, so P = (number of favourable selections)/(number of all selections), each counted with ⁿCᵣ.
teach.method: All selections: ⁿCᵣ. Favourable: choose the k of one kind and the r − k of the other kind, and multiply the two counts. For 'at least one', use 1 − P(none).

alternatives.title: List a small case
text: With 3 boys and 2 girls choosing 2, list all 10 pairs.
Count the pairs with one girl (6): the formula ²C₁ × ³C₁ = 6 matches.

families.title: Union, intersection, difference and complement of finite sets
explanations: union-intersection (conceptual): A ∪ B was read as the elements in both sets; the union takes every element that is in A or in B (or both).
product-not-lcm (conceptual): The common multiples were taken as the multiples of 6 × 2 = 12; numbers that are multiples of both 6 and 2 are the multiples of their LCM, 6.
difference-order (conceptual): The difference was taken the wrong way round; B − A keeps the elements of the first set that are not in the second.
common-not-removed (procedural): The common elements were not removed; B − A leaves out every element that is also in A.
complement-forgotten (procedural): The union was found but its complement was not taken; (A ∪ B)′ is everything in U outside A ∪ B.
de-morgan (conceptual): (A ∪ B)′ was taken as A′ ∪ B′; by De Morgan's law (A ∪ B)′ = A′ ∩ B′, the elements in neither set.

teach.idea: A ∪ B collects every element in A or in B, A ∩ B keeps only the elements in both, A − B keeps what is in A but not in B, and the complement A′ is everything in U outside A.
teach.method: First write A and B in roster form. Then go through U one element at a time and decide, from the definition, whether it belongs to the set asked for.

alternatives.title: Place the elements in a Venn diagram
text: Draw two overlapping circles A and B inside a rectangle U and write each element of U in its region: A only, both, B only, or outside both.
Then read off the regions the operation asks for: the union is all three circle regions, the intersection the middle, the complement of the union the outside.

alternatives.title: A membership table
text: Make a row for each element with two columns, 'in A?' and 'in B?', filled with yes or no.
Each operation is a rule on the two columns: ∪ needs at least one yes, ∩ two yeses, A − B yes then no.

families.title: Counting subsets and proper subsets of a finite set
explanations: empty-or-whole-left-out (conceptual): The empty set (or A itself) was left out; both ∅ and A are subsets of A.
whole-set-included (conceptual): A itself was counted; a proper subset of A must be different from A.
empty-removed (conceptual): The empty set was removed as well; ∅ is a proper subset of every non-empty set.
one-removed (procedural): Only one of ∅ and A was removed; non-empty proper subsets leave out both.
none-removed (procedural): All the subsets were counted; ∅ and A must both be removed.
all-subsets (procedural): Every subset was counted; only half of them contain a (pair each subset with the same subset with a added or removed).
double-not-power (conceptual): Each of the 12 elements was counted twice (2 × 12); each element is either in or out of a subset, independently, so the count is 2 multiplied by itself 12 times.
order-counted (conceptual): The 11 elements were counted in order (¹²P₁₁); a subset has no order, so it is ¹²C₁₁.
one-per-element (conceptual): Only the 12 subsets of the form {a} and {a, x} were counted; a can be joined by any subset of the other 11 elements.

teach.idea: Building a subset means deciding, for each element, in or out: two choices per element, so a set of n elements has 2ⁿ subsets, including ∅ and the set itself.
teach.method: Count all subsets as 2ⁿ, then remove what the question excludes: A itself for proper subsets, ∅ as well for non-empty proper subsets. Subsets of a fixed size r are ⁿCᵣ.

alternatives.title: List a small case
text: For {a, b}: ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b} — four subsets, 2².
Adding an element c doubles the list: every old subset, and every old subset with c added.

families.title: Counting with n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B)
explanations: only-part (conceptual): n(A ∪ B) − n(B) (or n(A ∪ B) − n(A)) was given; that counts the elements in only one of the sets, not those in both.
common-twice (conceptual): n(A) and n(B) were added; the 20 common elements are then counted twice, once in each set.
common-removed-twice (procedural): n(A ∩ B) was taken away twice; it is counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so it is taken away once.
common-not-removed (conceptual): n(A) was given; A − B leaves out the elements of A that are also in B.
wrong-set (procedural): n(A ∪ B) − n(A) was found; that is n(B − A), not n(A − B).
intersection-given (procedural): n(A ∩ B) was found and given; take it away from n(A) to get n(A − B).

teach.idea: When n(A) and n(B) are added, the elements in both sets are counted twice, so n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B).
teach.method: Write the formula, put in the three numbers you know and solve for the fourth. For 'A only', take n(A ∩ B) away from n(A).

alternatives.title: Fill the Venn regions from the middle
text: Write n(A ∩ B) in the overlap first.
Then A only = n(A) − overlap and B only = n(B) − overlap; the union is the three regions added.

families.title: Counting elements of A × B and relations from A to B
explanations: added (conceptual): n(A) and n(B) were added; each of the 10 elements of A pairs with each of the 10 elements of B, so they multiply.
pairs-not-subsets (conceptual): The number of ordered pairs was given; a relation is any subset of A × B, and a set of mn pairs has 2^(mn) subsets.
power-of-sum (procedural): 2 was raised to n(A) + n(B); A × B has 10 × 1 = 10 pairs, so the count is 2^10.
empty-relation-left-out (conceptual): The empty relation was left out; ∅ is a subset of A × B, so it is a relation too.
subtracted (conceptual): n(A) was subtracted from n(A × B); n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B), so divide by 10.

teach.idea: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a in A and b in B, so n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B). A relation from A to B is any subset of A × B.
teach.method: Multiply the sizes for the product. For the number of relations, raise 2 to the power n(A) × n(B).

alternatives.title: Draw the pairs as a grid
text: Write A down the side and B along the top: each cell is one ordered pair.
The grid has n(A) rows and n(B) columns; a relation is a choice of cells to tick.

families.title: Is a relation given by a rule reflexive, symmetric, transitive?
explanations: some-diagonal (conceptual): Some pairs (a, a) are in R, so R was called reflexive; reflexive needs (a, a) for every a in A, and (4, 4) is not in R.
transitive-a-equals-c (conceptual): Chains that come back to the start were skipped: (3, 1) and (1, 3) in R need (3, 3) in R too.
chain-missed (procedural): A chain was missed: (2, 1) and (1, 5) are in R, but (2, 5) is not.

teach.idea: Reflexive: every element is related to itself. Symmetric: whenever (a, b) is in R, so is (b, a). Transitive: whenever (a, b) and (b, c) are in R, so is (a, c) — including chains with a = c.
teach.method: Test the rule itself: put b = a for reflexive; swap a and b for symmetric; for transitive, take a chain (a, b), (b, c) and check (a, c). A single counter-example from A is enough to say 'not'.

alternatives.title: List the pairs first
text: Write out R as a list of pairs by going through every a and b in A.
Then check (a, a) for every a, the reverse of every pair, and every chain (a, b), (b, c).

alternatives.title: Write R as a table
text: Put a 1 in row a, column b when (a, b) is in R.

Reflexive: 1s all along the diagonal. Symmetric: the table equals its mirror image across the diagonal. Transitive: whenever row a has a 1 in column b and row b has a 1 in column c, row a has a 1 in column c.

families.title: The domain of a real function
explanations: end-left-out (procedural): x = 1/6 was left out; √0 = 0 is a real number, so the end point belongs to the domain.
sign-not-reversed (conceptual): Both sides were divided by −1 without reversing the inequality; dividing by a negative number reverses it.
b-sign (procedural): 1 was moved across without changing its sign.
root-rule-used (conceptual): The quadratic was made positive, as under a square root; a denominator only has to be non-zero, so just x = a and x = b are removed.
root-signs (procedural): The roots were read with the wrong signs: x² − 11x + 30 = (x − 5)(x − 6) is zero at x = 5 and x = 6.
sign-region (conceptual): The interval between the roots was chosen; the quadratic is negative there.
ends-left-out (procedural): The roots were left out; √0 = 0 is defined.
denominator-zero (conceptual): The roots 5 and 6 were included; there the denominator is √0 = 0.
minus-ignored (conceptual): The minus sign in front of x² was ignored; −x² + 11x − 30 = (x − 5)(6 − x) is ≥ 0 between the roots.

teach.idea: The domain of a real function is every real x for which the formula gives a real number: what is under a square root must be ≥ 0, and a denominator must not be 0.
teach.method: Write the condition (≥ 0, > 0 or ≠ 0), factorise any quadratic, decide the sign of each region between the roots, and write the answer in interval notation.

alternatives.title: A sign chart
text: Mark the roots on a number line; they cut it into regions.
Pick one number in each region and find the sign of the quadratic there; keep the regions that meet the condition, and decide each end point separately.

alternatives.title: Test numbers in f
text: Try a few values of x in the formula: if you need the square root of a negative number, or divide by zero, x is not in the domain.
The boundary values are where the quantity is exactly 0: test them separately.

families.title: The range of a quadratic function
explanations: f-at-zero (conceptual): f(0) = 84 was taken as the least value; the extreme value is at the vertex, x = 5.
direction (conceptual): The parabola was taken to open the other way; with a positive x² coefficient f has a least value.
end-open (procedural): 9 was left out; f(5) = 9, so it is in the range.
x-for-y (conceptual): The x-coordinate of the vertex (5) was used; the range is about the values of f, so use f(5).
vertex-sign (procedural): The vertex was put at x = −5; it is at x = −b/(2a) = 5.

teach.idea: Writing f(x) = a(x − h)² + k shows the range: (x − h)² takes every value ≥ 0, so f takes every value from k upwards when a > 0, and from k downwards when a < 0.
teach.method: Complete the square (or find the vertex at x = −b/(2a)), work out k = f(h), and write [k, ∞) or (−∞, k].

alternatives.title: Use the vertex formula
text: For ax² + bx + c the vertex is at x = −b/(2a).
Substitute it to get the least (a > 0) or greatest (a < 0) value; the range is the ray from there.

families.title: Is a quadratic on a restricted domain one-one, onto, both or neither?
explanations: square-never-one-one (conceptual): A quadratic was taken as never one-one; here the domain starts at 5, the vertex x = 5, so f only increases and different inputs give different outputs.
codomain-as-range (conceptual): The range was taken to be all of ℝ; on this domain f never goes below 5.
vertex-value-reached (conceptual): The least value 3 (at the vertex x = 4) was taken as reached; x = 4 is not in the domain, so f only reaches values from f(5) = 4 upwards.
vertex-inside (conceptual): The vertex x = 5 was not compared with the domain; it lies inside [4, ∞), so f goes down and then up: f(4) = f(6) = 6.

teach.idea: One-one: f(x₁) = f(x₂) only when x₁ = x₂. Onto: every element of the codomain is f(x) for some x in the domain. For a quadratic both depend on where the domain starts compared with the vertex.
teach.method: Complete the square to find the vertex (h, c). If the domain [d, ∞) starts at or to the right of h, f only increases (one-one) and its range is [f(d), ∞); otherwise f(d) = f(2h − d) and the range is [c, ∞). Compare the range with the codomain.

alternatives.title: Horizontal lines on the graph
text: Sketch the parabola and keep only the part over the domain [d, ∞).
One-one: no horizontal line meets it twice. Onto: every horizontal line at a height in the codomain meets it at least once.

families.title: A point on a transformed graph
explanations: shift-direction (conceptual): The graph was moved the wrong way; f(x + 2) takes the value f(5) when x = 3.
stretch-after-shift (procedural): 2 was added to 5 before multiplying by −1; in y = −f(x + 5) + 2 the value of f is multiplied by −1 first, and then 2 is added.
reflection-forgotten (conceptual): The −x inside f was ignored; it reflects the graph in the y-axis, so the x-coordinate changes sign before the shift.

teach.idea: In y = a·f(x − h) + v, the graph moves h to the right, is stretched by a (reflected if a < 0) and moves v up. A point (p, q) goes to (p + h, aq + v); f(h − x) also reflects it in the line x = h.
teach.method: Find the x that makes the input of f equal to p, then work out the output: multiply q by a, then add v.

alternatives.title: Track one point in a table
text: Write three columns: x, the input to f, and y.
Choose x so the input is p; then f gives q, and the outside numbers turn q into y.

families.title: Evaluating the greatest integer function
explanations: nearest (conceptual): The numbers were rounded to the nearest integer; [x] always goes down to the integer at or below x.
drop-decimals (conceptual): The decimal part was simply removed; for a negative number that moves up, but [x] is the integer at or below x: [−2.3] = −3.
