ceiling (recall): The integer above was taken; the greatest integer function takes the integer at or below x.

teach.idea: [x] is the greatest integer that is not more than x: on the number line it is the integer at x or the first one to its left. So [2.7] = 2 but [−2.7] = −3.
teach.method: Place each number on the number line and step left to the nearest integer (stay if it is already an integer), then add or subtract.

alternatives.title: Step left on the number line
text: Mark the number between two integers.
The greatest integer function always takes the left-hand one, even for negative numbers.

families.title: The corner point of a feasible region off the axes
explanations: intercepts-combined (conceptual): The smaller x-intercept and the smaller y-intercept were put together; the corner off the axes is where the two lines cross, found by solving them together.
swapped (procedural): The coordinates were written the wrong way round; give the x value first.

teach.idea: Each constraint ≤ is a half-plane bounded by a line; the corner points of the feasible region are where two boundary lines meet inside the region.
teach.method: Replace ≤ by = in the two constraints and solve the pair of equations (by elimination); check the point satisfies x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

alternatives.title: Eliminate one variable
text: Multiply the equations so that the y terms have the same coefficient, and subtract to find x.
Put x back into either equation to find y.

families.title: Solving |ax + b| = c
explanations: one-case (conceptual): Only 6x + 12 = 15 was solved; the modulus is also 15 when 6x + 12 = −15.
second-case-sign (procedural): In the second case the sign of 12 was lost: −(6x + 12) = 15 gives 6x + 12 = −15.
b-sign (procedural): 12 was moved across without changing its sign.

teach.idea: |A| is the distance of A from 0, so |A| = c (with c > 0) means A = c or A = −c: two equations.
teach.method: Write the two cases ax + b = c and ax + b = −c, and solve each.

alternatives.title: Distance on the number line
text: |ax + b| = c says ax is at distance c from −b.
Step c units left and right of −b to find the two values of ax, then divide by a.

families.title: Solving |ax + b| < c, ≤ c, > c, ≥ c
explanations: wrong-region (conceptual): The inside was chosen; |6x + 12| ≥ 4 means 6x + 12 is more than 4 from 0, on either side.
one-side (conceptual): Only 6x + 12 ≥ 4 was solved; the modulus also counts the negative side.
end-points (procedural): The end points were left out; with ≥ they belong to the answer.
b-sign (procedural): 12 was moved across without changing its sign.

teach.idea: |A| < c means A is within c of 0: −c < A < c. |A| > c means A is further than c from 0: A < −c or A > c.
teach.method: Rewrite without the modulus (one double inequality, or two inequalities joined by 'or'), solve for x, and write the answer in interval notation with the right brackets.

alternatives.title: Distance from a point
text: |ax + b| is the distance between ax and −b on the number line.
'Less than c' is the stretch of length 2c centred at −b; 'more than c' is everything outside it.

families.title: Solving a quadratic inequality
explanations: leading-sign (conceptual): The negative x² coefficient was ignored; −(x − 7)(x − 8) is positive between the roots and negative outside.
end-points (procedural): The roots were included; there the expression is 0, which does not satisfy a strict inequality.
root-signs (procedural): The roots were read with the wrong signs; the expression is zero at x = 7 and x = 8.
wrong-region (conceptual): The wrong region was chosen; (x − 6)(x − 8) is negative between 6 and 8 and positive outside.

teach.idea: A quadratic with roots a < b keeps one sign between the roots and the other sign outside them; the sign outside is the sign of the x² coefficient.
teach.method: Factorise, mark the roots on a number line, find the sign in each region, keep the regions the inequality asks for, and include the roots only for ≤ or ≥.

alternatives.title: Picture the parabola
text: With a positive x² coefficient the parabola opens upwards: it is below the x-axis only between the roots.
With a negative coefficient it opens downwards: it is above the x-axis only between the roots.

alternatives.title: A sign chart
text: Write the sign of each factor in each region.
Multiply the signs (and the sign of the leading number) to get the sign of the product.

families.title: Solving a rational inequality (x − a)/(x − b) compared with 0
explanations: multiplied-out (conceptual): Both sides were multiplied by x − 6 as if it were positive; its sign changes at x = 6, so compare signs of top and bottom instead.
wrong-region (conceptual): The wrong region was chosen; the fraction is negative between 6 and 8, where top and bottom have opposite signs.
denominator-zero (conceptual): x = 6 was included; there the denominator is 0 and the fraction is not defined.

teach.idea: A fraction is positive when top and bottom have the same sign and negative when they differ; it is 0 where the top is 0 and undefined where the bottom is 0.
teach.method: Mark the zeros of the top and of the bottom, find the sign of the fraction in each region, and keep the regions asked for. The zero of the bottom is always left out.

alternatives.title: Same sign as the product
text: (x − a)/(x − b) has the same sign as (x − a)(x − b) wherever x ≠ b.
Solve the product inequality, then remove x = b.

families.title: Partial fractions with two distinct linear factors
explanations: cover-up-sign (procedural): In the cover-up step the other factor was worked out the wrong way round: at x = 5 the factor x − 6 is −1, not 1.
not-divided (procedural): The numerator's value was not divided by the value of the other factor.
swapped (procedural): A and B were swapped; A goes with x − 5, found by putting x = 5.

teach.idea: (px + q)/((x − a)(x − b)) = A/(x − a) + B/(x − b) means px + q = A(x − b) + B(x − a) for every x, so choosing x = a and x = b each removes one unknown.
teach.method: Factorise the denominator, multiply through, then put x = a to find A and x = b to find B. Check at one more value of x.

alternatives.title: Compare coefficients
text: Expand A(x − b) + B(x − a) = (A + B)x − (Ab + Ba).
Match the x coefficient and the constant with px + q and solve the two equations for A and B.

families.title: Partial fractions with a linear and an irreducible quadratic factor
explanations: not-divided (procedural): N(5) was taken as A without dividing by 5² + 9 = 34.
x2-as-B (procedural): B was taken as the whole x² coefficient 7; the x² terms come from A·x² and Bx·x, so B = 7 − A.
c-sign (procedural): A sign slip matching the x terms: (Bx + C)(x − 5) gives (C − 5B)x.

teach.idea: A quadratic factor x² + k with no real roots needs a linear numerator Bx + C. Multiplying out, N(x) = A(x² + k) + (Bx + C)(x − a) holds for every x.
teach.method: Put x = a to find A. Then compare the x² coefficients to find B and the x (or constant) terms to find C.

alternatives.title: Three equations
text: Expand the right side and match the x², x and constant coefficients with N(x).
This gives three equations in A, B and C; solve them together.

families.title: Permutations of r out of n distinct objects
explanations: order-ignored (conceptual): The objects were chosen without order (³⁰C₄); in an arrangement the order matters.
repetition (conceptual): Every place was given all 30 choices; an object used in one place cannot be used again, so the choices go down by one each time.
all-arranged (procedural): All 10 objects were arranged (10!); only 7 places are filled.
divide-by-r (recall): 10! was divided by 7!; ¹⁰P₇ = 10!/(10 − 7)!.

teach.idea: Filling r places in order from n distinct objects: n choices for the first place, n − 1 for the second, and so on, so ⁿPᵣ = n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1) = n!/(n − r)!.
teach.method: Multiply r numbers, starting at n and going down by one each time.

alternatives.title: Draw the places as boxes
text: Draw r boxes in a row and write in each how many objects are still free to go there.
By the multiplication principle, multiply the numbers in the boxes.

families.title: Combinations: choosing r out of n
explanations: order-counted (conceptual): The 10 objects were counted in order (²⁰P₁₀); a selection has no order, so divide by 10!.
multiply-n-r (conceptual): 20 and 18 were multiplied; count the ordered choices 20 × 19 × … and divide by 18!.
divide-by-r-not-factorial (recall): ²⁰P₁₁ was divided by 11; each selection of 11 can be arranged in 11! ways, so divide by 11!.

teach.idea: Choosing without order: each group of r objects appears r! times among the ordered arrangements, so ⁿCᵣ = ⁿPᵣ / r! = n!/(r!(n − r)!).
teach.method: Use the smaller of r and n − r (ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ), multiply that many numbers down from n, and divide by its factorial.

alternatives.title: Pascal's triangle
text: Each entry of Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it; row n, place r (counting from 0) is ⁿCᵣ.
This is because a choice of r from n either includes a particular object or not: ⁿCᵣ = ⁿ⁻¹Cᵣ₋₁ + ⁿ⁻¹Cᵣ.

families.title: Selections with a condition: exactly k from one group
explanations: added (conceptual): The two choices were added; each choice of women goes with each choice of men, so multiply.
condition-ignored (conceptual): 3 were chosen from all 18 people; the condition fixes exactly 2 women and 1 man.
order-counted (conceptual): The members were arranged in order; a committee is a selection, so use combinations.

teach.idea: A condition splits the selection into independent parts: choose the women, choose the men, and multiply (every choice of one goes with every choice of the other).
teach.method: Work out ʷCₖ for the women and ᵐCᵣ₋ₖ for the men, then multiply.

alternatives.title: List a tiny case
text: With 2 women and 2 men, a committee of 2 with exactly 1 woman: 2 choices of woman × 2 choices of man = 4 committees.
Listing them shows each woman paired with each man.

families.title: Arrangements when some objects are identical
explanations: identical-as-distinct (conceptual): All 11 letters were treated as different (11!); swapping two equal letters gives the same arrangement.
counts-not-factorials (recall): The total was divided by the group sizes; divide by their factorials (the ways each group can be shuffled).
one-group-only (procedural): Only the largest group of equal letters was divided out; divide by the factorial of every group.

teach.idea: If all n objects were different there would be n! arrangements; each arrangement of identical objects is counted p! × q! × … times, once for every shuffle of equal objects.
teach.method: Work out n! and divide by the factorial of the size of each group of identical objects.

alternatives.title: Choose places for each colour
text: Choose the places for the first colour (ⁿCₚ), then for the second colour from the places left, and so on.
Multiply the choices: this gives the same number as n!/(p! q! …).

families.title: A coefficient in the expansion of (ax + b)ⁿ
explanations: powers-left-out (conceptual): Only ⁸C₇ was given; the term also carries (3x)⁷ and (3)¹, so their powers are part of the coefficient.
general-term-index (procedural): The general term was used with the wrong index: the term with x⁷ uses ⁸C₇ and the powers 7 and 1.
a-power-forgotten (procedural): The 3 in (3x)⁷ was not raised to the power 7.
sign-lost (procedural): The minus sign was dropped; (−1)¹ is negative (a negative number to an odd power), so the coefficient is negative.

teach.idea: The general term of (u + v)ⁿ is ⁿCᵣ uʳ vⁿ⁻ʳ. With u = ax and v = b, the term with xʳ is ⁿCᵣ aʳ bⁿ⁻ʳ xʳ.
teach.method: Pick the term whose power of x is r, then multiply ⁿCᵣ by aʳ and by bⁿ⁻ʳ, keeping the signs.

alternatives.title: Read the row of Pascal's triangle
text: Row n of Pascal's triangle gives ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, … ⁿCₙ.
Each one multiplies a power of ax and a power of b whose powers add up to n.

families.title: Expanding (ax + b)ⁿ
explanations: ends-only (conceptual): Only the first and last terms were written; (3x + 5)⁴ is not 81x⁴ + 625 — there are 5 terms.
no-binomial-coefficients (procedural): The binomial coefficients 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 were left out.
signs-lost (procedural): The signs were lost; odd powers of −1 are negative, so the signs alternate.

teach.idea: (u + v)ⁿ = ⁿC₀uⁿ + ⁿC₁uⁿ⁻¹v + … + ⁿCₙvⁿ: the power of u goes down while the power of v goes up, and the coefficients are a row of Pascal's triangle.
teach.method: Write the row of Pascal's triangle for n, then each term ⁿCᵣ (ax)ⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, and simplify each coefficient with its sign.

alternatives.title: Multiply step by step
text: (ax + b)² = a²x² + 2abx + b²; multiply by (ax + b) again for the cube, and so on.
This shows where the Pascal numbers come from: each new row adds neighbours.

families.title: The term independent of x in (xᵖ ± k/x^q)ⁿ
explanations: k-power-forgotten (procedural): Only ¹²C₆ was given; the term also carries (3)⁶ from k/x³.
sign-lost (procedural): (−1)⁵ is negative, since 5 is odd.
middle-term (conceptual): The middle term was taken; the constant term is where the powers of x cancel, which need not be the middle.
q-ignored (procedural): The power of x in the denominator was taken as 1; 1/x³ contributes x^(−3r).

teach.idea: In (xᵖ + k/x^q)ⁿ the general term is ⁿCᵣ (xᵖ)ⁿ⁻ʳ (k/x^q)ʳ = ⁿCᵣ kʳ x^(p(n − r) − qr). The term independent of x is the one whose power of x is 0.
teach.method: Write the power of x in the general term, set it equal to 0 to find r, then work out ⁿCᵣ kʳ.

alternatives.title: List the powers of x
text: Write the power of x in each term for r = 0, 1, 2, …: it goes down by p + q each time.
The term where the power reaches 0 is the constant term.

families.title: The nth term of a geometric progression
explanations: power-n (procedural): r was raised to the power 10; the 10th term is a r^9, because the first term has no factor r.
arithmetic (conceptual): The common difference was used as in an AP; each term here is 3 times the one before.
ar-power (procedural): (ar)^7 was worked out; only r is raised to the power, then multiply by a.

teach.idea: In a GP each term is the one before times r, so going from the 1st to the nth term multiplies by r exactly n − 1 times: aₙ = a r^(n − 1).
teach.method: Find r by dividing the second term by the first, then work out a r^(n − 1), keeping track of the sign.

alternatives.title: Keep multiplying
text: Write the terms out, multiplying by r each time, until you reach the term asked for.
Count the multiplications: one fewer than the term's position.

families.title: The sum of the first n terms of a GP
explanations: last-term (conceptual): The 7th term was found; the question asks for the sum of all 7 terms.
one-term-short (procedural): r^6 was used in the formula; Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) uses r^7.
divide-by-r (recall): The formula was divided by r; it is divided by r − 1.

teach.idea: Sₙ = a + ar + … + arⁿ⁻¹. Multiplying by r shifts every term along one place, so rSₙ − Sₙ = arⁿ − a and Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).
teach.method: Find a and r, then put them in Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), working out rⁿ with its sign first.

alternatives.title: Add the terms
text: For a few terms, list them and add.
Check that the formula gives the same total — then trust it for many terms.

families.title: The sum to infinity of a geometric series
explanations: plus-r (procedural): 1 + r was used; the sum to infinity is a/(1 − r), with r = 2/5.
a-left-out (procedural): The first term was left out; the sum is a/(1 − r), not 1/(1 − r).
first-terms-only (conceptual): Only the terms shown were added; the series goes on for ever, and the sum to infinity adds all of them.

teach.idea: When |r| < 1 the terms shrink towards 0 and the partial sums a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) approach a/(1 − r), because rⁿ → 0.
teach.method: Find r = second term ÷ first term, check |r| < 1, and work out a/(1 − r).

alternatives.title: Watch the partial sums
text: Add 1, 2, 3, 4 … terms and write each total down.
The totals get closer and closer to one number: that number is the sum to infinity.

families.title: The sum to infinity of an arithmetico-geometric series
explanations: gp-only (conceptual): Only the geometric part was summed, as if every coefficient were the first one; the coefficients grow by d each time.
one-minus-r-once (procedural): After subtracting rS from S, the result was not divided by 1 − r again.
d-without-r (procedural): The shifted series was taken to start with d instead of dr.

teach.idea: In an AGP the coefficients form an AP and the powers of r a GP. Subtracting rS from S lines up equal powers of r, and the differences of the AP are all d, leaving a GP.
teach.method: Write S and rS one place apart, subtract to get S(1 − r) = a + dr + dr² + ⋯ = a + dr/(1 − r), then divide by 1 − r.

alternatives.title: Use the formula
text: Check it by adding the first few terms: the totals approach your answer.

families.title: The harmonic mean of two numbers
explanations: arithmetic-mean (conceptual): The arithmetic mean was found; the harmonic mean is the reciprocal of the mean of the reciprocals.
not-inverted (procedural): The mean of the reciprocals was found but not turned back over.
geometric-mean (conceptual): The geometric mean √(ab) was found; the harmonic mean is 2ab/(a + b).

teach.idea: Numbers are in harmonic progression when their reciprocals are in AP. The harmonic mean H of a and b is the middle one: 1/H is the average of 1/a and 1/b, so H = 2ab/(a + b).
teach.method: Add the reciprocals, halve, and turn the result upside down — or use 2ab/(a + b) directly.

alternatives.title: Compare the three means
text: For positive a ≠ b, AM > GM > HM, and GM² = AM × HM.
So the harmonic mean should come out smaller than (a + b)/2 — a quick check.

families.title: Using the laws of logarithms: log N in terms of log 2 and log 3
explanations: five-as-sum (conceptual): log 5 was taken as log 2 + log 3, because 2 + 3 = 5; logs turn products into sums, and 5 = 10 ÷ 2, so log 5 = 1 − a.
decimal-ignored (procedural): The decimal point was ignored; 518.4 is a whole number divided by 10, which subtracts 1.
powers-not-multiplied (procedural): The powers were not brought down: log 2⁵ was taken as log 2; log xⁿ = n log x, so log 2⁵ = 5 log 2.

teach.idea: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x − log y and log xⁿ = n log x. With log 10 = 1, log 5 = log(10/2) = 1 − log 2.
teach.method: Write the number as a product of powers of 2, 3 and 5 (a decimal is a whole number over a power of 10), take logs term by term, and replace log 5 by 1 − a.

alternatives.title: Check with a calculator
text: Put these into your answer: it should match log of the number to four decimal places.

families.title: Evaluating a logarithm by writing both numbers as powers of one base
explanations: upside-down (conceptual): The exponents were divided the wrong way; log₃₄₃ x asks which power of 343 gives x, so it is 4/3.
subtract-exponents (procedural): The powers were subtracted; the logarithm is the power that turns the base into the number, here a quotient of the powers.
sign-lost (procedural): 1/7 = 7^-1: the power is negative.
divide-numbers (conceptual): 2401 was divided by 343; a logarithm is a power, not a quotient of the numbers.

teach.idea: log_B X = y means Bʸ = X. If B = cⁱ and X = cʲ, then (cⁱ)ʸ = cʲ, so iy = j and y = j/i.
teach.method: Write the base and the number as powers of the same prime, then divide the power of the number by the power of the base.

alternatives.title: Change of base
text: log_B X = log_c X / log_c B.
With X = cʲ and B = cⁱ this is j/i.

families.title: Solving log x + log(x ± c) = k
explanations: extraneous-kept (conceptual): The negative root was kept; log of a negative number is not defined, so x = −2401 is rejected.
sum-inside (conceptual): log x + log(x + 2400) was taken as log(2x + 2400); the sum of logs is the log of the product, x(x + 2400).

teach.idea: log x + log y = log(xy), and log_B N = k means N = Bᵏ. A logarithm is only defined for positive numbers, so every root must be checked.
teach.method: Combine the logs into one, rewrite as x(x ± c) = Bᵏ, solve the quadratic, and keep only roots that make both x and x ± c positive.

alternatives.title: Substitute each root
text: Put each root back into the original equation.
If any logarithm would have a zero or negative number inside, that root is not a solution.

families.title: Solving a quadratic with negative discriminant over ℂ
explanations: q-not-divided (procedural): √(164) was not divided by 2a = 6; the whole of −b ± √(b² − 4ac) is divided by 2a.
p-sign (procedural): The real part was taken as b/(2a); it is −b/(2a) = −4/3.
half-only (procedural): The imaginary part was divided by 2 only; divide by 2a = 6.

teach.idea: The quadratic formula works over ℂ: when b² − 4ac < 0, √(b² − 4ac) = i√(4ac − b²), so the roots are −b/(2a) ± i√(4ac − b²)/(2a), a conjugate pair.
teach.method: Find D = b² − 4ac, write √D = i√(−D) and simplify the surd, then divide both −b and √(−D) by 2a.

alternatives.title: Complete the square
text: Divide by a and write (x + b/(2a))² = (b² − 4ac)/(4a²), a negative number.
Take square roots using i: x + b/(2a) = ± i√(4ac − b²)/(2a).

families.title: A real quadratic from one complex root
explanations: sum-sign (procedural): p was taken as k × (sum of roots); the sum of the roots is −p/k, so p = −3 × 12 = −36.
i-squared (recall): (6 + 6i)(6 − 6i) was worked out with i² = +1; since i² = −1 the product is a² + b² = 72.
k-forgotten (procedural): The leading coefficient 3 was forgotten; the quadratic is 3(x² − (sum)x + product).

teach.idea: A polynomial with real coefficients has its non-real roots in conjugate pairs: if a + bi is a root, so is a − bi. Their sum is 2a and their product is a² + b².
teach.method: Write the quadratic as k(x² − (sum)x + product) and read off p and q.

alternatives.title: Substitute and match parts
text: Put x = a + bi into kx² + px + q and expand, using i² = −1.
The real part and the imaginary part must both be 0: two equations for p and q.

families.title: Converting between roster, set-builder and descriptive forms
explanations: strict-end (procedural): The last element 15 was left out; the description includes it.
count-off (procedural): The elements were counted wrongly: the description gives exactly 6 elements.
first-element (procedural): The first element was not checked: the set starts with 10.
square-as-double (prerequisite): n² was worked out as 2 × n; n² means n × n.
number-left-out (conceptual): 45 itself was left out; every number is a factor of itself.
one-left-out (conceptual): 1 was left out; 1 is a factor of every natural number.
prime-factors (conceptual): Only the prime factors were listed; the factors include 1, the number itself and every composite factor.
two-not-prime (conceptual): 2 was left out; 2 is a prime number (the only even prime).
odd-as-prime (conceptual): Odd numbers were taken as primes; 9, 15, 21, … are odd but not prime.

teach.idea: One set can be written three ways: roster form lists the elements in braces, set-builder form gives the rule {x : condition}, and descriptive form says it in words. All three must give exactly the same elements.
teach.method: To check a set-builder form, put n = 1, 2, 3, … (or test numbers) into the rule and list what it gives; compare with the roster, including the first and the last element.

alternatives.title: Make a table of n and x
text: Write n = 1, 2, 3, … in one row and the value the rule gives in the row below.
Stop at the last n the condition allows; the second row is the roster form.

alternatives.title: Test the ends
text: Most mistakes are at the ends: is the first element right, and is the last one included or not?
Check ≤ against < carefully.

families.title: Empty, singleton, finite, infinite, equal, equivalent and disjoint sets, subsets and power sets
explanations: universe-ignored (conceptual): The universe was ignored: there is no natural number strictly between 9 and 10.
empty-as-singleton (conceptual): The empty set was taken to have one element; ∅ has no elements at all (it is not {0}).
negative-root-missed (conceptual): Only x = 9 was found; x = −9 is an integer too and (−9)² = 81.
zero-as-element (conceptual): The set {0} was taken; x² + 81 is at least 81 for every real x, so no real number satisfies it.
large-as-finite (conceptual): The set was called finite because its numbers start from a fixed number; it has no last element, so it is infinite.
reals-as-integers (conceptual): There is no whole number between 9 and 10, so the set was called empty; x is a real number, and there are infinitely many real numbers between 9 and 10.
equal-as-equivalent (conceptual): The sets were taken as different because they are written differently; they have exactly the same elements, so they are equal.
equivalent-as-equal (conceptual): Sets with the same number of elements were taken as equal; equal sets must have the same elements, while equivalent sets only need n(A) = n(B).
equivalent-guess (procedural): The elements were not counted carefully; list both sets in roster form and count.
repeated-letters (conceptual): The repeated letters of RADAR were counted more than once; in a set each element is listed only once.
disjoint-not-equivalent (conceptual): Disjoint sets were taken as never equivalent; sets with no common element can still have the same number of elements.
equal-as-proper (conceptual): Equal sets were called a proper subset; A is a proper subset of B only when B has an element that A does not.
overlap-as-subset (conceptual): Sharing some elements was taken as being a subset; a subset needs EVERY element to be in the other set.
direction (conceptual): The subset sign was read the wrong way round: A ⊂ B means every element of A is in B.
empty-left-out (conceptual): ∅ was left out; the empty set is a subset of every set, so it is in P(A).
whole-left-out (conceptual): A itself was left out; every set is a subset of itself, so {8, 9} is in P(A).
elements-not-sets (conceptual): The elements 8 and 9 were written instead of the subsets {8} and {9}; the elements of P(A) are sets.

teach.idea: A set is empty (∅) if it has no elements, a singleton if it has one, finite if its elements can be counted to an end, and infinite otherwise. A = B when they have the same elements; A and B are equivalent when n(A) = n(B); disjoint when A ∩ B = ∅. A ⊂ B when every element of A is in B and B has more.
teach.method: First write each set in roster form (each element once), paying attention to the universe (ℕ, ℤ or ℝ). Then count, compare the elements one by one, and decide.

alternatives.title: Roster form first
text: Turn every set-builder form into a list; for letters of a word, write each letter only once.
With both lists in front of you, equal, equivalent, disjoint and subset can be read off.

alternatives.title: Build the power set by in-or-out
text: For each element decide in or out: for {a, b} that gives ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}.
The power set of a set with n elements has 2ⁿ elements, and each of them is a set.

families.title: Verifying the associative property of union and intersection
explanations: inner-only (procedural): Only the bracket B ∩ C was found; it must then be combined with the remaining set.
mixed-operations (conceptual): ∪ and ∩ were mixed up inside the bracket; every operation in (A ∩ B) ∩ C is an intersection.
union-intersection (conceptual): ∩ was read as all the elements together; an intersection keeps only elements in every set.

teach.idea: Union and intersection are associative: (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C) and (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C). They are also commutative: A ∪ B = B ∪ A and A ∩ B = B ∩ A.
teach.method: Work out the bracket first, then combine the result with the third set. Do the other grouping too; the two answers are the same set.

alternatives.title: Three-circle Venn diagram
text: Place each number of {1, …, 10} in its region of a three-circle Venn diagram.
A ∪ B ∪ C is everything inside any circle; A ∩ B ∩ C is the small middle region — the grouping does not matter.

alternatives.title: Test each element
text: For each number ask: is it in A? in B? in C?
For a union of all three it needs at least one yes; for an intersection it needs three yeses.

families.title: Counting with three overlapping sets in a survey
explanations: triple-not-added-back (procedural): In n(A ∪ B ∪ C) the 3 in all three were not added back.
union-given (procedural): n(A ∪ B ∪ C) was given; 'none' is the total minus that number.
only-first (procedural): Only the first group's 'only' count was found; 'exactly one' adds the people in only the first, only the second and only the third group.
at-least-one (conceptual): 'Exactly one' was taken as 'at least one'; people in two or three groups must be left out.
one-overlap (procedural): Only one of the two overlaps was taken away; people in the first group who are also in the third must be removed too.
just-added (conceptual): The three totals were simply added; everyone in two or three groups is then counted more than once.

teach.idea: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(B ∩ C) − n(C ∩ A) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C): adding the three totals counts the overlaps too often, subtracting the pairs removes the middle three times, so it is added back once.
teach.method: Draw three overlapping circles. Write n(A ∩ B ∩ C) in the middle, then each 'two only' region (pair minus middle), then each 'one only' region. Add the regions the question asks for.

alternatives.title: Fill the Venn diagram from the middle
text: Middle first: all three.
Then each pair region: n(A ∩ B) − middle, and so on; then each 'only' region: the total minus its three inner regions.

alternatives.title: Check the totals
text: The four regions inside circle A must add up to n(A); do the same for B and C.
If a region comes out negative, a number was taken away twice.

families.title: Sample spaces and events in set notation
explanations: order-ignored (conceptual): Outcomes like RG and GR were taken as the same; the first and second draws are different, so they are different outcomes.
outcome-missed (procedural): One outcome was missed; go through the outcomes systematically (a tree diagram helps).
complement (conceptual): The outcomes where the event does NOT happen were listed; the event is the set of outcomes where it does happen.
outcome-extra (procedural): An outcome was included that does not fit the description; check each outcome against the event.
another-outcome-missed (procedural): One outcome was missed; go through the outcomes systematically (a tree diagram helps).
replacement (conceptual): The first ball was taken as put back; without replacement the same colour cannot be drawn twice.

teach.idea: The sample space S of a random experiment is the set of all its possible outcomes; an event is a subset of S — the outcomes for which it happens.
teach.method: List the outcomes stage by stage (a tree diagram: every choice at the first stage, then every choice at the second). Then go through S and keep the outcomes that fit the event.

alternatives.title: A tree diagram
text: Draw a branch for each result of the first stage, and from each a branch for each result of the second.
Each path from the start to the end is one outcome; there are (choices at stage 1) × (choices at stage 2) of them.

alternatives.title: A two-way table
text: Write the first stage's results down the side and the second stage's across the top.
Each cell is one outcome of the sample space.

families.title: Deciding whether a relation is a function
explanations: many-one-not-function (conceptual): Two elements of A sharing an image was taken to stop R being a function; that is allowed (a many-one function). What is not allowed is ONE element with two images.
repeat-missed (procedural): An element of A appears in two pairs with different second entries; go through A = {1, 2, 3} one element at a time.
two-images-as-shared (procedural): The pairs were read the wrong way round (by their second entries); a function is about each element of A, the first entries.
missing-image (conceptual): Every listed element had one image, so R was called a function; a function from A must give an image to EVERY element of A.

teach.idea: A relation R from A to B is a function when every element of A has exactly one image in B. Two elements may share an image (many-one), but one element may not have two images, and none may be left without an image.
teach.method: Go through A one element at a time and count its pairs in R. If every count is exactly 1, R is a function. On a graph this is the vertical line test: no vertical line through an element of A meets the graph twice.

alternatives.title: Draw an arrow diagram
text: Write A in one oval and B in another, and draw an arrow for each pair.
A function has exactly one arrow leaving every element of A; arrows may arrive together.

alternatives.title: The vertical line test
text: Plot the pairs as points.
Above each element of A there must be exactly one point.

families.title: Naming a function: one-one or many-one, onto or into, identity or constant
explanations: codomain-check (procedural): f was called into because the codomain B was taken to need elements left over, as if the range were always smaller than B. Onto means every element of B is an image, and here every element of B is reached.
into-as-onto (conceptual): f was called onto because every element of A has an image; onto means every element of B is an image, and here some element of B is not reached (f is into).
many-one-missed (procedural): Two elements of A with the same image were missed; then f is many-one, not one-one.
identity-as-constant (conceptual): The identity was confused with a constant function; the identity's output changes with the input (f(x) = x).
constant-not-function (conceptual): Sending everything to the same element was taken as not being a proper function; it is the constant function.
one-one-as-identity (conceptual): A one-one function from A to A was taken as the identity; the identity sends EVERY element to itself.
repeat-as-constant (conceptual): Some repeated images were taken to make f constant; a constant function has only ONE image for all elements.

teach.idea: f : A → B is one-one if different elements have different images, and many-one otherwise; it is onto if every element of B is an image, and into otherwise. On A → A, the identity sends each x to x, and a constant function sends every x to one value.
teach.method: List the images f(a). Repeated images → many-one. Compare the set of images (the range) with B: equal → onto, smaller → into.

alternatives.title: Arrow diagram
text: Draw the arrows from A to B.
Two arrows meeting at one element: many-one. An element of B with no arrow: into.

alternatives.title: Compare range and codomain
text: Write the range {f(a) : a ∈ A}.
Onto means the range is the whole codomain B.

families.title: Recognising the graph of a standard function
explanations: confused-0-2 (conceptual): y = x³ was confused with y = x; x³ flattens near 0 and rises steeply further out.
confused-0-9 (conceptual): The sign of the slope was misread: y = −x goes down from left to right.
confused-1-11 (conceptual): y = −x² was confused with y = x²; −x² opens downwards.
confused-1-10 (conceptual): y = √x was confused with y = x²; x² is defined for negative x too.
confused-1-3 (conceptual): The V shape of y = |x| was confused with the curve y = x²; |x| is made of two straight pieces with a sharp corner.
confused-2-0 (conceptual): The straight line y = x was confused with y = x³; a cube curve bends.
confused-3-1 (conceptual): The parabola y = x² was confused with y = |x|; x² curves smoothly and is flat at the bottom.
confused-4-8 (conceptual): y = log₂ x was confused with y = 1/x; the reciprocal graph has two separate branches and never meets the axes.
confused-5-6 (conceptual): The step graph [x] was confused with signum; [x] jumps up by 1 at every integer.
confused-6-5 (conceptual): The signum graph was confused with the step graph; signum takes only the values −1, 0 and 1.
confused-7-8 (conceptual): y = log₂ x was confused with y = 2ˣ; 2ˣ exists for every x and is always above the x-axis.
confused-8-7 (conceptual): y = 2ˣ was confused with y = log₂ x; the two are mirror images in the line y = x.
confused-8-4 (conceptual): y = 1/x was confused with y = log₂ x; log₂ x exists only for x > 0 and crosses the x-axis at x = 1.
confused-9-0 (conceptual): The sign of the slope was misread: y = x goes up from left to right.
confused-10-1 (conceptual): y = x² was confused with y = √x; √x starts at the origin and exists only for x ≥ 0.
confused-11-1 (conceptual): y = x² was confused with y = −x²; x² opens upwards.

teach.idea: Each standard function has a recognisable graph: y = x a line through the origin, x² a parabola, x³ an S-shaped curve, |x| a V, 1/x two branches, sgn x three levels −1, 0, 1, [x] steps, 2ˣ an always-positive rising curve and log₂ x its mirror image for x > 0.
teach.method: Look at where the graph is defined, where it crosses the axes, whether it has corners or jumps and how it behaves far out; then check one or two points, e.g. x = 1 and x = 2, in each option.

alternatives.title: Check points
text: Read two or three points from the graph, for example at x = 0, 1 and 2.
Put those x-values into each option; only one gives all the y-values.

alternatives.title: Key features
text: Defined only for x > 0: log. Never below the x-axis: 2ˣ, |x| or x². A jump: signum or [x].
Shifting by k moves the whole graph up (k > 0) or down.

families.title: The multiplication and addition principles of counting
explanations: added (conceptual): The numbers of choices were added; each shirt goes with each pair of trousers and each pair of shoes, so the choices multiply.
repetition-mixed (conceptual): Every place was given all 9 choices; with no repetition the choices go down by one each time.
power-swapped (procedural): 4⁹ was worked out; with 9 choices for each of 4 places the count is 9⁴.
added-places (conceptual): The choices for the places were added; the places are filled one after another, so the choices multiply.
direct-forgotten (procedural): The 4 direct roads were left out; going directly is another way, so it is added.
all-multiplied (conceptual): The direct roads were multiplied in too; 'through Y' OR 'directly' are separate cases, so they are added.
all-added (conceptual): All the numbers were added; going through Y needs a road for the first part AND one for the second part, so those two multiply.
multiplied (conceptual): The numbers were multiplied; only ONE dish is chosen, from one group OR another, so by the addition principle they are added.

teach.idea: Multiplication principle: if one thing can be done in m ways and then another in n ways, both can be done in m × n ways. Addition principle: if a choice is either one of m things or one of n other things (not both), there are m + n ways.
teach.method: Ask: is it 'this AND then that' (multiply) or 'this OR that' (add)? For codes, count the choices for each place in turn; with no repetition, each place has one fewer choice.

alternatives.title: A tree diagram
text: Draw a branch for each first choice, and from each of them a branch for each second choice.
Count the ends of the branches: that is the product.

alternatives.title: AND multiplies, OR adds
text: Underline the words 'and then' (stages) and 'or' (cases) in the question.
Multiply across stages; add across cases.

families.title: Evaluating and simplifying expressions with factorials
explanations: difference (conceptual): 13!/12! was taken as (13 − 12)!; after cancelling, the factors 13 × … × 13 are left.
one-factor (procedural): Only the first factor 13 was kept; every factor from 13 down to 12 is left after cancelling.
divide-numbers (conceptual): 8!/4! was taken as (8/4)!; factorials do not divide like that. Cancel 4! from 8! = 8 × 7 × … × 1.
one-factor-scaled (procedural): 1/9! was rewritten with only one extra factor; 11! = 11 × 10 × 9!, so 1/9! = 110/11!.
second-not-scaled (procedural): 1/10! was not rewritten over 11!; it equals 11/11!.
one-factorial (procedural): Only 10! was divided out; the denominator also has 2!.
sum-factorial (conceptual): 10! × 2! was taken as (10 + 2)! = 12!, giving 1; a product of factorials is not the factorial of the sum.
smaller-factor (procedural): 210 = 15 × 14, and n!/(n − 2)! = n(n − 1), so n is the LARGER factor.

teach.idea: n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1, and n! = n × (n − 1)!. So a bigger factorial contains every smaller one: 8! = 8 × 7 × 6!.
teach.method: To simplify a quotient, write the bigger factorial down to the smaller one and cancel. To add fractions with factorials, rewrite each over the biggest factorial.

alternatives.title: Write the factors out
text: Write each factorial as a product of its factors.
Cross out the factors that appear on top and bottom; multiply what is left.

alternatives.title: The factorial chain
text: (n + 2)! = (n + 2)(n + 1) n!: each step up multiplies by the next number.

families.title: Using ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, ⁿPᵣ = r!·ⁿCᵣ and Pascal's rule
explanations: difference (conceptual): ⁿCₐ = ⁿC_b was read as a − b or b − a = n; the property is ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ, so 16 = n − 14.
larger-index (procedural): n was taken as the larger index 16; then ⁿC₁₄ and ⁿC₁₆ would be different.
no-factorial (recall): ⁿPᵣ ÷ ⁿCᵣ was taken as r; it is r! (each selection has r! arrangements), so r! = 120.
no-half (recall): ⁿC₂ was taken as n(n − 1); it is n(n − 1)/2.
one-less (procedural): n(n − 1) = 380 was solved with the smaller factor; n is the larger of the two consecutive numbers.
upper-index (conceptual): The upper index was kept as 15; Pascal's rule is ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ.
lower-index (procedural): The lower index was raised as well; ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ keeps r.

teach.idea: Choosing r to take is choosing n − r to leave, so ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ. Each selection of r can be arranged in r! ways, so ⁿPᵣ = r!·ⁿCᵣ. A selection of r from n + 1 either includes one particular object or not: ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ = ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁.
teach.method: For ⁿCₐ = ⁿC_b (a ≠ b), use a + b = n. Divide ⁿPᵣ by ⁿCᵣ to get r!. For a sum ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁, write ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ and evaluate.

alternatives.title: Pascal's triangle
text: Each entry is the sum of the two above it: that is Pascal's rule.
Each row reads the same from both ends: that is ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.

alternatives.title: Check by working out
text: Put your n or r back and evaluate both sides.
For small numbers, list the selections to see why the property holds.

families.title: Counting diagonals, triangles and lines with combinations
explanations: sides-counted (conceptual): All ²⁰C₂ = 190 segments were counted; 20 of them are sides, not diagonals.
no-half (procedural): n(n − 3) = 340 counts each diagonal twice (once from each end); divide by 2.
order-counted (conceptual): The three corners were counted in order; a triangle is the same whichever corner is named first, so use combinations.
collinear-ignored (conceptual): Every pair was counted as a separate line; all ¹²C₂ pairs of the collinear points give the same one line.
remove-pairs (procedural): ¹²C₂ was taken away; the choices that fail are the triples from the 12 collinear points, ¹²C₃.
line-not-added (procedural): The ¹²C₂ pairs on the common line were removed, but that line itself must be counted once: add 1.

teach.idea: A segment needs 2 points and a triangle 3 non-collinear points, with no order, so they are counted with ⁿC₂ and ⁿC₃. Then remove what does not count: the sides (for diagonals), or the choices from collinear points.
teach.method: Diagonals: ⁿC₂ − n = n(n − 3)/2. Triangles: ⁿC₃ − ᵐC₃. Lines: ⁿC₂ − ᵐC₂ + 1 (the collinear points give one line).

alternatives.title: Draw a small case
text: Draw a pentagon and its diagonals: there are 5, and ⁵C₂ − 5 = 5.
Draw 5 points with 3 on a line and count the triangles: ⁵C₃ − ³C₃ = 9.

alternatives.title: Count from one vertex
text: From each vertex of an n-gon, n − 3 diagonals start.
n(n − 3) counts each diagonal from both ends, so divide by 2.

families.title: Deciding whether order matters, and combining selection with arrangement
explanations: order-counted (conceptual): The students were counted in order; picking the same students in a different order gives the same group, so use ⁿCᵣ.
order-ignored (conceptual): The roles were ignored; the posts are different, so swapping two people gives a different result and order matters (ⁿPᵣ).
not-arranged (procedural): The letters were chosen but not arranged; each choice of 4 letters can be written in 4! = 24 orders.
added (conceptual): The vowel choices and the consonant choices were added; both are needed, so they multiply.
chair-forgotten (procedural): The chairperson was not chosen; each committee can pick its chairperson in 4 ways.
all-ordered (conceptual): All the members were arranged in order; only the chairperson is a special post, the others are not ordered.

teach.idea: Order matters when swapping two chosen things gives a different result (different posts, places, positions, a word); then count arrangements (ⁿPᵣ). If swapping gives the same result (a group, a team, a committee), count selections (ⁿCᵣ). Many problems first select, then arrange.
teach.method: Ask: if I swap two of the chosen, is it a different outcome? Select with combinations, then multiply by the number of arrangements (or of ways to fill the special posts).

alternatives.title: The swap test
text: Imagine two chosen people swapping places.
Different outcome: order matters (P). Same outcome: it does not (C).

alternatives.title: Select, then arrange
text: Step 1: choose the members (combinations, multiplied across groups).
Step 2: arrange or assign posts to the chosen (r! or r ways); multiply.

families.title: Arrangements with repetition, restrictions, around a circle, and the rank of a word
explanations: no-repetition (conceptual): Each letter was used at most once; repetition is allowed, so every place has all the letters to choose from.
power-swapped (procedural): 5¹⁰ was worked out; 5 places with 10 choices each give 10⁵.
group-not-arranged (procedural): The 'together' arrangements were counted without the 6 orders inside the block; there are 3! × 6! of them.
together-given (conceptual): The number of arrangements with them TOGETHER was given; 'not together' is all arrangements minus those.
row-count (conceptual): 8! counts arrangements in a row; on a necklace, turning and flipping do not give new necklaces.
flip-ignored (conceptual): The circle count (n − 1)! was given; a necklace can be turned over, which pairs up the arrangements, so divide by 2.
words-before (procedural): The number of words before it was given; its rank is one more than that.
used-letters-counted (procedural): Letters already used were counted again; at each place only the letters not yet used, and smaller than the word's letter, start earlier words.

teach.idea: With repetition each place has all n choices (nʳ). For 'together', glue the two into a block; for 'not together', subtract. Around a circle only relative positions count: (n − 1)!, and a necklace can also be flipped: (n − 1)!/2. A word's rank is 1 + the number of arrangements that come before it in dictionary order.
teach.method: Name the restriction, count with the matching rule, and check the answer with a very small case. For a rank, go letter by letter: (number of unused smaller letters) × (factorial of the places left), add them up and add 1.

alternatives.title: Try a small case
text: Three people A, B, C around a table: ABC, ACB — only 2 = (3 − 1)!.
Listing small cases shows why the rule works.

alternatives.title: A rank table
text: Write the word's letters in alphabetical order.
For each position, count the unused letters that come before the word's letter and multiply by the factorial of the positions left.

families.title: Building Pascal's triangle and reading binomial coefficients from it
explanations: copied (conceptual): The entry in the same position of the given row was copied; each new entry is the SUM of the two entries above it.
wrong-pair (procedural): The wrong pair of neighbours was added; position 11 of the new row is the sum of positions 10 and 11 of the row above.
position-off (procedural): The positions were counted from 1; the coefficient of ab⁹ is in position 9, counting the first 1 as position 0.
count-entries (conceptual): The number of entries (13) was given; the question asks for their sum.
double-n (conceptual): The sum was taken as 2 × 12; each row's sum is DOUBLE the sum of the row before, so it is 2¹².

teach.idea: Pascal's triangle starts with 1; each row starts and ends with 1, and every other entry is the sum of the two entries above it. Row n gives the coefficients ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, …, ⁿCₙ of (a + b)ⁿ.
teach.method: To build the next row, add each pair of neighbours and put a 1 at each end. The coefficient of aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ is the entry in position r (the first 1 is position 0).

alternatives.title: Write the triangle out
text: Write rows 0, 1, 2, … down the page, each one centred under the last.
Every entry is the sum of the two diagonally above it.

alternatives.title: Why it gives binomial coefficients
text: Expanding (a + b)ⁿ⁺¹ = (a + b)ⁿ(a + b): each term of the new row comes from two terms of the old one.
That is exactly the 'add the two above' rule.

families.title: Exact values and approximations by the binomial theorem
explanations: ends-only (conceptual): Only the first and last terms were kept: (1000 − 1)³ is not 1000³ − 1; the middle terms ⁿCᵣ 1000ⁿ⁻ʳ (−1)ʳ count too.
no-coefficients (procedural): The binomial coefficients were left out of the middle terms.
signs-lost (procedural): All the terms were added; the odd powers of −1 are negative, so the signs alternate.
two-terms (procedural): Only 1 + nx was used; the question asks for three terms, so ⁿC₂x² = 0.1125 is added too.
n-for-nc2 (recall): The x² term was given the coefficient n = 10; it is ⁿC₂ = 45.
x-not-squared (procedural): In the third term x was not squared: (0.05)² = 0.0025.

teach.idea: Writing a number close to a power of 10 as 10ᵏ ± a makes the binomial expansion easy to work out exactly. For (1 + x)ⁿ with x small, the terms x², x³, … shrink fast, so 1 + nx + ⁿC₂x² is already a good approximation.
teach.method: Exact: expand (10ᵏ + a)ⁿ term by term (keeping signs) and add. Approximation: write the base as 1 + x, work out nx and ⁿC₂x², and add them to 1.

alternatives.title: Watch the terms shrink
text: For x = 0.02 and n = 8: nx = 0.16, ⁿC₂x² = 0.0112, ⁿC₃x³ ≈ 0.0004.
Each term is much smaller than the one before, so three terms give a close value.

alternatives.title: Check with multiplication
text: For a small n, multiply the number by itself n times.
Compare with your binomial working: the exact values agree, the approximation is close.

families.title: The middle term or terms of (ax + b)ⁿ
explanations: term-number (procedural): The 4th term was taken; with 9 terms the middle one is the 5th, T₅, which uses r = 4.
powers-left-out (procedural): Only ⁹C₅ was used as the coefficient; 3⁴ and (3)⁵ belong to it too.
other-middle (procedural): The other middle term was given; the second middle term is T₆.
sign-lost (procedural): (−1)⁵ is negative, because 5 is odd.

teach.idea: (u + v)ⁿ has n + 1 terms, T₍ᵣ₊₁₎ = ⁿCᵣ uⁿ⁻ʳ vʳ. If n is even there is one middle term, T₍ₙ/₂₊₁₎; if n is odd there are two, T₍₍ₙ₊₁₎/₂₎ and T₍₍ₙ₊₃₎/₂₎.
teach.method: Count the terms, find which one is in the middle and its r, then work out ⁿCᵣ (ax)ⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ with signs.

alternatives.title: List the values of r
text: Write r = 0, 1, …, n in a row; the middle of the row is the middle term.
For an odd n the two numbers in the middle give the two middle terms.

alternatives.title: Use the symmetry
text: The coefficients ⁿCᵣ are symmetric, so the middle term has the largest binomial coefficient.
For n odd the two middle terms have equal binomial coefficients ⁿCₖ = ⁿCₖ₊₁.

families.title: Identifying a geometric progression
explanations: difference-as-ratio (conceptual): A constant difference was taken as a constant ratio; 729, −243, −1215, −2187, −3159, … adds −972 each time (an AP), while a GP multiplies by the same number each time.
few-terms-checked (procedural): Only the first three terms were checked; in 729, −243, 81, 405, 729, … the ratio changes after the third term. Check every pair of neighbours.
pattern-not-ratio (procedural): 729, −243, −2187, −5103, −8991, … follows a pattern, but not 'multiply by the same number'; divide each term by the one before to test it.

teach.idea: A sequence is a geometric progression when each term (after the first) is the previous term multiplied by the same non-zero number r, the common ratio: a, ar, ar², ar³, …
teach.method: Divide every term by the term before it. If all the ratios are equal, it is a GP; if any ratio is different, it is not. Checking only the first two terms is never enough.

alternatives.title: A row of ratios
text: Under each pair of neighbouring terms write term ÷ previous term.
A GP has the same number all along that row.

alternatives.title: Repeated growth
text: A GP grows (or shrinks) by the same factor every step, like money at compound interest.
An AP grows by the same amount every step, like a fixed weekly saving.

families.title: Growth, depreciation and compound interest with geometric progressions
explanations: simple-growth (conceptual): The change was worked out on the starting amount every year (80000 × 20% each year); each year's change is on the amount at the start of THAT year, so the amounts multiply by 1.2 each time.
n-minus-one (procedural): 3⁷ was used; after 8 hours there have been 8 multiplications by 3.
decay-as-growth (conceptual): The value was increased by 20% each year; depreciation takes the percentage away, so the ratio is 0.8.
linear (conceptual): 300 × 3 × 8 was worked out; the number is multiplied by 3 every hour, so it is 300 × 3⁸.

teach.idea: Growing by r% a year multiplies the amount by 1 + r/100 every year; losing r% multiplies it by 1 − r/100. So the amounts at the start, after 1 year, after 2 years, … form a GP: P, PR, PR², …, and after n years the amount is PRⁿ.
teach.method: Write the common ratio R (1.1 for 10% growth, 0.9 for 10% decrease), then work out P × Rⁿ. Note it is the (n + 1)th term, because the first term is the starting amount.

alternatives.title: A year-by-year table
text: Write the amount at the start, then add (or take away) the percentage of THAT amount for each year.
The table's numbers are the terms of the GP.

alternatives.title: Compare with simple growth
text: Simple growth adds the same amount every year: an AP.
Compound growth adds a percentage of the current amount: a GP, which pulls ahead over time.

families.title: Using the sum to infinity: recurring decimals, a bouncing ball, nested shapes
explanations: first-term-only (conceptual): Only the first block was turned into a fraction (98/100); the block repeats for ever, so all the terms of the series must be added.
nines (procedural): The two-digit block was put over 9; a block of two digits repeating goes over 99.
falls-only (conceptual): Only the distances going down were added; after each bounce the ball goes up AND comes down the same height.
first-drop-doubled (procedural): The first drop of 30 m was counted twice; the ball is dropped (only down), and each later height is travelled twice.
first-left-out (procedural): The first triangle was left out; its area 60 cm² is the first term.
side-ratio (conceptual): The areas were taken to go down by 1/4; joining midpoints makes the side 1/√2 times as long, so each area is HALF the one before.
half-ratio (conceptual): Each triangle was taken as half the one before; joining midpoints halves the sides, so the area is a QUARTER.

teach.idea: Many situations hide an infinite geometric series with |r| < 1: a recurring decimal 0.4545… = 45/100 + 45/10000 + …, the heights of a bouncing ball, the areas of shapes that shrink by the same factor each time. Its sum is a/(1 − r).
teach.method: Write the first term a and the ratio r of the repeating part, check |r| < 1, use a/(1 − r), and then add any part that is not repeated (the whole number, or the first drop of the ball).

alternatives.title: Write out the first few terms
text: Write the first three or four terms of the series in numbers.
Divide the second by the first to find r; check the third against the second.

alternatives.title: Check by algebra
text: This gives the same fraction as the geometric series.

families.title: Does a geometric series converge, and to what?
explanations: formula-without-check (conceptual): a/(1 − r) was used without checking |r| < 1; here r = 6/5, so the terms do not shrink and there is no sum to infinity.
alternating-diverges (conceptual): The changing signs were taken to mean the series has no sum; with |r| < 1 the terms shrink to 0 and the series still converges.
one-plus-r (procedural): 1 + r was used in the formula; the sum to infinity is a/(1 − r).
first-term-left-out (procedural): The first term was taken as ar; the series starts with a, so S∞ = a/(1 − r).

teach.idea: A geometric series a + ar + ar² + … converges (has a sum to infinity) exactly when |r| < 1; then the terms shrink to 0 and S∞ = a/(1 − r). If |r| ≥ 1 the terms do not shrink and the series diverges.
teach.method: Find r = (second term) ÷ (first term). If |r| < 1 work out a/(1 − r); otherwise say it diverges — never use the formula without this check.

alternatives.title: Watch the partial sums
text: Add 1, 2, 3, … terms and write each total.
If the totals settle down to one number the series converges; if they grow or keep jumping, it diverges.

alternatives.title: Place r on a number line
text: Mark −1 and 1.
Strictly between them: converges. At or beyond them: diverges.

families.title: Finding a parameter for which a quadratic has equal roots
explanations: four-forgotten (recall): The discriminant was taken as b² − ac; it is b² − 4ac.
no-root (procedural): k² = 1296 was found but the square root was not taken.
b-not-squared (procedural): b was not squared: the discriminant uses b² = 400.

teach.idea: ax² + bx + c = 0 has two equal real roots exactly when its discriminant b² − 4ac is 0 (then the parabola just touches the x-axis). If a coefficient contains k, setting the discriminant to 0 gives an equation for k.
teach.method: Write b² − 4ac with k in it, set it equal to 0 and solve for k. Keep only the values the question allows (positive k, or k ≠ 0).

alternatives.title: The graph touches the axis
text: Equal roots mean the graph of y = ax² + bx + c meets the x-axis at exactly one point, its vertex.
So the least (or greatest) value of the quadratic is 0.

alternatives.title: A perfect square
text: Equal roots mean ax² + bx + c = a(x − α)².
Compare coefficients: b = −2aα and c = aα², which gives b² = 4ac.

families.title: Values of a parameter for real or no real roots
explanations: strictness (procedural): The case of equal roots was included; then the roots are real, so the end point is left out.
direction (conceptual): The values giving real roots were found; no real roots needs b² − 4ac < 0.
four-forgotten (recall): The discriminant was taken as b² − ac; it is b² − 4ac.
one-side (conceptual): k² < 784 was solved as k < 28 only; a k below −28 also has k² > 784, so k must be greater than −28 too.

teach.idea: ax² + bx + c = 0 has real roots when b² − 4ac ≥ 0 (two different roots when > 0, equal roots when = 0) and no real roots when b² − 4ac < 0.
teach.method: Write the discriminant with k in it, write the inequality (≥ 0 for real roots, < 0 for none) and solve it for k; a k² inequality has two parts or one interval.

alternatives.title: Move the parabola
text: Changing the constant term moves the parabola up or down.
It meets the x-axis (real roots) only while its vertex is on or below the axis (for a > 0).

alternatives.title: Test a value of k
text: Pick a k in your interval and one outside.
Work out b² − 4ac for each; the signs must match the question.

families.title: Solving simple exponential equations by writing powers of one base
explanations: bracket (procedural): The power was not multiplied into the whole bracket: (c⁴)^(x + 2) = c^(4(x + 2)) and (c²)^(x − 1) = c^(2(x − 1)), so every term of the exponent is multiplied.
sign (procedural): A sign was lost when the x terms were collected; check by putting your answer back in.
upside-down (procedural): 4x = 5 was solved as x = 4/5; divide 5 by 4.
subtract (procedural): The powers were subtracted; (cⁱ)ˣ = c^(ix), so ix = the other power.

teach.idea: If aᵐ = aⁿ with a > 0, a ≠ 1, then m = n. So an exponential equation whose two sides are powers of the same number becomes an ordinary equation in the powers.
teach.method: Write each base as a power of one prime (9 = 3², 27 = 3³), use (cⁱ)ᵗ = c^(it) on the whole exponent, equate the exponents and solve.

alternatives.title: Take logarithms
text: Take log of both sides: (x + u) log A = (x + w) log B.
With A = cⁱ and B = cʲ, log A = i log c and log B = j log c, which gives the same equation.

alternatives.title: Check the answer
text: Put x back into both sides.
Both sides must come out as the same power of c.

families.title: Change of base: products and sums of logarithms
explanations: upside-down (procedural): log cʲ/log cⁱ = j/i was turned upside down (as i/j); it is 5/3.
two-logs (conceptual): The two reciprocals were each taken as 1/(the power); 1/log_A X = log_X A, and the two logs add to log_X(AB).
not-reciprocal (procedural): log_(AB) X was worked out instead of log_X(AB): since X = (AB)³, log_(AB) X = 3, but the sum 1/log_A X + 1/log_B X = log_X A + log_X B = log_X(AB), which is 1/3.

teach.idea: Change of base: log_a x = log x / log a (any base for both). So log_a b × log_b c = log_a c, and 1/log_a x = log_x a.
teach.method: Rewrite each logarithm as a quotient of logarithms to one base, cancel what is common, then evaluate using powers of the same prime.

alternatives.title: The chain rule for logs
text: log_a b × log_b c = log_a c: the middle number cancels, like units in a conversion.
Then write a and c as powers of one number.

alternatives.title: Check with a calculator
text: Work out each logarithm as log x ÷ log base.
Multiply or add; the result should be a simple fraction.

families.title: Integrating by partial fractions or by decomposition
explanations: cover-up-sign (procedural): In the cover-up step the other factor was worked out the wrong way round, so both partial-fraction numerators came out with the wrong sign.
swapped (procedural): A and B were swapped; A goes with x − 4, found by putting x = 4.
x-term-left-out (procedural): The 1 left after dividing was not integrated; ∫ 1 dx = x is part of the answer.
remainder-sign (procedural): The remainder was worked out as 4 − (5); x + 4 = (x − 5) + (4 + 5).

teach.idea: A fraction whose denominator factorises splits into simple fractions A/(x − a), each of which integrates to A log|x − a|. If the top has the same degree as the bottom, divide first.
teach.method: Factorise the denominator, find A and B (put x = a, then x = b), then integrate each part: ∫ A/(x − a) dx = A log|x − a|. For (x + k)/(x − a), write it as 1 + (a + k)/(x − a).

alternatives.title: Check by differentiating
text: Differentiate your answer: d/dx log|x − a| = 1/(x − a).
Add the results over a common denominator: you must get the integrand back.

alternatives.title: Compare coefficients
text: Write px + q = A(x − b) + B(x − a).
Matching the x terms and the constants gives two equations for A and B.

families.title: Reading an interval from its number-line picture
explanations: dots-swapped (conceptual): Filled and hollow dots were read the other way round: a filled dot means the end IS in the set (square bracket, ≤), a hollow dot that it is not (round bracket, <).
all-closed (procedural): Every end was written with a square bracket; look at each dot: only filled dots belong to the set.
direction (conceptual): The arrow was read the wrong way: the shading goes to the left, towards −∞.
inside (conceptual): The unshaded middle was written; the set is the shaded part, the two outer pieces.

teach.idea: On a number line, the shaded part is the set; a filled dot at an end means the end belongs to it ([ ] or ≤), a hollow dot that it does not (( ) or <), and an arrow that it goes on to ∞ or −∞ (always a round bracket).
teach.method: Read the left end and its dot, then the right end and its dot (or the arrow), and write the smaller end first. Two shaded pieces are joined with ∪.

alternatives.title: Test a few numbers
text: Pick a number inside the shading, one outside, and each end.
Your interval must contain exactly the numbers that are shaded (and the filled ends).

alternatives.title: Say it in words first
text: 'All numbers from −2, including −2, up to 3, not including 3' is [−2, 3).
Then turn each part of the sentence into a bracket.

families.title: Inserting arithmetic means between two numbers
explanations: divide-by-k (conceptual): The difference 62 − 20 was split into 5 equal parts; 5 means make 6 gaps between 20 and 62.
count-ends-as-gaps (procedural): The difference was split into 7 parts, as if the two given numbers were gaps too; there are 7 terms but only 6 gaps.
ends-listed (procedural): The two given numbers were listed as well; the means are only the numbers in between.

teach.idea: Inserting k arithmetic means between a and b makes an arithmetic progression of k + 2 terms with a first and b last, so b = a + (k + 1)d.
teach.method: Find d = (b − a)/(k + 1), then add d to a again and again to get the k means.

alternatives.title: Equal jumps on a number line
text: Mark a and b on a number line. The k means cut the distance into k + 1 equal jumps.
One jump is (b − a)/(k + 1); jump from a to get each mean.

families.title: Inserting geometric means between two numbers
explanations: arithmetic-means (conceptual): Equal differences were used; geometric means go up (or down) by the same FACTOR, not the same amount.
ends-listed (procedural): The two given numbers were listed as well; the means are only the numbers in between.
root-k (procedural): The ratio was found as the square root of 9/576; with 2 means there are 3 steps, so it is the cube root.

teach.idea: Inserting k geometric means between a and b makes a geometric progression of k + 2 terms, so b = a·r^(k + 1).
teach.method: Find r = (b/a)^(1/(k + 1)) (the positive root, since the means are positive), then multiply a by r again and again.

alternatives.title: The powers of r form an AP
text: The terms are a·r⁰, a·r¹, …, a·r^(k + 1): the powers 0, 1, …, k + 1 are equally spaced.
So b/a is r to the power (number of steps); try r = 2, 3, … until r^(k + 1) = b/a.

families.title: The least value of ax + b/x by AM ≥ GM
explanations: forgot-two (procedural): Only the GM √(360) was given; AM ≥ GM says (ax + b/x)/2 ≥ √(ab), so the sum itself is at least 2√(ab).
gave-x (procedural): The value of x where the least value happens (x = √(b/a)) was given, not the least value of the expression.
x-is-one (conceptual): x = 1 was put in; the least value is where the two terms are equal (ax = b/x), not at x = 1.

teach.idea: For positive p and q, (p + q)/2 ≥ √(pq), with equality exactly when p = q. Here p = ax and q = b/x have a fixed product ab.
teach.method: Multiply the two terms: (ax)(b/x) = ab. So ax + b/x ≥ 2√(ab), and the value 2√(ab) is reached when ax = b/x, i.e. x = √(b/a).

alternatives.title: Complete the square
text: A square is never negative, so the least value is 2√(ab), when the square is 0.

families.title: A coefficient in the binomial series for a rational index
explanations: power-of-k-left-out (procedural): The coefficient of yʳ in (1 + y)ⁿ was given, but y = 3x, so it must be multiplied by (3)³.
rising-factors (conceptual): The factors were taken as n(n + 1)(n + 2)…; the general term uses n(n − 1)(n − 2)… even when n is negative or a fraction.
no-factorial (recall): The product n(n − 1)… was not divided by 3!.
sign-of-k (procedural): The minus sign in 1 − x was dropped; (−1)³ is negative for an odd power.

teach.idea: For any rational n and |y| < 1, (1 + y)ⁿ = 1 + ny + n(n − 1)y²/2! + n(n − 1)(n − 2)y³/3! + …; when n is not a whole number the series never stops.
teach.method: The coefficient of yʳ is n(n − 1)…(n − r + 1)/r!. Put y = kx, so the coefficient of xʳ is that number times kʳ (keep the sign of k).

alternatives.title: Write out the first terms
text: Write 1 + n(kx) + [n(n − 1)/2](kx)² + [n(n − 1)(n − 2)/6](kx)³ with your n and k.
Simplify each bracket, then read off the term you need.

families.title: A coefficient in the exponential or logarithmic series
explanations: no-factorial (recall): The term was not divided by 5!; e^y = 1 + y + y²/2! + y³/3! + …
k-not-raised (procedural): The 4/3 inside was not raised to the power 5: the term is (4x/3)⁵.
divide-by-r (recall): The term was divided by 5, as in the log series; the exponential series divides by 5! = 120.
signs-not-alternating (recall): Every term of log(1 + y) was taken as positive; the signs alternate: y − y²/2 + y³/3 − …
factorial-for-log (recall): The term was divided by 5!; in the log series it is divided by 5 (the exponential series has the factorials).

teach.idea: eʸ = 1 + y + y²/2! + y³/3! + … for every y, and log(1 + y) = y − y²/2 + y³/3 − … for |y| < 1.
teach.method: Put y = kx. The coefficient of xʳ is kʳ/r! for eᵏˣ, and (−1)^(r + 1) kʳ/r for log(1 + kx).

alternatives.title: Where the log series comes from
text: d/dy log(1 + y) = 1/(1 + y) = 1 − y + y² − … (a geometric series).
Integrating term by term gives y − y²/2 + y³/3 − …, so the divisors are 1, 2, 3, … and the signs alternate.

families.title: The general term of a sequence from its first terms
explanations: n-not-n-minus-1 (procedural): aₙ = a + nd was used; the first term has no d added, so aₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
difference-reversed (procedural): The difference was worked out as a₁ − a₂ = −9; the common difference is a₂ − a₁ = 9 (later term minus earlier term).
constant-left-out (procedural): Only the step 9n was written; 9n gives 9 at n = 1, but the first term is 18, so a constant 9 must be added.
treated-as-ap (conceptual): Only the first difference was used, as if the sequence were an AP; here the differences themselves change, so aₙ has an n² term.
whole-second-difference (procedural): The coefficient of n² was taken as the second difference (2); it is half of it, because n² itself has second difference 2.
square-only (procedural): Only n² was matched to the first term; the n term is needed too (check a₂ and a₃).

teach.idea: A general term is a rule that gives aₙ straight from n. If the differences are constant (d), aₙ = dn + (a₁ − d); if the second differences are a constant 2, aₙ = n² + bn + c.
teach.method: Write the differences. Constant: the coefficient of n is d, then fix the constant from a₁. Second differences 2: write n² + bn + c and find b and c from a₁ and a₂.

alternatives.title: Test your rule
text: Put n = 1, 2, 3 into your rule and compare with the given terms.
If a₁ fits but a₂ does not, the coefficient of n is wrong; if all are off by the same number, the constant is wrong.

families.title: Writing an arithmetic series in sigma notation
explanations: no-shift (procedural): The k-th term was taken as a + kd; with k starting at 1 that skips the first term. It is a + (k − 1)d.
start-at-zero (procedural): k was started at 0 but still run to 12; that gives 13 terms.
one-short (conceptual): The upper limit was taken one too small; it is the number of terms, 12.
last-term-as-limit (conceptual): The last term was used as the upper limit; the upper limit counts the terms (12).

teach.idea: Σ (k = 1 to m) t(k) means t(1) + t(2) + … + t(m): the limits count the terms and the expression t(k) gives each one.
teach.method: Find the k-th term (for an AP, a + (k − 1)d), take the number of terms as the upper limit, and check by putting k = 1 and k = m.

alternatives.title: Expand each option
text: For each option write the terms for the lowest and highest k, and count how many values k takes.
The right option starts with the first term, ends with the last term and has the right number of terms.

families.title: A telescoping sum
explanations: wrong-last-term (procedural): The last fraction left after cancelling was taken as 1/120; that one cancels. The one left over is 1/124.
added-parts (procedural): The two remaining fractions were added; they come from a − sign in each partial fraction, so they are subtracted.
factor-left-out (procedural): The factor 1/4 from the partial fractions was left out: 1/((4k + …)(4k + … + 4)) = (1/4)[… − …].

teach.idea: If each term is a difference f(k) − f(k + 1), then in the sum all the middle parts cancel and only f(1) − f(n + 1) is left.
teach.method: Split 1/((dk + e)(dk + e + d)) into (1/d)[1/(dk + e) − 1/(dk + e + d)], write the first two and last terms to see the cancelling, and keep the first and the last fraction.

alternatives.title: Spot the pattern in partial sums
text: For 1/(k(k + 1)) the sums of 1, 2, 3 terms are 1/2, 2/3, 3/4.
The pattern n/(n + 1) is exactly 1 − 1/(n + 1): the first part minus the last part.

families.title: A sum using the standard sums of k, k² and k³
explanations: constant-once (conceptual): The constant 1 was added only once; Σ (k = 1 to 6) 1 adds it 6 times, giving 6.
square-of-sum (recall): Σk² was taken as (Σk)²; that is the rule for Σk³. Σk² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6.
one-short (procedural): The sum was stopped at k = 5; k runs up to 6.
cubes-over-two (recall): Σk³ was taken as n²(n + 1)²/2; it is [n(n + 1)/2]² = n²(n + 1)²/4.

teach.idea: Σ is linear: Σ(a·f(k) + b·g(k)) = aΣf(k) + bΣg(k), and the sum of a constant c over n terms is cn.
teach.method: Split into Σk³, Σk², Σk and Σ1, use [n(n + 1)/2]², n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, n(n + 1)/2 and n, then combine with the coefficients.

alternatives.title: Check with a small case
text: Put n = 2 into your working and compare with adding the first two terms by hand.
If they disagree, check the constant term (it is added n times) and which formula you used for each power.

families.title: Counting the elements of Cartesian products
explanations: upper-end-included (procedural): The end 8 was counted in A, but x < 8 leaves it out; A has 6 elements.
added (conceptual): The numbers of elements were added; each element of A pairs with each element of B, so n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B).
third-added (procedural): n(A × B) was found, then n(C) was added; A × B × C has a triple for every pair and every element of C.

product-commutes (conceptual): A × B and B × A were taken to be the same set, so only 30 pairs were counted; (1, a) is in A × B but (a, 1) is in B × A — different pairs — and no pair is in both, because A and B have no common element.
square-of-union (procedural): (A ∪ B) × (A ∪ B) was counted (11²); it also contains pairs like (1, 2) and (a, b) that are in neither A × B nor B × A.
union (conceptual): The union (A × B) ∪ (A × C) was counted; the intersection keeps only pairs whose second entry is in both B and C.
forgot-a (procedural): Only B ∩ C was counted; each of its 4 elements pairs with each of the 6 elements of A.

teach.idea: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Each of the n(A) first entries goes with each of the n(B) second entries, so n(A × B) = n(A)·n(B).
teach.method: Count each set first (list it if it is in set-builder form), then multiply. A × B and B × A have the same number of pairs, but different pairs: (a, b) ≠ (b, a) unless a = b.

alternatives.title: A grid of pairs
text: Draw a grid with a row for each element of A and a column for each element of B.
Each cell is one ordered pair, so the number of cells is rows × columns.

families.title: Reading the sets from a Cartesian product
explanations: swapped (conceptual): The first entries were read; B is made of the SECOND entries of the pairs in A × B.
all-numbers (procedural): Every number in the pairs was listed; only one position of each pair belongs to this set.

teach.idea: In A × B every pair has its first entry from A and its second entry from B, and every combination appears.
teach.method: To find A, collect the first entries of the pairs, writing each value once; to find B, collect the second entries.

alternatives.title: Put the pairs in a table
text: Make a table with one row for each different first entry and one column for each different second entry.
The row labels form A and the column labels form B.

families.title: Intersection, union and difference of intervals
explanations: reversed-difference (conceptual): B − A was found; A − B keeps the numbers of A that are NOT in B.
brackets-of-b-kept (procedural): B's own brackets were copied at the cut; when B is removed, an end that B includes is left OUT of A − B, and an end B leaves out stays IN.
ends-all-closed (procedural): Every end was written with a square bracket; check each end: is that number itself in the set?
intersection-instead (conceptual): The intersection was found; A ∪ B keeps every number that is in EITHER interval.
union-instead (conceptual): The union was found; A ∩ B keeps only the numbers that are in BOTH intervals.

teach.idea: An interval is a set of real numbers. A ∩ B keeps the numbers in both, A ∪ B the numbers in either, and A − B the numbers of A that are not in B. A square bracket includes its end; a round one leaves it out.
teach.method: Draw both intervals on one number line, shade what the operation keeps, then read off the ends, deciding for each end whether that number itself is in the result.

alternatives.title: Test points on the number line
text: Mark all four ends. Test one number in each gap and each end itself: is it in A? in B?
Keep the points the operation wants and join them into intervals.

families.title: Solving a double linear inequality
explanations: brackets-not-swapped (conceptual): The ends were swapped after dividing by −2, but the brackets were kept where they were; reversing the inequalities moves the strict end to the other side, so the brackets swap sides too.
middle-only (procedural): 9 was taken away from the middle only; whatever is done to the middle must be done to all three parts.
both-included (procedural): Both ends were included; only the end that comes from ≤ belongs to the solution set.

teach.idea: A double inequality is two inequalities at once; do the same thing to all three parts. Dividing by a negative number reverses both signs, so the left and right ends swap places.
teach.method: Subtract b from all three parts, divide all three by a (reversing the signs if a < 0), rewrite with the smaller number on the left, and use [ ] for ≤ and ( ) for <.

alternatives.title: Split into two inequalities
text: Solve p < ax + b and ax + b ≤ q separately.
The solution set is where both hold: the overlap of the two answers on a number line.

families.title: Matching a set of real numbers with its interval notation
explanations: strict-or-not (conceptual): Strict and non-strict were mixed up: > or < gives a round bracket, ≥ or ≤ a square one.
direction (conceptual): The direction was reversed: x > 6 means numbers to the right of 6, up to ∞.
brackets-swapped (conceptual): Square and round brackets were swapped: [ ] means the end IS included (≤), ( ) means it is not (<).
one-end-read (procedural): Only one end was checked; decide separately for the left end and for the right end whether it is included.

teach.idea: [ or ] means the end belongs to the set (≤, ≥); ( or ) means it does not (<, >). ∞ always gets a round bracket because it is not a real number.
teach.method: Look at each end on its own: is that number in the set? Then write the smaller end on the left and the larger on the right.
