alternatives.title: Filled and open dots
text: On a number line a filled dot is an included end ([ ]) and an open dot an excluded end (( )).
Draw the set, then translate each dot into a bracket.

families.title: The inverse of a linear or fractional linear function
explanations: reciprocal (conceptual): f⁻¹ was taken as 1/f(x); the inverse UNDOES f (f(f⁻¹(x)) = x), it is not the reciprocal.
undo-wrong-order (procedural): The steps were undone in the wrong order: f multiplies by 5 first and then adds 5, so f⁻¹ first takes away 5 and then divides by 5.
sign-of-b (procedural): 5 was moved across without changing its sign.
sign-slip (procedural): A sign was lost when the x terms were collected on one side; check by putting your answer into f.

teach.idea: f⁻¹ undoes f: y = f(x) exactly when x = f⁻¹(y). It exists because f is one-one and onto its codomain.
teach.method: Write y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y (for a fraction, multiply up and collect the x terms), then rename y as x.

alternatives.title: Check by composing
text: Pick a number, say x = 1, and work out f(1).
Put f(1) into your f⁻¹: you must get 1 back. Try a second number to be sure.

families.title: A value of an inverse function
explanations: f-not-inverse (conceptual): f(1) was worked out; f⁻¹(1) is the x for which f(x) = 1.
reciprocal (conceptual): 1/f(1) was given; f⁻¹ is the inverse function, not the reciprocal.
sign-slip (procedural): A sign was lost when the x terms were collected; check by putting your answer into f.

teach.idea: f⁻¹(t) is the number x with f(x) = t: the inverse runs the function backwards.
teach.method: Set (ax + b)/(cx + d) = t, multiply both sides by cx + d, collect the x terms and divide.

alternatives.title: Find f⁻¹(x) first
text: Find the formula f⁻¹(x) = (b − dx)/(cx − a).
Then put x = t into it.

families.title: Maximising by the corner-point method
explanations: infeasible-corner (conceptual): An axis intercept that breaks the other constraint was used as a corner; every corner must satisfy ALL the constraints.
intersection-only (procedural): Only the point where the two lines meet was checked; Z must be worked out at every corner of the feasible region.

teach.idea: A linear objective takes its greatest and least values over a bounded feasible region at corner points of the region.
teach.method: Draw each constraint line, find the corner points (axis intercepts and where lines meet) that satisfy every constraint, work out Z at each, and take the greatest.

alternatives.title: Slide the objective line
text: Draw px + qy = k for a small k and slide it outwards, keeping it parallel.
The last point of the region it touches gives the maximum.

families.title: Minimising over an unbounded feasible region
explanations: origin (conceptual): The origin was used as a corner; (0, 0) does not satisfy the ≥ constraints, so it is not in the feasible region.
infeasible-corner (conceptual): An axis intercept that breaks the other constraint was used; every corner must satisfy ALL the constraints.
intersection-only (procedural): Only the point where the two lines meet was checked; Z must be worked out at every corner.

teach.idea: With ≥ constraints the feasible region is unbounded, but if p, q > 0 then Z = px + qy still has a least value, at a corner point.
teach.method: Find the corner points (the intercepts that satisfy both constraints, and the meeting point), work out Z at each and take the least. For an unbounded region, check that the half-plane px + qy < (that value) has no point in common with the region.

alternatives.title: Slide the cost line inwards
text: Draw px + qy = k for a large k and slide it towards the origin.
The last point of the region it touches gives the minimum.

families.title: The optimal corner point of a linear programme
explanations: infeasible-corner (conceptual): An axis intercept that breaks the other constraint was chosen; check every corner in ALL the constraints.
intersection-only (procedural): The meeting point of the two lines was chosen without comparing Z at the other corners.

teach.idea: The optimal solution is the feasible point where Z is best; for a linear Z it is a corner point of the feasible region.
teach.method: List the corner points that satisfy every constraint, work out Z at each, and choose the corner with the greatest Z.

alternatives.title: A corner table
text: Make a table: corner point, then the value of Z.
Cross out any point that breaks a constraint before comparing.

families.title: Multiplying two 2 × 2 matrices
explanations: entry-by-entry (conceptual): Matching entries were multiplied; in a matrix product each entry is a row of A times a column of B, added up.
order-reversed (conceptual): BA was found; matrix multiplication is not commutative, and AB uses the rows of A with the columns of B.
row-by-row (procedural): Rows of A were multiplied with rows of B; use the COLUMNS of B.

teach.idea: Entry (i, j) of AB combines row i of A with column j of B: multiply matching entries and add. In general AB ≠ BA.
teach.method: For each of the four entries take a row of A and a column of B, multiply pairwise and add; keep the signs.

alternatives.title: Column by column
text: Column j of AB is A times column j of B.
So find A[e, g] and A[f, h] (as column vectors) and stand them side by side.

families.title: Solving a matrix equation kX ± A = B
explanations: not-divided (procedural): B + A is 4X, not X; every entry must still be divided by 4.
sign-of-a (procedural): A was moved to the other side without changing its sign: 4X = B + A.

teach.idea: Matrices are equal when every pair of matching entries is equal, so a matrix equation is solved like a number equation, entry by entry.
teach.method: Move A to the other side (subtract it, or add it if it was subtracted), then divide every entry by k.

alternatives.title: Four small equations
text: Write X = [[p, q], [r, s]] and compare entries: k·p ± a₁₁ = b₁₁, and so on.
Solve each of the four equations for one unknown.

families.title: A matrix product as a total bill
explanations: item-left-out (procedural): The third item was left out; a row of 3 quantities times a column of 3 prices has 3 products to add.
not-added (procedural): Each quantity was multiplied by its price, but the three products in a row were not added; QP has one entry per row of Q, the sum of those products.
rows-swapped (procedural): The two rows were written in the wrong order; row 1 of QP comes from row 1 of Q.
prices-reversed (procedural): The prices were paired with the quantities in the wrong order (the column read from the bottom up); the first entry of a row goes with the first entry of the column.

teach.idea: A row of quantities times a column of prices is a bill: each quantity is multiplied by its own price and the products are added. QP does this for every row at once.
teach.method: Check the orders: (2 × 3)(3 × 1) gives 2 × 1. For each row of Q, multiply the three entries by the three prices and add.

alternatives.title: Write it as two bills
text: Write each shop's bill as quantity × price + quantity × price + quantity × price.
The two totals, one under the other, are the column matrix QP.

families.title: Solving three equations by X = A⁻¹B
explanations: cofactors-not-transposed (procedural): The matrix of cofactors was used instead of its transpose; adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix.
det-sign (procedural): |A| was found with the wrong sign; check the signs in the expansion (+, −, + along the first row).
not-divided (procedural): adj A · B was not divided by |A|; A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|.

teach.idea: A system AX = B with |A| ≠ 0 has exactly one solution, X = A⁻¹B, and A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A.
teach.method: Find |A|; find the nine cofactors and transpose them to get adj A; multiply adj A by B and divide by |A|.

alternatives.title: Cramer's rule
text: x = |A₁|/|A|, y = |A₂|/|A|, z = |A₃|/|A|, where Aᵢ is A with column i replaced by B.
Check by substituting the values back into each equation.

families.title: Solving two equations with an inverse matrix
explanations: adj-signs (procedural): In the adjoint the off-diagonal entries were not negated; for [[a, b], [c, d]] the adjoint is [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
swapped (procedural): x and y were written the wrong way round; X = [[x], [y]], so the first entry of A⁻¹B is x.
not-divided (procedural): adj A · B was not divided by |A|; A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|.

teach.idea: If |A| ≠ 0 then A has an inverse and AX = B gives X = A⁻¹B. For a 2 × 2 matrix, A⁻¹ = (1/|A|)[[d, −b], [−c, a]].
teach.method: Find |A| = ad − bc, write the adjoint (swap a and d, negate b and c), multiply it by B and divide by |A|.

alternatives.title: Check in both equations
text: Put your x and y into the first equation, then the second.
Both totals must match B; if one does not, look again at the adjoint's signs.

families.title: A cubic whose roots are in progression
explanations: sign-of-sum (recall): The product of the roots was taken with the wrong sign; for ax³ + bx² + cx + d it is −d/a.
middle-only (procedural): Only the middle root was found; divide by (x − middle root) and solve the quadratic left over for the other two.

teach.idea: Roots in AP can be written a − d, a, a + d: their sum is 3a. Roots in GP can be written a/r, a, ar: their product is a³. Vieta then gives the middle root.
teach.method: For an AP, a = (−b/leading coefficient)/3; for a GP, a³ = −(constant)/(leading coefficient). Check a is a root, divide by (x − a) and solve the quadratic.

alternatives.title: Synthetic division
text: Once the middle root a is known, divide the coefficients by a in a synthetic-division table.
The bottom row gives the quadratic; factorise it for the other two roots.

families.title: Solving a cubic with the rational root theorem
explanations: leading-coefficient-ignored (procedural): The root 5/3 was given as 5: a factor of the leading coefficient 3 belongs in the denominator.
signs-reversed (recall): All the signs were reversed; if x − s is a factor then x = s (not −s) is a root.

teach.idea: If p/q (in lowest terms) is a root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient.
teach.method: List the possible p/q, test them (whole numbers first), divide by the factor you find and solve the quadratic that is left.

alternatives.title: Quick tests first
text: If the coefficients add to 0, x = 1 is a root; if p(−1) = 0, x = −1 is a root.
Each root found lowers the degree by one.

families.title: A cubic equation from a volume
explanations: cube-root (conceptual): The equation was treated as x³ = 84280, leaving out the terms in x² and x; for x > 0 those terms are positive, so the root is less than ∛84280 ≈ 44.
linear-only (procedural): Only the x term was kept: 24x = 82560 gives 3440, but x³ and 11x² also add to the left side, so the root is much smaller.

teach.idea: x(x + a)(x + b) = V expands to a cubic with one sign change, so it has exactly one positive root; a whole-number root divides the constant term V.
teach.method: Estimate: x is a little less than ∛V. Test the divisors of V near that estimate until one gives V.

alternatives.title: A trial table
text: Make a table of x and x(x + a)(x + b) for x = 1, 2, 3, …
The volume grows as x grows, so stop when you reach V.

families.title: Finding the other roots from a surd root
explanations: both-signs-changed (conceptual): Both parts of the root changed sign; the conjugate of 4 + √7 changes only the sign of the surd: 4 − √7.
rational-part-changed (conceptual): The sign of the whole-number part was changed; it is the surd part whose sign changes.
sum-sign (recall): The sum of the roots was taken as +(coefficient of x²); it is −(coefficient of x²).

teach.idea: If a polynomial has rational coefficients and u + √w is a root (√w irrational), then its conjugate u − √w is a root too.
teach.method: Multiply (x − (u + √w))(x − (u − √w)) = x² − 2ux + (u² − w), divide the cubic by this quadratic, and read the third root from the linear factor left over.

alternatives.title: Use the sum of the roots
text: The three roots add up to −(coefficient of x²).
The two conjugate roots add up to 2u, so the third root is −(coefficient of x²) − 2u.

families.title: Descartes' rule of signs
explanations: negatives-counted (conceptual): The number of negative coefficients was counted; the rule counts the CHANGES of sign from one non-zero coefficient to the next.
p-not-p-of-minus-x (procedural): The sign changes of p(x) were counted; negative roots need p(−x), where the odd powers change sign.
real-count-given (conceptual): The greatest possible number of real roots (1 + 4 = 5) was given; the question asks how many roots at least are NOT real: 5 − 5.
positive-only (procedural): Only the positive roots were taken away from 5; the negative roots (sign changes of p(−x)) are real too.
zeros-as-changes (procedural): Missing terms were counted as sign changes; skip the zero coefficients.

teach.idea: The number of positive roots of p(x) = 0 is at most the number of sign changes in its coefficients (and differs from it by an even number). For negative roots, count the changes in p(−x).
teach.method: Write the signs of the non-zero coefficients in order, skipping zeros, and count the changes. For p(−x), first change the sign of each odd-power coefficient.

alternatives.title: A row of signs
text: Under each power x⁵, x⁴, …, x⁰ write + or − (leave a gap for a missing power).
Draw a mark between each neighbouring pair of signs that differ; count the marks.

families.title: Symmetric functions of the roots of a cubic
explanations: product-sign (recall): αβγ was taken as +d/a; for a cubic it is −d/a.
pair-term-missing (procedural): The expansion missed the αβ + βγ + γα terms: (α + 1)(β + 1)(γ + 1) = αβγ + Σαβ + Σα + 1.
pair-sum-sign (procedural): (α + β + γ)² = Σα² + 2Σαβ, so Σα² = (Σα)² − 2Σαβ; the 2Σαβ was added instead of subtracted.
square-of-sum (conceptual): Σα² was taken as (Σα)²; squaring the sum also gives the cross terms 2(αβ + βγ + γα).
reciprocal-of-sum (conceptual): 1/(α + β + γ) was found; the sum of reciprocals is (αβ + βγ + γα)/αβγ.

teach.idea: For ax³ + bx² + cx + d = 0 with roots α, β, γ: α + β + γ = −b/a, αβ + βγ + γα = c/a and αβγ = −d/a.
teach.method: Rewrite the expression using only these three sums (e.g. α² + β² + γ² = (Σα)² − 2Σαβ, 1/α + 1/β + 1/γ = Σαβ/αβγ), then substitute.

alternatives.title: The signs alternate
text: Divide by a: x³ − (Σα)x² + (Σαβ)x − αβγ.
So the signs go −, +, − as you move along the coefficients.

families.title: Forming a quadratic with transformed roots
explanations: k-not-squared (procedural): The product was multiplied by −2; (−2α)(−2β) = 4αβ.
sum-sign (recall): The x coefficient was written as +(sum of roots); it is −(sum of roots).
wrong-direction (procedural): The shift went the wrong way: if y = α − 1, the new sum is (α + β) − 2.
identity-sign (procedural): α² + β² was taken as (α + β)² + 2αβ; it is (α + β)² − 2αβ.
product-not-squared (procedural): The product α²β² was taken as αβ; it is (αβ)².

teach.idea: A quadratic with leading coefficient 1 and zeros r₁, r₂ is x² − (r₁ + r₂)x + r₁r₂. For x² + px + q, α + β = −p and αβ = q.
teach.method: Write the new sum and product in terms of α + β and αβ (e.g. α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ), substitute, and write x² − (sum)x + (product).

alternatives.title: Substitute for x
text: If y = α + k then α = y − k: put x = y − k into x² + px + q = 0 and expand.
If y = kα, put x = y/k and multiply through by k² to clear the fractions.

families.title: The inverse of a 2 × 2 matrix
explanations: adjoint-only (procedural): The adjoint was given; A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|, so every entry must be divided by −24.
no-negation (procedural): a and d were swapped but b and c were not negated; adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
wrong-swap (procedural): The wrong pair was swapped: a and d change places, b and c only change sign.
determinant-added (prerequisite): The determinant was found as ad + bc; it is ad − bc.

teach.idea: A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A, and it exists only when |A| ≠ 0. For [[a, b], [c, d]], adj A = [[d, −b], [−c, a]].
teach.method: Find |A| = ad − bc; swap a and d, change the signs of b and c; divide every entry by |A|.

alternatives.title: Row-reduce [A | I]
text: Write A and I side by side and use row operations to turn A into I.
The same operations turn I into A⁻¹; check that AA⁻¹ = I.

families.title: The adjoint of a 3 × 3 matrix
explanations: not-transposed (procedural): The matrix of cofactors was given; adj A is its TRANSPOSE (rows become columns).
no-signs (procedural): The minors were used without the signs (−1)^(i + j); the cofactor of a position with i + j odd is minus its minor.

teach.idea: adj A is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors, and A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I, so A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| when |A| ≠ 0.
teach.method: For each entry find its minor (the 2 × 2 determinant left when its row and column are deleted), attach the sign (−1)^(i + j), then transpose the whole matrix.

alternatives.title: Check with A(adj A)
text: Multiply A by your adj A: every off-diagonal entry must be 0.
The diagonal entries must all equal |A|.

families.title: The rank of a 3 × 4 matrix
explanations: rows-counted (conceptual): The non-zero rows of the matrix as given were counted; first reduce it: one row is a combination of the other two, so it becomes a zero row.
one-row-removed (procedural): Only one row was reduced to zero; the third row is also a multiple of the first.
columns-counted (conceptual): The number of columns was taken; the rank is at most the number of rows (3) and is the number of non-zero rows in echelon form.

teach.idea: The rank is the number of non-zero rows in an echelon form: the number of rows that are not combinations of the others.
teach.method: Use row operations (swap rows, Rᵢ → Rᵢ − kRⱼ) to make zeros below each leading entry, then count the rows that are not all zero.

alternatives.title: The largest non-zero minor
text: The rank is the order of the largest square sub-matrix with a non-zero determinant.
Try the 3 × 3 minors (leave out one column at a time); if all are 0, try 2 × 2 minors.

families.title: Writing out the ordered pairs (or triples) of a Cartesian product
explanations: order-swapped (conceptual): The entries were written the wrong way round; in A × B × C the first entry comes from the first set named.
matched-only (conceptual): Only the first element was paired with the first, the second with the second; a Cartesian product pairs EVERY element of the first set with EVERY element of the second.
pair-missed (procedural): One triple was missed; there must be 8 of them (the product of the numbers of elements).
pair-once (conceptual): Each pair of different elements was written only once; (a, b) and (b, a) are different ordered pairs, and both belong to A × A.
same-left-out (conceptual): Pairs like (a, a) were left out; A × A contains every ordered pair from A, including pairs with equal entries.
third-set-ignored (conceptual): Only A × B was written; A × B × C is made of ordered TRIPLES (a, b, c).

teach.idea: A × B is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B; A × B × C is the set of all ordered triples (a, b, c). Order matters: (1, p) is not (p, 1).
teach.method: Take the first element of the first set and pair it with every element of the second set; then the next element; and so on. Check the count: n(A) × n(B) (× n(C)).

alternatives.title: A table of pairs
text: Write the first set down the side and the second across the top.
Each cell is one ordered pair; read them row by row.

alternatives.title: A tree for triples
text: Branch for each element of A, then for each element of B, then of C.
Each path from the root gives one ordered triple.

families.title: Equal ordered pairs
explanations: not-multiplied (procedural): x/3 = 2 was found, but not multiplied by 3 to get x.
sign-of-u (procedural): 3 was moved across without changing its sign.
half-forgotten (procedural): Adding the equations gives 2x; it must be divided by 2.
swapped (procedural): x and y were written the wrong way round; the answer is (x, y).
sign (procedural): A sign was lost when one equation was subtracted from the other; check by substituting.

teach.idea: (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c AND b = d: the order of the entries matters, so each position is compared on its own.
teach.method: Write first entry = first entry and second entry = second entry, then solve the two equations (together, if both contain x and y).

alternatives.title: Check by substituting
text: Put your x and y back into both entries of the left-hand pair.
You must get exactly the right-hand pair, in the same order.

families.title: Constructing a matrix from a rule aᵢⱼ (and its transpose)
explanations: from-zero (procedural): The rows and columns were numbered from 0; they start from 1, so the top-left entry is a₁₁.
not-transposed (procedural): A was given; the transpose Aᵀ turns each row of A into a column.
i-j-swapped (conceptual): i and j were swapped: i is the ROW number and j the COLUMN number, so a₁₂ is in row 1, column 2.

teach.idea: A = [aᵢⱼ] of order m × n has m rows and n columns; aᵢⱼ is the entry in row i and column j. The transpose Aᵀ has the rows of A as its columns, so it has order n × m.
teach.method: Draw an empty m × n grid. For each cell put in its row number i and column number j and work out the rule. For Aᵀ, write the first row of A as the first column, and so on.

alternatives.title: Label the cells
text: Write the label ij in each cell first (11, 12, 13 / 21, 22, 23).
Then replace each label by the value of the rule.

families.title: The order and the type of a matrix
explanations: columns-first (recall): The number of columns was given first; the order is (number of rows) × (number of columns).
entries-counted (conceptual): The number of entries was used; the order gives the numbers of rows and of columns.
confused-0-1 (conceptual): A single row was called a column matrix; a row matrix has one row, a column matrix one column.
confused-1-0 (conceptual): A single column was called a row matrix; a column matrix has one column.
confused-2-3 (conceptual): A square matrix with a non-zero entry off the diagonal was called diagonal; a diagonal matrix has zeros everywhere off the main diagonal.
confused-3-4 (conceptual): A diagonal matrix with different diagonal entries was called scalar; a scalar matrix has all its diagonal entries equal.
confused-4-5 (conceptual): A scalar matrix was called the identity; the identity has 1s on the diagonal.
confused-5-4 (conceptual): The identity was described only as a scalar matrix 'not the identity'; it IS the identity (scalar with k = 1).
confused-6-5 (conceptual): The zero matrix was called the identity; every entry of a zero matrix is 0.
confused-7-2 (conceptual): A rectangular matrix was called square; a square matrix has as many rows as columns.

teach.idea: The order of a matrix is rows × columns. A row matrix has one row, a column matrix one column, a square matrix as many rows as columns. A diagonal matrix is square with zeros off the main diagonal; a scalar matrix is diagonal with equal diagonal entries; the identity is scalar with 1s; a zero matrix has every entry 0.
teach.method: Count the rows, then the columns. Then check, from the most general to the most special: square? zeros off the diagonal? equal diagonal entries? are they 1? (or are all entries 0?)

alternatives.title: A ladder of types
text: square ⊃ diagonal ⊃ scalar ⊃ identity: each is a special case of the one before.
The most precise description is the lowest rung the matrix reaches.

families.title: Equality of matrices
explanations: swapped (procedural): x and y were written the wrong way round.
half-forgotten (procedural): Adding the two equations gives 2x; divide by 2.
halving (procedural): 2y = 12 was solved by subtracting 2; divide by 2.
sign (procedural): A number was moved across without changing its sign.

teach.idea: Two matrices are equal when they have the same order and every pair of corresponding entries is equal.
teach.method: Set each entry on the left equal to the entry in the same position on the right, then solve the equations you get.

alternatives.title: Check every entry
text: Put your values back into the left-hand matrix.
Every entry must match the right-hand matrix, position by position.

families.title: Modelling a situation with a matrix product
explanations: columns-swapped (procedural): The two columns of the needs matrix were put the other way round, so the totals came out in the wrong order; follow the order the question asks for.
rows-swapped (procedural): The producers were put in the other order; row 1 of the product comes from row 1 of the production matrix.
item-left-out (procedural): The third item was left out of each total; a row of 3 quantities times a column of 3 needs has 3 products to add.

teach.idea: When each of several producers makes several items, and each item needs fixed amounts of resources, the totals are a matrix product: (production matrix) × (needs per item matrix). The inner orders must match: (2 × 3)(3 × 2).
teach.method: Write one row per producer and one column per item for the production; one row per item and one column per resource for the needs. Multiply: each entry is a row of quantities times a column of needs, added up.

alternatives.title: Write each total as a sum
text: For producer P and resource 1: (number of item 1) × (need of item 1) + … for all three items.
The four totals, arranged by producer and resource, are the product matrix.

families.title: Word problems with three unknowns, solved by the inverse, Cramer's rule or Gaussian elimination
explanations: cofactors-not-transposed (procedural): The matrix of cofactors was used instead of its transpose; adj A is the TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix.
back-order (procedural): The values were written in the order they were found (z first); write the answer as (x, y, z).
det-sign (procedural): Δ was worked out with the wrong sign (check the + − + signs of the expansion); every value then changes sign.

teach.idea: Each fact in the story gives one linear equation in the three unknowns; together they form AX = B. With |A| ≠ 0 there is exactly one solution, found by X = A⁻¹B, by Cramer's rule (x = Δ₁/Δ, …) or by Gaussian elimination (row-reduce [A | B] and back-substitute).
teach.method: Name the unknowns (x, y, z), write one equation per fact, write A and B, then use the method asked for. Check the answer in every fact of the story.

alternatives.title: Cramer's rule
text: Δ = |A|; Δ₁ is |A| with column 1 replaced by B, and so on.
x = Δ₁/Δ, y = Δ₂/Δ, z = Δ₃/Δ.

alternatives.title: Gaussian elimination
text: Use row operations on [A | B] to make zeros below the diagonal.
Find z from the last row, then y, then x.

families.title: Linear programming: bounded, unbounded or infeasible?
explanations: corner-of-one-constraint (conceptual): Z was worked out at a corner of one constraint alone; first check that some point satisfies ALL the constraints — here none does.
intercept-as-max (conceptual): Z was worked out at the corner points, but the region goes on for ever in the direction where Z grows, so Z has no maximum.
wrong-corner (procedural): The larger corner value was chosen; compare Z at both corners and take the smaller.
unbounded-no-optimum (conceptual): An unbounded region was taken to have no optimal value; with positive costs Z still has a least value, at a corner.

teach.idea: Before using corner points, look at the feasible region. If no point satisfies every constraint, the problem is infeasible. If the region is unbounded, Z may have no maximum (or no minimum) — check whether Z can be made as large (or small) as you like inside it.
teach.method: Draw the constraints. Empty region: infeasible. Bounded region: evaluate Z at every corner. Unbounded region: evaluate Z at the corners, then test whether a better value is possible further out (for a maximum, the half-plane Z > M meets the region).

alternatives.title: Try a far-away point
text: Pick a feasible point far from the origin, such as (100, 100) if it is allowed.
If Z there beats every corner value, Z has no maximum.

families.title: Approximate values from the binomial, exponential and logarithmic series
explanations: two-terms (procedural): Only the first two terms were used; the question asks for three.
rising-factor (conceptual): The x² coefficient was taken as n(n + 1)/2; it is n(n − 1)/2, also for a negative or fractional n.
ten-forgotten (procedural): √109 = 10√(1 + 0.09); the factor 10 was left out.
no-factorial (recall): The x² term was not divided by 2! = 2; eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2! + …
signs (recall): All the terms were added; the logarithmic series alternates: x − x²/2 + x³/3 − …

teach.idea: For small x the later terms of a series are tiny, so the first few give a good approximation: (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx + n(n − 1)x²/2, eˣ ≈ 1 + x + x²/2, log(1 + x) ≈ x − x²/2 + x³/3.
teach.method: Write the number as (1 + x) with x small (√102 = 10(1 + 0.02)^(1/2)), work out each of the first terms as a decimal, and add them.

alternatives.title: How good is it?
text: With x = 0.02 the x² term is about 0.0004 and the x³ term about 0.000008.
So three terms are correct to about five decimal places.

families.title: Rotating and reflecting points with a 2 × 2 matrix
explanations: row-vector (procedural): The point was multiplied as a row, (x y)T, which uses the columns of T the wrong way; the image is T times the COLUMN [[x], [y]].
swapped (procedural): The coordinates of the image were written the wrong way round.

teach.idea: Multiplying a column [[x], [y]] by a 2 × 2 matrix moves the point (x, y); the matrix [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]] turns the plane through θ anticlockwise about the origin. Rotation and reflection matrices are orthogonal: TTᵀ = I.
teach.method: Work out T[[x], [y]]: first entry = (row 1 of T)·(x, y), second entry = (row 2 of T)·(x, y).

alternatives.title: Check with a sketch
text: Plot the point and imagine turning it (or folding the plane along the mirror line).
The image should be in the quadrant your sketch shows.

families.title: The inverse of an orthogonal matrix
explanations: matrix-itself (conceptual): A itself was given; A⁻¹ = Aᵀ, so rows become columns (they agree only when A is symmetric).
negated (conceptual): Every entry was negated; for an orthogonal matrix the inverse is the transpose, not −A or −Aᵀ.
k-not-divided (procedural): The factor 1/9 was left off; Aᵀ keeps the same factor.

teach.idea: A square matrix is orthogonal when AAᵀ = AᵀA = I. Then A⁻¹ = Aᵀ — no determinant or adjoint is needed. Rotations and reflections of the plane have orthogonal matrices.
teach.method: Check (or use, if given) AAᵀ = I, then write A⁻¹ = Aᵀ by turning the rows of A into columns.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Multiply A by your answer.
You must get I: 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere.

families.title: Encoding and decoding a message with a matrix
explanations: used-A (conceptual): The coded column was multiplied by A again; to decode, multiply by A⁻¹.
adjoint-signs (procedural): In A⁻¹ the off-diagonal entries were not negated; for [[a, b], [c, d]], A⁻¹ = (1/(ad − bc))[[d, −b], [−c, a]].
row-vector (procedural): M was multiplied as a row, (m₁ m₂)A; the code is A times the COLUMN M.
letters-swapped (procedural): The two letters were put in the wrong order in M.

teach.idea: A message can be hidden by multiplying columns of letter numbers by an invertible matrix A: C = AM. The receiver, who knows A, recovers M = A⁻¹C. A matrix with determinant ±1 has an inverse with whole-number entries.
teach.method: To encode, multiply A by the column of letter numbers. To decode, find A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A and multiply it by the coded column; then turn the numbers back into letters.

alternatives.title: Check by re-encoding
text: After decoding, multiply A by your answer.
You must get the coded column back.

families.title: The inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix by the Gauss–Jordan method
explanations: read-transposed (procedural): The right-hand block was read off column by column; A⁻¹ is the right half of [I | A⁻¹] read row by row.
left-half-only (conceptual): The row operations were done on A but not on I; the same operations must be applied to the whole row of [A | I].
sign-slip (procedural): A sign slip in a row operation Rᵢ → Rᵢ − kRⱼ left one entry with the wrong sign; check by multiplying A by your answer.

teach.idea: Each elementary row operation is multiplication on the left by an invertible matrix. If the operations turn A into I, their product is A⁻¹ — so doing the same operations to I produces A⁻¹.
teach.method: Write [A | I]. Make the first column (1, 0, 0) using row swaps and Rᵢ → Rᵢ + kRⱼ (and Rᵢ → cRᵢ), then the second column, then the third, always on whole rows. Read A⁻¹ from the right half and check AA⁻¹ = I.

alternatives.title: Compare with the adjoint method
text: A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| gives the same matrix.
Gauss–Jordan avoids nine 2 × 2 determinants and works for larger matrices too.

families.title: Solving a reciprocal equation
explanations: reciprocals-missed (conceptual): Only one root of each pair was given; in a reciprocal equation if t is a root then so is 1/t.
y-values (procedural): The values of y = x + 1/x were given; each value of y must be turned back into two values of x by solving x + 1/x = y.
minus-one-forgotten (procedural): The root x = −1 (the factor x + 1 of an odd-degree reciprocal equation) was left out.

teach.idea: A reciprocal equation is unchanged when x is replaced by 1/x: its coefficients read the same forwards and backwards (or with signs changed). So its roots come in pairs t, 1/t, and dividing by x² and putting y = x + 1/x halves the degree.
teach.method: For an odd degree, first take out the factor x + 1 (or x − 1). Divide by x², group (x² + 1/x²) and (x + 1/x), use x² + 1/x² = y² − 2, solve the quadratic in y, then solve x + 1/x = y for each y.

alternatives.title: Use the pairs
text: Try t = 2: if 2 is a root, so is 1/2, and (x − 2)(2x − 1) = 2x² − 5x + 2 is a factor.
Dividing by it leaves a quadratic for the other pair.

families.title: Equations reducible to quadratics: √x and exponential substitutions
explanations: y-given (procedural): The value of y = √x was given; x = y².
doubled (prerequisite): √x = y was undone by doubling; x = y² (y × y).
extraneous-kept (conceptual): √x = −8 was kept; √x is never negative, so x = 64 does not satisfy the equation.

teach.idea: Some equations that are not polynomials become quadratics after a substitution: x − 5√x + 6 = 0 is y² − 5y + 6 = 0 with y = √x, and 4^x − 6·2^x + 8 = 0 is y² − 6y + 8 = 0 with y = 2^x.
teach.method: Spot the substitution, solve the quadratic in y, then go back to x — and reject any value of y the substitution cannot take (√x ≥ 0, 2^x > 0). Check each x in the original equation.

alternatives.title: Check in the original
text: Put each value of x back into the equation you were given.
A value that fails (for example from √x = −3) is not a solution.

families.title: A volume condition giving a cubic equation
explanations: cube-root (conceptual): The box was treated as a cube (x³ = 10400); the other dimensions differ from x, so the x² term matters.
factor-two (procedural): The length 2x was taken as x; the volume is x × 2x × (x + a).

teach.idea: Writing the volume in terms of one unknown dimension gives a cubic equation. Only a positive root makes sense, and a whole-number root must divide the constant term.
teach.method: Write V = (length)(breadth)(height) in x, expand to a cubic = 0, then test whole numbers near ∛V (factors of the constant term) until one fits; check every dimension is positive.

alternatives.title: A table of volumes
text: Work out the volume for x = 1, 2, 3, …
The volume increases with x, so stop when you reach the given volume.

families.title: Roots and coefficients: the measurements of a box
explanations: half-area (procedural): αβ + βγ + γα was given; the box has two faces of each kind, so the surface area is 2(αβ + βγ + γα).
sum-only (procedural): α + β + γ was given; a cuboid has 4 edges of each length, so the total is 4(α + β + γ).
pair-sum (recall): The coefficient of x was used; the product of the roots is the constant term with its sign changed: αβγ = −(−729) = 729.
square-of-sum (conceptual): (α + β + γ)² was given; it includes 2(αβ + βγ + γα), which must be taken away to leave α² + β² + γ².
sign (procedural): 2(αβ + βγ + γα) was added instead of subtracted.

teach.idea: If α, β, γ are the roots of x³ − px² + qx − r = 0 then α + β + γ = p, αβ + βγ + γα = q and αβγ = r. For a box with edges α, β, γ these are a quarter of the edge length, half the surface area, and the volume.
teach.method: Read p, q and r from the equation (watch the signs), then write the quantity asked for in terms of them: surface area 2q, edges 4p, volume r, diagonal² = p² − 2q.

alternatives.title: Check by finding the edges
text: Try whole numbers in the cubic to find the three edges.
Measure the box from them; you get the same answers without solving.

families.title: Deciding the number of solutions of a 3 × 3 system by ranks
explanations: equal-ranks-infinite (conceptual): Equal ranks were read as 'infinitely many solutions'. Equal ranks mean the system is consistent; the solution is unique when that rank equals the number of unknowns (3).
rank-less-none (conceptual): ρ(A) < 3 was read as 'no solution'. When ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]) < 3 the system is consistent with infinitely many solutions.
equal-ranks-unique (conceptual): Equal ranks were taken to mean one solution; one solution needs the common rank to be 3, the number of unknowns.
singular-infinite (conceptual): ρ(A) = 2 was taken to mean infinitely many solutions without comparing with ρ([A | B]). Here the augmented matrix has rank 3, so the system is inconsistent.

teach.idea: AX = B is consistent exactly when ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]). If that common rank equals the number of unknowns there is one solution; if it is smaller there are infinitely many.
teach.method: Write [A | B], reduce it to echelon form with row operations, count the non-zero rows of A and of [A | B], and compare them with each other and with 3.

alternatives.title: Determinant first
text: Find |A|. If |A| ≠ 0 the system has exactly one solution.
If |A| = 0, replace each column of A by B in turn: if any of these determinants is non-zero there is no solution; here (with ρ(A) = 2) if all are zero there are infinitely many.

families.title: Finding the parameter values that make a system singular or consistent
explanations: solve-sign (procedural): |A| = −3λ − 3 = 0 was solved with a sign slip, giving λ = 1; moving −3 across changes its sign.
copy-row (conceptual): λ was chosen to copy the z-coefficient of the second equation; the third row must be the same combination of the first two rows in every column.
homogeneous-zero (conceptual): μ = 0 was chosen, as for a homogeneous system; here the third equation must be the same combination of the first two on the right side too.
just-add (procedural): The first two equations were simply added; the third row is 1R₁ − 1R₂, so the right side must be 1 × 1 − 1 × 5.
cofactor-sign (procedural): The determinant was expanded with a + sign on the middle term; the signs along a row are +, −, +.

teach.idea: A unique solution needs |A| ≠ 0. When |A| = 0 the third row is a combination of the other two; the system is consistent (infinitely many solutions) only if the right sides follow the same combination.
teach.method: For λ: expand |A| (it is linear in λ) and solve |A| = 0. For μ: find m, k with R₃ = mR₁ + kR₂ from the x and y columns, then μ = m b₁ + k b₂.

alternatives.title: Row-reduce with the letters
text: Row-reduce [A | B] keeping λ and μ as letters.
The last row becomes (0 0 λ − λ₀ | μ − μ₀): λ = λ₀ removes the pivot, and then μ = μ₀ makes the row all zeros.

families.title: Writing a 3 × 3 matrix as a symmetric plus a skew-symmetric matrix
explanations: wrong-order (procedural): A′ − A was used; Q = ½(A − A′). The other order gives −Q.
not-halved (procedural): A + A′ was not halved: P = ½(A + A′), so that P + Q gives back A.
transpose-as-symmetric (conceptual): A′ was given as the symmetric part; A′ is just A with rows and columns swapped, and is not symmetric unless A is.

teach.idea: (A + A′)′ = A′ + A, so ½(A + A′) is symmetric; (A − A′)′ = −(A − A′), so ½(A − A′) is skew-symmetric. Their sum is A.
teach.method: Write A′, add (for P) or subtract (for Q) entry by entry, and halve. Check: Q has zeros on its diagonal and P + Q = A.

alternatives.title: Average each pair
text: Look at a pair of entries in mirror positions, aᵢⱼ and aⱼᵢ.
P gets their average in both places; Q gets half their difference, with opposite signs in the two places.

families.title: The transpose of a product of 2 × 2 matrices
explanations: same-order (conceptual): A′B′ was found; the transpose of a product reverses the order: (AB)′ = B′A′.
no-transpose (procedural): AB was found but not transposed; swap its rows and columns.

teach.idea: Transposing swaps rows with columns, and for a product it reverses the order: (AB)′ = B′A′. (The sizes only fit in that order for non-square matrices.)
teach.method: Either find AB and transpose it, or transpose each matrix and multiply B′ by A′; both give the same matrix.

alternatives.title: Follow one entry
text: The (i, j) entry of (AB)′ is the (j, i) entry of AB: row j of A times column i of B.
That is column j of A′ times row i of B′, which is the (i, j) entry of B′A′.

families.title: The identity element and inverses for a binary operation
explanations: negative (conceptual): −6 (the inverse for ordinary addition) was given; the inverse b must satisfy 6 ∗ b = e for this operation's identity e.
identity-zero (conceptual): 6 ∗ b = 0 was solved; the identity of ∗ is −9, not 0.
identity-sign (procedural): a + e + 8 = a gives e = − 8; the sign was slipped.
reciprocal (conceptual): 1/5 (the ordinary inverse) was given; the inverse b must satisfy 5 ∗ b = e, where e = 9 is this operation's identity.
identity-one (conceptual): 6 ∗ b = 1 was solved; the identity of ∗ is 0, so solve 6 + b + 3(6)b = 0.

teach.idea: The identity e leaves every element unchanged: a ∗ e = e ∗ a = a. An inverse of a is an element b with a ∗ b = b ∗ a = e. Both depend on the rule, not on ordinary + or ×.
teach.method: Write a ∗ e = a with the rule and solve for e (it must not depend on a). Then write a ∗ b = e with the given a and solve for b.

alternatives.title: Guess and check
text: Try a candidate e with two or three different values of a: if a ∗ e = a every time, e is the identity.
For the inverse, work out a ∗ b with your b: you must get e.

families.title: Is a binary operation commutative, associative, both or neither?
explanations: product-term (conceptual): The rule looked too complicated to be associative; expand (a ∗ b) ∗ c and a ∗ (b ∗ c) fully: they are the same.
comm-implies-assoc (conceptual): Commutative was taken to mean associative as well; associativity must be checked separately with three elements.
equal-test (procedural): Commutativity was checked with a = b, where it always holds; try two different numbers.
not-comm-not-assoc (conceptual): Because the rule is not commutative it was assumed not associative either; check (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) on its own.

teach.idea: Commutative: a ∗ b = b ∗ a for all a, b. Associative: (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c) for all a, b, c. Either can hold without the other.
teach.method: Swap a and b in the rule and compare. Then work out (a ∗ b) ∗ c and a ∗ (b ∗ c) in full and compare. One counter-example (with actual numbers) is enough to show a property fails.

alternatives.title: Hunt for a counter-example
text: Try small numbers such as a = 1, b = 2, c = 3.
If the two sides differ, the property fails; if they agree for several choices, prove it with letters.

families.title: Classifying a function as one-one, onto or bijective
explanations: kind-0 (conceptual): A straight line was thought to miss some values; over ℝ every y is reached, at x = (y − 3)/3.
kind-1 (conceptual): x = (y − 3)/3 works over ℝ, but here inputs must be natural numbers: y = 1 has no natural-number input.
kind-2 (conceptual): Only the values y ≥ 3 were thought of; the codomain ℝ also contains values that x² never reaches.
kind-3 (conceptual): A square was assumed never to be onto; the codomain here is [3, ∞), and every y in it is reached. It is not one-one, since f(−1) = f(1).
kind-4 (conceptual): x² was assumed never to be one-one; here the domain is [0, ∞), so no negative inputs: f(x₁) = f(x₂) forces x₁ = x₂.
kind-5 (conceptual): Over ℤ the line 3x + 3 skips integers (it goes up in steps of 3), so it is not onto.
kind-6 (conceptual): x³ was treated like x²; but x³ is strictly increasing, so different inputs give different outputs.
kind-7 (conceptual): The square was assumed to reach every integer; most integers are not of this form.
kind-8 (conceptual): |x − 3| was thought one-one; f(2) = f(4), so it is not.

teach.idea: One-one: different inputs give different outputs. Onto: every element of the codomain is an output. Both depend on the domain and codomain, not only on the formula.
teach.method: For one-one, set f(x₁) = f(x₂) and see whether x₁ = x₂ follows. For onto, take any y in the codomain, solve f(x) = y, and check the solution lies in the domain.

alternatives.title: Horizontal lines
text: Draw horizontal lines y = c for c in the codomain.
One-one: no line meets the graph twice. Onto: every such line meets it at least once.

families.title: Testing a relation for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity
explanations: reflexive (conceptual): Reflexive needs (a, a) for EVERY a in A; one missing pair is enough to fail.
symmetric (conceptual): Every pair (a, b) needs its reverse (b, a) in R; one pair without its reverse is enough to fail.
transitive (conceptual): A chain such as (a, b), (b, a) needs (a, a) too; check every chain (a, b), (b, c) for (a, c).

teach.idea: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a in A. Symmetric: (a, b) ∈ R ⇒ (b, a) ∈ R. Transitive: (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R.
teach.method: Check the three properties one by one: list the (a, a) pairs; pair each element with its reverse; and for each pair (a, b) look for pairs starting with b.

alternatives.title: The relation matrix
text: Write a 3 × 3 table with a 1 in row a, column b when (a, b) ∈ R.
Reflexive: 1s on the diagonal. Symmetric: the table equals its mirror image. Transitive: wherever row a has a 1 in column b, row a must contain every 1 of row b.

families.title: The fewest pairs that make a relation an equivalence relation
explanations: reflexive-only (conceptual): Only the pairs (a, a) were added; an equivalence relation must also be symmetric and transitive.
no-transitive (procedural): Reflexive and symmetric pairs were added, but the pairs that transitivity forces (from chains (a, b), (b, c)) were missed.
unmentioned-elements (conceptual): Elements of A that do not appear in R were forgotten; each still needs its pair (a, a).

teach.idea: The smallest equivalence relation containing R splits A into classes of elements linked by R; within a class every element is related to every element.
teach.method: Join elements that appear together in a pair of R into classes; a class of n elements needs n² pairs; add up, then subtract the pairs R already has.

alternatives.title: Close it step by step
text: Add every (a, a); add the reverse of every pair; then add (a, c) for every chain (a, b), (b, c).
Repeat until nothing new appears, and count what you added.

families.title: The derivative from first principles
explanations: constant-kept (procedural): The constant 4 was kept; in f(x + h) − f(x) it cancels, so it does not appear in f′(x).
only-square (procedural): Only the x² term was worked out; the 5x term gives 5h/h = 5.
sign-lost (procedural): The minus sign was lost: k/(x + h + 5) − k/(x + 5) has numerator −kh.
not-squared (procedural): Only one bracket was kept in the denominator; after cancelling h, both (x + h + q) and (x + q) remain and become (x + q)².
half-lost (procedural): After rationalising, the denominator is √(x + h + q) + √(x + q), which tends to 2√(x + q); the 2 was lost.
cube-expanded-wrongly (prerequisite): (x + h)³ was expanded as x³ + h³; it is x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³.
sin-split (conceptual): sin(4x + 4h) was split as sin 4x + sin 4h; use sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.
cos-sign (recall): cos(A + B) − cos A tends to −sin A × B: the derivative of cos is −sin.
inner-lost (procedural): sin(4h)/h tends to 4, not 1: write it as 4 × sin(4h)/(4h).

teach.idea: f′(x) is the limit of the slope of a chord, [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h, as the second point slides towards the first (h → 0).
teach.method: Work out f(x + h) − f(x), simplify so that h is a factor of the top (expand, combine fractions, or rationalise a root), cancel h, then let h → 0.

alternatives.title: Shrink h with numbers
text: Pick x = 1 and work out the chord slope for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.
The slopes settle on a value: that is f′(1). The algebra does the same for every x at once.

families.title: Instantaneous velocity from a distance–time formula
explanations: position (conceptual): The distance at that moment was found; velocity is the rate of change of distance, ds/dt.
average (conceptual): The average velocity over the first 5 seconds (s ÷ t) was found; the instantaneous velocity is ds/dt at t = 5.

teach.idea: Velocity is the instantaneous rate of change of distance: the slope of the distance–time graph at that moment, ds/dt.
teach.method: Differentiate s term by term (d/dt tⁿ = n tⁿ⁻¹), then substitute the given time.

alternatives.title: Shrink the time interval
text: Average velocity from t₀ to t₀ + h is [s(t₀ + h) − s(t₀)]/h.
Work it out for h = 0.1 and h = 0.01: it approaches ds/dt at t₀.

families.title: Intervals where a cubic is increasing or decreasing
explanations: leading-sign (conceptual): The negative leading coefficient was ignored: f′ opens downwards, so it is positive between the roots and negative outside them.
root-signs (procedural): The roots of f′ were read with the wrong signs: x − 3 = 0 gives x = 3.
inside-outside (conceptual): The two kinds of interval were swapped: f′(x) = 6(x − 3)(x − 4) is negative between the roots and positive outside them.
one-piece (procedural): Only one piece was given; f′ has the same sign on (−∞, 3) and on (4, ∞), so both pieces belong to the answer.

teach.idea: f is strictly increasing where f′(x) > 0 and strictly decreasing where f′(x) < 0; the sign of f′ can only change at its roots.
teach.method: Differentiate and factorise f′. Mark the roots on a number line, test one value of x in each part, and collect the parts with the sign you need.

alternatives.title: A sign chart
text: Make a table with columns (−∞, α), (α, β), (β, ∞).
Write the sign of each factor of f′ in each column and multiply the signs.

families.title: The local maximum or minimum value of a cubic
explanations: x-for-value (procedural): The point where it happens (the x value) was given; the question asks for the value f(x) there.
max-min-swapped (conceptual): The two turning points were swapped: f′ changes from − to + at x = 4, which makes it the local minimum.

teach.idea: At a local maximum f′ changes from + to − (f″ < 0 there); at a local minimum from − to + (f″ > 0).
teach.method: Solve f′(x) = 0, decide which root is the maximum and which the minimum (first or second derivative test), then substitute that x into f.

alternatives.title: Second-derivative test
text: f″(x) = 12x − 6(α + β) for these cubics (times the sign of the leading term).
Negative f″ at a root means a local maximum; positive means a local minimum.

families.title: Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval
explanations: ends-only (conceptual): Only the end points were checked; the turning points inside the interval are candidates too.
turning-only (conceptual): Only the turning points were checked; on a closed interval the end points can give the absolute extreme.

teach.idea: A continuous function on a closed interval has an absolute maximum and minimum, and they occur either at a turning point inside or at an end point.
teach.method: Find the critical points inside [p, q]; evaluate f there and at p and q; the largest value is the absolute maximum, the smallest the absolute minimum.

alternatives.title: A table of candidates
text: List x = p, the critical points inside, and x = q in one row.
Write f(x) under each and circle the largest and the smallest.

families.title: Rates of change of related quantities
explanations: quantity (conceptual): The area (as a multiple of π) was found, not its rate of change.
rate-forgotten (procedural): dA/dr = 2πr was found but not multiplied by dr/dt = 5.
revenue (conceptual): The total revenue R(x) was found; the marginal revenue is its derivative R′(x).
average (conceptual): The revenue per item, R(x)/x, was found; the marginal revenue is R′(x).
one-term (procedural): Only the change in width was used; the area A = lb changes through both l and b: dA/dt = (dl/dt)b + l(db/dt).
sign (procedural): The length is decreasing, so dl/dt = −5; the minus sign was lost.

teach.idea: If a quantity Q depends on x and x changes with time, then dQ/dt = (dQ/dx) × (dx/dt): the rates are linked by the chain rule.
teach.method: Write the formula linking the quantities, differentiate both sides with respect to t, then substitute the values at the moment asked about.

alternatives.title: A small change in time
text: In a short time Δt, x changes by about (dx/dt)Δt.
Q then changes by about (dQ/dx) × (dx/dt)Δt; divide by Δt.

families.title: Areas bounded by a parabola, a cubic or a quadratic and the axis
explanations: half (conceptual): Only the part above the x-axis was found; the parabola is symmetric about the x-axis, so double it.
signed (conceptual): The curve is below the axis for 0 < x < 3; integrating straight through subtracted that part. Split at x = 3 and add the sizes.
from-zero (procedural): The region from x = −4 to 0 was left out.
above-only (procedural): Only the part from x = 3 to 9 (above the axis) was found; the part between 0 and 3 is also bounded by the curve and the axis.

teach.idea: Area is always positive: integrate the height |y| of the region. Where a curve dips below the x-axis, its integral there is negative, so split the interval at the crossing and add the sizes.
teach.method: Sketch the region, find where the curve meets the axis, write the area as a sum of integrals of positive heights (use symmetry where it helps), and evaluate.

alternatives.title: Horizontal strips
text: For y² = 4ax and x = c, take strips parallel to the x-axis: their length is c − y²/(4a).
Integrate from y = −2√(ac) to 2√(ac).

families.title: Choosing k to make a function continuous
explanations: move-sign (prerequisite): 3 was moved across without changing its sign: 3k + 3 = 30 was written as 3k = 30 + 3. Moving a number to the other side changes its sign: 3k = 30 − 3.
no-divide (procedural): The equation 3k + 3 = 30 was not finished: 3k = 27 was given as the answer, but k = 27 ÷ 3.
upside-down (procedural): The ratio was turned over, giving 5/6: the number in the sine goes on top, since sin(6x)/(5x) = (6/5) × sin(6x)/(6x), which tends to 6/5.
m-lost (procedural): sin(6x)/x was taken as 1; it tends to 6, since sin θ/θ → 1 needs θ = 6x in both places.
half-lost (procedural): After multiplying top and bottom by √(1 + 6x) + 1, the bottom has the factor √(1 + 6x) + 1, which tends to 2; that 2 was lost.
not-squared (procedural): 1 − cos(6x) = 2 sin²(6x/2), which gives (6x)²/2: the 6 is squared.
cube-factor (prerequisite): x³ − 216 was factorised as (x − 6)(x² + 36); it is (x − 6)(x² + 6x + 36).
zero (conceptual): 0/0 was taken as 0; it means the expression must be simplified (cancel x − 6) before substituting.

teach.idea: f is continuous at a when lim (x → a) f(x) exists and equals f(a): the left limit, the right limit and the value all agree.
teach.method: Find the limit of the formula near a (substitute for a polynomial; use sin θ/θ → 1, 1 − cos θ = 2 sin²(θ/2), rationalising or factorising otherwise), then set f(a) equal to it.

alternatives.title: Left value, right value
text: For a function in two pieces, work out each piece at x = a.
Continuity means the two values are equal: that is an equation for k.

families.title: Intervals of concavity of a cubic or quartic
explanations: swapped (conceptual): Upward and downward were swapped: y″ = 6(x − 4) is positive to the right of x = 4, so the curve is concave upward there.
one-piece (procedural): Only one piece was given; y″ > 0 on both outer pieces.
root-sign (procedural): y″ = 0 at x = 4, not −4: the sign was slipped.

teach.idea: A curve is concave upward where y″ > 0 (its slope is increasing) and concave downward where y″ < 0; points of inflection are where y″ changes sign.
teach.method: Differentiate twice, factorise y″, mark its roots on a number line and test the sign of y″ in each part.

alternatives.title: Watch the slope
text: Concave upward means the tangent slope increases as x increases, like a cup.
So check where y′ is increasing: that is where y″ > 0.

families.title: Definite integrals over [−a, a] using odd and even functions
explanations: all-vanish (conceptual): Every term was taken to vanish over a symmetric interval; only the odd part does. The even part kx² + m gives twice its integral from 0 to a.
not-doubled (procedural): The even part was integrated from 0 to a but not doubled: ∫₋ₐᵃ g = 2∫₀ᵃ g for an even g.

teach.idea: If f is odd (f(−x) = −f(x)), ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0: the areas on the two sides cancel. If f is even (f(−x) = f(x)), ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx.
teach.method: Split the integrand into its odd part and its even part, drop the odd part, and integrate the even part from 0 to a and double it.

alternatives.title: Substitute x = −t
text: Write ∫₋ₐᵃ f = ∫₋ₐ⁰ f + ∫₀ᵃ f and put x = −t in the first integral.
It becomes ∫₀ᵃ f(−t) dt, which is −∫₀ᵃ f for an odd f and +∫₀ᵃ f for an even f.

families.title: Definite integrals with the property ∫ f(x) dx = ∫ f(a + b − x) dx
explanations: not-halved (procedural): Adding the two forms of I gives 2I = ∫ 1 dx = 25; the last step, dividing by 2, was missed.
sum-of-limits (procedural): ∫ₐᵇ 1 dx = b − a = 25, not a + b.

teach.idea: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx: replacing x by a + b − x runs over the same interval backwards. For g(x)/(g(x) + g(a + b − x)), the two forms add up to 1.
teach.method: Call the integral I, write it again with x replaced by a + b − x, add the two: 2I = ∫ₐᵇ 1 dx = b − a, so I = (b − a)/2.

alternatives.title: Symmetry about the middle
text: At x and at a + b − x (mirror points about (a + b)/2) the integrand's values add up to 1.
So on average the integrand is ½, and the integral is ½ × (b − a).

families.title: Splitting the interval: |x − c| and the greatest integer function
explanations: no-split (conceptual): |x − 5| was integrated as x − 5 all the way; for x < 5 it is 5 − x, so split at x = 5.
right-only (procedural): Only the part from 5 to 6 was found; the part from 2 to 5 also counts.
as-x (conceptual): [x] was integrated as if it were x; [x] is constant on each interval [k, k + 1), so split at the integers.
one-too-many (procedural): The last unit interval was counted up to 6; the pieces are [2, 3), …, [5, 6), with values 2 to 5.

teach.idea: ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫ᶜᵇ f for any c in between. Split where the formula changes: at x = c for |x − c|, at each integer for [x].
teach.method: Find where the integrand changes its formula, split the interval there, write each piece without | | or [ ], integrate each piece and add.

alternatives.title: Count areas
text: |x − c| makes two triangles above the axis: (c − a)²/2 and (b − c)²/2.
[x] makes rectangles of width 1 and heights a, a + 1, …, b − 1 (below the axis when negative).

families.title: Choosing a and b to make a piecewise function differentiable
explanations: slope-without-x (procedural): The slopes were matched as a = 5, forgetting the 2x from x²: the left derivative at x = 3 is 2(3) + a.
sign-slip (procedural): 2(3) + a = 5 was solved as a = 5 + 6; subtract 2(3) = 6 from both sides instead.

teach.idea: Differentiable at c means the left and right derivatives at c are equal; this also needs f to be continuous at c (the pieces must meet).
teach.method: Match the slopes of the two pieces at x = c to find a; then match their values at x = c to find b.

alternatives.title: One tangent line
text: The line px + q must be the tangent to the parabola at x = c.
So the parabola must pass through (c, pc + q) with slope p there.

families.title: Separating the variables in an initial value problem
explanations: constant-in-exponent (procedural): log y = 2x² + 2x + C gives C = log 5, not 5; the constant was put into the exponent as 5.
y-dropped (conceptual): The y on the right was ignored and only (px + q) was integrated; divide by y first: dy/y = (px + q) dx.
constant-dropped (procedural): The constant was dropped; y(1) = 5 gives y = 5x⁴.
constant-added-late (procedural): The constant was added after taking exponentials; log y = p log x + C gives y = Axᵖ, a constant multiple.

teach.idea: When dy/dx is a function of x times a function of y, the variables can be separated: dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, and each side integrated.
teach.method: Divide by y, integrate both sides (log y on the left, the natural logarithm), add one constant, exponentiate, and use the initial condition to find the constant.

alternatives.title: Check by differentiating
text: Differentiate your y and see whether you get the right side of the equation.
Then put in the starting x and check you get the starting y.

families.title: The order and degree of a differential equation
explanations: largest-power (conceptual): The largest power anywhere was taken as the degree; the degree is the power of the highest-order derivative only.
swapped (recall): Order and degree were swapped: the order is how many times y is differentiated in the highest derivative; the degree is that derivative's power.

teach.idea: The order is that of the highest derivative in the equation; the degree (defined when the equation is a polynomial in the derivatives) is the power of that highest derivative.
teach.method: Find the derivative with the most dashes (the largest k in dᵏy/dxᵏ): that k is the order. Its power is the degree; powers of lower derivatives do not matter.

alternatives.title: Rewrite with dashes
text: Write dy/dx as y′, d²y/dx² as y″, d³y/dx³ as y‴.
The most dashes give the order; the power on that term gives the degree.

families.title: A linear differential equation with an integrating factor
explanations: constant-dropped (procedural): The constant of integration was dropped; y·x³ = … + C, and y(1) = −1 fixes C.
q-not-multiplied (procedural): The right side was integrated without multiplying it by the integrating factor x³: y·(IF) = ∫ Q·(IF) dx.

teach.idea: For dy/dx + Py = Q, multiplying by the integrating factor e^(∫P dx) turns the left side into the derivative of y × IF.
teach.method: Find IF = e^(∫P dx) (here xᵏ), write y × IF = ∫ Q × IF dx + C, divide by IF, and use the initial condition for C.

alternatives.title: See the product rule
text: d/dx (xᵏy) = xᵏ dy/dx + k xᵏ⁻¹ y = xᵏ (dy/dx + (k/x)y).
So multiplying the equation by xᵏ makes the left side d/dx (xᵏy).

families.title: A homogeneous differential equation with y = vx
explanations: constant-dropped (procedural): The constant of integration was dropped (taken as 0); the initial condition fixes it.
dv-for-dy (conceptual): With y = vx, dy/dx was taken as dv/dx; by the product rule dy/dx = v + x dv/dx.
two-lost (procedural): ∫ v dv = v²/2; the factor 2 was lost when solving for v².

teach.idea: In a homogeneous equation dy/dx depends only on y/x. Putting y = vx (so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx) turns it into a separable equation in v and x.
teach.method: Substitute y = vx and dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, simplify to x dv/dx = g(v), separate and integrate, put v = y/x back, and use the initial condition.

alternatives.title: Check your answer
text: Differentiate your y and work out the right side of the equation with it.
They must agree, and your y must equal the given value at x = 1.

families.title: Second-order derivatives
explanations: stopped-early (procedural): Only the first derivative was found; d²y/dx² means differentiate once more.
b-squared-sign (recall): The derivative of sin(3x) is +3cos(3x); a sign slip turned −b² into +b².
chain-once (procedural): The chain-rule factor 5 was used only once; each differentiation of (5x + 4) brings a factor 5.
product-once (procedural): Only the eᵃˣ factor was differentiated each time; the product rule also differentiates the x.
x-as-constant (procedural): x was treated as a constant multiplier; x sin ax is a product, so use the product rule.

teach.idea: The second derivative d²y/dx² is the derivative of dy/dx: how fast the slope itself is changing.
teach.method: Differentiate once (product and chain rules), simplify, then differentiate the result again; collect like terms at the end.

alternatives.title: Spot the pattern
text: For eᵃˣ times sin bx or cos bx, each differentiation keeps the factor eᵃˣ and mixes sin and cos.
Write dy/dx = eᵃˣ(…), then differentiate the bracket and the eᵃˣ again.

families.title: The differential equation satisfied by a family of functions
explanations: sign-p (procedural): The sign of p was slipped: the roots r of r² + pr + q = 0 add up to −p.
sign-q (procedural): The sign of q was slipped: the product of the roots is +q.
b-sign (recall): The derivative of cos is −sin; a sign slip turned a² + b² into a² − b².

teach.idea: y = eʳˣ satisfies y″ + py′ + qy = 0 exactly when r² + pr + q = 0. A family with two arbitrary constants comes from the two roots of that quadratic.
teach.method: Read off the roots r₁, r₂ from the exponents (a repeated root for (A + Bx)eᵐˣ, a ± ib for eᵃˣ(A cos bx + B sin bx)); then p = −(r₁ + r₂) and q = r₁r₂.

alternatives.title: Eliminate A and B
text: Write y, y′ and y″ in terms of A and B.
Combine them so that A and B cancel; the coefficients give p and q.

families.title: Domain and range of the principal value branches of the inverse trigonometric functions
explanations: branch-mix (recall): 0 was left in the range; cosec 0 is not defined, so cosec⁻¹ never gives 0.
domain-for-range (conceptual): The domain of cosec⁻¹ was given instead of its range: the range is the set of angles that cosec⁻¹ gives back.
range-for-domain (conceptual): The principal range of cosec⁻¹ was given instead of its domain: the domain is the set of numbers x that cosec⁻¹ accepts.
domain-mix (recall): 1/2 was accepted, as if cosec⁻¹ had the domain [−1, 1] of sin⁻¹; cosec θ is never strictly between −1 and 1, so cosec⁻¹(1/2) is not defined.
branch-edge (conceptual): 0 was taken as a value of cosec⁻¹; cosec 0 is not defined, so 0 is left out of [−π/2, π/2].

teach.idea: No trigonometric function is one-one on its whole domain, so to invert it we keep one piece on which it is one-one and takes every value once: the principal value branch. sin⁻¹ and cosec⁻¹ give angles in [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ and sec⁻¹ in [0, π], tan⁻¹ in (−π/2, π/2), cot⁻¹ in (0, π); sec⁻¹ leaves out π/2 and cosec⁻¹ leaves out 0.
teach.method: For the range, recall the branch and remove the angles where the function itself is not defined (π/2 for sec, 0 for cosec, the end points for tan and cot). For the domain, ask which values the function takes on the branch: [−1, 1] for sin and cos, every real number for tan and cot, x ≤ −1 or x ≥ 1 for sec and cosec.

alternatives.title: Reflect the graph
text: Draw y = sec x for 0 ≤ x ≤ π: it is not defined at π/2 and its values are ≤ −1 or ≥ 1.
Reflecting that piece in the line y = x gives y = sec⁻¹ x: its domain is the old set of values and its range is the old piece of x-axis.

families.title: Is a piecewise function continuous on ℝ or on an interval?
families.skill: continuity on a domain or an interval
explanations: pieces-polynomial (conceptual): Each piece is a polynomial, so f was taken to be continuous everywhere; at a point where the formula changes, the two pieces must also give the same value.
outside-point (procedural): The break at x = 3 was counted, but x = 3 is not in the interval; only points of the interval matter.
every-break (conceptual): Every point where the formula changes was taken to be a discontinuity; there f is continuous when the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and f(a) all agree.

teach.idea: A function is continuous on a set when it is continuous at every point of it. Polynomials are continuous everywhere, so a piecewise function can only fail where its formula changes, and there it fails exactly when the two pieces do not meet.
teach.method: List the points where the formula changes that lie in the set. At each one, work out the value of the left piece and of the right piece there (and f at the point). Equal values: continuous there; different: a discontinuity.

alternatives.title: Draw it without lifting the pencil
text: Sketch each piece on its own part of the number line.
At each change point, see whether the end of one piece meets the start of the next; a gap is a discontinuity.

families.title: Classifying a critical point by the second-derivative test
explanations: sign-rule-swapped (conceptual): The sign rule was swapped: f″ = 2 > 0 means the curve bends upward (a cup), which is a local minimum.
first-derivative (procedural): f′ was used in place of f″; f′ is 0 at every critical point, so it cannot decide. Differentiate once more and put the point into f″.

zero-as-min (conceptual): f″ = 0 at the point was read as if it were positive, so a minimum was concluded; the test decides only when f″ is strictly positive or strictly negative, and here it gives no conclusion (the first-derivative test is needed).

teach.idea: At a critical point c (f′(c) = 0): if f″(c) < 0 the graph bends downward there, so c is a local maximum; if f″(c) > 0 it bends upward, a local minimum; if f″(c) = 0 the test gives no conclusion.
teach.method: Differentiate twice, substitute the critical point into f″, and read the sign. If f″(c) = 0, say the test fails and use the first-derivative test instead.

alternatives.title: Cup or cap
text: f″ > 0: the slope is increasing, like the bottom of a cup — a minimum.
f″ < 0: the slope is decreasing, like the top of a cap — a maximum.

families.title: Areas bounded by straight lines and the coordinate axes
explanations: no-half (procedural): Each piece ∫ u(x − w) dx was evaluated without the ½ from integrating x, which doubles the area.
negative (conceptual): The line lies below the x-axis here, so the integral came out negative and was given as it is; an area is the size of the region, so take the absolute value.
from-zero (procedural): The integral was taken from x = 0 instead of from x = 2.
signed (conceptual): The line crosses the x-axis at x = −7/3; integrating straight through let the part below the axis cancel part of the area. Split at the crossing and add the sizes.
one-line (procedural): Only the part under the first line, from x = 3 to the meeting point x = 9/2, was found; beyond the meeting point the region lies under the second line.

teach.idea: The area between a curve and the x-axis is ∫ |y| dx; for straight lines the region is made of triangles and trapeziums, so integration must agree with ½ × base × height.
teach.method: Sketch the lines, find where they meet each other and the axes, split the interval at those points, write the height of the region on each part and integrate.

alternatives.title: Check with a triangle
text: Find the corners of the region from where the lines meet.
Its area by ½ × base × height (or two triangles) must equal the integral.

families.title: Areas of regions bounded by a circle and a straight line
explanations: no-triangle (procedural): The area under the circle from 0 to 12 (a quarter circle) was found, but the triangle under the line x + y = 12 must be taken away.
smaller-part (procedural): The smaller part cut off by the line was found; the question asks for the larger part, which is the whole circle minus it.
quarter (conceptual): The whole quarter circle in the first quadrant was given; the line through the centre cuts it, and only the part between the line and the axis is asked for.
other-axis (procedural): The angle between the line and the other axis (30°) was used; the region is between the line and the y-axis, an angle of 60°.
sector-only (procedural): The sector cut off by the two radii to the ends of the chord was found; the triangle between those radii and the chord must be taken away to leave the segment.

teach.idea: Under the circle x² + y² = r² the height above the x-axis is √(r² − x²), and ∫ √(r² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(r² − x²) + (r²/2) sin⁻¹(x/r). A region cut off by a line is (area under the circle) minus (area under the line).
teach.method: Sketch the circle and the line, find where they meet, write the area as ∫ (upper boundary − lower boundary) dx between those points (using symmetry where it helps), and evaluate; keep π and surds exact.

alternatives.title: Sector minus triangle
text: A chord cuts off a segment: the sector with angle θ (area ½r²θ) minus the triangle formed by the two radii (area ½r² sin θ).
A line through the centre cuts off a sector, whose area is (angle ÷ 360°) × πr².

families.title: Recovering a quantity from its rate of change and a starting value
explanations: constant-dropped (procedural): The fixed cost ₹1600 was left out; C(0) = 1600 gives the constant of integration.
rate-for-amount (conceptual): f′(5) was found; f(5) needs the antiderivative of f′.
constant-at-zero (procedural): The given value was used as if it were f(0); f(1) = 12 means the constant C satisfies 14 + C = 12.

teach.idea: If you know how fast a quantity changes, integrating the rate gives the quantity up to a constant; one known value (where it starts) fixes the constant.
teach.method: Find an antiderivative of the rate, add C, use the starting value to find C, then substitute the time (or amount) asked about.

alternatives.title: Start plus net change
text: The amount at the end = the amount at the start + ∫ (rate) over the time in between.
So s(T) = s(0) + ∫₀ᵀ v(t) dt.

families.title: The solution set of a system with infinitely many solutions
explanations: move-sign (procedural): The terms in t were moved to the right-hand side without changing their sign, which reverses the direction of the line of solutions.
order (procedural): The numbers were typed in the order x-constant, y-constant, x-coefficient, y-coefficient; the answer asks for (p, q, r, s) with x = p + qt and y = r + st.

teach.idea: When ρ(A) = ρ([A | B]) = 2 for three unknowns, one equation is a combination of the others and one unknown is free; the solutions form a line, described by one parameter.
teach.method: Keep two independent equations, put z = t, move the t terms to the right-hand side (changing their sign), and solve the two equations for x and y in terms of t.

alternatives.title: Check with two values of t
text: Put t = 0 and t = 1 into your x, y, z.
Both points must satisfy all three equations.

families.title: Tangents and normals to a curve, and the angle between two curves
families.skill: tangents, normals and angles between curves
explanations: through-origin (procedural): The slope 26 was found but the line was written as y = 26x, through the origin; it must pass through (2, 25).
intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted.
tangent-for-normal (conceptual): The tangent was given; the normal is perpendicular to it, so its slope is −1/m.
negative-only (procedural): The normal's slope was taken as −m = −4; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1, so it is −1/m = −1/4.
reciprocal-only (procedural): The normal's slope was taken as 1/m = 1/4; the minus sign was lost (perpendicular slopes multiply to −1).
plus-minus (recall): The formula was used with 1 − m₁m₂ in the denominator; tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
one-slope (conceptual): Only the slope of the first curve was given; the angle between the curves depends on both tangent slopes.

teach.idea: The tangent at a point has slope dy/dx there; the normal is perpendicular to it, with slope −1/(dy/dx). The angle between two curves where they meet is the angle between their tangents there.
teach.method: Find the point (x₁, y₁) and the slope m = f′(x₁). Tangent: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁); normal: y − y₁ = −(1/m)(x − x₁). For two curves, find both slopes m₁, m₂ at the meeting point and use tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.

alternatives.title: Draw the slopes
text: The tangent just touches the curve and has the curve's steepness at that point.
Turning it through a right angle about the point gives the normal.

families.title: Ordinary or partial, linear or non-linear: classifying a differential equation
explanations: coefficient-nonlinear (conceptual): The coefficient (eˣ) was taken to make the equation non-linear; coefficients may depend on the independent variable. Linearity is about the unknown function and its derivatives only.
rhs-nonlinear (conceptual): The term cos x was taken to make the equation non-linear; a term in x alone does not contain the unknown y, so it does not affect linearity.

missed-nonlinear (conceptual): The term that makes it non-linear (y multiplied by dy/dx) was missed; the unknown function and its derivatives must appear only to the first power and not multiplied together.
curly-d (recall): ∂ was read as an ordinary d; ∂ means a partial derivative, so the unknown depends on more than one variable and the equation is partial.

teach.idea: An ordinary differential equation has one independent variable (derivatives d/dx); a partial one has several (∂/∂x, ∂/∂y). It is linear when the unknown and its derivatives appear only to the first power, are not multiplied together and are not inside functions such as sin or e^( ).
teach.method: First look at the derivative signs: d means ordinary, ∂ means partial. Then check every term containing the unknown: a square, a product of the unknown with a derivative, or a function of the unknown makes it non-linear; coefficients that depend only on x do not.

alternatives.title: The superposition test
text: For a linear equation with right side 0, the sum of two solutions is again a solution.
Terms like y², y dy/dx or sin y break this, which is what non-linear means.

families.title: dy/dx = f(ax + y + c) by a substitution that separates the variables
explanations: v-for-y (procedural): The answer was left in terms of v; v = 3x + y + 3, so y is found by taking the other terms of v away from it.
back-sign (procedural): When going back from v to y, the other terms of v = 3x + y + 3 were added to v instead of being taken away.
constant-dropped (procedural): The constant of integration was taken as 0; at x = 0, v = 3, so tan⁻¹(v/3) = π/4 there.

teach.idea: When dy/dx is a function of one combination v = ax + y + c, that combination is the natural new unknown: dv/dx = a + dy/dx depends on v alone, so the variables separate.
teach.method: Put v = mx + y + c, so dy/dx = dv/dx − m. Rewrite the equation as dv/dx = g(v), separate and integrate (here ∫ dv/(v² + k²) = (1/k) tan⁻¹(v/k)), use the starting value, and finally write y = v − mx − c.

alternatives.title: Check by differentiating
text: Differentiate your y and compute (mx + y + c)² + k² − m with it.
They must agree, and y(0) must be the given value.

families.title: Binary operations modulo n, by a table and on matrices
families.skill: binary operations on finite sets, tables and matrices
