explanations: words-swapped (recall): 'Mutually exclusive' means no outcome in common; these events share an outcome, though together they cover every outcome (exhaustive).
cannot-be-both (conceptual): Events can be both: A and its complement have nothing in common and together cover every outcome.
different-means-exclusive (conceptual): Different events are not automatically mutually exclusive; look for an outcome that is in both sets.

teach.idea: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Exhaustive events cover the whole sample space (A ∪ B = S).
teach.method: Find A ∩ B: empty means mutually exclusive. Find A ∪ B: the whole sample space means exhaustive. Each property is checked separately.

alternatives.title: Tick each outcome
text: Write the outcomes 1 to 8 in a row; tick under A and under B.
A column with two ticks: not exclusive. A column with no tick: not exhaustive.

families.title: Bayes' theorem: which source produced it
explanations: shares-ignored (conceptual): The defect rates were compared without the machines' shares; a machine that makes more bolts also makes more of the defective ones. Multiply each rate by the share first.
joint-not-divided (procedural): P(machine and defective) was given; the bolt is known to be defective, so divide by the total probability of a defective bolt.
condition-reversed (conceptual): P(defective | machine B) = 9% was given; the question asks the reverse, P(machine B | defective).

teach.idea: Bayes' theorem reverses a condition: P(source | result) = P(source and result) / P(result), where P(result) adds up over all the sources (total probability).
teach.method: For each source multiply its share by its rate; add these for the total probability; divide the chosen source's product by the total.

alternatives.title: Count 10 000 items
text: Imagine 10 000 items: split them by share, then count the faulty ones from each source.
The answer is the faulty ones from the chosen source divided by all the faulty ones.

families.title: Bayes' theorem: which bag the ball came from
explanations: joint-not-divided (procedural): P(Bag I and red) was given; the ball is known to be red, so divide by the total probability of red, P(red) = P(Bag I and red) + P(Bag II and red).
condition-reversed (conceptual): P(red | Bag I) = 1/2 was given; the question asks the reverse, P(Bag I | red).
forward-question (conceptual): The probability that the ball is red was found (total probability); here the colour is known and the bag is asked, so that total is the denominator.
prior-only (conceptual): The chance of choosing Bag I before the draw, 5/6, was given; knowing the ball is red changes it.

teach.idea: Bayes' theorem turns the question round: P(Bag I | red) = P(Bag I and red) / P(red), and P(red) adds up the red branches of both bags (total probability).
teach.method: Draw a tree: first the bag (with the die's probabilities), then the colour. Multiply along each red branch; divide the Bag I red branch by the sum of both red branches.

alternatives.title: Count equally likely cases
text: Imagine many repeats: in 6 throws, f choose Bag I and the rest Bag II; scale up so the balls divide evenly.
Count all the red draws and the red draws from Bag I: the answer is the second count divided by the first.

families.title: Binomial probabilities
explanations: no-combinations (conceptual): pʳqⁿ⁻ʳ is the probability of one particular order; there are 9C8 = 9 orders, so multiply by 9.
one-value-only (conceptual): 'At most 8' includes every value from 0 up to 8, not only X = 8.
boundary-left-out (procedural): X = 8 itself belongs to 'X ≤ 8'; it was left out.
p-q-swapped (procedural): p was raised to the number of failures and q to the number of successes; it is pʳ qⁿ⁻ʳ with r successes.

teach.idea: In n independent trials with success probability p, any one order of r successes has probability pʳqⁿ⁻ʳ, and there are nCr such orders.
teach.method: Use P(X = k) = nCk pᵏ qⁿ⁻ᵏ with q = 1 − p. For 'at least' or 'at most', add the values needed, or use 1 minus the complement when that is shorter.

alternatives.title: Count the paths of a tree
text: Each trial branches into success (p) and failure (q).
Every path with r successes has the same probability; count the paths with nCr.

families.title: Mean and variance of a binomial distribution
explanations: variance-np (recall): The variance is npq; the factor q = 1 − p was left out.
variance-np-squared (recall): The variance is npq, not np².
p-q-swapped (procedural): Variance ÷ mean gives q = 1 − p, not p.

teach.idea: A binomial count is a sum of n independent 0–1 trials, each with mean p and variance pq, so the mean is np and the variance is npq.
teach.method: Mean = np, variance = npq with q = 1 − p. Going back: q = variance ÷ mean, p = 1 − q, n = mean ÷ p.

alternatives.title: Start from one trial
text: One trial scores 1 with probability p and 0 with probability q: mean p, variance p − p² = pq.
n independent trials add their means and their variances.

families.title: Adding and subtracting complex numbers, and the multiplicative inverse
explanations: parts-inverted (conceptual): Each part was turned upside down, 1/a + (1/b)i; 1/(a + bi) is found by multiplying the top and the bottom by the conjugate a − bi.
not-divided (procedural): The conjugate 6 − 3i was given without dividing by a² + b² = 45.
denominator-sign (procedural): (a + bi)(a − bi) was worked out as a² − b²; it is a² + b² = 45.
parts-mixed (procedural): A real part was combined with an imaginary part; add (or subtract) real parts with real parts and imaginary parts with imaginary parts.
subtracted (procedural): The second number was subtracted instead of added.
sign-imag (procedural): Only the real part of 3 + 2i was subtracted; the minus sign applies to both parts: −(c + di) = −c − di.

teach.idea: Complex numbers add and subtract part by part: real with real, imaginary with imaginary. The inverse 1/z uses the conjugate: z z̄ = a² + b² is a real number.
teach.method: For a sum or difference, combine the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. For 1/(a + bi), multiply the top and the bottom by a − bi to get (a − bi)/(a² + b²), then split into real and imaginary parts.

alternatives.title: Arrows in the Argand plane
text: Draw z₁ and z₂ as arrows from the origin; z₁ + z₂ is the diagonal of the parallelogram they make.
1/z points in the direction of z̄ and has length 1/|z|.

families.title: Conjugates of complex numbers and their properties
explanations: i-squared (recall): (a + bi)(a − bi) was expanded with i² = +1, giving a² − b²; i² = −1, so z z̄ = a² + b².
z-squared (conceptual): z was multiplied by itself instead of by its conjugate.
no-conjugate (procedural): The conjugate was not taken at all.
not-conjugated (procedural): The quotient was found but its conjugate was not taken.
negated (conceptual): Both parts were negated; the conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part only.
one-factor (conceptual): Only the first factor was conjugated; conj(z₁z₂) = z̄₁ z̄₂ needs both.
wrong-one (procedural): The conjugate of z₂ was taken instead of z₁.

teach.idea: The conjugate of z = a + bi is z̄ = a − bi: its reflection in the real axis. Conjugation respects arithmetic: conj(z₁ ± z₂) = z̄₁ ± z̄₂, conj(z₁z₂) = z̄₁z̄₂, conj(z₁/z₂) = z̄₁/z̄₂, and z z̄ = |z|² = a² + b².
teach.method: Either work out the product or quotient first and then change the sign of its imaginary part, or conjugate each number first and then combine them; both give the same answer.

alternatives.title: A mirror in the real axis
text: z̄ is z reflected in the real axis: same length, opposite angle.
Multiplying adds angles, so conj(z₁z₂) has angle −(θ₁ + θ₂), which is the angle of z̄₁z̄₂.

families.title: Slope from the inclination, and the inclination from the slope
explanations: cot (recall): cot 150° was used as the slope instead of tan 150°.
sign (conceptual): The sign was lost: a line with inclination between 90° and 180° slopes downwards, so tan 150° is negative.
intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted.
complement (recall): The angle with the y-axis was given; the inclination is measured from the positive x-axis.
acute-only (conceptual): The acute angle 30° was given; a negative slope means the line slopes downwards, so its inclination is obtuse.

teach.idea: The inclination θ of a line is the angle it makes with the positive x-axis (0° ≤ θ < 180°); its slope is m = tan θ. Upward lines have acute θ and positive slope; downward lines have obtuse θ and negative slope.
teach.method: Slope from the angle: m = tan θ (exact values for 30°, 45°, 60° and their supplements). Angle from the slope: find the acute angle with tan = |m|, and use 180° minus it when m is negative. Then y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

alternatives.title: Rise over run
text: Walk 1 unit to the right along the x-axis; the line rises tan θ units.
For 120° the line falls: tan 120° = −tan 60° = −√3.

families.title: Collinear points by equal slopes
explanations: run-over-rise (conceptual): The slope was taken as (change in x)/(change in y); slope is (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
order-mixed (procedural): The subtraction order was mixed (y₂ − y₁ over x₁ − x₂), which changes the sign of the slope.

teach.idea: Three points lie on one straight line exactly when the slope from the first to the second equals the slope from the first to the third (or from the second to the third).
teach.method: Work out the slope of AB, write the slope of AC with k in it, set them equal and solve for k.

alternatives.title: A triangle of zero area
text: Collinear points make a 'triangle' of area 0.
Set ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)| = 0 and solve for k.

families.title: Equations of lines in point–slope, intercept and normal form, and lines parallel to the axes
families.skill: forms of the equation of a line
explanations: intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted.
point-swapped (procedural): The coordinates of the point were swapped in y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
intercepts-swapped (procedural): The intercepts were put the wrong way round in x/a + y/b = 1: a is the x-intercept.
slope-sign (procedural): The slope came out as b/a; from x/a + y/b = 1, y = b − (b/a)x, so the slope is −b/a.
opposite (conceptual): The intercepts were taken as equal in size but opposite in sign (x − y = k); equal intercepts give x + y = k.
not-doubled (procedural): The coordinates of the midpoint were used as the intercepts; the intercepts are twice them.
other-coordinate (procedural): The midpoint's y-coordinate was used; a line parallel to the y-axis is x = (the x-coordinate).
ratio-reversed (procedural): The ratio was used the wrong way round: dividing AB in the ratio 1 : 2 gives (2y₁ + y₂)/3, nearer A.
midpoint (procedural): The midpoint was used instead of the point dividing in the ratio 1 : 2.
tan-slope (recall): tan ω was used as the slope of the line; ω is the angle of the perpendicular, so the line's slope is −cot ω.

teach.idea: A line is fixed by a point and a slope (y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)), by its intercepts (x/a + y/b = 1), or by the length p and direction ω of the perpendicular from the origin (x cos ω + y sin ω = p). Lines parallel to the axes are simply x = k or y = k.
teach.method: Pick the form that matches the data, put the numbers in, and rearrange to y = mx + c (or read off k for a line parallel to an axis).

alternatives.title: Check with the data
text: Put the given point into your answer: it must fit.
For intercepts, put y = 0 and x = 0 into your answer and see whether you get them back.

families.title: The parametric form of a line: the point at a given distance
explanations: cos-sin-swapped (recall): cos θ and sin θ were swapped: x changes by r cos θ and y by r sin θ.
sign-of-r (conceptual): The sign of r was ignored; a negative r means the point lies on the other side of A, against the direction θ.

teach.idea: Every point of the line through (x₁, y₁) with inclination θ can be written as x = x₁ + r cos θ, y = y₁ + r sin θ, where r is the signed distance from (x₁, y₁) along the line.
teach.method: Write cos θ and sin θ, put them into the parametric equations, then substitute the given r (negative r goes the other way).

alternatives.title: Walk along the line
text: Each unit of distance along the line moves you cos θ across and sin θ up.
So r units move you r cos θ across and r sin θ up.

families.title: From the general form Ax + By + C = 0: slope, intercepts, normal form, parallel and perpendicular lines
explanations: ratio-inverted (recall): The slope was taken as −B/A; from Ax + By + C = 0, y = −(A/B)x − C/B, so the slope is −A/B.
sign-lost (procedural): The minus sign was lost: putting y = 0 gives Ax = −C.
y-intercept (procedural): The y-intercept was given instead of the x-intercept.
no-root (recall): C was divided by A² + B² instead of by √(A² + B²).
plain-sum (procedural): C was divided by |A| + |B| instead of by √(A² + B²).
perpendicular-instead (conceptual): A perpendicular line was found; parallel lines have the same slope.
intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted.
parallel-instead (conceptual): A parallel line was found; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
p-negative (conceptual): The equation was divided by +√(A² + B²) whatever the sign of C, which can make p negative; p must be positive, which turns ω through 180°.
from-y-axis (procedural): The angle was measured from the y-axis; ω is measured from the positive x-axis.

teach.idea: Ax + By + C = 0 can be rewritten as y = −(A/B)x − C/B (slope and y-intercept), as x/(−C/A) + y/(−C/B) = 1 (intercepts), or, dividing by ∓√(A² + B²), as x cos ω + y sin ω = p with p > 0. Parallel lines share A : B; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
teach.method: Make y the subject to read the slope and y-intercept; move C across and divide to get the intercept form; divide by √(A² + B²), with the sign chosen to make the right-hand side positive, for the normal form.

alternatives.title: Use two points of the line
text: Put x = 0 to find where the line meets the y-axis, and y = 0 for the x-axis.
The slope is the rise between those points over the run.

families.title: Events as sets of outcomes: not A, A and B, A or B
families.skill: events as subsets of the sample space
explanations: a-itself (conceptual): The outcomes of A were listed; 'not A' (A′) is everything in S that is not in A.
and-for-or (conceptual): Only the outcomes in both A and B were listed; 'A or B' (A ∪ B) contains the outcomes in at least one of them.
or-for-and (conceptual): Every outcome in A or in B was listed; 'A and B' (A ∩ B) contains only the outcomes in both.
and-for-but-not (procedural): The outcomes in both A and B were listed; 'A but not B' keeps the outcomes of A that are not in B.
b-but-not-a (procedural): The outcomes of B that are not in A were listed; the event is A but not B.
not-both (conceptual): The outcomes not in both A and B together, (A ∩ B)′, were listed; 'neither A nor B' is (A ∪ B)′.

teach.idea: An event is a subset of the sample space S. 'A or B' is the union A ∪ B, 'A and B' the intersection A ∩ B, and 'not A' the complement A′ = S − A.
teach.method: List the outcomes of A and of B from S. Then: for A ∪ B take every outcome in either list; for A ∩ B only those in both; for A′ those of S not in A; for A ∩ B′ those of A not in B.

alternatives.title: A Venn diagram
text: Draw two overlapping circles A and B inside a rectangle S and write each outcome in its region.
Read the event off the diagram: the overlap is A ∩ B, both circles together A ∪ B, outside A is A′.

families.title: The addition theorem for three events
explanations: at-least-one (conceptual): P(A ∪ B ∪ C), the probability of at least one, was found; exactly one leaves out the outcomes that are in two or in all three events.
triple-left-out (procedural): P(A ∩ B ∩ C) was left out; subtracting the three pairs takes the triple overlap away three times after adding it three times, so it must be added back once.
pairs-not-subtracted (conceptual): The three probabilities were simply added; outcomes in two of the events are then counted twice, so the pairwise overlaps must be subtracted.
triple-subtracted (procedural): P(A ∩ B ∩ C) was subtracted instead of added.

triple-once (procedural): After subtracting twice the pairs, P(A ∩ B ∩ C) was added back only once; the triple region was counted three times in the singles and taken away six times with the pairs, so it must be added back three times.
pairs-once-exact (procedural): The pairs were subtracted only once; outcomes in exactly two events are counted twice in P(A) + P(B) + P(C), so for exactly one they must be taken away twice.

teach.idea: P(A ∪ B ∪ C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) − P(A ∩ B) − P(B ∩ C) − P(A ∩ C) + P(A ∩ B ∩ C): add the singles, take away the double counting of the pairs, and add back the triple overlap, which was taken away once too often.
teach.method: Add the three probabilities, subtract the three pairwise ones, add the triple one. For 'none of them', take the result away from 1. For 'exactly one', subtract the pairs twice and add the triple three times.

alternatives.title: Fill in a Venn diagram
text: Start from the centre: write the triple overlap, then each pair minus the triple, then each single minus what is already inside it.
Add all the regions inside the three circles.

families.title: One-point, two-point and Bernoulli distributions
explanations: q-for-p (procedural): The probability of failure was given; the mean of a Bernoulli variable is the probability of success p.
mean-for-variance (conceptual): The mean p was given instead of the variance.
p-squared (recall): p² was given; Var(X) = E(X²) − (E X)² = p − p² = p(1 − p).
average (conceptual): The two values were simply averaged; each value must be weighted by its probability.
swapped (procedural): The probabilities were attached to the wrong values.
ex2 (procedural): E(X²) was given; the variance is E(X²) − (E X)².
not-squared (procedural): (u − v) was not squared: Var(X) = (u − v)² p(1 − p).
value-for-variance (conceptual): The value itself was given; a variable that always takes the same value does not vary, so its variance is 0.

teach.idea: A one-point distribution always gives the same value (variance 0). A two-point distribution gives u with probability p and v with probability 1 − p; with u = 1 and v = 0 it is the Bernoulli distribution, with mean p and variance p(1 − p).
teach.method: Make the table of values and probabilities. Mean: Σ x P(x). Variance: Σ x² P(x) minus the square of the mean (for two points this simplifies to (u − v)² p(1 − p)).

alternatives.title: One trial of a binomial
text: A Bernoulli variable is a binomial with n = 1.
So its mean is np = p and its variance npq = p(1 − p).

families.title: Vector and Cartesian equations of a line in space
families.skill: equations of a line in space
explanations: denominators-as-written (procedural): The denominators were read as they stand; first make the coefficients of x, y and z equal to 1 (divide top and bottom by them, and turn (c − z) into −(z − c)).
signs-as-written (procedural): The point was read with the signs as written; (x − a)/l passes through x = a, so the + and − in the numerators change sign.
z-sign (procedural): The minus sign in front of z was left in the numerator; (c − Uz)/n = (z − c/U)/(−n/U).
b-as-direction (conceptual): The position vector of B was used as the direction; the direction is b⃗ − a⃗ (the vector from A to B).
ba (procedural): The direction was taken from B to A; with the form a⃗ + λ(b⃗ − a⃗) it is from A to B.

teach.idea: A line through the point A with direction b⃗ is r⃗ = a⃗ + λb⃗ (vector form), or (x − a₁)/b₁ = (y − a₂)/b₂ = (z − a₃)/b₃ (Cartesian form). The denominators are direction ratios and the numerators show the point.
teach.method: To convert Cartesian to vector form, first make the coefficients of x, y and z equal to +1 in the numerators (divide top and bottom), then read the point from the numerators and the direction from the denominators. Through two points, use b⃗ − a⃗ as the direction.

alternatives.title: Set each fraction equal to λ
text: Write (2x − 1)/3 = λ, so x = 1/2 + (3/2)λ; do the same for y and z.
The constant terms give the point and the coefficients of λ give the direction.

families.title: The point of intersection of two lines in space
families.skill: point of intersection of two lines
explanations: lambda-in-second (procedural): λ = 1 was put into the second line instead of μ = 1.
sign-of-lambda (procedural): The sign of λ was slipped: λ = −1 was used.

teach.idea: Two lines in space meet when some point is on both: a⃗ + λu⃗ = b⃗ + μv⃗ for one pair λ, μ. That is three equations in two unknowns; they intersect when the third equation agrees with the λ, μ found from two of them.
teach.method: Write the x, y and z equations, solve two of them for λ and μ, check the third, and substitute λ into the first line (or μ into the second).

alternatives.title: Check on both lines
text: Put your point into the Cartesian form of each line: all three fractions must be equal.
If they are equal for both lines, the point is on both.

families.title: The equation of a plane from three points, a point and a normal, its intercepts, a line and a point, or its normal form
explanations: d-sign (procedural): The constant came out with the wrong sign: n⃗ · (r⃗ − a⃗) = 0 gives n⃗ · r⃗ = n⃗ · a⃗.
intercepts-as-coefficients (conceptual): The intercepts were used as the coefficients (x0·x + y0·y + z0·z = 1); the intercept form is x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.
unit-forgotten (procedural): The distance was not multiplied by |n⃗| = 7; in r⃗ · n̂ = p the normal must be a unit vector.

teach.idea: A plane is fixed by a point A on it and a normal vector n⃗: n⃗ · (r⃗ − a⃗) = 0. Three points give the normal as (B − A) × (C − A); intercepts give x/a + y/b + z/c = 1; the normal form r⃗ · n̂ = p uses the unit normal and the distance p from the origin.
teach.method: Find a normal vector and a point from the data, write n⃗ · r⃗ = n⃗ · a⃗, clear fractions and remove any common factor.

alternatives.title: Check with the data
text: Put each given point into your equation: it must fit.
For intercepts, put two of x, y, z equal to 0 and see whether you get the intercept back.

families.title: The angle between two planes, or between a line and a plane
explanations: not-divided (procedural): Only the dot product was found; it must be divided by the product of the two lengths.
one-length (procedural): The dot product was divided by only one of the lengths.

cos-for-sin (conceptual): cos φ was found (as if the formula with the normal gave the cosine of the angle with the plane); the line makes 90° minus its angle with the normal, so the formula gives sin φ directly.

teach.idea: The angle between two planes is the angle between their normals: cos θ = |n⃗₁ · n⃗₂|/(|n⃗₁||n⃗₂|). A line with direction b⃗ makes an angle φ with a plane of normal n⃗ where sin φ = |b⃗ · n⃗|/(|b⃗||n⃗|), because the line makes 90° − φ with the normal.
teach.method: Read the normal vectors (the coefficients of x, y, z) and the line's direction, work out the dot product and the two lengths, and divide; simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: Look along the common line
text: Two planes meeting look like two lines when seen along their line of intersection.
The normals turn by the same angle as the planes, so the angle between the normals is the angle between the planes.

families.title: Tangents and normals to an ellipse or a hyperbola, with points in parametric form
families.skill: tangents and normals to ellipses and hyperbolas
explanations: tangent-for-normal (conceptual): The tangent was given; the normal is perpendicular to it at the same point.
intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted.
ellipse-rule (recall): The tangent rule for an ellipse (with +) was used; for a hyperbola it is xx₁/a² − yy₁/b² = 1.

teach.idea: The tangent to x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 at (x₁, y₁) is xx₁/a² + yy₁/b² = 1; for the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 it is xx₁/a² − yy₁/b² = 1. The normal is the perpendicular line through the same point. In parametric form the points are (a cos θ, b sin θ) and (a sec θ, b tan θ).
teach.method: Find the point (from θ if it is given in parametric form), write the tangent by the rule (or find dy/dx by implicit differentiation), and rearrange to y = mx + c; for the normal use slope −1/m through the point.

alternatives.title: Implicit differentiation
text: Differentiate x²/a² ± y²/b² = 1: 2x/a² ± 2y y′/b² = 0, so y′ = ∓ b²x/(a²y).
Put in the point to get the tangent's slope.

families.title: The angle bisectors of a pair of lines through the origin
families.skill: bisectors of a pair of lines
explanations: sign (procedural): a − b was used where b − a belongs: h(x² − y²) = (a − b)xy rearranges to x² − ((a − b)/h)xy − y² = 0.
2h (recall): The coefficient of xy (which is 2h) was used as h, so the answer came out halved.
upside-down (procedural): The fraction was turned over: h/(b − a) was used instead of (b − a)/h.

teach.idea: The two angle bisectors of the lines ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 are the lines whose points are equally far from both; together they are (x² − y²)/(a − b) = xy/h, that is h(x² − y²) − (a − b)xy = 0.
teach.method: Read a (the x² coefficient), 2h (the xy coefficient) and b (the y² coefficient), write h(x² − y²) = (a − b)xy and divide by h to get x² + kxy − y² = 0.

alternatives.title: Halve the angles
text: Find the two lines' inclinations θ₁ and θ₂.
The bisectors have inclinations (θ₁ + θ₂)/2 and (θ₁ + θ₂)/2 + 90°: they are perpendicular to each other.

families.title: Are two points on the same side of a line?
families.skill: position of points relative to a line
explanations: rule-reversed (conceptual): The rule was reversed: values of ax + by + c with the same sign mean the same side, opposite signs mean opposite sides.
c-left-out (procedural): The constant 3 was left out when the points were put into ax + by + c.

teach.idea: A line ax + by + c = 0 splits the plane into two half-planes: on one side ax + by + c is positive, on the other negative, and on the line it is zero.
teach.method: Put each point into ax + by + c. Same signs: the same side. Opposite signs: opposite sides. Zero: the point is on the line.

alternatives.title: Does PQ cross the line?
text: Join P and Q with a straight segment.
The points are on opposite sides exactly when the segment crosses the line.

families.title: A line through the point of intersection of two given lines
explanations: parallel-instead (conceptual): A parallel line was found; perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
intercept-sign (procedural): In y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), the term −m·x₁ was added instead of subtracted.
run-over-rise (conceptual): The slope was taken as (change in x)/(change in y); slope is rise over run.
perpendicular-instead (conceptual): A perpendicular line was found; parallel lines have the same slope.

teach.idea: For any λ, L₁ + λL₂ = 0 is a straight line through the point where L₁ = 0 and L₂ = 0 meet. One more condition (a point, or a slope) picks out the value of λ.
teach.method: Either solve L₁ = 0 and L₂ = 0 for the point of intersection and use the condition, or write L₁ + λL₂ = 0, apply the condition to find λ, and simplify.

alternatives.title: Find the point first
text: Solve the two equations together to get the point of intersection.
Then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) with the slope the condition gives.

families.title: Probability from a density function
explanations: density-not-area (conceptual): The density values were subtracted, f(5) − f(4); a probability is the AREA under f between 4 and 5, found by integrating.
power-not-divided (procedural): x³ was integrated to x⁴ without dividing by 4.
lower-limit-ignored (procedural): Only P(X ≤ 5) was found; the part below 4 must be taken away.

teach.idea: For a continuous random variable, probability is AREA under the density curve: P(b ≤ X ≤ c) is the integral of f(x) from b to c, and the whole area is 1.
teach.method: Integrate the density from the lower limit to the upper limit (or find F(x) = P(X ≤ x) first), then subtract: F(c) − F(b).

alternatives.title: Find the distribution function first
text: F(x) = ∫ f(t) dt from 0 to x. For f(x) = (n + 1)xⁿ/aⁿ⁺¹ this gives F(x) = (x/a)ⁿ⁺¹.
Check F(a) = 1, then P(b ≤ X ≤ c) = F(c) − F(b).

alternatives.title: See it as an area (when f is a straight line)
text: When f(x) = 2x/a², the graph from 0 to a is a triangle of base a and height 2/a: area 1.
P(X ≤ c) is the smaller triangle with base c and height 2c/a², whose area is c²/a².

families.title: The constant that makes a density function
explanations: lower-limit-ignored (procedural): The integral was taken from 0 instead of from 5; f is 0 below 5.
power-not-divided (procedural): x³ was integrated to x⁴ without dividing by 4.
height-one (conceptual): f(6) was set equal to 1; it is the total AREA under f that must be 1, not its largest value.

teach.idea: A density never gives negative values and the total area under it is exactly 1 (X must take some value).
teach.method: Integrate k xⁿ over the interval where f is not zero, set the result equal to 1 and solve for k.

alternatives.title: Start from the flat case
text: When n = 0, f is a rectangle of width hi − lo, so its height must be 1/(hi − lo).
For k xⁿ the same idea holds: area = k(hiⁿ⁺¹ − loⁿ⁺¹)/(n + 1) = 1.

families.title: Probabilities of independent events
explanations: exclusive-for-independent (conceptual): Independent events were treated as if they cannot happen together; independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
add-for-and (procedural): The probabilities were added; for both of two independent events to happen, multiply them.
no-overlap-taken (procedural): P(A) and P(B) were added without taking away P(A ∩ B), so the outcomes where both happen were counted twice.
union-as-product (conceptual): 'At least one' was worked out as 'both'.
exclusive-complement (procedural): 1 − P(A) − P(B) treats A and B as unable to happen together; for independent events use (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B)).
complement-of-both (conceptual): 'Neither' was taken as 'not both', 1 − P(A ∩ B); 'neither' means A does not happen AND B does not happen.
union-for-exactly-one (conceptual): P(A ∪ B) includes the outcomes where both happen; 'exactly one' leaves them out.
one-way-only (procedural): Only 'A but not B' was counted; 'B but not A' is the other way of exactly one happening.

teach.idea: A and B are independent when knowing that one happened does not change the chance of the other, so P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
teach.method: Multiply for 'both'. Use P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) for 'at least one', complements (1 − P) for 'not', and add the two separate ways for 'exactly one'.

alternatives.title: A 10 by 10 grid
text: Shade 10 × P(A) rows for A and 10 × P(B) columns for B in a 10 by 10 grid of equally likely squares.
Both is the overlap of rows and columns; count the squares you need and divide by 100.

families.title: Independent or mutually exclusive?
explanations: independent-means-apart (conceptual): 'Independent' was taken to mean 'cannot happen together'. That is mutually exclusive; independent means P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B).
counts-not-probabilities (procedural): n(A ∩ B) was compared with n(A) × n(B); the test uses probabilities: n(A ∩ B)/N against (n(A)/N) × (n(B)/N).

teach.idea: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Independent events have P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Two events that both can happen cannot be both.
teach.method: Count n(A), n(B) and n(A ∩ B). If n(A ∩ B) = 0 they are mutually exclusive. Otherwise compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A) × P(B).

alternatives.title: Does B change the chance of A?
text: Work out P(A) and P(A | B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(B).
If they are equal, knowing B tells you nothing about A: the events are independent.

families.title: Mean of a discrete random variable
explanations: divided-by-count (procedural): Σ x P(x) was divided by the number of values; the probabilities already do the averaging, so E(X) = Σ x P(x).
plain-average (conceptual): The four values were averaged as if equally likely; each value must be weighted by its probability.

teach.idea: The mean of a random variable is a weighted average: each value counts in proportion to its probability.
teach.method: Multiply each value x by its probability P(x) and add the products: E(X) = Σ x P(x).

alternatives.title: Imagine many trials
text: If the probabilities have denominator T, imagine T trials: value x turns up T × P(x) times.
Add all the results and divide by T: that average is E(X).

families.title: Variance of a discrete random variable
explanations: mean-square-missing (procedural): E(X²) was given as the variance; the square of the mean must be taken away: Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
mean-not-squared (procedural): E(X) was taken away instead of [E(X)]².
probabilities-ignored (conceptual): The four values were treated as equally likely; each squared deviation must be weighted by its probability.

teach.idea: The variance measures how far the values spread from the mean, each squared distance weighted by its probability.
teach.method: Find E(X) = Σ x P(x) and E(X²) = Σ x² P(x); then Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².

alternatives.title: Use deviations from the mean
text: Work out x − E(X) for each value and square it.
Multiply each square by P(x) and add: Var(X) = Σ (x − μ)² P(x).

families.title: The law of total probability (two bags)
explanations: bags-equally-likely (conceptual): The two bags were treated as equally likely; the die chooses Bag I with probability 5/6, not 1/2.
pooled-bags (conceptual): All the balls were put together in one bag; the bag is chosen first, so each bag's chance must be weighted by the chance of choosing it.
one-case-only (procedural): Only the Bag I case was counted; a red ball can also come from Bag II, so add both cases.

teach.idea: When the outcome can come about in separate ways (a partition: Bag I or Bag II), its probability is the sum over the ways of P(way) × P(outcome | way).
teach.method: List the cases, multiply the chance of each case by the chance of red in that case, and add: P(R) = P(E₁)P(R | E₁) + P(E₂)P(R | E₂).

alternatives.title: Draw a tree diagram
text: First branches: the bags, with their probabilities from the die.
Second branches: red or black from each bag. Multiply along each red path and add the paths.

families.title: A statement and its converse
explanations: converse-same-truth (conceptual): The converse was assumed to be true exactly when the statement is; a converse swaps the 'if' and 'then' parts and must be checked on its own.
one-example (procedural): One example where both parts are true was taken as proof; a general statement needs every case, and one counterexample shows it is false.

teach.idea: The converse of 'if P then Q' is 'if Q then P'. A statement can be true while its converse is false, so each needs its own check.
teach.method: Try to find a counterexample: a case where the 'if' part is true and the 'then' part is false. If none can exist, the statement is true; one counterexample makes it false.

alternatives.title: Think in factors
text: Every multiple of a is a multiple of b exactly when b divides a (6 → 3 works, 3 → 6 does not: 9).
For n² and n: if a has no square factor, every prime of a must already divide n.

families.title: A counterexample to a 'prime for every n' claim
explanations: obvious-factor-not-smallest (procedural): n = 281 makes every term a multiple of 281, so it is a counterexample, but the question asks for the SMALLEST one; check n = 1, 2, 3, … in order.

teach.idea: A claim about EVERY n is false as soon as one n fails; that n is a counterexample. Checking many n that work never proves the claim.
teach.method: Work out the value for n = 1, 2, 3, … in order and test each for a factor (try primes up to its square root). The first value with a factor gives the answer.

alternatives.title: Look for a forced factor
text: When n = c, every term of n² + an + c is a multiple of c, so the value cannot be prime.
That proves the claim false, but a smaller n may already fail: still check from n = 1.

families.title: True rows of a truth table
explanations: or-as-exclusive (conceptual): 'Or' was read as 'one but not both'; in logic A ∨ B is also true when both are true.
biconditional-as-and (conceptual): 'A if and only if B' was taken as true only when both are true; it is also true when both are false.
conditional-as-and (conceptual): 'If A then B' was taken as true only when A and B are both true; it is false ONLY when A is true and B is false.
conditional-reversed (conceptual): The conditional was read backwards (as 'if B then A'); A → B is false only when A is true and B is false.

teach.idea: A truth table lists every combination of truth values; the compound statement's value in each row follows from the connectives: ∧ needs both, ∨ needs at least one, A → B fails only for T → F, A ↔ B needs the same value.
teach.method: Write the 8 rows of p, q, r. Add a column for each negation, then for the bracket, then for the whole statement, and count the T's.

alternatives.title: Count the false rows instead
text: For an outer →, the statement is false only when the bracket is true and the last part is false.
Count those rows and take them away from 8.

families.title: Tautology, contradiction or contingency
explanations: first-row-only (procedural): Only the first row (p and q both true) was checked; a tautology must be true in EVERY row, a contradiction false in every row.
mostly-true (conceptual): A statement true in most rows was called a tautology; even one false row makes it a contingency.

teach.idea: A tautology is true in every row of its truth table, a contradiction is false in every row, and a contingency is true in some rows and false in others.
teach.method: Make the 4-row table for p and q, work out each bracket and then the whole statement, and look at the final column.

alternatives.title: Simplify with laws first
text: Replace A → B by ¬A ∨ B and use De Morgan's laws.
A ∨ ¬A is always true and A ∧ ¬A is always false; if the statement reduces to one of these, it is a tautology or a contradiction.

families.title: Variance of a frequency distribution
explanations: mean-not-squared (procedural): The mean was taken away instead of the square of the mean: σ² = Σfx²/N − x̄².
divide-by-n-minus-1 (conceptual): The sum of squared deviations was divided by N − 1 = 18; for the variance of a distribution divide by N = 19.
divide-by-values (procedural): Σf(x − x̄)² was divided by the number of different values (5) instead of the total frequency N.
frequencies-ignored (conceptual): The frequencies were ignored, as if each value appeared once.

teach.idea: Variance is the mean of the squared distances from the mean; squaring stops positive and negative deviations from cancelling.
teach.method: Find N = Σf, x̄ = Σfx/N and Σfx²/N, then σ² = Σfx²/N − x̄² (or Σf(x − x̄)²/N).

alternatives.title: Step-deviation (shortcut) method
text: Choose an assumed mean A (the middle value) and the gap h between values; let u = (x − A)/h.
Then σ² = h² [Σfu²/N − (Σfu/N)²]: the numbers stay small.

families.title: Standard deviation of raw data (exact)
explanations: variance-given (procedural): The variance was given; the standard deviation is its square root.
divide-by-n-minus-1 (conceptual): The squared deviations were divided by n − 1 = 5; for the standard deviation of these data divide by n = 6.
mean-deviation-given (conceptual): The mean of the distances from the mean (mean deviation) was found; the standard deviation squares the deviations first.

teach.idea: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it is in the same units as the data.
teach.method: Find the mean, the squared deviations (x − x̄)², their mean (the variance), then take the square root and simplify the surd.

alternatives.title: Use Σx² instead of deviations
text: σ² = Σx²/n − x̄² avoids fractions in the deviations.
With n = 6: σ = √(6Σx² − (Σx)²)/6.

families.title: Comparing consistency by the coefficient of variation
explanations: smaller-sd (conceptual): The smaller standard deviation was chosen; spread must be compared relative to the mean, CV = σ/x̄ × 100.
higher-mean (conceptual): The higher average was chosen; a higher mean means scoring more, not scoring more steadily.

teach.idea: The coefficient of variation CV = (σ/x̄) × 100 measures spread as a percentage of the mean, so groups with different means can be compared. The smaller CV is the more consistent.
teach.method: Work out CV for each batter, then choose the smaller one (equal CVs mean equally consistent).

alternatives.title: Compare without dividing
text: σ₁/x̄₁ < σ₂/x̄₂ exactly when σ₁ × x̄₂ < σ₂ × x̄₁.
Multiply across and compare the two whole numbers.

families.title: Mean deviation about the mean
explanations: signs-kept (conceptual): The deviations x − x̄ were added with their signs, and they always add up to 0; mean deviation uses the distances |x − x̄|.
divide-by-n-minus-1 (procedural): The sum of the distances was divided by 5; divide by the number of values, 6.
about-median (procedural): The distances were measured from the median; this question asks about the mean.

teach.idea: Mean deviation is the average DISTANCE of the values from the mean; distances are never negative, so signs are dropped.
teach.method: Find x̄, write each |x − x̄|, add them and divide by the number of values.

alternatives.title: Use the balance of the mean
text: The deviations above the mean add up to the same amount as those below it.
So M.D. = 2 × (sum of x − x̄ for the values above the mean) ÷ n.

families.title: Mean deviation about the median
explanations: middle-unsorted (procedural): The middle value of the list as written (27) was taken as the median; put the data in order first.
about-mean (procedural): The distances were measured from the mean; this question asks about the median.

teach.idea: The median is the middle value of the ORDERED data; the mean deviation about it is the average distance from it.
teach.method: Sort the data, take the 4th value as the median M, add the distances |x − M| and divide by 7.

alternatives.title: Top half minus bottom half
text: Distances from the median: the three largest values are above M, the three smallest below.
So the sum of distances = (sum of the top three) − (sum of the bottom three).

families.title: Exact values by compound-angle formulas
explanations: distribute (conceptual): tan(A − B) was split as tan A − tan B; tan does not distribute over a sum, so use the compound-angle formula.
formula-sign (recall): The sign in the denominator was wrong: tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B).

teach.idea: sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B, cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B, tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B): angles like 75° or 165° come from standard ones.
teach.method: Write down sin and cos (or tan) of each angle, substitute into the formula, multiply out the surds and simplify; rationalise a tan answer.

alternatives.title: Check with the unit circle
text: Locate A ± B on the unit circle: the quadrant tells you the sign of the answer.
For example cos(120° − 45°) = cos 75° must be positive and small (about 0.26).

families.title: Double-angle values from one ratio
explanations: double-the-ratio (conceptual): tan 2A was taken as 2 × tan A; doubling the angle does not double the ratio.
formula-mixed (recall): Two forms of the formula were mixed up: cos 2A = 1 − 2 sin²A = 2 cos²A − 1, not 1 − 2 cos²A.
quadrant-sign (conceptual): sin A was taken as positive; in this quadrant its sign must come from where A lies.

teach.idea: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A, cos 2A = cos²A − sin²A, tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 − tan²A); the quadrant fixes the sign of the ratio you work out.
teach.method: Use sin²A + cos²A = 1 to find the other ratio, give it the sign of its quadrant, then substitute into the double-angle formula.

alternatives.title: Draw the reference triangle
text: Sketch a right triangle with the given ratio (for example opposite 3, hypotenuse 5) and find the third side.
Put A in its quadrant: the x-side takes the sign of x there, the y-side the sign of y.

families.title: Products of sines and cosines as sums
explanations: sign-between-terms (recall): The two cosines were combined with the wrong sign, as cos(A − B) + cos(A + B); that sum is 2 cos A cos B. For 2 sin A sin B the two cosines are subtracted: cos(A − B) − cos(A + B).
halved (procedural): A ½ was put in front, from the form sin A sin B = ½[cos(A − B) − cos(A + B)]; here the product already carries the 2, so the ½ and the 2 cancel.
wrong-function (recall): Sines were written where the formula gives cosines: a product of two cosines becomes a sum of COSINES.
minus-dropped (procedural): The cosines were subtracted in the wrong order, cos(A + B) − cos(A − B); that is the negative of 2 sin A sin B.

teach.idea: Adding sin(A + B) and sin(A − B) cancels the cos A sin B parts and leaves 2 sin A cos B; the other three product formulas come the same way.
teach.method: Pick the formula for the product, put A = ax and B = bx, and write the angles A + B and A − B.

alternatives.title: Derive it from the compound-angle formulas
text: Write cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B and cos(A + B) = cos A cos B − sin A sin B.
Subtract: cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) = 2 sin A sin B.

families.title: Solutions of a trigonometric equation in 0 ≤ x < 2π
explanations: principal-only (conceptual): Only the principal value was given; tan takes each value once in every π, so look in every quadrant where it has this sign.
degrees-not-radians (procedural): The solutions were worked out in degrees and the degree numbers typed; in radians 180° is π, so 30° is π/6.
one-turn-only (procedural): Only angles 3x below 2π were used; when 0 ≤ x < 2π, 3x runs from 0 up to 6π.

teach.idea: sin and cos repeat every 2π and take each value twice per turn (tan repeats every π and takes each value once); the quadrant signs (All, Sin, Tan, Cos) tell you where.
teach.method: Find the reference angle from the standard values (π/6, π/4, π/3), place it in each quadrant where the function has the right sign, then (for kx) add multiples of 2π until kx reaches 2kπ, and divide by k.

alternatives.title: Read it off the graph
text: Sketch y = sin x for 0 to 2π and the line y = value.
Each crossing is a solution; for sin kx the graph squeezes k waves into 0 to 2π, so there are k times as many crossings.

families.title: General solution of a trigonometric equation
explanations: wrong-pattern (recall): The sine pattern was used for a tangent equation; tan y = tan α gives y = nπ + α, because tan repeats every π.
one-family-only (conceptual): Only every 2π was counted; tan repeats every π, so the solutions come every π (divided by the multiple of x).

teach.idea: sin y = sin α ⇔ y = nπ + (−1)ⁿα; cos y = cos α ⇔ y = 2nπ ± α; tan y = tan α ⇔ y = nπ + α (n any integer), with α the principal value.
teach.method: Write the right side as f(α) using the principal value, apply the matching general form to kx, then divide everything by k.

alternatives.title: List and check a few solutions
text: Put n = 0, 1, 2, −1 into an option and check each angle in the equation.
Also find the solutions in one turn from the quadrants: the right option must give all of them and nothing else.

families.title: Trigonometric functions of any angle
explanations: quadrant-sign (conceptual): The sign was wrong: in the quadrant of 1050°, cot is negative.
negative-ignored (conceptual): cot(−30°) was worked out as cot 30°; a negative angle is measured clockwise (sin, tan, cosec, cot change sign; cos and sec do not).

no-cofunction-change (procedural): The angle was written as a multiple of 90° plus 60°, but cot was kept; after an ODD multiple of 90° the function changes to its co-function (sin ↔ cos, tan ↔ cot, sec ↔ cosec).

teach.idea: Every angle has the same trigonometric values as its position on the unit circle; the value is the reference angle's value with the sign of the quadrant (All, Sin, Tan, Cos).
teach.method: Add or take away 360° until the angle is between 0° and 360°, find its reference angle (its distance from the x-axis), then attach the sign of the function in that quadrant.

alternatives.title: Allied-angle rules
text: Write the angle as 90° × n ± θ.
If n is even keep the function; if n is odd change to its co-function. Then fix the sign from the quadrant of the original angle.

families.title: The period of a trigonometric function
explanations: multiply-not-divide (procedural): The period was multiplied by the number in front of x; a bigger multiple of x makes the graph repeat SOONER, so divide.
period-mixed (recall): cot repeats every π, not every 2π.

teach.idea: sin, cos, sec and cosec repeat every 2π; tan and cot every π. Replacing x by kx makes the graph repeat k times as fast; the number in front and the shift inside do not change the period.
teach.method: Take the basic period (2π or π) and divide it by k.

alternatives.title: When does the inside complete a cycle?
text: The inside kx + c must grow by one basic period (2π or π).
kx grows by 2π when x grows by 2π/k: that is the period.

families.title: Degrees to radians
explanations: pi-dropped (procedural): The π was left out; 180° is π radians, so the answer is a fraction OF π.
factor-flipped (recall): The angle was multiplied by 180/π; to change degrees to radians multiply by π/180.
full-turn-as-pi (conceptual): A full turn was taken as π radians; a full turn is 2π radians, and π is a half turn (180°).

teach.idea: One radian is the angle whose arc equals the radius; a half turn, 180°, is π radians.
teach.method: Multiply the angle in degrees by π/180 and simplify the fraction.

families.title: Radians to degrees
explanations: denominator-dropped (procedural): π was replaced by 180° but the division by 5 was forgotten.
pi-as-full-turn (conceptual): π was replaced by 360°; π radians is a half turn, 180°.

teach.idea: π radians is 180°, so 1 radian = 180°/π (about 57.3°).
teach.method: Multiply by 180/π; with π in the angle, simply replace π by 180° and simplify.

alternatives.title: As a fraction of a half turn
text: kπ/d radians is k/d of a half turn.
So it is (k/d) × 180°.

families.title: Arc length and sector area
explanations: degrees-used (conceptual): The angle in degrees was multiplied by the radius; l = rθ needs θ in radians.
area-formula (recall): The sector-area formula ½r²θ was used; the arc length is rθ.
inverted (procedural): r was divided by l; from l = rθ, θ = l ÷ r.
multiplied (procedural): l and r were multiplied; θ = l ÷ r.
half-dropped (recall): The ½ was left out; the sector area is ½r²θ.
radius-not-squared (recall): r was not squared; the sector area is ½r²θ.

teach.idea: With θ in radians, the arc is θ radii long (l = rθ) and the sector is the fraction θ/2π of the circle (A = ½r²θ).
teach.method: Change degrees to radians first (× π/180), then use l = rθ or A = ½r²θ; to find θ use θ = l/r.

alternatives.title: Fraction of the whole circle
text: An angle of x° is x/360 of a full turn.
So the arc is (x/360) × 2πr and the sector is (x/360) × πr².

families.title: Finding a side with the sine rule
explanations: ratio-inverted (procedural): The sines were the wrong way up; a/sin A = b/sin B gives b = a sin B / sin A.
angles-proportional (conceptual): The sides were taken in the same ratio as the angles; sides are in the ratio of the SINES of the opposite angles.

teach.idea: In any triangle a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C: each side is proportional to the sine of the angle opposite it.
teach.method: Write a/sin A = b/sin B, put in the known values and solve for b; then simplify the surds.

alternatives.title: Drop a perpendicular
text: The height from C to AB equals b sin A and also a sin B.
So b sin A = a sin B, which is the sine rule.

families.title: The cosine of an angle from three sides
explanations: wrong-sign (recall): The squares were combined the wrong way; cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc), with the side opposite A taken away.
two-dropped (recall): The 2 in the denominator was left out: cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc).
wrong-angle (procedural): The formula for a different angle was used; for A, the side a (opposite A) is the one taken away.

teach.idea: The cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A extends Pythagoras: the extra term corrects for A not being 90°.
teach.method: Rearrange to cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc) and substitute; a negative answer means A is obtuse.

alternatives.title: Use coordinates
text: Put A at the origin and AB along the x-axis: B = (c, 0), C = (b cos A, b sin A).
Then a² = (b cos A − c)² + (b sin A)² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A.

families.title: Area of a triangle from two sides and the included angle
explanations: half-dropped (recall): The ½ was left out; the area is ½ab sin C (ab sin C is the parallelogram).
cos-for-sin (recall): cos C was used; the height of the triangle on side b is a sin C, so the area uses sin C.

teach.idea: Taking b as the base, the height is a sin C, so the area is ½ × b × a sin C.
teach.method: Multiply the two sides, multiply by sin of the angle between them, and halve.

alternatives.title: Check with Heron's formula
text: Find the third side with the cosine rule.
Then area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) with s half the perimeter.

families.title: Principal values of inverse trigonometric functions
explanations: outside-branch (conceptual): An angle outside the principal range was given for cosec⁻¹ of a negative number; its principal value lies between −π/2 and π/2, so it is negative here.
odd-rule-misused (conceptual): sec⁻¹(−x) was taken as −sec⁻¹(x); for cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ the rule is π − sec⁻¹(x), because their principal values lie between 0 and π.

teach.idea: Each inverse function returns one angle from its principal range: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹ in [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹ in [0, π]. That is why it has a single value.
teach.method: Find the standard angle whose ratio is the argument, then make sure it lies in the principal range: for a negative argument use −θ (sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹) or π − θ (cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cot⁻¹).

alternatives.title: Turn sec⁻¹, cosec⁻¹, cot⁻¹ into the basic three
text: sec⁻¹ x = cos⁻¹(1/x) and cosec⁻¹ x = sin⁻¹(1/x).
cot⁻¹ x = tan⁻¹(1/x) for x > 0, and π + tan⁻¹(1/x) for x < 0.

families.title: sin⁻¹(sin θ), cos⁻¹(cos θ) and tan⁻¹(tan θ)
explanations: cancel (conceptual): The inverse and the function were 'cancelled'; tan⁻¹(tan θ) = θ only when θ is in the principal range.
shift-no-reflect (procedural): A multiple of 2π was removed, but the angle was not brought into [0, π]: use cos(2π − θ) = cos θ.
period-2pi (recall): Multiples of 2π were removed; tan repeats every π, so remove multiples of π.

teach.idea: sin⁻¹(sin θ) is the angle in [−π/2, π/2] with the same sine as θ; it equals θ only when θ is already in that range (similarly [0, π] for cos⁻¹ and (−π/2, π/2) for tan⁻¹).
teach.method: Find an angle in the principal range with the same ratio: use sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(2π − θ) = cos θ, tan(θ − π) = tan θ, and add or remove whole turns.

alternatives.title: Use the unit circle
text: Mark θ on the unit circle. For sine, move to the point with the same height on the right half.
For cosine, move to the point with the same x on the upper half; for tangent, to the same line through the origin on the right half.

families.title: Linear combinations of vectors in components
explanations: scalar-first-only (procedural): The number in front of a vector was multiplied into its first component only; it multiplies every component.
minus-first-only (procedural): The minus sign before 2b was applied to its first component only; it changes the sign of every component.

teach.idea: Vectors in î, ĵ, k̂ form are added and scaled component by component, because î, ĵ and k̂ point in independent directions.
teach.method: Multiply every component of a by p and every component of b by q, then add the matching components.

alternatives.title: Write them as columns
text: Write each vector as a column of three numbers.
Scale each column, then add across each row.

families.title: Magnitude of the vector joining two points
explanations: root-missing (procedural): The square root was not taken; |AB| = √(x² + y² + z²).
added-points (conceptual): The position vectors were added; the vector AB is (position of B) − (position of A).
components-added (conceptual): The components were added without squaring; the length comes from Pythagoras in three dimensions.

teach.idea: The vector AB is OB − OA; its length is √(x² + y² + z²), Pythagoras used twice.
teach.method: Subtract A's components from B's, square the three differences, add, and take the square root (simplify the surd).

alternatives.title: The diagonal of a box
text: The differences are the edges of a box with A and B at opposite corners.
The floor diagonal is √(x² + y²); with the height z, the full diagonal is √(x² + y² + z²).

families.title: The section formula with position vectors
explanations: ratio-swapped (procedural): The ratio was used the wrong way round; for 3 : 4 from P, multiply q by 3 and p by 4.
external-as-internal (conceptual): The internal formula was used; for external division R lies outside PQ and r = (mq − np)/(m − n).
internal-as-external (conceptual): The external formula was used; for internal division r = (mq + np)/(m + n).

teach.idea: R divides PQ in m : n internally when PR : RQ = m : n with R between P and Q; then r = (mq + np)/(m + n). Externally, R is outside the segment and r = (mq − np)/(m − n).
teach.method: Choose the formula, multiply q by m and p by n, add (or subtract), and divide each component by m + n (or m − n).

alternatives.title: Walk along the segment
text: Internally, R is m/(m + n) of the way from P to Q: r = p + (m/(m + n))(q − p).
Externally, R = p + (m/(m − n))(q − p), which goes past Q (or behind P).

families.title: Direction cosines of a vector joining two points
explanations: ratios-given (conceptual): The direction ratios (the components of AB) were given; direction cosines are the components divided by the length |AB|.
reversed (procedural): The vector BA was used; AB is (B − A), and reversing it changes every sign.
divided-by-sum (conceptual): The components were divided by their sum; divide by the length √(a² + b² + c²), so that l² + m² + n² = 1.

teach.idea: The direction cosines (l, m, n) of a vector are the cosines of the angles it makes with the x-, y- and z-axes; they are the components of the unit vector, so l² + m² + n² = 1.
teach.method: Find the direction ratios B − A, find the length √(a² + b² + c²), divide each ratio by it and rationalise.

alternatives.title: Think of the angles
text: The angle α with the x-axis has cos α = (x-component)/(length), as in a right triangle.
Do the same for the y- and z-axes.

families.title: The angle between two vectors (cos θ)
explanations: dot-only (conceptual): Only a · b was found; cos θ = a · b / (|a| |b|), so divide by both lengths.
one-length (procedural): a · b was divided by |a| only; that is the projection of b on a. Divide by |a| |b|.

teach.idea: a · b = |a| |b| cos θ, and a · b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃; together they give the angle. a · b = 0 means the vectors are perpendicular.
teach.method: Multiply matching components and add (a · b), find |a| and |b|, then cos θ = a · b/(|a| |b|); rationalise.

alternatives.title: Use the cosine rule
text: a, b and a − b form a triangle with sides |a|, |b| and |a − b|.
cos θ = (|a|² + |b|² − |a − b|²)/(2|a||b|), the same as the dot-product formula.

families.title: Projection of one vector on another
explanations: wrong-length (procedural): a · b was divided by |a|; that is the projection of b on a. The projection on b divides by |b|.
dot-only (conceptual): Only a · b was found; the projection is a · b/|b|.
length-squared (procedural): a · b was divided by |b|²; that number scales b to give the projection VECTOR. The projection (a length) is a · b/|b|.

teach.idea: The projection of a on b is the length of a's shadow on the line of b: |a| cos θ = a · b/|b|. It is negative when the angle is obtuse.
teach.method: Find a · b and |b|, divide, and rationalise.

alternatives.title: Dot with the unit vector
text: Make b into a unit vector b̂ = b/|b|.
The projection is a · b̂.

families.title: The cross product in components
explanations: middle-sign (procedural): The ĵ component's minus sign was forgotten when expanding the determinant; the middle term is −(a₁b₃ − a₃b₁).
order-reversed (conceptual): b × a was found; the cross product changes sign when the order changes: a × b = −(b × a).
componentwise (conceptual): Matching components were multiplied; that is part of the dot product. The cross product uses the determinant.

teach.idea: a × b is a vector perpendicular to both a and b (right-hand rule), with length |a||b| sin θ, the area of the parallelogram on a and b.
teach.method: Expand the determinant with rows (î ĵ k̂), (a₁ a₂ a₃), (b₁ b₂ b₃): î(a₂b₃ − a₃b₂) − ĵ(a₁b₃ − a₃b₁) + k̂(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).

alternatives.title: The cyclic pattern
text: x: a₂b₃ − a₃b₂; y: a₃b₁ − a₁b₃; z: a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ (follow 1 → 2 → 3 → 1).
Check: the answer dotted with a, and with b, must give 0.

families.title: Area of a triangle by the cross product
explanations: half-dropped (recall): The ½ was left out; |AB × AC| is the area of the parallelogram, and the triangle is half of it.
root-missing (procedural): The square root of |AB × AC|² was not taken.

teach.idea: |AB × AC| = |AB||AC| sin A is the area of the parallelogram on AB and AC; the triangle is half of it.
teach.method: Find AB and AC, their cross product, its length, and halve it.

alternatives.title: Check with Heron's formula
text: Find the three side lengths with the distance formula.
Area = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), where s is half the perimeter.

families.title: The scalar triple product
explanations: middle-sign (procedural): The middle term of the expansion was added; the signs go +, −, + along the first row.
order-swapped (conceptual): Two of the vectors were swapped ([b a c]); swapping two rows changes the sign of the triple product.

teach.idea: [a b c] = a · (b × c) is the determinant with rows a, b, c; its size is the volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c, and it is 0 exactly when they are coplanar.
teach.method: Write the 3 × 3 determinant and expand along the first row with signs +, −, +.

alternatives.title: Cross first, then dot
text: Work out b × c as a vector.
Then dot it with a: multiply matching components and add.

families.title: Coplanar vectors: find λ
explanations: sign-slip (procedural): A sign slipped when solving the linear equation for λ; check by putting λ back into the determinant.
perpendicular-for-coplanar (conceptual): a · c = 0 was used (a perpendicular to c); coplanar means [a b c] = 0.

teach.idea: Three vectors are coplanar exactly when the parallelepiped they make is flat: [a b c] = 0.
teach.method: Write the determinant with rows a, b, c (λ in it), expand to get an expression in λ, set it equal to 0 and solve.

alternatives.title: c as a combination of a and b
text: Coplanar means c = xa + yb for some numbers x, y.
Find x and y from the î and ĵ components; the k̂ component then gives λ.

families.title: The vector triple product a × (b × c)
explanations: terms-swapped (recall): The two terms were swapped: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c.
bracket-moved (conceptual): (a × b) × c was found; the cross product is not associative, so the bracket matters.

teach.idea: a × (b × c) is perpendicular to b × c, so it lies in the plane of b and c: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b − (a · b)c.
teach.method: Work out the two dot products a · c and a · b, then form (a · c)b − (a · b)c component by component.

alternatives.title: Two cross products
text: Find b × c first.
Then cross a with that result; the answers agree.

families.title: The point on the unit circle for a real number t
explanations: swapped (recall): The coordinates were swapped; the x-coordinate is cos t and the y-coordinate is sin t.
quadrant-signs (conceptual): The signs were taken from the first quadrant; t = 23π/6 ends in a quadrant where y is negative.

teach.idea: On the unit circle, the real number t is an arc length; the point it reaches is (cos t, sin t). This defines sin and cos for every real number, and the quadrant of the point gives their signs.
teach.method: Change t to an angle (π = 180°), find the reference angle and its standard values, and give each coordinate the sign of its quadrant.

alternatives.title: Reflect a first-quadrant point
text: Find the point for the reference angle in the first quadrant, for example (√3/2, 1/2) for π/6.
Reflect it into the right quadrant: across the y-axis the x-coordinate changes sign, across the x-axis the y-coordinate does.

families.title: The signs of sin t and cos t for a real number t
explanations: degrees (conceptual): t = 12 was taken as 12°; here t is a real number (radians): π ≈ 3.14 is half a turn.
minus-ignored (procedural): The minus sign was ignored; a negative t goes clockwise from (1, 0).
coordinates-swapped (recall): The coordinates were read the wrong way round; cos t is the x-coordinate and sin t the y-coordinate.

teach.idea: P(t) = (cos t, sin t) lies in the quadrant reached after going t round the unit circle; cos t has the sign of the x-coordinate and sin t of the y-coordinate. One full turn is 2π ≈ 6.28, and the quadrants end at π/2 ≈ 1.57, π ≈ 3.14 and 3π/2 ≈ 4.71.
teach.method: Add or take away 2π until 0 ≤ t < 2π, compare t with π/2, π and 3π/2 to find the quadrant, and read the signs (All, Sin, Tan, Cos).

alternatives.title: Walk round the circle
text: Start at (1, 0) and walk t units anticlockwise (clockwise if t < 0) on a circle of radius 1.
Each quarter of the walk is about 1.57 units long.

families.title: Domain and range of the six trigonometric functions
explanations: range-for-domain (conceptual): The range of cos was given; cos is defined for every real x.
sec-range (conceptual): The range of sec and cosec was given; cos never goes beyond 5 in size.
factor-ignored (conceptual): The number 5 in front was ignored; it scales every value.
zeros-for-poles (conceptual): The points where cos 4x = 0 were left out; cot is undefined where sin 4x = 0.
k-ignored (conceptual): The 4 in 4x was ignored; cot 4x is undefined where 4x = nπ, so divide by 4.
bounded-like-sine (conceptual): cot was thought to stay between −5 and 5 like sine; near its asymptotes it takes every real value.
cos-range-used (conceptual): The range of cos was given; sec = 1/cos, so its size is never less than 5.

teach.idea: sin and cos are defined for every x and take values from −1 to 1; tan and sec are undefined where cos x = 0 (x = (2n + 1)π/2), cot and cosec where sin x = 0 (x = nπ); tan and cot take every real value; sec and cosec never lie strictly between −1 and 1.
teach.method: For a f(kx): the excluded x come from kx = (2n + 1)π/2 or kx = nπ, so divide by k; the range of sin, cos, sec, cosec is scaled by a, while tan and cot still take every real value.

alternatives.title: Read it from the graphs
text: The graph of tan x has vertical asymptotes at x = ±π/2, ±3π/2, …: those x are not in the domain.
The graph of sec x has U-shaped pieces above 1 and below −1, never in between.

families.title: Simplifying with the compound-angle formulas
explanations: function-changed (recall): cot was written; this pattern is the tangent formula, so it gives tan.
sign-pattern (recall): The sign was matched the wrong way: the sign in the numerator gives tan(A + B) or tan(A − B).

teach.idea: Read the formulas backwards: sin A cos B ± cos A sin B = sin(A ± B); cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B = cos(A ± B) (the sign flips); (tan A ± tan B)/(1 ∓ tan A tan B) = tan(A ± B).
teach.method: Match the pattern: which functions appear, in which order, and with which sign between the products. Then write the single function of kx ± mx.

alternatives.title: Check with x = 0 or a small x
text: Put a convenient value, like x = π/12, into the expression and into each option.
Only the right option gives the same number.

families.title: Half-angle values from one ratio
explanations: halve-the-ratio (conceptual): tan(A/2) was taken as half of tan A; halving the angle does not halve the ratio.
formula-swapped (recall): The two half-angle formulas were swapped: sin²(A/2) = (1 − cos A)/2 and cos²(A/2) = (1 + cos A)/2.
tan-formula-upside-down (recall): tan(A/2) was taken as (1 + cos A)/sin A; it is sin A/(1 + cos A) = (1 − cos A)/sin A.
half-angle-sign (conceptual): cos(A/2) was taken as positive; with π < A < 2π, A/2 lies between π/2 and π, where cosine is negative.

teach.idea: From cos A = 1 − 2 sin²(A/2) = 2 cos²(A/2) − 1: sin(A/2) = ±√((1 − cos A)/2), cos(A/2) = ±√((1 + cos A)/2), and tan(A/2) = sin A/(1 + cos A). The sign comes from the quadrant of A/2.
teach.method: Find cos A (and sin A) with its quadrant's sign, substitute into the half-angle formula, choose the sign from where A/2 lies (0 < A/2 < π), and rationalise.

alternatives.title: Start from the double-angle formula
text: Write cos A = 1 − 2 sin²(A/2) and solve for sin(A/2).
Then use 0 < A/2 < π: sine is positive there, cosine positive only when A < π.

families.title: Mean deviation of a frequency distribution
explanations: signs-kept (conceptual): The deviations were added with their signs; about the mean they always add up to 0. Mean deviation uses the distances |x − centre|.
divide-by-values (procedural): Σf|x − centre| was divided by 5, the number of classes; divide by N = Σf = 25.
frequencies-ignored (conceptual): The frequencies were ignored, as if each value appeared once.
about-median (procedural): The distances were measured from the median; this question asks about the mean.
about-mean (procedural): The distances were measured from the mean; this question asks about the median.

teach.idea: The mean deviation is the average distance of the observations from a centre (the mean or the median); in a frequency table each distance counts as often as its frequency, and for classes the mid-point stands for the class.
teach.method: Find N = Σf and the centre (mean = Σfx/N, or the median from the cumulative frequencies), then the distances |x − centre|, multiply by f, add, and divide by N.

alternatives.title: Use the balance about the mean
text: About the mean, the weighted distances above it add up to the same as those below.
So Σf|x − x̄| = 2 × (sum of f(x − x̄) over the values above the mean).

families.title: Variance of grouped data by the step-deviation method
explanations: h-squared-left-out (procedural): The bracket was not multiplied by h² = 400; u measures in class widths, so σ² = h²[Σfu²/N − (Σfu/N)²].
h-not-squared (procedural): The bracket was multiplied by h = 20 instead of h².
mean-term-left-out (procedural): (Σfu/N)² was not taken away; the step-deviation formula subtracts the square of the mean of u.
square-of-sum (procedural): (Σfd)² was found; Σfd² squares each deviation first, then multiplies by f and adds.
f-squared (procedural): Each fd was squared (f²d²); only the deviation is squared.

teach.idea: Shifting all the data by A does not change the variance, and dividing by h divides it by h²: so σ² = h²[Σfu²/N − (Σfu/N)²] with u = (x − A)/h, using the mid-points of the classes.
teach.method: Write the mid-points, choose A (a middle mid-point) and h, work out u, fu and fu², add the columns, and substitute.

alternatives.title: Assumed-mean method
text: With d = x − A (not divided by h): σ² = Σfd²/N − (Σfd/N)².
It gives the same variance with bigger numbers.

families.title: Area of a parallelogram by the cross product
explanations: triangle-half (recall): ½|a × b| was used; that is the triangle on a and b. The parallelogram is twice the triangle: |a × b|.
root-missing (procedural): The square root of |d₁ × d₂|² was not taken.
half-dropped (recall): The ½ was left out; with diagonals d₁ and d₂ the area is ½|d₁ × d₂| (the vectors are diagonals, not sides).

teach.idea: |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ is the base times the height of the parallelogram on a and b. If d₁ and d₂ are the diagonals, the sides are (d₁ ± d₂)/2, and the area is ½|d₁ × d₂|.
teach.method: Find the cross product with the determinant, then its length; halve it when the vectors given are the diagonals.

alternatives.title: Without the determinant
text: |a × b|² = |a|²|b|² − (a · b)².
Work out the lengths and the dot product, then take the square root.

families.title: Half-angle formulae in a triangle
explanations: formula-swapped (recall): The tangent formula was turned upside down: tan(A/2) = √((s − b)(s − c)/(s(s − a))).
root-missing (procedural): The square root was not taken; the formula gives the square of the half-angle ratio under the root.

teach.idea: With s = (a + b + c)/2, the cosine rule and cos A = 1 − 2 sin²(A/2) = 2 cos²(A/2) − 1 give sin(A/2) = √((s − b)(s − c)/(bc)), cos(A/2) = √(s(s − a)/(bc)) and tan(A/2) = √((s − b)(s − c)/(s(s − a))).
teach.method: Find s, the three numbers s − a, s − b, s − c, substitute into the formula, simplify the fraction under the root and rationalise.

alternatives.title: Go through cos A
text: Find cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc).
Then sin(A/2) = √((1 − cos A)/2): the same value.

families.title: Distances and heights with the sine and cosine rules
explanations: cos-sign (recall): cos 120° was taken as +½; cos 60° = ½ and cos 120° = −½.
pythagoras (conceptual): Pythagoras was used, as if the courses were at right angles; for any other angle use the cosine rule c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
wrong-angle (procedural): sin 60° was used for the angle at T; the angle of triangle ABT at T is 60° − 45° = 15°.
height-instead (procedural): The height of the tower was found; the question asks for the slant distance BT.

teach.idea: When the triangle in a problem is not right-angled, use the cosine rule (two sides and the angle between them give the third side) or the sine rule (a side and two angles give another side).
teach.method: Draw the triangle, mark what is known, find any missing angle from the angle sum (an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles), and apply the matching rule.

alternatives.title: Split into right triangles
text: Drop a perpendicular to make two right triangles.
Use sin, cos and Pythagoras in each: the result matches the sine or cosine rule.

families.title: Scalars, vectors and kinds of vectors
explanations: distance-confused (conceptual): Distance was taken as a vector; distance is only how far, while displacement also has a direction.
speed-confused (conceptual): Speed was taken as a vector; speed is only how fast (a size), while velocity also has a direction.
work-done-confused (conceptual): Work done was taken as a vector because it involves a force; work is a scalar (F · d), with no direction.
weight-confused (conceptual): Weight was taken as a scalar like mass; weight is a force pulling downwards, so it is a vector.
negative-not-collinear (conceptual): −a was taken as not collinear with a; a vector and its negative lie along the same line.
opposite-negative (conceptual): b was taken as the negative of a; −a has the same LENGTH as a, but here b is a larger multiple of −a.
same-direction-equal (conceptual): Vectors pointing the same way were taken as equal; equal vectors must also have the same length (here b is a multiple of a).
small-components-unit (conceptual): Components that are fractions less than 1 were taken to make a unit vector; a unit vector has LENGTH 1: √(x² + y² + z²) = 1.
head-to-tail (conceptual): Vectors joined head to tail were chosen; co-initial vectors both start at the same point.
same-end-point (conceptual): Vectors with the same END point were chosen; co-initial vectors have the same INITIAL (starting) point.

teach.idea: A scalar has only a size (mass, time, speed, work); a vector has a size and a direction (displacement, velocity, force). Equal vectors have the same length and direction; −a has the same length and the opposite direction; collinear vectors lie along parallel lines (b = λa); a unit vector has length 1; the zero vector has length 0; co-initial vectors start at the same point.
teach.method: Ask whether a direction is needed. For two vectors in components compare them: b = a (equal), b = −a (negative), b = λa (collinear), otherwise not collinear. For one vector find its length.

alternatives.title: Draw the arrows
text: Draw each vector as an arrow from its initial point.
Arrows on parallel lines are collinear; arrows from one point are co-initial; an arrow of length 1 is a unit vector.

families.title: Domain and range of the inverse trigonometric functions
explanations: range-for-domain (conceptual): The range of cos⁻¹ was given; its domain is the set of x for which cos⁻¹(x/4) is defined.
k-ignored (conceptual): The 4 was ignored; |x/4| ≥ 1 means |x| ≥ 4.
ends-left-out (conceptual): The end points were left out; sin⁻¹(1) = π/2 and sin⁻¹(−1) = −π/2 are values of sin⁻¹.
branches-swapped (conceptual): The range of tan⁻¹ was given; cot⁻¹ takes values between 0 and π.
bounded-domain (conceptual): cot⁻¹ was thought to need x/4 between −1 and 1 like sin⁻¹; tan and cot take every real value, so cot⁻¹ is defined for every x.
ends-included (conceptual): The end points were included; cot 0 and cot π are not defined.
sin-domain (conceptual): The domain of sin⁻¹ was given; cosec never has a value strictly between −1 and 1, so cosec⁻¹ needs |x/4| ≥ 1.
hole-forgotten (conceptual): 0 was not removed; it would need cosec 0, which is not defined.

teach.idea: Each inverse function undoes its function on one branch: sin⁻¹ has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹ [−1, 1] and [0, π]; tan⁻¹ ℝ and (−π/2, π/2); cot⁻¹ ℝ and (0, π); sec⁻¹ (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞) and [0, π] without π/2; cosec⁻¹ (−∞, −1] ∪ [1, ∞) and [−π/2, π/2] without 0.
teach.method: For f⁻¹(x/k), x/k must lie in the basic domain, so multiply its end points by k. For a·f⁻¹(x), multiply the range's end points by a.

alternatives.title: Reflect the restricted graph
text: The graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of the restricted graph of f in the line y = x.
So the domain and the range swap: the restricted domain of f is the range of f⁻¹.

families.title: Equations and sum formulae with inverse tangents
explanations: negative-root (procedural): Both roots of the quadratic were kept, or the negative one taken; for a negative x the left side is negative, so it cannot equal π/4.
denominator-sign (recall): The denominator was taken as 1 − uv; for a difference it is 1 + uv.
two-outside (conceptual): 2 tan⁻¹(1/a) was taken as tan⁻¹(2/a); doubling the angle is not doubling the tangent.

teach.idea: tan⁻¹ u ± tan⁻¹ v = tan⁻¹((u ± v)/(1 ∓ uv)) (for the sum, when uv < 1) comes from tan(A ± B). Taking tan of both sides turns an equation in inverse tangents into an ordinary equation.
teach.method: Combine the inverse tangents with the formula, take tan of both sides (tan(π/4) = 1), solve, and check each answer in the original equation (reject values that make the left side negative or break the condition).

alternatives.title: Think of angles
text: Let A = tan⁻¹ u and B = tan⁻¹ v, so tan A = u and tan B = v.
Then tan(A + B) = (u + v)/(1 − uv): this is the compound-angle formula.

families.title: The torque of a force about a point
explanations: order-reversed (conceptual): F × r was found; the torque is r × F, and the order changes the sign.
about-origin (procedural): The position vector of P (from the origin) was used; the torque about A uses the arm r = P − A.
