teach.idea: The torque (moment) of a force F acting at P about a point A is τ = r × F with r = AP = P − A: a vector perpendicular to r and F whose length |r||F| sin θ measures the turning effect.
teach.method: Find the arm r = P − A, then the cross product r × F with the determinant.

alternatives.title: Check perpendicularity
text: Your torque dotted with r, and with F, must be 0.
If not, a component of the cross product has a slip.

families.title: Volume of a parallelepiped or tetrahedron
explanations: tetra-sixth (recall): ⅙ was used; that is the tetrahedron. The parallelepiped is |[a b c]|.
sign-kept (conceptual): The triple product was negative and the sign was kept; a volume is the size |[a b c]|.
third-not-sixth (recall): A third of the triple product was taken (as for a pyramid on a parallelogram base); the tetrahedron is ⅙|[a b c]|.

teach.idea: |[a b c]| = |a · (b × c)| is the base area |b × c| times the height (the part of a along the normal): the volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c. The tetrahedron on the same three edges is ⅙ of it.
teach.method: Work out the determinant with rows a, b, c, take its absolute value, and divide by 6 for a tetrahedron.

alternatives.title: Base times height
text: The base parallelogram on b and c has area |b × c|.
The height is the projection of a on b × c; volume = base × height.

families.title: Probability mass function and distribution function from a sample space
explanations: values-equally-likely (conceptual): The 11 values of X were taken as equally likely; different values come from different numbers of outcomes, so count the outcomes.
strict (procedural): P(X < 4) was found; F(4) includes X = 4.
pmf-for-cdf (conceptual): P(X = 4) was given; F(4) = P(X ≤ 4) adds the probabilities of all values up to 4.

teach.idea: A random variable X gives a number to each outcome of the sample space. Its probability mass function p(x) = P(X = x) adds up the outcomes with each value; its distribution function F(x) = P(X ≤ x) adds p over all values up to x.
teach.method: List the sample space, write X beside each outcome, count how many outcomes give each value (divide by the total), and for F(k) add the probabilities of the values up to and including k.

alternatives.title: Make the table
text: Write the values of X in a row and their probabilities underneath.
A third row of running totals is F(x).

families.title: From a density to the distribution function, and back
explanations: density-given (conceptual): The density itself was given; F(x) is the area under f from the left end up to x.
power-not-divided (procedural): x⁴ was integrated to x⁵ without dividing by 5.
integrated (conceptual): F was integrated; the density is the DERIVATIVE of the distribution function, f(x) = F′(x).
power-not-brought-down (procedural): The power was reduced but not brought down in front: the derivative of x⁵ is 5x⁴.
from-zero (procedural): The area was measured from 0; the density is 0 below 5, so integrate from 5.

teach.idea: For a continuous random variable, F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫ f(t) dt from the left end up to x, and f(x) = F′(x) wherever F is differentiable: integrating and differentiating go back and forth.
teach.method: From f to F: integrate f from the start of the interval to x (check that F at the right end is 1). From F to f: differentiate F.

alternatives.title: Check the end points
text: F must be 0 at the left end and 1 at the right end of the interval.
f must be at least 0 and its total area must be 1.

families.title: Mean and variance of a continuous random variable; properties of expectation
explanations: density-mean (conceptual): f was integrated without the factor x; E(X) = ∫ x f(x) dx (the plain integral of f is 1).
midpoint (conceptual): The middle of the interval (the midpoint 3) was given; the mean is pulled towards where the density is larger.
ex2-as-variance (procedural): E(X²) was given; Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
mean-not-squared (procedural): E(X) was taken away instead of [E(X)]².
d-left-out (procedural): The constant 5 was left out; E(cX + d) = cE(X) + d.
c-not-squared (procedural): c was not squared; Var(cX + d) = c²Var(X).
d-added (conceptual): 5 was added; adding a constant shifts every value equally and does not change the spread.

teach.idea: For a density f, E(X) = ∫ x f(x) dx and Var(X) = ∫ x² f(x) dx − [E(X)]². For any random variable, E(cX + d) = cE(X) + d and Var(cX + d) = c²Var(X): shifting moves the mean but not the spread, scaling by c scales the spread by c².
teach.method: Integrate x f(x) (and x² f(x)) over the interval; for a linear change of X use the two properties.

alternatives.title: Test with a simple variable
text: Let X be μ − 1 or μ + 1 with probability ½ each.
Work out cX + d for both values: its mean is cμ + d, and its spread is c times as wide.

families.title: Statements, and the column of a truth table
explanations: open-sentence (conceptual): "x + 5 = 9." was taken as a statement; its truth depends on the unknown, so it is an open sentence, not a statement.
false-not-statement (conceptual): "9 is an even number." was taken as not a statement because it is false; a false sentence is still a statement — it has a definite truth value.
negation-ignored (conceptual): The ¬ (not) was ignored; ¬p is true exactly when p is false.
or-exclusive (conceptual): 'Or' was read as 'one but not both'; A ∨ B is also true when both are true.
conditional-as-and (conceptual): 'If A then B' was taken as true only when both are true; it is false ONLY when A is true and B is false.
biconditional-as-and (conceptual): 'A if and only if B' was taken as true only when both are true; it is also true when both are false.

teach.idea: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both. Questions, commands, exclamations and open sentences (whose truth depends on an unknown, like x + 3 = 7) are not statements. A truth table lists the truth value of a compound statement for every combination of p and q.
teach.method: For a sentence, ask: can it be called true or false as it stands? For a truth table, work out each bracket row by row (∧ needs both, ∨ needs at least one, → fails only for T → F, ↔ needs equal values), then the whole.

alternatives.title: Build column by column
text: Write the p and q columns: T T F F and T F T F.
Add a column for each negation and each bracket before the final column.

families.title: Choosing the equation that models a situation
explanations: bracket-too-wide (conceptual): The number taken away was put inside a bracket with x, so it was multiplied by 9 as well; in the story only x is multiplied by 9.
roles-swapped (procedural): The two numbers of the story were put in each other's places: 9 is the number that multiplies x, and 19 is taken away once.
give-away-added (conceptual): Giving away 19 sweets was written as adding 19; giving away makes the number smaller, so it is − 19.

teach.idea: An equation is the story written in symbols: the unknown is a letter, and each action in the story becomes an operation on it, in the same order.
teach.method: Name the unknown x. Follow the story: what multiplies x, what is added or taken away, and what the result equals. Check by putting a guessed number for x into both the story and the equation.

alternatives.title: Test with the story's number
text: Find the story's number by trying 1, 2, 3, … in the story itself.
Only the right equation is true for that number.

alternatives.title: Draw a bar model
text: Draw a equal bars for a × x, then a short piece for the number added.
The whole length is the result; the picture reads as ax + b = c.

families.title: Forming and solving a linear equation from a word problem
explanations: middle-number (procedural): The total was divided by 3, which gives the middle number of the three; the smallest is 1 less.
lost-the-number (conceptual): Only the 6x part was kept on the left; the smaller number x itself is part of the sum too.
added-once (procedural): 6 was added only once; it is added to each of the two numbers, so 2 × 6 = 12 goes into the equation.
half-perimeter (conceptual): The perimeter was taken as length + width; the perimeter goes all the way round, 2 × (length + width).
extra-once (procedural): The 8 cm was counted once; there are two lengths, so it appears twice: 2(2x + 8) = 4x + 16.
dropped-extra (conceptual): The 9 was left out, as if both numbers were the same.
bracket-not-expanded (procedural): 10(x + 10) was written as 10x + 10; the 10 multiplies both x and 10.

teach.idea: Call the number you are asked for x; the story then tells you how to build the total from x, and that is the equation.
teach.method: Write each quantity in terms of x, add them as the story says, set the result equal to the total, then undo: take away the constant, divide by the coefficient. Check in the story.

alternatives.title: Make a table
text: List each quantity in the story with its expression in x.
Add the expressions; the sum equals the given total.

alternatives.title: Guess, check, improve
text: Try a value of x in the story and see whether the total is too big or too small.
The equation does this in one step: it finds exactly the x that makes the total right.

families.title: Writing an algebraic expression from a statement in words
explanations: added-first (conceptual): The 2 was added before multiplying; “2 more than 9 times p” means work out 9 times p first, then add 2.
plus-for-times (recall): “9 times p” was written as p + 9; times means multiply.
less-than-reversed (conceptual): “9 less than” was written as 9 minus the rest; “9 less than something” is that something with 9 taken away.
subtract-first (conceptual): The 9 was taken away before multiplying; the multiplying by 7 comes first here.
no-bracket (procedural): The bracket was left out, so only p was multiplied by 9; the whole difference is multiplied.
order-reversed (conceptual): p was subtracted from 5; “5 is subtracted from p” means p − 5.
added-before-dividing (conceptual): 9 was added before dividing; the statement divides p by 8 first.
times-for-divide (recall): “divided by 8” was written as multiplying by 8.

teach.idea: A letter stands for any number; an expression is the list of operations done to it, written with + − × ÷ and brackets.
teach.method: Read the statement and find what is done first. Write that part, then the next operation on it. Use a bracket when a whole sum or difference is multiplied.

alternatives.title: Try it with a number first
text: Put a number such as 10 in place of the letter and work the statement out.
Write the same steps again with the letter instead of 10.

alternatives.title: A number machine
text: Imagine the letter going into a machine that does each operation in turn.
What comes out, written with the letter, is the expression.

families.title: Multiplying binomials and monomials with an area model
explanations: first-and-last (conceptual): Only the first terms and the last terms were multiplied; each term of one bracket multiplies each term of the other (four cells in the area model).
sum-and-product-swapped (procedural): The product 72 and the sum 17 were put in each other's places; the x term comes from adding, the number term from multiplying.
sign-of-product (procedural): The sign of a cell was lost: a negative times a positive is negative.
coefficients-left-out (procedural): The middle term was found as 5 + 5, without multiplying by 4 and 4; the two x cells are 4 × 5 and 5 × 4.
multiplied-powers (conceptual): The powers of x were multiplied; x³ × x³ means 3 factors of x and then 3 more, so the powers add.
added-numbers (procedural): The numbers 6 and 5 were added; the area of a rectangle multiplies its sides, numbers too.

teach.idea: A product of two brackets is the area of a rectangle whose sides are the brackets: split each side into its terms and the rectangle splits into smaller rectangles.
teach.method: Draw a grid with one bracket's terms across the top and the other's down the side. Multiply to fill each cell, then add the cells, collecting the like terms.

alternatives.title: Each term times each term
text: Multiply the first term of the first bracket by each term of the second, then the second term by each term of the second.
Add the four products and collect like terms.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Put x = 2 into the brackets and multiply.
Your expanded answer must give the same number at x = 2.

families.title: Deciding whether a list is an AP, with its first term and common difference
explanations: first-difference-only (conceptual): Only the first two terms were compared; in an AP every difference between neighbouring terms must be the same.
difference-reversed (procedural): The common difference was found as a term minus the next term; d is each term minus the one before it.

teach.idea: A list is an arithmetic progression when the same number is added each time: every term minus the one before it gives the same common difference d.
teach.method: Work out a₂ − a₁, a₃ − a₂, a₄ − a₃, …. If they are all equal, it is an AP with first term a₁ and that difference d; if any one differs, it is not an AP.

alternatives.title: Equal jumps on a number line
text: Mark the terms on a number line.
An AP makes jumps of the same size (to the left when d is negative).

alternatives.title: The middle term is the average
text: In an AP each term is the average of its two neighbours: 2a₂ = a₁ + a₃.
If this fails anywhere, the list is not an AP.

families.title: Which term, the nth term from the end, and the number of terms of an AP
explanations: forgot-plus-one (procedural): (l − a) ÷ d counts the steps between terms; the number of terms is one more.
from-the-start (conceptual): The 8th term from the start was found; from the end, start at the last term and go back.
n-steps (procedural): 8 steps were taken back from the last term; the 8th term from the end is 7 steps back.

teach.idea: In an AP aₙ = a + (n − 1)d: term n is n − 1 steps of size d after the first term. Read backwards from the last term l, the AP has first term l and difference −d.
teach.method: Which term is V: solve a + (n − 1)d = V for n. Number of terms: solve a + (n − 1)d = l. The nth term from the end: l − (n − 1)d.

alternatives.title: Count the steps
text: (V − a) ÷ d is how many steps of d lead from a to V.
Add 1 for the first term itself: that is the term number.

alternatives.title: Fence posts
text: Terms are like fence posts and differences like the gaps between them.
There is always one more post than gaps.

families.title: The sum of the first n terms of an AP
explanations: no-half (recall): The sum was not halved: pairing the first and last terms gives n/2 pairs, not n pairs.
n-not-n-minus-1 (procedural): (n − 1)d was written as nd; the last of 9 terms is only 8 steps after the first.
single-a (recall): The formula was used as n/2 × [a + (n − 1)d]; it is n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d] (the first term and the last term together).
last-times-n (conceptual): Every term was taken to be as large as the last one; the terms grow (or shrink) evenly, so their average is (first + last)/2.

teach.idea: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add: each pair of terms adds to the same total a + l, and there are n pairs, so 2Sₙ = n(a + l).
teach.method: Find the last term l = a + (n − 1)d, then Sₙ = n(a + l)/2, or in one step Sₙ = n/2 × [2a + (n − 1)d].

alternatives.title: Pair the ends
text: Pair the first with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on: every pair has the same sum.
Multiply that pair sum by the number of pairs, n/2.

alternatives.title: Average times number
text: The terms of an AP are spread evenly, so their average is (first + last)/2.
The sum is that average times the number of terms.

families.title: The condition for three numbers to be in AP
explanations: forgot-the-two (recall): The middle term was set equal to the sum of the other two; it is twice the middle term that equals that sum (the middle term is their average).
ends-equal (conceptual): The first and third terms were set equal; in an AP the gaps are equal, not the terms.

teach.idea: Three numbers are in AP exactly when the middle one is halfway between the others: b − a = c − b, or 2b = a + c.
teach.method: Write 2 × (middle expression) = (first) + (third), collect the k terms on one side and the numbers on the other, and divide.

alternatives.title: Equal gaps
text: Write the first gap (second − first) and the second gap (third − second) in terms of k.
Set them equal and solve.

alternatives.title: Check with the numbers
text: Put your k into the three expressions.
The three numbers you get must go up (or down) by the same amount.

families.title: Terms of a sequence from a general or a recursive rule
explanations: started-at-zero (procedural): The terms were found for n = 0, 1, 2, 3; the first term a₁ has n = 1.
bracket (procedural): The rule was used as 3(aₙ₋₁ + 1); multiply the term before by 3 first, then add 1.
rule-on-first (conceptual): The rule was applied to a₁ as well; a₁ = 6 is given, and the rule starts at a₂.

teach.idea: A general rule gives any term directly from its position n; a recursive rule gives each term from the one before, starting from a given first term. With aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d the sequence is an AP.
teach.method: General rule: substitute n = 1, 2, 3, 4. Recursive rule: start from a₁, then apply the rule to get a₂ from a₁, a₃ from a₂, and so on.

alternatives.title: A table of n and aₙ
text: Make two rows: n = 1, 2, 3, 4 and the terms.
For a recursive rule, fill each box using the box just before it.

alternatives.title: When is it an AP?
text: aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + d adds the same number each time: an AP.
aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 1 does not: the gaps keep changing.

families.title: An AP as points on a straight line
explanations: intercept-is-first-term (conceptual): The first term was taken as c; c is the value at n = 0, one step before the first term, so c = a − d.
order-swapped (procedural): The two numbers were given in the wrong order: the first term a comes first.
first-term-is-intercept (conceptual): The constant of the line was taken as the first term; the first term is the value at x = 1, so a = m + c.

teach.idea: aₙ = a + (n − 1)d = dn + (a − d) is a linear expression in n, so the points (n, aₙ) of an AP lie on a straight line whose slope is the common difference.
teach.method: Slope m = d. Intercept c = a − d (the value 'at n = 0'). Going back: d = m and a = m + c.

alternatives.title: From a table
text: Write n and aₙ in a table: aₙ rises by d whenever n rises by 1.
Step back from n = 1 to n = 0 to find where the line meets the y-axis.

alternatives.title: Fixed charge plus rate
text: A fare with a fixed charge and the same price for each kilometre grows in equal steps.
Its graph is a straight line; the price per kilometre is the slope.

families.title: Recognising a quadratic equation and writing it in standard form
explanations: signs-not-changed (procedural): Terms were moved from the right side to the left without changing their signs; moving + rx makes it − rx.
right-side-dropped (conceptual): Only the left side was expanded and the right side was forgotten; standard form needs everything on one side with 0 on the other.
x2-not-cancelled (conceptual): The x² on the right was not taken away from the x² on the left; they cancel, which leaves a linear equation.
x2-added (procedural): The x² on the right was added to the 2x² on the left; moving it across makes it − x².

teach.idea: A quadratic equation is one that can be written as ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. Whether it is quadratic shows only after expanding and collecting everything on one side: the x² terms may cancel.
teach.method: Expand every bracket, move all terms to the left (changing their signs), collect like terms. If an x² term remains, that is the standard form; if not, the equation is linear.

alternatives.title: Look for the highest power
text: After simplifying, the highest power of x decides the type.
Power 2: quadratic. Power 1 only: linear.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Put x = 1 into both sides of the original equation and find left − right.
Your standard form must give the same value at x = 1.

families.title: Solving ax² + bx + c = 0 by splitting the middle term
explanations: signs-of-roots (procedural): The numbers in the brackets were taken as the roots with their signs; ax + b = 0 gives x = −b/a.
not-divided (procedural): The coefficient of x in each bracket was not divided out: ax + b = 0 gives x = −b/a, not −b.
inverted (procedural): The fraction was turned upside down: ax + b = 0 gives x = −b/a, not −a/b.

teach.idea: Splitting the middle term reverses the expansion of (ax + b)(cx + d): the two middle products ad and bc multiply to ac × bd and add to the x coefficient.
teach.method: Multiply a by c; find two numbers with that product and with sum b; split bx into those two terms; group in pairs and factorise; set each bracket to 0.

alternatives.title: Use the quadratic formula
text: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a) gives the same two roots.
Here b² − 4ac is a perfect square, which is why the factors are rational.

alternatives.title: Check a root
text: Put each root back into ax² + bx + c.
It must give 0.

families.title: Solving a quadratic equation with the quadratic formula (irrational roots)
explanations: minus-b (procedural): The formula starts with −b; here b itself was used, which changes the sign of both roots.
plus-4ac (procedural): The discriminant was worked out as b² + 4ac; it is b² − 4ac = 21.
over-two (recall): Only 2 was put under the whole top; the denominator is 2a.

teach.idea: Completing the square on ax² + bx + c = 0 gives (x + b/2a)² = (b² − 4ac)/4a², so x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a: the formula works for every quadratic with real roots.
teach.method: Read a, b, c. Work out the discriminant b² − 4ac. Put it into x = (−b ± √D)/(2a), simplify the surd (√D = k√m), and cancel any common factor of all three numbers.

alternatives.title: Complete the square
text: Divide by a, move c/a to the right, add (b/2a)² to both sides.
Take the square root of both sides (±) and solve for x.

alternatives.title: Check with a calculator estimate
text: Work out each root as a decimal.
Put it back into ax² + bx + c: the result should be very close to 0.

families.title: Completing the square: x² + bx + c = (x + h)² + k
explanations: square-added (procedural): h² was added to c instead of taken away; (x + h)² already contains + h², so it must be removed again.
not-halved (recall): h was taken as the whole coefficient 10; (x + h)² = x² + 2hx + h², so h is half of it.
sign-of-h (procedural): The sign of h was changed; with + 10x the bracket is (x + 5).

teach.idea: (x + h)² = x² + 2hx + h². Choosing h = b/2 makes the x terms agree; the h² that comes with it is then corrected by k = c − h².
teach.method: Halve the coefficient of x to get h, square it, and subtract the square from c to get k. The equation x² + bx + c = 0 then becomes (x + h)² = −k, which can be solved by square roots.

alternatives.title: Complete the square with a picture
text: Draw x² as a square and bx as two strips of width b/2 on two sides.
The missing corner is (b/2)²: adding it completes a square of side x + b/2.

alternatives.title: Expand to check
text: Expand (x + h)² + k.
It must give back x² + bx + c exactly.

families.title: Quadratic word problems: numbers, ages and speeds
explanations: kept-impossible-root (conceptual): The negative root of the equation was given; a number of years, a speed or a positive number cannot be negative, so that root is rejected.
other-quantity (procedural): The larger number was given; the question asks for the smaller one.

teach.idea: A quantity multiplied by a related quantity gives an x² term, so these situations lead to quadratic equations. A quadratic has two roots, and the situation decides which one is the answer.
teach.method: Let x be the quantity asked for; write the other quantities in terms of x; form the equation and bring it to standard form; solve (factorise or use the formula); reject a root that cannot happen (negative ages, lengths or speeds).

alternatives.title: A table of quantities
text: For the train: write distance, speed and time (time = distance ÷ speed) for the usual and the faster journeys.
The difference of the two times gives the equation.

alternatives.title: Check in the story
text: Put your answer back into the words of the problem.
Every condition must be true, and every quantity must make sense.

families.title: The section formula: internal division, midpoint and points of trisection
explanations: ratio-reversed (procedural): The weights were swapped: for AP : PB = 2 : 1, B is multiplied by 2 and A by 1.
not-divided (procedural): The weighted sum was not divided by 2 + 1 = 3.
difference-halved (conceptual): The coordinates were subtracted instead of combined; the midpoint (and every section point) adds the weighted coordinates.

teach.idea: The point dividing AB in the ratio m : n is m/(m + n) of the way from A to B, in both coordinates: it is a weighted average of A and B, with B weighted by m and A by n.
teach.method: P = ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)). The midpoint is m = n = 1; the points of trisection are 1 : 2 and 2 : 1.

alternatives.title: Equal steps along the segment
text: Cut AB into m + n equal steps: each step is (B − A)/(m + n).
Walk m steps from A.

alternatives.title: Check with distances
text: Work out AP and PB with the distance formula.
Their ratio must be m : n.

families.title: The ratio in which a point or an axis divides a segment
explanations: reversed (procedural): The ratio was given the wrong way round; it is measured from A: AP : PB.
part-to-whole (conceptual): AP : AB was given; the ratio of division compares the two parts, AP : PB.
wrong-coordinate (conceptual): The y-coordinates were used; on the y-axis it is the x-coordinate that is 0, so the x-coordinates decide the ratio.

teach.idea: If P divides AB in the ratio λ : 1, each coordinate of P is (λx₂ + x₁)/(λ + 1). A point on the x-axis has y = 0, which gives one equation for λ.
teach.method: Write the ratio as λ : 1, put the known coordinate of P (or 0 for an axis) into the section formula, solve for λ, and write λ : 1 as a ratio of whole numbers.

alternatives.title: Compare the heights
text: For the x-axis, A and B are on opposite sides at heights |y₁| and |y₂|.
Similar triangles give the ratio |y₁| : |y₂|.

alternatives.title: Count equal steps
text: For a given point P, find how far it is from A and from B along the x direction.
Those two distances are in the ratio m : n.

families.title: The centroid of a triangle, and a missing vertex from the centroid
explanations: not-divided (recall): The coordinates were added but not divided by 3; the centroid is the average of the three vertices.
halved (recall): The sum was divided by 2, as for a midpoint; three vertices are averaged by dividing by 3.
no-times-3 (procedural): The coordinates of G were used without multiplying by 3; G is the average, so the three vertices add to 3 times G.
averaged-g (conceptual): G was treated as a vertex and the centroid of A, B and G was found; C is the unknown vertex.

teach.idea: The centroid, where the three medians meet, is the average of the three vertices: G = ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3). It lies two-thirds of the way along each median from its vertex.
teach.method: To find G, add the x-coordinates and divide by 3, and the same for y. To find a missing vertex, multiply G by 3 and subtract the two known vertices.

alternatives.title: Along a median
text: Find the midpoint M of BC.
G divides AM in the ratio 2 : 1: use the section formula.

alternatives.title: The balance point
text: A cardboard triangle balances on a pin at its centroid.
Each vertex has the same weight, so the balance point is their average.

families.title: Collinear points and the kind of triangle in space, by the distance formula
explanations: collinear-missed (conceptual): The three distances were found but not compared: when the two shorter distances add up to the longest, the three points lie on one line and there is no triangle.
pythagoras-not-tested (procedural): The triangle was named from its sides alone; test whether the two smaller squares add up to the largest square — then it is right-angled.
equal-sides-missed (procedural): Two of the distances are equal, which makes the triangle isosceles; compare the squared distances before taking square roots.
pythagoras-misread (procedural): The squared distances were compared wrongly; Pythagoras needs the two smaller squares to add up exactly to the largest.

teach.idea: The distance formula in space, √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²), gives the three side lengths. Their sizes decide the figure: collinear when two add to the third, right-angled when Pythagoras holds, isosceles when two are equal.
teach.method: Work out AB², BC² and AC². Test, in order: do the two shorter lengths add up to the longest (collinear)? Do the two smaller squares add up to the largest (right-angled)? Are two equal (isosceles)?

alternatives.title: With direction vectors
text: B − A and C − A are multiples of each other exactly when the points are collinear.
A zero dot product of two sides at a vertex means a right angle there.

alternatives.title: Compare squares, not roots
text: Keep the squared distances as whole numbers.
Equal squares mean equal sides; take square roots only to test collinearity.

families.title: The centroid of a triangle in space
explanations: not-divided (recall): The coordinates were added but not divided by 3.
halved (recall): The sum was divided by 2, as for a midpoint; the centroid averages three vertices.

teach.idea: As in the plane, the centroid of a triangle in space is the average of its vertices: G = ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3, (z₁ + z₂ + z₃)/3).
teach.method: Add the three x-coordinates and divide by 3; do the same for y and for z.

alternatives.title: Along a median
text: Find the midpoint M of BC.
The centroid divides AM in the ratio 2 : 1 (section formula in space).

families.title: The point dividing a segment in space externally
explanations: internal-used (conceptual): The internal formula (mB + nA)/(m + n) was used; external division subtracts: (mB − nA)/(m − n).
weights-swapped (procedural): The weights were swapped: B is multiplied by 4 and A by 3.

teach.idea: P divides AB externally in m : n when P is on line AB but outside the segment, with PA : PB = m : n. Replacing n by −n in the section formula gives P = (mB − nA)/(m − n).
teach.method: For each coordinate work out (m × B − n × A) and divide by m − n.

alternatives.title: Steps along the line
text: P is m/(m − n) of the vector AB away from A.
Find B − A, multiply by m/(m − n), add to A.

families.title: Estimating a limit from a table, and one-sided limits
explanations: undefined-means-zero (conceptual): Because f is not defined at x = 4, the limit was taken as 0; a limit is about the values near 4, which the table shows.
far-value (procedural): The value farthest from 4 in the table was rounded; the limit is what the values approach as x gets closest to 4.
other-side (conceptual): The rule for the other side of 5 was used; the right-hand limit uses the values for x > 5.

teach.idea: lim (x → a) f(x) is the value f(x) gets as close as we like to when x is close to a (on both sides), whatever happens at a itself. The left-hand limit uses only x < a, the right-hand limit only x > a; the limit exists when they are equal.
teach.method: From a table, look at the values for x nearest to a from each side and see what they settle on. For a piecewise rule, use the piece for that side and substitute x = a in it.

alternatives.title: Trace the graph
text: Move along the graph towards x = a from the left, then from the right.
The heights you approach are the left-hand and right-hand limits.

alternatives.title: Make x closer
text: Try x = a − 0.001 and x = a + 0.001 in the rule.
The two values tell you what f(x) approaches from each side.

families.title: Limits of rational functions: (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(xᵐ − aᵐ) and factorising
explanations: powers-dropped (procedural): Only the powers n and m were kept; the standard limit is naⁿ⁻¹, so the powers of a count too.
top-only (procedural): Only the top was treated with the standard limit; the bottom (x⁵ − 243) also tends to 0 and gives its own factor 5a⁴.
leading-terms (conceptual): The leading coefficients were divided, as for a limit at infinity; here x tends to a number, so factorise and cancel the common factor first.
zero-over-zero (conceptual): Direct substitution gives 0/0, which was taken as 0; 0/0 is not a value — it says a common factor must be cancelled.

teach.idea: When substitution gives 0/0, the top and the bottom share the factor x − a. Cancelling it (or using lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ for each part) leaves a function that can be evaluated at a.
teach.method: Factorise and cancel x − a, then substitute x = a. For (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(xᵐ − aᵐ), divide top and bottom by x − a: the limit is naⁿ⁻¹/(maᵐ⁻¹) = (n/m)aⁿ⁻ᵐ.

alternatives.title: Check with nearby values
text: Evaluate the function at x = a ± 0.001.
Both values should be very close to your answer.

alternatives.title: Divide out the factor
text: xⁿ − aⁿ = (x − a)(xⁿ⁻¹ + axⁿ⁻² + … + aⁿ⁻¹).
At x = a the second bracket has n terms each equal to aⁿ⁻¹.

families.title: lim (t → a) of c(tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a): the limit of an average rate
explanations: no-n (recall): The factor n = 4 was left out: lim (tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a) = naⁿ⁻¹.
power-not-lowered (recall): The power of a was not lowered: the standard limit is naⁿ⁻¹, not naⁿ.
c-dropped (procedural): The constant 6 in front was dropped; a constant factor stays in the limit.

teach.idea: (tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a) is an average rate of change of tⁿ between a and t; as t → a it approaches the instantaneous rate naⁿ⁻¹.
teach.method: Use lim (t → a) (tⁿ − aⁿ)/(t − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ and multiply by the constant in front.

alternatives.title: Factorise
text: t³ − a³ = (t − a)(t² + at + a²): cancel t − a.
Put t = a: a² + a² + a² = 3a².

families.title: Limits from the standard limits of sin x/x, (eˣ − 1)/x and log(1 + x)/x
explanations: upside-down (procedural): The fraction was turned over: the 9 inside the function goes on top.
always-one (conceptual): The standard limit was used as if it were 1 here; it is 1 only when the angle (or exponent) matches the denominator exactly, so first make 9x appear below.
no-half (recall): 1 − cos θ behaves like θ²/2 for small θ; the 1/2 was left out.
no-square (recall): 1 − cos 9x behaves like (9x)²/2 near 0, so a² appears, not a.

teach.idea: Near 0, sin θ, tan θ, e^θ − 1 and log(1 + θ) all behave like θ itself, so each of them divided by θ tends to 1; 1 − cos θ behaves like θ²/2.
teach.method: Make the standard form appear: sin ax/(bx) = (sin ax/(ax)) × (a/b), so the limit is a/b. Do the same for tan, eᵃˣ − 1 and log(1 + ax). For 1 − cos ax, use 2 sin²(ax/2).

alternatives.title: Check with a small x
text: Put x = 0.001 into the expression (in radians).
The value is very close to the limit.

alternatives.title: The first term of a series
text: sin ax ≈ ax, e^(ax) − 1 ≈ ax, log(1 + ax) ≈ ax and 1 − cos ax ≈ a²x²/2 for small x.
Replace and cancel the powers of x.

families.title: Limits by rationalising, and limits at infinity of rational functions
explanations: no-two (procedural): After rationalising, the bottom is x(√(9x + 36) + 6), which tends to 2 × 6; the 2 was left out.
constants (conceptual): The constant terms were divided; as x → ∞ the highest powers matter, and the constants become negligible.
leading-ratio (conceptual): The leading coefficients 9 and 6 were divided; the bottom has the higher power, so it grows much faster and the fraction tends to 0.

teach.idea: A 0/0 with a square root clears when you multiply by the conjugate: (√A − q)(√A + q) = A − q². At infinity, only the highest powers matter: divide top and bottom by the highest power of x in the denominator.
teach.method: Rationalise: multiply top and bottom by √(px + q²) + q, cancel x, substitute 0. At infinity: divide every term by x², let the terms with 1/x and 1/x² go to 0.

alternatives.title: Compare degrees
text: Same degree on top and bottom: the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients.
Bottom degree higher: the limit is 0.

alternatives.title: Try a big x
text: Put x = 1000 or x = 0.0001 into the expression.
The value shows what the limit must be.

families.title: Differentiating a sum and difference of several terms
explanations: constant-kept (recall): The constant 18 was kept; a constant does not change, so its derivative is 0.
power-not-lowered (recall): Each term was multiplied by its power but the power was not lowered by 1: d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹.
power-not-multiplied (recall): The powers were lowered but the coefficients were not multiplied by the old power.

teach.idea: The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor stays in front: d/dx [af + bg] = af′ + bg′. A constant term has derivative 0.
teach.method: Differentiate each term with d/dx xⁿ = nxⁿ⁻¹ (multiply by the power, then lower the power by 1), keep the signs, and drop the constant.

alternatives.title: Slopes add
text: The graph of f + g rises by what f and g rise together.
So the slope of a sum is the sum of the slopes.

alternatives.title: Check at a point
text: Find (f(2.001) − f(1.999))/0.002 with a calculator.
It should be very close to f′(2) from your answer.

families.title: The quotient rule
explanations: order-reversed (procedural): The top of the quotient rule was written as u v′ − v u′; the order is v u′ − u v′, so every sign came out reversed.
not-squared (recall): The bottom was not squared; the quotient rule divides by v².
derivative-over-derivative (conceptual): The derivative of the top was divided by the derivative of the bottom; a quotient is not differentiated part by part.

teach.idea: For y = u/v, a small change in x changes the top and the bottom; working it out gives (v u′ − u v′)/v². The minus sign makes the order matter.
teach.method: Name u (top) and v (bottom), find u′ and v′, put them into (v u′ − u v′)/v², and simplify the top.

alternatives.title: As a product
text: Write u/v = u × v⁻¹.
Use the product rule and the chain rule on v⁻¹: u′v⁻¹ − u v′ v⁻²; the same answer.

alternatives.title: Low d-high minus high d-low
text: Bottom times derivative of top, minus top times derivative of bottom, all over the bottom squared.

families.title: The chain rule for composite functions
explanations: inner-forgotten (conceptual): The outer function was differentiated but the result was not multiplied by the derivative of the inside.
power-not-lowered (recall): The power was not lowered by 1.
inside-changed (procedural): The inside function was differentiated as well as kept inside cos; the inside stays unchanged and its derivative multiplies.
cos-to-sin-sign (recall): The derivative of cos was taken as + sin; d/dx cos u = − sin u × u′.

teach.idea: A composite y = f(g(x)) changes with x through g: if x changes a little, g changes g′(x) times as much, and y changes f′(g) times that. So dy/dx = f′(g(x)) × g′(x).
teach.method: Name the inside u = g(x). Differentiate the outside as if u were the variable, keep u inside, then multiply by du/dx.

alternatives.title: Write it with u
text: Let u be the inside. Find dy/du and du/dx separately.
Multiply them and put u back in terms of x.

alternatives.title: Peel the layers
text: Differentiate from the outside in, one layer at a time.
Each layer you peel contributes one factor.

families.title: Derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions, and one function with respect to another
explanations: chain-dropped (procedural): The derivative of the inside, 9x, was not used: it multiplies by 9.
sign (recall): The minus sign from d/dx cos = −sin was lost.
square-dropped (recall): The square inside was lost: d/dx tan⁻¹u = u′/(1 + u²).
top-only (conceptual): Only x⁷ was differentiated; with respect to x⁵ the result is divided by the derivative of x⁵.
upside-down (procedural): The two derivatives were divided the wrong way round: d(sin)/d(cos) is (d sin/dx) ÷ (d cos/dx).

teach.idea: If y = sin⁻¹x then x = sin y, so dx/dy = cos y = √(1 − x²) and dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²); similarly for cos⁻¹ (with a minus sign) and tan⁻¹ (1/(1 + x²)). To differentiate y with respect to u, divide dy/dx by du/dx.
teach.method: Use d/dx sin⁻¹u = u′/√(1 − u²), d/dx cos⁻¹u = −u′/√(1 − u²), d/dx tan⁻¹u = u′/(1 + u²), then simplify. For 'with respect to', find both derivatives with respect to x and divide.

alternatives.title: Undo the inverse
text: Write y = tan⁻¹(x/a) as tan y = x/a.
Differentiate both sides: sec²y · dy/dx = 1/a, and sec²y = 1 + x²/a².

alternatives.title: Like a parametric derivative
text: Treat x as a parameter: y and u are both functions of x.
dy/du = (dy/dx)/(du/dx).

families.title: Derivatives of exponential and logarithmic functions
explanations: power-rule-on-e (conceptual): The power rule was used on e^(5x), as if 5x were a power: it was brought down in front and the exponent lowered by 1. The variable is in the exponent, so the power rule does not apply: d/dx e^(5x) = 5e^(5x).
exponent-factor (recall): The factor 5 from the exponent was left out: d/dx e^(5x) = 5e^(5x).
power-rule (conceptual): aˣ was differentiated like xⁿ; the variable is in the exponent: d/dx aˣ = aˣ log a.
no-log (recall): The factor log 7 was left out; only eˣ is its own derivative.
product-of-derivatives (conceptual): The two derivatives were multiplied; the product rule is u′v + uv′.
one-part (procedural): Only one part of the product rule was written.

teach.idea: eˣ is its own derivative, and log x (the inverse of eˣ) has derivative 1/x. Any aˣ is e^(x log a), so its derivative is aˣ log a.
teach.method: Use d/dx e^(ax) = a e^(ax), d/dx log x = 1/x, d/dx aˣ = aˣ log a, and the product rule for products.

alternatives.title: Rewrite with e
text: Write 2ˣ = e^(x log 2).
Use the chain rule: the inside x log 2 has derivative log 2.

alternatives.title: Growth in proportion
text: eˣ grows at a rate equal to its size.
aˣ grows at a rate equal to its size times log a.

families.title: Determinants of order 3, and the determinant of a product
explanations: middle-sign (procedural): The middle term was added; in the expansion along a row the signs go + − +, so the second term is subtracted.
forward-diagonals (conceptual): Only the three forward diagonals were added; the three backward diagonals must be subtracted as well (Sarrus' rule).
added (conceptual): |A| and |B| were added; the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants.
entrywise (conceptual): The matrices were multiplied entry by entry; matrix multiplication combines rows with columns (or use |AB| = |A||B|).

teach.idea: A 3 × 3 determinant is built from 2 × 2 ones: each entry of a row times its cofactor (its minor with the sign + − + …). The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants: |AB| = |A||B|.
teach.method: Expand along the first row: a₁₁(a₂₂a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₂) − a₁₂(a₂₁a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₁) + a₁₃(a₂₁a₃₂ − a₂₂a₃₁). Choose a row or column with zeros to save work.

alternatives.title: Sarrus' rule
text: Copy the first two columns to the right of the matrix.
Add the three products down to the right, subtract the three products down to the left.

alternatives.title: Make zeros first
text: Subtracting a multiple of one row from another does not change the determinant.
Make two zeros in a column, then expand along it.

families.title: An unknown vertex of a triangle of given area, by determinants
explanations: no-half (recall): The determinant was set equal to the area; the area is half the absolute value of the determinant, so the determinant is ± twice the area.
one-sign (conceptual): Only the positive value of the determinant was used; the absolute value means the determinant can be + or − twice the area, which gives two positions for the vertex.

teach.idea: The area of the triangle with vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃) is ½ |det[[x₁, y₁, 1], [x₂, y₂, 1], [x₃, y₃, 1]]|. With an unknown vertex the determinant is linear in k, and the absolute value gives two equations.
teach.method: Expand the determinant to get αk + β. Set αk + β = 2 × area and αk + β = −2 × area, and solve each.

alternatives.title: Two positions
text: The points that make a triangle of this area with the two known corners lie on two lines parallel to the side joining them, one on each side.
The line y = c meets each of these lines once: that is why there are two values of k.

alternatives.title: Check with the shoelace sum
text: Put each k back and work out ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Both must give the stated area.

families.title: The value that makes a 3 × 3 matrix singular, or a homogeneous system have a non-trivial solution
explanations: det-one (conceptual): The determinant was set non-zero (equal to 1); a non-zero determinant gives only the zero solution.
cofactor-sign (procedural): The sign of the cofactor at the unknown's place was missed (the signs alternate + − + in a checkerboard).

teach.idea: det A = 0 means the rows are dependent: the matrix has no inverse (singular), and the system AX = 0 has solutions besides X = 0. With one unknown entry the determinant is linear in it.
teach.method: Expand the determinant (along the row or column of the unknown is quickest), set it equal to 0, and solve the linear equation.

alternatives.title: Cofactor of the unknown
text: Expanding along the unknown's row: det = (its cofactor) × k + (the rest).
So k = −(the rest) ÷ (its cofactor).

alternatives.title: Dependent rows
text: When det = 0, one row is a combination of the others.
Then the equations do not pin down a single point: the system has infinitely many solutions through the origin.

families.title: The inverse of a 3 × 3 matrix
explanations: not-divided (procedural): The adjoint was given without dividing by |A| = −3.
not-transposed (procedural): The cofactor matrix was divided by |A| without transposing it; the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix.
minors (recall): Minors were used without their signs; each cofactor carries the sign (−1)^(i + j).

teach.idea: A · adj A = |A| I for every square matrix, so when |A| ≠ 0 the inverse is A⁻¹ = adj A / |A|. When |A| = 0 the matrix is singular and has no inverse.
teach.method: Find |A|. Find all nine cofactors (minors with signs + − + / − + − / + − +), transpose to get adj A, and divide every entry by |A|. Check that A·A⁻¹ = I.

alternatives.title: Row-reduce [A | I]
text: Write A next to the identity matrix.
Use row operations to turn A into I; the right-hand block becomes A⁻¹.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Multiply A by your answer.
Every diagonal entry must be 1 and every other entry 0.

families.title: Antiderivatives of the standard functions
explanations: differentiated (conceptual): Each term was differentiated instead of integrated; an antiderivative is a function whose derivative is the integrand.
power-not-divided (recall): ∫ x³ dx was written as x⁴; the new power also divides: x⁴/4.
trig-sign (recall): A sign was lost: ∫ sin x dx = −cos x, ∫ cos x dx = sin x and ∫ cosec²x dx = −cot x.

teach.idea: Integration undoes differentiation, so each standard derivative read backwards is a standard integral: (sin x)′ = cos x gives ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C, (tan x)′ = sec²x gives ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + C, (log|x|)′ = 1/x, and so on.
teach.method: Integrate term by term (constants stay in front): ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1), ∫ sin x = −cos x, ∫ cos x = sin x, ∫ sec²x = tan x, ∫ cosec²x = −cot x, ∫ sec x tan x = sec x, ∫ eˣ = eˣ, ∫ 1/x = log|x|; add one constant C.

alternatives.title: Differentiate to check
text: Differentiate your answer.
If you get back the integrand, the answer is right.

alternatives.title: Read the derivative table backwards
text: Write the table of standard derivatives.
Each line, read from right to left, is an integral.

families.title: Antiderivatives of f(ax + b)
explanations: not-divided (procedural): The result was not divided by 6; differentiating F(ax + b) brings out a factor a, so the integral must divide by it.
multiplied (procedural): The result was multiplied by 6 instead of divided; that is what differentiating does.
power-not-divided (recall): The new power 5 was not used to divide.

teach.idea: By the chain rule, d/dx F(ax + b) = a F′(ax + b). So to integrate f(ax + b), take the usual antiderivative F at ax + b and divide by a.
teach.method: Integrate as if ax + b were x, then divide by a: ∫ cos(ax + b) dx = sin(ax + b)/a + C, ∫ (ax + b)ⁿ dx = (ax + b)ⁿ⁺¹/(a(n + 1)) + C, ∫ 1/(ax + b) dx = log|ax + b|/a + C.

alternatives.title: Substitute u = ax + b
text: Let u = ax + b, so du = a dx and dx = du/a.
Integrate in u and put back u = ax + b.

alternatives.title: Differentiate back
text: Differentiate your answer with the chain rule.
The factor a must cancel the 1/a.

families.title: Finding a function from its derivative and one value
explanations: no-constant (conceptual): The constant of integration was left out; the given value of f is there to find it.
powers-not-divided (recall): The powers were raised but not divided by the new power.
constant-is-value (procedural): C was taken to be 45; that is only true when the given value is at x = 0.

teach.idea: All the antiderivatives of f′ differ by a constant: their graphs are the same curve shifted up or down. One known value picks out the one curve that passes through that point.
teach.method: Integrate f′ term by term, add C, substitute the given x and f(x), and solve for C.

alternatives.title: A family of curves
text: Sketch y = F(x) + C for several C: parallel copies of one curve.
The given point lies on exactly one of them.

alternatives.title: Check both conditions
text: Differentiate your answer: it must give f′(x).
Put in the given x: it must give the given value.

families.title: Integration using trigonometric identities and substitution
explanations: power-rule-on-sin (conceptual): sin²(ax) was integrated like a power of x; there is no power rule for sin, so rewrite it with the double-angle identity first.
identity-sign (recall): The identity was used with the wrong sign: cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2.
power-rule-on-cos (conceptual): cos²(ax) was integrated like a power of x; rewrite it with the double-angle identity first.
product-of-integrals (conceptual): The two factors were integrated separately and multiplied; the integral of a product is not the product of the integrals.
minus-x (recall): tan²θ was integrated as if it were sec²θ; tan²θ = sec²θ − 1, so a − x appears.
power-rule-on-tan (conceptual): tan² was integrated like a power of x.
top-times-log (procedural): The top was kept in front of the logarithm; after substituting u = bottom, the top together with dx is exactly du.
factor-forgotten (procedural): du = 12x dx, so x dx = du/12; the factor 1/12 was left out.

teach.idea: Powers and products of sines and cosines are not standard integrals, but trigonometric identities turn them into sums of single sines and cosines, which are. A substitution u = g(x) works when g′(x) is also present.
teach.method: Rewrite: sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2, cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2, tan²θ = sec²θ − 1, 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B). Then integrate term by term. For f′(x)/f(x) the answer is log|f(x)| + C.

alternatives.title: Substitute and change dx
text: Choose u as the inside function; write du in terms of dx.
Every x must disappear before integrating in u.

alternatives.title: Differentiate back
text: Differentiate your answer.
Use the identity again to see it equals the integrand.

families.title: Integrals of the standard forms 1/(x² − a²), 1/(a² − x²), 1/√(x² ± a²), √(x² ± a²) and (px + q)/(x² + bx + c)
explanations: no-factor (procedural): The factor 1/9 from du = 9 dx was left out.
swap (recall): The fraction inside the logarithm was turned upside down, which changes the sign of the answer.
no-x (recall): The u inside the logarithm was left out: the form is log|u + √(u² − a²)|.
power (conceptual): The power rule was used as if the top were the derivative of the inside; it is not, so this is the standard logarithmic form.
no-log (recall): Only the first part of the standard result was written; the logarithm part is needed too.
half-log (recall): The coefficient of the logarithm is a²/2, not a².
first-only (procedural): Only the log|x² + bx + c| part was integrated; after writing px + q = (p/2)(2x + b) + B, the constant B gives a second, standard-form integral.
log-sign (recall): The logarithm part was added; for √(x² − a²) it is subtracted: (x/2)√(x² − a²) − (a²/2) log|x + √(x² − a²)|.

teach.idea: Completing the square turns x² + bx + c into (x + h)² ± a², and each such shape has a standard antiderivative; a linear top px + q is split into a multiple of the bottom's derivative plus a constant.
teach.method: Complete the square; match the form; write the standard result with u = x + h. For (px + q)/(x² + bx + c), write px + q = (p/2)(2x + b) + B: the first part gives (p/2) log|x² + bx + c|, the second a standard form.

alternatives.title: Partial fractions
text: Integrating gives (1/2a)(log|x − a| − log|x + a|), the same result.

alternatives.title: Differentiate back
text: Differentiate your answer.
It must give back the integrand at every x where both are defined.

families.title: Definite integrals of 1/(x² + a²), 1/√(a² − x²) and √(a² − x²)
explanations: degrees (recall): The angle was given in degrees; in calculus, angles are in radians.
no-one-over-a (recall): The factor 1/a = 1/9 in front of tan⁻¹ was left out.
sixty-degrees (recall): sin⁻¹(1/2) was taken as π/3; the angle whose sine is 1/2 is π/6.
whole-circle (conceptual): The area of the whole circle was given; from 0 to a under the upper half is a quarter of the circle.
half-circle (conceptual): Half the circle was given; this integral is a quarter of the circle (from 0 to a only).

teach.idea: d/dx tan⁻¹(x/a) = a/(a² + x²) and d/dx sin⁻¹(x/a) = 1/√(a² − x²), so these integrands have inverse trigonometric antiderivatives; their values at the limits are standard angles. ∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx is a quarter of a circle of radius a.
teach.method: ∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ √(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. Evaluate at the limits in radians.

alternatives.title: Substitute x = a tan θ or x = a sin θ
text: With x = a tan θ, dx = a sec²θ dθ and x² + a² = a² sec²θ: the integrand becomes (1/a) dθ.
Change the limits to angles and integrate.

alternatives.title: A quarter circle
text: y = √(a² − x²) is the upper half of the circle x² + y² = a².
From 0 to a it covers a quarter of the area πa².

families.title: Integrating by partial fractions: repeated factors and improper fractions
explanations: sign (recall): ∫ dx/(x − a)² was taken as +1/(x − a); differentiating 1/(x − a) gives −1/(x − a)², so the integral is −1/(x − a).
all-logs (conceptual): The repeated factor was integrated as a logarithm too; only 1/(x − a) gives a logarithm, 1/(x − a)² is a power.
no-division (procedural): The fraction was split without dividing first; when the top's degree is not less than the bottom's, the polynomial part (here 1, giving x) comes first.
swap (procedural): The two partial-fraction constants were attached to the wrong factors.

teach.idea: A repeated factor (x − a)² needs two partial fractions, A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²: the first integrates to a logarithm, the second to a power, −B/(x − a). An improper fraction (top degree ≥ bottom degree) is first divided to give a polynomial plus a proper fraction.
teach.method: If needed, divide. Split the proper part into partial fractions, find the constants (cover-up or comparing coefficients), integrate each term, add C.

alternatives.title: Substitute u = x − a
text: For a repeated factor, put u = x − a: the top becomes Au + B.
∫ (Au + B)/u² du = A log|u| − B/u.

alternatives.title: Differentiate back
text: Differentiate your answer and add the fractions.
You must get the original integrand.

families.title: Integration by parts, Bernoulli's formula and ∫ eˣ[f(x) + f′(x)] dx
explanations: sign (procedural): The remaining integral was added; by parts subtracts it.
product (conceptual): Each factor was integrated separately and the results multiplied; the integral of a product is not the product of the integrals.
first-only (procedural): Only uv was written; the remaining integral −∫ v du still has to be worked out.
fp (recall): eˣ f′(x) was given; the rule is ∫ eˣ[f + f′] dx = eˣ f(x) + C.
kept-both (conceptual): The bracket was kept as it is; the whole bracket combines into eˣ f(x).
stopped-early (procedural): Bernoulli's formula was stopped too early; continue until the derivative of x² reaches 0 (three terms).
signs-not-alternating (recall): The signs in Bernoulli's formula alternate + − + − …; here they were all taken as +.

teach.idea: The product rule read backwards gives ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du. Choose u to be the factor that becomes simpler when differentiated (x, x², log x); repeated parts on x² gives Bernoulli's formula with alternating signs.
teach.method: Pick u and dv (ILATE order: inverse trig, log, algebraic, trig, exponential for u). Find du and v, write uv − ∫ v du, and integrate the last part. For eˣ[f + f′], the answer is eˣ f + C at once.

alternatives.title: The table method
text: Column 1: u, u′, u″, … down to 0. Column 2: v, then its integrals v₁, v₂, v₃.
Multiply along the diagonals with signs + − + and add.

alternatives.title: Differentiate back
text: Differentiate your answer with the product rule.
All terms but the integrand must cancel.

families.title: A definite integral by substitution: ∫ c t/√(t² + d²) dt
explanations: lower-limit (procedural): The lower limit was taken to give 0; at t = 0, u = 400 and √u = 20, which must be subtracted.
missed-half (procedural): du = 2t dt, so t dt = du/2; the factor 1/2 was left out.

teach.idea: When the integrand contains a function and (a multiple of) its derivative, substitute u for the function: t dt is half of d(t² + d²). The limits change with the variable.
teach.method: Let u = t² + d², so t dt = du/2. Change the limits (t = 0 gives u = d², t = b gives u = b² + d²), integrate (1/2)u^(−1/2) to √u, and subtract.

alternatives.title: Back-substitute instead
text: Find the antiderivative √(t² + d²) first.
Evaluate it at t = b and t = 0 and subtract.

alternatives.title: Check the derivative
text: d/dt √(t² + d²) = t/√(t² + d²).
So the integral is the change in √(t² + d²).

families.title: Definite integrals of polynomials by the fundamental theorem
explanations: reversed (procedural): F(lower) − F(upper) was worked out; it is F(upper) − F(lower).
powers-not-divided (recall): The powers were raised without dividing by the new powers.
integrand-difference (conceptual): The integrand itself was evaluated at the limits; the antiderivative must be used.
upper-only (procedural): Only F(6) was worked out; the fundamental theorem subtracts the value at the lower limit, F(2).

teach.idea: If F′ = f, then ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a): the total accumulated by a rate f is the change in its antiderivative (distance is the change in position).
teach.method: Find an antiderivative F (no constant is needed), work out F(b) and F(a), and subtract.

alternatives.title: Area under the graph
text: Where f > 0, the integral is the area between the graph and the x-axis from a to b.
A rough sketch tells you whether the answer is sensible.

alternatives.title: Set out F in a table
text: Write each term of F, its value at b and at a.
Subtract column by column and add.

families.title: A definite integral as the limit of a sum
explanations: sum-r (recall): Σr was taken as n² instead of about n²/2 (it is n(n + 1)/2); equivalently ∫₀¹ x dx is 1/2, not 1.
sum-r2 (recall): Σr² was taken as about n³/2; it is n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, about n³/3 (∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3).
each-term-one (conceptual): Each term was treated as if it were 1/n, giving the factor alone; the terms shrink as r grows, following 1/(1 + x²).
half-pi (recall): tan⁻¹(1) was taken as π/2; it is π/4.
power-not-raised (recall): ∫₀¹ xᵐ dx was taken as 1/m; it is 1/(m + 1).

teach.idea: ∫ from 0 to 1 of f(x) dx is the limit of the sums (1/n)[f(1/n) + f(2/n) + … + f(n/n)]: n thin rectangles of width 1/n under the graph. A sum of this shape can be evaluated by integrating.
teach.method: Take out a factor 1/n and write the rest of each term in terms of r/n only; call r/n = x, so the limit is ∫ from 0 to 1 of f(x) dx. Integrate.

alternatives.title: Use the sum formulas
text: Substitute, divide by the power of n, and let n → ∞.

alternatives.title: Rectangles under a curve
text: Each term is the area of a thin rectangle of width 1/n and height f(r/n).
As n grows, the rectangles fill the area under the curve.

families.title: Definite integrals by parts and Bernoulli's formula
explanations: signs-not-alternating (recall): The signs in Bernoulli's formula (or in u v − ∫ v du) were not alternated; they go + − + − ….
lower-limit-dropped (procedural): The value at the lower limit was taken as 0 without working it out; it must be subtracted.

teach.idea: Repeated integration by parts on xⁿ times eˣ, sin x or cos x lowers the power of x each time until it disappears; Bernoulli's formula writes all the steps at once with alternating signs. Then the fundamental theorem gives the value.
teach.method: Write the antiderivative with Bernoulli's formula (u = xⁿ and its derivatives, v and its repeated integrals, signs + − + …), then substitute the upper and the lower limit and subtract.

alternatives.title: The table method
text: List the derivatives of xⁿ down to 0, and the integrals of eˣ (or sin x, cos x) next to them.
Multiply along the diagonals with alternating signs.

alternatives.title: Estimate the size
text: e ≈ 2.718 and π ≈ 3.142: work out your exact answer as a decimal.
It must be positive here and smaller than the largest value of the integrand times the length of the interval.

families.title: Integrals with inverse trigonometric answers: 1/(x² + a²), 1/√(a² − x²), √(a² − x²) and forms reducible to them
explanations: no-1/a (recall): The factor 1/a = 1/6 in front of tan⁻¹ was left out.
inside (recall): tan⁻¹ x was used instead of tan⁻¹(x/7); the a² inside the bracket gives x/a.
extra-1/a (recall): A factor 1/a was put in front, as for tan⁻¹; the sin⁻¹ form has none.
tan (conceptual): The tan⁻¹ form was used; with a square root of a² − x² the form is sin⁻¹(x/a).
no-shift (procedural): After completing the square, u = x + h was not put back: the answer must contain (x + h)/a.
log-only (procedural): Only the x part was integrated; the constant on top gives a second, tan⁻¹ part.
log-coef (procedural): The x part was integrated as c log(x² + a²); the derivative of x² + a² is 2x, so the coefficient is c/2.
no-inverse (recall): Only the first part of the standard result was written; the (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) part is needed too.
coef (recall): The coefficient of sin⁻¹ is a²/2, not a².

teach.idea: d/dx tan⁻¹(x/a) = a/(x² + a²) and d/dx sin⁻¹(x/a) = 1/√(a² − x²), so these integrands have inverse trigonometric antiderivatives. Completing the square brings x² + bx + c to (x + h)² ± a², the same forms with u = x + h.
teach.method: ∫ dx/(x² + a²) = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ √(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. For a linear top, split it into a multiple of the bottom's derivative (a logarithm) and a constant (a tan⁻¹).

alternatives.title: Substitute x = a tan θ or x = a sin θ
text: With x = a tan θ: dx = a sec²θ dθ and x² + a² = a² sec²θ, so the integrand becomes (1/a) dθ.
θ = tan⁻¹(x/a) gives the answer.

alternatives.title: Differentiate back
text: Differentiate your answer with the chain rule.
The factor from the inside x/a must cancel the 1/a in front (or produce it).

families.title: Integrating by partial fractions with an irreducible quadratic factor
explanations: no-tan (conceptual): The whole (Bx + C)/(x² + a²) part was integrated as a logarithm; only the Bx part is (half) the derivative of the bottom, and the constant C gives (C/a) tan⁻¹(x/a).
log-coef (procedural): Bx/(x² + a²) was integrated as B log(x² + a²); the derivative of x² + a² is 2x, so the coefficient is B/2.
no-1/a (recall): The factor 1/a = 1/4 in front of tan⁻¹ was left out.

teach.idea: A factor x² + a² that does not factorise needs a linear top: (Bx + C)/(x² + a²). Its x part integrates to a logarithm and its constant part to a tan⁻¹.
teach.method: Write the integrand as A/(x − r) + (Bx + C)/(x² + a²); find A by putting x = r, then B and C by comparing the x² and constant terms. Integrate: A log|x − r| + (B/2) log(x² + a²) + (C/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C.

alternatives.title: Compare coefficients
text: Multiply out A(x² + a²) + (Bx + C)(x − r).
Match the coefficients of x², x and the constant with the given top.

alternatives.title: Differentiate back
text: Differentiate each part of your answer.
Adding the three fractions must give back the integrand.

families.title: Dividing by repeated subtraction
explanations: counted-the-start (procedural): The starting number 98 was counted as one of the take-aways, so the count came out one too many. Count only the times 9 is taken away.
stopped-early (procedural): The taking away stopped one step early: 17 is still 9 or more, so 9 can be taken away once more.
times-for-left (conceptual): The number of take-aways was given; the question asks what is left at the end.
assumed-exact (conceptual): It was assumed the taking away ends exactly at 0, but 98 is not a multiple of 9.
left-for-times (conceptual): The number left at the end was given; the question asks how many times the number was taken away.

teach.idea: Dividing asks how many times a number can be taken away: each take-away is one equal group.
teach.method: Keep subtracting the divisor and count the subtractions; stop when what is left is smaller than the divisor. That is the remainder.

alternatives.title: Make groups and count them
text: Put out counters for the number.
Move them away in groups of the divisor; count the groups and the counters left.

families.title: The multiplication fact behind a division
explanations: multiply-the-dividend (conceptual): The number being divided (120) was multiplied again. A division undoes a multiplication: 10 groups of the answer make 120.
fact-slip (prerequisite): The fact 10 × 12 is not yet reliable, so a fact one group away was chosen.

teach.idea: Multiplication and division are opposites: if d groups of q make n, then n ÷ d = q and n ÷ q = d.
teach.method: To check n ÷ d = q, multiply the divisor by the answer: d × q should give n.

alternatives.title: Rows of an array
text: Arrange the objects in rows, one row for each share.
Rows × objects in a row gives the total: that is the multiplication fact.

families.title: Building the 13 to 19 times tables
explanations: ten-part-left-out (procedural): Only the 9 × 10 part was worked out; the 10 × 10 part must be added on.
added-not-multiplied (procedural): 9 was added instead of 9 × 10: both parts of 19 are multiplied by 10.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (9 × 10) is not yet reliable.
not-doubled (procedural): The 9 times fact was given without doubling it; 18 is twice 9, so the answer is twice as big.
added-for-double (conceptual): 9 was added to the fact instead of doubling it: 18 groups of 10 is two lots of 9 groups.
not-halved (procedural): The 5 × 10 part was taken as 10 × 10 again; it is half of it.
only-half (procedural): Only the half (5 × 10) was given; the 10 × 10 part must be added.

teach.idea: A new table can be built from known ones: 14 groups is 10 groups and 4 groups, or two lots of 7 groups.
teach.method: Split the number into 10 and the rest and add the two facts, or double a table you know (14 = 2 × 7, 16 = 2 × 8).

alternatives.title: Split the array
text: Draw the product as an array of rows and columns.
Cut it after 10 columns: the two smaller arrays are facts you know; add them.

families.title: Products by doubling and halving or a nearest multiple
explanations: no-adjust (procedural): 100 × 25 was given without the last step: 101 is one more than 100, so one group of 25 must be added.
adjust-by-one (conceptual): 1 was added instead of one whole group of 25.
wrong-way (procedural): The group of 25 was taken away; 101 groups is more than 100 groups.
halved-only (procedural): 48 was halved but 125 was not doubled: halving one factor and doubling the other keeps the product the same.
doubled-both (conceptual): Both numbers were doubled; that makes the product four times as big.

teach.idea: Doubling one factor and halving the other leaves the product unchanged; a factor next to a multiple of ten is that multiple minus (or plus) one group.

alternatives.title: Reshape a rectangle
text: Think of x × y as a rectangle of squares.
Cut it in half along one side and put the halves end to end: twice as long, half as wide, the same squares.

families.title: Multiplying with partial products
explanations: dropped-zero (conceptual): 999 was multiplied by 1 instead of 10: multiplying by 1 ten makes 1 ten of 999, so the answer ends in 0.
tens-as-ones (conceptual): 997 was multiplied by 7 instead of 70: the tens digit of 73 stands for 70, so that partial product ends in 0.
one-partial-product (procedural): Only one partial product was found; 997 × 73 needs both 997 × 70 and 997 × 3, added together.
multiplied-place-by-place (conceptual): Digits were multiplied only with the digit in the same place (tens with tens, ones with ones); every part of one number multiplies every part of the other.
used-ones (procedural): 999 × 6 was given; that is the other partial product.

teach.idea: Splitting a factor by place value turns one hard product into easier ones: 47 × 36 = 47 × 30 + 47 × 6.
teach.method: Multiply by the tens (the answer ends in 0), multiply by the ones, then add the partial products.

alternatives.title: An area model
text: Draw a rectangle with sides split by place value, e.g. 40 + 7 and 30 + 6.
Find the area of each small rectangle (40 × 30, 7 × 30, 40 × 6, 7 × 6) and add them all.

families.title: Multiplying with the lattice method
explanations: box-halves-swapped (procedural): The two halves of the boxes were read the wrong way round: the upper-left half holds the tens and the lower-right half the ones.
no-carry (procedural): Only the ones digit of each diagonal total was written; when a diagonal adds up to 10 or more, the tens are carried to the next diagonal.
ones-halves-only (procedural): Only the ones halves were added; a diagonal also runs through the tens halves of the boxes below and to the right.
wrong-diagonal (procedural): The diagonals were counted from the wrong end or one too far along; the ones diagonal is the single half-box at the bottom right.

teach.idea: The lattice keeps every digit product in its place: each diagonal collects the digits of one place value.
teach.method: Fill each box with the product of its digits (tens above the slash, ones below), add along the diagonals from the bottom right, and carry when a total is 10 or more.

alternatives.title: Check with partial products
text: Split one number by place value: 46 × 23 = 46 × 20 + 46 × 3.
Both methods add the same digit products; the lattice just lines them up on diagonals.

families.title: Long division with a remainder, and dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder
explanations: one-group-off (recall): A multiplication fact with 39 slipped by one group in one step.
remainder-too-big (procedural): One group too few was taken: a remainder is always less than the divisor 39.
quotient-for-remainder (conceptual): The quotient was given; the remainder is what is left after the last subtraction.
remainder-left-out (procedural): Only divisor × quotient was found; the remainder 33 must be added on.
remainder-to-quotient (procedural): The remainder was added to the quotient before multiplying; it is added after: 39 × 212 + 33.
subtracted-remainder (conceptual): The remainder was taken away; it is what was left over, so it is added back.
first-step-remainder (procedural): The remainder of the first step was given; the division continues to the last digit.
dropped-zero (procedural): A zero in the quotient was left out: when the divisor does not go into a step, a 0 is written in the quotient.

teach.idea: Long division shares out one place at a time; the remainder is what is left when no more full groups fit, and it is always less than the divisor.
teach.method: Divide, multiply, subtract and bring down the next digit, again and again. Check: divisor × quotient + remainder = dividend.

alternatives.title: Take away big chunks
text: Take away easy multiples of the divisor: 100 groups, 10 groups, single groups.
Add up the groups taken away (the quotient); what is left at the end is the remainder.

families.title: Dividing mentally by splitting or by halving
explanations: rest-not-divided (procedural): Only the first part (810) was divided; the other part (81) must be divided by 9 too.
first-part-only (procedural): Only 810 ÷ 9 was given; the answers for both parts are added.
halved-once-too-few (procedural): The halving stopped one time too soon: dividing by 16 means halving 4 times.
halved-once (conceptual): The number was halved only once; halving once divides by 2, not by 16.

teach.idea: A dividend can be split into parts that are easy to divide; dividing by 4 or 8 is halving two or three times.
teach.method: Split into a multiple of 10 × divisor and the rest, divide each part and add. For ÷ 8, halve, halve and halve again.

alternatives.title: Share in two rounds
text: Share the big part first: 80 among 4 is 20 each.
Then share what is left: 16 among 4 is 4 each. Each share gets 20 + 4 = 24.

families.title: Equal fractions from folding paper
explanations: strips-over-parts (conceptual): The coloured strips were counted, but the whole sheet was counted in small parts: the top and the bottom must count the same size of part.
top-only (conceptual): Only the coloured parts were multiplied; folding again cuts the whole sheet into more parts too, so the bottom number grows as well.
added-folds (conceptual): 5 was added to the top and the bottom; cutting every strip into 5 parts multiplies the number of parts by 5.

teach.idea: Folding again cuts every part into the same number of smaller parts: the coloured amount does not change, so a/b = (a × k)/(b × k).
teach.method: Count all the small parts (the new bottom number) and the coloured small parts (the new top number).

alternatives.title: Two strips side by side
text: Draw one strip in thirds with one third coloured, and an equal strip in sixths.
The coloured length is the same: it covers 2 of the sixths, so 1/3 = 2/6.

families.title: Reducing a fraction to its lowest terms
explanations: bottom-only (procedural): Only the bottom number was divided; to keep the fraction equal, the top and the bottom are divided by the same number.
left-as-is (conceptual): The fraction was taken to be in lowest terms already, but 99 and 108 are both divisible by 9.
partly-reduced (procedural): Top and bottom were divided by 3, but they still share a factor: keep dividing until the only common factor is 1 (or divide by the highest common factor, 9, at once).

teach.idea: Dividing the top and the bottom by the same number gives an equal fraction; in lowest terms they have no common factor except 1.
teach.method: Find the highest common factor of the top and the bottom and divide both by it (or keep dividing by common factors until none is left).

alternatives.title: Cancel prime factors
text: Write the top and the bottom as products of primes: 18/24 = (2 × 3 × 3)/(2 × 2 × 2 × 3).
Cancel the primes they share: what is left is 3/4.

families.title: Telling like fractions from unlike fractions
explanations: same-top (conceptual): Fractions with the same numerator were taken as like fractions; like fractions have the same denominator (the same size of part).
equal-means-like (conceptual): Equal (equivalent) fractions were taken as like fractions; they show the same amount, but their denominators differ, so they are unlike.

teach.idea: Like fractions count the same size of part: their denominators are equal. Unlike fractions have different denominators.
teach.method: Look only at the denominators (the bottom numbers): if they are the same, the fractions are like fractions.

alternatives.title: Same-sized pieces
text: 2/7 and 5/7 are both counted in sevenths: same-sized pieces.
2/7 and 2/9 have the same number of pieces but different sizes, so they are unlike.

families.title: Adding and subtracting unlike and mixed fractions
explanations: add-tops-and-bottoms (conceptual): The whole numbers were subtracted, and the tops and the bottoms were subtracted separately; unlike fractions must first be written with the same denominator.
improper-left (procedural): The answer was left as an improper fraction; the question asks for a mixed number when the answer is more than 1.
wholes-dropped (procedural): Only the fraction parts were worked out; the whole numbers must be included too.
not-simplified (procedural): The fraction part was not reduced: 16 and 30 still have a common factor.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): 7/9 is smaller than 9/10, so the fractions were subtracted the other way round; regroup 1 whole from the whole number into the fraction part first.

teach.idea: Fractions can be added or subtracted only when they count the same size of piece; mixed numbers can be written as improper fractions first.
teach.method: Change mixed numbers to improper fractions, write both with a common denominator, add or subtract the tops, then simplify and change back to a mixed number.

alternatives.title: Wholes and parts separately
text: Add (or subtract) the whole numbers, then the fraction parts with a common denominator.
If the fraction part being taken away is bigger, regroup 1 whole as a fraction first; if the fraction parts add to more than 1, carry 1 whole.

families.title: Fraction word problems with whole numbers
explanations: multiply-both (conceptual): Top and bottom were both multiplied by 9: that gives an equal fraction, not 9 lots of it.
multiply-bottom (procedural): The bottom was multiplied; 9 glasses of 11/12 litre is 9 × 11 pieces of the same size.
add-whole (conceptual): 9 was added to the top; 9 glasses means 9 lots.
no-divide (procedural): The number of students was multiplied by 11 but not divided by 12.
one-part-only (procedural): Only 1/12 of the class was found (108 ÷ 12); 11/12 is 11 of those parts.
upside-down (conceptual): The class was divided by 9 and multiplied by 11; 9/11 of a number means divide by 11, then multiply by 9.

teach.idea: k lots of a/b is k × a pieces of size 1/b; a/b of a number is a of its b equal parts.
teach.method: For k × a/b, multiply the top by k. For a/b of N, divide N by b, then multiply by a.

alternatives.title: A bar model
text: Draw the whole amount as a bar cut into b equal parts.
Each part is the whole ÷ b; shade a parts and add them up.

families.title: A fraction product in an area model
explanations: counted-all-shaded (conceptual): Every shaded rectangle was counted; the product is only the part shaded in both colours (the overlap).
added-rows-columns (conceptual): The shaded columns and rows were added (7 + 7); the overlap has 7 columns of 7 rectangles.
one-colour (procedural): Only the blue part (7/8) was given; the product is the overlap of the two colours.
