added-fractions (conceptual): Tops and bottoms were added; in the area model the product is the overlap: (top × top) out of (bottom × bottom) small rectangles.

teach.idea: a/b × c/d is the part of a whole that is both a/b one way and c/d the other way: an overlap of a × c small rectangles out of b × d.
teach.method: Cut the rectangle into b columns and d rows, shade a columns and c rows, and count the overlap over the total: (a × c)/(b × d).

alternatives.title: A fraction of a fraction
text: Take 3/4 of the rectangle, then shade 2/3 of that piece: the overlap is the product.

families.title: Statistical questions, other questions and statements
explanations: one-answer (conceptual): The question was taken to have one answer; it asks about many people whose answers vary, so answering it needs data: it is statistical.
any-number-question (conceptual): A question with one answer was taken as statistical; it asks about one person, so no data that vary are needed.
data-is-statistical (conceptual): A sentence that gives a piece of data was taken as a statistical question; it tells a fact and asks nothing.
statement-as-question (procedural): The sentence was read as a question; it ends with a full stop and tells something.

teach.idea: A statistical question expects answers that vary, so it is answered by collecting data from many people or times; a question with one fixed answer is not statistical, and a statement asks nothing.
teach.method: Ask: is it a question? If so, would different people (or days) give different answers? If yes, it is statistical.

alternatives.title: Imagine the survey
text: Picture going round with a clipboard to answer it.
If you would need to ask many people and write down many answers, it is a statistical question; if one look gives the answer, it is not.

families.title: Writing a repeated product in exponential form
explanations: powers-swapped (procedural): The two counts were given the wrong way round: b appears 5 times and m appears 4 times.
counted-signs (procedural): The multiplication signs were counted instead of the factors; the power is how many times the base is a factor.
total-count (conceptual): All the factors were counted together; each base gets its own power.

teach.idea: A power is a short way of writing a repeated product: aⁿ means n factors of a multiplied together.
teach.method: Group equal factors together, count how many there are of each, and write each count as the power of its base.

alternatives.title: Tally the factors
text: Go along the product and put a tally mark under its base each time a factor appears.
The tally for each base is its power: 2 × 5 × 2 × 2 = 2³ × 5¹.

families.title: Writing a number as a product of prime powers
explanations: each-prime-once (conceptual): Each prime was given the power 1; the power counts how many times that prime divides the number.
one-division-missed (procedural): One division by 2 was missed: keep dividing by a prime until it no longer divides.

teach.idea: Every whole number greater than 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way; powers say how many times each prime appears.
teach.method: Divide by 2 as often as possible, then by 3, 5 and 7, counting the divisions: the counts are the powers.

alternatives.title: A factor tree
text: Split the number into two factors and keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime.
Count how many times each prime appears at the ends of the branches.

families.title: The zero exponent
explanations: zero-power-zero (conceptual): A zero power was taken as 0; 12⁵ ÷ 12⁵ is a number divided by itself, so it is 1.
zero-power-base (conceptual): A zero power was taken as the number itself; a⁰ = 1, because a⁰ = aᵐ ÷ aᵐ.

teach.idea: aᵐ ÷ aᵐ = aᵐ⁻ᵐ = a⁰, and a number divided by itself is 1, so a⁰ = 1 for any a ≠ 0.
teach.method: Replace every zero power by 1, then work out the rest.

alternatives.title: Follow the pattern
text: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2: each step down divides by 2.
One more step down: 2⁰ = 2 ÷ 2 = 1.

families.title: Fractional exponents and radicals
explanations: upside-down (conceptual): The fraction was turned upside down; the power inside (9) is the numerator and the root (8) the denominator.
root-as-subtraction (procedural): The root was taken away from the power (9 − 8); a 8th root divides the power by 8.
negative-value (conceptual): A negative power was taken to give a negative number; it gives the reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
sign-ignored (procedural): The minus sign in the power was left out; it turns the answer into its reciprocal.
times-the-fraction (conceptual): 100000 was multiplied by 4/5; a fractional power means a root and a power, not a multiplication.
root-as-division (conceptual): The square root of 100 was taken as 100 ÷ 2; the root is the number that, multiplied by itself 2 times, gives 100.
root-only (procedural): Only the 5th root was taken; the numerator 4 is a power still to be applied.
power-only (procedural): Only the power 3 was applied; the denominator 2 means a root too.
multiplied (conceptual): The power and the root were multiplied; a 8th root divides the power by 8.

teach.idea: a^(p/q) is the q-th root of a, raised to the power p: (ᵠ√a)ᵖ = ᵠ√(aᵖ). A negative power gives the reciprocal.
teach.method: Take the root first (the denominator), then the power (the numerator); for a negative power, take the reciprocal at the end.

alternatives.title: Use the law (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ
text: Write the base as a power: 27 = 3³.

families.title: Reasoning about remainders
explanations: multiplied (procedural): The remainders were multiplied; for a sum, the remainders are added.
added (procedural): The remainders were added; for a product, the remainders are multiplied.
added-remainder (procedural): 11 was added to 130; the number must be a multiple of 12 plus 11, and 130 is not a multiple of 12.
next-multiple (procedural): The next multiple of 12 was given; it leaves remainder 0, so 11 more is needed.
below (procedural): That number leaves the right remainder but is not greater than 130.
counted-multiples (conceptual): The multiples of 12 were counted; the numbers wanted are one multiple of 12 plus 9, starting at 9 itself.
off-by-one (procedural): The first number (11) or the last one was left out or counted twice.
not-reduced (procedural): The remainders were multiplied, but 64 is not less than 12: divide it by 12 again to get the remainder.

teach.idea: Only the remainders matter: a number is a multiple of d plus its remainder, so the remainder of a sum (or product) is the remainder of the sum (or product) of the remainders.
teach.method: Combine the remainders, then divide by d again if the result is d or more. Numbers leaving remainder r are r, r + d, r + 2d, …

alternatives.title: A clock with d hours
text: Think of a clock face numbered 0 to d − 1: counting on past d − 1 comes back to 0.
Adding remainders is moving round the clock; where you stop is the remainder.

families.title: Estimating a large product by rounding
explanations: zero-lost (procedural): A zero was lost when multiplying; count the zeros in both rounded numbers and write them all after the product of the first digits.
zero-extra (procedural): One zero too many was written; the zeros of the answer are the zeros of the two rounded numbers together.
rounded-down (procedural): Both numbers were cut down to their first digit instead of rounded to the nearest; look at the next digit: 5 or more rounds up.

teach.idea: Rounding each factor to its greatest place gives an easy product that is close to the real one: a quick check of size.
teach.method: Round each number, multiply the first digits, then write all the zeros of both rounded numbers: 5,000 × 40 = 20 × 10,000 = 2,00,000.

families.title: Percentage of one quantity in another, and percentage change
explanations: part-as-percent (conceptual): The part (171) was given as the percentage; a percentage compares the part with the whole, out of 100.
upside-down (conceptual): The whole was divided by the part; the percentage is part ÷ whole × 100.
change-as-percent (conceptual): The change in rupees (₹171) was given; the percentage change compares it with the original price.
change-only (procedural): Only the decrease (95% of 180) was given; it must be taken from the original amount.
rupees-for-percent (conceptual): ₹95 was taken away; 95% of ₹180 is ₹171.
new-as-base (conceptual): The change was compared with the new price; percentage change is always worked out on the original amount (₹180).

teach.idea: A percentage compares a part with a whole out of 100; a percentage change compares the change with the ORIGINAL amount.
teach.method: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100. Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100. To increase by p%, add p% of the amount (or multiply by (100 + p)/100).

alternatives.title: Scale to 100
text: Ask: if the whole were 100, how big would the part be?

families.title: Overhead expenses and the marked price
explanations: added-discount-of-sp (conceptual): 50% of the selling price was added back; the discount was 50% of the marked price, so the selling price is 50% of it.
discount-taken-again (procedural): The discount was taken off the selling price again; the marked price is more than the selling price.
overheads-left-out (conceptual): The repair cost was left out; the cost price includes overhead expenses: ₹1000 + ₹120 = ₹1120.
amount-for-percent (procedural): The loss in rupees (₹177) was given; the question asks for it as a percentage of the cost price.
rupees-added (conceptual): ₹5 was added; the discount is 5% of the marked price, not ₹5.
percent-of-sp (conceptual): The profit or loss was compared with the selling price; it is always a percentage of the cost price.

teach.idea: Overheads (repairs, transport) are part of what was spent, so they belong in the cost price; a discount is a percentage of the marked price.
teach.method: CP = price paid + overheads; profit % = profit ÷ CP × 100. If the discount is d%, the selling price is (100 − d)% of the marked price, so MP = SP × 100 ÷ (100 − d).

alternatives.title: A bar of 100 parts
text: Draw the marked price as a bar of 100 equal parts.
The discount takes away d parts; the selling price is the other 100 − d parts. Find one part, then all 100.

families.title: The price or concentration of a mixture
explanations: plain-average (conceptual): The two prices were averaged; there is more of one than the other (9 and 3), so each must be weighted by its quantity.
weights-swapped (procedural): Each quantity was multiplied by the other one's price; match each quantity with its own.
total-not-shared (procedural): The total cost was found but not divided by the total quantity (12).

teach.idea: The price (or strength) of a mixture is a weighted mean: each part counts as much as its quantity.
teach.method: Find the total cost (or total sugar) of all the parts, then divide by the total quantity.

alternatives.title: A balance on a line
text: Mark the two prices on a number line; the mixture's price lies between them.
It lies nearer the price there is more of: with 3 kg and 1 kg, it is three quarters of the way towards the 3 kg price.

families.title: Are four numbers in proportion?
explanations: first-pair-only (procedural): Only the first terms were checked (the third is a multiple of the first); the fourth must be the same multiple of the second.
differences-differ (conceptual): The differences were compared and found unequal; in a proportion the ratios are equal, so the differences usually are not.
same-difference (conceptual): The numbers were taken to be in proportion because they go up by the same amount; a proportion needs the same ratio (the same multiplier), not the same difference.

teach.idea: a, b, c, d are in proportion when a : b = c : d, that is, when the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: a × d = b × c.
teach.method: Multiply the first and the last numbers, then the middle two. Equal products: in proportion; different: not in proportion.

alternatives.title: Simplify both ratios
text: Write a : b and c : d in simplest form.
If the simplest forms are the same, the four numbers are in proportion.

families.title: The missing term of a proportion
explanations: wrong-pair (procedural): The wrong pair was multiplied: it is the extremes (first and last) against the means (middle two).
additive (conceptual): The same difference was used instead of the same multiplier; in a proportion the second ratio is the first one scaled.

teach.idea: In a : b :: c : d the product of the extremes equals the product of the means: a × d = b × c.
teach.method: Multiply the two known terms that pair up (extremes or means), then divide by the known term of the other pair.

alternatives.title: The unitary method
text: Find what 1 of the first quantity goes with: 4 cm for 10 km is 2.5 km for 1 cm.
Then scale up to the number you need.

families.title: Do two quantities vary directly?
explanations: equal-steps-expected (conceptual): y was expected to go up by the same amount as x; in direct variation y ÷ x stays the same, so y goes up by k times as much.
both-increase (conceptual): Both quantities increase together, but that is not enough: in direct variation y ÷ x is the same for every pair (and y = 0 when x = 0).

teach.idea: Two quantities vary directly when y = kx: y ÷ x is the same for every pair, so doubling x doubles y.
teach.method: Work out y ÷ x for each column of the table. All equal: direct variation. Any different: not direct variation.

alternatives.title: Double and check
text: Find two columns where x doubles (or triples).
In direct variation y must double (or triple) too; if it does not, the quantities do not vary directly.

families.title: A missing value from the mean, and deviations from the mean
explanations: four-for-five (procedural): The total was taken as 4 × 25; there are five numbers, so their total is 5 × 25.
mean-as-value (conceptual): The fifth number was taken to be the mean (25); the fifth number balances the others, so it is usually different.
sign-flipped (procedural): The sum of the four deviations (10) was given; the fifth must balance it, so it has the opposite sign.
value-for-deviation (conceptual): The fifth value was given; its deviation is the value minus the mean.
mean-of-four (conceptual): The mean of the four given numbers was found; the question asks for the number that makes the mean of all five equal to 24.

teach.idea: The mean is the balance point of the data: the deviations above it exactly balance those below, so they add up to 0. The total is the mean times the count.
teach.method: Missing value: total = mean × number of values; subtract the values you know. Deviation: add the known deviations and take the opposite.

alternatives.title: A seesaw
text: Put the values on a number line as weights and the mean as the pivot.
Distances to the left and to the right of the mean balance: the missing value sits where the seesaw levels.

families.title: The median of data in a frequency table
explanations: mode-for-median (conceptual): The value with the highest frequency was given; that is the mode. The median is the middle value when all the data are in order.
median-of-frequencies (conceptual): The middle of the frequencies was found; the median is a value of the data, found by counting through the frequencies.
middle-of-table (conceptual): The middle row of the table was taken; the median is the middle of all the data, so the frequencies count how many times each value appears.

teach.idea: In a frequency table each value appears as many times as its frequency; the median is the middle value of that full ordered list.
teach.method: Add the frequencies to get n. Find the middle position ((n + 1)/2 for odd n). Keep a running total of the frequencies until it reaches that position: that row's value is the median.

alternatives.title: Write the list out
text: Write each value as many times as its frequency, in order.
Cross off one from each end, again and again: the value left in the middle is the median.

families.title: Conditional probability from P(A ∩ B) and P(B)
explanations: multiplied (conceptual): P(A ∩ B) and P(B) were multiplied; given B, the probability is the share of B taken by A ∩ B: divide.
intersection-as-answer (conceptual): P(A ∩ B) was given; knowing that B happened makes B the whole, so divide by P(B).
upside-down (procedural): P(B) was divided by P(A ∩ B); it is P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B).
complement-of-intersection (conceptual): 1 − P(A ∩ B) was found; the complement must also be taken within B: 1 − P(A ∩ B)/P(B).
divided (procedural): P(A | B) was divided by P(B); the multiplication theorem multiplies: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B).
conditional-as-joint (conceptual): P(A | B) was given as P(A ∩ B); the joint probability also needs the chance that B happens.
no-complement (procedural): P(A | B) was found but not taken from 1; P(A′ | B) = 1 − P(A | B).

teach.idea: Given that B happened, B becomes the whole sample space: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B). Conditional probabilities given B obey the usual rules, e.g. P(A′ | B) = 1 − P(A | B).
teach.method: Divide P(A ∩ B) by P(B). For a joint probability, multiply: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B).

alternatives.title: Imagine 20 equally likely cases
text: With probabilities in twentieths, picture 20 students: P(B) = 0.6 means 12 of them are in B.
If 7 are in both, then among the 12 in B the chance of A is 7/12.

families.title: The multiplication theorem: drawing two without replacement
explanations: with-replacement (conceptual): The bag was treated as unchanged for the second draw; without replacement there is one ball fewer, so the second probability is out of 19.
second-unchanged-red (procedural): The number of red balls was not reduced for the second draw: after one red is taken, 9 red are left among 19.
either-order (procedural): Both orders (red then blue, blue then red) were counted; the question fixes the order: red first.
one-colour-only (procedural): Only both red was counted; both blue is the same colour too, so add its probability.
without-for-with (procedural): The second draw was treated as if the first ball stayed out; it was put back, so the bag is the same for both draws.
added (conceptual): The two probabilities were added; for 'first and second' they are multiplied.

teach.idea: The multiplication theorem: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B | A). Without replacement the second draw depends on the first: there is one ball fewer.
teach.method: Probability of the first draw times the probability of the second given the first; add the separate ways when more than one outcome counts.

alternatives.title: A tree diagram
text: Draw two branches for the first ball and, from each, two for the second with the new counts.
Multiply along a path; add the paths that give the event.

families.title: Comparing the volumes of two boxes
explanations: taller-is-bigger (conceptual): The taller box was taken to be the bigger one; a shorter box can hold more if it is longer or wider.
added-edges (conceptual): The lengths of the edges were added and compared; volume counts the cubes, which is length × width × height.

teach.idea: The volume of a box made of unit cubes is how many cubes it holds: length × width × height, not how big its edges look.
teach.method: Work out the number of cubes in each box (one layer × the number of layers) and compare the two numbers.

alternatives.title: Compare layer by layer
text: Count the cubes in one layer of each box (length × width).
Multiply by the number of layers, then compare.

families.title: The cost of fencing a rectangle
explanations: area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The area was used; a fence goes round the edge, so it is the perimeter that is paid for.
two-sides-only (procedural): Only one length and one width were fenced; a rectangle has two of each.
perimeter-only (procedural): The length of fencing (132 m) was given; each metre costs ₹50.

teach.idea: A fence (or a border) runs along the edge, so its length is the perimeter; the cost is that length times the price of one metre.
teach.method: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width); then multiply by the cost per metre.

alternatives.title: Walk round the edge
text: Imagine walking round the garden: along a length, a width, a length and a width.
Add those four sides to get the metres of fence, then pay for each metre.

families.title: The centres of a triangle and the lines that meet there
explanations: midpoint-means-circumcentre (conceptual): The midpoints were noticed and the point was taken to be the circumcentre. Lines from the corners to the midpoints of the opposite sides are medians, and medians meet at the centroid; the circumcentre comes from lines through the midpoints at right angles to the sides.

right-angle-means-circumcentre (conceptual): The right angles were noticed and the point was taken to be the circumcentre. Lines from the corners at right angles to the opposite sides are altitudes; they meet at the orthocentre. The lines for the circumcentre go through the midpoints of the sides, not through the corners.

right-angle-means-orthocentre (conceptual): The lines at right angles to the sides were taken to be altitudes. An altitude starts at a corner; these lines start at the midpoints of the sides, so they are perpendicular bisectors, and they meet at the circumcentre.

midpoint-means-centroid (conceptual): The midpoints were noticed and the point was taken to be the centroid. The centroid comes from lines joining each corner to a midpoint (medians); lines through the midpoints at right angles to the sides meet at the circumcentre.

bisector-as-median (conceptual): The line was taken to end at the midpoint of MN because it halves the angle. Halving the angle makes it an angle bisector; it reaches the midpoint only when the two sides at the corner are equal.

corners-for-sides (conceptual): Being equally far from the three corners was mixed up with being equally far from the three sides. The point equally far from the corners is the circumcentre; equally far from the sides is the incentre.

sides-for-corners (conceptual): Being equally far from the three sides was mixed up with being equally far from the three corners. Equally far from the sides is the incentre; equally far from the corners is the circumcentre.

inside-means-incentre (conceptual): A point well inside the triangle was taken to be the incentre. The incentre lies on the angle bisectors; a point on the line from a corner to a midpoint, two thirds of the way along, is the centroid.

circumcircle-for-incircle (conceptual): The circle through the corners was mixed up with the circle inside that touches the sides. The circle through the three corners has its centre at the circumcentre; the circle touching the three sides has its centre at the incentre.
incircle-for-circumcircle (conceptual): The circle inside touching the sides was mixed up with the circle through the corners. The circle that touches the three sides has its centre at the incentre.

right-corner-circumcentre (conceptual): The circumcentre was placed at the right-angled corner. In a right triangle the circumcentre is the midpoint of the longest side LN. The two shorter sides are themselves altitudes, so the altitudes meet at the right-angled corner: the orthocentre.

midpoint-is-centroid (conceptual): The midpoint of a side was taken to be the centroid. The centroid is two thirds of the way along each median, always inside the triangle. The midpoint of the longest side of a right triangle is equally far from all three corners, so it is the circumcentre.
balance-at-incentre (conceptual): The balance point was taken to be the centre of the circle inside the triangle. A triangle balances where its medians meet, at the centroid.

centroid-perp-bisectors (conceptual): Both medians and perpendicular bisectors use the midpoints of the sides, and they were mixed up. Medians join each corner to the midpoint of the opposite side, and they meet at the centroid.
orthocentre-perp-bisectors (conceptual): Both altitudes and perpendicular bisectors meet a side at right angles, and they were mixed up. Altitudes start at the corners; they meet at the orthocentre.

circumcentre-altitudes (conceptual): Both altitudes and perpendicular bisectors meet a side at right angles, and they were mixed up. The circumcentre is equally far from the corners, so it lies on the perpendicular bisectors, which go through the midpoints of the sides.
incentre-perp-bisectors (conceptual): The incentre was mixed up with the circumcentre. The incentre is equally far from the three sides, so it lies on the bisectors of the angles.

altitude-as-perp-bisector (conceptual): LD meets MN at a right angle, so it was called the perpendicular bisector. A perpendicular bisector must also pass through the midpoint of MN; a line from a corner at right angles to the opposite side is an altitude.

median-as-bisector (conceptual): The line was taken to halve the angle at L because it halves the opposite side. It usually does not halve the angle; a line from a corner to the midpoint of the opposite side is a median.

perp-bisector-as-altitude (conceptual): The line was taken to be an altitude because of the right angle. An altitude starts at a corner; this line goes through the midpoint and need not pass through L, so it is the perpendicular bisector.

teach.idea: A triangle has four kinds of special lines, three of each kind, and the three of a kind always meet at one point: medians at the centroid, altitudes at the orthocentre, perpendicular bisectors of the sides at the circumcentre, and angle bisectors at the incentre.
teach.method: Ask what each line does. Corner to midpoint of the opposite side: median (centroid, the balance point). Corner, at right angles to the opposite side: altitude (orthocentre). Through a midpoint at right angles: perpendicular bisector (circumcentre, equally far from the corners). Halving an angle: angle bisector (incentre, equally far from the sides).

alternatives.title: Fold a paper triangle
text: Fold one corner onto another: the crease is the perpendicular bisector of that side, and every point on it is equally far from the two corners. The three such creases meet at the circumcentre.
Fold one side onto the next so the crease runs through their corner: that crease halves the angle. The three such creases meet at the incentre, equally far from the sides.

alternatives.title: Two circles, two centres
text: The circle through the three corners is the circumcircle; its centre is the circumcentre (circum = around).
The circle inside touching the three sides is the incircle; its centre is the incentre (in = inside).

families.title: The centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1
explanations: ratio-reversed (conceptual): The 2 : 1 was taken the wrong way round, with the shorter part next to the corner. The centroid is nearer the midpoint D: AG is the longer part (2 parts) and GD the shorter (1 part).
centroid-at-middle (conceptual): G was taken to be the midpoint of the median. It is not halfway: it is two thirds of the way from the corner A to D.
double-for-whole (procedural): AG was doubled to get AD. AG is 2 of the 3 equal parts of AD, so one part is AG ÷ 2 and AD is 3 such parts.
other-part (procedural): The whole median AD was found instead of GD. GD is only the short part between G and D.
whole-for-part (procedural): The whole median AD was found instead of AG. AG is the long part from the corner A to G, without GD.
part-for-whole (procedural): Only AG was found. AD is the whole median: AG + GD.

teach.idea: The three medians of a triangle meet at the centroid G, and G cuts each median into two parts in the ratio 2 : 1, the longer part next to the corner. So AG is 2/3 of AD and GD is 1/3 of AD.
teach.method: Split the median into 3 equal parts. AG is 2 parts, GD is 1 part, AD is all 3. Find one part from the length you know, then multiply.

alternatives.title: Three equal steps
text: Walk from A to D in three equal steps. After two steps you are at G; one more step reaches D.
If AD = 12 cm, each step is 4 cm: AG = 8 cm and GD = 4 cm.

alternatives.title: Average the corners
text: With coordinates, G is the average of the three corners: A(0, 6), B(−3, 0), C(3, 0) give G(0, 2), and D, the midpoint of BC, is (0, 0).
Along AD, A is 6 units from D and G is 2 units from D: AG = 4, GD = 2, which is 2 : 1.

families.title: The angle between two angle bisectors at the incentre
explanations: minus-for-plus (recall): The rule was remembered as 90° − ∠A/2. The two half-angles at B and C add up to (180° − 160°) ÷ 2 = 10°, which is less than 90°, so ∠BIC is more than 90°.
whole-angles (conceptual): ∠BIC was taken to equal ∠A, as if IB and IC took the whole angles at B and C. They take only half of each.
supplement (conceptual): ∠BIC and ∠A were taken to add up to 180°. They do not: ∠BIC = 90° + ∠A/2.
a-not-halved (procedural): ∠A was not halved: ∠BIC = 90° + 88°/2, not 90° + 88°.
one-halved (procedural): Only one of the two angles was halved. Both IB and IC are bisectors, so both ∠B and ∠C are halved.
sum-in-rule (recall): The rule 90° + half the angle was used with ∠B + ∠C in place of ∠A. The rule uses ∠A = 180° − 140° − 20° = 20°.
not-doubled (procedural): 170° − 90° = 80° is only half of ∠A, since ∠BIC = 90° + ∠A/2. Double it.

teach.idea: IB and IC cut ∠B and ∠C in half, so in △BIC the angles at B and C add up to half of (∠B + ∠C) = half of (180° − ∠A). What is left of 180° is ∠BIC = 90° + ∠A/2.
teach.method: Find ∠B + ∠C (180° − ∠A if only ∠A is given), halve it, and take the result from 180°. Going backwards: ∠A = 2 × (∠BIC − 90°).

alternatives.title: Work it through with numbers
text: Take ∠B = 70° and ∠C = 50°. The bisectors make 35° and 25° at B and C inside △BIC.

alternatives.title: Check with special triangles
text: In an equilateral triangle every angle is 60°, the halves are 30° and 30°, and ∠BIC = 120° = 90° + 30°.
As ∠A gets close to 0°, B and C nearly fill 180°, their halves nearly fill 90°, and ∠BIC gets close to 90°: so ∠BIC is always more than 90°.
